title: Somali pirates hijack Iranian vessel with 23 crew
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Somali pirates seized an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali guards near Somalia's northeastern coast, the EU's Indian Ocean maritime security center said.
Somali pirates hijacked an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 23 crew members near the coast of northeastern Somalia, according to the European Union's Indian Ocean maritime security center (MSCIO).
The vessel was carrying 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali guards, the center said.
No information on the condition or safety of the crew was available at the time the report was published.

title: Greek Shipowner Opens STEM Centre at US Maritime Academy
body: Greek shipowner Vangelis Marinakis has supported the creation of a state-of-the-art STEM centre at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy in the United States, honouring his late father, Miltiadis Marinakis, and helping prepare future maritime professionals for the industry’s technological and environmental challenges. The 4,000-square-metre facility, named Miltiadis Marinakis Hall, recently opened at the Academy in Cape Cod. Rear Admiral Francis McDonald, the Academy’s president, and Vangelis Marinakis, founder and chairman of Capital Maritime & Trading Corp., attended the inauguration. Marinakis funded the building through a donation. The new centre houses laboratories for construction, electronics, control systems, biology, physics and chemistry. All Academy students will use the facilities, regardless of their specialisation. During the opening ceremony, McDonald and Academy officials showed Marinakis around the building, where teaching and research activities had already begun. The Academy is also developing new programmes in automated control, programming and robotics, while exploring the early stages of a nuclear energy specialisation. McDonald described the centre as an important addition to the campus that the Academy could not otherwise have built. He thanked Marinakis for his generosity, saying the donation had given students something special that would benefit generations to come. He also highlighted the Academy’s strong reputation and demand for its graduates. Twice a year, more than 150 organisations visit the campus, bringing over 500 recruitment representatives and advertising more than 1,000 jobs at sea and ashore. They compete for approximately 350 graduating students. McDonald noted that female enrolment had doubled over the past decade, reaching around 80 students in each intake of 400. The Academy began admitting women in 1977. The first female engineer aboard its new training ship is also an Academy graduate. Marinakis receives Distinguished Service Award During the ceremony, McDonald presented Marinakis with the Academy’s Distinguished Service Award. The formal programme also featured speeches by McDonald, Marinakis, Massachusetts state representative Steven Xiarhos and the Academy’s Provost, Commander Brigid Pavilonis. McDonald said the building’s location made it particularly fitting for the Marinakis family. Its rooftop offers panoramic views of the Academy’s new training ship, Patriot State, as well as the campus football fields — two areas closely associated with the family’s history. He also stressed the responsibility that came with naming the building after the Marinakis family, saying the Academy recognised the significance of the honour and the expectations it carried. For Vangelis Marinakis, the inauguration held deep personal meaning. The centre commemorates his father while investing in the education of young people at a time when shipping requires broader scientific knowledge and advanced technical skills. “Today is a very special day, not only for the Massachusetts Maritime Academy, but also for me personally and for my family,” Marinakis said. He described the Academy as an institution that had shaped maritime excellence for almost 150 years and said the opening represented much more than the inauguration of a new STEM centre. Honouring his father’s maritime legacy Marinakis said the decision to support the project stemmed from his father’s lifelong connection with the sea. His father, Miltiadis Marinakis, graduated from a similar maritime academy almost 75 years ago. A marine engineer, he began his career working on offshore oil platforms, tankers and dry-bulk vessels. “He devoted his life to the sea,” Marinakis said, recalling his father’s belief in education and the potential of young people. He described him as a man guided by hard work, integrity, resilience and deep respect for seafarers. “For him, shipping was never simply an industry. It was a passion, a legacy and a way of life,” Marinakis said. His father often reminded him that while steel builds ships, the true strength of maritime power lies in the courage, knowledge and character of the people who serve aboard them. Marinakis said three generations of his family had regarded the sea as their home and that their passion for shipping came with a responsibility to leave the world better than they had found it. He quoted Greek author Nikos Kazantzakis, urging the students to embrace responsibility and take ownership of their actions. “Always love responsibility and take it upon yourselves,” he told them. Preparing maritime professionals for a changing industry Marinakis also highlighted the importance of shipping to global economic development and national prosperity, saying that the industry moves the world. He described Miltiadis Marinakis Hall as the Academy’s first building with the potential to achieve net-zero energy consumption. He said its design reflected the industry’s growing commitment to environmental responsibility, innovation and future generations. “Shipping stands on the threshold of a new era, facing unprecedented challenges,” he said. “Twenty-first-century seafarers must be more than skilled maritime professionals. They must be scientists, engineers, innovators and visionary leaders.” He pointed to conflicts in the Red Sea, the Arabian Gulf, Russia and Ukraine, which are changing maritime routes and highlighting shipping’s vital role in global trade and the international economy. He also identified energy efficiency and sustainability as major challenges, with emerging technologies expected to reduce the environmental footprint of ships while improving their performance. Meeting these demands, he said, requires professionals with new knowledge and skills, alongside practical experience. Marinakis also referred to renewed efforts in the United States to strengthen the commercial fleet and shipbuilding industry. He argued that investment in maritime higher education was essential to developing the skilled workforce needed to support those ambitions. “Shipping, above all, is about its people. They are its most valuable asset,” he said, adding that the Academy’s educational work could help revitalise American shipping through US-flagged vessels built in the United States. He also pointed to the White House maritime plan published in February 2026, which identifies education and training as one of its four main pillars. The plan highlights workforce and skills shortages in shipyards and maritime professions and includes measures to support the six state maritime academies, including Massachusetts. A bridge between Greek maritime tradition and American education Marinakis said his support for the Academy also reflected his belief in the importance of higher education in shipping. He pointed out that although Greece ranks among the world’s leading maritime nations, studies at its corresponding maritime academies do not form part of the university education system. He described the new building as a symbolic bridge between Greece’s centuries-old seafaring tradition and the academic excellence and technological innovation of the United States. “Greece and the United States share an enduring bond based on freedom, democracy and a deep respect for the sea,” he said. Addressing the students, Marinakis said the building existed for future maritime leaders and expressed his hope that generations of cadets would draw inspiration from it, pursue ambitious goals and expand the boundaries of what they could achieve. He urged them to remain true to their word, describing a person’s word as the greatest contract in shipping. For the students, the Greek name on the building has already become part of everyday campus life. Cypriot cadet Nikos Pattichis, who addressed the ceremony on behalf of the student body, praised Marinakis’s vision and investment, saying they could help make the Academy the world’s leading maritime institution. He also spoke about the emotional significance of seeing a Greek name on campus while studying far from home. “Distance also makes us miss our homeland more,” he said. “It was a great surprise to see Mr Marinakis, and I am very happy that every day I will see a building with a Greek name here at the university.” (Source: AMNA) Advertising  ( window.advanced_ads_ready || jQuery( document ).ready ).call( null, function() {var $greek2slider2624846735 = jQuery( ".greek-2slider-2624846735" );$greek2slider2624846735.on( "unslider.ready", function() { jQuery( "div.custom-slider ul li" ).css( "display", "block" ); });$greek2slider2624846735.unslider({ delay:6000, autoplay:true, nav:false, arrows:false, infinite:true });$greek2slider2624846735.on("mouseover", function() {$greek2slider2624846735.unslider("stop");}).on("mouseout", function() {$greek2slider2624846735.unslider("start");});}); The post Greek Shipowner Opens STEM Centre at US Maritime Academy appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Elga coal terminal reaching design capacity
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. The Elga Port Marine Coal Terminal has reached its design capacity, shipping 2.5 million metric tons of coal in October 2026, which corresponds to 30 million metric tons in annual equivalent, the press service of Ellga Management Company reported.
"The port reaching its design capacity is an important milestone in the development of the Elga industrial and logistics cluster. The created infrastructure, the Pacific Railway and the coal terminal, fully unlocks the potential of the Elgin deposit and ensures efficient and uninterrupted coal delivery to consumers in key markets for the company," Elga CEO Alexander Isaev said, cited by the press service.
This result is the consequence of large-scale investments and the coordinated work of the entire project team, Isaev noted.
The Pacific Railway was launched in September 2025, Elga said. The 531-kilometer mainline connects the Elga coal deposit in Yakutia) with the marine terminal at Cape Manorsky in the Khabarovsk Region, on the coast of the Sea of Okhotsk. The design throughput capacity of the railway is up to 50 million metric tons of coal per year.
In 2025, 35.1 million metric tons of coal were mined at the Elga deposit, and by the end of 2026, the mining volume will exceed 40 million metric tons.

title: Encroachment along Pokuase-Nsawam Highway raises road safety concerns at Dobro
body: Concerns over road safety and the progress of construction works along the Pokuase–Nsawam Highway have resurfaced following the emergence of container shops, sand and chippings businesses, and concrete mixer rental services within a road buffer zone at Dobro in the Eastern Region. The development comes despite a previous demolition exercise undertaken to remove structures encroaching on the 90-metre road reservation ahead of the highway’s construction. The affected area, particularly the stretch in front of fruit processing company Blue Skies, has become a point of concern, with containers and heavy-duty tipper trucks occupying space between the main highway and the road linking to Dobro. The activities have raised questions about compliance with road reservation requirements and the enforcement of regulations intended to protect road infrastructure and ensure the safety of motorists and pedestrians. The presence of commercial activities along the narrow stretch could pose significant risks to road users, particularly when heavy-duty trucks enter or exit the roadside businesses. The movement of these vehicles, coupled with the limited space available, could obstruct traffic and increase the risk of collisions and injuries involving motorists and pedestrians. Additional concerns have been raised about containers positioned directly beneath high-voltage electricity transmission pylons, potentially exposing people operating within the area to safety risks. Beyond the immediate dangers, the encroachment could interfere with ongoing road construction by occupying space required for road works and associated infrastructure. Management of Blue Skies has expressed concern about the situation, warning of its potential implications for road safety, construction activities, factory operations and the company’s public image. The company’s Head of Estates, Prince Asimani, says the activities along the stretch require urgent attention from the relevant authorities to prevent possible accidents and other consequences. According to him, Blue Skies had previously reached an agreement with the chiefs of Dobro to landscape the area. However, the landscaping was destroyed during road construction, leaving the company concerned about the subsequent use of the space for commercial activities. Management believes the current development requires investigation and appropriate action to ensure the area is used in accordance with applicable road reservation requirements. The Municipal Assembly has responded to the concerns, assuring that it will take the necessary steps to remove facilities encroaching on the affected areas. The assurance follows concerns raised by Blue Skies over the presence of container shops, heavy-duty trucks and other commercial activities along the stretch near its factory at Dobro. The Assembly’s response is expected to bring renewed attention to enforcement efforts aimed at protecting the road reservation, improving safety and preventing further encroachment. Blue Skies says it has written to the Municipal Chief Executive and the Coordinating Director to draw their attention to the situation and seek intervention. Management is also appealing to the Ministry of Roads and Highways, the Eastern Regional Minister, the Municipal Assembly, the police and other responsible authorities to ensure the concerns are addressed. The company is particularly worried that failure to address the situation could expose motorists, pedestrians and prospective customers to danger while undermining efforts to improve road transport along the corridor. The situation at Dobro has renewed concerns about the sustainability of enforcement measures following the earlier demolition exercise along the Pokuase–Nsawam Highway. Road reservations are intended to protect space for road infrastructure, improve visibility and support the safe movement of vehicles and pedestrians. The reappearance of commercial activities within the affected stretch has consequently raised questions about monitoring and enforcement to prevent renewed encroachment. The Municipal Assembly’s assurance to remove the encroaching facilities will therefore be crucial in addressing the concerns and ensuring that commercial activities do not compromise public safety or ongoing road construction.

title: itel Energy offers 48-hour repairs, product replacement to customers at exhibition
body: itel Energy, a clean energy and power solutions brand, has promised to repair or replace faulty solar power equipment within 48 hours for customers across Nigeria as part of its after-sales support. The company reemphasized their commitment during the Nigeria Energy exhibition week in Lagos, where it showcased new products and showed distributors, installers, both new and existing customers how its after-sales service works. The company said it offers remote services, home visits and product replacement where necessary. According to the company, after-sales service is an important consideration for households and businesses switching from petrol and diesel generators to solar power, because a faulty inverter or battery can disrupt electricity supply and business operations. Speaking on the sidelines at the exhibition, the Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of SunFi, a major distributor of itel Energy products, Rotimi Thomas, said the commitment boosted customers’ confidence in the products distributed through the company. “The 48-hour resolution commitment from itel Energy is very important for us as a distribution platform because we don’t make the product and when a consumer buys a product through SunFi, they’re actually really buying a trusted service,” Thomas said. He explained that customers needed assurance that equipment would be repaired or replaced when problems arose, rather than being left to deal with faults after purchase. “That trust comes from the type of equipment that we use and the promise of being able to replace or repair the assets when there’s a problem,” he said. Thomas also urged customers to look beyond warranty periods when choosing solar equipment, saying the speed and quality of support during the warranty period were equally important. “But even more important than that five-year warranty is what happens before the five years or during the five-year period. How do you respond when I report that I have a problem with the product now?” Thomas said the cost of solar systems remained a barrier to adoption, adding that the company offers instalment payment plans for households and businesses unable to pay the full amount. According to him, about 30 to 40 per cent of prospective customers still request payment plans, which shows the need for financing options that make clean energy more accessible. He said some customers preferred to pay between 10 and 30 per cent upfront and spread the balance over three, six, 12 or 24 months, or longer. Meanwhile, itel Energy’s Country Service Manager, Emmanuel Kumuyi, said most common complaints reported by customers included overloading, protection issues and incorrect installation. He said some problems arose when solar panels, inverters and batteries were not properly matched to the user’s power requirements. Kumuyi advised customers to use certified engineers for installation and to ensure that their systems were correctly configured. He explained that when a customer reports a fault, the company’s service agents document the complaint and refer it to an engineer for remote assistance. According to him, if the problem cannot be resolved remotely, an engineer is assigned to visit the customer’s premises. Where necessary, component or product replacement is initiated in line with the applicable warranty terms. The company’s National Distributor Manager, Lucky Ovenseri, said itel Energy had distribution coverage across Nigeria’s 36 states, with showrooms and dedicated energy after-sales centres in major cities, including Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Ibadan and Kano. He said the company also operated a replacement policy under which customers could receive another unit while their faulty equipment was being handled. At the exhibition, itel Energy showcased its newly launched PowerTank 1000 and IP54 11kW Hybrid Inverter, targeting customers with different electricity needs. The PowerTank 1000 demonstration featured a powered mini-chiller and a water dispenser, while visitors interested in the 11kW hybrid inverter sought information about pricing, installation, warranty coverage and its ability to support higher power demands. The company currently has 5 Flagship service centers, and over 200 service centers across more than 60 cities, backed by Carlcare and Transsion Group’s network of 2,000+ service centers spread across Sub-saharan Africa,Middle-East,and Asia. title: Countdown until US midterm elections are over feels like waiting for war with Iran - editorial
body: Wednesday, 3 p.m. Dentist.Thursday, 4 p.m. Pick up the children.Friday, 11 a.m. Resume war with Iran.Don't forget to put it in your calendar.It is a ridiculous way to discuss a war, particularly one whose consequences could be felt across the Middle East. Yet it is becoming difficult to escape the impression that renewed fighting with the Islamic Republic has been penciled into the diary, awaiting only a convenient date.First came Israel's election. Now Americans go to the polls on Tuesday for their midterms. Once those votes are counted, the thinking goes, Washington and Jerusalem can return to the unfinished business of Iran.The headlines this weekend have done little to dispel that impression. On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States had largely destroyed Iran's nuclear capabilities but still had “one or two sites” to deal with, including the underground facility known as Pickaxe Mountain. “We can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters.Ten minutes. Barely enough time for a coffee, apparently, and sufficient to settle what remains of the Iranian nuclear question.Electoral timetable feels like a countdownTrump also spoke with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, amid reports of American preparations for renewed strikes. The Post reported that US military aircraft have delivered equipment to the region, while Washington and Israel continue coordinating their plans.None of this means a strike has been ordered. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump “hasn't made a decision” and still prefers a diplomatic solution. Trump himself said negotiations were progressing, although he questioned Tehran's reliability. The distinction matters: military planning can be intended to strengthen diplomacy as much as to prepare for its failure.Nevertheless, the electoral timetable is hard to ignore. Trump explicitly ruled out attacking Iran before November 3.Reports have also described an Israeli operation contemplated for October that did not proceed amid American opposition. Whether these accounts capture every consideration behind the decisions is another matter. But the public message has been unmistakable: there are dates on which war is apparently less convenient than others.Of course, governments must weigh domestic political circumstances before committing their countries to military action.Democracies cannot operate in a vacuum, and leaders have an obligation to consider the public they represent. There is, however, something deeply uncomfortable about the suggestion that an Iranian nuclear facility can remain an intolerable danger on Monday but become a suitable target only after Tuesday's ballots have been cast.Countdown seems to downplay importance of the decisionIran's threat is not imaginary. Its nuclear ambitions, ballistic missiles, support for armed proxies, and repeated threats against Israel have given successive Israeli governments ample reason for concern. Tehran's leaders have also made clear that further attacks would invite retaliation, potentially against American allies and civilian infrastructure throughout the region. Israelis know well that even successful operations can carry a heavy price at home.That is precisely why the conversation should be more serious than the current countdown suggests. What, exactly, would another campaign achieve? Is the objective to destroy the remaining nuclear infrastructure, prevent Iran from rebuilding its missile arsenal, force a credible agreement, or create conditions in which Iranians themselves can finally determine their country's future?These objectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A 10-minute strike might destroy a facility. It cannot, by itself, resolve the political and strategic problem posed by the Islamic Republic. Nor should anyone assume that Tehran will respond according to the timetable Washington prefers.Civilians deserve to know impacts of what leaders are preparingFor the Iranian people, who have endured repression, economic hardship, and the regime's brutality, this is considerably more than a discussion about American polling dates. For Israelis, too, the stakes are measured in lives, not campaign cycles.Israel must retain the freedom to act against genuine threats, and the United States must not allow Tehran to use negotiations indefinitely as cover for rebuilding its capabilities. But decisions of such consequence require clear objectives, sober judgment, and an honest explanation of the risks.The public deserves to know whether leaders are preparing a limited operation, a prolonged confrontation, or another round whose ending nobody can confidently predict.The calendar may tell us when the elections are over. It cannot tell us when war is necessary, still less when it will end.

title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 2, 2026
body: The naira’s exchange rate against the US dollar remains a major focus for businesses, importers, investors and Nigerians who depend on foreign currency for international transactions. The Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market are two major segments of Nigeria’s foreign exchange market, with rates varying according to currency supply, demand and market conditions. As of Monday, November 2, 2026, the latest available figures indicate that the official NFEM rate stood at ₦1,346.26 per dollar, while the parallel market quoted the dollar at approximately ₦1,386.36. Official NFEM exchange rate Data published by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) showed that the naira traded at an average rate of ₦1,346.2565 per dollar on Friday, October 30, the latest available official trading data ahead of Monday’s session. The official market also recorded a closing rate of ₦1,346.00 per dollar, reflecting a marginal improvement from the previous trading session. The NFEM rate is determined by the volume-weighted average of transactions in the official foreign exchange market. It serves as the benchmark for official foreign currency transactions in Nigeria. Central Bank of Nigeria Dollar to naira black market rate today In the parallel market, commonly known as the black market, currency dealers quoted the dollar at approximately ₦1,380.59 for buying and ₦1,386.36 for selling as of Sunday, November 1. This means Nigerians seeking to purchase one dollar from parallel market operators would need approximately ₦1,386, although the actual amount may vary depending on the dealer and location. The parallel market rates are indicative and may change throughout the day in response to foreign exchange demand and supply. Difference between official and parallel market rates The difference between the latest official NFEM weighted average of ₦1,346.26 and the parallel market selling rate of ₦1,386.36 is approximately ₦40.10 per dollar. The gap reflects differences in foreign exchange supply, demand and pricing across the two markets. For individuals and businesses purchasing dollars, the parallel market selling rate remains an important consideration, particularly for transactions that cannot be processed through official banking channels. How much is $100 in naira today? At the latest available official NFEM rate of ₦1,346.26, $100 is equivalent to approximately ₦134,626. At the parallel market selling rate of ₦1,386.36, $100 would cost approximately ₦138,636. These figures are indicative and do not necessarily represent the final rates offered by banks or individual currency dealers. Nigerians are advised to confirm prevailing exchange rates with their banks or licensed Bureau de Change operators before conducting foreign exchange transactions. title: Air defenses down 154 out of 193 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine since evening
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force Command reported this on Telegram .
On the night of November 1-2 (from 18:00 on November 1), Russia attacked Ukraine with 193 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (75 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from Oryol, Kursk and Bryansk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 154 enemy UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (58 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and drones of other types.
More than six attack drones are still in Ukrainian airspace.
Hits by enemy weapons were recorded at 26 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at nine locations.

title: US Calls Turkey-Libya Maritime Deal “Unhelpful and Provocative” as Greece Defends Crete
body: Washington has described the ratification of the Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum as “unhelpful and provocative”, adding its voice to the criticism of a deal that Greece says ignores the maritime rights of Crete and other Greek islands. “The announcement of the ratification of the Turkish-Libyan delimitation memorandum of understanding has raised tensions in the region and is unhelpful and provocative — and our position on this matter has not changed,” a US State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital . The spokesperson urged all countries in the Eastern Mediterranean to settle maritime disputes through good-faith negotiations, noted that Greece and Türkiye are both NATO allies and encouraged the two to work through their differences bilaterally. “Peaceful resolution of such disputes opens the way for commercial investment and exploration that will benefit the entire region,” the spokesperson said. The firmer wording replaced an earlier State Department response that did not pass judgement on the memorandum. As Greek City Times has reported, the statement was revised after work by the US Embassy in Athens and the Greek Embassy in Washington. What Libya approved On 20 October, Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives, which is aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar, voted unanimously to approve the memorandum Türkiye signed in Istanbul in November 2019 with Libya’s then Tripoli-based Government of National Accord, the Libyan News Agency reported. The vote overturned the parliament’s 2020 rejection of the deal and its decision to cut political ties with Ankara. The memorandum claims a shared maritime boundary between Türkiye and Libya south-east of Crete. Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have rejected it since it was signed. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Anadolu in Brussels on 21 October that it was “an entirely legitimate agreement, both from a legal and a political perspective”, adding: “There is no need to debate it.” He said Ankara had regarded the agreement as valid since 2019. Athens: “The memorandum will not be implemented” Greece’s Foreign Ministry said the memorandum “remains illegal, null and void”, pointing out that Türkiye and Libya “do not have opposite or adjacent coasts” and that the deal “disregards the Greek islands and their entitlement to maritime zones under UNCLOS”. Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis was blunter in a radio interview with Mega News 104.6 the following day: “The memorandum will not be implemented. And it will not be implemented for the simple reason that it produces no legal effects whatsoever, as it is entirely contrary to international law.” He noted that Greece had already launched tenders for offshore blocks south of Crete, inside the area the memorandum covers. Athens has since taken the fight to the United Nations. On 26 October, Greece delivered a statement in New York on behalf of Bahrain, Cyprus, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, the European Union and itself, declaring the memorandum “null and void”. On 29 October the dispute reached the Security Council. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, chairing a debate under Greece’s presidency, accused the two countries of drawing an artificial boundary that ignores Crete, Rhodes, Karpathos and Kasos. Turkish Ambassador Ahmet Yıldız replied that “this Council is not a court for delimiting maritime zones”, while Greek Ambassador Aglaia Balta answered: “Geography cannot be reshaped. This is not a slogan,” euro2day.gr reported. Europe, Israel and US energy interests European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 20 October that the agreement “infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void”, and reaffirmed solidarity with Greece and Cyprus. Israel’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the ratification. “Regretfully, once again we see Turkey working to destabilise the east Mediterranean region,” it said, Reuters reported. Endy Zemenides, executive director of the Hellenic American Leadership Council, told Fox News Digital the memorandum “effectively denies maritime rights and zones of Crete” and “specifically infringes on U.S. companies and U.S. energy policy”. He described Crete as “NATO’s southernmost base”. US energy giant Chevron holds exploration blocks south of Crete and is expected to begin seismic surveys there in December, Proto Thema reported. title: Anyma Fuses Ancient Greece and AI as ÆDEN Lights Up Athens
body: Athens’ Olympic Athletic Centre became a giant digital canvas on Saturday 31 October, when Anyma brought his audiovisual show ÆDEN to Greece for the first time – and gave it a distinctly ancient Greek flavour. Anyma, the stage name of Italian-American DJ and producer Matteo Milleri, performed at OAKA’s Wall of Nations in Marousi before a crowd that in.gr and loaded.gr both put at more than 15,000. Both reviews say he took the stage at 10.15pm and played for more than two hours, while loaded.gr notes that Italian brothers Mathame warmed up the crowd with an hour-long set beforehand. The bill also featured Naples project 19:26, a back-to-back set from Jast and SLVR, Henri Bergmann and Athens-born Chris IDH. The event was presented by P+US, Primer Music Festival and Dreamstar Events, CNN Greece reported. Ancient Greece meets artificial intelligence Anyma’s shows are known for treating the visuals as seriously as the music, and ÆDEN is built around a huge video wall, 3D figures, lasers and synchronised lighting. What made the Athens night stand out for local audiences was the way it drew on antiquity. According to mad.gr and in.gr, mythological figures, classical statues and towering columns were woven into the digital scenery. Familiar forms from classical sculpture reappeared with metallic, machine-like features, as though lifted out of the ancient world and dropped into a distant future. In.gr noted that Anyma has named antiquity as one of the main sources of inspiration for ÆDEN, with classical art, Greco-Roman aesthetics and mythology shaping both the stage design and the look of the show. The idea, it wrote, is a dialogue between past and future in which human creativity, technology and artificial intelligence sit side by side. Ethnos ’ reviewer was first struck by the sheer size of the projections, then by the detail – the movement of the bodies and surfaces that looked like marble or metal. Reviewers agreed the production was the real star of the night, with in.gr describing the music as familiar Anyma territory and the visuals as the element that lifted the experience. View this post on Instagram From Coachella and the Sphere to OAKA ÆDEN premiered at Coachella in April before setting off on a world tour that has already taken in London, Gdańsk, Vancouver, Milan and Sydney, with Mumbai, Abu Dhabi, Bangkok, Paris and São Paulo among the dates still to come. “It was a dream to see this come to life on such a stage,” Anyma wrote on Instagram after the Coachella premiere. “Now let’s go on tour.” The tour follows his landmark residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas, Afterlife Presents Anyma: The End of Genesys. He was the first electronic act to headline the venue, and the 12-night run from December 2024 to March 2025 drew more than 200,000 fans, Billboard reported. In Athens, fans were quick to share clips from the night, including this one posted on TikTok. Anyma in Athens #anyma #fy #viral #aeden For a show about where humanity and technology are heading, there were few more fitting places to stage it than the city where so much of Western art and thought began. title: Mitsotakis Sets Priorities and Election Preparations for 2027
body: Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis will hold a Cabinet meeting at the Maximos Mansion in Athens today Monday, 2 November, to review key government priorities for each ministry through the end of the current parliamentary term. The meeting begins at 11:00, with ministers presenting their proposals following opening remarks by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State Kostis Hatzidakis and Minister of State Akis Skertsos. Deputy Infrastructure and Transport Minister Georgios Kotsiras will present a report entitled “Urban Transport: Tangible Progress and the Future”. Labour and Social Security Minister Niki Kerameus will outline a bill setting rules for the use of artificial intelligence in the labour market and protecting workers on digital platforms. The legislation will incorporate EU Directive 2024/2831 into Greek law. Justice Minister Giorgos Floridis will present legislation to transform the Judicial Police into a Security Corps. Deputy Education, Religious Affairs and Sports Minister Giannis Vroutsis will introduce a bill aligning Greek law with the World Anti-Doping Agency’s revised Anti-Doping Code. Interior Minister Theodoros Livanios and Development Minister Takis Theodorikakos will also present legislative bills covering various provisions within their respective ministries. New Democracy prepares for 2027 elections Immediately after the Cabinet meeting, Mitsotakis will travel to Piraeus for the first meeting of New Democracy’s Executive Secretariat under the composition established following the party’s recent congress. The members include Mitsotakis, Hatzidakis, Adonis Georgiadis, Konstantinos Kyranakis, Maximos Charakopoulos, Ioannis Smyrlis, Orfeas Georgiou, Maria-Alexandra Kefala, Dimitrios Kairidis, Athanasios Papanathasis, Stavros Papasotiriou, Asimina Skondra, Panagiotis Palpanas, Christina Patrikakou, Georgios Tsakoumis and Konstantinos Tsiagliotis. The prime minister is expected to issue instructions and place the party on election alert ahead of the 2027 national elections. Sources at the party’s headquarters in Piraeus say at least six months remain before the elections are called. However, organisational preparations have already begun, with Mitsotakis and party teams stepping up visits across Greece. Konstantinos Kyranakis, Ioannis Smyrlis, Stelios Kontadakis and Thanasis Nezis coordinate the party teams’ nationwide activities. The same sources say New Democracy’s secretary will present a review of visits carried out since the summer in Western Greece, the Peloponnese, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, Central and Western Macedonia, Epirus, the Dodecanese and the Ionian Islands. He will also outline plans for future visits, initiatives to involve party members in drafting the government programme, and efforts to renew the party organisation and prepare its candidate lists. title: How a vampire drawing helped La Salle’s Joaquin Tovera vanquish rival Ateneo
body: MANILA, Philippines – For any Ateneo-La Salle rivalry in any UAAP sport, the tension and pressure are always more palpable than other games, no matter the current stakes. Players and coaches alike sometimes prepare a bit more, spend more time mentally psyching themselves up, or simply do things they don’t normally do. Joaquin Tovera idly draws on the coach’s whiteboard with a marker. Ahead of one of the most crucial showdowns in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament, the Blue Eagles and Green Archers found themselves locked with identical records squarely in the middle of the pack heading to Saturday, October 31. The way the needle moves in this particular match could dictate how the rest of the season would go for either side. Tovera, meanwhile, continued to draw, mimicking the vampire the La Salle team had set up in time for a chilling Halloween encounter. Hours after drawing perhaps a pair of fangs or a cape, the 19-year-old dynamo was on the Araneta Coliseum court among thousands, this time drawing up winning plays for others or himself — his own fangs bared against Ateneo’s own scrappy band of brothers. He traded the vampire’s cape for a hero’s one, as he eventually led the defending champions to an exhilarating 76-73 overtime win to the tune of 21 points, 7 rebounds, and 6 assists, and spent all the power he had before being helped off the floor after multiple bad ankle rolls. Tovera did not care too much for roaring, clashing seas of blue and green around him, for the game was like his drawing on the board before the game: simply black and white. Win, or lose. In his own lane, own zone Head coach Topex Robinson, who saw Tovera scribbling before the rivalry match and joked if the soft-spoken guard was planning to take over his job, emphasized this defining moment as to why his rookie is just on a different lane as the rest. “I was like, ‘Do you know how important this game is again?’ [He said] ‘Yes coach, but I love to draw,’” Robinson recounted post-game. “We hope that Joaquin stays to be that young guy who just enjoys basketball and doesn’t care what the ramifications are of what he does.” “We’re just so fortunate that he has a good support system with these guys. Every time he makes a mistake, you’ll always see one of them trying to pacify him. We’re so fortunate to have these guys guiding in his rookie year. Hopefully, he gets to appreciate the support that he gets.” Never mind the pressure of righting a title defense gone sideways early. Never mind the pressure of needing to step up right as your mentor and leader goes down. In the two games since graduating star Jacob Cortez went down with an injury, the Fil-Am youngster from NBA player breeding ground Chino Hills in California has averaged MVP-caliber numbers of 18 points, 7 rebounds, and 7.5 assists on 44% shooting. Though potential has always been there the moment Tovera stepped into the UAAP, this is the first stretch of games where his grace under pressure has been truly tested, especially after the Archers went down with an alarming 3-4 record to end the first round before rebounding to 6-4. Ever a kid of few words, Tovera simply said he wanted to do what’s best for the team, and essentially hold the fort while Cortez recovers for the final stretch of his collegiate career. His La Salle kuyas , however, have much more to say about his character, extending well beyond his years. “He’s been huge for us these past three games. He’s had really good contributions,” said veteran guard JC Macalalag. “I just tried to remind him of what he can do. Being able to facilitate the team and control the tempo at a young age leaves a lot of room for improvement.” “For me, it’s just his composure that really stands out the most, with how he’s able to stay poised under pressure,” added former Ateneo prospect Mason Amos. “Time and time again, he tends to deliver for us, and as a kuya, I’m really proud of his efforts, and proud of him not getting emotional when things get rough for him. He just keeps moving forward and that’s something that I can really say about Joaquin.” – Rappler.com

title: Kofi Arko Nokoe commissions Apataim cassava factory to boost local processing
body: The Apataim Cassava Factory Project in the Evalue Ajomoro Gwira Constituency has been commissioned, marking a step towards expanding local cassava processing, creating jobs and improving incomes for farmers and processors. The commissioning ceremony was held on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, with the Member of Parliament for the area, Kofi Arko Nokoe, and the Municipal Chief Executive for Nzema East, Herbert Kuah Dickson, participating in the event. Mr Nokoe expressed gratitude to the United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) and the Climate Adaptive Living Facility for sponsoring and supporting the project, which is expected to strengthen the local agricultural value chain. He said the factory would provide an opportunity to add value to cassava produced in the area, reduce post-harvest losses and create employment opportunities, while improving the livelihoods of farmers and processors. The MP said the project reflected the importance of partnerships in delivering development initiatives that respond to the needs of local communities. He reaffirmed his commitment to working with development partners and other stakeholders to promote sustainable economic opportunities and accelerate development across Evalue Ajomoro Gwira.

title: Ukraine suffers 8,300 casualties in past week — military expert
body:
LUGANSK, November 2. /TASS/. Ukraine lost 8,300 soldiers and foreign mercenaries killed or wounded over the past week, with Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicting the heaviest losses, military expert Andrey Marochko said.
"The enemy lost around 8,310 Ukrainian militants and mercenaries killed or wounded over the past week. Ukrainian armed formations suffered their heaviest personnel losses in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Center, which operates in the Donetsk People’s Republic and the Dnepropetrovsk Region," he wrote on VK after analyzing Russian Defense Ministry data.
Russian troops also destroyed 6,900 fixed-wing drones, 11 vessels, 29 field artillery pieces, 52 electronic warfare and counter-battery systems, and nearly 700 Ukrainian combat vehicles of various types over that period, Marochko added.

title: George Calombaris Calls Athens ‘the New Berlin’ and Hosts Travellers
body: Chef George Calombaris will host up to 20 travellers in Athens for seven days in June 2027, calling the Greek capital “the new Berlin”. The George Calombaris Athens journey is run with Melbourne-based travel platform Quro Collective . Prices start from AUD $8,999 per person, twin share, with a $500 deposit to secure a place, Quro said. As a result, travellers will meet the chefs, bartenders and producers in the former MasterChef Australia judge’s circle. Calombaris will make the introductions. “Athens is a city that, for me, is the new Berlin, but there’s still a lot of people out there who don’t know Athens through my lens,” Calombaris said. Inside the George Calombaris Athens itinerary The first full day begins with a souvlaki crawl led by Calombaris and Greek food creator IKON5. Stops include Kapsa, the shop of chef Christoforos Peskias. Next, Peskias joins the group at Varvakeios Market, which has supplied the city’s kitchens since 1886. He then hosts lunch at his restaurant, Dopios. Chef Polychronis Damalas will also take travellers to a farmers’ market. Afterwards, they lunch at Raw Bata, where Greek ingredients meet Japanese influences. Pastry chef Stelios Parliaros welcomes the group into Sweet Alchemy, the shop he opened in 1982. At Ergon House, guests move from the ground-floor food market into the kitchen for a hands-on cooking class with Calombaris. At the Metaxa cellars in Kifisia, travellers enter barrel rooms normally closed to the public. They then create their own blend alongside the Metaxa Master and Calombaris. In the evenings, the George Calombaris Athens trip turns to cocktails. At The Clumsies , the group meets co-owners Vasilis Kyritsis and Nikos Bakoulis. Their bar reached No. 3 on the World’s 50 Best Bars list in 2020. The same pair are also behind Line, named number one in the inaugural Europe’s 50 Best Bars list in June 2026. “I can’t wait for you to meet these boys,” Calombaris said. “They have the number one bar in Europe right now. And you get to come inside with me.” Price, hotel and island extension Travellers stay six nights at the Perianth Hotel on Agias Eirinis Square, with daily breakfast. A local guide and coach transfers on scheduled days are included. However, international flights, travel insurance and airport transfers are not included. Optional paid add-ons, such as an Acropolis visit or a Greek wine masterclass, cost extra. After the George Calombaris Athens week, an optional extension adds three nights each on Milos and Paros. It costs from an additional AUD $4,999, including ferries and transfers. Calombaris opened his first restaurant, The Press Club, in Melbourne in 2006. Since then, he has competed at the Bocuse d’Or and published five cookbooks. He also runs Auto Greek, an annual Melbourne pop-up based on his trips to Athens. Greek City Times reported on his Gold Coast venture earlier in October. He is now Culinary Director for new hospitality projects across Sydney. Bookings for the George Calombaris Athens journey opened on 30 October through Quro Collective. title: Lyre Camp Revives Ancient Greek Music on Mount Olympus
body: People from 11 countries travelled to Mount Olympus in September to learn to play the ancient Greek lyre, reconnecting with a musical tradition that had fallen silent for centuries. Photos provided by Mr Koumartzis. From China, the United States and Canada to Chile, England and Ukraine, 50 participants gathered on Greece’s highest mountain for the third annual Lyre Camp. For the first time, the event took place on Mount Olympus, offering students an opportunity to explore ancient Greek music in the mythical home of the gods. The multi-day programme combined practical lyre lessons with philosophy, history and group music-making. Participants attended two consecutive week-long sessions, with 25 students in each. “We wanted from the outset to create an opportunity for people who had previously studied the ancient lyre mainly through a screen to meet in person, share their musical experiences and, of course, get to know Greece,” Theodoros Koumartzis told the Athens-Macedonian News Agency (AMNA). “This year, Mount Olympus itself provided a very strong incentive for them to travel here.” Koumartzis leads the camp alongside Lina Palera and Thanasis Kleopas. All three are musicians with international careers and extensive experience in reviving, teaching and developing contemporary artistic applications for the ancient Greek lyre. A typical day began at 8am with readings from ancient philosophy accompanied by the lyre. For an hour, participants explored ancient philosophical texts and examined the connections between music, philosophy and everyday life. After breakfast, students joined group lessons divided into three levels: beginners, advanced and highly advanced. The classes catered both to people with no previous musical experience and professional musicians interested in exploring the instrument’s possibilities. Afternoon sessions offered individual tuition, allowing each participant to work one-to-one with one of the three instructors. Special presentations on ancient music and its instruments followed in the evenings. The week culminated in a student concert, where participants performed a melody they had prepared together during the lessons. Those who wished could also take the stage individually, performing either solo or accompanied by one of the instructors. From a workshop in Kilkis to an international musical community The story behind Lyre Camp began with efforts to reconstruct ancient Greek musical instruments. “We began reconstructing these instruments in 2014, establishing our workshop in Europós, Kilkis, and working with Aristotle University of Thessaloniki to study archaeological depictions and ancient texts describing their construction,” Koumartzis said. The initiative led to the development of the family-run Luthieros Music Instruments workshop, which makes ancient musical instruments. The team later established the SEIKILO Museum of Ancient Music in Thessaloniki, where it holds weekly ancient Greek lyre lessons. Another milestone came in 2020 with the launch of the Lyre Academy, the world’s first online platform offering ancient Greek lyre lessons in English. “Many people bought the instruments and then asked us, ‘I have the lyre. Now how can I learn to play it?’ So we created the Academy and developed educational books alongside it,” Koumartzis explained. The Academy now offers a comprehensive four-year curriculum for everyone from beginners to professional musicians. During the COVID-19 pandemic, demand for online lessons grew internationally, attracting students from around the world. This prompted the organisers to establish Lyre Camp, bringing the Academy’s online community together in person so students could meet, play music and exchange experiences. The first two camps took place on the island of Aegina, mainly because of its easy access from Athens. However, the announcement that the third edition would move to Mount Olympus generated strong interest, prompting the organisers to schedule two separate week-long sessions. Lyre Camp 2027 already attracting strong interest The organisers have already filled all 25 places for the first week of the 2027 Lyre Camp on Mount Olympus. They expect to announce a second week shortly, giving more people the opportunity to take part. title: Greece Introduces New Gender Pay Transparency Rules
body: Greece introduced new pay transparency and equal pay rules on Sunday, 1 November 2026, requiring private-sector employers to explain how they determine salaries and ensure that women and men receive equal pay for equal work or work of equal value. The new framework, established under Law 5316/2026 to implement European Directive 2023/970, introduces specific obligations for employers and strengthens workers’ rights to salary information during recruitment and throughout their employment. At the heart of the legislation lies the principle that employers must determine salaries according to the work employees perform and its value, rather than their gender. The measures require employers to establish objective salary structures, disclose pay information to job applicants and existing employees, identify unjustified wage differences and take corrective action when they find inequalities. The framework also strengthens workers’ protection and their ability to seek equal treatment and fair remuneration. Employers Must Establish Objective Pay Structures From 1 November 2026, all employers, regardless of the number of people they employ, must introduce and apply pay structures that guarantee equal pay for equal work or work of equal value. Employers must document these structures in writing, ensure they allow comparisons between different positions, establish a review procedure and clearly identify the components of remuneration for each employee category. Employers must assess positions using objective criteria that do not discriminate on the basis of gender. They will develop these criteria in agreement with employee representatives, where such representatives exist. The criteria include: Skills; Effort; Responsibility; Working conditions. Employers may also consider other factors relevant to a particular job or position, including seniority and relevant non-technical skills. Employers covered by a collective labour agreement may use the job classifications and salary scales set out in that agreement. The new framework also requires companies to monitor their internal gender pay gaps and identify unjustified differences at an early stage. Businesses must report information on the overall gender pay gap, the gender gap in bonuses, the median pay gap and pay differences across employee categories. If employers identify differences that objective, gender-neutral factors cannot justify — such as greater experience, higher qualifications or the requirements of a position — they must take corrective action under the prescribed procedures. What Changes for Job Advertisements and Recruitment Pay transparency begins before an employer hires a new employee. Under the new rules, job advertisements, recruitment notices and other vacancy announcements cannot refer to an applicant’s gender or family status. Employers also cannot use criteria that result in direct or indirect gender discrimination. Job applicants have the right to learn the starting salary or salary range for a position before their first interview. Employers must base this information on objective, gender-neutral criteria and include details of any applicable collective labour agreement. Employers also cannot ask candidates how much they earned in previous jobs. This restriction aims to prevent existing pay inequalities from carrying over into new employment. Instead, employers must determine salaries according to the requirements of the position, candidates’ qualifications and objective assessment criteria. As a result, applicants will know the salary framework before pursuing a position, without their previous earnings influencing the employer’s offer. Employees Gain the Right to Request Salary Information The legislation gives employees the right to request written information about their individual pay level and the average pay levels, broken down by gender, for employees performing equal work or work of equal value. Employers must respond within a reasonable period and, in all cases, within two months of receiving a request. They must also inform employees every year about this right and explain how they can exercise it. Employers must provide the information while respecting personal data protection and confidentiality requirements. When Employers Must Conduct a Joint Pay Assessment The new framework establishes a joint pay assessment mechanism that employers must activate when three conditions occur together: The average pay difference between women and men reaches at least 5% in any employee category. Objective, gender-neutral criteria cannot justify the difference. The employer fails to correct the difference within six months of submitting the relevant pay information. The assessment aims to identify unjustified pay differences, establish measures to address them and prevent them from recurring. The process requires employers and employee representatives to: Record the proportion of women and men in each employee category. Examine average pay levels for women and men. Analyse additional and variable components of remuneration. Record pay differences and investigate their causes using objective, gender-neutral criteria agreed between the employer and employee representatives. Examine the proportion of women and men who received a pay improvement after returning from maternity, paternity, parental or carers’ leave, where such improvements occurred within the relevant employee category during the period of leave. If the assessment identifies unjustified differences, employers must determine the necessary corrective measures and evaluate their effectiveness. They must also consider the findings of previous joint pay assessments. Employees Gain Stronger Rights to Challenge Pay Inequality The new legislation strengthens employees’ ability to seek redress when they experience unequal pay. Workers will be able to lodge complaints with the Labour Inspectorate or take their cases to court. They may also seek support from the Greek Ombudsman and trade unions, within their respective areas of responsibility. The framework therefore goes beyond simply giving employees access to salary information. It establishes procedures to identify, document and correct unjustified pay differences. According to the Ministry of Labour, the objective is to make equal pay for equal work or work of equal value a practical reality through transparent procedures, objective assessment criteria and effective action against unjustified wage inequalities.
