title: I confronted religious merchants in Kaduna to achieve peace — Uba Sani
body: By Charles Kumolu For years, Kaduna State was synonymous with ethno-religious violence, communal distrust, and bloodshed, with successive administrations struggling to end the cycle of killings that fractured communities and undermined the state’s economic and social life. But Governor Uba Sani believes the tide has turned, insisting that the peace being experienced in the state is the product of deliberate efforts to dismantle what he calls the “merchants of ethno-religious crises,” promote inclusive governance, and address the economic conditions that fuel insecurity. From Southern Kaduna to Birnin Gwari, he says, the emphasis has been on rebuilding trust, taking development to neglected communities, and making citizens see one another as partners rather than adversaries. In this interview with a team of editors from Vanguard Newspapers, the governor explains the thinking behind his Kaduna Model, how his administration secured the release of 222 captives in Birnin Gwari through the reopening of markets, and why he believes economic empowerment is central to sustainable peace. He also responds to allegations of intolerance toward opposition politicians, speaks on the role of political elites in exploiting ethnic and religious divisions, and outlines his administration’s efforts to reposition Kaduna through agriculture, rural roads, transportation, and sports infrastructure. In Rivers State’s history, it was once known as Rivers of Blood. About 10 years ago, Kaduna was known as a state of blood, crisis, and bloodshed. How were you able to restore peace, especially in Southern Kaduna? When we came in, the first thing we looked at was recognising the fact that our state is the most diverse state in Nigeria. Of course, I agree with you that the number of lives we lost in Kaduna in the last 20 years, before we came, was more than the number of lives lost because of insurgency, kidnapping, and banditry. Knowing that, we believed that for us to claim any success as a government, we must bring our people together. The only way we could do that was by ensuring that we created a state where everyone would be carried along in whatever we were doing. Of course, we decided to run a system that would bring everyone together, which is a highly inclusive government. For us, inclusivity isn’t just about bringing people to sit with us. It’s about taking development to every part of Kaduna State. When we came in, we looked at the deficits in terms of infrastructure, healthcare, and education. We looked at this holistically, and we believed it was the only way we could address injustice and marginalisation. Some people felt they were not treated like citizens of our state. We believed that doing that really demanded that we relegate politics and elevate governance. Doing that, of course, could sometimes be difficult because when you are elected as a governor, you have people who work with you. The first thing they tell you is to consider people who voted for you and ignore those who did not. But when we came in, it was not about who voted for us and who did not; it wasn’t the issue at all. It was about carrying everyone along. So, we really tried to put that aside and focus on carrying everyone along, including those who did not vote for us. We took development to every part of Kaduna State, irrespective of party, religious, or ethnic affiliation. Of course, a lot of people have been talking about the Kaduna Model, asking how we did it. That is because in the last three and a half years in Kaduna, we have not experienced a single ethno-religious crisis, which is highly unprecedented. But for me, the Kaduna Model is nothing difficult. It’s about running a state where you carry everyone along and, as much as possible, be fair to everyone. Of course, human beings want justice. Sometimes you might work with people who are certainly merchants. When I say merchants, I mean people who only survive whenever there is an ethno-religious crisis. You have to eliminate them within the system. If you don’t eliminate them within the system, the problem will continue. We tried as much as possible to eliminate those merchants, which was actually very difficult. That was because some of them also felt they were part of the system, and they also helped to win the election. That was the first battle you have to encounter as a leader. Did you say merchants? Yes, ethno-religious merchants. For me, it takes a lot of political will to do that because they also feel they have a stake. Probably some of them contributed significantly to making one win the election. But then, along that line, of course, I had issues with many people who probably misunderstood my ideology. I tried to explain to some that they need to go back. Happily, I look at my antecedents. I am not just a normal politician. I’m someone who spent many years fighting for justice, equality, democracy, and the rule of law. So, putting my ideology aside is very difficult. I paid my dues. I went to detention five times fighting for democracy in Nigeria. I was in the Senate. I would have been comfortable. But I decided to contest for the governorship of my state simply because I wasn’t happy about how toxic our state was. People didn’t trust one another. I was not comfortable with how the state was divided along the locations where people lived. People go to work together and eat together as family and friends. But when they close their offices, they go to different places because nobody trusts one another. I felt Kaduna State was the most important city in all of Northern Nigeria. At that time, I believed the only thing we needed to do was restore the glory of our state. Today, I’m happy. Gradually, we are restoring the glory of our state. Everyone now feels comfortable. Everyone wants to stay in Kaduna. That was the reason why, when the president wanted to launch his campaign, he chose Kaduna. The Kaduna of the past is different from the Kaduna of today. Everyone feels Kaduna is home now. We quickly abolished the issue of citizen and indigene dichotomy because our strength is in our diversity. But most importantly, we are highly cosmopolitan. That is the reason we don’t look at things through the lenses of religion, geography, or ethnicity. After three and a half years, have you achieved the Kaduna of your dream? Yes, I can say that largely. But I still believe we can do more, simply because we cannot rest. We must consolidate. When I say merchants, the merchants are not going to give up. I’m not sure we have completely defeated them. We have done a lot. If we rest, they will take us back. I remember when we were trying to choose our deputy governor; a lot of people thought it was difficult. But I said, no, this is a new Kaduna. Nobody will worry about whether it is a Muslim or a Christian. We have moved beyond that. When we decided to make a decision, people thought there would be issues. Nobody said a word. In three years, we have done a lot to promote interfaith harmony in our state. All the leaders of both religions who didn’t sit at the same table now sit together. They understand poverty has no ethnic or tribal mark. It has no respect for religion or ethnicity. The poor man is a poor man. The only thing is that they believe we need to work together. They put that aside and now think about how to move us forward. Because at the end of the day, the elites still live together. It’s only the poor people who are separated. Who is really working to ensure the poor people remain separated? It is the elites. It was an easy decision to say, look, the elites cannot live together while the poor people live separately. You cannot do that. I will not accept that. When I came in, in the first month, I was giving people a lot of land. There were some I gave land to in a particular place. They sold it because they said they could not live in such a place. Today, I’m working to ensure that everyone lives together. Just like the people living together, the downtrodden must also live together without suspicion. For me, in Kaduna, it is not the number of bridges we built. It’s not the number of roads we constructed. It’s about the unity of our state. Like I always say, Kaduna is not only the political capital of Northern Nigeria; it’s both a political and spiritual capital, I can tell you for free. That’s the reason why, whenever there’s any religious crisis in Kaduna, virtually everything within the Middle Belt and even the far North-East may be affected. In the last three years, there were some religious crises in Benue and Plateau, but there was nothing in Kaduna. If it happens in Kaduna, it will happen in several states. But it could happen anywhere; it will not come to Kaduna. That is how strategic Kaduna is. It is the heartbeat of the Middle Belt in Nigeria. People don’t understand that. A lot of people never gave us a chance. But we said, look, it was not an issue that happened spontaneously. It’s a creation of some selfish politicians who divided our people to achieve their selfish political aims. That was easy for us because the only way to demolish it was to not do what they used to do—to let people understand that we must live together as one family. You recognise this diversity as one of the strengths of Kaduna. But there’s now a growing noise that is getting louder. It is said that you are not tolerating opposition politicians, especially at gatherings… I just talked about merchants. Maybe you have to understand what I mean by merchants. You can do something in other states, and it’s fine, but in Kaduna it’s not possible. If you go to the media house and insult Uba Sani one million times, I will thank you for that because this is democracy. I also challenged successive military governments, and I paid the price by going to prison. But look, what we have done in Kaduna—and I made it clear, and I still have no apology—is that in Kaduna, because of our diversity, you cannot come and say anything to incite the people. I’m fighting the merchants, and I will continue to fight them because I realise that the reason for all those religious crises is that the merchants create problems while innocent people in the villages die. I made it clear. Talk politics, but don’t talk about ethno-religious issues in Kaduna. I have looked through the constitution as a civil rights activist for many years, and I have not seen where freedom of speech has given me the right to say something that can result in the loss of lives of innocent and gullible people who are not educated. I don’t believe in that. If it happens, honestly speaking, I will certainly go after that person. I said it many times. I have no apology for that. But if you go and say, I’m against this party, it’s okay. But as long as I always wake up in the morning and go through my oath, and I read my oath every two or three days, I see that it is my responsibility to protect the lives and properties of the people of Kaduna. If you come to say anything that can affect the lives and properties of innocent people, honestly speaking, I will go after you. I fought for the rule of law in this country. You see, I’m not just a normal activist. If you ask any activist in Nigeria, I was probably the closest to Chief Gani Fawehinmi. You can ask anyone. Chief Gani always told us, honestly speaking, at the heat of the struggle, that we can do anything. If you are someone groomed by Gani like me, who lived in his house for four years, you would agree with me that our training by Chief Gani was to respect constituted authority. Gani would be arrested today by the police. Tomorrow, he would come out, and we would write a statement against the police; he would tell us to drop it. We would ask him why, and he would say, as we are sitting now in my parlour eating, someone called you and said that somebody is getting into your house, and the lives of your family and your wife were under threat. Who would you call? We would say the police. Then he would ask: Why do you want to destroy them? It is their job. For me, that was my training. That’s how I was groomed. I believe in the rule of law. If you do something that can affect the lives of innocent people, as a governor, I will just allow the law to take its course. If you go to court, you will sort it out because I am not a judge. I will help you to face the judiciary, certainly. If you have a good lawyer, fine. If you don’t have a good lawyer, sort it out. I’m not apologising for this. And that’s the reason why I’m keeping Kaduna safe. If I had not done that, I can tell you, the merchants would have defeated us. And if the merchants defeated us, today, I wouldn’t have been going to Southern Kaduna. For the last six months, when I went to Birnin Gwari, I stopped on the road. I saw farmers in the market. Ten metres away, there were more than 200 cows. I asked them if they were not the ones killing themselves before, and they said yes. I said, why did you stop? One of them said they no longer see the people who were instigating them. If you move from there to the Southern part of Kaduna, where people died every day, nobody is dying. The farmers are there. The cows are there. Why are they not fighting? It is because I’m destroying the merchants one by one, and I’ll continue to destroy them. One merchant could ruin the lives of 1,000 innocent people. What did you do, or how did you get rid of the warlords, the terrorist kingpins, that terrorised the state? Birnin Gwari is a clear case study. It wasn’t rocket science. Birnin Gwari was the epicentre of insurgency in the whole of Nigeria. I went to Birnin Gwari and met the Emir. The Emir of Birnin Gwari had been there for almost 40 years. I told him, why is it that people are being kidnapped every day in this place? When I was in the Senate, I represented the central zone. Every day, in the National Assembly, we stood up for a minute of silence because people had lost their lives. I made an effort to create state police. It was my bill in the Senate. I was defeated. We moved on. But in the absence of state police, which I believe was the only solution, there must be another solution. We had to look at the symptoms and drivers of insecurity. There must be symptoms. What are the symptoms? What are the drivers? You have to study it holistically. The insecurity in the Northwestern part of Nigeria has no relationship with the insecurity in the North-East. That’s the first thing. On insecurity, you have to understand that the North-East is largely ideological. The North-West is poverty and economy. Instead of successive governments resolving it, they didn’t do that. It also created a trust deficit between the people and government. How do you do it? You must allow the process to be driven by the communities because they don’t trust government any longer. That’s what we meant. And I asked them what they wanted. I don’t pay ransom. I don’t know bandits. The Emir of Birnin Gwari told me every bandit around the area was born in Birnin Gwari in his presence. The solution became nearer. Most bandits in his area are under the age of 40. They were born while he was watching them. I said, what is the problem? He said the problem was the economy. He said two major markets—the grains market and the livestock market—were closed for nine years. No government could open them. I went there and said I wanted to open the markets. I opened the markets. But I told them I had a condition. As we were speaking at the time, 222 people in Birnin Gwari were already with the bandits. I told them that I would open the market, but ensure that in the next one week, the 222 would be released. Because he knew the parents of the bandits, he intervened. We opened the markets. Within five days, all the captives were released. That was the first step. The second step was asking the Emir of Birnin Gwari what he needed again. At that time, most of the schools were closed. All their hospitals were closed because of bandits. We opened all the schools. The market started booming. As I’m speaking with you, every day you can go to Birnin Gwari. One farmer made N1.7 billion from grains. Now in Birnin Gwari, every day you have lorries filled with maize and other grains, numbering about 35, going to Lagos. In addition, more than 50 trucks of cows go to Lagos. They even requested a new market. I’m building a new grain market and a new livestock market, the biggest ever in Kaduna. As we are speaking, Birnin Gwari has not seen one kilometre of road in 20 years. I had to take the CGC, the company constructing roads in Abuja, to construct 36 kilometres of road in Birnin Gwari, cutting across 77 farming communities. They’ve never seen that in their lives. Nobody wants to kidnap any more. So underdevelopment was part of the problem? Yes, because it’s the economy. That’s number one. We took the same model to other areas and resolved the issues there. That’s the reason we were able to reclaim 500,000 hectares of abandoned farmland. Last year, when people wanted to go to Mecca, I was telling Mr President that the Chairman of the Hajj Commission wrote letters to all the states that we should subsidise the Hajj. I said I don’t subsidise going to Hajj. I build roads in Kaduna. For that reason, even for me as a Muslim, it is clear. If you cannot afford it, you don’t have to go. I didn’t subsidise it. The chairman of the Hajj Commission came back to me after the deadline was over and told me Kaduna is still number one in Nigeria. And I said, do you know why we’re number one? I said, the economy is booming. The farmers come to farms. When I look at the analysis, 70 per cent are farmers from rural areas, not even in the town. The people in the town are poor. The people in the metropolitan part of Kaduna, the city, are poor. The rich ones are in the rural areas. Not only that; that is why, out of the 1,315 kilometres being constructed in Kaduna, 800 kilometres are in the rural areas, connecting farms with markets. It was largely the economy. How much was the budget for agriculture when we came in? N1.4 billion. Today, the budget for agriculture in Kaduna is N110 billion. We surpassed the Malabo Declaration of 2014 of 10 per cent. We’re at 12 per cent. We’re leading Nigeria in agriculture. That’s why we were the first state in Nigeria to launch our SAPZ, Special Agro-Processing Zone. Not only that; we were the second state in the whole of Nigeria to have an agricultural quality centre, where we can have all our grains certified for exportation. On transportation, when Makinde opened his bus terminal, there were about a thousand buses. We are concluding ours next month. The President promised to commission it. There are 5,000 buses. It’s the biggest ultra-modern bus terminal in Nigeria. When Sardauna was alive, he built Ahmadu Bello Stadium in 1964. It was one of the leading stadiums, apart from the national stadium in Lagos. Then the one in Kaduna was one of the two major stadiums hosting FIFA tournaments. Ahmadu Bello Stadium deteriorated and became obsolete. The last time we hosted any FIFA event in Kaduna was almost 2016, right? It was a junior football tournament. I went to the president and told him the dream of Sardauna was destroyed. I said we needed to bring back Ahmadu Bello Stadium. He said, what do we do? He said, what do you want, Comrade? I said, give it to me. He said, what do you want to do? I said, Mr President, I will demolish it. As we are speaking, Ahmadu Bello Stadium has been demolished. I am rebuilding it into a 33,000-capacity stadium to be completed in December. It will be the only stadium with a hybrid pitch. Uyo is grass. The stadium here is grass. To put a hybrid pitch alone is over N2 billion. We are gradually bringing glory. I told Mr President that the just-concluded FIFA tournament in the US fetched $24 billion. Morocco, at the last AFCON, made $1.6 billion. The new stadium we are constructing would generate revenue and contribute to the economy. title: Abu Dhabi agrees OpenAI deals to transform government services and education
body: Abu Dhabi has teamed up with global tech company OpenAI on a series of landmark deals aimed at harnessing artificial intelligence across sectors including the government, investment, food and education. The agreements were signed after a meeting between Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. Mr Altman hailed the UAE for setting a "bold, global standard" for the integration of AI across both the public and private sectors. "We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation.” The Abu Dhabi government and OpenAI will launch the world's first AI-native Machine-Readable Government initiative, which is being heralded as a key step in the emirate's goal to become the world's first AI-native government. The high-tech project will translate a defined set of government policies and regulations into machine-readable form, enabling AI-powered systems to assist officials with routine regulatory compliance assessments, including those related to issuing permits and certificates. Each assessment is traceable to the governing rule, while government officials retain oversight and accountability for final decisions. Led and governed by the Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE), MRG’s first pilot is already in production with the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority (Adafsa), focused on food imports. The technology will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure based in the UAE. Investing in the future Under the plans, Mubadala, Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to deploy advanced AI capabilities to support investment analysis, opportunity identification and risk assessment, with the goal of ensuring more informed investment decisions. In addition, Inception42 and OpenAI signed a five-year agreement to enable the adoption of Open AI's Frontier platform across government, enterprise and education. OpenAI and Inception42 will jointly support AI adoption across government, enterprise and education in the UAE. They will collaborate to deliver enterprise solutions for large UAE organisations, pairing OpenAI’s Frontier platform and AI engineering expertise with Inception42’s applied AI capabilities and consultancy-led professional services programmes.

title: Police with assault rifles begin Sydney patrols in wake of Bondi attack
body: A new police unit armed with military assault rifles has begun patrolling the streets of Sydney, in an Australian-first measure set up in response to the Bondi Beach attack last December.The Armed Response Command will deploy at major events, crowded public spaces, sporting venues, and places of worship to conduct "high visibility" patrols, New South Wales state police said. The A$94 million ($66.08 million) unit is composed of 250 police officers armed with Australian combat assault rifles.The measure is the first of its kind in Australia, where the presence of heavily armed police officers is rare.Police unit established in response to Bondi shootingThe move comes after two men opened fire on a Jewish celebration at the famous beach, killing 15 people in an antisemitic attack motivated by Islamic State ideology."The tragic events at Bondi demonstrated the devastating consequences when an alleged armed offender attacks innocent people," the unit's commander, Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans, said."ARC ensures we have highly trained officers in the right places, with the right equipment, ready to act when seconds matter."Amnesty International Australia said the introduction of heavily armed police patrols in Sydney raised "serious questions about the increasing militarisation of policing and the safeguards in place to protect human rights.

title: Tempi Train Crash Trial Continues with 21 Witnesses This Week
body: The trial over the deadly Tempi train crash continues today at the Three-Member Court of Appeal for Felonies, with 21 witnesses scheduled to testify across three hearings this week. Six witnesses will appear today, including relatives of Vaio Vlachos and Ioannis Voutsinas, two of the 57 people who died in the February 2023 disaster. Vaggelis Vlachos, brother of Vaio Vlachos, heads today’s witness list. Court Continues to Hear Survivors’ Testimony The court is also continuing to hear from passengers who survived the collision. During the past two weeks, witnesses who travelled mainly in the second and third carriages of the Intercity train have given evidence. Last week, the presiding judge questioned survivors from the second carriage mainly about the minutes immediately before and after the collision. The questions covered where passengers saw flames, whether they noticed any unusual smells, whether the train stopped at any point after leaving Larissa railway station, and how fast it travelled before the crash at Tempi. Court Orders Documents on Railway Safety Last week, the presiding judge also announced the court’s decision on requests submitted by Loukas Apostolidis, a lawyer supporting the prosecution. Apostolidis had requested European Commission documents concerning railway safety in Greece and the summoning of the transport ministry’s former secretaries-general who served between 2016 and 2023. The court reserved its decision on whether to summon the former officials. However, it approved the request for documents. The ruling orders the Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Infrastructure and Transport to submit Greek translations of European Commission warning letters and other legal documents covering the period from 2016 to 2026. The documents concern Greece’s compliance, or failure to comply, with its railway safety obligations. Court Awaits Stationmaster’s Mobile Phone Report The court is also awaiting a forensic report from the Hellenic Police Directorate of Criminal Investigations concerning the mobile phone of the accused night-shift stationmaster. Authorities seized the phone after the crash. The presiding judge ordered the examination during the hearing on 29 September and called for the report’s submission as soon as possible. The forensic examination will cover incoming and outgoing calls, incoming and outgoing SMS and MMS messages, and data applications such as Viber. title: Why a new war on Iran could backfire on Israeli regime
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Israeli media and a retired general are warning that a new war against Iran would be a strategic error, risking a wider Persian Gulf crisis and deeper domestic troubles for Tel Aviv.
The experience of the recent war with Iran has shown that resorting to the military option against Tehran, contrary to the calculations of its architects, is not only not a guarantee for achieving political and security objectives, but can also bring heavy costs and unpredictable consequences for its initiators. Now, under conditions in which some political and military circles of the Zionist regime speak of the possibility of a new round of confrontation with Iran, the media and military figures of this regime are warning about the consequences of such a decision.
The Hebrew-language newspaper Haaretz, in a report, has emphasized that the start of a new round of conflict with Iran could be a strategic error; an error whose consequences will not be limited to Iran's borders and the occupied territories and may even involve the countries of the Persian Gulf region in a widespread crisis. This assessment shows that concern about the expansion of the scope of confrontation with Iran has become one of the serious topics in Israel's media and political circles.
In this regard, Itzhak Brik, a retired general of the Zionist regime's army, in a note in the Ma'ariv newspaper, has warned about the possibility of Donald Trump, the American president, and Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of the Zionist regime, moving toward a new military action against Iran. According to Brik, if American and Israeli decision-makers move toward such an action under the influence of political calculations and domestic developments, its consequences will go far beyond a bilateral confrontation.
This retired general believes that renewed confrontation with Iran can spread the fire of crisis across the region, intensify the Zionist regime's internal problems, and place this regime in a situation from which exit will be very difficult. The importance of this warning increases when we know that Brik speaks from within Israel's military structure, and his assessment is based on an understanding of this regime's military capacities, operational limitations, and vulnerabilities.
One of the most important lessons of the recent war with Iran is the change in Israel's and America's security calculations regarding the costs of military action against Tehran. In the past, part of the decision-making circles in Tel Aviv imagined that weapons superiority and the possession of American military support could provide the possibility of imposing will on Iran. However, practical experience showed that entering a military confrontation with Iran does not mean beginning a path whose end can be easily determined.
Iran, possessing diverse military capacities, extensive strategic geography, and the ability to use various instruments of power, has the possibility of raising the costs of action against it to a level beyond the opposing side's initial calculations. For this reason, any decision to start a new round of confrontation must be made by taking into account a set of military, security, and economic consequences; consequences whose control may slip out of the hands of the initiators of the crisis.
Under such circumstances, the issue is not only the extent of possible damage to Israel's military targets. The expansion of the scope of conflict can also affect vital infrastructure, economic centers, energy facilities, and important transportation routes in the region. The countries of the Persian Gulf region, due to their geographical position and their role in the global energy market, are vulnerable to the consequences of a widespread crisis. Any disruption in the security of this region can transfer its economic effects to global markets, energy prices, and international trade.
From this perspective, Haaretz's warning about the possibility of the crisis expanding to the Persian Gulf countries is not merely a limited security concern, but expresses the economic and geopolitical dimensions of a possible confrontation with Iran. In other words, the decision for renewed war with Tehran can impose costs on various actors that do not necessarily have a clear place in Tel Aviv's and Washington's initial calculations.
Israel's Internal Crisis; A Determining Variable
Another important point in Brik's warning is the emphasis on the effect of a possible confrontation with Iran on the internal situation of the Zionist regime. This regime faces a set of political, social, and security challenges, and any widespread military crisis can increase pressure on its political and economic structure.
Under such conditions, decision-making about entering a new confrontation may be influenced by the political considerations of Israel's leaders rather than being based on a realistic assessment of security interests and costs. Netanyahu also faces numerous pressures and challenges in the domestic political atmosphere, and this issue highlights the necessity of separating the Zionist regime's strategic interests from its government's short-term political considerations. On the other hand, America's entry into such an equation will not be cost-free either. Washington must strike a balance between supporting Israel, maintaining the security of its forces and facilities in the region, and preventing the expansion of the crisis in the Persian Gulf. The wider the scope of the confrontation becomes, the more America's political and military costs will also increase. Therefore, support for a new military action does not necessarily mean the ability to control all its consequences.
Why Is Renewed Confrontation with Iran Not Strategic?
The set of these developments shows that the main issue for Tel Aviv and Washington is not merely the possibility of starting a new military action; rather, the fundamental question is the ability to achieve the desired result and control its consequences. Starting a military operation may be technically possible, but this by no means guarantees that the desired political and security objectives will be realized.
The experience of the past eight months has also shown that Iran possesses the necessary capacity to respond and impose costs on the opposing side. This experience has made the calculations related to confrontation with Tehran more complex and has shown that Iran cannot be considered an actor that, in the face of military pressure, will suffice merely with limited and predictable reactions.
In fact, one of the most important factors of Iran's deterrence is the ability to link military capacities with geopolitical position and to influence the region's security equations. This very issue causes any military action against Iran to probably be accompanied by a set of chain consequences whose containment will not be easy for America and the Zionist regime.
Ultimately, the warnings published in Haaretz and Ma'ariv should be seen as a sign of the existence of serious concern in part of Israel's media and military circles about the costs of renewed confrontation with Iran. These warnings indicate that even within the Zionist regime, this reality has been taken into consideration that military superiority alone is not a guarantee of political and strategic victory.
For Tel Aviv and Washington, the issue is no longer merely choosing between military action and non-action; rather, it is choosing between accepting the new realities of the region and entering a crisis whose dimensions and costs may be far beyond initial predictions. From this perspective, the start of a new round of confrontation with Iran is not a display of power, but can be the beginning of a strategic error with widespread consequences for the entire region.

title: Talks with RSF on transition to civilian rule in Sudan expected within weeks, says UN envoy
body: The UN plans to hold talks “before Christmas” with Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on the transition to civilian rule, following meetings with parties close to the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the anti-war coalition, a UN official said. Pekka Haavisto, the UN special envoy for Sudan, told The National that diplomatic momentum is strong to end the devastating war despite other crises in the region, including the US-Iran conflict and the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia . The SAF's chief Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, vowing to continue fighting until his rivals are defeated. The RSF and its commander Gen Mohamed Dagalo - also known as Hemedti - meanwhile, have yet to make clear commitments to the peace proposals on the table. However, recent reports by a UN fact-finding mission accusing both sides of committing crimes, coupled with mounting US pressure, suggest that diplomatic efforts may have a window of opportunity. In an interview at the Manama Dialogue annual security forum in Bahrain, Mr Haavisto said “good meetings” had already taken place with parties close to the SAF and with an anti-war coalition led by former prime minister Abdalla Hamdok. He added that a Quintet meeting with the RSF and its allies could take place in Addis Ababa. “In our last meeting in October in Addis Ababa, we got a feeling that we’re advancing. That was a good meeting with the anti-war coalition, already talking about the substance of the transition to a civilian government,” he explained. “We got a similar feeling when talking to the democratic bloc in SAF-controlled areas. We are still waiting for a meeting with Hemedti’s bloc to take place before Christmas.” The UN has been working alongside the European Union, African Union, Arab League and Intergovernmental Authority on Development as part of the group known as the Quintet, which is pushing for peace in Sudan. But on the ground, the situation is less promising. Drone attacks have been devastating against civilians, most recently escalating in Abyei, Kordofan and Darfur among others. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned the attacks, which have also hit civilian infrastructure such as water plants, humanitarian lorries and hospitals. 'War against civlians' Last week, UN -appointed investigators warned that the Sudanese city of Al Obeid is living in “constant fear” due to drone strikes from one side in the civil war and arrests and torture by the other. Drone strikes by the RSF have killed and injured civilians. Meanwhile, thousands of people have been arrested by the SAF security cells, said Mona Rishmawi, one of the mission’s experts, adding that people were detained and tortured in Al Obeid Central Prison and other “unofficial locations”. In September, evidence revealed that the SAF not only used chemical weapons in the devastating war but also built a secret stockpile that it later sought to conceal, Mr Haavisto said he agrees with the categorisation that Sudan is not only a civil war, but a “war against civilians”. “Diplomatically, the efforts are strong, and now even more strong than some years ago, so there’s strong engagement by many parties on the diplomatic front,” he said, lauding efforts by the Quintet but also by the Quad – made up of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the US and the UAE – which has been pushing for civilian rule in the war-torn country. The war broke out in April 2023 amid a power struggle between the SAF and the RSF over civilian rule and the planned integration of the rival bodies. Repeated diplomatic initiatives have failed to secure a lasting ceasefire. The conflict has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, according to the UN World Food Programme . The US, which is pushing for an arms embargo that covers all of Sudan, has said that there is “no future” for either of Sudan’s two warring generals in the country’s political leadership.

title: Insecurity: As 30 State Houses of Assembly Okay State Police…
body: With 30 State Houses of Assembly endorsing state police, Nigeria moves closer to decentralised policing. But constitutional approval, operational legislation, funding, safeguards and implementation challenges remain critical to success, writes Sunday Aborisade . Nigeria’s decades-long debate over the establishment of state police appears to be approaching a decisive turning point, following the endorsement of the proposed constitutional amendment by no fewer than 30 State Houses of Assembly. The development, announced by the Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, represents a significant milestone in efforts to decentralise the country’s security architecture and introduce a policing arrangement that allows state governments to establish their own police services alongside the existing federal structure. For a country grappling with banditry, kidnapping, terrorism, communal conflicts and other violent crimes, the proposed reform has far-reaching implications for national security, federalism and the protection of lives and property. However, beyond the excitement generated by the legislative breakthrough, Nigerians must understand two separate but interconnected initiatives: the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, which seeks to provide constitutional authority for state police, and the proposed National Policing Bill, 2026, which will establish the operational, administrative and regulatory framework. While the former provides the constitutional foundation, the latter prescribes the institutional arrangements, standards and safeguards required to implement the reform. This distinction is important because approval of the constitutional amendment does not automatically authorise governors to recruit police officers, establish commands or commence independent policing operations. Advocates of state police have consistently argued that Nigeria’s centralised policing structure has become inadequate for a federation of its size, population and security complexities. They maintain that a single national police organisation cannot always respond effectively to the peculiar security challenges confronting communities across 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. State governments, being closer to their communities, are considered better positioned to identify local threats, understand the terrain, communicate in indigenous languages and develop intelligence networks capable of preventing criminal activities. Opponents, however, fear that governors could turn state police formations into instruments of political intimidation, persecution of opponents and suppression of dissent. Others question the financial capacity of several states to maintain properly equipped and professionally trained police organisations. Despite these concerns, the National Assembly has taken the process considerably further. The Senate passed the State Police Constitution Alteration Bill on June 24, 2026, while the House of Representatives approved it on July 23. Following the passage by both chambers, the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, transmitted the proposal to the 36 State Houses of Assembly on September 16 for consideration and approval. Under Section 9(2) of the 1999 Constitution, an alteration requires resolutions from not less than two-thirds of all State Houses of Assembly. With 36 states, the constitutional requirement is 24. On October 23, the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill announced that the required threshold had been achieved. Six days later, on October 29, Bamidele disclosed that the National Assembly had received formal reports indicating that at least 30 state assemblies had endorsed the amendment. Although the constitutional requirement had already been satisfied upon securing 24 approvals, the additional endorsements provide a broader political foundation for the proposed reform. Bamidele, who is also Vice Chairman of the Senate Committee on the Review of the 1999 Constitution, described the development as a historic breakthrough. He said the National Assembly intended to complete the outstanding legislative procedures and transmit the amendment to President Bola Tinubu for assent latest by December 2026. The remaining procedures include the consideration and collation of reports from the state legislatures and the passage of the necessary resolutions by both chambers before transmission to the President. The Senate Leader stressed that the proposed reform was not intended to establish state armies or weaken the Federal Government’s authority. Rather, it would create state-led, community-based policing arrangements operating within constitutional safeguards, professional standards, oversight mechanisms and human rights protections. Perhaps the most important issue in the ongoing debate is the distinction between the constitutional amendment and the National Policing Bill. The Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, provides the legal authority for Nigeria to move from its existing centralised police arrangement towards a dual structure comprising the Federal Police Service and State Police Services. In practical terms, it removes the constitutional obstacles preventing individual states from establishing their own police organisations. The National Policing Bill, on the other hand, will provide the operational framework, including recruitment requirements, training procedures, institutional responsibilities, accountability mechanisms, funding arrangements and minimum professional standards. This means constitutional permission does not automatically translate into operational readiness. The Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, chaired by the President’s Chief of Staff, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, was established to develop the comprehensive legislative framework. On October 19, the group submitted the draft National Policing Bill, 2026, alongside 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation. The proposed legislation is expected to address existing legal provisions designed around a single national police organisation that may become inconsistent with the introduction of state police services. The official National Policing Bill information portal explains that the constitutional amendment is enabling and phased. Under the proposed arrangement, a state may possess the constitutional authority to establish its police service but cannot commence operational policing until it has enacted the necessary state legislation and obtained certification that it meets the national minimum standards prescribed by an Act of the National Assembly. Consequently, the constitutional amendment and the National Policing Bill must progress together. One establishes the legal foundation, while the other provides the institutional machinery for implementation. The proposed arrangement will introduce two levels of police administration: the Federal Police Service, retaining responsibility for national policing functions and federal offences, and individual State Police Services established by states that satisfy the necessary legal, administrative, operational and financial requirements. The intention is to enable state police officers to respond more directly to security threats within their jurisdictions, while federal police retain responsibilities requiring national coordination. These include terrorism, organised crime, federal offences and security challenges extending beyond individual state boundaries. The final legislation will determine the precise division of responsibilities and command structures. Cooperation will also be essential. Kidnapping incidents involving the movement of victims or suspects across state boundaries, for instance, will require coordinated operations between affected state police formations and federal security agencies. Similarly, organised criminal networks operating across several states cannot be effectively confronted without intelligence sharing, integrated criminal information management and clearly defined command responsibilities. The success of the proposed system will therefore depend on cooperation rather than competition between the different levels of policing. One of the strongest objections to state police has been the fear that governors could deploy the new institutions against political opponents, critics and democratic activities. These concerns cannot be dismissed, particularly in a political environment where relationships between state governments and opposition parties are often characterised by intense rivalry. For this reason, the proposed National Policing Bill places considerable emphasis on accountability, independent oversight, professional standards and human rights protection. Its framework identifies critical areas requiring regulation, including recruitment, vetting, training, discipline, complaints management, firearms control, financial sustainability and institutional supervision. It also envisages independent oversight arrangements and state-readiness certification before any state police service can commence operations. Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, had earlier emphasised that the proposed legislation was intended to prevent state police from becoming instruments of political persecution. For the reform to enjoy public confidence, state police institutions must remain accountable to the Constitution and the law rather than the personal interests of governors or political office holders. Independent complaints mechanisms, transparent recruitment, professional discipline and judicial oversight will therefore be indispensable. Another major challenge concerns the financial implications of establishing and maintaining state police organisations. Nigeria’s 36 states have different revenue profiles, economic capacities and competing development priorities. While some may possess the resources to establish modern police formations, others could struggle to finance recruitment, training, salaries, pensions, equipment, vehicles, communication facilities and operational accommodation. Establishing a police organisation goes beyond recruiting officers and providing uniforms. It requires sustainable funding, continuous professional development, adequate equipment and institutional structures capable of maintaining acceptable operational standards. The National Policing Bill is expected to address these concerns through provisions dealing with sustainable financing, national standards and possible grant support. Importantly, states that are not immediately ready to establish their own police services are expected to continue benefiting from the Federal Police. This phased arrangement is intended to prevent the reform from creating security gaps in states that cannot immediately establish independent police formations. Nevertheless, the National Assembly must ensure that the final legislation clearly defines funding responsibilities and transparent criteria for determining when a state is financially and institutionally ready. Without such provisions, decentralised policing could create significant disparities in security capacity across the federation. Developments surrounding state police have also acquired a political dimension ahead of the 2027 general election. Speaking when members of the Arewa Revival Project, a northern youth organisation with membership across the 19 northern states, visited him in Abuja, Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio expressed optimism that Nigeria could soon embrace decentralised policing. He disclosed that about 30 state assemblies had endorsed the constitutional amendment, describing the development as an important step towards improving national security. Akpabio also used the occasion to canvass support for President Tinubu’s re-election, urging the northern youths to mobilise grassroots backing for the administration. His remarks reflected the growing intersection between governance, security reforms and electoral politics as political parties and their supporters prepare for the next general election. However, the proposed establishment of state police should be treated as a national institutional reform rather than a partisan political achievement. Its ultimate success or failure will affect Nigerians irrespective of their political affiliations or the parties controlling their respective states. With the constitutional threshold achieved, attention will now shift to the outstanding legislative and executive responsibilities. First, the National Assembly must complete the collation and consideration of reports received from the State Houses of Assembly. Both chambers must then pass the necessary resolutions before transmitting the constitutional amendment to the President for assent. Bamidele has indicated that the National Assembly intends to conclude these procedures by December 2026. Second, the Presidential Working Group must complete the review and validation of the National Policing Bill and its accompanying consequential amendments before the proposed legislation undergoes the necessary executive and legislative processes. Third, the National Assembly must scrutinise the operational framework, particularly its provisions on federal and state jurisdictions, recruitment, funding, oversight, intelligence sharing, human rights and accountability. Fourth, individual states will be expected to enact enabling laws and demonstrate their readiness to establish police services. This means that even after the constitutional amendment and National Policing Act have been completed, the commencement of operations will depend on each state’s compliance with prescribed conditions. Consequently, some states may establish their police services earlier than others, depending on their financial and institutional preparedness. Interestingly, Bamidele’s address at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies, Kuru, went beyond the state police debate to raise another important question about the quality of lawmaking in Nigeria. He argued that the performance of the 10th National Assembly should not be judged principally by the number of bills passed into law but by their measurable impact on citizens. He cited legislation on student loans, minimum wage, taxation, social investment, electoral administration, cybercrime, insurance and regional development commissions as examples of the Assembly’s legislative interventions. The Senate Leader, however, acknowledged that good laws alone cannot guarantee good governance. Legislation, he argued, must be relevant, evidence-based, implementable, adequately funded, properly administered, effectively monitored and periodically reviewed. That argument is particularly relevant to the state police initiative. Nigeria has enacted several laws and established numerous institutions, but implementation has frequently remained a major challenge. The establishment of state police must therefore not become another constitutional milestone celebrated primarily through speeches, ceremonies and political declarations. Its real value will be determined by whether it reduces criminal activities, improves intelligence gathering, strengthens community confidence and makes the protection of lives and property more effective. The National Assembly must ensure that the final legislation establishes measurable performance standards and mechanisms for holding federal and state police authorities accountable. Governors, on their part, must demonstrate that their commitment to state police goes beyond the political attraction of controlling another security institution. Ultimately, the endorsement of the constitutional amendment by at least 30 state assemblies represents an important development in Nigeria’s search for a more responsive security architecture. But the journey is not over. The constitutional amendment must be completed, the National Policing Bill must become law, states must establish the necessary institutions and the prescribed safeguards must be enforced. For Nigerians, the central expectation is straightforward: a policing system that responds faster to emergencies, understands local security challenges, prevents crimes more effectively and protects citizens without fear or favour. The real measure of this reform will not be the number of state police commands established or officers recruited, but whether Nigerians can live, work, travel and conduct their daily activities with greater security and confidence.

title: OPEC+ holds December oil output steady to support market stability
body: By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, have agreed to maintain their September 2026 required production levels for December to support stability in the global oil market. The countries — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — reached the agreement at a virtual meeting on November 1, 2026, where they reviewed “global market conditions and outlook”. The seven producers, which announced additional voluntary production adjustments in April and November 2023, decided to retain their existing production requirements for December. In a statement after the meeting, the countries reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation among oil-producing nations and stability in the international market. The statement read: “The seven participating countries decided to maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026.” The countries also reiterated their “collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation”, the framework guiding collaboration between OPEC members and participating non-OPEC oil producers. They added that they would continue to monitor developments in the global oil market through regular consultations. “The seven OPEC+ countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review market conditions. The next meeting will be held on 29 November 2026,” the statement said. The seven countries’ combined required production level for December stands at 31.01 million barrels per day (bpd), according to the accompanying production schedule. Saudi Arabia has the highest required production level at 10.478 million bpd, followed by Russia with 9.949 million bpd and Iraq with 4.431 million bpd. Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman have required production levels of 2.676 million bpd, 1.628 million bpd, 1.007 million bpd and 841,000 bpd, respectively. Reacting to the development in an interview, an energy analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the decision could support international crude oil prices, with positive implications for Nigeria’s revenue and foreign exchange earnings. title: Germany’s Gen Z protests turn violent as riots, looting erupt in major cities
body: Violence erupted in several German cities on Saturday as Gen Zs took to the streets to protest a myriad of issues, including rising living costs and underfunding of schools. The violent demonstrations in Germany come in the wake of similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of protests. The French protests, which were over high cost of living and underfunding of education, resulted in large-scale looting and destruction of properties. The protests in Germany, organised by Gen Z regelt, loosely translated as “Gen Zs got this’’, took place in more than 30 cities, with thousands taking part. The young Germans are also opposing public spending cuts and the potential return of compulsory military service. The protests, which were largely peaceful by day, assumed a violent dimension at night, with police forced to fire water cannons and pepper spray in Frankfurt, Hamburg, Cologne and Leipzig. Masked rioters smashed shop windows and looted stores in Frankfurt, hurling Molotov cocktails, fireworks and stones at police. Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters in Frankfurt. “We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology,” Roman Poseck, the state interior minister, said. Frankfurt police reportedly took around 30 people into custody, following the violent protests. In Hamburg, protesters fired pyrotechnics at police and set barricades on fire, with the officers responding with water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds. Rioters also smashed shop windows and set rubbish bins on fire. Lina Friedrich, spokesperson for Gen Z regelt, said the demonstrations were “to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion.” “What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service, and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden,” Friedrich said. title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike oil facility in Russia's Samara Oblast in overnight attack
body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated. Ukrainian drones reportedly struck an oil facility in Russia's Samara Oblast in an overnight attack on Nov. 2.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Supernova+ and Exilenova+ reported that Ukrainian drones had struck the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station in the city of Prosvet, around 835 kilometers (520 miles) northeast of Ukraine's border.
Eyewitness footage from local residents shows smoke rising above the city in the early morning light.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the targets or extent of damage from the strikes.
The Prosvet facility, a major node in Russia's oil pipeline network, consists of pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. According to Ukraine's General Staff, the station blends oil from western Siberia and other oil-producing regions of Russia to produce export-grade fuel for the Russian armed forces.
The site has been the target of multiple Ukrainian strikes in recent weeks. On Oct. 7, large fires engulfed the facility after being struck by Ukrainian drones.
The latest attack comes as Ukraine continues strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, following reports that Kyiv had opted to adopt U.S. President Donald Trump 's unilaterally imposed energy ceasefire with Russia.
Senior Ukrainian officials confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv never agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil sites on Oct. 31.
In overnight attacks on Nov. 1, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian oil refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast.
Since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine has engaged in a sustained campaign of long-range drone strikes on Russian energy facilities, focusing on oil refineries and fuel depots, which are critical to sustaining Russia's war effort.

title: GHS contains yellow fever outbreak after confirming four cases
body: The Ghana Health Service (GHS) says it has contained a yellow fever outbreak recorded between September and the first half of October, after laboratory tests confirmed four cases in parts of the country. Director-General of the GHS, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, said the cases were detected in Sissala West, Wa West, Etu and Nadowli-Kaleo, with samples sent to Dakar, Senegal, for confirmation. Speaking on TV3 on Sunday, November 1, 2026, he said health authorities responded by rolling out vaccination interventions to prevent further spread of the disease. “We had an outbreak of yellow fever, but it has been curtailed. Between September and the first half of October, we recorded cases, more than two in this case, that came confirmed from Dakar,” he said. Dr Akoriyea confirmed that four cases had been officially established, adding that the vaccination exercise formed part of measures taken to bring the outbreak under control. He also disclosed that the GHS was investigating reports of deaths in some affected communities to establish whether they were caused by yellow fever, as has been speculated.

title: Diri has betrayed Bayelsa to APC, says Dickson; ‘We won’t respond’ — Gov’s aide
body: By Samuel Oyadongha Yenagoa—Former Bayelsa State Governor, Seriake Dickson, has accused his successor, Governor Douye Diri, of surrendering government they built together to a party that never won the state through the ballot. Dickson, who spoke in a statement following his homecoming to Bayelsa, weekend, which witnessed the commissioning of the NDC state secretariat, said the governor’s decision to join the APC amounted to ‘donating’ the state to a party he claimed had never won Bayelsa through the ballot. The National Leader of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) said he had deliberately refrained from commenting extensively on developments in the state to avoid creating political tension and preserve peace. He, however, declared that the time had come to make his political position clear, accusing Diri of abandoning the political structure that nurtured and supported his emergence as governor. He said: “Every single one of the people in the current government was nurtured and supported for years by me.” The former governor recalled that Diri served as his Executive Secretary, Deputy Chief of Staff, member of the House of Representatives and Senator before succeeding him as governor. Dickson said his decision to support Diri’s emergence was informed by the need to sustain Ijaw political leadership and promote fairness among the different local government areas in Bayelsa. He alleged that his successor had now turned against those who supported his political journey, accusing the administration of pettiness, propaganda, blackmail and victimisation. “Our victory was donated free of charge to the APC, making all of us overnight opposition members in our own state, in a government we formed, in a governorship I crafted, and an administration we worked hard to put in power,” he said. Dickson maintained that the APC had never defeated him or won Bayelsa State at the polls, claiming that his political influence had prevented the party from taking control of the state since 2015. He expressed disappointment that Diri had aligned with the APC without securing what he described as corresponding benefits for Bayelsa from the Federal Government. The senator also criticised the Federal Government over what he described as inadequate infrastructure development and insufficient representation of Bayelsa and the Niger Delta in federal appointments. He, however, urged his supporters to remain peaceful and avoid personal attacks against the governor. “As I said, children may deny their father, but fathers do not deny children. The governor is still my person, my brother, my compatriot and our governor. But he is now someone I disagree with, as he and the people in his government are wrong with the direction they are taking our state to,” he said. Diri won’t respond — Aide An aide to Governor Diri, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the governor would not respond to Dickson’s allegations. “The governor doesn’t want to respond to him. That’s just the truth. Everybody is free to say whatever they want to say. We decided we don’t want to make any issue out of it. We are focused on what we want to do for Bayelsans. Let Bayelsans be the judge. That’s all we care about,” the aide said. Miriki faults Dickson’s remarks Technical Adviser to the Bayelsa State Governor on General Duties, Miriki Ebikibina, described Dickson’s comment as unfortunate, urging the former governor to exercise restraint and uphold the dignity expected of a former chief executive of the state and a serving senator. He questioned the propriety of Senator Dickson’s remarks, considering the political support and opportunities he received from former President Goodluck Jonathan, including his appointments as a commissioner and Attorney-General, as well as his emergence as a member of the House of Representatives and later as governor of Bayelsa State. Ebikibina also recalled the political circumstances surrounding Dickson’s emergence as the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, claiming that party stakeholders, including former President Jonathan and King A.J. Turner, played significant roles in securing his candidacy and electoral victory. He called on Senator Dickson and the NDC to emulate the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, whom he described as having focused his campaign on issues rather than personal attacks. According to Ebikibina, “the Diri administration’s achievements reflect purposeful leadership and effective governance. Political disagreements should not overshadow constructive engagement on issues affecting the state.” Obi to Tinubu: You’re tired, quit 2027 race Meanwhile, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress ,NDC, Peter Obi, has asked President Bola Tinubu to abandon his re-election bid in 2027, declaring that Nigeria needs a leader with the energy and capacity to tackle the country’s worsening economic and security challenges. Obi, who urged Tinubu to retire from the presidential race and return home to rest, said Nigerians could no longer afford leadership that, in his view, lacked the drive to confront the country’s mounting problems. The former Anambra State governor spoke on Friday in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, during the commissioning of the NDC campaign office and secretariat. He accused the All Progressives Congress-led Federal Government of failing to address widespread poverty, hunger, unemployment, insecurity, poor healthcare and inadequate electricity supply. He said millions of Nigerians could no longer afford basic necessities, while access to quality healthcare, education and employment remained a major challenge. Taking a direct swipe at Tinubu’s second-term ambition, Obi said, “The man is tired. He needs to go home. Tinubu must go and rest. We want him to go and rest. “Today, we have a country that produces the highest number of poor people in the world. Today, we have a country where our people are hungry. Nigerians don’t know where the next meal will come from.” He lamented that the collapse of public healthcare had forced some Nigerians to resort to spiritual interventions instead of seeking medical attention, while poor educational infrastructure and unemployment continued to undermine the country’s development. Outlining his party’s agenda, Obi said an NDC government would prioritise national unity, security, domestic production, accountability and job creation. “We are telling you that NDC is coming to build a new Nigeria that is possible. We want to move Nigeria from consumption to production. We will start by uniting the country,” he said. He pledged to strengthen public institutions, tackle insecurity and guarantee equal opportunities for Nigerians, irrespective of their ethnic or geographical backgrounds. title: Iran FM Araghchi arrives in Ashgabat for high-profile talks
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi arrived in Turkmen capital of Ashgabat on Monday to meet with high-ranking officials of the country.
According to the scheduled program, Iran’s top diplomat will hold talks with high-ranking officials of the host country and will discuss strengthening cooperation and expanding bilateral cooperation in various political and economic fields.
The Iranian foreign minister arrived in Ashgabat on Monday at the head of a diplomatic and economic delegation.

title: Adnoc signs agreement with OpenAI and G42 to deploy Frontier AI
body: Adnoc has signed an agreement with OpenAI and G42 to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier technology, as it seeks to expand AI use across its operations. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, met OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman on Monday and witnessed the agreement, signed by G42 through its subsidiary Inception42. The project will integrate advanced AI capabilities across Adnoc’s operations, enabling more connected operational, investment and commercial decision-making to improve efficiency and productivity. The technology will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure based in the UAE. The deal marks another step towards fulfilling Adnoc’s ambition to become the world’s most technology and AI-enabled energy company. It was one of four agreements signed between Abu Dhabi-based entities and OpenAI, spanning the government, energy and investment sectors. “Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone,” Mr Altman said. “We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation.” The Abu Dhabi government and OpenAI also launched what they described as the world’s first AI-native Machine-Readable Government initiative, part of the emirate’s goal to become the world’s first fully AI-native government. The initiative converts a set of government policies and regulations into a format AI systems can read, so they can help officials with routine compliance assessments, such as issuing permits and certificates. Officials keep oversight of and accountability for final decisions. Led by the Department of Government Enablement, its first pilot is already running with the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority and focuses on food imports. Mubadala , Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply AI to investment analysis, opportunity identification and risk assessment. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to support the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education in the UAE.

title: 3 feared dead, 5 rescued as two-storey building collapses in Osun
body: By Shina Abubakar OSOGBO—THREE persons have been confirmed dead and five rescued alive after a two-storey commercial building under construction collapsed at Owode-Ede, in Ede North Local Government Area of Osun State. The incident occurred at Zone 8, Oke Alaafia Community, at about 11pm on Friday, prompting a rescue operation by the Federal Fire Service and other emergency responders. In a statement, the spokesperson for the Federal Fire Service, Osun State Command, DSF Ojo Omoyemi Olamide, said the command received a distress call through its emergency line at about 11:30pm and immediately mobilised personnel to the scene. She said the five rescued victims were taken to Idera Specialist Hospital, Ede, for urgent medical attention, while the three bodies recovered were handed over to the Nigeria Police Force, A Division, Ede. “The incident involved a two-storey shopping complex used for commercial purposes. The building consists of six shops on the upper floor, six shops on the middle floor and two stores on the ground floor, covering an area of about 50m by 100m. “Preliminary investigation reveals that structural defects and the use of substandard materials are suspected to be the cause of the collapse,” she stated. Olamide said the rescue operation was completed and personnel returned to the station at about 9:26am on Saturday. She added that the estimated property loss was N100 million, while property worth approximately N150 million was saved. The operation was conducted in collaboration with the Osun State Fire Service, Ede Station; the Nigeria Police Force, A Division, Ede; and personnel of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), Owode-Ede Division. title: Ghana will become hostile territory for drug traffickers – Kumadoe
body: Security analyst Richard Kumadoe says Ghana is stepping up efforts to disrupt international drug trafficking networks, warning that traffickers who use the country as a transit point risk arrest either locally or at their intended destinations. He said security agencies were deepening intelligence-sharing and international cooperation to track suspected traffickers and dismantle networks operating across national borders. Speaking on Channel One TV on Sunday, November 1, Mr Kumadoe said authorities could use controlled delivery operations to monitor suspicious consignments and allow shipments to proceed under surveillance to facilitate arrests further along the trafficking chain. “If you use our territory or our environment, here will become very hostile to you in such a way that we either get you arrested here or we will send you with a package away with a tip-off so that you’ll be arrested in wherever you are going as your final destination,” he said. His comments followed the arrest of a Syrian passenger in Lebanon after 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine were discovered in his luggage. The passenger, identified only as B.H., had travelled from Accra to Beirut aboard a Middle East Airlines flight. Mr Kumadoe said the seizure was connected to a controlled delivery operation involving Ghanaian and Lebanese authorities, intended to help identify other individuals linked to the shipment. He said the approach demonstrated the importance of intelligence-led enforcement, with security agencies working beyond Ghana’s borders to track suspects and disrupt trafficking networks rather than concentrating solely on drug seizures at entry and exit points. He added that stronger cooperation among security agencies and investment in screening technology would be critical to preventing traffickers from exploiting Ghana as a transit route.

title: Court restrains EFCC from arresting Honda executives, associates, dealers
body: By Innocent Anaba A Lagos State High Court has restrained the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) from arresting or detaining Honda Manufacturing (Nigeria) Limited, Honda Automobile Western Africa Limited and more than 200 other applicants in connection with a pending investigation. Justice Olukayode Ogunjobi granted the first prayer in the applicants’ motion for interim injunction after it was moved by their counsel, Chief Bolaji Ayorinde, SAN. The applicants, comprising the two Honda companies, their officers, dealers, distributors, business associates and other individuals and businesses, sought protection of their fundamental rights over the EFCC investigation. They sought orders restraining the commission and its officers from arresting or detaining them, compelling them to report for questioning, issuing further invitations, or harassing, intimidating or threatening them with arrest. The applicants also asked the court to prevent the EFCC from restricting their liberty without complying with the Constitution, the Administration of Criminal Justice Act and other applicable laws. The court granted prayer one. , holding that the relief covered prayers two to six.The suit was brought under Sections 34, 35, 37, 40, 43 and 46 of the 1999 Constitution as amended, and relevant provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. (Ratification and Enforcement) Act. The matter was adjourned to November 23, 2026, for further proceedings.
