title: Gunmen abduct Plateau varsity student, shoot another in Bokkos
body: By Golok Nanmwa JOS—GUNMEN suspected to be kidnappers have abducted a 100-level female student of Plateau State University (PLASU), Bokkos, and shot another person during an attack on an off-campus student residential area in Bokkos Local Government Area of Plateau State. The incidents occurred on Saturday at about 8:40pm, raising concerns over the safety of students living outside the university campus. A student, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed the abduction to journalists in Jos on Sunday, saying the victim had gone out with another female student when she was seized. “Yes, the student was taken away by the attackers last night, and we have not seen her since then. She lives off-campus, but I don’t know her personally,” the student said. He lamented the growing insecurity in the area and appealed to security agencies to ensure the safe rescue of the abducted student. A university staff member, who also spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly, said the institution was aware of the incident. “The university is aware of a reported shooting incident in one of the off-campus student residential areas. This would be the second such incident in four weeks,” he said. “While the incident did not occur within the university campus, which remains our direct responsibility to secure, we are deeply concerned that any of our students living off-campus should face such threats to their safety,” he added. The staff member said the administration of Prof. Shadrack Best had made concerted efforts to provide safe on-campus accommodation for all students. “However, due to severe financial constraints, the university is currently only able to accommodate about 1,000 students in its dormitories,” he stated. “The university appreciates the support of its Visitor and Plateau State Governor, Barr. Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, as well as the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, TETFund, for providing critical infrastructure at the institution,” he said. “The university will continue to engage relevant authorities to expand both accommodation and security for our nearly 20,000 students,” he added. Efforts to reach the Plateau State Police Command’s Public Relations Officer, SP Alfred Alabo, for comments were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report. title: Ukrainian Navy destroys six Russian aircraft, ten multiple launch rocket systems in October
body:
The Ukrainian Navy reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
"Military units and formations of the Ukrainian Navy, both as part of task groups and independently, continue to carry out their missions with honor and courage to repel the Russian Federation's full-scale armed aggression," the statement said.
According to the Ukrainian Navy, successful combat operations resulted in the following estimated Russian losses in October: approximately 373 personnel killed or wounded; six aircraft; 123 vehicles; ten multiple launch rocket systems; seven artillery systems; one cruise missile; 8,218 FPV drones; 17 operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles; 690 attack drones; three ammunition depots; and 190 Shahed-136/131 drones.
The Russian army also lost seven watercraft, three naval mines, two air defense systems, one armored combat vehicle and one unmanned surface vessel (USV) as a result of Ukrainian Navy operations.

title: EPL: Havertz fires Arsenal to 1-0 win at Anfield
body:
German Striker, Kai Havertz scored the only goal for Arsenal as they won 1- 0 against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.
Champions Arsenal took the lead in the 16th minute when Havertz tapped in a low cross from Declan Rice after Liverpool failed to play the ball out of defence.
But Mikel Arteta’s side held on and defended superbly their first Premier League win at Anfield in 14 years.
The win puts Arsenal on top of the table with 24 points, ahead of Manchester City, on 21 after losing at home to Brighton and Hove Albion on Saturday.
The defeat leaves Liverpool nine points behind Arsenal in fifth place.

title: The Saudi-UAE split is ending. That may be bad news for Yemen.
body:
A sharp break last year left the Gulf allies at odds. Now, they're reentering the fight against the Houthis, with divergent goals.
The Houthis’ lightning advances in Yemen have given Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates an opening to set aside their differences after a notable rupture over the country’s political makeup less than a year ago.
However, even if a unified threat manages to bind them together, their unresolved disagreements over the future of Yemen could limit the effectiveness of renewed military cooperation against the Houthis and deepen fragmentation elsewhere in Yemen.
At least for now, both countries have signaled a willingness to compartmentalize their disputes. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman’s meeting with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed on October 18 provided a public indication of renewed dialogue, with bin Salman praising the “historical relations between our two brotherly countries.”
The official readout did not announce a Yemen military agreement, but the Guardian separately reported that Abu Dhabi had agreed to resume payments to government-aligned forces it had previously backed in southern Yemen, a region where it has long sought influence. In exchange, Saudi Arabia’s air force would provide support for those forces against the Houthis.
Further details of Emirati involvement remain scarce. But numerous prominent Saudi and Emirati media outlets have published conciliatory commentary following the recent meeting, emphasizing the shared benefits of cooperation and calling for an end to public feuding.
The shift in tone signals an effort to sideline the December 2025 rupture in relations, which saw UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) forces capture large parts of the Hadramawt and al-Mahra provinces bordering Saudi Arabia.
The advance, which Riyadh viewed as a direct threat to its national security within its southern neighbor, triggered severe public recriminations.
It also led to a Saudi-led airstrike on a weapons shipment at Mukalla port that it said had arrived in support of the STC, and an abrupt demand for the remaining UAE forces to leave Yemen, along with the severe weakening of the STC.
That confrontation exposed competing visions for Yemen that had strained their intervention from the outset.
Although both led a war against the Houthis, known officially as Ansar Allah, starting in 2015, Riyadh backed the internationally-recognized government, while Abu Dhabi cultivated southern armed groups, including the separatist STC.
The Saudis wanted a unified government capable of defeating the Houthis, while the UAE prioritized advancing southern Yemen’s independence via the STC in a bid to gain control over ports, including Aden, which lies near the mouth of the Red Sea.
Those differences flared up in 2019, when STC and government forces fought for control of Aden, until a marriage of convenience saw Riyadh and Abu Dhabi unify these factions into a fragile power-sharing agreement .
Nevertheless, describing this simply as Saudi support for the internationally-recognized government against Emirati support for separatists would obscure both countries’ reliance on myriad local armed partners. Those relationships offer Abu Dhabi a means of re-engaging without returning its own forces to the battlefield.
The UAE is unlikely to fight the Houthis directly as it did in the previous stage of the war. The Houthis had previously struck Emirati territory, notably in 2022, showcasing the risks for the UAE, whose economy relies on projecting an image of a secure commercial oasis in an otherwise turbulent region.
And having already faced intensive Iranian missile and drone attacks since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran , Abu Dhabi may be more inclined to limit its role to supporting local anti-Houthi factions, particularly given the Houthis’ markedly improved strike capabilities.
Still, even though Emirati involvement in Yemen would likely prove secretive, it could play a critical role in the coalition.
Abu Dhabi has built influence through relationships with capable local militias – including the Giants Brigades and Tarek Saleh’s National Resistance Forces – and a wider network of commercial and security interests. Although some major Emirati-backed factions merged into the Saudi-led military structures in Yemen following Abu Dhabi’s withdrawal of direct funding last year, residual command networks and personal loyalties remain intact.
Therefore, Abu Dhabi maintains significant leverage, which it can tap into by rapidly reactivating financial and logistical support. The question is whether it will use that power to boost the coalition or counter Riyadh, including by constraining its options in the south.
Indeed, the real danger is that Riyadh and Abu Dhabi will each maintain their own channels of influence and back parallel structures that end up causing fractures in territories beyond Houthi control.
Beyond geostrategic differences, there are potential ideological clashes. One longstanding source of friction is the Islamist Islah party, which is allegedly tied to the Muslim Brotherhood. Despite both governments’ hostility towards the Muslim Brotherhood, Riyadh has maintained relationships with Islah politicians within the internationally-recognized government.
Abu Dhabi, meanwhile, has seen no room for compromise. The UAE has reportedly even hired mercenaries to assassinate the faction’s leaders.
As long as Riyadh insists on working with Islah as a pragmatic means of strengthening the anti-Houthi coalition, this disagreement alone may hinder the level of support that Abu Dhabi will provide for government-backed forces.
Agreement on confronting the Houthis therefore does not necessarily extend to agreement on which Yemeni actors should be empowered.
Disagreements over who should govern Yemen could also complicate decisions about how to fight the Houthis and on what terms to negotiate. Since the U.N.-brokered ceasefire in April 2022, Riyadh has spent years seeking a negotiated exit from Yemen’s war, but the renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi territory — including deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport and attacks on oil infrastructure — have shown the limits of its containment policy, which aims to check Houthi advances without a return to full-scale war.
Regional factors matter too. Saudi Arabia has already called on Turkey, Pakistan and Egypt for defensive support against Houthi strikes, in line with the Mecca Defense Alliance, signaling that it is looking beyond its traditional reliance on the UAE.
That could deepen divisions and suggest that Riyadh increasingly views its alliance with Abu Dhabi as less essential. Meanwhile, divisions among various anti-Houthi groups remain deep. Southern factions are still divided over independence, autonomy, the distribution of power and their relationship with the rest of the country, reflecting longstanding tensions that predate Yemen’s unification in 1990.
Ultimately, any Saudi-UAE military coordination will remain fragile so long as the two Gulf powers continue to pursue conflicting endgames for Yemen.
The real test is whether any renewed cooperation yields accountable financing, coherent command structures and a political process that genuinely includes Yemen’s competing factions.
Without those elements, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi may very well end up assembling a coalition that will fight the Houthis today but crumble tomorrow, further fueling the instability that has long plagued Yemen.

title: Panic over El-Sayed has GOP resurrecting toxic 9/11-era tropes
body:
Republicans are now accusing the Democratic Senate nominee as posing threat to American national security
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) had a dire warning for Michigan voters last Wednesday: Electing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate could cost American lives.
Speaking at a GOP campaign event in Grosse Pointe Woods, Cruz accused El-Sayed of being a “passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood,” warning that if he were elected and given a seat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, “there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result.”
Several Republicans on next week’s midterm ballot spoke at the event, but Cruz reserved most of his time for El-Sayed, who is facing former Rep. Mike Rogers in the race for an open Senate seat in Michigan.
Cruz’s remarks are among the harshest in an escalating campaign of attacks on El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate. From President Donald Trump to prominent Republican lawmakers like Cruz, conservative commentators are portraying the Democratic nominee as not only a political opponent, but as a potential threat to American national security.
The attacks revive a familiar strain of fear-mongering post-9/11 politics, where Muslim candidates — even non- Muslim candidates — were accused of supporting Islamist extremism and described as potential dangers to the country. This escalating barrage of criticism comes as El-Sayed and Rogers are locked in a tight race for what could prove to be a decisive Senate seat. The latest RealClearPolitics average shows the Democratic leading by 3.5 percentage points.
The attacks started as soon as El-Sayed won the nomination in August, when Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) called him “a TERRORIST” and “a RADICAL ISLAMIST who will do everything he can to destroy America.”
Since then, the rhetoric has only intensified. Trump has targeted him frequently, calling El-Sayed a “ jihadist , who would be “the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector.” After introducing the father of a man who died on Flight 93 on Sept. 11, 2001, at a recent event, the president compared the Michigan Democrat to the 9/11 hijackers.
A number of Republicans, including Trump and the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund PAC, have said El-Sayed wants to bring “Sharia law” to the United States, recycling another common talking point from the early 2010s. (El-Sayed is not the only Muslim politicians to face similar attacks based on their religion; Tuberville’s pinned tweet highlights an image of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani next to the Twin Towers blowing up, with the caption “The enemy is inside the gates.”)
One Republican Senator said El-Sayed “can be nowhere near Washington, D.C.” because he does not understand that “Jesus came here for our salvation.”
Two hawkish Republican columnists took to the pages of the Daily Signal and the Wall Street Journal to emphasize Cruz's point that, unlike appointed government officials, El-Sayed, if elected, will not have to pass a background check in order to access classified materials.
“Rumor has it that El-Sayed covets a seat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee,” wrote Republican commentator Josh Hammer. “That’s a perfect perch for a senatorial fifth column.”
The critics offer little explanation of how El-Sayed's election would pose a threat to national security. Republicans making the accusations have not presented evidence that he has engaged in extremist activity or would misuse access to classified information.
They have largely pointed to El-Sayed’s past statements supporting Egyptian protesters against the 30-year dictatorship of President Hosni Mubarak and Egypt's democratic transition in 2011 and 2012. At the time, El-Sayed argued that the U.S. should support the protesters despite the possibility of the Muslim Brotherhood taking power, which, he said, contrary to some Americans’ fears, would “look nothing like Iran.”
That position was well within the mainstream at the time. The late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), for example, urged the Obama administration to do a “better job of encouraging democracy" in the Middle East , despite the “influence” of groups like Muslim Brotherhood, because “the “status quo” was destined to lead to “much more violence.” Though he remained critical of the group, McCain also met with members of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt on at least two occasions and called for the release of members of the group’s leadership after they were removed from power.
Critics have also cited allegations that his family has historical ties to the organization, a once-popular group in Egypt that promoted governance based on Islamic principles. Mohamed Morsi, who was the leader of the Muslim Brotherhood’s political wing, briefly served as the first democratically-elected president of Egypt before his ouster in a military coup.
In a recent ad, Rogers declared that “Abdul El-Sayed’s radical ideology is a threat to our national security” and has repeatedly accused him of being “connected to” the Muslim Brotherhood.
During Morsi’s presidency, Rogers, then a member of the House of Representatives, said there were “moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to” and voted to continue sending aid to Cairo during Morsi's presidency.
Critics of this approach say framing El-Sayed, who has spent most his career as a public health administrator, as a threat to national security is an attempt to redirect attention away from the issues voters actually care about, like the economy, health care, or the ongoing war in Iran , which appear to be losing electoral issues for the Republican Party as the midterms near. As the journalist Ken Klippenstein recently wrote on his Substack, “It’s a ploy to shift the debate from concerns that the public has to that of think tank ‘experts’ and the professional commentators.”
As the campaign entered its final weekend, the tendency to cast Muslims as national security risks and the desire to revive the peak of post-9/11 threat inflation had reached a new extreme.
Speaking to the New York Post on Saturday, Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre invoked one of that era’s most recognizable symbols.“He’s a better fit for Guantanamo Bay than the halls of Congress,” she said, adding that “Michiganders should keep this jihadist as far away from power as possible.”

title: Monarch’s murder: Nwifuru seeks death penalty for kidnappers
body: By Jeff Agbodo Ebonyi State Government has forwarded an executive bill to the State House of Assembly seeking to make kidnapping a capital offence punishable by death without an option of alternative punishment. Governor Francis Nwifuru disclosed this at the weekend during the funeral of the slain traditional ruler of Ndufu-Alike autonomous community in Ikwo Local Government Area, HRH Eze Francis Igwe. Igwe, father of the immediate past Deputy Governor of Ebonyi State, Eric Igwe, was abducted on Sunday, March 1, while on his way to church. He was reportedly killed by his abductors a day after. Speaking at the funeral, conducted by the Assemblies of God Church, Nwifuru lamented what he described as the moral deterioration among Nigerian youths, expressing concern about their readiness to assume leadership positions in the future. He also pledged to implement any court decision against those arrested over the monarch’s murder, adding that the proposed legislation was intended to deter kidnapping and abduction in the state. The governor said: “I am worried about our present-day youths taking up leadership positions tomorrow. Some of our youths are not well informed, and they act so irrationally. “I am concerned because, with some of their attitudinal dispositions, there seems to be no future for our youths. “The youths need to have a rethink concerning certain actions of theirs, especially as concerns their attitudes towards community leaders. They should desist from treating their leaders as holders of their destinies.” He warned that the monarch’s murder should be the last such incident in Ikwo and other parts of the state. “I will not wait to execute the decision of the court over the murderers of this monarch, HRH Eze Francis Igwe. We have sent a bill to the House of Assembly to make kidnapping attract the death sentence by hanging in the state, with no other option. This should serve as a deterrent to those planning a kidnap, whether for political reasons or otherwise,” the governor said. Nwifuru described the late monarch as a forthright, vocal and astute parliamentarian who represented his people effectively in the old Anambra State and attracted development projects to his community, including the popular Folk Technical College, which has produced prominent Nigerians. In tributes, former governors Sam Egwu and Martin Elechi, as well as former Senate President, Anyim Pius Anyim, described the deceased as a statesman, peacemaker, renowned educationist, administrator and passionate leader who left enduring legacies. They urged the family and the Ikwo people to take solace in his contributions to society. In his tribute, the monarch’s first son, Igwe, described his father as a devoted family man and role model who guided him on family life, religion, politics and culture. He said the circumstances surrounding his father’s death remained difficult for the family to comprehend but expressed confidence that his legacies would endure across generations. Thanking sympathisers and well-wishers who attended the funeral, Igwe disclosed that his father’s last wish was for Governor Nwifuru to secure a second term. Earlier, in a sermon titled, “Prepare for Eternity”, the General Superintendent of Assemblies of God, Nigeria, Rev. Dr. Abel Amadi, represented by the church’s General Treasurer, Rev. Dr. Gabriel Michael, urged Christians to remain prepared for eternity, noting that no one knew the hour of their death. title: GRASAG-UG, UGSRC warn students against unauthorised protest over accommodation fees
body: The Graduate Students’ Association of Ghana (GRASAG-UG) and the University of Ghana Students’ Representative Council (UGSRC) have urged students to stay away from a planned demonstration over accommodation fees, warning that the group organising the protest is not recognised under the university’s governance system. The Concerned Students’ Movement of the University of Ghana has announced plans to demonstrate on Monday, November 2, against a proposed 26 per cent increase in accommodation charges at university halls and facilities managed by the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL). In a joint communiqué issued on Sunday, November 1, the two recognised student bodies said they shared concerns about the rising cost of accommodation but cautioned students against joining protests that might breach university regulations or the Public Order Act, 1994 (Act 491). “We clarify that the group currently mobilising for a demonstration on Monday, November 2, is unrecognised and unregistered within the University’s governance framework,” the statement said. They added: “To protect students from legal jeopardy, disciplinary action, or public safety risks, students are strongly advised not to participate in demonstrations that do not comply with university regulations or the Public Order Act, 1994 (Act 491).” The warning comes amid ongoing negotiations between student leaders and UGEL over the proposed accommodation charges. UGEL initially proposed a 26 per cent increase across university-managed halls and enterprise hostels for the next academic year, but the proposal was rejected by GRASAG-UG, UGSRC and Junior Common Room (JCR) executives at a residence meeting. Following further discussions, UGEL presented revised increases ranging from 15 to 19 per cent, depending on room categories and facilities. The student leadership, however, said the revised rates remained unacceptable and did not sufficiently address the financial pressure on students. GRASAG-UG and UGSRC said negotiations had yet to produce an agreement, adding that the Office of the Dean of Students had held an initial meeting with representatives of the group planning the demonstration. The two bodies reaffirmed their commitment to protecting students’ interests and said they would continue engaging the relevant stakeholders to reach an acceptable outcome. “GRASAG and UGSRC remain fully committed to protecting student welfare and ensuring that no student is priced out of higher education,” they said. They urged students to remain calm and exercise restraint while the discussions continued, adding that further updates would be shared through their official communication channels as consultations progressed.

title: 2027: Obi will win Bayelsa, Niger Delta, Nigeria — Dickson
body: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — National Leader of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Senator Seriake Dickson, has expressed confidence that the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, will win Bayelsa State, the Niger Delta and the country at large in the January 16, 2027 general election. Dickson also declared that the All Progressives Congress (APC) had nothing to offer the people of Bayelsa, accusing the ruling party of failing to deliver meaningful infrastructure, including roads and bridges, to the state and the wider Niger Delta region. The former Bayelsa State governor spoke during a visit to his home state and community, Toru-Orua, alongside Obi and other NDC leaders. In a statement posted on his Facebook page on Sunday, Dickson claimed that the APC had never defeated him politically or won Bayelsa State through the ballot. He also boasted that he had been the major obstacle preventing the APC from winning the state since 2015, despite the defeat of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) at the federal level. “The APC never defeated me and they have never won Bayelsa on the ballot. I have been the obstacle stopping them from winning Bayelsa since 2015, even with the defeat of the PDP at the centre,” he said. Dickson accused Governor Douye Diri, whom he said he had supported and helped bring to power, of handing the state over to the APC, thereby turning him and his political associates into opposition members in an administration they helped establish. He, however, described Diri as his brother and compatriot, saying their disagreement was over the political direction of the state. “The governor is still my person, my brother, my compatriot and our governor. But he is now someone I disagree with, as he and the people in his government are wrong with the direction they are taking our state to,” Dickson said. The senator said he had deliberately refrained from making extensive public comments on the political developments in the state to preserve peace and prevent a crisis. He, however, urged his supporters and Bayelsans to make their political positions known ahead of the 2027 elections, while appealing to them to remain peaceful and avoid attacks, threats or abuses against political opponents. Dickson also alleged that some of his supporters had experienced intimidation, harassment and dismissal from political appointments, although he did not provide specific details to substantiate the claims. He maintained that his opposition to the APC was informed by what he described as the absence of tangible federal development projects, life-changing policies and adequate representation for the Niger Delta in federal appointments. According to him, the NDC is committed to equity, justice and an inclusive Nigeria, insisting that the interests of the Niger Delta must be pursued alongside those of other regions. The former governor urged party members to mobilise across their communities and constituencies, promising to join them in the campaigns. He also called on them to resist electoral intimidation and any unlawful attempts by security personnel or electoral officials to undermine the will of voters. “Those who claim to be popular should test that popularity at the polls and allow the votes to count,” he said. Dickson said he was accompanied on the visit by Obi, the Director-General of the NDC National Campaign Council, Mallam Ibrahim Abdulkarim, and other party leaders. He thanked the party’s National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas, members of the National Working Committee, state and local government executives, ward chairmen and other stakeholders for their participation in the visit. He also disclosed that the delegation commissioned the party’s state secretariat before proceeding to his country home in Toru-Orua, where they were received by traditional rulers, chiefs, elders, youths, women and other residents. Dickson said he introduced Obi to the people of Bayelsa and urged them to support and vote for him, as well as other NDC candidates in the 2027 elections. He further called on the people to honour the legacies of political figures associated with the Niger Delta struggle, including Harold Dapabiriye, the late Chief Melford Okilo, Isaac Adaka Boro, former Bayelsa governor Diepreye Alamieyeseigha and the late Pa Edwin Clark. The senator also recalled his role in the emergence of Diri as governor, saying his succession decision was informed by the need to sustain Ijaw political leadership and promote fairness among communities in Bayelsa. He alleged that the state’s political transition to the APC had undermined the sacrifices made by him and other party members to establish the current political structure. The visit also featured cultural performances, including an Ijaw traditional war boat regatta organised in Dickson’s honour, which he said he was pleased to share with Obi. He thanked the people of Bayelsa, traditional institutions, party supporters, security agencies, musicians and media organisations for their participation in the visit. title: How melted nylon additive keeps plantain chips crunchy
body: By Elizabeth Adegbesan For some years, plantain chip has been one of Nigeria’s ultimate snacks which is affordable, accessible, and portable. But as inflation hovers at historic highs, a sinister economic survival tactic has crept into the informal food sector. Read Also: NAFDAC secures five-year jail term for fake Goya oil manufacturer Economy&Lifestyle discovered that to cut costs and keep chips crispy for days, some street entrepreneurs are turning to a dangerous additive: melted cellophane bags. The cost of a crunch The mathematics of running a small-scale food business in Nigeria today is brutal. The price of vegetable oil, cooking gas, and raw plantains has tripled over the last two years. For vendors like Halima Mohammed, who operates a roadside frying station, the pressure to maintain profit margins without raising prices is suffocating. “If I increase the price of a small pack from N200 to N400, the students will walk away. “People don’t have money. So, vendors look for shortcuts to make the oil last longer and keep the chips from getting soggy in humidity.” The “shortcut” involves tossing polyethylene plastic bags directly into the scalding oil. As the plastic melts, it blends with the vegetable oil, creating a glazing agent. When the plantain slices are fried in this mixture, they form a glassy, ultra-crisp outer shell. Crucially for vendors, the plastic coating prevents the chips from absorbing moisture, extending their shelf life from two days to over two weeks. A lifestyle of hustle and denial In the underbelly of Nigeria’s entrepreneurial ecosystem, the practice is an open secret, driven by sheer desperation. The lifestyle of a micro-entrepreneur in Nigeria is defined by any-way-raw-iron—a slang term for survival by any means necessary. With no safety nets and a failing grid that forces reliance on expensive petrol generators, the boundary between ethical business and hazardous malpractice has blurred. Osaro Jimoh, a distributor who supplies packaged chips to traffic vendors on the , admitted that the market rewards the longest-lasting product. “The boys selling in traffic need chips that stay crunchy under the hot sun for days. If the chips go soft, the motorists will throw them back at us. Nobody asks how the crunch is made; they just want the crunch. “I don’t know the preservative used to achieve such crunchiness.” For the millions of consumers who rely on these cheap snacks to get through grueling multi-hour commutes, the lifestyle implications are passive but deadly. Plastic-infused oil releases carcinogenic compounds, heavy metals, and microplastics into the food, posing severe long-term risks to liver and kidney health. The regulatory blindspot Agencies have repeatedly warned the public against consuming street foods prepared with plastic additives. However, enforcing regulations in a vast, informal economy is nearly impossible. Millions of fryers operate out of residential backyards, unbranded and untraceable. Public health advocate, Dr. Duro Ifagbemi, emphasized the gravity of the situation. “We are looking at a ticking time bomb of gastrointestinal complications and cancer cases,” he warned. “But you cannot solve a public health crisis without addressing the economic reality. “When people are starving, long-term health risks feel invisible compared to immediate poverty.” Surviving at all costs Though Mohammed denied using the plastic trick herself but acknowledges that the economic system pushes many over the edge. “Nigeria makes entrepreneurs out of necessity, not out of choice. “When the government makes it impossible to do business cleanly, people will find a way to survive in the dirt.” Until the macroeconomic pressures ease, the crisp snap of a roadside plantain chip will carry a cost far heavier than the few Naira exchanged on the asphalt. Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.
The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.
Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations , the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

title: Gully erosion destroys 30 houses, cuts off Edo communities
body: By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY — No fewer than 30 houses have been destroyed by a ravaging gully erosion at Agor-Uwagboe community in Oredo Local Government Area of Edo State. The erosion has also cut off the community’s access road linking it with Ofumwengbe and Egbiri communities, leaving residents with limited means of movement. To ease the situation, residents have constructed a makeshift wooden bridge to enable motorcycles conveying passengers to cross the affected area. Residents of the community on Sunday staged a peaceful protest to draw the attention of the Edo State Government to their worsening situation. Speaking during the protest, a community member, Mr Ernest Uwagboe, said the gully was gradually extending into the community, threatening more homes and property. He warned that the entire community could be consumed by the erosion within three years if the state government failed to urgently intervene. The community’s spokesman, Kenneth Adoni, said residents had written several letters to relevant government agencies seeking assistance but had yet to receive any intervention. He appealed to Governor Monday Okpebholo to come to their aid, lamenting the hardship caused by the erosion. “We are begging Governor Monday Okpebholo to come and help us. For the past three years, the gully has caused lots of problems. We cannot cross to other communities. Whenever it rains, children cannot go to school,” he said. The residents called on the state government to urgently address the erosion menace and restore access to neighbouring communities to prevent further destruction and alleviate their hardship. title: Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, top stories this morning
body:
News in Azerbaijan , Armenia , Georgia . Top stories from local media, photos, videos and trending comments.
● Armenia has officially launched its new biometric passport system at a ceremony in Yerevan. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said the passports meet all modern international standards and cannot be forged. “This is a very important innovation in terms of increasing international trust in our citizens and our state. But most importantly, this biometric passport system should make life easier for the people of Armenia,” he said.
● More than 1,300 people have already registered to obtain the new biometric passports, Interior Minister Arpine Sargsyan said. She noted that Armenia can now join the system of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).
● Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan met in Yerevan with executives from major international companies in the passenger transport sector. Those attending included IN Groupe head Yan Hage, IN Groupe representative and HayPass board member Isabelle Loiseau, and Corporación América Airports director Martin Eurnekian. They discussed the introduction of biometric passports in Armenia. Pashinyan described the new passports as a strategic step towards improving public services and advancing Armenia’s visa liberalisation process with the EU.
● Armenia is among 29 countries where Russia allows information and advisory centres providing assistance with consular matters to operate.
● Russia’s Foreign Ministry has denied reports that Moscow refused to approve Samvel Mkrtchyan’s appointment as Armenia’s new ambassador to Russia. The Armenian newspaper Hraparak had previously reported the alleged refusal, suggesting it might be linked to Mkrtchyan’s long diplomatic career in European countries. The paper also wrote that Armenia’s current ambassador to Russia, Gurgen Arsenyan, had said goodbye to representatives of various Russian circles in the summer and returned to Armenia in August. He later travelled back to Moscow and resumed his duties.
Samvel Mkrtchyan was appointed Armenia’s ambassador to Poland in November 2018. Before that, he headed Armenia’s diplomatic mission in Lebanon, represented the country at NATO and led the Foreign Ministry’s Department for Arms Control and International Security.
● The Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin marked the 27th anniversary of the enthronement of Karekin II, Supreme Patriarch and Catholicos of All Armenians. A festive liturgy and patriarchal service were held, and the Skevra reliquary containing the relics of saints was brought out for veneration. Heads of dioceses and pilgrims attended the service, which was led by Bishop Mushegh Babayan. In his sermon, he called Karekin II “one of the outstanding patriarchs” and said he had assumed the throne at a time when Armenia and the Armenian people were just beginning the difficult path of independence.
● Nearly 1,000 lorries are waiting to cross from Russia into Georgia along one of the key transit routes for Armenia, which has no common border with Russia. North Ossetian head Sergey Menyailo said the road was open to traffic but did not explain what had caused the build-up.
● Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and his associates gathered in a courtyard in Yerevan for a traditional khash meal – a traditional soup made from beef trotters. Tables were set up under tents and served by specially hired waiters.
● Halloween was marked by noisy and conflicting celebrations in central Yerevan. Hundreds of people took to the streets in costumes, while others held anti-Halloween placards and sang songs in praise of Jesus.
PHOTO: An exhibition in central Yerevan marking the launch of the biometric passport system.
● A new controversy has erupted in Georgia over stray dogs. TV Pirveli has broadcast disturbing footage which, according to the programme, shows dog remains being buried at night in a cemetery in Tbilisi. Animal rights activists are demanding that the Prosecutor’s Office investigate, exhume the remains and conduct an independent examination, including checks for microchips and comparisons with reports of missing dogs from across Georgia. They also want investigators to establish how many animals were euthanised, which drugs were used, and who authorised the procedures and on what grounds.
Tbilisi’s Animal Monitoring Agency denies allegations of mass, deliberate killing, saying the site is designated for animals that have died from illness, accidents or natural causes. On 1 November, the Interior Ministry announced an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which covers cruelty to animals.
● The Constitutional Court of Georgia concluded the oral submissions phase on 30 October in a case brought by ruling party MPs seeking to ban five opposition parties. Hearings will resume on 9 November with the questioning phase. Court President Revaz Nadaraia said the parties would be questioned first, followed by the respondents. Public Defender Levan Ioseliani said he would submit his own opinion to the court, setting out international standards.
● The ruling party’s lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties has drawn criticism from several international organisations. The Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe (ALDE) called for the lawsuit to be withdrawn and urged the EU to “impose targeted sanctions on those responsible for repression”. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee condemned the move, while OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Mykyta Poturaiev expressed concern. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze responded to ALDE’s statement, saying: “Such statements constitute a gross interference in the independence of Georgia’s judiciary.”
● The 11th meeting of the Georgia-Azerbaijan Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation was held in Georgia, co-chaired by Prime Ministers Irakli Kobakhidze and Ali Asadov. Following the meeting, Kobakhidze said the two countries had agreed to accelerate the delimitation and demarcation of their shared border. He noted that there had been no progress in recent years and that 15 sections remained unresolved. The disputed areas include the David Gareji monastery complex and its surrounding territory.
● Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said renowned opera singer Paata Burchuladze, convicted in connection with the 4 October attempt to seize the presidential administration, could “get out of prison very easily if he expresses remorse and admits his guilt”. Kobakhidze said public calls for Burchuladze’s unconditional release ran counter to the rule of law. Several activists convicted in the same case have already been released after reaching plea agreements with the Prosecutor’s Office.
● Georgia’s State Security Service said a Georgian citizen illegally detained by Russian occupation forces near the village of Bershueti in Gori Municipality, in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, was released on 31 October. The EU Monitoring Mission’s hotline was used to secure his release.
● Tbilisi held its 46th Saturday march. The slogan of the most recent demonstrations has been “Georgia against [oligarch] Ivanishvili”. Continuous pro-European protests have been taking place in Georgia since 28 November 2024, when the ruling Georgian Dream party announced that it was suspending the country’s EU accession talks until the end of 2028.
Podcast “Protests in Georgia” – video and photos.
● Parliament has passed in its third reading a law allowing the national energy regulator to set household natural gas tariffs based on consumption levels. Currently, the price per cubic metre is the same regardless of how much gas a household uses. The existing tariff expires in December.
Photo: Animal rights activists are staging a protest outside the Government administration building.
● APA TV reporter Sanan Bahramli was assaulted while covering a major fire at the site of a former meat-processing plant in Baku. The attacker, who identified himself as a security guard, insulted the journalist, physically assaulted him and damaged the news crew’s equipment. He was later identified as Heydar Sardarov. Police detained him and opened a criminal case. Azerbaijan’s Media Council condemned the attack and called for an objective investigation.
● A suspected mass food poisoning incident occurred at the Qizil Qaya restaurant in Baku’s Nizami district. Fourteen people reported symptoms of food poisoning and five were hospitalised. The Food Safety Agency is investigating.
● Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry welcomed the nomination of OSCE Secretary General Feridun Sinirlioğlu for the post of UN Secretary General.
● President Ilham Aliyev congratulated Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Revolution Day, describing the Algerian people’s struggle for independence as a symbol of heroism, national unity and the pursuit of freedom. He expressed confidence that bilateral cooperation would continue to expand.
● The 11th meeting of the Azerbaijan-Georgia Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation was held in Georgia, co-chaired by the two prime ministers, Ali Asadov and Irakli Kobakhidze. They discussed trade, energy, transport, investment and the development of the Middle Corridor. The meeting concluded with the signing of cooperation documents in customs and agriculture. Asadov said Azerbaijan was Georgia’s largest investor, with nearly $4 billion invested in its economy. Kobakhidze said Georgia intended to accelerate the process of delimiting and demarcating the shared border.
● The total value of Azerbaijan’s environmental start-up ecosystem has approached $600 million. Vusal Gasimli, head of the Centre for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communication, said the country had 161 start-ups in the sector and that the ecosystem’s value had grown by more than 7% over the past year. Azerbaijan ranks 81st worldwide by this measure.
● Azerbaijan marked the first anniversary of the country’s first-ever heart transplant, also the first in the South Caucasus. A conference in Baku heard that more than 1,500 people in the country are currently waiting for organ transplants, including over 50 who need a heart transplant. Around 1,800 people have registered as posthumous organ donors. Specialists say that despite growing interest in donation, demand for transplants still exceeds available capacity.
● Baku will host the World Fire and Rescue Sport Championships for men and women from 2 to 8 November. More than 400 athletes from over 20 countries are expected to take part. Competitors will compete in four events: climbing a training tower using an assault ladder, a 100-metre obstacle course, a 4×100-metre fire relay and a combat deployment event.
● The sixth Victory Run charity race was held in Baku to mark the anniversary of Azerbaijan’s victory in the Second Karabakh War. More than 2,000 people took part in the 10-kilometre race, the highest turnout since the event was first held in 2021. Bakhtiyar Asgarli and Anna Yusupova won the race. All registration fees will go to the YASHAT Foundation, which supports families of military personnel killed or wounded in wars.
● Azerbaijan topped the overall team standings in the individual events at the European Judo Championships for athletes under 23 in Naples. Aydar Baghirov won gold in the under-100kg category, while Kenan Nasibov took gold in the over-100kg category. Nasibov became European U-23 champion for the second consecutive year.
● Around 70 animals of various species have been released into the Jabrayil, Lachin and Kalbajar districts as part of efforts to restore biodiversity. They include 40 gazelles, five falcons, four East Caucasian tur, ten partridges and three bezoar goats, the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources said. Authorities have also announced the restoration of nature reserves and the creation of a Karabakh National Park covering more than 88,000 hectares.
● Statistics: More than 8.4 tonnes of drugs and psychotropic substances, with an estimated value of 246.3 million manats (around $145 million), were seized from illegal circulation in Azerbaijan between January and September. A total of 4,352 people, including 117 women and 50 foreign nationals, were held criminally liable for drug-related offences.
PHOTO: Two projects by Azerbaijani artists Orkhan and Elvin Nabizade were presented at Baku’s Stone Chronicle Museum. The first, “Ancient Stone, Modern Memory”, draws on the Gobustan rock carvings and depicts Azerbaijan’s wildlife, including the Caucasian leopard, gazelle, grey wolf and brown bear. The second, “Radius of Responsibility”, explores the relationship between humans and wildlife through an interactive format. The presentation was attended by Leyla Aliyeva, vice-president of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Arzu Aliyeva, head of the Baku Media Centre and daughters of the president.
