title: Nana Simopoulos Continues to Redefine The Musical Language
body: After four decades of musical exploration, Nana Simopoulos continues to redefine the boundaries of artistic expression, weaving together cultures, traditions and sounds into a deeply personal musical language. An acclaimed composer, guitarist and visionary artist, she has collaborated with legendary musicians, explored diverse musical landscapes and embraced the expressive possibilities of orchestral composition and immersive art. Rooted in her Greek heritage yet inspired by the musical traditions of the world, her work reflects a lifelong search for connection, emotion and truth. Today, her artistic journey is guided not by technical virtuosity or recognition, but by the beauty of silence, the power of melody and music’s extraordinary ability to unite people across generations and cultures. After four decades of composing and performing, how has your relationship with music changed? What do you hear, feel, or look for in music today that perhaps you didn’t when you began your career? When I first started, I thought technique, speed, timing and proving what I could do were the most important things in music. I was focused on getting every note in its exact right place. Today, four decades later, what is important to me has completely changed. What I look for now is the silence between the notes, the breathing space and pure honesty. Technical difficulty doesn’t matter to me anymore; what matters is how much truth and emotion a piece carries. Today, I hear music with my whole body, not just my ears. I look for the kind of sound that makes you stop thinking and simply feel. Your music has always brought together different cultures, instruments, rhythms and traditions while maintaining a strong sense of melody. What continues to draw you toward musical dialogue across cultures and how has your understanding of that dialogue evolved over the years? When I was younger, bringing together different instruments—like the sitar, the mandolin, or jazz guitar—felt like an adventure. I wanted to see how they sounded together. Over the years, I came to realize that this dialogue between cultures isn’t just an experiment; it’s the most effective way we have to understand one another. Melody is our common language. No matter what culture I encounter, when a strong melody is present, everyone feels the same underlying emotions: joy, sadness, nostalgia. Today, I’m not trying to simply ‘blend’ genres. I let each tradition keep its own distinct color and beauty, and I just invite them to sit at the same table and talk like old friends. You are now focusing strongly on orchestral music and your new album of original orchestral works. What is it about the orchestra that speaks to you at this stage of your life and career and what do you want this new body of work to express? The orchestra is the largest canvas available to me as a composer. At this stage in my life, I feel I’ve accumulated so many experiences and memories that I needed a big, rich sound to hold them all. In an orchestra, dozens of musicians breathe together, play together, and form a single, powerful wave of sound. What I want this new body of work to express above all is unity. I want to show that even though we live in a world filled with noise, isolation, and screens, the human spirit can still come together to create something beautiful, alive, and deeply moving. Your collaboration with the Nostos Youth Orchestra brings your music into conversation with a younger generation of musicians. What have these young performers taught you and what do you hope they take away from working with your music? These young musicians from the Nostos Orchestra—from the Music School of Alimos—have given me so much energy! They remind me why I fell in love with music when I was their age. They’ve taught me to look at music once again with fresh eyes and pure excitement, free from the fatigue that sometimes comes with a long career. What I hope they take away from working with me is a sense of freedom. I want them to know that music doesn’t have rigid boundaries, and there’s nothing to be afraid of. You don’t have to put yourself in a box. You can play classical music while carrying rock energy, zeibekiko rhythms, or Eastern textures inside you. I want them to feel that music is an open door, and most importantly, I want to help them discover a deeper, more visceral way of listening—listening not just with their ears to hit the right notes, but with their whole body and heart. You have recently expanded your work into immersive visual environments, including Perennial Land at the Morris Museum. How does composing for an installation or digital landscape change the way you think about melody, silence, space and emotion compared with writing for the concert stage? When you write for the concert stage, the audience sits in rows and looks straight ahead. But when you write for an installation like Perennial Land , people walk through the space. The sound isn’t just in front of you—it surrounds you. That completely shifted my approach. It taught me to give music much more space. Silence became even more crucial. The melody doesn’t need to push forward constantly; it can float in the air, allowing visitors to feel as though they are physically living inside the emotion. It’s like building a home out of sound that someone can walk into, experience, and find stillness in. You have collaborated with extraordinary artists from very different musical worlds, from Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins to Ustad Sultan Khan and Dave Liebman. Looking back, which collaborations changed you most deeply as an artist and what did you learn from those encounters that remains with you today? Every one of these extraordinary artists reshaped a part of who I am. From Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins, I learned what true rhythm and ‘deep sound’ mean in jazz—they taught me to listen with my heart. From Ustad Sultan Khan in India, I learned about the spiritual side of music and how a single note can bring tears to your eyes. What I learned from all of them—and what stays with me every day—is humility. The greater the artist, the more humble they are before the music. They didn’t play for their egos; they played to serve the sound. That is what I try to do every single day. Your career has involved enormous creative commitments—composing, performing, conducting large multicultural ensembles, teaching and working across film, theatre, dance and visual art. What role has your family played in making that life possible and how have the people closest to you influenced your creative journey? My family means everything to me. Without them, none of this would have been possible. A life in music involves constant travel, long hours of isolation, and a lot of uncertainty. Having people by your side who truly understand you, love you, and support you is the greatest gift. My loved ones are my anchor. They keep me grounded when life gets overwhelming. And the memories of my family—like my grandfather playing the mandolin, or my parents and their deep roots in Greece—are the very foundation of my music. Every note I write carries a piece of the love I received from them. You began your career in a very different musical and cultural landscape. If you could speak to the young composer and musician you were at the beginning of your journey, what would you tell her now—and what do you think she would find surprising about the artist you have become? If I could talk to that young girl just starting, I would tell her: ‘Don’t be afraid. Trust your heart, be yourself and don’t try to be anyone else. Your journey is going to be beautiful—just keep working with love.’ I think she would be completely surprised to see where I am today! She’d probably be amazed that her guitar found its way to the Indian sitar, but most of all, she would be thrilled to see herself conducting a symphony orchestra in Greece, performing her own compositions. She would be proud that she never lost her passion. At this point in your life, what are you still curious about? Are there musical territories, collaborators, instruments, forms, or artistic disciplines that you feel you have yet to explore? I am still curious about everything! Curiosity is what keeps us young. And I learn new things every day. I want to keep exploring large orchestral works, but I also want to experiment with artists from entirely different fields—perhaps collaborating more with architecture, theater, or new artistic mediums that connect sound with nature. There are still so many instruments and rhythms in the world that I haven’t touched yet! I feel like my journey is truly just beginning, and I can’t wait to see what’s around the corner. When you look toward the years ahead, what is the music you most want to make? Beyond projects and performances, what do you hope your work will leave with listeners—and what does “success” as an artist mean to you now? When I look toward the years ahead, I want to make music that brings together the worlds that have shaped me—jazz, improvisation, African, Indian and Byzantine, contemporary and classical and the sounds and traditions of Greek folk music. I was never interested in fitting into a particular category, but more interested in creating a musical language that feels genuinely my own. I want to continue to make music that has emotional depth, but also mystery—that gives the listener something to discover. I’m especially drawn to the idea of music that can create a sense of place, memory, movement, and connection between different cultures and traditions. At this point in my life, success is less about recognition or the number of performances. Of course, I would love for the music to reach large audiences and to be performed by great orchestras. But ultimately, success would be knowing that I made the music I needed to make, without compromising who I am—and that somewhere, it moved someone, made them curious, or stayed with them after the music ended. I think that is what I hope to leave behind: not simply recordings or scores, but a body of work that reflects a life lived across different worlds and continues to speak to people after I’m no longer there to explain it. title: IMF mission wraps up Ghana PCI review this week as economic targets take centre stage
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission to Ghana is expected to conclude its first Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) review engagement this week, with economic targets and the country’s macroeconomic framework likely to dominate the final discussions. Sources say the closing engagements will review Ghana’s performance against quantitative targets for the year ending September, along with policies to sustain recent economic gains. The mission is expected to hold a final round of discussions with Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson and Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Asiama. The team, led by Dr Ruben Atoyan, may also meet members of Parliament, including the Finance Committee. The final discussions follow engagements with civil society organisations and visits to facilities, including the Tema Oil Refinery. The mission has also discussed the banking sector, energy, Ghana’s debt position and ongoing reforms at some state-owned banks. What the team has covered so far Ghana’s fiscal performance, revenue mobilisation and preparations for the 2027 Budget have featured prominently in the discussions, sources say. The team has examined economic performance during the first nine months of the year and the policies needed to sustain recent gains. Further engagements are expected to cover expenditure management for the rest of the year and spending plans for 2027. These discussions come as the government prepares to prioritise infrastructure investment in the upcoming budget. On monetary policy, the mission has discussed Ghana’s inflation-targeting framework and foreign exchange arrangements. Sources say the team has also assessed the Bank of Ghana’s financial position, international reserves and measures to safeguard its independence. The review forms part of Ghana’s engagement with the IMF under the PCI, a framework designed to support economic stability and sustain policy reforms without providing direct funding. PCI programme and what it means for Ghana The PCI allows countries to maintain close policy engagement with the IMF without borrowing under the instrument. It supports the design and implementation of economic reforms. It also helps demonstrate policy credibility to investors and development partners. Its objectives include strengthening macroeconomic stability, addressing economic imbalances and building resilience against shocks. Although the instrument provides no direct financing, participating countries must pursue policies that meet standards comparable to those under IMF lending arrangements. The IMF assesses performance through scheduled reviews, typically every six months. The PCI requires approval from the IMF Executive Board. This distinguishes it from a Staff-Monitored Programme, an informal arrangement between IMF staff and a member country. For Ghana, the review provides an opportunity to demonstrate progress on policy commitments and reinforce confidence in its economic programme.

title: Fresh woes for pupils in Niger
body: At least 12 pupils of Madarasatul Nurul Islam, Maikujeri community in Rafi Local Government Area of Niger State have been reportedly kidnapped by bandits. Daily Trust gathered that the children were abducted around 10am on Saturday while harvesting maize on their teacher’s farm on the outskirts of the town. A resident, Mohammed Adamu, told Daily Trust that the children were already on their way home when the bandits struck and picked them. An Okada man identified as Tasi’u, who attempted to escape, was reportedly shot and is currently receiving treatment at the IBB Specialist Hospital in Minna, the state capital. How bureaucracy leaves power equipment rotting in ports Sokoto: Concerns over attack on ADC guber candidate’s convoy Another source close to the Quranic school told one of our correspondents that 13 people, including 12 female pupils of the school and the younger brother of the school’s proprietor, Mallam Mainasara, were kidnapped. He said the victims, aged between nine and 14, were abducted as they stopped by a borehole to wash themselves and drink water after leaving the farm. According to him, the pupils had been working on the farm with their teacher when the teacher received information that bandits were advancing towards the area. He said the teacher immediately instructed the pupils to return home while he also left on his motorcycle. “While on their way home, the pupils reportedly stopped at a borehole to wash their bodies and drink water. It was at that point that the armed men swooped on them and whisked them away,” he said. The source further disclosed that some women were also abducted from another farm in the area. When contacted, the spokesperson for the Niger Police Command, SP Wasiu Abiodun, promised to verify the information and revert. The police spokesperson, however, revealed that six people were rescued but was silent on the abduction of the pupils. He said, “On 29th October, 2026, at about 12.30pm, joint security tactical teams during a clearance and rescue operation around Pandogari Rafi LGA rescued six abducted victims who were reportedly kidnapped by some hoodlums on 28th October, 2026 at about 12 pm in their farms at Mahangi village via Pandogari. “The victims were abducted and taken to Hanawanka forest where they were rescued unhurt. They were later received at Kagara Div for debriefing and medical attention ahead of reunion with their relatives.” Map of Niger State with red cycle indicating the LGA where the incident took place Dozens of farmers displaced Similarly, dozens of farming communities in Borgu, Mariga, Mashegu and Rijau LGAs have continued to flee their homes following the renewed bandits’ attacks. The affected farmers told Daily Trust that their farm produce, including rice, soyabeans and maize, is wasting on their farms because bandits have stopped them from harvesting. Ibrahim Ayuba, a resident of one of the affected communities in Mariga LGA told Daily Trust that their farm produce including rice, white beans, soyabeans have been left to waste due to attacks and kidnapping of farmers from their homes and on their farms. He said, “Currently, for about 14 to 19 days now, bandits have occupied some villages in Mariga, including Ragada, Maburya, Mazame, Kuimo and Kura, as well as villages in Rijau Local Government Area, which include Inana, Idaci, among others. “This situation has forced people to flee their homes for days. The attacks have resulted in the loss of three lives and injured many others, alongside allegations of sexual assault against women. “The people from the affected areas are currently in the towns of Warari, Gulbin Boka, and Rijau. Just tonight, we received reports of an attempted new attack in Kuimo, which has forced the residents of that area to flee again in the middle of the night. As for the farms, they are truly in a critical state; if the soybeans and rice do not receive immediate attention and care, they will go to waste.” Recent abductions in Niger It has been 72 days since over 500 Worshippers were kidnapped from Juma’at mosques in Dekara and four other communities. Families said the abductors have yet to communicate with them since the incident. Terrorists had invaded four Juma’at mosques in Dekara, Gbezhin, Sabon-Gida and Kpenya simultaneously on August 21, 2026 and took away Worshippers. On 15 June bandits attacked farmlands in Pandogari District of Rafi LGA and killed one Dauda Galadima, a resident of the nearby Ruba village. They also abducted five farmers on their fields, including Nasiru Yakubu and his son, Bilyaminu. On July 24, gunmen raided Tashar Hajiya community in Niger State at about 2:30 a.m., killing one 25-year-old Mustafa Murtala and abducting three residents, one Alhaji Baza Baza, his wife and one of their daughters. On September 27, 47 farmers were abducted while harvesting groundnuts on their farms in Tugan-Rimi, Mariga LGA of the state. Daily Trust also recalls that on November 21, 2025, 230 pupils and students as well as staff members were kidnapped at St. Mary’s Primary and Secondary School in Papiri, Agwara LGA. The victims were later rescued through an operation coordinated by the Office of the National Security Adviser after several weeks in captivity. Also in November 2025, terrorists kidnapped an unspecified number of travellers along the Wawa–Luma Road in Borgu LGA, Niger State. According to a source, two passenger vehicles heading to Gupanti and Lumma communities were intercepted, and all occupants were abducted. However, farmers in Mariga, Borgu , Mashegu, Rijau told Daily Trust that attacks and kidnappings have become a daily occurrence. Forest security key to ending abductions – Experts A Senior Security Consultant, Auwal Bala Durumin Iya, has called on the federal government to strengthen security in Nigeria’s forests to address the persistent abduction of students, including Almajiri pupils and conventional schoolchildren. Durumin Iya, who is also a Quality and Internal Quality Assurance Manager of Homeland Security in Nigeria, said securing forests was critical to protecting rural communities and urban centres from kidnappers. He made the call while reacting to the reported abduction of some Almajiri pupils in Niger State while they were returning from their teacher’s farm. He said kidnappers deliberately targeted schoolchildren because their abduction attracted widespread public attention, putting pressure on governments and security agencies. According to him, the publicity generated by such incidents also creates fear among residents and could force communities to submit to the demands and directives of criminal groups. “When they kidnap students or Almajiri pupils, the attention of the public goes directly to that kidnapping, and they want wider publicity. When they get wider publicity, it means the students or community will put pressure on security personnel and the government. It also creates more fear in the community so that people may obey their orders, thereby distracting the government and security personnel,” he said. The security expert identified the establishment of a specialised forest security system, which he described as a forest marshal arrangement, as one of the measures needed to tackle the menace. He explained that the proposed forest marshals should be educated and properly trained personnel with the capacity to secure both thick and thin forests across the country. “When our forests become secure, our villages will also become secure. And when our villages are secure, the urban areas will be more secure,” he said. Recent bandits attack in Niger State Durumin Iya noted that many kidnapping incidents, particularly random and conventional abductions, occurred around forest areas, making the protection of such locations essential to preventing attacks on surrounding communities. He also proposed the establishment of an independent Centre for Intelligent Research to conduct professional security research and provide governments with early warnings and policy recommendations. He said the centre would bring together security professionals and researchers to study emerging threats and anticipate security developments within specific areas, including possible incidents in the following six months. According to him, findings from such research would be documented and communicated to relevant authorities to enable them to develop effective strategies for tackling security challenges in forests, rural communities and urban centres. The security consultant further advocated the adoption of a Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) programme to identify and develop the skills of Nigerians who possess practical knowledge and competencies but lack formal education. He said recognising such skills would enable government and relevant institutions to support individuals in developing their abilities, producing goods and services and creating employment opportunities. “Many people in Nigeria did not go to school, but they have competence, skills and knowledge. When you recognise their knowledge, they can produce and train many young people coming up. “The government does not have to provide employment for everybody. When their skills are recognised, the government can connect them with other government opportunities, non-governmental organisations, companies and individuals who have the resources to purchase their products. “That way, they can employ more people than the government,” he said. He urged the government to consider the three proposals as part of broader efforts to address insecurity, strengthen community protection and reduce unemployment, which he said could help tackle some of the conditions that expose communities to criminal activities. Weighing into the matter, a security and counter-terrorism expert, Chidi Omeje, in an interview with one of our correspondents, explained that intelligence gathering must be strengthened. Omeje also listed security of Nigeria’s forests and porous borders as part of broader ways to resolve issues of kidnapping, adding that the military alone could not solve the menace. The expert said, “To stem the tide of kidnapping in Nigeria, we must stop treating kidnapping merely as a military problem and confront it as a governance, intelligence and law-enforcement failure. “Strengthen intelligence gathering at the grassroots, dismantle kidnapping networks and their financiers, secure our forests and porous borders, improve inter-agency collaboration, and ensure the swift prosecution of perpetrators. “The police must lead internal security operations, with the military providing support where necessary. Above all, tackle the poverty, unemployment and criminal economies that sustain recruitment into these gangs. “Kidnapping will not end through force alone; it requires actionable intelligence, political will, effective law enforcement and good governance.” What is driving Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis – Ex-NIA DG Meanwhile, a former Director-General of the National Intelligence Agency (NIA), Ambassador Ahmed Rufai, has said Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis is being sustained by a complex network of terrorist groups, criminal bandit militias, informants and financial facilitators, Rufai said the motives behind abductions had evolved from fundraising and recruitment to political propaganda and prisoner exchanges, making the country’s security challenge more complicated. He spoke at the Global Security Forum in Doha – Qatar, an annual international gathering of senior government officials, security experts, academics and journalists. Explaining Nigeria’s kidnapping situation, the former intelligence chief identified three broad categories of perpetrators: terrorist groups, bandit militias and other criminal gangs. He said Boko Haram, which operates in parts of the country, was affiliated with terrorist organisations in the Sahel and beyond, adding that its early abductions were aimed at raising funds and recruiting young men and women into its ranks. According to him, bandit militias, on the other hand, engage in criminal kidnapping, often targeting individuals and communities to collect ransom. “It’s a kind of economy hostage-taking,” he said. Rufai said the motives of the different groups had increasingly overlapped, with terrorist organisations sometimes working alongside criminal militias to carry out mass abductions. He said such operations were intended not only to raise money but also to serve as propaganda and demonstrate the groups’ continued activities, particularly when security forces intensified their operations against them. The former NIA chief cited the Abuja-Kaduna train attack, in which about 100 passengers were abducted, as an example of collaboration between terrorist and criminal groups. He estimated that between $1 million and $2 million was collected as ransom, saying the money was channelled to Ansaru in the Sahel region. Rufai said the pattern of kidnapping had also expanded to the abduction of schoolchildren and worshippers, both Muslims and Christians, with some incidents now aimed at securing the release of detained members of the groups. He, however, noted that negotiations for prisoner exchanges could become difficult when the individuals whose release was being demanded had already been killed during security operations. Beyond the perpetrators, Rufai identified a network of informants, financial facilitators and other criminal collaborators as key elements sustaining kidnapping operations. He said informants provide information about potential targets, while financial systems, including cryptocurrencies and small financial outfits, are used to launder ransom proceeds. “They use a lot of informants that tell them about their targets, their potential targets,” he said. On possible responses, Rufai said approaches to hostage-taking should depend on the motives and identities of the perpetrators. He advocated discreet, back-channel negotiations in cases where terrorist groups abduct victims primarily for money, involving trusted intermediaries and contact persons.

title: EDITORIAL: 2027: Voting candidates of popular choice, not by threats
body:
Campaigns for the 2027 general elections have begun, sparking candidates’ waves of peripatetic movement across the country to seek votes. It also offers political parties the opportunity for strategic engagements toward consolidation of their support bases, and how to flip their opponents’ strongholds.
However, some pseudo-democrats have introduced harassment and intimidation into this electoral process, demanding that citizens vote only for their parties or else all hell will be let loose. This is ominous, and it should be contained by law enforcement agencies.
In Ebonyi State, Governor Francis Nwifuru threatened to remove from office any local government chairperson who failed to ensure victory for the All Progressives Congress (APC). Pupils of a primary school in the state were made to sing President Bola Tinubu’s political anthem, “Tinubu, On Your Mandate We Shall Stand,” by a federal lawmaker for the exercise books and pencils given to them. This is totally wrong.
The governor, while swearing in the 13 local government area chairpersons in September, said, “As a local government chairman, if you like, go and sleep so that another person will take over your house. You will not stop us (APC) from winning. But when we win, we will remove you.”
Mr Nwifuru’s stance smacks of impunity and intolerance. His action stands condemned. Under the 1999 Constitution as amended, the governor does not have the power to remove any local government chairperson, or engineer the illegality through councillors.
By his conduct, he has demonstrated the councils’ lack of autonomy or independence in his state. This should worry all Nigerians who crave the effective operation of the 774 local governments, enshrined in the constitution, as the third tier of government in Nigeria.
These councils were created for governance to permeate the grassroots, which insulates them from governors’ control. In July 2024, a Supreme Court judgment, which ruled that their federal allocations be paid directly to their accounts, was further amplification of this point.
Unfortunately, the governor is not alone in this despicable act. A commissioner in Borno State, Sainna Buba, in charge of Youths and Sports Development, in August, threatened to flog whoever would not vote for the APC candidates in 2027. He said, “This government is our government; follow us and enjoy honey. As for those who refuse to follow us, they will be flogged.” Interestingly, the commissioner spewed these obnoxious fumes when a Tinubu campaign support group, City Boys Movement, was inaugurated in the state.
The malady is spreading fast, giving a foretaste of what is ahead as electioneering gathers steam, and even the elections in January and February next year. The Chairman of Kuje Area Council in Abuja, Samuel Shekwolo, has told residents that anyone not prepared to support the APC in 2027 should leave the area.
Inflammatory rhetoric like this should be seen as alien to democracy. Kuje Council, for goodness sake, is not the property of any political party. Undoubtedly, these vibes of political intolerance thrive where multi-party democracy is enfeebled or does not matter.
It is no wonder, therefore, that Peter Obi, the presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), was blocked from moving around in Benue State by hired thugs recently, when he was in the state to visit communities affected by violent attacks and mass murders.
That show of shame seems to have official imprimatur. It is inexplicable why thugs in large numbers, with cudgels and other dangerous weapons, stood in front of the police, chanting that Mr Obi was a persona non grata, and could not be arrested. Mr Obi departed the state without accomplishing his mission.
The state chapter of the NDC had written to the state Commissioner of Police, Cletus Nwadiogbu, notifying him of the visit; and he, in turn, notified the state governor, Hyacinth Alia, who had warned Mr Obi last year not to visit his state without his permission, when Mr Obi faced a similar situation.
It took angry public condemnation for the State Police Command to arrest, a day later, 46 suspects who purportedly participated in the mass thuggery. We doubt the identities of these suspects. The police boss needs to explain why his officials could not apprehend even one of the thugs in real time, as they blocked Mr Obi’s convoy. His clarification that the police avoided using force to disperse the thugs when they were within reach is specious. The subsequent arrests, in our view, seem like damage control.
Let us be clear: the right to free movement of persons is a fundamental right, guaranteed under the 1999 Constitution, in Section 41. It is restricted only in specific lawful cases of criminality and investigations. None of them applied in the Peter Obi case. Electioneering has officially been flagged off, which further makes the police, or the state authorities’ explanations, hard to put.
PREMIUM TIMES had hitherto expressed concerns about these anti-democratic tendencies, and the need for the police to decisively deal with their purveyors to avoid possible subversion of the 2027 general elections.
Beyond the police interrogation of the senator who asked APC members to kill Accord Party members in the last Osun State governorship election, and his fellow traveller who insisted that voters must vote for only the APC candidate, their prosecution remains a far cry.
These outlaws, wherever they may be found, can only be stopped in their strides by enforcement of the law to serve as deterrence. Therefore, the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, should put an end to these growing anomalies in the democratic space.
Candidates get votes in an election, not by coercion, harassment and intimidation of citizens, but by persuasion and presentation of convincing manifestos that address the existential crises of the people. Any shortcut is dubious and an abuse of the electoral process.

title: Pakistan International Airlines receives first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner
body: Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) has received its first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, with the aircraft arriving at Islamabad International Airport (ISB) from London Heathrow (LHR) on November 1, 2026. The aircraft operated the flight under PIA flight number PK786. The arrival marks the first time a Boeing 787 Dreamliner has been introduced by a Pakistani airline. The aircraft, however, is not a new purchase. It has been leased from Norwegian carrier Norse Atlantic Airways under an agreement covering two Boeing 787-9s. The deal was signed in October and is based on an Aircraft, Crew, Maintenance and Insurance (ACMI) arrangement, commonly known as a wet lease. Norse Atlantic provides the aircraft and crew and remains responsible for maintenance and insurance, while PIA uses the aircraft for its own passenger services. According to Pakistani media reports , the aircraft is approximately eight years old and completed its first commercial flight in May 2018. It has a reported seating capacity of 358 passengers and is equipped with an in-flight entertainment system. More capacity for UK routes The main reason behind the agreement is PIA’s plan to increase its capacity between Pakistan and the United Kingdom. The airline returned to the London market on March 29, 2026, after a six-year absence. Its comeback followed the lifting of restrictions that had prevented Pakistani airlines from operating flights to the UK. Since then, PIA has been working to increase its presence in the market. The airline has planned additional services connecting Islamabad and Lahore with London Heathrow and Manchester, with the leased Boeing 787-9s intended to operate several of these routes. RELATED PIA to install lie-flat seats in Boeing 777 cabin overhaul According to published schedule information, the first aircraft is scheduled to replace Boeing 777 equipment on selected London services, with Manchester operations also planned. The second Dreamliner is expected to provide further capacity once it joins the operation. The post Pakistan International Airlines receives first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Alterra's investments designed to hedge against AI bubble, says chief executive
body: Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate vehicle , has designed its artificial intelligence investment strategy to protect it against a much talked about bubble in the sector, its chief executive has told The National . The fund's focus on investing in energy systems powered by AI and not directly into the technology is serving as a “hedge” against any potential bubble that may burst in the booming industry, Majid Al Suwaidi said. “We're investing in the only place that our portfolio touches the AI story – through the energy systems. What is great with our investment thesis is that we don't invest directly in AI infrastructure,” he said in an interview. “Those energy systems, regardless of whether it's powering AI or powering a factory, homes, schools, or hospitals, that power will still be needed. So, in a way, Alterra and the investments we make are a really good hedge against a bubble in AI.” Mr Al Suwaidi's comments come as Abu Dhabi-based Alterra gives a vote of confidence to the technology by investing in one of Europe's biggest sovereign AI companies. On Monday, Alterra announced that it had partnered with Milan-based Domyn to develop a proprietary climate intelligence system that the former will own and control, which will pave the way towards becoming an AI-native company, Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Once we've built that core system, we can then extend that to other aspects of the business and truly become an AI-native organisation,” he said. The system, which will be developed in phases, will “come into the fore” next year, he added. “To pick up these technologies and apply them very early in our development means that we will be able to use AI or our analytics to … take advantage of the power of this technology.” Alterra did not disclose the value of its investment in Domyn, which was formerly known as iGenius and founded by former Apple employee Uljan Sharka. Domyn has raised $1.1 billion in debt financing over the past two years and is valued at about $2 billion. In June, the European Commission chose Europa, a project led by Domyn, to develop an open-source AI model covering all 24 official languages in the EU. “The way we're designing the system is that it can be evergreen in the sense that as new models are being built or as new developments happen within the technology that they can be plugged in immediately and we can upgrade our system,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. The partnership with Domyn mirrors his confidence in the AI sector, where the bubble debate is hot. Recently, two of the biggest names in asset management, Citadel chief executive Ken Griffin and Blackstone president Jon Gray, gave negative and positive views, respectively. Mr Al Suwaidi acknowledged that there is a bubble “in some ways”, but managing expectations and doing due diligence to make sound investment decisions will help contain potential ill-effects. “Any time you have a new asset class, a bubble is developed … and bubbles can be good if managed and bad if they burst … it just remains to be seen how long it will continue to grow and whether we can manage it in a prudent way so that it doesn't burst with negative consequences,” he said. “We know for sure that this technology is going to be critical to our future economic development, and how we use it becomes increasingly important, and we're discovering that, so there's going to be winners and losers in that process.” Alterra's mandate is to raise $250 billion globally by 2030 to create a fairer climate finance system. Its chairman is Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. It is less than three years since Alterra's launch at the Cop28 climate conference hosted by the UAE. Since then, Alterra has grown into three funds – Acceleration, Transformation and Opportunity – with five global investment partners: Brookfield Asset Management, BlackRock, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, KKR and TPG. It also has more than 60 direct and indirect portfolio companies across more than 40 countries, supporting more than 100GW of renewable energy capacity. Alterra's capital activity is also accelerating. More than $51 billion in expected equity capital across its fund and co-investment activities has been mobilised, with preliminary mobilisation ratios of more than 10 times for its Acceleration Fund and over four times for the Transformation Fund, excluding Alterra's own capital and deal-level debt. Recent investments also show the breadth of Alterra's expansion, including Inkia in Peru, Wireless Logic alongside General Atlantic, and Jeppesen ForeFlight with Thoma Bravo. “What Alterra has shown through our success in the climate realm is that you can achieve the same goals, but in an economically prudent way,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Something that is very unique, and very underreported is how successful we've been in our model.”

title: The next phase of UAE-China energy co-operation will be built on shared expertise
body: As energy systems become more digital, more complex and more interconnected, the value of a partnership is no longer measured solely by the capital invested or the resources produced. Increasingly, it is measured by the ability to solve technical challenges together, deploy innovation at scale and build the expertise needed for long-term energy security. The UAE and China have built one of the most significant energy relationships in the global economy. As China remains a major energy consumer and the UAE continues to invest across both conventional and emerging energy systems, the partnership is increasingly expanding beyond trade and investment towards technology, expertise and operational collaboration. The evolution of the partnership between the China National Petroleum Company and Adnoc illustrates this shift. Over time, co-operation has expanded beyond investment and production towards shared technical capability, applying new approaches to reservoirs, drilling, digitalisation and lower-carbon operations and translating them into measurable results in the field. This year, CNPC joined Adnoc and other international partners in the Bab Gas Cap concession, which is expected to produce 1.5 billion cubic feet of gas per day. CNPC is also a partner in the development of the Umm Shaif Gas Cap, expected to unlock more than 600 million cubic feet a day by 2030. At Umm Shaif , the technical challenge is as important as the scale. The gas sits above an oil reservoir that has been producing for decades. Developing one resource while protecting reservoir pressure and oil recovery requires refined management, exactly the kind of challenge that requires close collaboration between partners over many years. In 2017, CNPC became asset leader for the North East Bab oilfield group and established a technical centre to deepen technical collaboration with Adnoc. Since then, the partnership has applied advanced technologies to address complex reservoir challenges, helping to double annual production across the field group while improving operational efficiency and reducing unit technical cost. Similar results have been achieved beyond NEB, with enhanced reservoir evaluation and development optimisation at Al Yasat onshore-offshore project helping unlock additional resource potential and exceed second-phase production targets. This demonstrates how long-term technical collaboration can create value by embedding expertise into the day-to-day development and operation of energy assets. That principle is increasingly important as the industry brings new technologies into conventional operations. CNPC has supported Adnoc in addressing technical challenges around CO2 storage wells, while also exploring cleaner energy, electrification, automation, intelligent completions and advanced well designs. The goal should not be technology for technology’s sake. It is to use the right technology where it can improve recovery, reduce operational complexity, strengthen asset integrity or bring down the cost per barrel. Practical innovation is already producing measurable results. Closer-spaced water injection has increased output by more than 20 per cent in major fields, while advanced completion techniques and new gas-management solutions have improved performance without adding operational complexity and cost. The CNPC Monobore Expandable Casing Technology was successfully applied in Al Yasat and broke a world record in casing diameter and operation length. This solution will save time and reduce drilling cost in similar scenarios across all Adnoc fields. These are very different technologies solving very different problems. What connects them is a focus on practical operating results. That shift from experimentation to deployment is increasingly visible across Abu Dhabi’s energy sector, and artificial intelligence is becoming a powerful example of this shift. Adnoc is now using an AI-enabled platform across more than 120 drilling rigs, helping engineers monitor operations, identify potential issues earlier and manage larger volumes of information more efficiently. Robotics are also moving into day-to-day industrial applications, including the inspection of infrastructure and hazardous environments. For energy companies, this changes the question. It is now about how quickly a proven application can move from a technical discussion stage to field trial and verification to industrial-scale deployment across complex operating assets. Experience matters in making that transition. More than 150 technologies have now been registered for application within the onshore project, covering areas including reservoir development and optimisation, enhanced oil recovery, intelligent well completions and reservoir treatment. Hundreds of technical workshops and discussions also take place each year across development, drilling, completion and digitalisation, helping turn technical exchange into a more continuous way of working. As the industry works to produce resources more efficiently, integrate digital technologies and manage emissions, deeper technical capability will need to develop alongside long-term investment But the numbers themselves are less important than the capability built around them: engineers and operators who can understand a problem, pilot a solution, adapt it to local conditions and decide whether it can deliver value at scale. At a time when global energy demand continues to rise and energy systems face growing pressure to deliver affordability and reliability and lower greenhouse gas emissions simultaneously, operational efficiency is becoming a strategic priority. Technical capability is increasingly an element of energy security itself. The next phase of China-UAE energy co-operation should build on that model. As the industry works to produce resources more efficiently, integrate AI and digital technologies and manage emissions, deeper technical capability will need to develop alongside long-term investment. These questions are increasingly shaping industry discussions globally and will feature prominently at Adipec , where the focus is shifting from what technologies such as AI, robotics and advanced analytics might achieve in future to how they are already delivering measurable value today. Adipec’s expanded technology programme reflects that shift, with applications ranging from reservoir modelling and autonomous operations to infrastructure inspection and robotics. For me, that is where the most useful conversation lies. Technology transfer is rarely a one-off transaction. It develops through working together repeatedly, sharing best practices on operation and building enough trust to verify new approaches in demanding environments. For CNPC and Adnoc, years of co-operation have created that foundation. The opportunity now is to turn technical collaboration into an even greater source of shared capability and value. As energy systems become more complex and interconnected, the strongest partnerships will increasingly be defined not only by the resources they develop, but by the knowledge , expertise and innovation they build together.

title: US economy under Donald Trump in five charts
body: A nervous US electorate is heading to polling stations across the country for Tuesday's midterm elections , and their personal finances could determine which way control in Congress swings. Recent polling suggests President Donald Trump 's shifting tariff policies, war with Iran and overall handling of the economy will be major issues this week for voters, who say they have been affected by higher prices at the petrol pumps and on grocery shelves. Half of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important this year”, with health care costs and the war in Iran also top among 11 issues rated in an October 29 Gallup poll. Roughly four in 10 voters rate income and wealth distribution (44 per cent) and petrol costs (42 per cent) as extremely important. Forty-seven per cent of registered voters said the cost of living would be the single most important factor in their votes this week, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in August. Only 17 per cent approve of Mr Trump's handling of the cost of living, while an AP-Norc poll found 26 per cent approve of his handling of the economy overall. A Chicago Council poll also found 71 per cent of Americans think US tariffs on imports have been bad for the economy, and 81 per cent said they have been bad for their cost of living. Although not a particular macroeconomic data point, the Consumer Confidence Survey measures attitudes, buying intentions and holiday plans, inflation expectations, and where people believe stock prices and interest rates are heading. In this way, it can offer a key insight into perceptions on the economy. Fergus McCormick, senior economist at the Conference Board, said “consumers continued to express frustration with rising costs” in October, with most references pointing to the high cost of goods, groceries and petrol. Easing petrol prices saw some recovery in the Consumer Confidence Index, which rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, although confidence remains on a long-term and persistent downwards trend. Moreover, consumers are planning for less spending on services and goods over the next six months, reflecting enduring inflation. Despite this anxiety, consumer spending rose at a 3.4 per cent pace in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department data, showing the US economy has remained resilient amid the energy price shock caused by the Iran war. Strong business spending also accounted for US GDP to grow at a 3.4 per cent annual pace in the July to September period. US inflation has significantly eased since peaking at 9.1 per cent in 2022, and fell to 3 per cent when Mr Trump began his second term in office in January 2025. Headline inflation fell as low as 2.3 per cent in April that year. But inflation picked up again after he imposed a sweeping set of tariffs on nearly every trading partner. The disinflation process now appears stalled, and the Iran war has led to surging energy prices couple with AI-driven investment. Petrol prices accounted for nearly half of the all-items increase in September, when CPI inflation clocked in at 3.7 per cent. Even after stripping away food and energy, inflation still gained 0.3 per cent on a monthly basis and 2.6 per cent year on year. It has been nearly six years since CPI inflation registered at 2 per cent. Seventy-nine per cent of Americans agreed that prices at the pump were higher now compared to 38 per cent in February, a dramatic shift in perceptions since the Iran war began, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in September. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's energy supplies, has pushed up global energy costs. Even the US, the world's top crude producer, has not been fully insulated. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries have exacerbated rising costs for diesel , which powers the lorries that transport food and other goods. The average driver is currently paying $4.20 for a gallon of petrol today, an increase of $1.17 from the same time last year, according to automotive group AAA. Of the six “swing states” in this year's midterm election cycle, only Georgia's petrol prices are below the national average. Diesel prices have also soared to $6.32, compared to $3.68 a gallon a year ago. The Federal Reserve was in the middle of an easing cycle when Mr Trump returned to office last year. While the Fed's announcements on short-term interest rates grab headlines, they also influence the 10-year Treasury yield through market expectations and the inflation outlook. The 10-year Treasury is the global benchmark for interest rates, car loans, corporate borrowing and consumer mortgages. Energy-driven inflation, the massive AI buildout and heavy government debt issuance have weighed on the bond market in recent months, with yields on the 10- and 30-year Treasury at levels unseen in nearly a quarter century. At the same time, the Fed has begun a new tightening cycle and has raised expectations it will raise rates further before the year ends. This combination of factors has plagued the housing market, where fixed 30-year mortgage rates climbed as high as 7.4 per cent before pulling back slightly to 7.24 per cent, compared to last year at 6.17 per cent. That means a homebuyer refinancing or purchasing a home would face higher borrowing costs on their monthly payments. Mr Trump frequently uses the stock market as an economic barometer. After suffering brief dips during last year's tariff row and the early days of the Iran war, Wall Street's major indices have surged. The S&P 500 has climbed more than 10 per cent this year and hit a new record-high of 7,818.93 on October 6, though disappointing earnings reports are fuelling a new wave of investor concerns over the AI buildout and the massive investment powering it. AI investment has been cited as the major driver behind the surge. The Magnificent Seven stocks – Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Tesla – make up 34 per cent of the S&P 500. This leads to what economists classify as a K-shaped economy, in which high-earners who own assets such as stocks see their wealth climb while workers relying on pay cheques fall behind as living costs increase.

title: Petrol drops to GH¢16.38, diesel rises to GH¢18.45 as OMCs adjust pump prices
body: Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have begun adjusting pump prices for the first pricing window in November, with petrol prices falling and diesel prices rising. Star Oil took the lead over the weekend, reducing petrol from GH¢16.45 to GH¢16.38 per litre. It increased diesel from GH¢17.95 to GH¢18.45 per litre. Other major fuel retailers told JoyBusiness they will adjust prices later today or later this week. The changes follow projections by the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies (COMAC) for the November 1–15, 2026 pricing window. The chamber projected a reduction of up to 3.35% in petrol prices, a 1.50% increase in diesel prices, and a 0.81% rise in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices. Separate indicative figures from JoyBusiness put petrol at GH¢17.02 per litre and diesel at GH¢18.99. Actual pump prices will vary across marketing companies. COMAC attributed the mixed outlook to changes in international petroleum prices, a stronger cedi and government–industry intervention to cushion diesel consumers. Crude oil prices fell by 1.90% during the review period, but refined product prices moved in different directions. International petrol prices declined by 4.97%, while diesel prices rose by 3.54%. LPG prices rose the most, up 21.33%. The cedi, meanwhile, appreciated by 0.70% to GH¢11.7326 to the US dollar. This was based on average bank rates between October 12 and October 27, 2026. According to COMAC, foreign exchange interventions by the Ghana Gold Board over the past three weeks provided modest support for the currency. The chamber also cited a planned $1.5 billion injection to support the cedi ahead of the festive period. The stronger currency is expected to help moderate the impact of international price increases on consumers. For diesel, adjustments to the Energy Sector Shortfall and Debt Repayment Levy and selected statutory margins remain in place for one month to cushion the increase. “The total value of the intervention remains unchanged, maintaining the Government–industry burden-sharing arrangement introduced on 16 April 2026 to moderate increases in diesel prices at the pumps,” COMAC said.

title: How bureaucracy leaves power equipment rotting in ports
body: Recent revelations that more than 300 containers of critical electricity equipment imported by the Federal Government remained stranded at Nigerian ports for years have exposed the administrative bottlenecks and institutional inefficiencies undermining efforts to improve electricity supply across the country, experts have said. The equipment, some of which have reportedly been trapped in the ports for close to two decades, were procured under various government-funded and development-partner-supported electricity projects, including the National Integrated Power Project (NIPP), Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) donor-funded projects and the Presidential Power Initiative (PPI). Despite their importance to the country’s electricity infrastructure, the equipment have been unable to reach their intended destinations because of unresolved import documentation, disagreements over duty exemptions, mounting shipping demurrage, port charges and bureaucratic delays involving government agencies. President Bola Tinubu has consequently directed the immediate clearance of the stranded containers, a move that has generated mixed reactions among stakeholders in the power sector. Tinubu approved purchase of SUVs for FCT traditional rulers – Wike N4.6trn lost to building collapse in 4 years – Report While some experts have welcomed the directive as a demonstration of political will to address longstanding challenges in the electricity industry, others believe the development exposes years of institutional failures that cannot be resolved through presidential orders alone. What power minister said Minister of Power, Olasunkanmi Joseph Tegbe, who disclosed the presidential directive after the Federal Executive Council (FEC) meeting at the State House, expressed dismay that equipment meant to strengthen the country’s electricity infrastructure could remain abandoned at the ports for such an extended period. Tegbe said: “Those containers are not empty. It is appalling to see that we find ourselves in such situations. “They were imported by the Federal Government through the Ministry of Power/Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) under various power projects over the years.” However, industry experts said the circumstances surrounding the stranded equipment reveal structural weaknesses in government procurement, importation and project implementation processes. Nigeria has an installed electricity generation capacity of approximately 13,014.40 MW to 13,625 MW, while available or generated power fluctuates between 4,000 MW and 5,403 MW. This was largely attributed to ageing or inadequate infrastructure to support transmission and power distribution. It would be recalled that the Niger Delta Power Holding Company Limited (NDPHC) recently recovered abandoned power equipment worth billions of naira from various seaports across the country, following an intervention by the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA). The Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of NDPHC, Jennifer Adighije, said during a visit to the NPA in August that the released items were in 110 abandoned containers and 216 packages. Some experts called for a critical evaluation of the equipment in order to retrieve those that are still useful. A former Chief Technical Officer, Presidential Power Initiative (PPI) and MD/CEO, Idfon Power Engineering Consultants (iPEC) Limited, Engr. Idowu Oyebanjo, said the situation arose when the projects were awarded to contractors at low cost without demurrage. According to him, some of the contracts are structured on Cost, Insurance and Freight (CIF) Lagos terms, meaning the equipment are delivered to the Lagos port without sufficient arrangements to ensure their prompt clearance and transportation to the project sites. He explained that the difficulties begin even before the containers arrive in Nigeria, as critical import documentation and duty exemption approvals are often not completed before shipment. Oyebanjo stated that upon the arrival of the containers and notification sent to the shipping agents, the agents approach TCN to obtain an Import Duty Exemption Certificate (IDEC). However, TCN would reportedly inform them that the relevant file was with the Ministry of Power, while the ministry, in turn, would say it was with the Ministry of Finance. He added that the Ministry of Finance often views the imported equipment as potential revenue for the government and consequently seeks to impose a five per cent import duty. He noted that such equipment should ordinarily benefit from the relevant government exemptions, considering that they were imported specifically for public electricity infrastructure projects. According to him, some of the consignments arrive without properly processed Form M, the mandatory import declaration form; Pre-Arrival Assessment Report (PAAR); Standards Organisation of Nigeria Conformity Assessment Programme (SONCAP) certification; and Import Duty Exemption Certificate (IDEC). These omissions, he said, leave the equipment exposed to additional clearance requirements and charges. Oyebanjo said the situation becomes more complicated after the containers spend 90 days at the ports without clearance. He disclosed that a particular batch of 22 containers accumulated liabilities of N483.88m because of the conflicting classifications and the continued accumulation of shipping charges. Providing details of the contents of the containers, Oyebanjo said they include critical electricity infrastructure approved by the Federal Executive Council for various transmission projects. Among the equipment are 300 Mega Volt-Ampere (MVA), 330/132/33 kilovolt (kV) transformers intended for Ikeja West, Gas Insulated Switchgear (GIS) spares, 33kV double-circuit lines for Katampe and materials for the proposed Super Grid. He said some of the equipment had remained in the ports for about 20 years. Oyebanjo alleged that the prolonged delays had also created opportunities for an auction racket, claiming that some overtime cargo were auctioned to cronies at about 10 per cent of their value before being resold to TCN. ‘How to avoid recurrence’ To prevent a recurrence, he recommended the establishment of a dedicated TCN desk at the Nigeria Customs Service, rather than leaving the process entirely within the purview of the Ministry of Finance. Such a desk, he said, should operate with pre-approved duty waivers to ensure that documentation and clearance arrangements are completed before the equipment arrive in the country. He also called for a change in the procurement structure for future electricity projects, recommending that all new contracts adopt Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) arrangements, under which contractors would be responsible for delivering equipment to the project sites rather than simply bringing them to Lagos ports under CIF terms. On his part, a power expert, Engr. Ibrahim Sulu said since 2016, presidential approvals have cleared stranded power equipment again and again, only for it to pile up. He said the country needs a standing rule that does not depend on whoever is minister, adding that all contracts are Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) to the project site, with the contractor bearing demurrage. A power stakeholder, Duru Oguzie, expressed dismay over the prolonged abandonment of the equipment, describing the situation as evidence of a lack of patriotism among some Nigerians entrusted with managing public resources. He criticised the Nigeria Customs Service for allowing the equipment to remain stranded for years when they could have been released earlier for use in the country’s electricity infrastructure. He described the development as a show of shame, arguing that the equipment had lost much of its potential value to the country because of the prolonged delays. Oguzie urged the Federal Government to maintain zero revenue charges on the stranded electricity equipment to ensure their immediate release. He argued that the government should prioritise the national interest and the potential benefits of deploying the equipment rather than focusing on revenue collection from assets already procured with public funds or development financing. However, another stakeholder, Saka Mohammad, questioned the political narrative surrounding the presidential directive. He said the applause generated by the presidential directive was undeserved because the clearance of the equipment should be viewed within the broader context of the government’s responsibility to address the longstanding weaknesses in the power sector. He maintained that the Federal Government should take more proactive measures to ensure that the problems responsible for the abandonment of critical electricity equipment do not recur. However, energy expert Rasheed Adeleke described the clearance of the stranded equipment as a positive development that could support improvements in the electricity sector. He lamented that the equipment had remained trapped at the ports for almost two decades, saying the situation exposed the persistent institutional failures and unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles slowing the development of Nigeria’s power infrastructure. Beyond the stranded equipment, concerns have also been raised about the direction of the country’s transmission infrastructure development and the feasibility of some newly announced projects. A competent source with knowledge of the industry said, “Now, as elections approach, the President has promised Nigerians that he will fix the power sector and end estimated billing. He even challenged Nigerians not to vote for him if he fails to deliver on these two promises. “They have now introduced the East-West transmission project without publishing the necessary details, technical studies or implementation plan. Yet, they claim it will be completed in two years and add 14,000MW to the national grid. This is being presented to Nigerians without adequately explaining the technical and commercial realities.” The source added, “Electricity is not generated simply by making political promises. It requires properly coordinated investments in generation, transmission and distribution, supported by credible technical studies, financing and implementation capacity. “Without addressing these fundamental issues, the promise of adding 14,000MW in two years raises serious questions about the feasibility and credibility of the project.”

title: Tinubu approved purchase of SUVs for FCT traditional rulers – Wike
body: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has approved the procurement of brand-new Sport Utility Vehicles (SUVs) for newly upgraded traditional rulers across the Federal Capital Territory. The Minister of the FCT, Nyesom Wike, disclosed this on Saturday, in Abuja at the Rainbow Coalition Stakeholders Rally and unveiling of FCT National Assembly candidates, organised by the FCT Stakeholders Assembly at the Old Parade Ground. This was contained in a statement issued by the Deputy Director, Press, Office of the FCT Minister, Rabi Musa Umar. The rally brought together traditional rulers, the six area council chairmen, leaders of indigenous communities, youth and women groups, and party leaders across divides, including the APC and PDP chairmen in the FCT, who jointly endorsed President Tinubu for a second term in 2027, alongside Senator Philip Tanimu Aduda for FCT Senate, Hon. John Gabaya for Abuja North and Hon. Danladi Chiya for Abuja South Federal Constituencies. How bureaucracy leaves power equipment rotting in ports Fresh woes for pupils in Niger According to the statement, the minister attributed the presidential gesture on SUVs to recognition of the vital roles traditional rulers play in preserving culture and maintaining peace, noting that the President’s approval of the upgrade of traditional stools, which was abandoned for 27 years, underscores his commitment to the FCT. “Mr President has said that you cannot just answer royal fathers by mouth. You cannot just answer royal fathers by entering Keke Napep. You cannot answer royal fathers by entering Okada. That all of you, by the grace of God, before December, you will go with your SUV cars. “If there is any traditional institution that needs to be treated well, that needs empowerment, it’s the traditional institution of the Federal Capital Territory”, the statement quoted Wike as saying. Charging supporters to translate endorsement into votes, the FCT Minister declared a strict grassroots mandate ahead of the January 16, 2027 election. “Deliver your polling unit, deliver your ward, deliver your local government, deliver your state”, he said. He warned against claiming victory without grassroots contribution. “I don’t want to hear: I lost my polling unit, but we won. If you lose your polling unit, don’t say we won because you never contributed to the victory. So, everybody go home, it’s an operation to deliver your polling unit”, Wike stated. “We shall never make the mistake we made in 2023. When you realise a mistake, you correct it. To God be the glory, come January 2027, Senator Philip Tanimu Aduda will be elected because he identifies with you and cares about you”, Wike said, questioning whether the incumbent Senator had ever called constituents for a meeting or moved a bill for FCT. To empower youth mobilisation for the election, the minister announced President Tinubu’s approval of four buses for FCT youths and fixed November 10 for an interactive session with youths across the six area councils. He also promised a separate engagement with persons with disabilities, stressing that “disability does not mean you do not have capacity”.

title: N4.6trn lost to building collapse in 4 years – Report
body: The recurring incidents of building collapse in Nigeria has again raised questions on structural and regulatory supervision in the real estate sector. Checks by Daily Trust show that about N4.6 trillion has been lost to building collapse which led to the destruction of goods and valuable items. Additionally, between January 2020 and June 2026, Nigeria recorded dozens of building collapses that killed hundreds and injured many more. Nationwide, more than 650 collapses have killed over 1,600 people since 1974, according to figures the Federal Government cited last month. Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital accounts for over half of all recorded incidents. High-profile collapses there in 2021, 2022 and 2024 claimed dozens of lives and destroyed livelihoods. Fresh woes for pupils in Niger How bureaucracy leaves power equipment rotting in ports Consequently, incidents continue to climb: residential blocks, commercial properties and even schools have given way, often during heavy rains or while occupants slept. These are not isolated tragedies but symptoms of systemic failure in materials quality, regulation and enforcement. Experts attribute these incidents to substandard block-moulding combined with defective materials , unprofessional construction practices, inadequate supervision and the push to cut costs In Nigeria, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON), state works ministries and local councils are mandated by law to regulate and and ensure that building materials are up to standards N4.6trn lost The Chartered Institute of Forensics and Certified Fraud Investigators of Nigeria (CIFCFIN), in partnership with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) and the Nigeria Building and Road Research Institute (NBRRI) has set up an initiative to curb building collapses, noting that Nigeria is currently lossing trillions Speaking at the induction of the inaugural cohort of CEFFI professionals, Dr Iliyasu Gashinbaki, President and Chairman of the Governing Council of CIFCFIN, said the initiative stemmed from disturbing findings in a 2026 engineering study. According to Gashinbaki, the study identified 111 validated building-collapse incidents in Nigeria between 2015 and 2025. He said the incidents resulted in 321 deaths and 344 injuries, representing an average of approximately 32 deaths and 34 injuries annually within the dataset. Gashinbaki added that fire-related losses were equally sobering. He said a recent analysis of documented incidents between 2022 and 2025 estimated at least N4.6 trillion in destroyed goods, property and business assets. He said this amounted to roughly N1.15 trillion annually across the dataset. Gashinbaki said the figures demonstrated the need for Nigeria to move from reactive responses to evidence-based investigation and accountability.Buy Maps He said the CEFFI initiative would bring together engineering, forensic science, law, regulation and investigation to strengthen the response to engineering failures. He said a recent analysis of documented incidents between 2022 and 2025 estimated at least N4.6 trillion in destroyed goods, property and business assets. He said this amounted to roughly N1.15 trillion annually across the dataset. Gashinbaki said the figures demonstrated the need for Nigeria to move from reactive responses to evidence-based investigation and accountability.Buy Maps He said the CEFFI initiative would bring together engineering, forensic science, law, regulation and investigation to strengthen the response to engineering failures. “Where there is suspected negligence, fraud, malpractice or deliberate compromise of safety, properly conducted forensic engineering can preserve the technical evidence required,” he said. He urged regulators, project owners, contractors, professional bodies and law-enforcement agencies to ensure that engineering failures did not end with repairs, abandonment or silence. Gashinbaki said the initiative would help promote safer infrastructure, stronger institutions, better stewardship of public resources and the protection of human life. Only recently, Daily Trust reports that one person was injured after a five-storey building under construction partially collapsed on Durban Street, Wuse II, Abuja. The National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA, confirmed the incident, which occurred at about 6:30 pm on Saturday, October 17, 2026. In a statement issued by its Press Unit, the agency said its Abuja Operations Office received an alert about the collapse and immediately activated relevant emergency response agencies. NEMA said the FCT Fire Service and its AYA Emergency Response Ambulance Bay team were among the responders mobilised to the scene to coordinate search and rescue operations. The agency confirmed that no life was lost in the incident, while the injured worker was evacuated to a nearby hospital for medical attention. What can be done Two measures matter most. First, criminal and civil liability must extend to manufacturers, suppliers and complicit professionals where negligence leads to collapse, with State Houses of Assembly legislating penalties stiff enough to deter, alongside whistleblower protection. Second, SON must move from paper standards to street-level enforcement: mandatory certification for block producers, regular market sampling and lab testing, and tighter import checks. Supporting this, local councils should license and inspect block-moulding sites, publishing lists of certified producers and revoking licenses for repeat offenders. Approval processes must include mandatory on-site inspection at foundation, lintel and roof stages, not just at submission – with inspectors trained, equipped and rotated to reduce corruption. Digital permit platforms publishing inspection status would add pressure that paper files cannot.

title: Sokoto: Concerns over attack on ADC guber candidate’s convoy
body: The African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the All Progressives Congress (APC) have traded blame following an attack on the convoy of the ADC governorship candidate in Sokoto, Manir Muhammad Dan’iya. Dan’iya had alleged that personnel of the Marshal and Community Guard, state-owned security outfits, attacked his convoy around the Sokoto Airport at about 9 pm on Friday, October 30, shortly after he escorted former governor Aminu Waziri Tambuwal to the airport. The ADC candidate, in a statement by his media aide, Aminu Abdullahi, claimed that security personnel blocked his convoy and prevented it from passing, allegedly acting on orders from above to stop ADC members from entering Sokoto. He alleged that gunshots were fired during the confrontation, his vehicle was damaged, and two Department of State Services (DSS) officers attached to his security team were detained. Presidency makes case for power rotation, insists south needs to complete 8 years N4.6trn lost to building collapse in 4 years – Report Dan’iya described the incident as a threat to his life and called on the police, the DSS and other relevant authorities to investigate the matter and establish those responsible. The ADC candidate further alleged that earlier in the day, personnel of the security outfits had been deployed at entry points into the state, where vehicles bearing ADC inscriptions were reportedly stopped from entering. The Director-General of the ADC campaign council, Bello Muhammad Goronyo, called on the Inspector-General of Police and the Department of State Services (DSS) to investigate the alleged attack on Dan’iya. Goronyo, in a statement, described the incident as a threat to the safety of the party’s governorship candidate and members of his entourage. He maintained that no governor, political party or security commander had the authority to prevent citizens from entering a state because of their political affiliation. The ADC director-general also accused the state government of allegedly deploying public security resources for partisan activities, arguing that security personnel should concentrate on addressing banditry, kidnapping and other security challenges facing communities. However, the APC dismissed the allegations, describing them as fabricated claims intended to attract public sympathy and divert attention from the ADC’s political challenges. The state APC Chairman, Alhaji Haruna Adiya, said the allegations were part of what he described as a propaganda campaign against the state government. Adiya, in a statement, questioned the credibility of the account, particularly the claim that personnel of the state security outfits detained DSS officers and interfered with their vehicles. He also faulted what he described as inconsistencies in the ADC’s account of the incident, arguing that while the party’s media aide reportedly claimed that security personnel prevented Dan’iya from entering Sokoto metropolis, the candidate’s statement indicated that he had visited different locations in the city to pay condolence visits and attend to other engagements. The APC chairman also dismissed claims that security personnel were deployed to restrict ADC members from entering the state, explaining that Sokoto was preparing to host a major traditional title conferment ceremony scheduled for Sunday. He said the event was expected to attract prominent personalities and visitors from different parts of the country, making adequate security arrangements necessary. Analyst condemns attack Speaking on the issue, Dr Aminu Hayatu, a political scientist at Bayero University, Kano (BUK), said the growing tension between political parties in some states was being fuelled by alleged attempts to suppress opposition activities.
