He warned that the situation could degenerate into widespread violence ahead of the 2027 general elections. He said although heightened political tension was expected as the country moved closer to another election, the pattern of developments in some states over the past month suggested that the situation required serious attention. He said the alleged restrictions, which he claimed were deliberately targeted and controlled by actors within the ruling party, had deepened opposition grievances over the political environment ahead of the elections. According to him, the growing frustration had also contributed to retaliatory actions by opposition supporters, who sometimes resorted to tearing down ruling party banners whenever they sighted APC members or their campaign activities. He warned that the situation could trigger more political violence as the election approached and potentially worsen during the polls if urgent steps were not taken. Hayatu said security agencies had a critical role to play in containing the situation. He, however, stressed that they could only do so by remaining neutral and resisting attempts by political actors to use them as instruments of intimidation or suppression. He said the perceived involvement of security operatives in actions against opposition parties could further undermine confidence in the electoral process. He argued that political parties must be allowed to operate freely and enjoy a level playing field to prevent existing tensions from escalating and threatening the conduct of free and fair elections. Hayatu said suspicions that the ruling party was attempting to influence the electoral process had also contributed to the growing political hostility, noting that civil society organisations had raised concerns about the situation. He urged political stakeholders to take the warning signs seriously. He described Nigeria as an increasingly fragile polity, already grappling with economic difficulties and persistent security challenges, saying the addition of political violence could further destabilise the country. The political scientist said the violence witnessed in Sokoto reflected what had been happening quietly in some parts of the North, warning that the situation could spread to other states if left unchecked.

title: Kwankwaso alleges plot to stop NDC candidate
body: The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, has accused Kano State Governor Abba Yusuf of plotting to disqualify the party’s governorship candidate, Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo, ahead of the 2027 election. Daily Trust has reported how Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) deleted Gwarzo’s name from its updated governorship candidate in the state and said it was due to a court order. The commission however clarified that it has no problem with the candidate, adding that his omission was in compliance with the court. But speaking at a press briefing in Kano on Sunday, Kwankwaso alleged that the governor initially sought to use INEC to remove the NDC candidate from the ballot but later resorted to the courts when that move failed. According to him, Governor Yusuf had realised that he made a political mistake and had since been making frantic efforts to prevent the NDC from participating in the governorship contest. ”What he wanted was for INEC to declare that there was no governorship candidate in Kano. When that did not happen, they went to court seeking the disqualification of our candidate,” Kwankwaso said. The former Kano governor alleged that associates of the governor secretly instituted legal action against the party and INEC in a bid to secure a court order without attracting public attention. He claimed that the case was structured in a manner that would prevent the affected candidate from becoming aware of the proceedings until after judgment had been delivered. Kwankwaso, however, insisted that the NDC candidate had no constitutional or legal impediment that could warrant disqualification. ”Our candidates have no issues relating to age, educational qualification or any other constitutional requirement. There is nothing that should stop them from contesting the election,” he said. The NDC vice-presidential candidate further accused the governor and his allies of attempting to avoid electoral competition rather than face the party at the polls. ”They do not want to contest against us. They believe that once they occupy government offices, they can do whatever they want. But Kano voters will decide,” he said. Speaking of previous political developments in the state, Kwankwaso recalled that a court ruling had once removed a candidate before he was subsequently reinstated ahead of an election that his party eventually won. He expressed confidence that the electorate would reject what he described as attempts to undermine democratic choice in the state. Kwankwaso also urged supporters, particularly young people, to verify their voter registration status and remain politically active. He maintained that the NDC would participate in the election and defeat its opponents at the polls. Efforts to obtain the reaction of Governor Yusuf on the allegations were unsuccessful as calls made to the governor’s spokesperson, Sanusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, were neither answered nor returned as at the time of filing this report.

title: Presidency makes case for power rotation, insists south needs to complete 8 years
body: The Presidency has charged the North to honour the current eight-year tenure of the South, in the interest of “reciprocity and national stability.” Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, stated this in Kano on Sunday during the Grand Inauguration & Strategic Media Awards Ceremony of Matan Arewa 4 Tinubu Again (MATA). She said Nigeria’s national stability hangs by a “slender thread,” demanding that the North honour the unwritten power rotation pact and allow the South to complete its eight-year tenure, warning that breaking this trust could jeopardise the country’s unity. According to her, Nigeria’s power rotation arrangement is not a sectional concession but a reciprocal compact that has stabilised the Fourth Republic. Making a veiled reference to former Vice President and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, who she recalled attended and participated in the famous Kaduna meeting where the power rotation agreement was reached, Abdulmajid argued that the North cannot sacrifice the stability of Nigeria for the ambition of one man. Tracing the origin to Kaduna, she noted that when military rule ended, patriots negotiated a framework for unity, maintaining, just as he said, “And present in that room was Atiku Abubakar himself, as later confirmed by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume. Insisting on the power rotation arrangement, the presidency said, “In 1999, when the guns of military rule finally fell silent, this nation did not just switch governments—we made a sacred promise. Our founding patriots gathered in Kaduna with one urgent, defining question echo-chambered in their minds: How do we keep Nigeria one? “And from that sacred deliberation came a compact: not a sectional concession, but a reciprocal agreement. This gentleman’s agreement decreed that power must rotate between North and South every eight years—an arrangement to guarantee fairness, to ensure stability, and to guarantee that no Nigerian ever feels like a stranger in his own country.” On how the arrangement worked, Abdulmajid said it survived because it was honoured. “This is not fiction. This is our history. And how did it work? It worked because we honoured it. In 1999, we gave it to the South—Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, eight years, from 1999 to 2007. Then we gave it to the North: Umaru Musa Yar’Adua in 2007. But death, a painful death, cut his tenure short in 2010. “His vice, Goodluck Jonathan from the South, took over. The North felt cheated. The North said our turn was not complete, and that agitation was legitimate. What happened? In 2015, power returned to the North. The late former President Muhammadu Buhari, eight full years, 2015 to 2023! The sequence was restored! The principle survived,” she stated. The presidency contended that the agreement is a two-way street and the North has already taken its full benefit. “My people, the agreement is reciprocal; it is a two-way street. The North has already taken its full benefit after eight solid years under Buhari. You cannot eat your cake and still demand another man’s cake,” Abdulmajid said The presidential aide stressed that stability requires reciprocity, recalling that the current President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, a Southerner, worked tirelessly for the late General Muhammadu Buhari to emerge victorious when the North demanded power must return after Jonathan’s tenure. “That same logic applies today. You cannot abandon a principle when it becomes inconvenient. If you do, you tell the world that the agreement was never a principle at all—merely a temporary tactic. And if we destroy trust today, what will we use to negotiate tomorrow? Let us be honest. Much of this noise against the South completing its term is not a matter of principle. It is personal ambition,” she queried. Abdulmajid said, “Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar tells us zoning is “self-defeating.” But he participated in and benefited from zoned arrangements in 2015 and 2019 when they favored his ambition! When rotation opened the door for him, it was acceptable. When it stands in his way, it becomes “intellectually dishonest.” “Shall we sacrifice Nigeria’s stability for one man’s ambition? The North’s genuine interest is not served by that; the North’s interest is stable inclusion. The guarantee that power will return to you only lives if we honour the compact today.” On his part, Kano State Governor, Abba Kabir Yusuf, corroborated Abdulmajid’s position, saying the unity of Nigeria can only be guaranteed by fair play and inclusivity. The governor who was represented by his Director-General of Media and Publicity, Sunusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, argued that reversing the existing rotational arrangement will paint the North in ignoble light, even as he urged the region to maintain the status quo by re-electing President Tinubu for a second term. In his remarks, former Governor of Jigawa State and immediate past Minister of Defence, Mohammad Abubakar Badaru, said the Renewed Hope Administration of President Tinubu has benefited the North more than any other part of Nigeria.

title: Tompolo joins ‘Rainbow Coalition’ for Tinubu in Osun
body: ​​In a display of political alignment, a high-powered coalition featuring High Chief Government Ekpemupolo (Tompolo), Osun State Governor Senator Ademola Adeleke, and Minister of Marine and Blue Economy Adegboyega Oyetola has set an ambitious target of 1.5 million votes for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in Osun State. ​The alliance unveiled their goal at the weekend in Osogbo, the state capital, during the official inauguration of the state and local government chapters of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement. At the event, Tompolo donated 30 operational vehicles alongside a substantial cache of campaign materials. ​Delivering his keynote address through Chief Kestin Pondi, Managing Director of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, Tompolo who serves as the Grand Patron of the movement urged Osun residents to rally behind President Tinubu as a son of the South-West. He challenged the electorate to deliver between 90 and 100 percent of the total votes cast to guarantee the seamless continuation of the administration’s economic reforms. ​“We are in Osun State canvassing for votes for a man who has done so well for the South-West because we believe in his reformation agenda,” Tompolo stated through his representative. He highlighted early structural reforms, enhanced federal revenue allocations to state governments, prompt salary disbursements, and macroeconomic stabilization efforts as compelling reasons for continuity. ​“Most leaders would have delayed tough reforms until a second term, but President Tinubu initiated his immediately because he puts Nigeria first,” Tompolo added. ​Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke, represented by Deputy Governor Kola Adewusi, characterized the alliance as a “Rainbow Coalition” transcending traditional party boundaries to ensure a decisive victory for the President. ​Adeleke commended Tompolo for launching the nationwide advocacy drive and implored political stakeholders to bury past rivalries. ​“Our unity of purpose and shared determination to secure Mr. President’s re-election is clearly demonstrated by this gathering of supporters across party lines,” Adeleke noted. “All coalition partners must set aside historical political antagonisms and work together to deliver between 1.5 and 2 million votes for Mr. President.” ​Reinforcing the message, Marine and Blue Economy Minister Adegboyega Oyetola represented by the APC 2026 governorship candidate, Bola Oyebamiji emphasized that support for President Tinubu has broadened beyond traditional party lines.

title: 2027 permutations favour Tinubu – Deputy Senate President
body: The Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Barau Jibrin, has expressed optimism that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu will emerge victorious in the January 16, presidential election, citing the prevailing political situation in the country. Barau stated this at the weekend during the inauguration of campaign committees for Dawakin Tofa, Tofa and Rimin Gado Local Government Areas of Kano State, where he charged party members to work towards securing victory for all candidates of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the forthcoming general elections. In a statement issued by his media aide, Ismail Mudashir, the Deputy President of the Senate said the foundation laid by President Tinubu during his first term would yield the desired results in his second term. He expressed appreciation to party leaders, elected representatives, local government chairmen, Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf and other stakeholders for their support and commitment to the APC, assuring that the unity and cooperation currently being enjoyed by the party would be sustained. “Based on the assessments of political analysts and the current state of Nigerian politics, all indications suggest that, Bola Ahmed Tinubu will win the presidential election,” he said. He noted that Kano, being one of the largest states in the country and second only to Lagos in terms of the latest registered voters, deserved greater attention and opportunities from the Federal Government. According to him, the Governor’s decision to lead the people from the New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP) to the APC was a strategic move that have enhanced Kano’s political relevance and improved its access to developmental opportunities. The Deputy President of the Senate expressed confidence that the political unity achieved in Kano would translate into tangible benefits for the people, particularly with the alignment of councillors, local government chairmen, state legislators, members of the National Assembly and the Governor under the APC. He added that the coming elections would usher in a new phase of political and developmental activities, with elected representatives expected to contribute meaningfully to the development of their respective constituencies. Barau explained that the campaign committees were carefully constituted to accommodate party leaders, members of the party’s executive committees, former and serving legislators, councillors, local government chairmen, new party members and respected elders.

title: Russia Deploys Rare MiG-35 Fighters for Low Cost Air Defence Against Ukrainain Drones
body: The Russian Aerospace Forces have begun using MiG-35 fighters to intercept Ukrainian long-range unmanned aerial vehicles attacking targets deep inside Russian territory. According to a report published by Ukrainian defence outlet Defense Express in late October, the deployment was highlighted by an image shared by the aviation-focused Soniashnyk open-source intelligence community, reportedly taken from inside a Russian MiG-35 cockpit during a mission to counter Ukrainian drones. With only six of the aircraft believed to have been produced, their reported use in homeland air defence illustrates the growing demands Ukrainian long-range strikes are placing on Russian military resources. The MiG-35 has the lowest sustainment costs of any fighter type in Russian service, reflecting the fact that the aircraft are considerably smaller than the Su-30, Su-34 and Su-35 fighters that form the backbone of the fleet. With these heavier fighter types all being derivatives of the Soviet Su-27 heavyweight air superiority fighter, the MiG-35 was developed in parallel as a derivative of the MiG-29 medium weight fighter , which while having a much smaller radar and more limited weapons payload, also requires much less maintenance and is considerably less costly to operate. The MiG-35 was developed primarily for export, but has gained no orders in large part due to competition from the more advanced Chinese J-10C fighter. Limited domestic demand as reflected the fact that doctrine in post-Soviet Russia has deprioritised the fielding of medium or lightweight combat jets. The MiG-35’s deployment has occurred as Ukraine continues to expand its long-range drone campaign against Russian military installations, airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries and other strategic targets. Ukrainian unmanned aircraft have repeatedly penetrated Russian airspace to strike targets far from the front lines, forcing Moscow to distribute air defence resources across a vast territory. The resulting demands extend beyond surface-to-air missile systems, with fighter aircraft, radar networks, electronic warfare systems and mobile air defence teams all contributing to the effort to detect and intercept incoming drones. Fighter aircraft can offer advantages when countering long-range drones, particularly when targets are detected far from defended installations. Their speed allows them to cover large distances quickly, while onboard sensors and air-to-air weapons can provide another layer of interception capability alongside ground-based defences. Employing advanced fighters against comparatively inexpensive unmanned aircraft can create an unfavourable cost exchange, particularly if expensive guided missiles are required to destroy individual drones. The effectiveness of this approach also depends on the ability to detect relatively small targets flying at low altitudes and to engage them without exposing the aircraft to unnecessary risks. The MiG-35’s mounting of onboard cannon and compatibility with gun pods, combined with its very high manoeuvrability and low sustainment costs, makes it a potentially optimal fighter for such operations. Although older MiG-29s are widely in service, they cost considerably more to operate and require more maintenance than the MiG-35 due to their less efficient Soviet era designs. The Russian Aerospace Forces have deployed A-50U airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) systems to provide support to missile defence efforts, in particular to help intercept FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strikes against high value strategic targets. This gained particular attention after Russian air defences in shot down more than five of the missiles in the early hours of June 5. It remains highly possible that the MiG-35 could be integrated with such operations, with support from the A-50’s powerful airborne radar potentially compensating for the limited power of the fighters’ own onboard sensors. It is likely that Russian government-linked sources will seek to publicise the MiG-35’s combat successes as part of renewed efforts to market the fighter type for export.

title: 'Suspicious object' enters Latvian airspace near Belarus, Russia border
body:
Latvian armed forces announced that a flying object had briefly entered the country's airspace near its border with Russia and Belarus on Nov. 1.
"Take action!" the Latvian military wrote on X. "We inform you that there is a threat in the airspace of Latvia. Go indoors, follow the two-wall principle! Follow official announcements. If you notice a low-flying or suspicious object, do not approach it."
The incursion occurred around the border towns of Kraslava and Ludza in southeast Latvia .
Less than an hour after the initial announcement, the Latvian military declared that the incursion had ended and the threat had left.
The Latvian military later said it had deployed a BLAZE interceptor drone in response to the incursion and had activated its self-destruct protocol to avoid entering and violating Russian or Belarusian airspace.
It is not yet clear where the flying device, likely a drone, originated from.
The incursion comes after drones repeatedly violated the airspace of Poland, Baltic nations, and other nations along NATO's eastern flank in recent months.
An unidentified object, likely a drone, entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded on Oct. 18, sending residents to shelters and damaging a civilian vehicle, according to Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda. NATO fighter jets were then scrambled in response to the incident,
On Oct. 17, two Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones flying in Romanian national airspace, the country's Defense Ministry announced.
Threats to NATO airspace come amid warnings from European leaders that Russia could utilize drones to wage hybrid attacks on the alliance, testing its Article 5 commitments.
Ukrainian drones have also unintentionally entered NATO airspace while launching attacks on targets deep in Russia.
In June, a drone with a 5-kilogram warhead was found in southern Estonia after a Ukrainian attack on Russia.
Ukrainian strikes against Russian Baltic Sea terminals and other strategic targets have previously resulted in Ukraine's drones crashing on the territory of the Baltic countries and Finland, as Russia seeks to divert attacking unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with electronic warfare.

title: APC’s assault on democracy will fail says ADC campaign
body: The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has condemned what it described as a “sustained, coordinated and state-sponsored assault on democracy, freedom of association and the constitutional right of Nigerians to political participation under the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.” The Council said the unfolding incidents across the country went beyond ordinary political rivalry, alleging that they represented a disturbing pattern of intimidation, harassment and suppression of opposition voices. These are calculated “atrocious actions skewed to scare Nigerians ahead of the general elections.” In a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC-PCC recalled a series of incidents, including “attacks on its leaders and members in Kaduna, the reported assault on its Sokoto State governorship candidate, Alhaji Munir Dan Iya, by operatives of the Sokoto Marshals along Airport Road, Sokoto, and alleged attacks on other opposition figures.” ADC also cited the reported demolition of its governorship campaign office in Kebbi State and the alleged denial of a campaign venue in Enugu State to the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Mr Peter Obi. The Council further referenced the reported attacks on the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, and other opposition voices, describing the incidents as part of what it called an “emerging pattern of political intolerance.” According to the ADC-PCC, the alleged attacks, denial of campaign venues, arrests, harassment and intimidation of opposition figures raise serious concerns about the state of democratic freedoms and political pluralism in Nigeria. The Council maintained that no government, regardless of its political or institutional strength, could successfully suppress the democratic aspirations of Nigerians, recalling that popular resistance contributed to the collapse of former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s third-term agenda. ADC also argued that President Tinubu and the APC enjoyed the benefits of political participation and opposition politics when they were outside government, insisting that those same democratic freedoms must be guaranteed to all political parties and their members. The ADC-PCC expressed concern over the continued detention of its Vice Chairman and former Governor of Kaduna State, Mallam Nasir El-Rufai, alleging that he was being unlawfully held and denied his right to bail. It warned that the circumstances surrounding his detention would not weaken the party, adding that the international community was watching developments in Nigeria. “The world is watching, and the burden of this illegality rests squarely on those responsible,” the Council stated. The campaign council further alleged that financial inducements were being deployed to compromise individuals and weaken opposition ranks, but insisted that Nigerians would not surrender their constitutional rights for monetary or material benefits. The ADC-PCC called on Nigerians to remain committed to defending democratic values, freedom of association and the right to political choice, regardless of political affiliation.

title: In Mountain Province, a solemn path of smoke and fire honors the dead
body: SAGADA, Philippines – Traced back to the arrival of the Anglican mission in the early 1900s, this unique tradition has deeply influenced local culture and beliefs in the Mountain Province. Panag-apoy, a solemn practice observed by Sagada locals every November 1, All Saints’ Day, honors the dead through smoke and fire. It is also known as “Pagdedenet,” a Kankanaey term meaning “to light the fire.” Instead of candles, locals use pine fatwood as it is rich in resin and cannot be put out easily by the wind and light rains. Photo by Kenosis Yap The lighting of fire on graves holds meaning for both tribal and Anglican beliefs, serving as an act of remembrance meant to warm and guide the spirits of departed loved ones. Panag-apoy starts with a Holy Mass to remember the departed members of the community. In some towns across the province, names of the deceased locals are read aloud during the service. The local priest then blesses the graves, including candles and flowers at the cemetery, signaling locals to light their saeng or saleng — small bundles of fatwood placed on top of graves. As the fire burns, the cemetery glows orange as smoke fills the sky. The fire from each grave commemorates a soul who was once part of the local community. Photo by Jyor So Locals and officials stress that Panag-apoy is not a festival, despite the influx of tourists in recent years due to social media posts. While residents appreciate visitors, the swelling crowds, they say, have disrupted the solemnity and sacredness of the tradition. The light burning the fatwood is believed to be the light of Jesus guiding the souls of the departed. Photo by Kenosis Yap This year, the local government of Sagada limited visitor access to preserve the solemnity of the occasion. Tourists may only observe the practice from 7 pm to 9 pm, and drone cameras are not allowed. Tourists quietly take photos of the sacred practice. Photo by Jyor So The ritual unfolds in silence as the youth watch their elders light the saeng , passing the sacred tradition to the next generation. Even late at night, locals continue to arrive and light up fires for their loved ones. Photo by Kenosis Yap. – Rappler.com

title: Two unknown projectiles struck tanker off Saudi Arabia
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Two unknown projectiles have struck the port side of a tanker, the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency says.
UKMTO said the attack took place at 23:47 GMT on Sunday, about 72 nautical miles (133km) east of the Saudi Arabian coastal city of Khafji.
“All crew are accounted for and there is no reported environmental impact at this time,” it added.

title: Justice for the dead miners
body: The 10-member Independent Committee to Investigate the Reported Deaths of 33 People in NSCDC Custody on September 17, 2026, headed by Mr Jonathan Kure, a retired Deputy Director-General of the Department of State Services, submitted its report last week, a few weeks after its constitution. In its report, the committee provided a thorough and far-reaching account of the circumstances surrounding the tragic incident, leaving no doubt that it painstakingly examined the facts, reviewed available evidence and engaged relevant stakeholders before arriving at its recommendations. In line with earlier eyewitness accounts, the committee found that the deaths of the detained miners resulted from environmental asphyxia caused by severe overcrowding, poor ventilation, extreme heat and dehydration in an unsuitable detention facility. The panel concluded that the tragedy was entirely preventable and stemmed from unlawful detention conditions, failure of duty of care, inadequate supervision and the disregard of repeated distress calls from detainees who pleaded for help throughout the night. Before the investigation, officials of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State sought to explain the deaths as possibly resulting from an unspecified disease outbreak. They later stated that the cause of death had not yet been established. That position was a disservice to the Nigerian people, who fund the activities of the NSCDC. Rejecting the disease outbreak claim, the committee further established that the arrests and detention of the alleged illegal miners were carried out without proper planning or authorisation. In its report, the committee made a series of recommendations aimed at ensuring accountability, justice and institutional reform. Foremost among them was that officers found culpable in the deaths of the detainees should be dismissed from service and prosecuted in accordance with the law. Significantly, the committee identified the officers involved and specified the roles each played in what amounted to an unnecessary loss of 37 lives. The committee also urged the federal government to provide compensation to the victims’ families, educational support for their dependants, and medical and psychological care for survivors and affected relatives. In addition, it called for a formal government apology in recognition of the gravity of the tragedy. On the institutional front, the panel recommended a comprehensive overhaul of detention practices within the NSCDC. This should include upgrading detention facilities, ensuring stricter adherence to constitutional safeguards and human rights standards, enhancing the supervision of detainees, improving officer training, and strengthening oversight and accountability mechanisms. The committee further stressed the need for proper operational planning, record-keeping and authorisation procedures for future enforcement operations, warning that systemic failures and negligence must never again be allowed to cause such a preventable loss of life. International human rights law and Section 33 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria guarantee the right to life, a fundamental right that does not cease to apply simply because a person is under arrest or in detention. Detainees and inmates remain entitled to the protection of the law, humane treatment, access to medical care where necessary, and the constitutional safeguards of due process and fair hearing. The committee’s findings indicate that the deceased detainees repeatedly cried out for help and showed signs of severe distress before their deaths, yet those warnings were allegedly ignored. No domestic law or international human rights standard permits security personnel to stand by while people in their custody face a life-threatening emergency. The reported failure to respond raises serious questions about the training, judgment and conduct of the officers involved. Whether the neglect resulted from inadequate human rights training, gross indifference or an attempt to conceal wrongdoing, the tragedy represents a profound breach of the duty of care owed to every person in lawful custody. While the officers directly implicated in the deaths of the detained miners must face the full weight of the law, it would be a grave mistake to treat the Niger State tragedy merely as the misconduct of a few individuals. The findings of the Independent Investigative Committee point to deeper institutional weaknesses, including poor supervision, inadequate detention conditions, operational failures and disregard for established standards of care. The needless loss of lives has inevitably placed the NSCDC under intense public scrutiny and raised troubling questions about its procedures, oversight mechanisms and accountability structures. The government must therefore go beyond disciplining culpable officers and undertake a comprehensive review of the organisation’s operations nationwide. Such a review should examine detention practices, operational protocols, training standards, command responsibility and compliance with constitutional and human rights obligations. The tragedy in Niger State should serve as a wake-up call and an opportunity for meaningful reform. Anything short of a thorough institutional overhaul would risk leaving the conditions that produced this disaster unchanged, thereby exposing citizens to similar tragedies in the future.

title: A book launch with a difference
body: The public presentation of the book Tinubu: From Renewed Hope to Despair was a launch like no other – for two reasons. First, the launch came beset with all sorts of controversies. The book’s title alone was enough to draw the ire of those in government, particularly in an election period. It was supposed to have been launched at a ceremony billed to take place at Arewa House, Kaduna, on October 15. For some inexplicable reason, ABU Zaria, which owns Arewa House, scuttled the ceremony a few days before the event. To compound matters, the launching committee could not lay their hands on any alternative venue in Kaduna. It looked as if unseen forces had directed all hoteliers and event-centre owners to stay clear of this book launch. That made the book singularly popular and aroused the interest of yours sincerely to look forward to where else the launch would take place. Fortunately, the editors chose to come to the Yar’Adua Centre in Abuja. Somehow, the unseen forces did not interfere, and the launch went ahead on October 16. Secondly, during the ceremony, the authors offered the book at the ridiculous fee of only N5000. Prof. Abubakar Siddique Mohammed, who made the announcement, explained that producing the book cost about N4000 per copy and that they added only N1000 to offset residual expenses, including transportation and venue hire. I was stunned by this candid revelation. I recall that in this year alone, I witnessed ceremonies in the same venue, where book prices at the launch ranged from the princely sum of N50,000 to the outrageous amount of N100,000 per copy. But this is typical of the publishers, Centre for Democratic Development, Research and Training (Ceddert), whose primary aim was not profit but delivering an informed treatise to the public, at basic cost. The centre itself was established in the early 1990s by a group of high-minded professionals from ABU’s history department led by their mentor, the indomitable Dr Yusuf Bala Usman. Since his death in 2005, Professors Siddiq Mohammed, Alkassum Abba, Aliyu Sanusi, and a host of others, all in the mould of town-and-gown public intellectuals, have carried the banner of Ceddert even higher. Over the years, the centre has been quite prodigious in churning out well-researched papers on many social issues affecting the north of the country. I have particularly noted their contributions to the debate on the Almajiri and rural banditry issues. The gathering that morning at the Yar’Adua Centre was like a festive affair, a meeting of old friends, many from the university days of the 1970s. I spotted Adamu Maina Waziri, the ABU SUG President during my time in the 1974/75 session and Dr Usman Bugaje, also an active student leader of the time. Also present were those known to be in the trenches as field politicians and civil rights activists. These included, among others, the SDP presidential candidate, Adewole Adebayo; the ADC vice-presidential candidate, Rotimi Amaechi; the PRP Chairman, Dr Hakeem Baba Ahmed; Dr Usman Yusuf; and Prof Jibrin Ibrahim, who gave a riveting keynote address. As you would expect, many rousing speeches were made at the occasion. However, Prof. Mohammed put the contents of the book in perspective. Quoting from an earlier Ceddert press statement, he said: “There is nothing in this book that is not already in the public domain. The book examines the record of the Tinubu administration, interrogates its policies and assesses their implications for Nigeria’s economy, security, national unity and democratic development. Its purpose is to contribute to public understanding and stimulate informed debate. These are legitimate and necessary activities in any democracy. “If those in power disagree with our analysis or conclusions, they are free to challenge them with evidence, reasoned arguments and alternative explanations. They may publish their own assessments, organise public discussions or respond directly to the issues raised in the book. What they should not do is seek to prevent the public from hearing arguments they dislike. The proper response to criticism is engagement, not suppression.” The book itself is divided into seven chapters, with each of the four editors taking one or two. As its compelling blurb explains, the book critically analyses President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s policies, “examines the first three years of the administration against the promises that preceded it and the realities Nigerians experienced. The book interrogates the widening gap between policy intentions and lived experience, focusing on the consequences of economic reforms for household incomes, food prices, purchasing power, public debt, agriculture, industry and infrastructure. Beyond the economy, the book examines concerns over national unity, federal character, regional equity and the changing geography of federal power. It considers whether the distribution of political appointments, federal institutions, infrastructure and economic opportunities is strengthening or straining confidence in Nigeria’s federal system.” On reading the book, one is immediately struck by the thorough preparations undertaken by the editors. Their data collection from verifiable sources was meticulous. Their analyses are very profound. Their conclusions and verdict may seem brutal, but this does not detract from the book’s overall quality. The book is good reading material for those of us trying to make sense of how we came to be where we are now. It might even be more of a recommended read for those at the top levels of government.

title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
body: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country’s development. Photos he shared on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers, and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials rarely undergo military training. Participants include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa, and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia’s ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. “Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory,” he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government’s ambitions.

title: INEC, purge the register before it is too late
body: A face that belongs to no one should not choose who governs Nigeria. When the Independent National Electoral Commission announced that it would embed artificial intelligence in the conduct of the 2027 elections, eyebrows were raised. Who would regulate INEC’s use of a technology so powerful and so open to abuse? The commission offered assurances. The fears remained. With the display of the preliminary voters’ register, those fears are becoming manifest. Barely a month after INEC announced that its register had crossed 103 million names, Nigerians scrolling through it found faces that did not look human. Faces with the unmistakable sheen of artificial intelligence. INEC first called them “suspected” images and said the online register did not reflect ongoing data clean-up. Three days later, its own Director of ICT, Lawrence Bayode, went further. Some registration officers, he said, had used their official logins to add questionable records in several states. Some of the photographs were AI-generated. Others reflected “very bad registration.” That is not a rumour from a partisan blogger. That is an admission from inside the commission. And it raises questions INEC has not yet answered. How many records were added this way? In which states and wards? Which officers did it, and on whose instruction? Will they be prosecuted? Silence on these questions is not an option. The commission plans to certify the final register on December 15. Once that happens, every fake name on it becomes a legal entry, a ballot waiting for a hand. The window to clean the register is not months. It is weeks. But care is needed. Social media is awash with figures: 20 million AI voters, even 50 million. None of these numbers has come with a method, a sample or a single verifiable dataset. Inflated claims do the riggers’ work for them. They tell the young voter in Gombe or Ogbomoso that his vote is already stolen, so why bother? A demoralised electorate is the easiest one to defeat. The truth is serious enough without exaggeration. INEC has admitted that insiders manipulated the register. The scale is unknown. That alone should alarm every Nigerian, whatever their party. It should also alarm INEC, because the commission’s credibility is its only real asset. Its chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, has said that “algorithms will not and must never decide the 2027 votes.” But Nigerians will judge the commission by what it does before December 15, not by what it says at conferences. So what must INEC do? First, publish the numbers. The commission says its Automated Biometric Identification System flagged the irregularities. Then it knows how many records were flagged. It should publish that figure, broken down by state and local government, and update it weekly until certification. Second, purge the fakes in public view. Every record removed should be listed, with the reason for removal: duplicate, deceased, underage, fabricated image. Political parties and accredited observers should be invited to witness the process and test the results. Third, hand over the register. The Electoral Act entitles political parties to copies of the voter register. INEC should release the cleaned version early enough for parties, civil society and the media to audit it before certification, not after. Fourth, name and sanction the officers involved. If staff used official logins to plant fake voters, that is not “very bad registration.” It is an electoral offence, and it should be prosecuted as one. Fifth, extend the timeline if necessary. If the clean-up cannot be completed credibly by December 15, INEC should say so and adjust. A delayed, clean register is better than a punctual, poisoned one. INEC cannot do this alone, nor should it be trusted to. The National Assembly’s committees on electoral matters must summon the commission and demand a full account of every AI system it uses: what it does, who supplied it and who audits it. The question Nigerians asked at the start remains unanswered: no law today regulates how INEC deploys artificial intelligence. That gap must be closed by regulation before the election, not by apology after it. Political parties must stop treating the register as INEC’s business alone. Every party has agents in every ward. Let them check the names against the people they know. And the media must do what journalism exists to do: verify. Pick the wards. Find the names. Photograph the faces. Report what is proven, and label what is not. Ordinary citizens have a role too. Check your own details on the register. Report entries you know to be false. Collect your PVC. On election day, stay to watch the count and photograph the result sheet at your polling unit. A fake name in the register does not steal an election by itself. Someone still has to vote it, and that vote must still survive the collation centre. But the register is the foundation. Build the election on a corrupted list, and every result that follows will carry a question mark. Nigeria has been here before. Ghost workers on the payroll. Ghost beneficiaries in social investment programmes. Now the ghosts have learned to use artificial intelligence. The farmer who will walk two kilometres to vote in January deserves to know that his ballot will be counted alongside real neighbours, not invented ones. That is the least a democracy owes him. INEC has six weeks. It should use every one of them.

title: Trump suggests potential new measures against Iran if no deal is reached
body:
WASHINGTON, November 2. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has stated that the United States may take further action against Iran if no agreement is reached with the Islamic Republic.
"The only reason why I'm not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can," he told supporters. "But at some point, we're going to have to give them the hammer," Trump said speaking at a rally for Republican supporters in the state of Iowa, ahead of the midterm congressional elections.
Prior to the rally, Trump also told reporters regarding the conflict with Iran: "We'll put it away very soon, one way or the other. Either they'll make a deal or we'll just end it, end it the, I guess you could say, maybe the easy way." He provided no further details.
On October 8, Trump stated that the US had no intention of launching strikes against Iran before the midterm congressional elections, scheduled for November 3. On Saturday, he asserted that negotiations with Tehran were progressing well, though he expressed skepticism regarding Iran’s trustworthiness. He also declined to give a definitive answer when asked whether he planned to resume military action against the Islamic Republic next week. According to the news outlet Axios, Trump does not intend to resume military operations against Iran immediately following the midterm elections, as he prefers to focus on negotiations with Tehran.

title: Arewa must confront rise of religious extremism
body: Until the killing of Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka in Katsina State, I had never heard his name. I had never listened to his sermons, watched his videos or familiarised myself with his religious teachings. I therefore have no opinion on his beliefs, his theological positions or what he represented. I may take time to understand his teachings, but that is not the subject of this article. His death is relevant here only because it triggered an unusually heated exchange across social media, bringing me face to face with something that has troubled me deeply over the past few days. What I have witnessed is an increasingly disturbing exchange among young Nigerian Muslims, many seemingly in their twenties and thirties, debating the differences between Islamic religious movements and traditions. Videos of clerics are being circulated, shared and defended by their followers. Some are being used to attack opposing interpretations of Islam, while others contain statements that are difficult to reconcile with the values of compassion, restraint and respect for human life that should underpin religious teaching. The exchanges involve adherents of Izala and other Salafi-oriented currents, as well as followers of Sufi traditions, including the Tijaniyya and other tariqas. These are not uniform communities, and their theological differences should not be confused with support for violence. However, the hostility and some of the utterances being circulated are deeply concerning. For four days, it has been difficult to open my X timeline without encountering another video or argument arising from this controversy. What is particularly troubling is not simply that people disagree about religious doctrine. Disagreement is neither new nor inherently dangerous. Muslims have different schools of thought, traditions and interpretations, and there is room for robust theological debate. What should concern us is the growing willingness of some voices to justify hatred, dehumanisation and violence in the name of defending religious positions. When young people begin to consume, defend and reproduce such messages as ordinary religious discourse, we must ask ourselves what kind of society we are preparing them to inherit. I have seen a video in which a cleric reportedly claimed that parents should kill a ten-year-old child who refuses to observe Salah, presenting this as an Islamic instruction. That is an extremely dangerous misrepresentation. The commonly cited Hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud about teaching children to pray at seven and disciplining them at ten does not instruct parents to kill their children. The Quran expressly prohibits killing children. Yet statements of this nature can circulate widely, acquire credibility because of the religious authority of the speaker and reach young people who may not have the knowledge to challenge them. Other videos have been even more disturbing. One showed a group of young people in uniforms resembling those of a religious organisation chanting threats to obtain weapons and attack people attending churches in Enugu and Plateau. The organisation publicly disowned the statements and called for an investigation. That response should be acknowledged. However, the recording itself raises serious questions about how young people are being influenced, what they are being taught to regard as acceptable and how easily violent rhetoric can become a collective performance. I want to emphasise that this is not an argument about Muslims against Christians. It is not even primarily an argument about the relationship between Muslims and people of other faiths. What I have been observing is a problem emerging within Muslim communities themselves. It is about Muslims being encouraged to regard other Muslims as enemies because they follow a different school of thought, belong to another religious movement or interpret certain texts differently. If we cannot tolerate differences among ourselves, what hope do we have of building a society in which people of different faiths can coexist peacefully? The implications go far beyond the arguments currently playing out online. Arewa has spent years confronting organised violent extremism. Boko Haram, ISWAP and other armed groups have inflicted enormous damage on communities, institutions, education, livelihoods and the bonds that hold the region. Governments have invested heavily in military operations, intelligence gathering and other security interventions to contain these threats. Yet I fear we are paying insufficient attention to another dimension of the problem: the possibility that we are creating the conditions for a generation of individualised extremists. A young person may never join Boko Haram, ISWAP, Ansaru or any other organised group. They may never enter a terrorist camp, receive weapons training or have direct contact with an insurgent commander. But if they spend years consuming messages that teach them to hate people who disagree with them, that portray other Muslims as legitimate targets, or that present violence as a religious obligation, they may eventually develop an extremist worldview of their own. They may act independently, without belonging to any recognised organisation. This is not to suggest that every young person who encounters such content will become violent. It is to recognise that the normalisation of violent ideology creates a risk that we cannot afford to ignore. We may spend the next decade dismantling organised terrorist networks only to discover that the ideas sustaining violence have become more widely distributed among individuals who are difficult to identify through conventional security structures. In that situation, the challenge will be considerably more complex. How do we confront an extremist who has no organisational affiliation, whose radicalisation has taken place through years of online exposure, and who believes that violence is a legitimate expression of faith? Prevention must therefore begin long before an individual becomes a security threat. This is why I believe the federal and state governments across Northern Nigeria must take a much firmer position on the regulation of public religious preaching. Not everyone should be able to wake up one morning, declare themselves a religious authority and use a public platform to issue inflammatory opinions or dangerous religious instructions without accountability. A sermon delivered in a mosque does not remain within that mosque. It can be recorded, uploaded and circulated to thousands, sometimes millions, of people. A speaker who addresses a relatively small congregation may end up influencing young people across the country. Regulation, however, must be properly designed. Nigeria’s Constitution protects freedom of religion and expression. These rights must not be undermined by governments seeking to control legitimate theological debate or silence religious criticism. But freedom of religion cannot be a licence to incite murder, threaten communities or promote violence. The distinction must be clear, and the law must be applied fairly, transparently and consistently. Some states already have legal and administrative arrangements for regulating public preaching and religious institutions. The question is whether these mechanisms are effective, whether they are being properly enforced and whether they adequately address sermons that are recorded and distributed online. Governments should review existing frameworks and work with recognised Islamic institutions, respected scholars from different traditions, legal experts, child protection professionals and security agencies to establish credible standards for public religious instruction. There should be clear qualifications and accountability requirements for those occupying public preaching platforms, effective complaints mechanisms and independent procedures for investigating credible allegations of incitement. Regulation must target dangerous conduct, not theological disagreement. Saudi Arabia is not a model that should be copied wholesale, nor should any country be treated as an example in every aspect of religious governance. However, its system of formal requirements for the appointment of mosque imams demonstrates that public religious leadership can be subject to institutional standards. Nigeria must develop an approach suited to its own constitutional and religious context, rather than treating the regulation of public preaching as an impossible undertaking. Religious leaders themselves must also recognise the responsibility that comes with influence. Scholars who understand the Quran, Hadith and Islamic jurisprudence have a duty to challenge dangerous distortions of religious teachings. They cannot leave the task of correcting misinformation entirely to government or security agencies. When a cleric makes a statement that encourages violence, other respected scholars should be prepared to challenge it publicly and explain why it is unacceptable. Silence can create the impression that such statements are legitimate or uncontested. Parents, schools and communities must also pay attention to what young people are consuming online. Religious education should cultivate understanding, discipline, compassion and respect for human life. Children must be encouraged to ask questions, examine claims and seek guidance from knowledgeable and responsible adults. We cannot assume that everything delivered in the language of religion is necessarily sound or harmless. The governors of Arewa and the federal government must understand the urgency of this challenge. One of the greatest acts of service they can render to Arewa is to confront the spread of religious extremism before it becomes even more deeply embedded in the communities. This is not a problem that can be postponed until the next security emergency. It is already demanding attention. I am genuinely concerned about the environment in which our children are growing up. If we continue to allow hatred to be dressed up as religious instruction, if we allow young people to consume calls for violence as ordinary online content, and if public religious platforms remain beyond meaningful accountability, we should not be surprised by the consequences. I may be generous in giving us another ten years, but the danger could emerge much sooner. Arewa cannot afford another generation raised to believe that religious disagreement is a justification for hatred or that violence is an acceptable defence of faith. We have already lost too much to organised extremism. We must not allow its ideology to become so normalised that the next threat comes from individuals who no longer need an organisation to tell them whom to hate or whom to kill. The time to act is now, before the ticking time bomb within our own communities becomes another tragedy we will claim we never saw coming.

title: Liverpool v Arsenal ratings: Van Dijk 8, Isak 6; Gabriel 9, Havertz 7
body: Arsenal moved three points clear at the top of the Premier League after a battling 1-0 win over Liverpool on Sunday that earned the Gunners a first victory at Anfield in 14 years. A first-half finish from Kai Havertz was enough to earn the reigning champions all three points, moving them above Manchester City, who lost at home to Brighton on Saturday. Liverpool will be frustrated to come away with nothing, but a combination of wayward finishing, calls not going their way and a resolute Arsenal defence meant Andoni Iraola's side missed out on a return to the top four. The Gunners, meanwhile, bounced back from their shock League Cup exit at Fleetwood Town in midweek. Arsenal have won eight out of nine league games this season, conceding just five goals, and head into the midweek Uefa Champions League match away to Slavia Prague in fine form. Liverpool will be hoping for a return to winning ways at Fenerbahce. What they said: Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk: "Disappointment. We play at home; we had some opportunities. We tried everything. We could have done a bit better in the last 15 minutes to get more balls in the box. It wasn't enough today, and that's why disappointment is the feeling I'm having. When we conceded, we played much better. Alexis [Mac Allister] could have changed the game." Arsenal scorer Kai Havertz: “This means a lot to the whole football club, and it's been 14 years [since Arsenal won at Anfield]; that is a crazy stat, and I think that we are all happy that we gave it to them today. I think we all know what this stadium is about and what the fans are about. Liverpool have big players and they can show their quality. We knew that this was coming for us and we all stuck together and defended together.” Liverpool ratings: Alisson Becker – 7/10: His sloppy pass out from the back started the move that led to Arsenal's opener. Superb one-handed save to turn low Tzolis out for a corner in the second half. Ronald Araujo – 7/10: Defender on loan from Barcelona didn't put a foot wrong all night and was a real physical presence in the home defence. Jeremy Jacquet – 8/10: One vital last-ditch recovery tackle to stop Odegaard getting a free shot on goal and has a really tight partnership with Van Dijk. Virgil van Dijk – 8/10: Brilliant reading of the game to get in front of Havertz to deny the German a second goal in the second half. Remains the driving force for the team. Milos Kerkez – 6/10: Sent one weak shot wide of the target when well placed. One beauty of a cross to set up a chance for Mac Allister, but frustrated home fans at times with poor distribution. Booked for a trip on Madueke. Alexis Mac Allister – 6/10: Went down demanding a penalty after a slight pull in the first half but rightly waved off. Should have levelled scores just before break but sent a header over bar. Shameful play-acting after touching heads with Madueke during incident that saw Argentine booked after arguing with Timber. Trey Nyoni – 8/10: First league start for teenager who could have been booked in a first minute for standing on the back of Odegaard's ankle. Impressive passing performance in midfield. 4 - Liverpool have scored just four goals at Anfield in the Premier League this season, their joint-fewest after five home matches in a top-flight campaign (also four in 1913-14 and 2012-13). Restricted. pic.twitter.com/te1GNFW7VI — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) November 1, 2026 Florian Wirtz – 7/10: Unlucky to see a curling free-kick come back off the crossbar. A key factor in Liverpool's relentless pressing. Bradley Barcola – 7/10: Record signing started on the left and caused Arsenal's defence problems, more so in the first half. One brilliant cross in the 20th minute from that flank deserved a finishing touch. Booked for a foul on Timber. Cody Gakpo – 6/10: Another Liverpool player who went down looking for a penalty in the opening half with no joy as Liverpool poured forward hunting for a leveller. One desperately poor cross with teammates waiting in the box elicited mass groans around Anfield. Alexander Isak – 6/10: Hit a shot wide of target in the first half. Sent another effort high and wide 10 minutes after half-time as Liverpool failed to register a shot on target despite 17 attempts on goal. Substitutes Dominik Szoboszlai (On for Nyoni, 58') – 6/10: Welcome sight for Liverpool fans but no chance to produce a moment of magic. Rio Ngumoha (On for Gakpo, 81') – 6/10: Had one shot turned out for a corner in added time. Lewis Koumas (On for Wirtz, 81') – N/A. Kostas Tsimikas (On for Kerkez, 81') – N/A. Victor Munoz (On for Araujo, 81') – N/A. Arsenal ratings: David Raya – 7/10: Scrambled a Van Dijk header out for a corner under pressure from Isak. Beaten all ends up by Wirtz free-kick that hit the bar. Booked for time-wasting. Jurrien Timber – 7/10: Could have conceded a penalty for a shirt pull on Isak. Had his hands full dealing with Barcola but stuck to his task and tried to get forward to support Madueke when possible. Ezri Konsa – 9/10: Up against it as Liverpool piled forward for much of the match, but the Gunners have now kept a clean sheet in six of their nine league games this season. Gabriel – 9/10: Went down embarrassingly in the opening minutes after being brushed in the face by Isak's hand but was a rock at the back for Arsenal, who gave a defensive masterclass in the face of intense pressure. Riccardo Calafiori – 8/10: This Arsenal backline continues to be something special and incredibly tough to break through, and the Italian was a key part of that at Anfield. Declan Rice – 8/10: Excellent overlap run followed by a low cross to set up Havertz's opening goal. Had a low shot easily saved by Alisson. A machine in the middle of the park whose energy is infectious. 24 - @Arsenal 's 24 points are the most by a team after nine games of a Premier League season since the Gunners themselves in 2022-23 (also 24). Only in 2004-05 and 2007-08 have they ever had more at this stage of a PL campaign (25 in both). Hungry. pic.twitter.com/JMu2gherPt — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) November 1, 2026 Bruno Guimaraes – 6/10: Marked one first-half interception in his own area by celebrating wildly in front of away fans. The Brazilian was given no time on the ball by relentless Liverpool press. Martin Odegaard – 7/10: Captain pressed high to take advantage of Alisson's poor pass, winning an interception and starting the move for Havertz's goal. Like Guimaraes, not given a moment's peace in possession. Noni Madueke – 7/10: Winger was involved in the build-up to Havertz's goal. Booked for taking down Barcola and stopping a counter-attack. Christos Tzolis – 7/10: Back in action for the first time after a hamstring injury, the Greek winger thought he had scored his first Arsenal goal with 15 minutes left only for Alisson to pull off a fine save. Kai Havertz – 7/10: Perfectly placed to tap in Rice's cross after 16 minutes. Nearly did the same with a cross-cum-shot from Guimaraes 10 minutes later. The German scores big goals in big matches. Substitutes Miles Lewis-Skelley (On for Guimaraes, 62') – 7/10: Picked up a harsh booking for a foul but helped Arsenal see out the match. Piero Hincapie (On for Tzolis, 84') – N/A. body:

title: China state broadcaster pulls Real Madrid match over Mbappé joke
body: China’s state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite an apology from the club’s star striker, Kylian Mbappé, for his “ill-judged” remarks about the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong. Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme “that makes [him] laugh the most” was the one in which his face is superimposed on a “Chinese dictator” resembling Mao. China Media Group, CCTV’s parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches after the furore, which also led several Chinese brands to drop Mbappé. China’s foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé’s apology “seriously”. Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised. China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them “an absolute prerequisite” for moving past the incident. It has acknowledged the apologies but has not said how long the broadcast blackout will last. Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” he had said. The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country’s past. Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China, died in 1976. During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society. This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities. It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city. Morey later backtracked after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors, and commercial partners. “I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives,” Morey later wrote. “I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors…I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention.” Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 on Sunday, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham, and Yan Diomande.

title: Russian athletes have no place in Finland if Moscow continues war, Foreign Minister says
body:
Yle reported this, according to Ukrinform.
“I intend to pursue the necessary measures in the coming days,” the Foreign Minister of Finland said.
Valtonen previously said she would call for a complete ban on issuing visas to Russian tourists to the EU.
Recently, five Finnish Members of the European Parliament signed a demand for new sanctions and visa restrictions against Russia.
The demand is aimed at preventing Russia’s national ice hockey teams from returning to international tournaments.
According to the signatories, host countries need to explore options for restricting the entry of Russian nationals.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Lausanne, Switzerland, ordered the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) to allow Russian national ice hockey teams to compete in international tournaments.

title: Trump doesn't intend to resume strikes against Iran right after midterm elections — Axios
body:
WASHINGTON, November 1. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump does not intend at this stage to resume military action against Iran immediately following the midterm Congressional elections scheduled for November 3, the US news outlet Axios reported.
According to its sources, Trump had a phone conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday. They discussed "the state of U.S. negotiations with Iran and how quickly to return to combat," Axios wrote referring to one Israeli and one U.S. source.
The outlet reported that "Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out — a strategy Netanyahu is concerned about."
An Israeli source called the conversation "tough," while a US official described it as "direct."
On Saturday, Trump stated that negotiations with Tehran are progressing well, but expressed doubt about Iran’s trustworthiness. He also declined to provide a definitive answer when asked whether he plans to resume military action against the Islamic Republic next week.
Earlier, Axios reported that a defeat for the Republican Party in the US midterm Congressional elections could prompt Trump to resume large-scale military operations against Iran. According to its data, opinions regarding potential attacks on the republic differ within the US administration. The MS NOW television channel previously noted, citing sources, that the US might resume strikes against Iran the day after the midterm congressional elections scheduled for November 3.

title: ‘Every venue will sell out’ — I will demand $500,000 if I tour with Wizkid – Davido
body: Afrobeats singer Davido said a joint tour with Wizkid would sell out venues worldwide, adding that he would demand $500,000 per show. Davido made the statement during an appearance on the IONWANNATALK show, where he discussed the possibility of recording music and touring with his colleague. However, he expressed uncertainty about whether a joint song with Wizkid would become a hit, citing the D’banj and 2Baba collaboration as an example. “If Wizkid and I do a song together, I don’t know if it will pop because when D’banj and 2Baba did a record together, it didn’t really pop,” Davido said. But he was more confident about touring together, saying, “If we tour together, I’ll ask for $500,000 per show because I know every venue will sell out.” The singer also said he and Wizkid hadn’t recorded a song together in about 10 years, explaining that they hadn’t collaborated because they couldn’t work together. Davido said he hadn’t been in the same mental space with Wizkid, adding that people had different opinions on whether their rivalry had made them bigger or whether working together would boost their careers. He also spoke about moving past disagreements, saying it takes maturity to admit when your feelings have changed. “I felt that way at some point but not anymore, and it takes a great man to do that,” he said.

title: Four Sacred Stops on a Boeotia Pilgrimage, From Hosios Loukas to Thebes
body: A Boeotia pilgrimage leads travellers beyond Arachova to Byzantine gold, a monastery that sheltered the fighters of 1821 and a Roman tomb linked to Saint Luke. Arachova and the slopes of Parnassus have long defined this region for travellers. But behind them lies an inland of castle towns, archaeological treasures, mountains and a dense web of religious monuments. Some of those monuments recall the glory of the middle Byzantine era, while others still echo the 1821 Revolution. Many also remain living monastic communities, so each stop on a Boeotia pilgrimage opens a window onto local life. Four stops on a Boeotia pilgrimage The Region of Central Greece now places religious and pilgrimage tourism at the front of its promotion . It also wants to link the leading monasteries and churches with the area’s wider culture and food. Its Boeotia pilgrimage takes in four distinct stops. They are Hosios Loukas, the Makariotissa Monastery, the Church of Saint Luke the Evangelist and Megali Panagia in Thebes. Because the sites sit close together, a Boeotia pilgrimage can fit into one day. Visitors can admire gold mosaics in the morning, then reach a monastery on the fir-covered slopes of Mount Helicon by midday. After an afternoon among the Christian traces of Thebes, the day can end with Boeotian wine and local flavours. Byzantine gold at Hosios Loukas On the western foothills of Helicon, the Monastery of Hosios Loukas grew around the revered figure of Hosios Loukas of Steiri. It is still perhaps the finest example of middle Byzantine architecture in Greece. Since 1990, it has featured on the UNESCO World Heritage List , together with the monasteries of Daphni and Nea Moni on Chios. Inside the gate stand the 10th-century Church of the Panagia, the 11th-century katholikon, or main church, a crypt, cells and galleries. Its katholikon mosaics, among the finest surviving Byzantine art anywhere, make a fitting start to a Boeotia pilgrimage. When daylight enters through the dome windows, the gold tesserae seem to come alive. The relic of the saint returned from Venice in 1986, while the candlelit crypt below holds his original tomb. Cheese and revolution at Makariotissa Perched near Domvraina, the Makariotissa Monastery offers a different picture of monastic life. It underwent major renovations in 1609, then again in 1802. In 1821, it became a key local stronghold of the Revolution, serving as a base and refuge for the troops of Georgios Karaiskakis . A new brotherhood revived Makariotissa in 1992, and since then worship and production have gone hand in hand. The monks raise livestock and keep alive traditional cheesemaking. Every day, their modern dairy inside the monastery produces fresh milk, strained yoghurt and rizogalo, a creamy rice pudding. It also keeps the community self-sufficient. Saint Luke’s tomb in Thebes On a Boeotia pilgrimage, Thebes brings a name known around the world. Its story evokes the myth of Oedipus, the sacrifice of Antigone and the military genius of Epaminondas . Beneath that ancient layer, however, lies an equally deep Christian story. In the city’s south-east stands the Pilgrimage Church of Saint Luke the Evangelist, a landmark on any Boeotia pilgrimage. Church tradition holds that the Evangelist, a physician and icon painter , chose Thebes as his final stop, where he lived, taught and died. Inside, a Roman marble sarcophagus from the 2nd century AD is linked to his first burial. Then, in 357 AD, his relics went to Constantinople and, after centuries of travel through Europe, ended up in Italy. Finally, on 17 September 2000, part of the relics returned to Thebes and rest again in the ancient marble tomb. A church built like a stone book On the western side of the historic centre, the Church of Agios Dimitrios is better known as Megali Panagia. The present church opened in spring 1867, because the earthquakes of 1853 had destroyed the older building. Its architect, Ioannis Filippotis of Tinos, set ancient fragments, early Christian pieces and Byzantine carvings from the surrounding area into its outer walls. As a result, the building reads like a book of stone. At its heart hangs the icon of Megali Panagia, which tradition attributes to Saint Luke himself. That link also ties it to the previous stop, creating a small themed route within the city. Planning a Boeotia pilgrimage all year Beyond the four stops, a Boeotia pilgrimage can also reach Orchomenos, Chaeronea, Livadeia with its running waters, Plataea, Thespies and Helicon. Villages, trails through fir and oak forests and a proud food tradition complete the picture. Pilgrimage tourism also stays relevant 365 days a year, since monasteries draw visitors in every season. At the same time, the big religious feasts offer further reasons to escape. The region hopes a Boeotia pilgrimage, backed by culture, food and quality stays, will turn day trips into longer visits. Fani Papathoma, Deputy Regional Governor for Tourism and Culture of Central Greece, said: “From Hosios Loukas and Makariotissa to the Holy Church of Saint Luke the Evangelist and Megali Panagia, we are showcasing places that continue to speak of Boeotia, its history and its tradition.
