The Justice Department has issued new subpoenas in a criminal investigation into the election, CBS News reported, and the Trump administration is suing to block the election from being certified if Sen. Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion." President Trump says both Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state-level investigation , and said Thursday the probe could "impact whether somebody is seated in the U.S. Senate."
A Peltola campaign spokesperson pushed back, calling Dunleavy's comments a "threat to overrule the will of Alaska voters."
"Mary won't be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted," the spokesperson said.
As the controversy over the two Dan Sullivans draws nationwide reactions, CBS News visited remote Petersburg, Alaska, to look for one person who hasn't spoken out — Daniel J. Sullivan.
The retired teacher hails from the small fishing town, located on an island in southeastern Alaska that's only accessible by air or sea. In prior interviews , he has insisted he isn't trying to trick people and is genuinely interested in becoming a senator.
CBS News visited his house, only to find no one home.
But we spoke with a friend and former colleague who said Daniel J. Sullivan wouldn't do anything malicious.
"I wouldn't be surprised if this was actually, some campaign person may have come up with this idea," Mary Ellen Anderson said. "Whether Dan bought into it or not, I don't know. I don't think so. I can't imagine him being used that way."
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will make a joint appearance with Rep. Haley Stevens at an event in Detroit on Sunday, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, marking one of their only side-by-side campaign events since facing off in the primary.
The Associated Press was first to report the event.
Stevens endorsed El-Sayed, but the former rivals — who offered starkly differing visions for the future of their party during the primary — largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.
On Wednesday, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News he plans to vote for Republican nominee Mike Rogers, arguing El-Sayed — a vehement critic of Israel — had acted "recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community."
In a CNN interview later that day, Stevens reaffirmed her support for El-Sayed, saying, "We're a household divided." She added that El-Sayed still needs to work to win undecided voters.
Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it.
Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ad's planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million.
The divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. That was despite the two having not seen each other for nearly 50 years. Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
Ramaswamy had defended the ad, though a later version trimmed some portions.
Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement that Ramaswamy "should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it's totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio."
President Trump and Vice President JD Vance said they supported the decision to air the ad. The president said he told Ramaswamy to leave it on the air, adding "she's fair game."
The Justice Department has issued grand jury subpoenas to state and local officials in California, according to sources with direct knowledge and copies seen by CBS News.
The move escalates a dispute over allegations by the federal government that the state may have as many as 20,000 non-citizens registered to vote ahead of the midterm elections.
The subpoenas were issued between Oct. 21 and 24. News of the subpoenas came not long after a judge rejected the Trump administration's bid to require California election officials to separate out tens of thousands of mail ballots.
"There's a lot of pissed-off farmers right now at Trump and Marshall," said Kansas farmer Jeff Preisser, "because you see the situation we're in."
In the final stretch of Kansas' unexpectedly competitive Senate race between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton, the Preisser family laid out their situation for CBS News, handing over a piece of paper detailing their heightened expenses.
It cost them $737,375 more to operate their farm in 2026 than last year, almost entirely due to higher diesel and fertilizer costs wrought by the Iran war. Meanwhile, drought, low commodity prices and trade wars have cut their revenue by $325,000.
The squeeze has pushed Kansas farms to the edge — scrambling farmers' political loyalties.
Voting in the midterms is already well underway, with 44.8 million Americans already casting ballots as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida Election Lab .
That includes nearly 23.6 million in-person early votes and 21.3 million returned mail ballots.

title: Battlegroup North drone crew strikes Ukrainian Kozak armored combat vehicle in Sumy Region
body:
KURSK, November 2. /TASS/. An FPV drone crew from Russia’s Battlegroup North has destroyed a Kozak armored combat vehicle (ACV) of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in a forest in the Sumy Region, a company commander with the call sign Taiga told TASS.
"By using a reconnaissance UAV a drone crew from the Battlegroup North detected an enemy Kozak ACV concealed in a specially prepared revetment in a forest in the Sumy Region. After analyzing the gathered intelligence, a decision was made to engage the enemy's ACV. FPV drones were deployed against the target, and the enemy's armored vehicle was successfully destroyed," he said.
It is noted that UAV crews continue to strike Ukrainian Armed Forces weaponry, equipment, military facilities, and personnel on a daily basis, which is recorded in real time by objective monitoring systems.

title: More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy in London
body: More than 300 people have been arrested during a protest supporting the banned Palestine Action group outside the US embassy, police have said. Hundreds of people gathered at Nine Elms in London on Saturday, with many holding signs reading phrases such as: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that it made 325 arrests. The force added on social media that 320 of them were for “expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act”. At least 4,000 arrests have been made in relation to the group, which was proscribed in July 2025. The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action’s ban under terrorism legislation , after the group’s co-founder was granted permission to appeal it. The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal. Officers on Saturday made arrests into the evening, taking people to police vans for transfer, to the applause of many protesters, some of whom chanted: “Free, free Palestine.” In some instances, officers had to carry demonstrators who refused to walk. Retired lawyer Charles Allison – who was taken by police in the afternoon – had travelled from Cumbria to participate. He said he feared for people’s civil liberties, which he said were “being devalued and watered down”. “I hope the Supreme Court justices – they won’t necessarily be influenced by it [the protest] – but I hope that they will take a long-term view of what is happening in this country and decide that the proscription was unlawful, as I believe it was,” the 75-year-old said. David Bolden, another protester awaiting arrest called the ban an “absurd law”. Defend Our Juries, which has been co-ordinating a series of protests over the ban, said the number of people detained this weekend took the total over 4,000 arrests since the group was proscribed, calling it “truly dystopian”. According to Home Office figures seen by the BBC, 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026. Along with the 134 people arrested outside Westminster Magistrates Court earlier this year and those on Saturday brings the total up to 4,089. The BBC has contacted the Met to confirm any figures it might hold. Amnesty International UK has criticised the arrests and called for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action. Defend Our Juries called the arrests “unjust” and an assault on free speech.

title: Arab Americans who backed Trump in 2024 are abandoning his party for Abdul El-Sayed
body: Yahya Basha stands outside his hospital north of Detroit, surrounded by new blue signs he has put up: Abdul for US Senate. He hired two people to guard the signs round the clock after they were repeatedly stolen. Some passers-by honk and give a thumbs-up, while others have called to complain. It is a significant pivot for Dr Basha, 80, a Syrian-American physician and longtime community leader in Michigan. Two years ago, he met Donald Trump and his team and helped build support for the Republican presidential candidate among Arab and Muslim American voters in the state. He still keeps a selfie he took with Mr Trump on his phone. Both men are smiling, while Mr Trump's eyes are closed. In 2024, many Arab Americans were furious with the administration of Joe Biden, Mr Trump's Democratic predecessor, over its handling of the war in Gaza. Throughout the conflict, they felt their efforts to be heard on the issue had failed. Dr Basha says the Trump team was, by contrast, very receptive to their concerns at the time. So he donated to the campaign and organised meetings with Arab-American leaders. But like many Arab Americans, his support for Mr Trump and the Republican Party has since dissipated amid discontent over the President's handling of the economy and the war in Gaza, as well as his decision to launch a new war in Iran. Before Tuesday's midterm elections , Dr Basha has thrown his support behind Abdul El-Sayed , the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan, despite being pleased with Mr Trump's approach to Syria. He says he has personally donated about $500,000 to Mr El-Sayed's campaign – more than he has ever given to a single candidate – and helped him raise even more from Arab and Muslim Americans in Michigan and elsewhere. “I'm happy with the President's support for Syria, for stability and safety, for an end to wars in Syria and for a united Syria,” Dr Basha says. “But at the same time, I don't want religion to become his comedy material.” If Mr El-Sayed wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. But for weeks, Mr Trump has mocked his name at rallies and online, repeatedly referring to him as “Mohammed”. The comments have deeply offended many Muslims, particularly in Michigan, a state Mr Trump has won twice. “He is using a racist platform and attacking Abdul because of his name, and focusing on his religion, his mother or grandmother or sister. That's very cheap,” Dr Basha says. Mr El-Sayed's opponent, Mike Rogers , a Trump ally, has also attacked him, claiming that the candidate and members of his family have connections to armed groups in the Middle East – allegations he has repeatedly denied. Mr El-Sayed, 42, has campaigned on universal health care, ending state collaboration with federal immigration enforcement and stopping military funding for wars abroad. Foreign policy has also been a major focus of his campaign. Mr El-Sayed has described Israel's conduct in Gaza as genocide and opposes further US military aid to the country. He has argued that the US should instead prioritise funding domestic needs, such as education and health, a message that has resonated with many residents. Candace Kawatso, 69, is a retired teacher from Detroit Public Schools. She said several of her students had suffered from lead poisoning, a longstanding public-health problem in Michigan, particularly in Detroit and Flint. One of her third-grade pupils became almost blind. Ms Kawatso helped her to obtain free glasses after hers broke, through a programme championed by Mr El-Sayed when he was a public health administrator. “He had the water tested for lead and had children in Detroit public schools tested for lead. He wants public schools to be more equitable. He wants everybody to have access to great public schools and health care,” Ms Kawatso said. 'Zero' support Michigan is one of a handful of closely watched swing states, where the outcome of the Senate race could help to determine control of the chamber. It is also home to the largest concentration of Arab Americans in the US. They make up about 5 per cent of the state's voters. Wasel Yousef, a longtime Republican and community organiser, said support for Mr Trump among the community was now essentially “zero”. “Arabs feel like Republicans have pushed them out,” Mr Yousef says. Although he still plans to vote for Mr Rogers, he says he has been unable to help the Republican campaign among Arab and Muslim Americans. Much of the community's trust in the party has been lost. Mr Yousef says he helped Mr Rogers to hold meetings with the Chaldean community and other Christian Arabs in Dearborn, where he retains some support. Two years ago, Bishara Bahbah, a Palestinian American and longtime Democrat, established the group Arab Americans for Trump. The organisation played a significant role in rallying support for Mr Trump, particularly in Dearborn. He went on to win Dearborn in 2024, securing more than 42 per cent of the vote. Mr Bahbah said he had received personal assurances from Mr Trump and his team that the President wanted to end the conflict in Gaza – a sharp contrast with what he described as the Biden administration's refusal to heed calls to rein in Israel. Although he credits Mr Trump with securing a ceasefire in Gaza, he says little has been done since to ease the suffering of Palestinians there. Last year, he changed the group's name to Arab Americans for Peace after Mr Trump discussed the possibility of the US taking over Gaza . He says he is deeply offended by Mr Trump's recent remarks about Mr El-Sayed. “People's names are very important to them. They're their identity, and you can't make fun of people's names,” he says. Low approvals The Republican Party is heading into the election just as its leader, Mr Trump, has a historically low approval rating stuck in the low to mid-30s. Many Americans are unhappy with the ever-rising cost of living, including increases in food and fuel prices. The war in Iran has also proved deeply unpopular. Mr Rogers has campaigned on reviving the state's manufacturing industry, lowering the cost of living and strengthening public safety. In recent weeks, he has sought to distance himself from Mr Trump on two issues that have become liabilities in Michigan: tariffs on Canada and the war in Iran. In campaign ads he said, “Canada is not our enemy”, and urged a quick end to the Iran conflict, because of its impact on energy costs and household budgets. Neither ad names Mr Trump. “The challenge for Rogers is that a lot of the affordability crisis and gas prices tend to impact white, working-class voters most because they do a lot of driving,” said John Feehery, a Republican strategist. Midterm elections tend to attract low turnouts, but this year is set to buck that trend, with high numbers of early votes already cast. The party of the sitting President historically loses seats in the House of Representatives. "Typically a president, whether he's good or bad, Republican or Democrat, loses the midterms. Nobody's ever explained why," Mr Trump said from the Oval Office on Friday. "But I think we have a shot at doing well. Maybe very well." In Grosse Pointe, a wealthy suburb of Detroit, a Republican campaign headquarters is neatly arranged, with signs, billboards and campaign flyers displayed on tables. Leslie, a volunteer, said she was initially drawn to Mr Trump because she saw him as a political outsider capable of disrupting a system she considered broken. She welcomed his first-term efforts to shake up Washington. But she believes he has since become more like the establishment politicians he once promised to challenge. “Trump was a disruptor and I was pro that,” said Leslie, who asked to be identified by her first name only. She sees Mr Rogers as a more traditional Republican, particularly on fiscal issues and the concerns of working-class people. “I feel like Trump has moved away from that position,” she said. Although she remains a Trump voter, she said she was increasingly uncomfortable with his behaviour and the direction of his presidency. “I can't stand all the name-calling. I can't stand it,” Leslie said. Amy said she was drawn to Mr Rogers because of his stance on public safety. She was turned off by Democrats, including Mr El-Sayed, who she said supported reducing the number of armed police officers. “The violence around here, the gunshots at night. I know that's about gun control and all that, but we need to – you can't take away our police,” she said. “You don't need as many police, but you need them.” 'This is America' Amer Zahr, a comedian and activist, says Arab support for Mr Trump two years ago was not a rejection of the Democratic party, but a move to punish Mr Biden. "It wasn't an embrace of Republicans, it was a middle finger to the Democrats," Mr Zahr says. With early voting already under way, volunteers were gathering outside a voting centre in Dearborn. The latest forecast by On Point Politics shows that nearly 1.5 million votes have already been cast in Michigan, with the Democrats ahead by nearly 15 percentage points. Adel Mozip, a Democratic candidate for the Dearborn school board, said parents were concerned about their children's education and school funding. At the state level, he said, residents were also worried about rising prices, inflation and the cost of health care. “I never imagined, as a Muslim and Arab American, that we would have somebody who's running in Grand Rapids, who's getting so many fans in Traverse City, and his name is 11 letters, and that's just a first name [Mr El-Sayed's full first name is Abdulrahman], who sounds like me, who prays like me,” Mr Mozip said. “But this is America.”

title: How Canada’s resource wealth makes it a strategic partner for the UAE and Europe
body: “Worthy Canadian initiative” is a common joke for the world’s most boring headline. But, threatened by the US, Canada is launching initiatives that could be more world-shaping than worthy. The UAE and the EU have become two vertices of the triangle including this northern resource giant. The Canada-EU summit concluded in Montreal, one of the most European cities in North America, on Friday. Though Prime Minister Mark Carney’s hopes of “associate membership” may not be granted in so many words, a much closer relationship is on the cards. And on Tuesday, the UAE signed a comprehensive economic partnership with Ottawa . The UAE committed $50 billion of investment in the country last year. This has a strong energy component: Abu Dhabi’s renewable energy champion Masdar concluded a co-operation agreement with federal agency Natural Resources Canada. Simultaneously, Dubai’s DP World is discussing developing the northern port of Churchill, on Hudson Bay, with access to the Arctic and Atlantic oceans. Rail connects it to the Pacific. Canada’s official Latin motto translates as “From Sea to Sea”, and some have proposed amending it to “From Sea to Sea to Sea” to respect the northern ocean. Churchill’s operator suggests it could be part of an Asia-Europe trade corridor that would be as fast and more secure than traditional routes through the Red Sea. The fast-warming Arctic, itself a warning of dangerous climate change, is opening up new shipping routes through previously ice-choked straits. These moves span four global trends. First, the need for other great and middle powers to build alliances and lessen dependence on an increasingly erratic US, a revanchist Russia and a potentially overbearing China. Second, the creation of alternative transport routes as maritime security comes under threat . Third, the construction of new trade architecture while other countries try to demolish it. Fourth, the search for reliable providers of critical resources. Resource superpowers The UAE and Canada may not have much in common geographically, but they are resource superpowers. While the UAE’s bounty concentrates mostly on hydrocarbons, the northern nation has those, plus many others. At nearly 6.2 million barrels per day, it is the fourth-biggest oil producer in the world and, depending on your view of Venezuela, the second or third-largest reserves owner. It is fifth in gas output, and its shale resources ensure plenty of room to grow production. The Shell-led LNG Canada in British Columbia began exporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) last June, with an ideal geography to supply Asia. LNG Canada is set to double capacity by the early 2030s, and two other projects are due to start in 2027 and 2028. Bloomberg last month suggested that Adnoc’s international unit XRG was interested in taking a stake in LNG Canada. The company already bought Calgary's Nova Chemicals in a $13.4 billion deal last March. Canada is first in the world in extracting potash, a crucial fertiliser, second in uranium mining , and fourth in gold, platinum and nickel mining and aluminium smelting. And it is an agricultural hothouse, with huge exports of wheat, oilseed, livestock, wood and other crops. For the new strategic minerals, as well as nickel for batteries, it is a growing producer of lithium and natural graphite. It has important deposits of titanium and vanadium, crucial metals for aerospace and defence technology. In the famous and geopolitically sensitive rare earths , it has no commercial mines today, but holds large resources, and several projects are being developed. Finally, its cool climate, open land and abundance of cheap, zero-carbon hydropower – where it is the third-biggest generator in the world – make it a good site for data centres . This commodity wealth makes it tremendously attractive as a partner to the EU: a stable, Western, free-market democracy, and closer than the similarly advantaged Australia. It is further from the UAE, but many of the same attractions apply. In turn, Canada needs good friends. Seventy-six per cent of its exports go to its overbearing southern neighbour. The EU, China and the UK are each of similar weight, with about 4 per cent to 5 per cent each. This dependence makes Canada vulnerable to the US's arm-twisting with tariffs. While Canada will no doubt expand trade with China, that brings its own political exposure. A recent preliminary referendum on independence for the hydrocarbon heartland province of Alberta, backed by right-wing voices in the US, was heavily defeated. But Canadians are not amused by “51st state” taunts. They saw how their Arctic neighbour, Greenland , was intimidated by the White House, which eyes enviously its rare earths and possible oil. New routes, new partnerships Transport barriers mean Canada does not earn full value for its resources. American natural gas producers might complain about low prices, currently $2.86 per million British thermal units. Europeans’ wallets are emptied, and their energy-intensive industries hollowed out by paying around $30, as they suffer from the cut-off of LNG from the Gulf. But the wholesale price in Alberta, Canada’s main producing region, is just $1.40 per MMBtu. It is a similar story for oil. With only one pipeline to the Pacific, Albertan producers are hostage to the US market. Western Canadian crude usually sells at about a $12 per barrel discount to the US’s West Texas Intermediate. That differential has now widened to $31 per barrel. Mr Carney has sought to promote new pipelines, to integrate the national electricity grid, and in general to recharge the Canadian economy by diversifying exports and slashing inter-provincial trading barriers. Broadening its transport infrastructure is a crucial element and needs deep-pocketed investors with a long time horizon. Full development of the Churchill port and rail corridor alone will cost $57 billion. It will not replace Suez or Panama, but the current war in the Gulf shows how valuable back-up plans can become. Like Western countries in general, Canada also struggles less with mining critical minerals and more with processing them. Investors are deterred by high costs, lack of access to proprietary technologies, and the tendency of China to undercut competitors. This may be a fruitful area for triangular UAE-EU-Canada co-operation, whether investing in metals refineries in Canada or in the Gulf, as part of an integrated supply chain. Diversification – of allies, trading partners, transport routes and commodity providers – seems like a good policy today. Although technically hydrocarbon competitors, the UAE and Canada have much to complement with Europe. A new geography mingles the warm waters of the Gulf with the chilly north.

title: At Adipec, energy’s big chance to power the AI boom
body: Artificial intelligence is transforming the energy industry, while its growing appetite for electricity demands urgent attention. As Adipec opens on Monday, the key question for stakeholders is how to turn this technological promise into a more resilient energy system. The four-day gathering, held annually in Abu Dhabi since 1984, takes place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty. Global energy markets have been disrupted by geopolitical turmoil, with the threat to vital shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz adding to concerns over supply. Yet energy flows continue from the UAE and the wider region. And demand for energy remains strong, particularly from Asian countries, whose delegations are expected to attend in record numbers . The participation of 2,260 exhibitors, 181,000 pre-registered visitors, 40 government ministers and 12,000 conference delegates further underlines the value of a forum that brings together producers, consumers and investors to address their shared challenges. This year, AI is central to that conversation. New research jointly conducted by Adnoc, XRG and Microsoft shows that 62 per cent of surveyed energy leaders now rank the technology among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42 per cent last year. Almost nine in 10 increased spending on it, while 63 per cent expect returns on existing investments to cover or exceed costs. Ramping up energy production can only partially meet this surging demand. Investment must be made to modernise grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation, too The benefits that AI brings to the energy industry are increasingly becoming clear as it moves from pilot programmes to wider adoption. It is reportedly already improving maintenance, enhancing production, making hazardous inspections safer and helping balance complex electricity networks. These are practical, tangible gains for an industry that is today confronting unpredictable supply and growing demand. And of course, this technology is creating new supply demands. According to the survey, nearly three quarters of respondents expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030, while only 52 per cent believe existing infrastructure can meet the additional demand. A separate Adipec survey found that 81 per cent of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts. Increasing energy production can only partially meet this surging demand. Investment must be made to modernise grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation, too. Adnoc’s advancements across the oil production ecosystem is taking these developments into account. Masdar’s ambitions in the US data-centre market show how renewable energy can help meet computing needs. But reliable supply will require a mix of technologies, supported by infrastructure capable of delivering electricity when and where it is needed. The central theme of last year’s Adipec was “Knowledge is power, but now power is knowledge”, meaning the electricity needed for AI processing. That equation is being tested by geopolitical strain and rising electricity demand – which is why one of this year’s themes, “Performance under pressure: energy systems in a new era”, could not be more relevant today as the energy industry focuses on building resilience. The answers on how to achieve this, it is hoped, can be found at Adipec over the next four days.

title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
body: Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported. An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured. The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injuries to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a “particularly sophisticated” incendiary device. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a Molotov cocktail at a police line was “what I call a murder attempt”, adding officers were working to find the perpetrators. Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools. Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities. There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week’s protests, the French interior ministry said. But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported. The officer – part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry – said his unit “suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries”. Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device “had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail”. “We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters,” he said. “These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state.” Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said. French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by “grenades”. France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests. Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend , as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

title: Brent crude oil price falls below $111 per barrel for the first time since October 22
body:
MOSCOW, November 2 /TASS/. The price of a January Brent crude oil futures contract on the London-based ICE exchange has fallen below $111 per barrel for the first time since October 22, 2026, according to trading data.
As of 05:04 a.m. Moscow time (03:04 a.m.), the price of Brent was down 0.52% at $110.98 per barrel.
By 05:14 a.m. Moscow time (03:14 a.m.), Brent was trading at $110.68 per barrel (-0.79%).

title: Poultry Division without a hen
body: One of the most funnily memorable stories I ever heard from a state governor was in 2001, when then Borno State Governor Mala Kachallah paid us a visit at New Nigerian, where I was the editor. He had left his state capital, Maiduguri in some turmoil because the state NLC branch was demanding implementation of the newly approved national minimum wage. The governor said BOSG was handicapped because it had the second largest number of civil servants in Nigeria, 30,000, so he had to retrench some workers before he could implement the new wage. NLC rejected that option. To give us an idea of the problem he faced, Kachallah said, “The Poultry Division of the Borno State Ministry of Agriculture; their last hen died in 1981, but they have 571 staffers, and every year they bring a promotion list.” Eleven years later, I heard a slightly different complaint from Borno State Governor Kashim Shettima. In response to Boko Haram attacks, he had banned motorcycles from Maiduguri streets and instead bought 5,000 tricycles, all of which were sold to beneficiaries at a discounted price, to be paid for instalmentally. Many beneficiaries turned around, sold them at an even lower price and squandered the money. The governor was unhappy; he wondered if such attitude can happen anywhere else. I said, “Sir, take heart. I don’t know about the South, but in almost every Northern state, the same thing will happen if you sell anything on loan at a discounted price.” The Kachallah/Shettima worry in Borno reminded me of what then Niger State Governor Musa Inuwa told me in 1993. He had proposed to retrench some skilled civil servants and instead get for them bank loans to set up businesses. They rejected the plan and threatened to go on strike. Inuwa said, “Niger State Scholarships Board has eight typists but only three typewriters. Niger State Ministry of Works has 60 skilled artisans, carpenters, electricians and plumbers who are not doing any work. They are to be found sitting in front of the ministry’s premises, and small thing they will say “Strike! Strike!” I used to think that governors are well fed, but on two occasions I encountered a hungry governor. In 1993, Governor Musa Inuwa gave me an 8am appointment in Minna but when I arrived at his office, he had a sudden visitor in Abia State Governor Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu. I had to wait for two hours until he escorted Onu out of town. When I was ushered into his office, he apologized for keeping me waiting, said we should proceed with the interview, even though he had not eaten his breakfast. So I said, “Sir, please have your breakfast. I will wait in CPS’s office.” He was very grateful! In 2002, Jigawa State Governor Ibrahim Saminu Turaki arrived very late for an interview at New Nigerian. An hour into the interview, he suddenly said he was very hungry, and asked if the man who used to sell roasted meat at nearby NEPA roundabout was still there. Staffers rushed out and brought hot roasted meat. The governor retreated into the MD’s office, ate his fill, and returned to continue the interview. Most memorable was Abacha-era Works Minister Major General Abdulkarim Adisa’s press conference in Abuja. A reporter audaciously asked him why he awarded contracts only to his friends. The rambunctious Adisa said, “Those who say I give contracts only to my friends, I pray to God to make them minister so that they will give contracts to their enemies.” In 2000AD, as Editor of New Nigerian, I accompanied my managing director Dr. Omar Faruk Ibrahim to Sokoto to pacify Governor Attahiru Bafarawa. He was very angry because, in our inside page, his picture was used to illustrate a story about a Sokoto magistrate court that convicted two homosexuals. Bafarawa was certain that New Nigerian’s Sokoto reporter planted it that way to embarrass him. We struggled to convince him that the reporter was far away from the production center and could not possibly know how a sub editor carelessly designed that page. In 1991, very fresh into my journalism career as a Citizen magazine reporter, I was in Katsina to interview military governor Colonel John Yahaya Madaki. As we sat in the visitors’ room, Madaki saw us on a CCTV camera. He stormed out, chased away a woman and a male contractor, then came for me and said, “Who are you?” His Chief Press Secretary Abubakar Yar’adua quickly intervened and said he brought me. I was ushered into the office and sat in the conference area. Madaki left his desk, came near me and sat on the center table, his starched khaki menacingly rubbing my leg. I was young and audacious then, so I said, “Sir, please sit down on the chair.” The Jungle Expert exploded; “This is my office! I will sit down where I want! If you don’t want, pack your things and go!” But we had a rich two-hour interview. My next explosive gubernatorial interview came 18 years later, with Adamawa State Governor Murtala Nyako in Abuja. Two of us were ushered to the dining table where the governor sat. Looking at the other man, he said, “Girigiri [Second Republic Senator Girigiri Lawan of Yobe], I asked you to come because I am going to talk to this journalist, and I do not trust him.” Turning to me, he said, “You, you hate the people of Adamawa State!” I quickly replied, “Sir, I was born in Adamawa State.” “It’s a lie!” “It is true!” “When?” “In Northern Nigeria. My father was the D.O in Mubi.” Nyako then changed tack and said, “I know why you are mischievous. It is because your family’s cattle have finished. There is no person more evil than a Fulani man whose cattle has finished.” I said, “Sir, my grandfather left behind many cows.” “How many?” I said, “Up to 30.” He said, “My father left behind 15,000 cows!” Katsina State Governor Umaru Musa Yar’adua was one of the gentlest governors I interviewed, in 2001. I [audaciously] asked him why he drove a car with three commissioners to go on a condolence visit, why he stopped at a roadside kiosk to buy cigarettes, and why, as governor, he prayed under a Tsamiya tree instead of entering the Friday mosque to pray beside the Emir. Malam Umaru looked at me quietly and said, “I have been praying under that tree for 18 years. Why should I enter the mosque and pray beside the Emir, only to come out again one day when I am no longer the governor and resume praying under that tree? You see, all these things, my fear is for women and children. Me, any day I lose privileges, I can adjust, but when women and children are used to something, they find it difficult to adjust. It is the cause of the corruption all around.” In 1992, I interviewed Sokoto State Governor Malam Yahaya Abdulkarim and asked him about a protracted quarrel between himself and Senator Garba Ila Gada. The governor looked at me and said, “Turn off your tape recorder.” He then said, “You know the real reason for this quarrel between me and him? It is because he wants this chair.” I once asked former Abia State governor and then ANPP national chairman Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu about the fiasco at ANPP’s 1999 Kaduna convention, when he was nominated as presidential candidate and then substituted with AD candidate Olu Falae. Onu laughed heartily and said, “My brother, it is something you do not wish to happen even to your worst enemy.” In 2001, Kogi State Governor Abubakar Audu invited me to Lokoja to mark two years of his administration. When I was ushered in, he said no interview until I first toured his projects. His Chief Press Secretary then grabbed a car and we charged through the state until well after dusk, inspecting roads, housing projects, the Audu Oyigi eye hospital and the then new Abubakar Audu University at Ayingba. On our way back I told the CPS that I was really impressed with what I saw. So he said, “When we go to see Oga, please praise him! My Oga likes praise. Please praise him very well, and agbada will flow!” Small fry like me, I once found myself settling a quarrel between two governors. Former Zamfara State governor Senator Ahmed Sani came to my Abuja office in 2009 and said, “I come to report your friend [his successor, Governor Mahmud Aliyu Shinkafi].” He told me that he went to Government House to see the governor, was told that he was praying in the mosque, so he waited for him in his office. After a very long wait, he asked what was delaying the governor’s return, and the office messenger told him that when the governor heard that Yarima was waiting for him in the office, he summoned his car to the mosque and sneaked away. I then sent a message to Governor Shinkafi and said “Sir, Yarima has reported you to me.” The very gentle Shinkafi replied that he will be in Abuja in two days and will send for me, which he did. I told him what Yarima said, and he said, “Yarima was wrong!” That there was going to be an ANPP primaries contest in Bakura LGA, and he asked Yarima who was his preferred candidate, but he said both men were the same to him. The two men went for the primaries and after one of them won, Yarima said he preferred the other one. “That was why I went away.” For the first [and possibly the last] time in my life, I found myself scolding a sitting governor. I said, “Sir, you made a mistake by going away. As the Governor, you should have stayed and told him firmly that he was wrong. But by sneaking away, you spoilt the case.”

title: Thousands of jobs at Virgin Media O2 to be cut
body: Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff face redundancy risk as the telecoms firm seeks to cut costs amid billions of pounds in debt and tougher competition. The broadband provider has not finalised how many roles it will cut, but the BBC understands it is likely to be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce. VMO2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is facing competition from both smaller providers and giants like BT, which has agreed to acquire rival TalkTalk, a move VMO2 has firmly opposed. VMO2 declined to comment. The Prospect union, which represents VMO2 staff, said the cuts were “disappointing and very unsettling”. Deputy general secretary Noel McClean said it was “committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected”. The majority of affected staff will be in non-customer-facing roles, and senior leadership changes are already underway, the BBC has been told. VMO2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers alongside the job cuts first reported by Sky News. As of 30 June, VMO2’s total debt stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm’s latest accounts. Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper “altnets” like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre. VMO2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by VMO2’s owners. However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from VMO2. BT share price jump At the time, VMO2 called the BT takeover a “stitch-up”, which allowed its rival to “tighten its grip” over the market. BT said its deal provided “a safety net” for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover. On Friday, BT’s share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported VMO2 was close to agreeing a deal to use its rival’s fibre broadband network. VMO2 was minded to go ahead with the plans after halting upgrades and expansion of its own infrastructure to ease concerns over its debt pile, the paper reported. The BBC has been told the deal is very close and that VMO2 is highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday.

title: Kentridge’s Orpheus Show Draws Queues at Athens Archaeological Museum
body: Long queues formed outside the National Archaeological Museum in Athens on Sunday, as crowds came to see the new William Kentridge exhibition on the myth of Orpheus. The Hellenic Ministry of Culture shared a photo of the line on the museum steps in a Facebook post . It pointed to “two reasons” for the crowds, starting with the “amazing” new show. Sunday 1 November was also the first free-admission Sunday of the winter season at state museums and sites. Free entry then applies on the first and third Sundays of each month until 31 March. Orpheus meets the museum’s ancient treasures Titled “Imitate the Sleep of Stones – Orpheus and Eurydice: Transformation and Return”, the show opened on 30 October and runs until 24 January 2027. Curator Burcu Fikretoğlu put it together, according to the museum . The South African artist William Kentridge, born in Johannesburg in 1955, works across drawing, film and theatre, as well as opera. In this show, his works sit beside ancient objects tied to music, death and transformation. First, rust-coloured steel figures and paper tree silhouettes by William Kentridge stand among the kouroi, sphinxes and grave monuments. They then lead visitors to the central hall, where a diorama uses the 19th-century stage trick known as “Pepper’s Ghost”. In addition, the antiquities on show include a Corinthian red-figure krater (c. 400–375 BC) showing Orpheus playing the lyre. An ivory lyre from the Menidi tholos tomb, dating to the 14th–13th century BC, joins it. A white kylix by the Pistoxenos Painter (c. 470 BC), on loan from the Acropolis Museum, also features. It shows Orpheus raising his lyre as a Thracian woman attacks him. Linked to the Greek National Opera’s L’Orfeo The exhibition opened on the eve of the premiere of Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo, which William Kentridge directs for the Greek National Opera at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. Like the show, it has international backing, as a co-production with Glyndebourne and New York’s Metropolitan Opera. Culture Minister Lina Mendoni called the show “emblematic”. In her words, the works “converse with selected antiquities” around the myth of Orpheus and “life, love, death”. For his part, William Kentridge said he was “very happy” to show his work in Athens. The museum itself, which earlier extended its Mycenaean exhibition , faces its own transformation as the Chipperfield extension moves ahead. Until 15 November, the museum at 44 28is Oktovriou (Patission) Street opens 8am to 8pm, except Tuesdays (1pm to 8pm). Standard admission costs €20, and the next free Sunday falls on 15 November.
