title: Our Commitment to Ndi Enugu: The Journey So Far
body: GUEST COLUMNIST BY PETER MBAH First let me begin by giving my profound gratitude to the entire Management and Staff of Godfrey Okoye University and its other collaborators for this excellent forum – and the opportunity it offers for an enriching dialogue. My dear people of Enugu State, I want to begin today by asking you to remember something. Think back to May 2023, when we first assumed office. Think about the condition of our state, the difficulties we faced, and the expectations we had gradually learned to live without. I want us to be honest about that period, because unless we remember where we began, it becomes difficult to appreciate the distance we have travelled. There was a time when Monday was no longer an ordinary working day in Enugu. Shops remained closed. Roads were deserted. Parents were afraid to send their children to school. People who depended on their daily earnings had to surrender an entire day’s income because others had decided they should remain indoors. Consider what that meant for a woman selling food in the market. Her customers were at home, her produce was deteriorating, and the money she needed to support her family would not be earned that day. Or the young man who had borrowed money to start a business, only to discover that one working day in every week had effectively been taken away from him. Our children who lost a whole academic year before their compulsory external exam paper fell on a Monday. That was the reality we inherited. Our roads were in poor condition. Public services had deteriorated. Many schools were struggling to provide the kind of education our children deserved. Our health facilities needed substantial investment. And Enugu, a city that had once been the natural centre of commercial, political and cultural life across the region, was gradually losing that position. Businesses were looking elsewhere. Major events were moving to other cities. Our airport had barely two incoming flights a day. Perhaps the greatest danger was that we might begin to accept these conditions as normal. Because when people live with the same difficulties for long enough, their expectations begin to change. They stop asking what is possible and concentrate instead on getting through the day. I knew we could do better. I had spent much of my working life building businesses, dealing with challenges and making decisions about the future. I understood that Enugu possessed enormous resources, but I also knew that those resources would achieve very little unless we created the conditions for people to use them. Our greatest resource was already here: the people of Enugu. What was missing was a clear direction, the determination to pursue it, and a government prepared to take responsibility for the results. When I presented my original Statement of Purpose, I set out an ambition that some people considered almost impossible. We proposed to grow Enugu’s economy from approximately $4.4 billion to at least $30 billion within eight years, making our state one of Nigeria’s three leading economies. We also committed ourselves to the long-term ambition of eliminating poverty. Those were enormous goals. I knew that. But I wanted us to understand the scale of the change required. An economy cannot grow substantially if businesses cannot operate safely, if electricity is unreliable, if roads are impassable, or if young people leave school without the skills they need. These problems are connected. They have to be addressed together. So, we began by identifying the foundations of a functioning state: security, education, healthcare, infrastructure, productive industries and institutions capable of delivering results. And we made some difficult choices. We committed an unusually large share of our resources to education because we recognised that the future of Enugu would depend upon the abilities of its children. We began restoring security and normal economic activity. We invested in roads and transport, planned improvements to healthcare and set about attracting the businesses and industries that would create employment. I also knew that government itself had to change. For too long, public announcements had been treated as achievements. A project could be celebrated at its commencement and then disappear from public attention. I wanted a different standard. If we promise a school, people should be able to visit it. If we announce a road, they should be able to travel on it. If we say that public services are improving, citizens should be able to tell us whether that is true. This is why accountability, measurable performance and public participation were written into our original Statement of Purpose. We were asking the people of Enugu to place their confidence in a programme of substantial change. We therefore had an obligation to demonstrate, through our work, that their confidence was justified. Distinguished Guests, Today, I can stand before you and point to changes that have taken place across our state. One of the earliest and most important was the restoration of normal activity on Mondays. I remember how deeply the sit-at-home restrictions had affected people’s lives. The fear was real, and the economic consequences were considerable. Today, people are going about their business with a freedom that had been denied to them for far too long. A trader can plan a full working week. Children can attend school. Businesses can receive customers, move goods and keep their employees working. It may seem strange that we should celebrate something as ordinary as being able to go to work on Monday. But anyone who lived through those years understands its importance. Security gave us a foundation upon which other changes could begin. We turned our attention to the condition of our roads and the movement of people around the state. Road construction is often discussed in kilometres and contract values. Most people experience it rather differently. They know the road that used to damage their vehicles, the journey that took too long, or the difficulty of getting produce from a farm to a market. These are the experiences that matter. We have undertaken substantial road development and begun introducing a more organised transport system, including new buses and terminals. Our ambition is to make movement around Enugu safer, more comfortable and more dependable, while connecting communities to the opportunities being created across the state. The same thinking informs our work in aviation. When we assumed office, Enugu had barely two incoming flights a day. In our recent review, we counted more than fifteen. That change tells us something about the renewed interest in our state. Through Enugu Air and our wider aviation plans, we want to strengthen the connections between Enugu, the rest of Nigeria and international markets. A businessperson should be able to reach customers and partners without unnecessary difficulty. Investors should be able to visit our state. People who have made their lives elsewhere should find it easier to return, visit family and participate in our economy. Of course, improved air travel alone will not transform the life of someone living in a rural community. But a growing economy needs these connections, and our responsibility is to ensure that the opportunities they generate reach much further. That brings me to education. I have always believed that the most important investment we can make is in the abilities of our children. Consider the world into which a child entering school today will eventually graduate. Technology is already changing the way people work. Some occupations will disappear, others will be transformed, and entirely new industries will emerge. That child needs an education that prepares them to think independently, solve problems, communicate well and adapt to circumstances we cannot yet predict. This is the thinking behind our 260 Smart Green Schools, designed to bring a new standard of education to every ward in Enugu State. We want children in our rural communities to have access to the kind of learning opportunities that parents might once have believed were available only in the most privileged schools. Imagine what that could mean for a family whose children are the first generation to receive such an education. A daughter might develop the skills to build an agricultural business using modern methods. A son might become an engineer, a software developer or a skilled technician. Another child might become a teacher or a healthcare professional and return to serve the community in which they grew up. We cannot know exactly what each child will become. But we can give them a stronger foundation from which to choose. That is why education occupies such a central place in our development programme. And we must ensure that the economy grows alongside it. There would be little satisfaction in educating a generation of talented young people if they could find no opportunity to put their abilities to work. Our plans for agriculture, industry, technology, energy and commerce are intended to create those opportunities. Take agriculture: Enugu has fertile land, experienced farmers and communities with generations of knowledge about food production. Yet many farmers still struggle with poor access to equipment, storage, processing facilities and markets. They work hard, take considerable risks and often receive too little of the final value of what they produce. We want to build an agricultural economy in which more of that value remains here. Think of a farmer who grows cassava. If the crop can be processed locally, it creates work beyond the farm. Someone operates the equipment. Someone maintains it. Someone packages the finished product. Others transport and sell it. The income generated by that activity can support families and create further businesses within the community. Now imagine similar opportunities developing around other crops and agricultural products across Enugu. That is the practical meaning of agricultural industrialisation. Our plans for energy and industrial development follow the same logic. Reliable electricity can change the prospects of a small business. A tailor can work more efficiently. A food processor can preserve produce. A manufacturer can operate equipment without constantly depending on expensive alternative power. We have set out major ambitions for increasing electricity generation and attracting industrial investment because these are essential to the kind of economy we want to build. Some of these undertakings are long-term. Their benefits will develop over several years, and we must be realistic about the work involved. But we cannot afford to postpone them. I also want to speak about healthcare. For a parent with a sick child, the most important question is whether good medical attention is available when it is needed. For an expectant mother, it is whether she can receive proper care during pregnancy and childbirth. For an elderly person, it is whether treatment can be obtained without travelling an unreasonable distance or placing an impossible burden on the family. These are the circumstances against which our healthcare investments must be judged. We have been working to improve primary healthcare facilities and strengthen services across the state. We are also investing in the wider systems needed to make healthcare more effective. There is still work ahead, particularly in ensuring that improvements reach every community. And I want to acknowledge that openly. I know that some people listening today are already experiencing the benefits of the changes we have made. Others are still waiting for a road to be completed, a facility to become fully operational, or a new economic opportunity to reach their community. I understand that frustration. A government must be judged by the experiences of all its citizens, including those who have yet to see the full benefit of its work. That is why our programme must continue, and why we must remain willing to listen and make corrections. Now consider the larger investments we are pursuing. We are working to expand Enugu’s aviation connections, develop tourism destinations, attract major hospitality investment, improve electricity supply and create new areas for business and residential development. Some people will understandably ask what these projects have to do with their daily lives. It is a fair question. A new hotel can bring visitors and create demand for food, transport, maintenance, laundry, construction and many other services. A tourism destination can support local businesses. Better electricity can make investment in manufacturing more attractive. But government must do more than hope that these benefits spread. We must help our people acquire the skills, access the finance and establish the businesses that allow them to participate. A large project should create possibilities for many smaller enterprises. That is how economic development begins to reach into households and communities. We have made substantial progress in restoring Enugu’s position as a place where people want to live, work, invest and visit. The changes are visible, and the scale of our ambition is becoming clearer. We should take pride in what has been achieved, while recognising how much remains to be done. My fellow citizens, there is a reason I have spent time today looking back at where we began and examining the progress we have made. I want us to understand the opportunity now before us. We are living through a period of extraordinary change. Technology is reshaping industries across the world. The way food is produced, goods are manufactured, businesses are managed and knowledge is shared is changing faster than at any previous point in our lives. The opportunities created by these changes are considerable, but they will not be distributed equally. Places that invest in education, infrastructure, skills and productive enterprise will be better prepared to benefit. Those that fail to prepare may find themselves falling further behind. This matters enormously for Enugu. We have a young population, talented people, valuable natural resources and a long history of enterprise. We also have a generation of children growing up at a time when the possibilities available to them could be greater than anything their parents experienced. But those possibilities depend upon the choices we make now. A young person who wants to establish a business needs more than encouragement. They need access to skills, customers, finance and dependable infrastructure. A farmer who wants to increase production needs practical support and a market in which the additional effort can be rewarded. A community that wants better healthcare or education needs functioning institutions and a government that responds to its concerns. These are the connections we must strengthen in the years ahead. Our Statement of Purpose was built around the ambition of creating a productive economy and improving the lives of our people. That remains our direction. The next phase must deepen the work already begun, bring projects into full operation and extend their benefits to communities that are still waiting. We must also create more opportunities for our young people to participate in the industries of the future. The development of technology, modern agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and other productive sectors will require a workforce with new capabilities. Our schools, training institutions, businesses and government agencies must work together to develop them. There is urgency in this work because time matters. A child who receives a poor education today cannot simply recover those years later. A business that closes because it cannot operate may never reopen. A talented young person who leaves because there is no opportunity at home may build their future somewhere else. We cannot afford to lose another generation of potential. And this is why the moment before us is so important. The foundations we have begun to establish give us an opportunity to move faster and achieve more. The decisions we make over the coming years will determine how widely the benefits of this transformation are shared and how firmly they become established. I believe Enugu is capable of becoming one of the great centres of economic and social progress in Nigeria. But that future will depend upon the continued effort of government, the confidence of investors, the enterprise of our businesses and the participation of our people. Which brings me to the most important invitation I want to make today. My dear people of Enugu, when we began this journey, I asked you to believe that our state could become something greater. Today, I am asking you to become more deeply involved in making that future a reality. Government can create the conditions for progress, but the energy that sustains it comes from the people. It comes from the teacher who takes responsibility for the children in her classroom, the business owner who trains young employees, the farmer who introduces a better method of production, and the community that comes together to solve a problem. It also comes from citizens who ask difficult questions, demand accountability and contribute their ideas to the decisions that affect them. I want that relationship between government and citizens to grow stronger. Our original Statement of Purpose committed us to transparent government, measurable performance and public participation. These commitments matter because people are more likely to take responsibility for something when they understand it and have a meaningful voice in shaping it. When a new school opens in your community, I want you to regard its success as a shared responsibility. The government must provide the facilities, teachers and resources. Parents and community leaders also have an important part to play in supporting the children who attend it. When a new road connects your community to a market, I want us to consider the businesses and opportunities that connection could support. When an investment creates the possibility of employment, I want our young people to be ready with the skills and determination to take advantage of it. And when government falls short, I want citizens to speak up and help us identify what needs to improve. This is how a stronger relationship between the people and their institutions is built. I am particularly conscious of the responsibility we carry towards the next generation. Our children will inherit the state we leave behind. They will live with the consequences of our decisions, our investments and the opportunities we either created or failed to recognise. And I believe that when they look back upon this period in Enugu’s history, they should be able to say that something important happened here. That a generation of people looked honestly at the condition of their state, decided it could do better and began the difficult work of changing its future. That the progress continued because people across Enugu chose to participate. We have already seen what can happen when a state begins to regain its confidence. People return to their businesses. Investment begins to grow. New institutions emerge. Young people see possibilities that were previously difficult to imagine. There is a growing sense that Enugu is moving forward again. But the greatest part of this journey is still before us. I spoke earlier about the dawn. In May 2023, we stood at the beginning of a new day. There was uncertainty about what lay ahead, but we knew that the time had come to change direction. Today, the first light has given way to morning. We can see the work taking shape around us, and we can begin to appreciate the scale of what is possible. We are now in the heat of the morning, when the real labour of the day must be done. And I want every citizen of Enugu to recognise the importance of this hour. Because history sometimes gives a people an opportunity to change the direction of their future. Such opportunities do not remain open indefinitely. The world is moving quickly, and we must be prepared to move with it. This is one moment in the long history of Enugu. This is a moment of extraordinary possibility for our people. And I believe this is the moment we must seize. The work we have begun needs the commitment of all of us. I ask you to bring your ideas, your skills, your enterprise and your experience into the life of our state. Take an interest in what is happening in your community. Help us identify problems and develop practical solutions. Encourage our young people to learn, create and build their futures here. We have the opportunity to leave something of lasting value to those who come after us: A state with stronger institutions, a more productive economy, better opportunities for its children and communities whose people can take pride in what they have achieved together. That is the Enugu I want us to build. And I believe we have reached the point in our history when we can begin to make that ambition real. My fellow citizens, the morning is upon us. There is much work ahead, and I am ready to continue that work with you. Ndi Enugu, Tomorrow Is Here. Thank you. Mbah, Govenor of Enugu State, presented the manifesto performance scorecard at Godfrey Okoye University, Enugu

title: Samples for two suspected Ebola cases in Nigeria turn out negative
body: Health authorities in Nigeria investigating two suspected Ebola cases in the country’s northeast region confirmed that samples tested negative after two rounds of testing, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention said on Sunday. Officials said the two individuals had been isolated while they carried out contact identification, listing and laboratory testing in a post on X. Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more ​than a decade last week in a Swiss woman who had travelled to Uganda and then returned ​to the capital, Abuja, in central Nigeria. ​ She and her husband were evacuated to Switzerland on Monday. ‌It ⁠remains the only confirmed case of the disease in the country up to date. The centre of Africa’s Ebola outbreak is in ​the Democratic Republic ​of Congo, ⁠where more than 5,000 people have died since it was declared in ​May. Kenya and Uganda have also ​reported ⁠cases. No approved treatments or vaccines exist to combat the rare Bundibugyo species ​behind the Congo outbreak.

title: Oil slips more than 1% as talks continue on ending Iran war
body: Oil prices slipped more than 1% on ‌Monday after Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures fell $1.59, or 1.40%, to $111.84 a barrel by 0011 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude ​was $102.56 a barrel, down $1.56, or 1.50%. Brent ended October at its highest ⁠level in six months amid concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate ​again after Tuesday’s US midterm elections . “Oil is seeing a technical pullback this morning ​after last week’s strong gains,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. “Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation ​over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices ​for now.” However, the market remained alert to the possibility that rhetoric around Iran could ‌be ⁠ratcheted higher and push Brent toward $120 after the midterm elections, Waterer said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the “ongoing and progressing” talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared ​for “both defence and diplomacy”. ​The talks come ⁠amid attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz that are driving up global energy and shipping costs. In ​October, Saudi Arabia increased crude exports versus September despite attacks by ​the Iran-aligned ⁠Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, two of three ship-tracking companies said. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia, or OPEC+, kept December production ⁠targets ​steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more policy ​adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from ​the Iran war.

title: I wasted my first earnings from music – Don Jazzy
body: Veteran record producer and music executive Michael Collins Ajereh, popularly known as Don Jazzy, revealed that he spent his first major earnings on frivolities rather than investing or using them wisely. Speaking in a recent episode of the On The Grind podcast, Jazzy explained that he later got the hint and started investing his subsequent earnings, especially in new artists. He said that because of his investments in record labels and other businesses, he doesn’t have to work again. He advised young people to prioritise investing as soon as they start making money, rather than spending excessively on frivolities. Don Jazzy said, “The first big money I got from music, I lavished it. I bought 50 bottles of champagne and went clubbing. But I quickly got my act together and invested in signing new artistes. Now I don’t have to work ever again. “You don’t necessarily have to invest in a record label, but the money you are making in your youth, invest it in a lucrative business as opposed to wasting it on frivolities.”

title: Kwankwaso, Yusuf: South Must Retain Power in 2027
body: Igbo torn between emotion and reason, declares Soludo Says those who couldn’t defeat Tinubu out of power won’t do so now Unites APGA, APC, PDP, Accord in Anambra for president’s re-election Akpabio: Akwa Ibom’ll deliver South-South’s highest votes to Tinubu Urges APC factions to unite Deji Elumoye, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja, David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka and Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano The Vice Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Rabiu Kwankwaso; Kano State Governor, Abba Kabir Yusuf, and Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, yesterday insisted that the South should retain power in 2027, warning against breaking the existing rotational arrangement between the North and the South. While Kwankwaso warned former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) against disrupting the zoning arrangement, Yusuf and Abdulmajid argued that allowing the South to complete its eight-year tenure was necessary for national stability, reciprocity and peaceful coexistence. Also yesterday, Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, said the Igbo were torn between emotion and reason ahead of the 2027 elections, urging them to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, while Senate President Godswill Akpabio assured that Akwa Ibom State would deliver the highest votes for the President in the South-South. It’s Still Turn of South in 2027, Kwankwaso Warns Atiku, ADC Kwankwaso has warned Atiku not to disrupt the zoning system by contesting, urging him to allow the system to continue by supporting Mr. Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South. Kwankwaso, who stated this during an interactive session with journalists at his residence in Kano, yesterday, also warned the ADC against causing confusion over the rotational presidency between the North and the South. He said even though zoning was not enshrined in the constitution, common sense dictates that if one part of the country rules for two terms, the other region should be allowed to take over. According to the former governor, fielding any candidate from the North would not help the country’s peaceful coexistence but will rather create confusion and disharmony among Nigerians. “Atiku should not disrupt the system by contesting at this point in time. He should allow the system to continue by supporting Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South.” Kwankwaso recalled how he contested for president three consecutive times but decided to abandon his ambition to allow the Southern part of the country to produce Mr. Peter Obi. “What is happening in the ADC will not help us. Some people want to create confusion by bringing a candidate from the North, knowing full well that it is still the turn of the South. After Obi presidency, it will return to the north. “I sacrificed my ambition for Peter Obi because he is credible and from the South. We share common goals and ideology. We are strong and can manage the affairs of this country with ease,” he added. The Kwankwasiyya leader stressed that for the Nigerian system to be balanced, Obi from the South should be given the opportunity to steer the affairs of the presidency. Yusuf, Presidential Aide Insist on Power Rotation Specifically, the Presidency justified the existing power rotation between the North and the South by urging the North to honour the current eight-year tenure being served by the South to completion, in the interest of reciprocity and national stability. It said Nigeria’s national stability hangs by a slender thread, demanding that the North honour the unwritten power rotation pact and allow the South to complete its full eight-year tenure, warning that breaking this foundational trust could jeopardise the country’s unity. Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, stated this in Kano during the Grand Inauguration & Strategic Media Awards Ceremony of Matan Arewa 4 Tinubu Again (MATA). According to her, Nigeria’s power rotation arrangement was not a sectional concession but a reciprocal compact that has stabilised the Fourth Republic. In a veiled reference to Atiku, who she recalled attended and participated in the famous Kaduna meeting where the power rotation agreement was reached, Abdulmajid argued that the North cannot sacrifice the stability of Nigeria for the ambition of one man. Tracing the origin to Kaduna, she noted that when military rule ended, patriots negotiated a framework for unity, maintaining that, “present in that room was Atiku Abubakar himself, as later confirmed by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume. “Chief Sunday Awoniyi, the great Northern elder, stood up in 1998 and declared that the North should not field a candidate, in order to heal the wounds of June 12 and soothe the pain of the South.” She further listed other patriots who shaped the understanding to include Dr. Chuba Okadigbo, speaking for the South; Alhaji Abubakar Rimi, speaking for the North; Dr. Alex Ekwueme, and Dr. Okwesilieze Nwodo. Insisting on the power rotation arrangement, the Presidency said, “In 1999, when the guns of military rule finally fell silent, this nation did not just switch governments—we made a sacred promise. Our founding patriots gathered in Kaduna with one urgent, defining question echo-chambered in their minds: How do we keep Nigeria one? “And from that sacred deliberation came a compact: not a sectional concession, but a reciprocal agreement. This gentleman’s agreement decreed that power must rotate between North and South every eight years—an arrangement to guarantee fairness, to ensure stability, and to guarantee that no Nigerian ever feels like a stranger in his own country.” On how the arrangement worked, Abdulmajid said it survived because it was honoured. “This is not fiction. This is our history. And how did it work? It worked because we honoured it. In 1999, we gave it to the South—Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, eight years, from 1999 to 2007. Then we gave it to the North: Umaru Musa Yar’Adua in 2007. But death, a painful death, cut his tenure short in 2010. “His vice, Goodluck Jonathan from the South, took over. The North felt cheated. The North said our turn was not complete, and that agitation was legitimate. What happened? In 2015, power returned to the North. The late former President Muhammadu Buhari, eight full years, 2015 to 2023! The sequence was restored! The principle survived,” she stated. The Presidency contended that the agreement was a two-way street and the North has already taken its full benefit. “My people, listen to me. The agreement is reciprocal; it is a two-way street. The North has already taken its full benefit after eight solid years under Buhari. You cannot eat your cake and still demand another man’s cake,” Abdulmajid said. The presidential aide stressed that stability requires reciprocity, recalling that the current President, a Southerner, worked tirelessly for the late General Muhammadu Buhari to emerge victorious when the North demanded power must return after Jonathan’s tenure. “That same logic applies today. You cannot abandon a principle when it becomes inconvenient. If you do, you tell the world that the agreement was never a principle at all—merely a temporary tactic. And if we destroy trust today, what will we use to negotiate tomorrow? Let us be honest. Much of this noise against the South completing its term is not a matter of principle. It is personal ambition,” she queried. Attributing opposition to the South completing its term to personal ambition, Abdulmajid said, “Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar tells us zoning is “self-defeating.” But he participated in and benefited from zoned arrangements in 2015 and 2019 when they favored his ambition! When rotation opened the door for him, it was acceptable. When it stands in his way, it becomes “intellectually dishonest.” “Shall we sacrifice Nigeria’s stability for one man’s ambition? The North’s genuine interest is not served by that; the North’s interest is stable inclusion. The guarantee that power will return to you only lives if we honour the compact today.” The Presidency appealed to the North not to break the sacred promise that binds nation, urging the people of the region to rise together and complete the Southern tenure, describing it as not merely an election. “This is for our honour. This is for reciprocity. This is for the enduring stability and peaceful coexistence of our great nation. That is exactly what the re-election of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term stands for. That is the future we build today,” it added. Also speaking, Governor Yusuf corroborated Abdulmajid’s position, saying the unity of Nigeria could only be guaranteed by fair play and inclusivity. The Governor who was represented by his Director-General of Media and Publicity, Sunusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, argued that reversing the existing rotational arrangement would paint the North in ignoble light, even as he urged the region to maintain the status quo by re-electing President Tinubu for a second term. In his remarks, former Governor of Jigawa State and immediate past Minister of Defence, Mohammad Abubakar Badaru, said the Renewed Hope Administration of President Tinubu has benefited the North more than any other part of Nigeria. Badaru listed major completed road projects to include the 88km Zuba-Jere section and the 81km Abuja-Kaduna section of the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Highway commissioned in October 2026, the 77km Kaduna-Pambeguwa road, Yakasai-Badume-Damargu-Marken Zalli roads in Kano, and the Jimeta Bridge in Yola. On social infrastructure, Badaru cited completed health facilities such as Gadon Kaya PHC in Kano, three Polio Emergency Centers in Katsina, Kano and Sokoto, pharmacy lab at ABUTH Zaria, 50-bed mental health center at UNIMAID, and infertility center at ATBUTH Bauchi, plus ongoing upgrades at Bichi General Hospital and deployment of 79 CNG ambulances. Igbo Torn Between Emotion and Reason in 2027 Elections, Declares Soludo Soludo has summarised the disposition of the Ndigbo ahead of the 2027 elections, saying they were torn between emotions and reason in the forthcoming presidential election, but advised that it was better to embrace reason than work on emotion. Soludo was referring to the support being given by most Igbo people to Obi, who is from the region. Speaking at a stakeholders’ meeting of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), All Progressives Congress (APC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and Accord Party, which he convened in Awka as the Anambra State Coordinator of the Presidential Campaign Committee of APC, Soludo insisted that those who couldn’t win Tinubu when he was not in power should not expect to win him now that he was in charge. Speaking at the well-attended meeting which had members of the four political parties in attendance, Soludo insisted that there would be consequences for not supporting Tinubu if he won reelection next year. He said: “This is a grand coalition for the progress, prosperity, security, and welfare of Nigeria and of course, Anambra. This is a battle for the soul of Ndigbo and Anambra, a battle between emotion and reason. Emotion will always dominate, but reason will eventually triumph. “We have clamoured for the presidency since 1978, we have held many positions in Nigeria except president. So, how do we get there? We need partnerships. Politics is about interest, we are not doing Tinubu any favour by supporting him, rather we are doing ourselves a favour. We did not vote for him in 2023, yet he won, and some people want us to repeat the same mistake?” Soludo said he was sure of Tinubu’s victory next year, saying, “A warrior who you couldn’t beat when he was sleeping in 2023, is it now that he is fully awake that you think you can defeat him? It can’t happen. Show me anywhere in the world that anyone has taken power from a powerful incumbent president? “Ndigbo have been playing politics of protest and it is not in our own favour. Our brother who is running for president (Peter Obi) is my friend. We are close, our families are close and we will remain close. The only place where we disagree with each other is in politics. We cannot keep deceiving our people. “In politics, there is not prize for second position, that is why I say we should not throw away our votes. We must remember there is consequence for running and failing. So, for Ndigbo, this is a battle between temporary emotion and reason. “If we back Tinubu for a second term, after his tenure, power will move to the north, and when it comes to the South again, we will be able to negotiate with other regions in the South to support us because we supported them when they needed us.” The Governor insisted that he was not supporting Tinubu’s reelection for any percuniary gains, adding that after winning a second term as governor, he was done with election contest. He said: “I grew up in the era when we used to say – speak the truth and shame the devil. In 2023 I even wrote it down that he (Obi) will fail. I wrote that at best he would come third, and what later happened? This time, I’m saying it again that he will fail. Once you go to election with fragmented opposition, the incumbent will carry the day. “I’m saying this truth because I care for Igbo. I’m no longer contesting any election after my second term, so I can retire to my village and be enjoying fresh palm wine, but it is the future of Ndigbo that we are fighting for. That is why I’m shouting because I know that contesting and failing has serious consequences.” Soludo charged all parties in the coalition to go out and scout for votes to ensure a resounding victory for Tinubu on January 16, 2026. He said parties must adopt a door-to-door campaign strategy to be able to reach undecided voters, insisting that securing victory for Tinubu in Anambra will give the state the right to negotiate for favours in his second term. He also scored the president high on projects being done in the state, saying only victory will give him the courage to complete the projects when he returns. “Tinubu is doing many projects in Anambra State. We want to support him to ensure that he returns to complete them. There are numerous other projects that we would want him to do, but you can only ask for them if you are a member of the inner chamber. “We need to partner the federal government for some projects. Our roads need to be motorable, there is the gas pipeline project, rail project, erosion menace. Some of these are not things a state can take on with just FAAC, and the only way the federal government can come to our aid is if we are partners,” Soludo said. Akpabio: Akwa Ibom’ll Deliver South-South’s Highest Votes for Tinubu in 2027 The President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, has assured President Bola Tinubu and the leadership of the APC that Akwa Ibom State would deliver the highest number of votes for the ruling party’s presidential candidate in the South-South geopolitical zone in the January 16, 2027 general election. Akpabio, according to a statement from his Media Office, gave the assurance yesterday, at a special religious service organised to dedicate the APC’s 2027 election campaigns to God at the International Christian Worship Centre, Uyo, the Akwa Ibom State capital. The service, which had the theme, ‘We Are Well Able,’ brought together party leaders, government officials, political stakeholders and supporters to seek divine guidance for the party ahead of the forthcoming general election. The Senate President, who called on APC members in the state to close ranks and present a united front, said the party could only translate its electoral ambitions into reality if internal divisions and disagreements were set aside. He attributed his emergence as President of the Senate to the support of Tinubu, describing the development as an opportunity for Akwa Ibom State to demonstrate its appreciation through massive electoral support for the President. He said, “An Akwa Ibom son, through the support of Mr. President, is today the President of the Senate and the number three citizen of Nigeria. Whether you like him or not, he is there today. “The only way to thank Mr. President for that support is to give him all our votes. From what I have seen here today, Akwa Ibom State will give Mr. President the highest number of votes in the South-South region.” In an address titled ‘One Family, One Destiny, One Akwa Ibom Under God,’ the statement explained that Akpabio emphasised the importance of unity, inclusiveness and peaceful coexistence among members of the APC, warning against divisions based on the length of membership or political affiliation. He maintained that the party should operate as one family in which old and new members enjoy equal opportunities to contribute to its growth and electoral success. He said, “In the APC family, there should be no aborigines and no newcomers; no landlords and no tenants; no first-class members and no second-class members. There should be only one big family, united by a common purpose and a shared responsibility. “Those who were here yesterday have a history to honour, and those who arrived today have contributions to make. Neither history nor arrival should become an instrument of exclusion.” Using a biblical illustration from John 14:2, the Senate President said there was sufficient political space for every member of the party, irrespective of when they joined. He said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ declared in John 14:2: ‘In my Father’s house are many mansions.’ Let me borrow that beautiful imagery today. In this house, there are many mansions, enough for everyone! “There is room for the pioneer and room for the newcomer; room for the elder and room for the youth; room for those who laid the foundation and room for those who will raise the roof. “Nobody needs to demolish another person’s mansion to find accommodation, and nobody needs to extinguish another person’s candle for his own light to shine. We may have arrived through different doors, but we must learn to live under one roof,” he added. Akpabio further urged political leaders and party members to ensure that their political ambitions did not override the welfare and aspirations of the people. He said political activities should reflect the moral values of the faith professed by the people, stressing that electoral campaigns must respect human dignity and promote peaceful coexistence. “Therefore, our politics must reflect our faith, our campaigns must honour human dignity, and our ambitions must never become greater than the welfare of our people,” he stated. The Senate President also described Akwa Ibom as a developing success story, attributing the state’s progress to purposeful leadership, peace and sustained development. According to him, the state’s achievements should not be measured solely by physical infrastructure but also by its ability to strengthen relationships among its people and restore public confidence in governance. He said, “Akwa Ibom has become a Nigerian wonder story, a testimony to the possibilities of purposeful leadership, peace and development. “Our state is demonstrating that progress is not merely about the roads we construct or the buildings we erect, but also about the bridges we build between people and the hope we restore in human hearts. “We must preserve this progress and ensure that the chapters yet to be written are greater than those already written,” he said. He also linked the state’s development to the broader national interest, insisting that Akwa Ibom could not achieve sustainable prosperity in isolation from the challenges confronting other parts of the country. Akpabio said, “Akwa Ibom’s greatness is inseparable from Nigeria’s greatness. We cannot desire peace in Uyo and be indifferent to insecurity elsewhere in our federation, nor celebrate prosperity in our communities while ignoring hardship in other parts of our country. “Nigeria is not merely the nation to which Akwa Ibom belongs; it is the larger destiny to which Akwa Ibom contributes,” he said. He urged political stakeholders to demonstrate national solidarity through their actions and strengthen the foundations of democracy. Earlier, Governor Umo Eno thanked the people of Akwa Ibom for their support during the last election and appealed for even greater backing for Tinubu, Akpabio, himself and other APC candidates in the 2027 general election. The governor also reaffirmed his commitment to serving the people with the fear of God, expressing the hope that they would give him another mandate to continue his administration’s development agenda. He urged residents to sustain their support for the APC, describing the forthcoming election as an opportunity to consolidate the party’s political fortunes and development efforts in the state.

title: Atiku Accuses APC Presidential Campaign of Obscuring President’s Unfulfilled Promises
body: · ADC council says ruling party’s sustained assault on democracy will fail Chuks Okocha in Abuja President candidate of African Democratic Congress (ADC) and former Vice President, Atiku Abubakar, has accused the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council of seeking to obscure President Bola Tinubu’s unfulfilled electricity promise with a long recital of laws, committees, bonds, and projects. Atiku made the accusation in a statement by Director of Strategic Communication, ADC Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC), Phrank Shaibu. Separately, ADC-PCC condemned what it called sustained, coordinated, and state-sponsored assault on democracy, freedom of association, and the constitutional right of Nigerians to political participation under the Tinubu administration. It, however, declared that the assaults would fail and democracy was bound to survive and outlive APC. Atiku said, in the statement by ADC-PCC, “The APC should spare Nigerians the spectacle of celebrating paperwork while homes and businesses remain in darkness. “After three and a half years, families still struggle to keep their homes lit. Traders and small business owners spend scarce resources on alternative power, yet struggle to keep their businesses alive.” ADC campaign council said, “Nigerians are billed for electricity they cannot rely on. President Tinubu promised steady power and an end to estimated billing. That promise has not been kept. “Across Nigeria, consumers are placed in Bands A, B, C, D and E and charged different rates. In many areas, Band A customers pay about N209.50 per unit before VAT. Rates for the other bands vary by state and electricity provider. ”Yet across every band, the same hardship endures: the power fails, but the bill arrives. No family should have to weigh the cost of electricity against the cost of food. No business should be left to pay more while receiving less.” ADC added, “The government now says it plans to end electricity subsidies from 2027, even as it insists there will be no immediate tariff increase. Nigerians are entitled to a clear answer: what will happen to their bills when the subsidy ends?” The ADC presidential candidate promised that if elected, “I will work with state governments and regulators, within the law, to abolish the present band system and replace it with a fair, transparent and affordable framework that protects households and holds power companies accountable for the electricity they deliver. “Steady power that Nigerians can afford will be a national priority.” Insisting that Tinubu had no justification for seeking another term, the ADC campaign council stated, “When President Tinubu campaigned in 2022, he made an unmistakable commitment. He said: ‘If I don’t give you constant electricity for four years, when I come back for a second term, don’t vote for me.’ “Nigerians have lived through those four years. They do not need his campaign council to interpret his words for them. They need him to answer for them. “His administration has not built a single new generation infrastructure of its own to increase Nigeria’s power capacity. Yet it has floated a multitrillion naira bond programme to settle legacy debts owed to generation companies, without showing Nigerians how this financial intervention has produced the steady electricity they were promised. ”Paying old debts is not the same as building new power infrastructure. Bonds cannot be presented as a substitute for power in people’s homes.” ADC also accused the Tinubu government of worsening the power woes with unjustifiable energy taxes. It stated, “Meanwhile, Nigerians face VAT on electricity, and the Nigeria Tax Act provides for a five per cent surcharge on certain fossil fuels, including petrol and diesel. “The government says the surcharge has not been activated and would require a ministerial order. At a time when families already struggle to meet the cost of energy, Nigerians deserve to know why another potential charge has been placed before them. “Dele Alake’s statement cannot light a home. Signing a law is not electricity. Raising a bond is not electricity. Approving a project is not power delivered. Nigerians cannot cook, study, work or sustain a business on announcements. ”President Tinubu invited Nigerians to judge him by his performance. They have done so. What they seek is simple: reliable electricity they can afford, and a government that keeps its word.” APC’s Sustained Assault On Democracy Will Fail, Says ADC Presidential Campaign ADC-PCC condemned what it described as organised assault on democracy and freedom of association and political participation under the administration of Tinubu, declaring that the assaults will fail, as democracy will outlive APC. The council said the unfolding incidents across the country went beyond ordinary political rivalry. It alleged that the incidents represented a disturbing pattern of intimidation, harassment, and suppression of opposition voices. The council said the Tinubu government had engaged in calculated atrocious actions skewed to scare Nigerians ahead of the general election. In a statement signed by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, ADC-PCC recalled a series of incidents, including attacks on its leaders and members in Kaduna, the reported assault on its Sokoto State governorship candidate, Alhaji Munir Dan Iya, by operatives of the Sokoto Marshals along Airport Road, Sokoto, and alleged attacks on other opposition figures. It also cited the reported demolition of its governorship campaign office in Kebbi State and the alleged denial of a campaign venue in Enugu State to Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Mr Peter Obi. The council further referenced the reported attacks on the presidential candidate of African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, and other opposition voices, describing the incidents as part of an emerging pattern of political intolerance. According to ADC-PCC, the attacks, denial of campaign venues, arrests, harassment, and intimidation of opposition figures raised serious concerns about the state of democratic freedoms and political pluralism in Nigeria. The council maintained that no government, regardless of its political or institutional strength, could successfully suppress the democratic aspirations of Nigerians, recalling that popular resistance contributed to the collapse of former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s third-term agenda. It also stated that Tinubu and APC enjoyed the benefits of political participation and opposition politics when they were outside government, insisting that those same democratic freedoms must be guaranteed to all political parties and their members. Sharing Atiku’s thoughts, ADC-PCC also described as an afterthought the attempt by Alake and APC-PCC to rewrite Tinubu’s categorical 2023 electricity pledge through selective quotations and elaborate explanations. Reacting to comments by Alake, Ologbondiyan maintained that Tinubu was unequivocal when he told Nigerians not to vote for him for a second term if he failed to deliver electricity during his first tenure. According to ADC-PCC, Nigerians have not forgotten the president’s words. His commitment was clear and unambiguous: “Don’t vote for me for second term if I fail to deliver electricity.” The council said no amount of selective editing, additional paragraphs, or grammatical gymnastics could erase that commitment from the consciousness of Nigerians. It said rather than end estimated billing, the Tinubu administration had presided over increased electricity bills, leaving many households struggling to afford power supply. ADC-PCC further observed that businesses, including hospitality facilities, had been forced to ration electricity by switching off power for guests during daytime hours to contain operating costs. It also criticised the introduction of discriminatory tariff classifications under Bands A, B, C and others, stating that consumers continue to pay more without receiving reliable electricity supply.

title: Hackers breach Russia's statistics agency, obtain data on Russian losses in Ukraine
body:
That is according to Reform.news , Ukrinform reports.
Silent Crow said the hackers had gained access to the agency's central office, its regional branches and the Main Interregional Center for the Processing and Dissemination of Statistical Information.
The group added that they had taken control of around 25,000 computers.
The hackers also claim to have exfiltrated around 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, databases and official information.
According to them, the materials obtained include information on Russia's military losses in its war against Ukraine.

title: 50 Greek-American Candidates Contest US Midterm Elections
body: At least 50 candidates of Greek descent are contesting the November 3, 2026, US midterm elections, seeking political office across 20 states at federal, state and local levels. Running as Democrats and Republicans, the candidates reflect the growing political presence of Greek Americans and their continued involvement in shaping the country’s political future. The elections will determine control of the US Congress, alongside numerous governorship, state and local government positions, making the vote a significant moment for the Greek-American community. Greek-American candidate targets US Senate One of the most closely watched contests involving a candidate of Greek descent is the New Hampshire Senate race. Democratic Congressman Chris Pappas is challenging former Republican senator John Sununu for the seat. Pappas has represented New Hampshire’s First Congressional District since 2019 and is seeking to advance to the US Senate. If elected, he would become the first Greek-American senator since Olympia Snowe left office in 2013. Greek-American candidates seek House seats Several Greek-American lawmakers are also seeking election or re-election to the US House of Representatives. They include Republicans Gus Bilirakis, Mike Haridopolos, Jimmy Patronis and Nicole Malliotakis, alongside Democrats Dina Titus and Maggie Goodlander. Their work in Congress has covered issues including foreign policy, national security, healthcare and the economy. Several have also been active in promoting stronger relations between the United States, Greece and Cyprus. Candidates across state governments Greek-American political representation extends well beyond Washington, with candidates competing for influential positions in state administrations. California Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis is seeking election as state treasurer, while Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias is campaigning for another term. Other prominent candidates include Nevada Lieutenant Governor Stavros Anthony, Massachusetts State Auditor Diana DiZoglio and Connecticut Lieutenant Governor Susan Bysiewicz, who are seeking to retain their respective positions. Candidates of Greek descent are also contesting seats in state legislatures, county administrations and judicial offices. Their campaigns span New York, Pennsylvania, Florida, Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia, Kentucky, Oregon and Arizona, among other states. Greek-American political influence crosses party lines The participation of Greek-American candidates from both major political parties highlights the community’s bipartisan presence in American public life. Their political influence also carries significance for Greece and Cyprus, particularly as Washington continues to shape policy across the Eastern Mediterranean. Members of Congress can influence decisions involving defence cooperation with Greece, relations with Turkey, energy security and the Cyprus issue. The bipartisan Congressional Hellenic Caucus provides an important platform for lawmakers to promote issues affecting Greece and Cyprus within the US political system. A significant election for the Greek diaspora With at least 50 candidates of Greek descent competing across 20 states, the November 3 elections represent a major moment for Greek-American political participation. The results will determine how many candidates secure elected office and the extent of Greek-American representation across federal, state and local institutions. For the Greek diaspora, the election is also an opportunity to demonstrate its continued influence in American public life and its capacity to contribute to decisions shaping the country’s domestic and international policies.
