title: Sanwo-Olu, CIBN Task Banks on Productive Lending to Drive Industrial Growth
body: Nume Ekeghe Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu; President and Chairman of Council of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN), Dele Alabi and former Group Chief Executive Officer of FBN Holdings Plc, Mallam Bello Maccido, have urged banks to channel funds raised through the recent recapitalisation exercise towards productive lending to businesses, particularly SMEs and manufacturers, to accelerate industrial growth.\They made the call at the CIBN Fellowship Investiture Ceremony held in Lagos over the weekend.\Speaking at the event, Sanwo-Olu said the success of the recapitalisation exercise would ultimately depend on how effectively the additional capital was deployed to support productive enterprises, expand industries and create economic opportunities. He identified access to affordable, long-term financing as one of the major constraints facing Nigerian businesses, urging banks to increase lending to sectors capable of driving sustainable growth. “But raising capital is only the beginning. The two major obstacles, in our view, are how effectively that capital supports productive enterprises, how it helps industrial expansion, and how it creates economic opportunities for every Nigerian,” the governor said. He noted that manufacturers needed financing to acquire machinery, fund production and compete internationally, while agricultural businesses required capital to strengthen storage and processing capacity. He also called for increased support for start-ups, particularly young businesses requiring seed capital to establish and expand their operations. Sanwo-Olu stressed that the banking industry had a critical role to play in growing the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) segment, noting that improved access to financing would broaden economic participation. Earlier, Alabi said the recapitalisation programme had mobilised N4.65 trillion in fresh capital through the Nigerian capital market, with 33 banks meeting the new capital requirements. He described the development as evidence of the resilience of the banking industry and the growing depth of the country’s financial markets. However, he said the priority must now shift towards ensuring that the strengthened capital base translates into investments in industries, infrastructure, business expansion and job creation. “The question before us is no longer whether our banks have sufficient capital, but whether that capital will translate into new industries, expanded businesses, better infrastructure, thriving SMEs, sustainable jobs, and shared prosperity,” Alabi said. He said Nigeria had a significant opportunity to deploy the additional capital towards manufacturing, agriculture, infrastructure, energy and technology. Also speaking, Maccido urged banks to reconsider their asset allocation strategies, warning against excessive concentration in treasury instruments at the expense of lending to the real sector. Citing a World Bank report, he said that since the completion of the recapitalisation exercise in March 2026, treasury bills had increased as a proportion of banks’ total assets from 18 per cent to 22 per cent, while loans had remained unchanged at 22 per cent. He described the trend as a concern, urging banks to direct more capital towards industries that could support economic transformation. “So, I’m appealing to you, my friends and fellow bankers, as I move into the advisory world, having grown older in banking. We need to look at the critical industries necessary to drive the transformation of our economy,” he said. Maccido argued that lending was not merely a regulatory obligation but a profitable business that offered banks multiple income streams, including interest income, foreign exchange earnings, letters of credit commissions and other fees. “Lending itself is a very good business because the income streams from lending are diverse. From interest income to exchange income, letters of credit commissions and other fees, there is quite a wide array of income streams that banks can generate from lending. So, lending is not something you are doing simply because the regulatory authorities are pushing or forcing you to do it. You are actually making money from it,” he said. He further noted that lending to carefully selected sectors, including SMEs, could deliver higher net yields than treasury instruments, given the relatively lower returns associated with risk-free assets. Maccido urged banks to prioritise manufacturing, industrial parks and other critical sectors that would strengthen domestic production. “I would like to see us focus on manufacturing, industrial parks and other critical sectors that will drive the creation of a productive economy. That is the whole essence of the recapitalisation exercise stipulated by the CBN,” he said.

title: 22 Firms Report N12.1tn PBT in 9 Months Despite Macro-economic Headwinds
body: Kayode Tokede Despite macroeconomic headwinds, MTN Nigeria Communications Plc and 21 other listed companies on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) reported N12.1 trillion profit before tax in nine months ended September 30, 2026. This represent a 35.4 per cent Year-on-Year (YoY) increase over N8.94 trillion reported in recorded in the same period in 2025. The 22 companies that are made up of cement manufacturing, financial institutions, and others generated an estimated N7.6 trillion profit after tax in nine months of 2026, up by 22.1per cent when compared to N6.2 trillion in nine months of 2025. In the period under review, the economy weathered insecurity, weak purchasing power despite inflation easing, among others. Nigeria’s inflation eased to 14.63 per cent as of September 2026 from 15.15 per cent December 2025, while the Naira at the closed September 30, 2026 at N1,331.50 against the dollar from N1,478.00 against the dollar September 30, 2025. Also, the ongoing unrest in the Middle East between US/Israel and Iran has impacted on global oil prices, led to uncertainties and companies in Nigeria felt the impact. After navigating heightened uncertainty and trade barriers last year, the global economy now faces a fresh shock from the war in the Middle East. Growth is projected to slow to 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.2per cent in 2027, weighed down by rising geopolitical tensions. Meanwhile, analysis of the companies’ unaudited result and accounts for nine months ended September 2026 showed that MTN Nigeria Communications Plc recorded the highest profit followed by Dangote Cement Plc and Seplat Energy Plc. MTN declared N1.79 trillion profit before tax in nine months of 2026, about 59.4 per cent from N1.13 trillion reported in nine months of 2025. The Chief Executive Officer, MTN Nigeria Communications, Mr. Karl Toriola in a statement said: “We delivered a very strong third quarter, reversing the temporary slowdown in Q2. Service revenue grew 19.7per cent (8.4per cent QoQ), with growth accelerating each month to 21.6per cent in September. “Profitability grew even faster: Q3 EBITDA rose 32.8 per cent (12.5per cent QoQ) and the EBITDA margin widened by 5.8 per cent to 58.7 per cent. For the nine months, service revenue grew 23.7per cent with an EBITDA margin of 56.9 per cent. Both are comfortably within the guidance of ‘at least low-20per cent’ revenue growth and a ‘mid-to-high-50per cent’ margin. “Growth is increasingly volume-led, driven by more users, deeper data adoption, higher usage and rising demand for home broadband, supported by continued investment in network coverage, capacity and quality. In fintech, core mobile money revenue more than doubled, up 102.2per cent, while our airtime and data credit service continued to recover following its resumption under a multi-partner model, with revenue up 78.5per cent in Q2.” Dangote Cement announced N1.47trillion profit before tax, which is 41.45 per cent increase over N1,04 trillion in corresponding period of 2025, while Seplat Energy declared N1.34 trillion profit before tax, which is 52.7 per cent growth from N878.99 billion in nine months of 2025. The Chief Executive Officer, Dangote Cement, Arvind Pathak in a statement said: “The Group delivered a record performance in the nine months ended September 2026. Revenue rose 19.6per cent to N3.77 trillion, EBITDA rose 23.7per cent to N1.77 trillion at a 46.8per cent margin, and profit after tax grew 31.2per cent to a record N974.8 billion, driven by volume growth, broader market reach, and disciplined execution of our strategic priorities.” He added that, “As we enter the final quarter, our priorities remain clear: sustain volume growth, protect margins through cost discipline, expand our regional market presence, and complete our strategic capacity investments. With record profitability, record cash generation and a net-cash balance sheet, we approach these priorities from a position of strength unmatched among African cement producers.” Capital market analysts stressed that Nigerian companies have been resilient over the years despite facing significant economic challenges such as double-digit inflation, 23 per cent interest rate and ongoing security concerns, An Investment Banker and Stockbroker, Mr. Tajudeen Olayinka stated that the profit generation for nine months of 2026 is a reflection of improved economic indicators in Nigeria. He said, “There was an increase in the price of petrol and diesel and these companies passed the cost effect to customers that eventually impacted on their profit generation.” He added that Nigeria companies remain resilient amid growing challenges.

title: New Upgrades to China’s Top Stealth Fighter Detailed in Rare Report: J-20 Continues to Evolve in Service
body: Chinese state media has revealed further details of upgrades to the J-20 fifth generation fighter, highlighting improvements to engine performance, aerodynamic design and sensor systems. A report published by CCTV described the aircraft family’s evolution as part of a broader transformation of the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF), with commentators cited having emphasised that the J-20 is increasingly intended to operate as part of an integrated combat network rather than solely as an individual air-superiority fighter. The J-20 family is also being integrated with a broader range of Chinese combat aircraft and support platforms, including KJ-500 and KJ-3000 AEW&C systems, YY-20 aerial tankers, and J-16 multirole fighters, allowing the Air Force to link stealth aircraft with airborne surveillance, logistical support and additional strike platforms, improving the potential for coordinated operations across a larger battlespace. The upgraded single-seat J-20A incorporates visible changes to the aircraft’s forward fuselage and sensor configuration. One is a raised section behind the cockpit, with a smoother transition between the canopy and the fuselage. Wang suggested that the revised profile could improve aerodynamic performance and support higher-speed flight, although no quantitative performance data were provided. Another change is a protruding component beneath the nose, which Wang said incorporates eight optical lenses, compared with six on the earlier configuration. The revised arrangement may indicate improvements to the aircraft’s electro-optical detection capabilities, potentially enhancing its ability to detect and track targets, including low-observable aircraft. Such sensors could contribute to the J-20A’s effectiveness in networked operations, complementing its radar and other onboard systems. The report highlights that a major milestone in the program was the transition to domestically developed WS-10C engines, which first entered service in 2021. Military commentator Wang Mingliang said the engines provide greater thrust, supporting higher speeds, sustained supersonic cruise and high-load manoeuvres. While the WS-10C was designed as a stopgap, production more recently transitioned to the much more capable WS-15 next generation engine, which is thought to have entered service in 2025. The J-20’s first demonstrator first flew in January 2011, after which the program was able to progress to serial production in little over four years, which represented less than half the time of any other fighter of its generation. Entering service in 2017, its rate of incremental upgrades appear to have far exceeded those made to any other fighter type. The speed at which China’s defence sector was able to move between the first prototype and demonstrator flights, the initiation of serial production, and the bringing of the J-20 into service in February 2017, bore a sharp contrast to rival fifth generation fighter programs in Russia and the United States, with the F-22, F-35 and Su-57 all seeing their first full units formed a full 14-15 years after the first demonstrator flights. This speed was key to allowing China to bridge the gap with the United States in its fifth generation fighter capabilities. The J-20’s production scale would increase significantly from 2021 after the WS-10C entered service, with the fighter J-20 today is in production at over three times the scale of any other twin engine fighter at an estimated 100-120 aircraft per year. It is today widely considered the world’s premier air superiority fighter, with the similarly advanced American F-35 being a much smaller aircraft less well optimised for air-to-air operations, while the Russian Su-57 is considered technologically far behind.

title: YPM Pledges to Deliver 2mVotes for Tinubu, Yayi, Others
body: James Sowole in Abeokuta A major political campaign group for All Progressives Congress (APC) candidates in the 2027 elections in Ogun State, Yayi Progressives Movement (YPM), had promised to deliver not less than two million votes for President Bola Tinubu and also to ensure that the party’s governorship candidate, Senator Solomon Adeola, emerged as the next governor of the Gateway State in 2027. The group also promised to work assiduously to ensure that the Ogun East Senatorial Candidate, Prince Dapo Abiodun, and House of Representatives and State Assembly candidates emerged victorious in the senatorial district. The Convener of YPM, Hon. Amstrong Tope Akintunde, revealed the determination of the group while speaking at the Ogun East Mega Rally organised by the Yayi Progressives Movement. The event, held at the Otunba Dipo Dina Stadium in Ijebu-Ode, served as a major political grassroots mobilisation in support of the re -election of Tinubu and other party candidates for the forthcoming elections. The stadium gathering was preceded by a rally around several streets in the town as political groups, artisan federations, market associations, and youth bodies from all nine local government areas in Ogun East assembled early in the morning to declare their support for the APC. Drummers, cultural troupes, and motorbikes led the procession, with participants chanting slogans supporting Senator Adeola’s legislative track record, highlighting his tenure as the chairman of the Senate Committee on Appropriations. Prominent leaders, legislators, and council chairmen from Ogun East attended the rally and reaffirmed their solidarity with Governor Dapo Abiodun’s administration and also backed YAYI’s vision to succeed him. As part of the proceedings, YPM leaders inaugurated over 1,100 ‘Artisan Ambassadors’ across various trades (tailors, mechanics, carpenters, and hairdressers) to build grassroots structures across the senatorial district. Speakers urged members to continue supporting President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s economic reforms and Governor Abiodun’s ongoing infrastructure projects across Ogun State. Speaking at the stadium, the convener of the movement, Akintunde Armstrong, stated that the rally, which is one of two more to come, will continue to serve as a spring point for political mobilisation as the nation approaches the 2027 general election. “Today, we are sounding it loud and clear that in Ogun State, it is only APC. We will replicate this rally in Ogun Central and Ogun West soon. This massive support is organic, and it will continue until all our candidates are delivered,” he added. In his remarks, Senator Adeola lauded the massive grassroots support movement from YPM, adding that his belief in youth renaissance is reassured. “I came in here, and I was marvelled at the sea of heads in solidarity walk for our party, the APC. I heard some of you have been here since 7 a.m. Whatever is making you come this far is a reassurance that my belief in the youths of our country is never misplaced,” he said. Meanwhile, the Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, while introducing the Ogun East candidates, stated that votes for the APC must be from top to bottom, adding that Ogun State must give President Bola Ahmed Tinubu united votes. “We have promised our president two million votes, and not a single vote must be lost; after all, there is no opposition in Ogun State,” he maintained.

title: Nine killed in Florida Learjet crash after pilots report icing and turbulence
body: Nine people were killed when a Learjet 60 crashed in Florida’s Palm Beach County on November 1, 2026, after its crew reported icing and turbulence, requested a climb and then declared an emergency during a rapid descent. The aircraft was flying from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) in Texas to North Eleuthera Airport (ELH) in the Bahamas. The Learjet crashed near Cresthaven at approximately 12:50 local time, according to the FAA. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that everyone aboard died. Dashcam video shows the jet descending almost vertically beneath dark clouds before striking the ground beside a busy road and erupting in a fireball. The impact left a large crater near homes and passing vehicles. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground being killed or injured. In still frames from the dashcam video, the Learjet appears to be missing its horizontal stabilizer. Minutes before the crash, the crew reported turbulence causing altitude deviations of as much as 700 feet, according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC. “We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers. The crew subsequently reported precipitation and requested a climb. Shortly afterward, the pilot declared an emergency, reporting descent rates increasing from 8,000 to 10,000 and then 20,000 feet per minute, along with an overspeed condition. Flightradar24 identified the aircraft as N722BD. Its tracking data showed the jet departing Austin at 09:37 local time and flying east toward the Bahamas. Near Naples, Florida, the aircraft began descending toward 35,000 feet. The crew later requested a climb to 37,000 feet. The aircraft briefly climbed at approximately 12:48 before entering a steep descending right turn. Its reported descent rate exceeded 32,000 feet per minute, with the last altitude received by Flightradar24 showing 8,750 feet at 12:49:22. Rain and strong thunderstorms were affecting South Florida that day. The National Weather Service said an upper-level low moving over the state was bringing moisture and widespread storms. A flood watch covered Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties at the time of the crash. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office closed Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North as emergency crews worked at the scene. Local officials were arranging shelter and assistance for approximately 600 nearby residents affected by the crash. Authorities had not released the occupants’ names or confirmed how many were passengers and crew. The NTSB is leading the investigation, with FAA assistance. The board dispatched investigators to arrive Sunday and Monday and announced plans for a November 2 media briefing in West Palm Beach. The post Nine killed in Florida Learjet crash after pilots report icing and turbulence appeared first on AeroTime .

title: 'I don't know what came over me': Vandal leaves apology on altar of Maronite church in Nahariya
body: Members of Nahariya's Christian community of South Lebanon Army (SLA) veterans were shocked on Sunday after worshippers discovered smashed statues and vandalized religious images inside a prayer hall used as a church by the community.According to Father Yosef Yaakov, spokesperson for the Maronite community in Israel, a note written in English was left on the altar asking for forgiveness. Nahariya police opened an investigation into the incident, emphasizing that all possible leads were being examined.The prayer hall is on municipal property adjacent to a municipal garden and serves the Lebanese Maronite community for prayer and religious ceremonies.The community numbers approximately 1,100 people. Several dozen worshippers attend Sunday services, while hundreds gather for religious holidays.'I don't know what got into me': Apology left on altarYaakov said the vandalism was discovered at approximately 5:30 p.m., when a worshipper entered the hall ahead of a prayer service scheduled for 7 p.m.According to Yaakov, whoever damaged the statues and religious images left a note on the altar apologizing for the act and including a statement along the lines of "I don't know what came over me."Yaakov stressed that the identities of those responsible and their motives remained unknown."We are waiting for the police to investigate," he said, adding that it was too early to determine whether the vandalism was motivated by religious hatred.As the community awaits the results of the investigation, Yaakov described the pain felt by worshippers over the damage to a place of profound personal and religious significance.He said the incident had caused anger and distress, as well as a feeling among community members that they were unwelcome.Yaakov noted that families with children also attend services at the hall and that the vandalism had raised concerns about their safety, undermining the sense of security in a place where worshippers seek peace and spiritual comfort.Maronite Church condemns vandalism: 'We will not respond to destruction with hatred'The Maronite Archdiocese in Haifa issued a statement strongly condemning the incident.The archdiocese described the vandalism as an attack on the sanctity of a place of worship and on the right of believers to practice their religion freely, safely, and with dignity.Church leaders called on the authorities to investigate the incident, identify those responsible, and bring them to justice. They also demanded measures to protect the prayer hall and prevent similar incidents from recurring.The archdiocese emphasized that the community would continue holding religious services at the site despite the damage."We will not allow this act of vandalism to deter us from exercising our natural right to pray and worship God. We will continue to use this hall and hold our prayers there, with faith, determination, and peace," the statement said.The archdiocese further declared that "we do not respond to harm with harm, and we do not respond to destruction with hatred."However, church leaders stressed that tolerance did not mean remaining silent in the face of harm or relinquishing their rights.Police: 'All avenues of investigation are being examined'Israel Police said the Nahariya police station had immediately opened an investigation after receiving a complaint about the vandalism.Investigators were carrying out a range of investigative activities, and all possible avenues of inquiry were being examined, police said."The Israel Police views seriously any violation of holy places and freedom of worship, and will act decisively, exhausting all means at its disposal to locate those responsible for the act and bring them to justice," police emphasized.

title: A new starting point for Oman-China relations: HM
body:
His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik and the Xi Jinping, President of the People's Republic of China, held an expanded session of official talks at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing as part of His Majesty's state visit to the People's Republic of China. The session reviewed existing fields of cooperation between the two friendly nations and explored avenues to enhance them, particularly in technology and innovation, artificial intelligence, energy, renewable energy, manufacturing, logistics, digital trade, and food security, alongside boosting integration between economic zones and ports. His Majesty the Sultan delivered a speech on this occasion. The full text of the speech reads as follows: “Your Excellency President Xi Jinping, President of the friendly People’s Republic of China: It is a great pleasure to be here in your esteemed country, the friendly People’s Republic of China—a nation that has long served as a civilizational and humanitarian bridge between the East and the West, besides being a hub for cultural radiance and intellectual diversity. We express our deepest appreciation for the warm welcome and hospitality extended to us—a testimony to the genuine character of the friendly Chinese people and the deep-rooted friendship and mutual respect that bind our two nations and peoples. We take this opportunity to affirm the depth of the historical ties between the friendly People’s Republic of China and the Sultanate of Oman. We reiterate our commitment and direct support for the development of these relations, which have recently seen rapid growth across economic, commercial and investment sectors. I am accompanied on this visit by a number of ministers concerned, with the aim of exploring further opportunities for cooperation between our two countries. We also view this visit as a new starting point for the joint march of Omani-Chinese relations. Since their inception, the relations between our two countries have witnessed continuous, positive development. Your nation has become the Sultanate of Oman’s primary trading partner; over the past few years, direct investments by Chinese companies in our country—in partnership with the Oman Investment Authority (OIA)—have reached more than 33 billion Chinese yuan. Furthermore, the scope of our partnership has expanded to encompass energy, industry, infrastructure, logistics, and advanced technologies.

His Majesty the Sultan delivered a speech on this occasion. The full text of the speech reads as follows:
“Your Excellency President Xi Jinping, President of the friendly People’s Republic of China:
It is a great pleasure to be here in your esteemed country, the friendly People’s Republic of China—a nation that has long served as a civilizational and humanitarian bridge between the East and the West, besides being a hub for cultural radiance and intellectual diversity. We express our deepest appreciation for the warm welcome and hospitality extended to us—a testimony to the genuine character of the friendly Chinese people and the deep-rooted friendship and mutual respect that bind our two nations and peoples.
We take this opportunity to affirm the depth of the historical ties between the friendly People’s Republic of China and the Sultanate of Oman. We reiterate our commitment and direct support for the development of these relations, which have recently seen rapid growth across economic, commercial and investment sectors. I am accompanied on this visit by a number of ministers concerned, with the aim of exploring further opportunities for cooperation between our two countries. We also view this visit as a new starting point for the joint march of Omani-Chinese relations.
Since their inception, the relations between our two countries have witnessed continuous, positive development. Your nation has become the Sultanate of Oman’s primary trading partner; over the past few years, direct investments by Chinese companies in our country—in partnership with the Oman Investment Authority (OIA)—have reached more than 33 billion Chinese yuan.
Furthermore, the scope of our partnership has expanded to encompass energy, industry, infrastructure, logistics, and advanced technologies.
We perceive this evolution as a qualitative shift in the nature of the economic ties between our two nations, establishing a more diverse and profound partnership—one rooted in the exchange of expertise, joint investment, the development of productive capacities, and the advancement of knowledge- and technology-based industries. We attach special importance to these relations, with the hope of increasing the volume of trade and encouraging the establishment of projects—through joint investment funds—across a number of strategic sectors.
These include industries related to renewable energy, artificial intelligence, digital technologies, space, and defense. We also look to foster cooperation between our educational and training institutions to advance research and innovation in fields such as technology, healthcare, and food security. Furthermore, we emphasize the significance of continued cultural cooperation, which contributes to the enrichment of knowledge and fosters cross-cultural engagement among our peoples.
We also place particular importance on collaboration between investment and financial institutions, as this creates opportunities to explore and develop diverse, vital, and strategic partnerships.
The Sultanate of Oman is open to entering into a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with the People's Republic of China. We are confident that such an agreement would open new avenues for trade and investment, facilitate and enhance commercial and investment exchanges between our two nations, and create broader prospects for mutual benefits and shared interests. Mr. President,
We would like to express our admiration for your model of governance, which has succeeded in transforming your country into a major global economic power—one whose influence extends well beyond China’s borders and has contributed to the economic advancement of many friendly nations. We share your vision that human beings are the central focus and the ultimate objective of this economic development. Furthermore, we clearly recognize and deeply appreciate the fact that your economic approach is free from any political agendas or hegemonic ambitions.
Geography and maritime trade routes have long fostered closer ties between the Sultanate of Oman and China.
Today, the strategic geographical location of Oman’s ports offers significant advantages, facilitating the connection of global markets and supply chains through the Sultanate’s ports, economic zones, and industrial areas—all of which are benefiting from ongoing development in infrastructure and logistical capabilities. Therefore, we view the "Belt and Road" initiative—which you launched—and "Oman Vision 2040" as frameworks that offer extensive opportunities for integrating the development agendas of our two countries. This is particularly true in sectors such as advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, green hydrogen, modern technologies, the digital economy, and logistics services.
he rapid transformations currently unfolding globally—accompanied by shifts in lifestyles and challenges related to climate change, energy, food and health security, and the stability of supply chains—all underscore the vital importance of partnerships built upon trust, mutual reliance, and interconnected interests. We believe that development and stability are inextricably linked. The prosperity of nations requires an environment defined by security, peace, respect for state sovereignty, and adherence to international law—an environment where disputes are resolved through peaceful means and resources are directed toward construction and development. While we value your leadership role in this regard, we also call for continued coordination with the People’s Republic of China in a manner that serves our mutual interests and contributes to the enhancement of international security, stability, and cooperation. We express our deep appreciation for China’s positions on key issues concerning our region.
Furthermore, we reaffirm the Sultanate of Oman’s steadfast commitment to the "One China" principle, as well as our support for China’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. This firm stance within our foreign policy reflects the mutual respect and political trust that have characterized our bilateral relations for decades.
Just as the ancient maritime Silk Roads once linked the ports and peoples of our two nations, our ambition today is to extend bridges of cooperation between our institutions, economies, and centers for research and innovation. We aim to evolve our partnership—moving beyond mere connectivity through trade routes toward a deeper integration in shaping the future.
We reiterate our sincere appreciation and profound gratitude for this gracious invitation. We look forward to continuing our work with you to consolidate our partnership and friendship, in a manner that brings prosperity and development to our peoples, and contributes to the advancement of peace, stability, and flourishing. We extend our best wishes to the friendly Chinese people for continued progress and prosperity."

title: Zelensky attempting to undermine position of Republicans in the US — Dmitriev
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky does not seem to learn from previous mistakes as he continues attempts to undermine the position of the Republican Party ahead of the US midterm congressional elections, Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian Presidential Special Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), said.
"Zelensky keeps lecturing President Trump. Zelensky doesn’t seem to learn from previous mistakes as he continues trying to undermine Republicans before the midterms," Dmitriev wrote on the social media platform X.
He was commenting on Zelensky’s remarks in an interview with Fox News about a potential energy ceasefire.
"If the American president thinks that this war has influence on the prices [for electricity in the US], so he can ask energy ceasefire [at the negotiations in Abu Dhabi]," Zelensky said, as quoted by Fox News journalist Trey Yingst on his X profile.

title: Enugu Govt, Humatrix Partner to Create 100,000 Jobs via BPO
body: Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt The Enugu State Government and Humatrix Limited have signed a partnership agreement to establish a Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) hub in the state. The long-term target is to create over 100,000 jobs for young people and positioning Enugu as a leading destination for digital services in Nigeria and Africa. The agreement, signed at Government House, Enugu, marks the implementation phase of the initiative, which aligns with Governor Peter Mbah’s economic diversification agenda, human capital development policy and drive to attract private investment. Speaking at the ceremony, Director of Humatrix Limited, Dr Dakuku Peterside, said the company chose Enugu after assessing its investment climate, policy consistency and the state government’s commitment to economic transformation. He said, “It was very easy for us to choose Enugu. Enugu is investing, and there is consistency. Most importantly, we have a supportive environment. These are core things any business would request to scale.” Peterside disclosed that the company would commence operations with a 750-seat BPO centre, expand to over 2,000 seats within the first year and target 100,000 jobs within five years. Also speaking, the Special Adviser to the Governor on MSME and Digital Economy, Mr Arinze Chilo-Offiah, said the partnership represented a significant step towards actualising the governor’s vision of growing Enugu’s economy from $4.4 billion to $30 billion. He explained that the Enugu Talent City Initiative was designed to position the state as a leading digital services and outsourcing hub in Nigeria and Africa, attracting global companies, creating employment and enabling young people to work for international clients from Enugu. In his remarks, Governor Mbah said the partnership was consistent with his administration’s commitment to ensuring that young people could acquire relevant skills, secure rewarding employment and build their futures in Enugu rather than leave the state in search of opportunities.

title: Stakeholders Laud Ogun Free Trade Zone’s Education Programme
body: James Sowole in Abeokuta Education stakeholders and community leaders in Igbesa, Ado-Odo/Ota Local Government Area in Ogun State have commended the Ogun–Guangdong Free Trade Zone (OGFTZ) for its sustained investment in educational development across its host communities. The leaders described the OGFTZ interventions as significant contributions to improving learning opportunities, nurturing talents and shaping the future of young people. The stakeholders, who spoke during separate interactions with journalists, highlighted the impact of its educational initiatives, particularly the establishment of the China–Nigeria Friendship Model School, scholarship opportunities for deserving students and various academic, sporting and extracurricular programmes. Speaking on the zone’s contributions, Mr. Joseph Ibikunle, head of Academics and School Services at the Ado-Odo/Ota Local Government Education Authority, described OGFTZ’s educational interventions in the community for the past 15 years as remarkable and worthy of commendation. Ibikunle noted that the zone had consistently supported learners through interventions in school infrastructure, the provision of educational materials, and scholarship opportunities for deserving students. According to him, these sustained contributions had positively influenced the learning environment and created opportunities for students across the host communities. He expressed appreciation to the management of OGFTZ for its continued commitment to educational development, urging the organisation to sustain its interventions, which he said had made a meaningful difference in the lives of learners across the local government. Also speaking, High Chief Ezekiel Adewumi Durojaiye, the Otunba Amona of Igbesa, identified the establishment of the China–Nigeria Friendship Model School as one of the most significant contributions of the zone to the community. He observed that since the arrival of OGFTZ and the establishment of the school, Igbesa had increasingly become associated with China, to the extent that residents and visitors sometimes jokingly refer to the town as “China in Nigeria.” Describing the school’s impact as remarkable, Durojaiye recalled discussions surrounding its development during the visit of the Chinese Consul-General, expressing optimism that the institution would continue to grow. He said the community would welcome the expansion of the school to accommodate secondary education, and eventually, tertiary-level programmes, adding that such development would further strengthen educational opportunities for children in the area. In a similar account, Chief Ajidagba Jamiu, family head of Ilu Idofin in Igbesa, highlighted the personal impact of the zone’s educational intervention, revealing that four of his children attended the China–Nigeria Friendship School. He also disclosed that some indigenes of the community had benefited from OGFTZ-funded scholarships to study in China and had completed their studies, with some now working in their respective professional fields. While expressing appreciation for the zone’s contributions, he appealed for an expansion of the scholarship programme to accommodate more students from the host communities. He noted that increasing the number of scholarship beneficiaries would give more young people access to quality education and the opportunity to acquire knowledge and skills that could contribute to the development of their communities. The Chairman of the Igbesa Educational Committee, Alhaji Saheed Animashaun, also commended the OGFTZ partnership for its consistent educational and developmental programmes over the past three years. According to him, the zone has maintained a deliberate commitment to organising initiatives that promote the educational advancement and overall development of children in the host communities, with hardly a year passing without at least one programme designed for their benefit. He identified the annual Children’s Day celebrations, which bring together primary and secondary school pupils, as one of the initiatives through which the Zone recognises and encourages young people. Beyond the celebrations, Animashaun said OGFTZ had consistently organised academic, sporting and cultural competitions, including quiz and recitation contests, football, athletics and dancing competitions, providing platforms for students to discover and develop their abilities. He explained that these activities had helped build students’ confidence, encouraged healthy competition and demonstrated that public schools in the host communities are home to talented, intelligent and promising young people. The Education Committee chairman particularly emphasised the importance of these initiatives in identifying and nurturing talents beyond the conventional classroom environment. He added that participating students were rewarded with various gifts and prizes, including musical instruments, mowing machines, educational materials and other useful items, describing the incentives as additional motivation for students to work harder and pursue excellence. Animashaun maintained that investment in education remained one of the most valuable contributions any organisation could make to society, noting that developing the intellectual capacity and talents of young people was essential to building responsible future leaders. He, therefore, expressed appreciation to OGFTZ for its sustained commitment to educational development, urging the Zone to continue its interventions for the benefit of present and future generations.

title: Adewunmi Identifies Strategic Priorities to Boost Sustainable Electricity
body: Chinedu Eze The President of the Lagos Country Club, Seyi Adewunmi, has identified strategies priorities that must be achieved for Nigeria to have sustainable and affordable power accessible to over 230 million of its population. In his welcome address during the Business Forum 3.0 organized by the Club at the weekend in Lagos, with the theme: “Energy Costs and Business Survival: Driving Profitability Amidst Nigeria’s Power Crisis.” Adewunmi said that for Nigeria to become industrialized, create jobs for its teaming youths, the country must solve the intractable problem of power supply. To solve this problem, Adewunmi identifies these priorities, which include the strengthening of electricity generation. “This calls for reliable gas supply, adequate infrastructure, diligent maintenance of existing power plants, and investment in a prudent mix of gas-fired, hydroelectric and renewable sources. New capacity is important, but we must equally ensure that the facilities we already have deliver their full potential,” he said. He said Nigeria must resolve the bottlenecks in transmission and distribution, noting that electricity generated means little if it cannot reach homes and businesses efficiently. “Investment in transmission lines, substations, transformers, distribution networks and modern grid management must be accelerated, even as technical and commercial losses are reduced,” he said.

title: Beyond Giving: How Companies Can Use Corporate Philanthropy to Build Stronger, Self-sustaining Communities
body: Sam Ogbemi Daibo For decades, the relationship between companies and their host communities in Nigeria has largely been defined by projects. A company builds a classroom, renovates a health centre, provides boreholes, awards scholarships or rehabilitates a road. These interventions can be valuable. They meet real needs and often improve lives. But after decades of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), we must ask a harder question: have these projects created communities that are economically stronger, institutionally capable and increasingly able to sustain their own development? Too often, the answer is no. Nigeria’s next development challenge is therefore not simply to do more CSR. It is to move beyond CSR—from delivering community projects to investing in community systems. The distinction matters. A project asks: What can we build for this community? Community investment asks: What can we build with this community that strengthens its institutions, expands economic opportunity and continues creating value long after the intervention ends? That shift changes everything. From Beneficiaries to Development Partners The Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) presents an important opportunity to rethink this relationship in Nigeria’s oil- and gas-producing communities. Through Host Community Development Trusts (HCDTs), the PIA provides a framework for communities to participate more systematically in identifying and advancing their development priorities. But establishing HCDTs is only the beginning. Their long-term value will depend on whether they become credible, accountable and capable institutions for community development. That requires more than funding projects. It requires strong governance, participatory planning, accountability, evidence-based decision-making and sustained collaboration among communities, operators, regulators and other stakeholders. This lesson has been reinforced through PIND’s work with HCDTs under the Bridges Project. The experience points to a simple but important conclusion: the real value of an HCDT should not be measured only by the projects it funds, but by its ability to govern resources responsibly, engage its stakeholders, track results and make increasingly strategic development investments. As the Bridges Project concludes, one question has become particularly important: what happens after the project ends? It is a question that should be asked of every corporate-community intervention in Nigeria. Build Economies, Not Just Infrastructure Community investment also requires us to rethink what successful development looks like. A vocational training centre is useful. But its value multiplies when training responds to market demand, employers participate, graduates can access finance and businesses have customers. A solar mini-grid provides electricity. But when that electricity powers enterprises, increases productivity and creates opportunities for local service providers, it becomes part of a local economic system. Agricultural support becomes more sustainable when farmers are connected to processors, finance, technology and reliable markets rather than receiving inputs year after year. The objective should not be for communities to permanently wait for the next corporate intervention. It should be communities with stronger institutions and local economies capable of attracting investment, creating livelihoods and sustaining development. That requires a fundamental change in mindset: from companies as providers and communities as beneficiaries, to companies and communities as development partners. New Compact for Corporate- c ommunity Relations This principle extends far beyond oil and gas. As investment expands across mining, agriculture, renewable energy, manufacturing and infrastructure, Nigeria needs a new compact between businesses and the communities in which they operate. For companies, this is not philanthropy dressed in new language. Strong local economies, trusted institutions and constructive community relationships can contribute to more stable and sustainable operating environments. For communities, it means moving beyond one-off benefits towards institutions, capabilities and economic opportunities that endure. For government and regulators, it means encouraging long-term community value rather than measuring success simply by the number of projects completed. And for development organisations, it requires recognising that our greatest legacy may not be the projects we leave behind, but the systems, capabilities and relationships that continue to function after we leave. At the Bridges Project Impact Summit, stakeholders are being challenged to answer three questions: What changed? What was learned? What happens next? That final question is perhaps the most important because sustainability begins when ownership outlives intervention. From Projects to Prosperity Nigeria will continue to need schools, roads, health facilities, water systems and other community infrastructure. The argument is not that companies should stop building projects. It is that projects should become building blocks of stronger community systems—not the final measure of development. So perhaps the question companies should ask is no longer: What project can we give this community? But: What can we invest in together that will make this community stronger long after we are gone? That is the shift from CSR to community investment. And it may be one of the most important shifts Nigeria can make in moving communities from being recipients of development to owners of their prosperity. . Sam Daibo is the E xecutive D irector of the Foundation for Partnership Initiatives in the Niger Delta (PIND).

title: Access Bank Appoints Kumapayi DMD, African Subsidiaries, Bamisebi ED, IT
body: Nume Eekeghe Access Bank Plc has announced the appointed Oluseyi Kumapayi as Deputy Managing Director, African Subsidiaries, and Olanrewaju Bamisebi as Executive Director, Information Technology and Digitalisation, as its parent company, Access Holdings Plc, moves to strengthen operational efficiency, profitability and technology-driven growth. The Holdings company in a statement noted that the appointments which received the approval of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), took effect from October 27 and October 28, 2026, respectively. Kumapayi was elevated from his previous position as Executive Director, African Subsidiaries, while Bamisebi joins the board of Access Bank from Access Holdings, where he held the position of Executive Director, Information Technology and Digitalisation. The appointments reflect the Group’s shift from expanding its footprint to extracting greater value from its existing businesses, with increased emphasis on profitability, capital efficiency, operational performance and sustainable shareholder returns. Kumapayi brings more than 25 years of banking experience spanning financial management, strategy, risk, treasury and business development. He joined Access Bank in 2002 and served as Group Chief Financial Officer from 2007 to 2020, before becoming Executive Director, African Subsidiaries, in November 2020. In his new role, he will continue overseeing the Bank’s African operations, with an expanded mandate to improve subsidiary profitability, capital productivity and operational efficiency, while strengthening business integration across the markets. He will also support the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer in the broader leadership and strategic management of the Bank. Kumapayi is a Fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria and holds an Executive MBA from IMD, Lausanne, as well as an Executive Master’s degree in Digital Transformation and Innovation Leadership from IE University, Madrid. He is also an alumnus of Harvard Business School’s General Management Programme. Bamisebi, who has over 20 years of experience in technology transformation, digital banking and enterprise systems, previously held senior positions at Equity Group Holdings Limited, including Group Director, Information Technology and Operations, and Managing Director of Finserve Africa. He also served as Group Chief Information Officer at Diamond Bank and held other technology leadership positions within Nigeria’s financial services industry. At Access Bank, he will lead the technology and digitalisation agenda, focusing on modernising technology platforms, strengthening cybersecurity and operational resilience, improving efficiency and accelerating digital solutions to enhance customer experience and business performance. His appointment also transfers executive responsibility for technology transformation from the holding company directly to the Bank, bringing technology investment closer to its commercial and operational priorities. Commenting on the appointments, Group Chairman, Access Holdings Plc, Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, said the Group was focused on converting its extensive banking presence into stronger financial performance and improved returns. “Access Holdings has built a substantial banking franchise across Africa and beyond. Our strategic priority is now to translate that scale into superior performance, greater efficiency, stronger returns on capital and sustainable value for shareholders. “These appointments reflect that priority. Mr. Kumapayi’s elevation reinforces our determination to improve the performance and contribution of our African subsidiaries, while Mr. Bamisebi’s appointment reflects a deliberate decision to bring executive technology leadership closer to the Bank’s operations, customers and commercial priorities. “We believe that clearer accountability, stronger execution and disciplined investment in technology will be critical to the next phase of our development. Both executives bring the experience and leadership required to advance these objectives.” Also commenting, Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Access Bank Plc, Roosevelt Ogbonna, said the Bank would prioritise productivity, efficiency and profitability while making better use of its capital, technology and existing market presence. “Our focus is on building a more productive, efficient and profitable banking institution, making better use of our capital, technology and established market presence. “Across our African subsidiaries, the emphasis will be on improving returns, strengthening execution and capturing greater value from our existing franchise. In technology, our priority is to simplify platforms, improve reliability, accelerate innovation and deliver better outcomes for our customers at a lower cost to serve. “By integrating executive technology leadership more directly into the Bank’s management structure, we are strengthening the connection between technology investment and business performance. I look forward to working with both executives as we deliver on these priorities.”

title: Luminate: Nigeria Shows Global Tech Giants Not Beyond Reach
body: Kayode Tokede The Chief Executive Officer of Luminate, Melanie Hui, yesterday praised Nigeria as a leading example of how African countries can shape the global artificial intelligence economy rather than simply consume it. She pointed to the country’s regulators, workers and innovators as proof that the continent is already setting its own terms. Hui gave the keynote address at the Build 2026 Conference in Abuja. The audience included the Honourable Minister of Communication, Innovation and Digital Economy, heads of government parastatals, members of the diplomatic community and members of the Nigeria AI Collective. She said research Luminate commissioned this year on the continent’s AI landscape “found not only patterns of extraction and inequality. It found imagination and leadership.” “Here, there are important reasons for optimism,” she said. Hui cited the action Nigeria’s competition authority took against Meta over data exploitation and discriminatory practices. She said this showed that “global tech companies are not beyond the reach of national institutions.” She also praised app-based drivers in Nigeria for securing government recognition for Africa’s first e-hailing trade union. She said innovators across Nigeria are “using locally built, practical technology to serve the underserved: from bringing reliable banking for rural communities to tackling massive crop losses.” Her examples from elsewhere on the continent were litigation in Kenya establishing that global technology companies can be brought before Kenyan courts civil society coalitions in South Africa challenging bulk surveillance at the Constitutional Court AI-assisted learning materials in local languages helping children in Mali drones extending healthcare to remote islands in Uganda

title: Funding: Why Stronger Partnerships Are Essential to Unlocking Nigeria’s Investment Potential
body: Richard Madiebo Nigeria is not a country short of opportunities. Across its states and economic sectors, there are infrastructure projects waiting to be developed, agricultural value chains capable of supporting greater productivity, businesses seeking opportunities to expand and communities whose economic prospects could be transformed by well-directed investment. From the possibilities of industrial development to the growing interest in technology, trade and renewable energy, the country’s economic potential remains considerable. Yet, between identifying these opportunities and translating them into projects that create jobs, strengthen institutions and improve livelihoods lies one of Nigeria’s most persistent development challenges: the ability to mobilise the right resources, build credible partnerships and convert investment intentions into measurable results. For years, conversations about economic development have understandably focused on the availability of funding. Governments require resources to deliver infrastructure and public services. Businesses need capital to expand operations, while development institutions seek opportunities that align financial commitments with sustainable outcomes. But experience continues to demonstrate that access to capital, while important, is rarely sufficient on its own. A project may attract investor interest without having the institutional capacity required for execution. An investment opportunity may appear commercially attractive but lack the financial structures needed to manage its risks. Similarly, a partnership may bring together influential stakeholders without establishing a clear pathway from agreement to implementation. The real opportunity for Nigeria, therefore, lies not only in attracting more investment, but in strengthening the systems, relationships and institutional capabilities that enable investment to deliver lasting economic value. Development Finance and Access to Capital Development finance remains an important instrument for supporting economic transformation, particularly in sectors where long-term financing needs, infrastructure requirements or investment risks may limit the availability of conventional commercial funding. Through appropriate financing structures, technical assistance, guarantees and partnerships, development finance institutions can help support projects with significant economic and social potential. However, effective development financing requires a clear understanding of the relationship between funding, project readiness and execution capacity. Consider a state government seeking to develop an agricultural processing hub. The opportunity may be compelling: improved market access for farmers, increased local processing capacity, employment opportunities and stronger regional trade. Yet translating that ambition into a viable investment requires more than securing an initial financial commitment. There must be clarity around infrastructure requirements, commercial demand, financial sustainability, governance arrangements, environmental and social considerations, and the responsibilities of participating institutions. Investors need confidence that the project is appropriately structured. Development partners require assurance that resources will be deployed towards clearly defined objectives. Governments must also establish mechanisms for accountability and continuity. These considerations reinforce an important principle: investment readiness is just as critical as investment availability. By strengthening project preparation, financial governance and institutional capacity, Nigeria can improve its ability to attract suitable financing and maximise the value of available development resources. Turning Partnerships to Economic Growth As development priorities become increasingly complex, collaboration between governments, development institutions, private investors and financial service providers is no longer merely desirable. It is essential. No single institution possesses all the financial resources, technical expertise, market knowledge and operational capabilities required to address Nigeria’s development needs. Government provides policy direction, public infrastructure priorities and the enabling environment. Development finance institutions contribute specialised financing instruments and technical expertise. Private sector organisations bring investment, innovation and operational capacity. Financial institutions, meanwhile, play an important role in connecting these interests through banking relationships, financial intermediation, appropriate transaction structures and the management of financial flows. The effectiveness of these partnerships, however, depends on the clarity of their shared objectives. Partnerships must move beyond expressions of interest and ceremonial agreements to clearly defined responsibilities, realistic implementation plans and measurable outcomes. A successful collaboration should answer fundamental questions: What specific problem is being addressed? What resources and capabilities are required? How will risks be allocated and managed? What constitutes success, and how will progress be evaluated? Equally important is the ability of institutions to sustain these relationships beyond individual projects, leadership transitions or immediate funding cycles. Where trust, transparency and accountability are embedded in the partnership structure, the potential for long-term value creation becomes significantly stronger. Strengthening Public Institutions The public sector occupies a particularly important position in Nigeria’s investment landscape. Across federal, state and local government institutions, decisions regarding infrastructure development, revenue management, financial administration and public service delivery directly influence the environment in which businesses and investors operate. Consequently, strengthening public financial management is not simply an administrative priority. It is also an important component of investment readiness. Effective revenue collection, reliable financial reporting, transparent transaction processes and improved reconciliation can support stronger financial administration and more informed planning. For institutions seeking to attract development funding or collaborate with investment partners, these capabilities can contribute to the credibility and reliability of their financial operations. Digital financial infrastructure presents opportunities in this regard. Technology-enabled collections, payment processing, transaction monitoring and reporting can help institutions improve operational visibility, reduce unnecessary manual processes and strengthen financial controls when appropriately implemented. However, digital transformation should not be viewed as a substitute for good governance. The introduction of technology must be accompanied by reliable systems, institutional accountability, effective oversight and the capacity of people to use those systems appropriately. Ultimately, progress is achieved not merely by adopting digital platforms, but by improving the quality, transparency and efficiency of the underlying financial processes. Unlocking Opportunities Nigeria’s investment ambitions also extend beyond its borders. International development partners, multilateral institutions, foreign investors and Nigerians living abroad represent important sources of financial relationships, expertise, entrepreneurial networks and potential investment opportunities. The Nigerian diaspora, in particular, maintains significant economic and social connections with the country. Beyond supporting families and meeting financial obligations at home, Nigerians abroad contribute professional expertise, international business experience and valuable connections across markets. These capabilities present opportunities for deeper participation in enterprise development, investment partnerships and broader economic activities. However, encouraging sustainable engagement requires more than appealing to patriotic sentiment or highlighting potential financial returns. Investors and professionals operating across borders need credible information, suitable financial structures, transparent processes and confidence in the institutions through which they engage. International development partners similarly require clarity regarding regulatory conditions, project viability, implementation arrangements and accountability. Strengthening these foundations can help Nigeria develop more productive relationships with global investors and development institutions, while creating clearer pathways for Nigerians abroad to participate in relevant economic opportunities. For financial institutions, this also highlights the importance of facilitating appropriate cross-border banking relationships, reliable payment processes and access to financial information that enables more informed decisions. Evolving Role of Financial Institutions As Nigeria pursues greater investment and economic diversification, financial institutions have an increasingly important role in supporting the relationships and systems required for sustainable growth. This responsibility extends beyond providing conventional banking services. Banks can contribute to investment conversations by connecting stakeholders, facilitating financial transactions, supporting institutional banking requirements and helping businesses and public sector organisations navigate relevant financial processes. Their understanding of customer needs, sectoral activities and financial infrastructure can also provide practical perspectives on the challenges that affect investment implementation. At Fidelity Bank, we recognise that supporting economic development requires sustained engagement with the institutions, businesses and communities that drive it. Our work across public sector banking, collections, digital financial services and other business segments reinforces the importance of providing relevant financial solutions while building relationships that contribute to long-term economic value. This approach recognises that economic development is interconnected. Stronger public institutions can support a more conducive investment environment. More efficient financial processes can improve business operations. Better access to appropriate banking solutions can facilitate commercial activities, while productive partnerships can create opportunities that extend across industries and communities. The challenge is to connect these different elements in ways that respond to real economic needs. It is equally important to recognise that financial institutions cannot independently resolve structural development challenges. Meaningful progress depends on effective collaboration among government, regulators, development partners, investors, businesses and other stakeholders. From Conversations to Concrete Outcomes Nigeria’s development future will be shaped not only by the resources it attracts, but also by how effectively those resources are mobilised, managed and translated into productive outcomes. The next phase of investment engagement must therefore place greater emphasis on the quality of partnerships, institutional preparedness and practical implementation. Development finance conversations should lead to stronger project pipelines and better-informed investment decisions. Partnerships should establish clearer responsibilities and pathways for execution. Financial innovation should contribute to improved efficiency, transparency and confidence. Most importantly, stakeholders must remain focused on outcomes that extend beyond the immediate transaction or agreement. These considerations are central to Fidelity Bank’s upcoming high-level stakeholder webinar, themed “From Partnerships to Impact: Unlocking Development Finance and Investment Opportunities in Nigeria,” scheduled for Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The engagement will bring together perspectives from government, development finance institutions, international partners, investors and the private sector to examine opportunities for strengthening collaboration and unlocking sustainable investment in Nigeria. Beyond the exchange of ideas, conversations of this nature can contribute to a deeper understanding of the responsibilities, opportunities and practical considerations involved in advancing national development. For Nigeria, the real measure of progress will not be the number of investment conversations held or partnerships announced. It will be the extent to which those efforts produce viable projects, strengthen institutions, expand economic opportunities and improve lives. The country has no shortage of possibilities. What it needs is a stronger connection between ambition and execution, between available capital and investment readiness, and between partnerships and measurable development impact. That is where the next chapter of Nigeria’s investment story must begin. .Richard Madiebo is the Divisional Head, Public Sector & Collections, Fidelity Bank Plc. Fidelity Bank’s high-level stakeholder webinar holds on November 3, 2026, at 10:00am WAT. Registration: www.fidelitybank.ng/publicsectorwebinar/

title: NCC to Curb Influx of Fake SIM-enabled Devices with Device Checker
body: Emma Okonji The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), has announced its intention to introduce Device Checker, a technology tool that allows mobile device merchants to verify if the model of devices they are importing into Nigeria has been type-approved by the NCC. According to NCC, the initiative will help reduce influx of fake and substandard mobile devices that are SIM-enabled in Nigeria, with a view to addressing network distortion and frequency jam, often caused by substandard devices that were smuggled into the country. NCC therefore warned that henceforth, any existing SIM-enabled device that has not been type approved by NCC, would be blocked from accessing any network in Nigeria, and advised device users, especially mobile phone users to verify if the device they are interested in purchasing, is type approved by the NCC. Speaking during a press conference in Lagos, the Executive Vice Chairman of NCC, Dr. Aminu Maida, said the purpose of the briefing was to update the public on the implementation of the NCC Device Checker Platform, an initiative designed to strengthen Type Approval compliance, protect consumers, and enhance the integrity of communications devices used on Nigerian networks. Maida, who was represented by the Director/Zonal Controller, Lagos Zonal Office of the NCC, Mr. Tunji Jimoh, said: “As Nigeria’s digital economy continues to expand, it is important that devices connected to our networks comply with established technical and regulatory standards. The Device Checker Platform supports the verification of the Type Approval status of SIM-enabled devices and helps address the circulation of non-compliant, counterfeit, cloned, and unauthorised devices in the market.” According to Maida, to further simplify compliance processes, NCC has developed a user-friendly Device Checker application that enables authorised stakeholders to quickly scan device IMEIs and upload information directly to the platform, improving efficiency and ease of compliance.

title: Police forward Ashie Moore case docket to AG for prosecution over alleged theft
body: By Isaac Yeboah The Ghana Police Service has forwarded the case docket involving Greater Accra Regional Chairman of the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC), Emmanuel Nii Ashie Moore, to the Attorney-General’s Department for prosecution over allegations of stealing from a Singaporean businessman. The forwarding of the docket, with a covering letter dated October 28, 2026, marks a new development in a case that has been under police investigation since 2025, and in which the Attorney-General’s Department had, as far back as March 16, 2026, advised that Mr Ashie Moore be prosecuted. Ashie Moore, on the other hand, has vehemently denied any wrongdoing, insisting that the allegations constitute a smear campaign against his political acumen. The latest police action brings the case a step closer to prosecution, following months of investigations and questions over when the Attorney-General’s directive would translate into formal prosecutorial action. The case stems from a complaint by Singaporean businessman Toh You Kang, who accused Mr Ashie Moore of taking his personal belongings, including his passport, luxury luggage, electronic gadgets and US$10,000 in cash, while he was in police custody in June 2025. The Attorney-General’s Department, after reviewing the police investigation docket, advised that Mr Ashie Moore be charged with stealing, contrary to Section 124 of the Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29). The advice, issued by Senior State Attorney Nana Ama A. Prempeh, followed an assessment of statements from the complainant, the suspect and police investigators, as well as CCTV footage and a cybercrime analysis report obtained from Fiesta Residences in Cantonments, Accra. How the case started According to the investigation docket, Mr You Kang travelled to Ghana in May 2025 following an invitation from Mr Ashie Moore for a proposed business investment. The complainant told investigators that he had been introduced to the NDC regional chairman through a business associate and arrived at the Kotoka International Airport on May 28, 2025, accompanied by a second suspect, identified as Luibing Liang, a Chinese national. He alleged that upon arrival, Mr Ashie Moore took custody of his Singaporean passport under the pretext of facilitating VIP clearance procedures. The complainant was subsequently accommodated at Fiesta Residences in Cantonments before being taken to a property in Adenta, which he said was presented as Mr Ashie Moore’s residence. There, according to his account, he was accused of fraud and asked to pay US$5.5 million. He alleged that Mr Ashie Moore threatened police involvement and detention if he failed to comply. Mr You Kang was subsequently arrested on May 28, 2025, following a complaint of defrauding by false pretences lodged by Mr Ashie Moore. A police investigator, Detective Corporal David Agbeve, told investigators that he led a team to arrest the businessman at a residence in Adenta at about 10 p.m. that day. The complainant was cautioned and charged on May 29 before being arraigned in court on May 30, 2025, and remanded into custody. Missing belongings and hotel CCTV footage The alleged stealing at the centre of the prosecution’s advice concerns the complainant’s personal belongings at Fiesta Residences while he was in police custody. Mr You Kang told investigators that he encountered difficulties retrieving his medication and luggage from the hotel during his detention. A police officer, D/Cpl. Agbeve, said he accompanied the complainant to what they initially believed was Fiesta Royale Hotel in Dzorwulu, but they subsequently established that his accommodation was at Fiesta Residences in Cantonments. The officer said the complainant’s lawyer confirmed the correct location and indicated that hotel management had locked him out of his room over alleged indebtedness. According to the investigator, Mr Ashie Moore later brought medication the complainant had requested to the Accra Central Police Station cells. When questioned about how he obtained the medication, Mr Ashie Moore reportedly said he had appealed to the hotel management to retrieve it from the complainant’s luggage. The case was subsequently reassigned to another investigator, who indicated that he would follow up with the hotel management to retrieve the complainant’s belongings. Mr You Kang later alleged that while he was in custody, Mr Ashie Moore and others had checked him out of the hotel and removed his personal effects. The missing items listed in his statement included a Louis Vuitton duffle bag, a Bugatti luggage bag, four mobile phones, an iPad, credit and debit cards, house keys, two luxury vehicle keys, watches, clothing, perfumes, accessories, medication, his Singaporean passport and US$10,000 in cash. He told investigators that none of the items had been returned to him. Police investigation and evidence The matter was referred to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) of the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) Headquarters following a petition submitted on behalf of the complainant by Cletus Bayor on June 27, 2025. Chief Inspector Gabriel Ametame, an investigator with the SIU, told the police that the petition alleged that Mr Ashie Moore had collected the complainant’s personal belongings from Fiesta Residences after his arrest and remand. The police subsequently obtained a court order directing the management of Fiesta Residences to produce CCTV footage covering the relevant period. According to the statement of Detective Chief Inspector Timothy B. Asamoah of the SIU, who received the docket on July 24, 2025, investigators reviewed the footage alongside a cybercrime analysis report. The analysis provided a chronological account of activities at the hotel, including the arrival of individuals, the movement of luggage and the handling and retrieval of items considered relevant to the investigation. Following an examination of the footage and other investigative findings, Mr Ashie Moore was charged with stealing on July 28, 2025. He, however, denied the allegation in his statement to the police, maintaining that he had not taken the complainant’s belongings and did not have any of the items in his possession. Attorney-General’s directive In her legal advice dated March 16, 2026, Senior State Attorney Nana Ama A. Prempeh said a review of the entire docket, including the statements of the complainant, the suspect and investigating officers, the CCTV footage and the accompanying cybercrime analysis report, provided sufficient evidence to support a charge of stealing against Mr Ashie Moore. The advice noted that the CCTV footage corroborated the removal of the complainant’s luggage from the hotel by Mr Ashie Moore and other unidentified persons. It also identified what it described as unexplained circumstances surrounding the suspect’s possession of the complainant’s medication and how the passport eventually came to be deposited at the High Court Registry. The Attorney-General’s Department concluded that the circumstances supported an inference that the complainant’s belongings had been dishonestly appropriated without lawful justification. It consequently directed the police to charge Mr Ashie Moore with stealing under Section 124 of Act 29, obtain a charge statement from him and forward it to the Law Office. The duplicate SIU docket, with reference number R.O. 204/2025, was retained for prosecution. The police forwarding of the case docket on October 28 is the latest indication that the process is advancing following the Attorney-General’s assessment. Passport deposited at High Court Registry The whereabouts of the Singaporean businessman’s passport also featured in the investigation.
