title: Nigerian families and survivors seek justice over miners’ deaths
body: Families of 37 artisanal miners who died in custody in Nigeria want ‌swift justice and the return of property seized during their arrest, saying no financial compensation will make up for their loss. A presidential panel on Tuesday found that the detainees, who were suspected of being illegal miners, had died ​from overcrowding, extreme heat, dehydration and neglect while being held by the Nigeria Security ​and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State last month. Nigeria’s government welcomed the panel’s findings, and Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said it had sent the report to the Attorney General for immediate judicial action. He did not respond to requests for comment on when victims’ families ​and survivors would receive compensation. The deaths, including of teenagers, triggered protests in Nigeria, raising new concerns about conditions in detention facilities and the treatment of suspects awaiting trial. “What we wanted was for our children to be alive and ​return to us,” said Zainab Salihu, whose son was among the dead. She said the deaths in ​detention had led to the deterioration of the health of her husband, who later died. Reuters was unable to ‌verify ⁠the circumstances of her husband’s death. “No matter how much money they give us, it will never bring our children back,” Salihu said. Dantala Tanko, whose 25-year-old son Suleiman died in detention, is struggling to come to terms with his loss. “Now he is gone, and this is deeply painful for me. ​I know he will ​never return,” he said ⁠after praying at his son’s grave. Some survivors said they appreciated the investigation’s findings, but wanted accountability. “Officers who demonstrate such disregard for human life should ​not remain in positions of authority. They must be held accountable, and ​appropriate disciplinary action ⁠should be taken,” said 25-year-old Dauda Shehu. Abdulsalam Yakubu, 23, said government action had been slow. He said he wanted the government to return motorcycles, phones, mining equipment and gold, which he said had ⁠been ​seized during the victims’ arrest. “We have suffered enough. We are ​asking for justice, the promised support, and the return of our property so that we can begin to rebuild our ​lives,” he told Reuters.

title: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest Formula 1 world champion
body:
MEXICO CITY, November 2. /TASS/. Mercedes' Italian driver Kimi Antonelli has set a new record as the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history.
Antonelli clinched his maiden title at the age of 20 years and 69 days, shattering the previous record held by Germany’s Sebastian Vettel, who won his first championship in 2010 at 23 years and 134 days.
As TASS reported earlier, Antonelli clinched his historic Formula 1 championship following the Mexico Grand Prix.

title: Nigeria says troops kill 48 Islamist fighters after attacks in Borno, Yobe bases
body: Nigerian troops, backed by air support, repelled ​attacks by Islamist fighters on military ‌positions in the northeastern Borno and Yobe states, killing 48 insurgents, the military said ​on Friday. Attacks by Islamist groups Boko ​Haram and its splinter Islamic State ⁠West Africa Province (ISWAP) on military positions ​in the region have surged in recent weeks ​despite years of military operations aimed at containing the 17-year insurgency in northeastern Nigeria. Military spokesperson ​Captain Mohammed Goni said troops foiled ​overnight attacks by Boko Haram and ISWAP fighters ‌on ⁠Bitta in Borno and a military training school in Buni Yadi, Yobe Air-backed troops in Bitta repelled an overnight assault ​before launching ​a counter-offensive ⁠against ISWAP fighters who attacked the military school in ​Buni Yadi, with fighting continuing into ​the ⁠early hours of Friday, Goni said The military said one soldier was killed and ⁠two ​were lightly wounded and ​receiving treatment.

title: King Charles’ sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
body: King Charles has since 2022 expressed sorrow for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has ‌long resisted: an apology. That balancing act will likely be tested at next week’s Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders backing a reparations campaign through the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are expected to press their case. Buckingham Palace has indicated Charles would not apologise on behalf of Britain, which has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over ​its role in the transatlantic slave trade. Speaking in the Bahamas on Tuesday ahead of a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting that begins ​on Sunday, Charles said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past,” ⁠and said leaders from affected countries would discuss the issue at the summit. But Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas’ National Reparations Committee, said that ​did not go far enough. “We do not need more carefully crafted words about healing,” she said in a statement. “We need action equal with the scale ​of the harm inflicted.” On Friday, about 15 people protested ahead of the king’s arrival in Georgetown, Guyana. They gathered outside the Umana Yana, a conical palm-thatched hut originally built for the 1972 Non-Aligned Foreign Ministers Conference, where Charles later delivered a speech. “It’s an opportunity to try to impress upon him this historic responsibility for what took place ​here,” said Terence Campbell, a member of parliament for the opposition APNU, who stood among the protesters holding a banner that read: “No apology will ​return what was stolen. Reparations now!” ROYAL LINKS TO SLAVERY UNDER SCRUTINY From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery ‌by ⁠European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database. Alan Lester, a University of Sussex historian whose research spans the legacies of slavery and empire, said opponents of the reparations movement had “successfully weaponised” the idea that reparations simply meant writing a cheque, an idea that few Western governments will countenance. Instead, Caribbean leaders often frame their demands in terms ​of debt relief, development finance, education, ​healthcare and climate resilience, measures ⁠they say would address inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism. “I think King Charles III is in a difficult position because you can express sorrow about something, but an apology goes much further,” royal commentator Afua Hagan said. Buckingham Palace ​said in 2023 that Charles had given his support to research that was examining the monarchy’s links ​to slavery after the ⁠Guardian newspaper reported on a document showing a historical connection. In a more recent finding, independent researcher Desiree Baptiste told Reuters her forthcoming book, “George IV, Empire, and Objects of Prestige,” would cite House of Lords papers and other British government records showing that profits derived from enslaved labour helped fund furniture and decorative ⁠work commissioned ​by George IV at royal residences. In response, the Royal Collection Trust, a charity that maintains and displays artworks and historic objects held in trust by the king, said ongoing research helps it keep its records “continually under review in order to improve the information presented on ​an object or subject”.

title: MWI Book Club: Project Maven
body:
Welcome to the MWI Book Club, a podcast predicated on the idea that a military that reads is a military that wins wars. On this episode, cohosts John Amble and Theo Lipsky read a new account of the rise of artificial intelligence in US military operations: Project Maven: A Marine Colonel, His Team, and the Dawn of AI Warfare , by Katrina Manson.
The book follows a Marine intelligence officer named Drew Cukor through the post-9/11 wars as he encounters troubles with the US military’s intelligence and communications architecture—then seeks to overcome them with artificial intelligence. What emerges is Project Maven. Along the way, the reader gets a panoramic view of conflict in the twenty-firstcentury and US the national security enterprise.
Many questions arise from the Project Maven story: Can the US joint force integrate artificial intelligence into its operations? Should it? What are the best uses of artificial intelligence for military operations? Are any of its promises false? What does it take to change a large bureaucracy? And is such change always worth the cost?
In their close read of the book, John and Theo explore these questions and more. You can listen to the full episode below or find it on Apple Podcasts or your favorite podcast app. While you’re there be sure to subscribe so you don’t miss December’s episode, featuring a discussion about John Steinbeck’s World War II novel The Moon Is Down . And if you’ve enjoyed the first four episodes of the MWI Book Club , please leave a rating or give it a review, which helps new listeners to find the podcast.
Lastly, if you have ideas about what books we should consider next, don’t hesitate to reach out at john.amble@westpoint.edu or theodore.lipsky@westpoint.edu .

title: China and Indonesia Launch First Major Joint Exercises in 14 Years as Major Fighter Deliveries Loom
body: China and Indonesia have resumed their Sharp Knife series of joint army counter-terrorism exercises after a 14-year hiatus, with the latest iteration focusing on hostage-rescue operations in mountainous terrain and coordination between manned and unmanned systems. The Sharp Knife 2026 exercise is being held in Guangdong Province in southern China from late October to early November, and is the third exercise in the series, following earlier drills in 2011 and 2012. The training is designed to improve the two militaries’ ability to conduct counter-terrorism operations in difficult terrain. Activities include mountain climbing, the use of specialised vehicles, helicopter rappelling, close-quarters assaults and cooperation between personnel and unmanned platforms. The exercise also includes specialist training in reconnaissance, communications, unmanned systems and sniping, alongside tactical coordination and comprehensive drills involving mixed groups of Chinese and Indonesian troops. China and Indonesia have faced common terror threats primarily form Turkish-backed jihadist groups such as the East Turkestan Islamic Party, which have maintained a presence in Indonesia, and carried out large scale attacks on civilians in Central Asia, China and Thailand. The renewed exercises are intended to strengthen practical military cooperation and improve the ability of both forces to operate together. Beyond counter-terrorism, Chinese commentary has highlighted potential applications in tackling transnational crime, including telecommunications fraud and human trafficking. The two countries have also expanded high-level security dialogue, including through a joint foreign and defence ministerial mechanism established in 2025. Chinese military commentator Song Zhongping has highlgihted that the scenario involves a coordinated sequence of operations to rescue hostages held in mountainous and forested areas. Drones would conduct initial reconnaissance, followed by ground teams using climbing techniques and specialised vehicles to approach and isolate the target area. Helicopters could then insert personnel by rappelling, before troops conduct close-quarters assaults to locate and free hostages. The previous Sharp Knife exercises were held in Bandung, Indonesia, in June 2011 and Jinan, China, in July 2012. The initiation of joint exercises has occurred amid growing signs if strengthening defence cooperation between Beijing and Jakarta, including Indonesia’s large scale procurement of J-10C fighter aircraft to form the new backbone of its combat aviation fleet. Indonesian Defence Minister Sjafrie Sjamseoddin first confirmed the planned procurement of J-10C fighters on October 16, 2025, while Indonesian sources in early October 2026 reported that the country’s armed forces were preparing to receive their first J-10C fighters within six months. Local sources in June widely reported that the country’s defence ministry has doubled orders from 42 to 84 fighters, potentially making Indonesia by far the largest foreign operator of the type. Acquiring such a large number of J-10s would allow the Air Force to phase all its older fighter types out of service, including the U.S. F-5 and F-16, and the Russian Su-27 and Su-30. The strengthening of defence cooperation reflects a broader bolstering of economic ties between Jakarta and Beijing, which has included tremendous Chinese investment in infrastructure and large scale technology transfers.

title: UK PM Burnham says he is ‘open’ to formal apology for slavery, but rules out reparations
body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to calls for a formal apology for Britain’s historical role in slavery, ​before attending next week’s Commonwealth summit at which he is likely to face demands ‌for financial reparations. Writing in the Guardian newspaper, Burnham said Britain was “offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade”, in which at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into ​slavery. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state ​will form an important part of this process, and I am open ⁠to them,” he added. But Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations , writing: “I do not think that ​British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in ​a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.” From the 15th to the 19th century, millions of Africans were sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated ​3.2 million people across the Atlantic, according to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Ahead of the Commonwealth ​Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, a spokesperson for King Charles said he “will not shy away ‌from confronting ⁠the most shameful aspects of the past” during his visit. A spokesperson for Charles — head of the Commonwealth group of 56 nations, mainly former British colonies — added: “It would not be appropriate for him to address matters of particular policy relating to the UK government’s position.” Charles ​continues to receive ​treatment for cancer, though ⁠a senior Buckingham Palace aide said he was “working as hard as ever, across time zones with packed schedules”. Caribbean leaders are expected to press demands for reparations, which they have often framed in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare, and climate resilience. Burnham also wrote in the Guardian that he wanted to “launch a new drive on debt”, including by helping more vulnerable countries “repay over a longer ⁠time period ​and with better rates”. Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston ​Browne welcomed Burnham’s comments and proposals for practical assistance, though he added in a Facebook post: “The Caribbean’s longstanding position ​on reparatory justice remains unchanged.”

title: U.S. Air Force Needs 250 Blended-Wing Airborne Tankers to Prepare for War Against China
body: The U.S. Air Force has been urged to acquire 250 advanced blended-wing-body (BWB) aerial refuelling aircraft to improve its ability to sustain large-scale air operations in the western Pacific during a potential conflict with China. A report published by the Hudson Institute argues that existing tanker fleets would struggle to support operations across the vast distances of the Pacific, particularly if Chinese missile strikes rendered forward and intermediate airfields unusable. The proposed aircraft would combine substantially greater fuel offload capacity and range with improved aerodynamic efficiency, allowing them to refuel combat aircraft farther from their bases and closer to contested areas. The report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations , warns that by 2035, Chinese forces could be capable of suppressing large-scale tanker operations from many of the forward and intermediate airfields on which U.S. air power traditionally depends. The authors of the report argue that the Boeing KC-46A Pegasus, which is gradually replacing the ageing KC-135 Stratotanker, lacks the range and fuel offload capacity required to sustain large-scale operations across the Pacific under these conditions. The KC-46A can carry approximately 212,000 pounds of fuel, while the proposed medium-sized BWB tanker would carry approximately 300,000 pounds, while its more efficient aerodynamic configuration could allow it to deliver substantially more fuel over longer distances. According to the Hudson analysis, a fleet of 250 such aircraft could refuel more than twice as many force packages as an equivalent number of KC-46As, or provide refuelling at more than twice the distance. At longer ranges and higher fuel offloads, the performance advantage could be greater still. Other assessments have contended that existing tankers’ survivability against long range missile attacks is increasingly limited, with China fielding a range of well optimised ‘tanker killer’ assets . The fact that Chinese fighters on average have much longer ranges than their American counterparts, with the country’s top fighter the J-20 having over double the range of the F-35 or F-22, further exacerbates the need for a survivable tanker to bridge the gap. Analysts have thus posited that a tanker with advanced stealth capabilities is necessary, although the affordability of this remains in serious question. Designs for advanced stealth tankers have been put forward by a number of major defence producers, including Lockheed Martin. The U.S. Air Force has faced growing difficulties sustaining its aerial refuelling fleet, with its ability to sustain global air operations increasingly constrained by the age of its KC-135 Stratotankers and continuing problems with the newer KC-46 . A September assessment by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the condition and sustainment of the tanker fleet had deteriorated significantly, while the service’s transition from the KC-135 to the KC-46 has failed to proceed quickly enough to prevent a growing capability gap. The development is particularly significant given the dependence of the U.S. Armed Forces on aerial refuelling to project air power over the enormous distances separating American bases from potential theatres of operations. The full mission capability of the tanker fleet — the proportion of aircraft able to perform all their assigned missions — declined substantially between 2019 and 2025. The KC-135 has been the backbone of American aerial refuelling for more than six decades, with the aircraft first entering service in 1957.

title: FAA: Plane crashes in Palm Beach, Florida after rapid dive, killing nine passengers
body: US authorities are launching an investigation after a plane crashed into a residential area in Florida, killing all nine people on board on Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said.The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the circumstances surrounding the plane's crash in Palm Beach County.  The flight was supposed to go from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas to the Bahamas, CNN reported. It descended 27,000 feet in under a minute before tracking data cut off, the report added. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the crash as looking "like a missile going down." According to DeSantis, there are no reports of any casualties on the ground, but the crash caused a significant debris field. Some 600 people were left in need of shelter on the ground due to the crash, CNN cited a county official as saying. Pilot reported ice accumulation, turbulence before emergencyThe pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft minutes before the crash, as well as moderate turbulence, radioing the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center, CNN wrote. “We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot said.Moments later, the pilot declared an emergency. “We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot said. “We are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000 feet per minute … We're going to crash into the ground.”Scattered storms were reported in the area at the time of the crash, but it is unclear whether the storm contributed to the incident.

title: Debibi United stun Hearts to end Phobians winning streak
body: Hearts of Oak’s three-match winning streak came to an end after a 1-0 defeat to Debibi United at Debibi Presby Park .Sarkodie Demetrous’s effort in the 51st minute handed the debutants a their first topflight. Victory brings reprieve for the time being, lifting them out of the relegation zone for the first time this season. The Phobians, meanwhile, have dropped to third on the league table.

title: Not every artist I signed will become global – Don Jazzy
body: Renowned music executive Michael Collins Ajereh, popularly known as Don Jazzy, has explained that being signed to his record label doesn’t guarantee global success. Speaking in a recent livestream with popular forex trader Habby Forex, Don Jazzy said the music business is risky, even if it is not as volatile as forex trading. He pointed out that not every artist he signed to his record label would become a global star and make a lot of money for the label. The Mavin Records boss noted that as long as an artist is better than they were before they joined the label, that is already a success for them. “The forex market is just something I do for fun. Music still takes most of my time, and my other businesses are not as volatile and risky as the forex market. But not every artist I signed will become global. Just like in trading, there is risk in the music business, too. But to us, as long as you are better today than yesterday as an artist, you are a success,” he said. Don Jazzy has nurtured and played significant roles in the careers of Nigerian artists who rose to global prominence, including D’Banj, Tiwa Savage, Rema, and, most recently, Ayra Starr.

title: Student denies charges in Bishop Obinim GH¢1.5m theft case
body: A 23-year-old student accused of stealing GH¢1.5 million belonging to Bishop Daniel Obinim has pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit a crime, to wit, theft. Ohemaa Serwaa Abigail Owusu Ansah made her second appearance before an Adenta Circuit Court on Friday. At her previous appearance, the court admitted her to bail in the sum of GH¢1 million, with two sureties, one to be justified with landed property, but deferred taking her plea. Chief Inspector Maxwell Lanyo, prosecuting, told the court that the complainant was Bishop Obinim, founder of the International Godsway Church, and that the accused was his friend. The prosecution said that on October 13, 2026, the accused visited Bishop Obinim at his Lakeside residence. During their conversation in his room, the complainant left for church, leaving her at the house. The following morning, at about 0700 hours, Bishop Obinim discovered that his safe had been broken into and GH¢1.5 million stolen. When confronted, the accused allegedly told him that she had contacted her father’s worker, identified as Owusu, who arranged for two young men to meet her at the bishop’s residence. She allegedly led the men into the room and showed them the safe, which they broke open before taking the money and leaving. The prosecution said the accused was arrested on October 16, 2026, at about 1400 hours and escorted to the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) headquarters. In her caution statement, she allegedly admitted to inviting the two men to the complainant’s residence to break into the safe and steal the money. The prosecution said investigations were ongoing.

title: Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC spokesperson says
body: Two oil tankers exploded after hitting Iranian mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy spokesperson announced in a statement to the state media channel Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting on Sunday.The tankers "were in violation of regulations," the spokesperson said, explaining that they were traveling on "an unauthorized route in the Strait.""One of the vessels is a supertanker; it is currently engulfed in flames following a powerful explosion," the statement added.The IRGC spokesperson added that oil tankers had switched off the navigation and identification systems, as they wanted " to pass covertly through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz with the support of the terrorist US military.""Following the incident, [the tanker] was brought to a halt," he added.UKMTO: Separate tanker hit by projectile in HormuzAn oil tanker passing through the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile earlier on Sunday, the United Kingdom Maritime and Trade Operations (UKMTO) Center announced.UKMTO WARNING 191-26 Click here to view the full warning⤵️ https://t.co/6GC5YjtGp6 #MaritimeSecurity #MarSec https://t.co/9aM1J3gZyA— UKMTO Operations Centre (@UK_MTO) November 1, 2026The master of a nearby tanker reported that the other vessel had been struck, UKMTO explained.The incidents come amid repeated attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil export routes, since the outbreak of the conflict between the US and Iran in February.Iran has hit vessels it says have violated its restrictions on passage through the strategic waterway, as it seeks to assert control over the strait and exert pressure on Washington.On Friday, the IRGC Navy spokesperson said that two oil tankers that switched off their navigation systems were involved in an incident and stopped in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring radio warnings and attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway.Iran also said on Friday that it destroyed a US unmanned vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the US military.Tanker struck by two projectiles near Saudi Arabia, UKMTO saysA tanker traveling southeast through the Gulf was struck by two unidentified projectiles on its port side, 72 nautical miles east of Saudi Arabia's Ras al-Khafji, UKMTO said on Monday.All crew members were accounted for, and no environmental impact had been reported, the UKMTO added.

title: Investors turn to 'Big Short' strategies as AI stocks tumble, fears of a market crash rise - report
body: Investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence's potential to transform the global economy has fueled massive bets on the sector; however, growing concerns about a possible downturn are prompting investors to seek financial protection against losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.“We're seeing really significant demand from folks looking to protect downside,” said Stephen Solaka, a senior vice president at Gateway Investment Advisers.Investors and technology executives are increasingly turning to financial instruments such as put options and credit-default swaps to protect their investments.Put options give investors the right to sell shares at a predetermined price before a specified date. For shareholders seeking protection, these contracts can limit potential losses if stock prices fall sharply, although investors must pay a premium for that protection.A combination of rising borrowing costs for major data center projects and chip purchases, falling share prices among AI companies, and a broader stock market selloff has heightened concerns about the sector's financial outlook.Friday's technology stock selloff wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value. The Nasdaq 100 index fell 3.4%, while the broader S&P 500 dropped 1.8%. The S&P 500's technology sector was hit particularly hard, declining more than 4.2%, NBC News reported Friday.AI companies keep pursuing billions in funding, even amid selloffThe growing demand for financial protection comes as AI companies continue seeking enormous amounts of capital to fund infrastructure development and expansion.According to Solaka, some investors have accumulated such substantial gains from technology stocks that they now prioritize protecting their wealth over pursuing further returns.“These people have made so much money, they're quitting to hedge their stock,” Solaka said, adding that some companies restrict employees' trades.For example, trading in put options tied to AI cloud infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to record levels in October and remained elevated, according to data from Cboe Global Markets.AI investors turn to credit-default swaps to hedge against debt risksInvestors are also turning to credit-default swaps, financial contracts that protect against a borrower failing to repay its debt.According to the report, the cost of insuring against debt defaults by major technology companies, including Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, rose over the past month to its highest level since 2021.“There were no exceptions, suggesting broad market concern about the sector rather than idiosyncratic credit events at individual companies,” said Eugene Grinberg, a co-founder of bond data provider Solve.As investment in AI infrastructure grows, trading firm Jump Trading has begun offering financial contracts that allow companies to protect themselves against a potential collapse in the price of computing power.For example, companies renting out Nvidia chips could use these contracts to lock in a minimum rental price, protecting revenue if demand for AI computing power falls.The growing demand for financial protection is reminiscent of the events depicted in The Big Short, when investors used credit-default swaps to bet against mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 financial crisis. Unlike those investors, however, many of today's technology shareholders are not necessarily betting on a market collapse, but seeking to protect gains accumulated during the AI boom.

title: Ablakwa and the Evacuation of the Unborn
body: By Jimmy Aglah Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, our commitment to future generations became so impressive that we began evacuating citizens before they were born. Other countries were making plans for 2034 and 2036. We were already bringing their inhabitants home from South Africa. For years, politicians had been accused of doing nothing for the unborn. Here, at last, was documentary evidence that the unborn had benefited from foreign policy. Somewhere, a couple yet to meet could apparently rest assured that their future child had already escaped xenophobia. Then the Ghana High Commission in Pretoria arrived with an explanation and spoilt a perfectly good national miracle. Passport expiry dates had been entered as dates of birth in records affecting 15 evacuees. The mission accepted responsibility, supplied corrections and maintained that the people concerned were genuine passengers who had received their allowances. The Republic had rescued human beings after all; it was the spreadsheet that had travelled into the future. A clerical error, certainly. Those who have never attached the wrong document to an email may cast the first keyboard. Nevertheless, when a public record gives a grown person several years to wait before being born, somebody should notice before the document leaves the office. The elder who inspects the cooking pot does not wait for the soup to reach the funeral before discovering that the salt container fell inside. The underlying operation deserved better paperwork. According to government, 1,964 Ghanaians were brought home between 27 May and 4 September 2026 following xenophobic violence and intimidation in South Africa, at a reported cost of GH¢49.72 million. For families waiting anxiously for their relatives, an aircraft arriving safely was no small achievement. A person being chased by danger does not pause to compare airline legroom. But when the passengers have reached safety and the welcome embraces are over, the accountant must also be allowed to arrive. He is an inconvenient guest, admittedly. While everybody admires the rescue photographs, he wants to know which voucher belongs to which payment. Such people can ruin a thanksgiving service with one innocent question. The Minority says the documents leave more than GH¢16.4 million requiring explanation and wants an independent audit. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa rejects the allegation of unaccounted funds and has presented records in defence of the expenditure. These remain disputed accounting claims, not established findings of theft. In the Republic, that distinction requires protection, because a suspicion can be arrested, tried and sentenced on morning radio before the auditor has switched on his computer. Still, saving lives and explaining expenditure should get along quite comfortably. The farmer who carries a neighbour’s child out of a flooded river deserves gratitude. If he subsequently submits a bill for three canoes, the village may respectfully ask where the other two were parked. Appreciation does not make the village treasurer redundant. Unfortunately, our politics has developed a wonderful arrangement under which every request for a receipt must first undergo examination for ingratitude. Then the envelopes joined the rescue operation. The announced package was GH¢5,000 for reintegration and GH¢500 for transport per evacuee. JoyNews reported that at least three people it contacted said they received GH¢2,000. Ablakwa disputes the underpayment claims, saying beneficiaries received two envelopes, were encouraged to verify their contents and had made no complaints to his ministry. Two envelopes, yet such a large national conversation. Our grandparents used one envelope to summon an entire extended family to a funeral. We now require payment records, beneficiary interviews and ministerial explanations to establish the contents of two. Surely this is a matter that records and verification can settle. Ask the people concerned, examine the acknowledgements and trace the payments. The woman who sells tomatoes knows that when the money in the drawer disagrees with the sales book, praising the beauty of the tomatoes will not reconcile the figures. But reconciliation is a modest occupation. It produces neither a triumphant press conference nor a particularly satisfying party slogan. The controversy has consequently acquired a longer travel itinerary. Ablakwa’s defence included a request for a special audit of evacuation exercises undertaken since 2017. Let those records be examined too. The public purse has no family head whose permission must be sought before opening an old cupboard. What a splendid family gathering that promises to be: present officials arriving with explanations, former officials arriving with recollections, and everybody remembering precisely which cupboard contains somebody else’s difficulties. Yet the person asked about today’s missing goat should help search today’s bush, even if he has excellent information about the neighbour’s poultry losses in 2017. Both matters can be investigated. The goat need not remain missing while a historical commission interviews the chickens. “He who seeks equity must come with clean hands,” we are reminded. A fine maxim, although its practical application in our politics usually involves an exhaustive inspection of the opponent’s fingers. Soap is always urgently required across the aisle. Let the standard apply all round. Those demanding scrutiny should welcome it when their own records are called. Those defending expenditure should welcome the patient checking that can establish their case. A clean account gains nothing from being surrounded by party supporters shouting that it is clean. Meanwhile, the people rescued from danger deserve to rebuild their lives without becoming permanent exhibits in our political quarrel. Their journey home should not leave them stranded between competing press conferences. The Republic has successfully brought its citizens back from South Africa. With the same determination, it should now bring the records into agreement. The aircraft has landed. We cannot spend the rest of the year at the airport waiting for the arithmetic.

title: Veteran whose daughter died in military training exercise named Silver Cross Mother
body:
A veteran whose daughter died during a military training exercise in 2002 has been named the 2026 National Silver Cross Mother.
The Royal Canadian Legion says Virginia Hicks will place a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Nov. 11, an annual tradition on behalf of Canadian mothers who have lost a child serving in the Canadian military.
Hicks’ daughter Mariebeth Short died on Sept. 23, 2002 during a training exercise in Petawawa, Ont., when the light armoured vehicle she was training in rolled over.
The Royal Canadian Legion says Hicks’ family has a long history of military service and she served in the Canadian Armed Forces for 29 years, working in supply and logistics.
This year’s Remembrance Day ceremony comes just weeks after four Canadian soldiers were killed and dozens more were injured during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.
Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed in a grass fire last month.
Strong, sudden winds propelled the nearby fire toward 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry who were conducting two exercises in the military base’s training area, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy with support from the RCMP.
Hicks says she has much in common with all mothers who have lost a child serving in the military.
“We all share the same sorrow, we all share the same bravery, and same love and respect for our children as we do for any other child who has passed,” she said in a statement.

title: Zaporizhzhia region provides UAH 105M worth of military equipment to Ukrainian forces in October
body:
Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, announced this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
"We continue to systematically and promptly meet the needs of the military on the Zaporizhzhia front. In October, 45 Defense Forces units received equipment worth more than UAH 105 million," Semikin said.
According to him, funds from the region's joint defense fund were used to purchase and deliver more than 1,040 FPV drones, wings, aircraft and quadcopters, as well as 12 vehicles, 35 electronic intelligence/electronic warfare systems, and more than 560 power supply devices, communication equipment and office equipment.
In addition, the military received more than 2,470 pieces of equipment and batteries for unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as over 5,400 remote mining devices.

title: Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion at 20 years old
body: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli became Formula One’s youngest world champion at ‌20 on Sunday, in a red-flagged, ​restarted Mexico City Grand Prix won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. The first ​Italian champion since 1953 finished ​third, sobbing with joy over the team radio as he ​took the chequered flag ​at the high-altitude Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, ‌with ⁠his overall lead now an unassailable 119 points. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton started from ​pole position ​and ⁠took a close second place on an ​afternoon of drama ​with ⁠two safety cars, multiple crashes and an agonising ⁠33-minute ​halt with 25 ​of the 71 laps remaining.

title: World No. 1-bound Zverev loses to De Minaur
body: Alexander Zverev lost his first match since securing the men’s world number one ranking, falling to Alex de Minaur in a semi-final upset at the Vienna Open. German top seed Zverev, who will replace Jannik Sinner at the summit of the men’s rankings on Monday, lost 4-6 6-1 6-7 (4-7) to the Australian fifth seed. Victory means 27-year-old De Minaur has leapfrogged Spain’s Rafael Jodar in the race to qualify for the season-ending ATP Finals. “Super proud with how I handled the situation,” said De Minaur “I played on my terms. I was going to go out swinging and playing the right type of tennis, and that’s what made the difference today.” After losing the first set, Zverev overpowered De Minaur in the second before a hard-fought decider. With neither player able to create a break point opportunity, it was De Minaur who held his nerve in the resulting tie-break as he wrapped up victory inside two hours and 30 minutes. De Minaur will face Spanish second seed Carlos Alcaraz in the final after he beat Daniil Medvedev in straight sets. The seven-time Grand Slam-winner secured a 6-4 7-6 (7-2) victory over the Russian third seed to reach his fifth final of the year. The win extended Alcaraz’s unbeaten run at ATP 500 events to 25 matches with the 23-year-old last suffering defeat at that level to Holger Rune at the Barcelona Open in April 2025. De Minaur will be competing in his fourth final of the year with his sole title coming at the Rotterdam Open in February.

title: U.S. Army prioritizes industrial modernization, supply-chain resilience and research partnerships
body: Telle has called for the Army to “evolve at the speed of business” and build a “seamless, frictionless, symbiotic relationship with American ingenuity.” The work in Arkansas brings those priorities to three areas: Pine Bluff Arsenal’s industrial transformation, Walmart’s experience managing disruption and the University of Arkansas’s logistics and materials research. At Pine Bluff Arsenal, the ARSENAL READY campaign aims to replace a reactive sustainment model with a continuously operating, modernized defense industrial park. Launched last year, the initiative relies on public-private partnerships, expanded enhanced-use leasing and a broader portfolio of activities. Pine Bluff produces capabilities with few domestic alternatives, including its role as the nation’s sole-source producer of white phosphorus munitions. It is also a primary manufacturer of tactical smoke, pyrotechnics and illumination rounds, with designated expertise in non-lethal ammunition, chemical and biological defense equipment, filtration and textiles. The transformation supports the Department of War’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative to revitalize the defense and organic industrial base. Pine Bluff’s infrastructure covers 15,000 acres and includes more than 500 buildings and over one million square feet of explosive storage. At Walmart’s headquarters and Global Security Operations Center, discussions focused on how a geographically dispersed organization maintains visibility across its operations and responds to disruption. Army and company representatives exchanged lessons on managing supply chains through natural disasters, changing security conditions and emerging global events. The military application is sustaining forces when conditions change and established supply routes face disruption. Telle said exchanges with private-sector leaders offer valuable perspectives on resilience and crisis response as the Army works to support joint operations. At the University of Arkansas, discussions with engineering and business researchers addressed supply-chain management, contested logistics and advanced materials. Developing future leaders with those skills formed part of the agenda alongside using academic expertise to address military sustainment problems. “If we are going to become more efficient, effective, and ultimately dominant on the battlefield, we must fully harness what we already have in America, which is the amazing spirit of ingenuity in our entrepreneurial capital markets and world-class research institutions,” Telle said. “We see that on full display here in Northwest Arkansas.” The university’s Multi-User Silicon Carbide Research and Fabrication Facility provides a platform for semiconductor fabrication and technologies that could support next-generation defense systems. Its Civil Engineering Research and Education Center is working on large-scale structural testing, 3D-printed structures and fast-setting cement, with potential uses in military infrastructure and rapid-deployment logistics.

title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
body:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., speaks to reporters in March 2026, in Washington. Murphy suffered a stroke on Saturday and is expected to recover. Allison Robbert/AP hide caption
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

title: Shock Basel loss dents Djokovic’s ATP Finals hopes
body: Novak Djokovic’s hopes of making a record 19th appearance at the ATP Finals have been dented by a surprise defeat against Jan-Lennard Struff at the Swiss Indoors in Basel. Playing in the tournament for the first time in 15 years, the 39-year-old lost 6-7 (4-7) 7-5 7-6 (7-5), the first time Struff has beaten him in nine meetings. “I knew I needed to go for it. There was only one way to play it. So, I was very, very happy,” said the world number 27. “I knew I had to play my best tennis to have a chance. He beat me very, very easily the last eight times. So, I’m very, very happy and pleased with the performance.” The year’s top-eight performers qualify for the ATP event in Turin and this result leaves Djokovic – the men’s game’s record 24-time Grand Slam winner – 11th in the standings. Djokovic admitted he expected to feel “a little rusty” after beating Frenchman Ugo Humbert on Wednesday, but now faces a fight to reach the final as he is outside the top 10 for the first time since 2018. Rafael Jodar holds the final qualifying spot in ninth place, because number one Jannik Sinner is injured and will not take part. Djokovic is 319 points behind Jodar, but he can move up the rankings at the Paris Masters in November. The Serb aims to overtake Roger Federer with his 19th appearance in the Turin final. He has won the event a record seven times and missed the past two editions with injury, but the last time he failed to qualify on merit was in 2017, when injury affected his season. Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton have their places confirmed for the showpiece event in Italy from 15-22 November, although American Shelton also surprisingly lost in Basel. The top seed lost 6-3 6-7 (4-7) 7-6 (7-1) to Swiss wildcard Jerome Kym, who is ranked 222nd in the world.

title: Gulf region on edge as Qatar leads talks with Iran to stave off new U.S. attacks
body:
Qatar has been leading intense mediation efforts over the past 72 hours to prevent a new round of possible U.S. attacks on Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections. The uncertainty has the entire Gulf region on edge.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: Meanwhile, the U.S. and Israel are planning for possible strikes on Iran after Tuesday's midterms, and Qatar has been leading intense mediation efforts over the past 72 hours to try to prevent that from happening. The uncertainty of what comes next has the entire Gulf region on edge. NPR's international correspondent Aya Batrawy is in Bahrain, and she's with us to talk about all this. Hi, Aya. AYA BATRAWY, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha. PFEIFFER: To start us off, a two-part question - what do these mediation efforts look like, and what has President Trump said, if anything, about how likely another attack on Iran is? BATRAWY: All right. So Qatar has been really tight-lipped about what's been going on. They did have some mediators visiting Tehran, and also Iran had a delegation in Doha, Qatar - all of this over the past 72 hours. But Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, today, was quoted in Iranian state media saying there's still no definitive conclusion to these mediation efforts. But he said there is talk of a two-day plan. That would include basically the Iranians not attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz to allow for direct talks to begin again between Washington and Tehran. And Trump was asked about the possibility of restarting the war with Iran. He was at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago, and he said, we're not in that much of a hurry. Have a listen. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We've knocked out almost every piece of military equipment there. We've knocked out a lot of their manufacturing capabilities. We've knocked out the nuclear. We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes. BATRAWY: So as you heard there, President Trump isn't really saying what he might do after Tuesday's elections. Now, everyone I have been speaking to in the Gulf - from senior European diplomats to Arab military generals - no one has any idea what Trump will do, but the lives of tens of millions of people in the Gulf hinge on his decision. PFEIFFER: And we have heard President Trump say many times that Iran is essentially finished. We heard him say that again in the cut you just played for us. Based on your reporting, how true is that? BATRAWY: Yeah. I mean, Iran was hit hard after the U.S. and Israel launched this war eight months ago, killing the country's supreme leader, top military commanders, taking out many of its ships, missile production sites. But even after eight months of war and crippling U.S. economic sanctions, the war has not toppled Iran's regime as Israel said it was its stated goal. And Iran's Revolutionary Guard force is still very capable of inflicting pain on Gulf Arab countries. These are some of the world's most important oil and gas producers, and this war and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused oil and gas prices to rise globally. Brent crude oil is 60% higher today than it was before the war. PFEIFFER: Aya, you said that Iran could inflict pain on other Gulf Arab countries. Is Iran saying what it would do if it's attacked again? BATRAWY: Yes. The message from Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, to senior commanders of Iran's armed forces this weekend is that any threat to the country must be met with an immediate response that is, quote, "without geographical limitations." Now, Iran's state media says this means that any new Israeli or U.S. attacks on Iran will inflict even greater damage than we have already seen. PFEIFFER: We mentioned that you are in Bahrain. Are you seeing signs of damage? Is it evident where you are? BATRAWY: Yeah. So Bahrain is an island nation. It's a tiny country in the Persian Gulf, with Iran as its much larger neighbor to the East, and it's home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet. But on the first day of this war on February 28, Iran hit back at U.S. military sites across the region, and they hit here on the 5th Fleet's logistics hub and warehouses. So you can't take photos of facilities like this here in Bahrain that have been hit, but you can see the damage to the 5th Fleet's hub right there from the highway. I could see radar equipment that had been hit, and I could see charred and blackened warehouses where the 5th Fleet logistics hub is. And there used to be 8,000 military personnel on this base before the war, and now it's down to less than a hundred. Now, I have been at the Manama Dialogue - it's a security forum here in Bahrain. And today, Bahrain's foreign minister, Abdullatif Al Zayani, spoke of the many missiles and drones fired at his country by Iran, not just at U.S. military sites but also civilian infrastructure. And he noted that Iran's Revolutionary Guard this month has made new threats to hit undersea internet cables that carry data through the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf States if a war resumes. Have a listen. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ABDULLATIF AL ZAYANI: This follows the same pattern we have seen at sea - a shared artery is being used as a tool of pressure and threat. BATRAWY: And Iran did hit Amazon data centers at the peak of this war in the United Arab Emirates in Bahrain. PFEIFFER: Aya, you mentioned that you're at a security forum. Given that security is top of mind for the whole region now, what kind of emotions, sort of emotional tenor, conversations are you hearing at that event? BATRAWY: Yeah. I mean, Gulf Arab states - they view Iran as a top threat to their security, but it is still their neighbor. And so while they welcome U.S. pressure on Iran, they did not and do not want war with Iran. Even the United Arab Emirates, which has strong ties with both the U.S. and Israel and has the most hawkish policy in the Gulf on Iran, does not want more war. Senior Emerati diplomat, Anwar Gargash, said it clearly today at the summit. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ANWAR GARGASH: We really have to deal with this crisis with a lot of wisdom, with political tools being our main tools and with the understanding that military solutions will only complicate the current, very complicated scene that we have and will not actually bring any quick off-ramp to the solution. BATRAWY: Yeah. So as you heard him say there, military solutions will not bring a quick off-ramp here. And, you know, places like Dubai known as safe havens to invest in and spend your vacations in - that's all been shaken by this war. Economies across the Gulf are suffering. And don't forget Saudi Arabia is struggling now to protect its airports and oil facilities from attacks by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. So the united message here from the Gulf is that more attacks on Iran will be devastating. PFEIFFER: And the ripple effects of the war are rippling all across the region, for sure. That is NPR's international correspondent Aya Batrawy. Aya, thank you. BATRAWY: Thank you, Sacha. (SOUNDBITE OF BADBADNOTGOOD AND GHOSTFACE KILLAH'S "EXPERIENCE") Copyright © 2026 NPR. title: Bellingham scores 50th goal as Alexander-Arnold gets rare start
body: Jude Bellingham scored his 50th goal for Real Madrid as his side backed up last week’s El Clásico win with a statement victory at Racing Santander. The visitors were awarded an 11th-minute penalty when Matteo Prati dragged down Kylian Mbappe and the French forward found the net from the spot. Bellingham doubled Real’s lead in the 21st minute, driving from the halfway line, dinking the ball over the onrushing keeper and into an empty net. Record signing Yan Diomande hit a third before half-time, volleying home an effort after a half-cleared corner. Mbappe also hit the post in the 59th minute with a curling effort from the edge of the box. Santander then had a late penalty overturned by the video assistant referee after it ruled that Aurelien Tchouameni’s handball was accidental and came after the ball deflected off the midfielder’s boot. Bellingham’s goal was his 50th in all competitions for the Spanish giants since he joined the club as a 19-year-old for £88.5m from Borussia Dortmund in 2023. The 23-year-old former Birmingham City player has made 154 appearances for Real and has also recorded 37 assists. He put the ball in the net for a second time on Sunday, but the referee ruled his calm, late finish into the bottom corner offside. The win means Real have won their past five matches in all competitions and are just three points off La Liga leaders and rivals Barcelona, whom they beat 2-1 in their previous match. Jose Mourinho’s side are on an excellent run and have only lost two games this season, with their last defeat coming against rivals Atletico Madrid on September 20. Mourinho gave England full-back Trent Alexander-Arnold a rare start, and the former Liverpool defender almost earned an early assist, but teammate Arda Guler curled his cut-back just wide. Alexander-Arnold, 28, has started only five of Real Madrid’s 14 games this season, with Denzel Dumfries and midfielder Federico Valverde often preferred at right-back.

title: Iliana Iotova leads Bulgarian presidential election — CEC
body:
SOFIA, November 2. /TASS/. Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission (CEC) has released the first official vote count from the second round of the presidential election.
According to data published on the CEC website, Bulgarian’s incumbent President Iliana Iotova and her vice-presidential running mate Kiril Valchev are leading with 57.943% of the vote. Their challengers, Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, have secured 39.007%.
The initial results are based on the processing of 17.39% of the election commission protocols as of 11:00 p.m. local time (09:00 p.m. GMT).

title: MTN Ghana pays GH¢9bn to state, earns GH¢7.8bn profit in first 9 months of 2026
body: MTN Ghana paid GH¢9 billion in direct and indirect taxes to the state in the first nine months of 2026, surpassing its profit after tax of GH¢7.8 billion for the same period, according to the company’s latest unaudited financial statements. The nine-month results ended September 30, 2026, show the company’s significant contribution to public finances, with tax payments rising from GH¢7.3 billion in the prior year to GH¢9.0 billion. In addition to the direct and indirect taxes, the company also paid GH¢533.6 million in fees and levies to government agencies. Although the tax outlay exceeded the bottom line, MTN Ghana still delivered robust profitability, with profit after tax up 43.0 per cent year-on-year to GH¢7.8 billion. This growth was driven by a 33.5 per cent surge in service revenue to GH¢23.2 billion, underpinned by strong performance in the data, digital, and Mobile Money segments. Data revenue was the primary growth engine, surging 44.5 per cent to GH¢13.5 billion, supported by a 16.1 per cent increase in active data subscribers to 22.0 million. Digital revenue nearly doubled, rising 98.0 per cent to GH¢642 million, while Mobile Money revenue rose 24.4 per cent to GH¢5.4 billion. The company’s Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation rose 40.6 per cent to GH¢14.3 billion, and the EBITDA margin expanded 3.1 percentage points to 61.5 per cent. Profit before tax rose to GH¢11.4 billion, up 47.0 per cent. The financial statement also reported tax expense of GH¢3.6 billion for the period, up from GH¢2.3 billion in the prior year, reflecting higher taxable earnings. Despite this heavy tax burden and substantial capital expenditure of GH¢3.2 billion, the company’s earnings per share rose 42.9 per cent to GH¢0.586. Commenting on the performance, MTN Ghana CEO Stephen Blewett attributed the results to the resilience and diversification of the company’s growth engines. He also noted that the business made significant investments in network capacity, including acquiring 5G spectrum in the 700 MHz and 3 GHz bands for US$202 million. The company declared a third-quarter interim dividend of GH¢0.03 per share, with MobileMoney Fintech LTD declaring a similar dividend to its shareholders.

title: I’ll tell my players to dive in future – Iraola
body: Andoni Iraola says that he will tell his players to go down in future after Liverpool were denied a penalty in Sunday’s defeat by Arsenal . With Liverpool trailing 1-0 after Kai Havertz’s opener, Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak’s shirt in the first half as Isak went for a header from Bradley Barcola’s cross. However, the Liverpool striker stayed on his feet, and referee Andy Madley did not point to the spot. Stuart Attwell, on video assistant referee (VAR) duty, ruled there wasn’t enough in the tug to overturn the decision, but Iraola disagreed. “There is a clear grab of the shirt,” the Spaniard told Match of the Day. “Alex [Isak] was just in front of him; he was going to head in front of the goal but couldn’t because he grabbed the shirt. “If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100%. It should be like this, but that’s how it is. Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor; otherwise, they won’t call it.” On what the answer is going forward, Iraola added: “The answer is you have to dive, if you don’t dive they won’t call it.” Isak turned and spoke to Timber after the incident, but did not appeal to the referee after staying on his feet. Iraola told Sky Sports that going forward, managers should tell their players to go to the floor. On if he will tell Isak that going forward, he added: “Yes, definitely.” He elaborated in his news conference when asked by BBC Sport if he would have to tell his players to be more smart, going forward. “It’s a shame you ask me this question, but honestly, yes, we have to tell them, go down, because they’re not going to call it otherwise. Then referees complain about why they go down. Because if you don’t go down, you don’t call it. Then it’s like, no, you are all the time going down,” said Iraola. “But I think Alex is honest. He tries to go for the ball, everyone can see live straight away that there is a clear, clear pull.” The understanding is that because there was minimal contact and it was a slight tug on the shirt, rather than a sustained holding offence, the play was allowed to continue. Iraola conceded in his news conference that “it is not going to change anything” if Pro Ref, the Premier League’s refereeing body, was to offer an apology about the incident. Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann told BBC Sport: “Timber takes a huge risk by grabbing the shirt. It could easily have been given on another day. “It’s right on the limit. It has to be sustained holding – some will say it was sustained, some will say it wasn’t. But it’s interesting that Isak didn’t even appeal.” Liverpool also had another penalty appeal waved away when Cody Gakpo went down in the box under pressure from Christos Tzolis. ‘It’s an odd reaction from Isak’ Liverpool did not have any shots on target against Arsenal Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy said the decision came at a pivotal point in the game. “I think Arsenal got lucky,” he told Match of the Day. “If Isak maybe makes a bit more of it. I hate to see players exaggerate, but he’s going to score. It’s a big moment in the game “I feel for the referee because it happened so quickly. I thought there was enough for VAR to have another look and give him another look. If he made more of it, maybe they would have given it on-field.” Gary Neville agreed that, for a centre-forward, it was an unusual reaction from Isak, who failed to connect with the ball due to the pull. “The argument around Isak and whether he should have made more of it, it’s unnatural not to make more of it,” he said on Sky during commentary of the game. “When you get pulled and you’re just about to score a goal, you normally complain like crazy. It’d a very odd reaction from Isak not to react.” Asked if Isak should have reacted more, Liverpool skipper Virgil van Dijk said: “We have 50 cameras. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras. Everyone has seen it. In the end it wasn’t given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal .”

title: Fitch Solutions maintains nearly 6% growth rate for Ghana in 2026, but expects economy to lose momentum in 2027
body: Fitch Solutions has maintained its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast of nearly 6.0% for Ghana in 2026. According to the UK-based firm, the Ghanaian economy has remained largely insulated from global developments over the past year, supported by elevated gold prices, low domestic inflation, and the transmission of the Bank of Ghana’s (BoG) 1,400 basis points easing cycle. “While elevated oil prices have increased the energy import bill, Ghana remains broadly net neutral in oil trade thanks to the Jubilee and TEN offshore fields, with the oil trade deficit coming in at just 0.3% of GDP in Q2 [Quarter 2} 2026”. “With our Commodities team forecasting gold prices to remain elevated at US$4,200/oz [per ounce], we expect the current account surplus to remain sizeable at 5.3% of GDP in 2027, supporting Ghana’s reserve position and limiting exchange-rate depreciation”, it added. Nonetheless, Fitch Solutions expects the economy to lose some momentum, with growth slowing from 5.9% in 2026 to 4.7% in 2027. This will be caused in part by inflation rising from an annual average of 4.7% in 2026 to 11.3% in 2027, reflecting unfavourable base effects, rapid money supply growth, and higher global food prices linked to El Niño. Combined with slower credit growth as the BoG resumes monetary tightening, the UK-based firm pointed out that these factors will weigh on domestic demand. For most Sub-Saharan African economies, it pointed out that a more persistent inflationary environment will erode purchasing power and weigh on private consumption and business activity, creating a headwind to growth in 2027. For oil-exporting markets, however, elevated energy prices will continue to support export earnings and fiscal revenues by more than we had earlier anticipated, providing a temporary boost to growth prospects.

title: Tinubu’s 2023 Electricity Pledge Taken Out Of Context, Says APC Campaign Council
body: The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has defended President Bola Tinubu’s 2023 campaign promise to end estimated billing and ensure stable electricity supply, saying his remarks have been taken out of context. In a statement on Sunday, the council’s spokesperson, Dele Alake, said Tinubu made the pledge while addressing members of the Organised Private Sector (OPS) in Lagos ahead of the 2023 general elections. Alake said the then presidential candidate had outlined plans to address longstanding structural and institutional challenges in the power sector, particularly the burden of estimated billing on households and businesses. He recalled Tinubu’s words at the meeting: “Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills anymore. A promise made will be a promise kept. “If I don’t keep the promise and I come for a second term, don’t vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn’t deliver.” The APC spokesperson argued that some recent commentaries had omitted the concluding part of the statement, in which Tinubu said he would provide Nigerians with adequate reasons if he failed to fulfil the pledge before seeking a second term. He maintained that the president’s commitment should be assessed alongside his administration’s interventions in the electricity sector since assuming office in 2023. According to Alake, Tinubu signed the Electricity Act 2023 on June 9, less than two weeks after taking office, allowing state governments to participate in electricity generation, transmission and distribution. He listed Lagos, Enugu, Abia, Ekiti, Oyo, Kaduna and Niger among the states that have established electricity regulatory agencies to take advantage of the legislation and attract private investment. On metering, Alake said the administration launched the Presidential Metering Initiative to address a backlog of more than seven million unmetered electricity customers, adding that over 1.5 million customers had been metered under the programme in the last three years. He also said the government had taken steps to address more than ₦6 trillion in legacy debts accumulated between 2015 and 2025, while introducing a ₦4 trillion bond programme to settle verified obligations to power generation and gas companies. The spokesperson said the first and second tranches of the bond programme had raised more than ₦1.2 trillion towards settling the debts owed to 21 generation companies and gas suppliers. Alake further listed investments in substations, grid expansion and renewable energy projects among the administration’s efforts to improve electricity supply. He said the Rural Electrification Agency had connected universities, hospitals and rural communities to solar power, while the government had unveiled plans to modernise the Osogbo Grid Control Centre and construct an East-West super grid. On transmission infrastructure, he said the administration reviewed the Presidential Power Initiative inherited from the late President Muhammadu Buhari and signed an acceleration agreement with its German partners in December 2023. He added that the Federal Executive Council approved the first batch of five Transmission Company of Nigeria substations for upgrades in December 2024, with another set of projects approved in June 2026 to construct eight new substations and upgrade four existing ones. Alake said the administration had also introduced different electricity service bands and adjusted tariffs towards cost-reflective levels to improve the financial position of distribution companies, while putting measures in place to protect low-income households. He acknowledged that efforts to resolve the power sector crisis were still ongoing but insisted that Tinubu remained committed to his campaign promise. “As he seeks Nigerians’ mandate for a second term in office, he will proudly present his scorecard in the power sector and clearly tell Nigerians what remains to be done,” he said. The post Tinubu’s 2023 Electricity Pledge Taken Out Of Context, Says APC Campaign Council appeared first on Channels Television .
