title: Jet carrying 9 crashes in Florida neighbourhood, U.S. officials confirm
body:
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway, creating a giant fiery crater in the pavement.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed on social media that all nine people on the Learjet 60 plane were killed. He did not comment on whether any injuries or deaths had been reported on the ground in Palm Beach County.
He said the FAA was sending a team to the scene to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s (NTSB) investigation.
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
“This is definitely a tragedy,” he said.
He said the tail number for the flight was N722BD.
Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.
The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.
A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for approximately two hours following the crash.
The circumstances of the crash remained under investigation.
— with files from Global News’ Sean Previl

title: AI-Generated Photos: We Are Already Cleaning Up Our Register – INEC
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it has commenced the process of cleaning up its preliminary Register of Voters following the identification of records with suspected AI-generated photographs and other irregularities. The commission’s Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, said on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics that its Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) had flagged 268 records for review. “What we are currently doing now is looking at all these 268 records that ABIS already flagged as AI-generated or even something of irregularities,” he said. Bayode explained that some people allegedly used their official credentials to create questionable profiles, exploiting a registration option designed for persons with disabilities who do not have complete fingers or have no fingers. According to him, the option, known as special registration, was used to deceive the system and was among the irregularities detected by ABIS. He said the commission had begun cleaning up the affected records. “Those that we have seen, we are cleaning up,” Bayode said. Bayode Lawrence However, he clarified that not every photograph enhanced with artificial intelligence would be removed, distinguishing between images generated entirely by AI and genuine photographs improved with AI tools on mobile phones. “Those that we know it is the AI on the phone that helped enhance their pictures, we can’t exclude such people because it was the AI on the phone that does that. Such people will still be on the register but those AI-generated, those photographs, all these will be removed. We are already looking at them,” he said. The controversy followed the publication of INEC’s preliminary Register of Voters online on October 26, after screenshots circulated on social media showing questionable photographs attached to voter records, including entries from parts of Edo State. The concerns also included allegations of duplicate entries and reports that names of deceased persons appeared on the register. In response, INEC said the online version was the same preliminary register displayed physically at Registration Areas nationwide from October 9 to 15. It explained that the publication did not reflect all the data-cleanup activities already in progress. The commission also said the register was not yet the final certified version and that the display, claims and objections exercise was designed to allow members of the public to identify inaccuracies and questionable entries before certification. INEC has said it will complete the necessary verification, adjudication and data-cleanup processes before certifying the final Register of Voters on December 15, 2026. The post AI-Generated Photos: We Are Already Cleaning Up Our Register – INEC appeared first on Channels Television .

title: MPs to vote for NPT pullout unanimously if Leader agrees
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – A member of the Iranian Parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission says Iran’s parliament will unanimously vote for reconsidering continued NPT membership if asked.
Former Iranian Foreign Minister and lawmaker Manouchehr Mottaki told national TV on Sunday night that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has been turned into an instrument against Iran despite Tehran’s responses to questions concerning its nuclear activities. He said the agency had failed to fulfill its expected commitments.
Referring to growing calls inside Iran for withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), he said that Iran had been a member for more than half a century but it has so far benefited from only a limited portion of the advantages provided under the treaty.
The lawmaker said that the MPs receive around 200 text messages a day urging for withdrawal from the NPT, adding that withdrawal has also become a demand voiced by some members of the public.
Motaki said he believed the time had come to consider leaving the treaty, although he stressed that the decision fell within the authority of the country’s Commander-in-Chief, namely the Leader.

title: King Charles to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
body: King Charles III is to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said. The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was “open” to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery – a change in the government’s stance. The Palace was reportedly told in advance of Burnham’s comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not changed his speech in light of them. The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck to his predecessors’ policy and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described “endless talk about apologies” as a “distraction” from solving current problems. She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards.” The King will speak at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM). He “will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit”, a Palace spokesperson said. “You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond.” When asked about the King’s reaction to the prime minister’s comments, the spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the King to address matters of policy relating to “the UK government’s position”. The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK’s colonial legacy in the region. On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the “suffering of the past”. In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed. Buckingham Palace said the visit was a chance for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK. Royal sources have stressed that decisions about an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace. “His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope,” a Royal aide said. “He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to ‘bat for Britain’, the Realms and wider Commonwealth.” In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a “brutal and barbaric violation”, and that Britain “must face up to the past”. King Charles will welcome his pledge in the article to strengthen the Commonwealth as an organisation, which he views as a powerful vehicle for change. The King will deliver the opening speech at CHOGM, which brings together leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth. Each biennial meeting has a theme, and this year’s is officially called Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth. Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua, and as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, it reminded everyone of the week’s intended focus. Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation that the Commonwealth’s “prosperity” must be “shared prosperity”. “True partnership requires mutual respect; it requires listening; it requires fairness.” A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together.” The King, they said, “contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions”. The King has had a difficult few months, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer. In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK in August with his wife, Meghan, and their two children. Asked whether the King was confident his approach to family matters had been right in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. “Yes,” a senior aide told the BBC. “That is why he takes the actions he does – and has done.” On serious allegations about Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to comment publicly: “We wouldn’t comment on private family matters.” The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024, and the Palace says he remains on a “positive trajectory”. In hot, humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day Caribbean tour.

title: WATCH: IDF uncovers Hezbollah posters in child’s bedroom, weapons in southern Lebanon civilian home
body: IDF troops operating in the security zone in southern Lebanon uncovered Hezbollah terrorist paraphernalia and multiple weapons in a civilian home, the military revealed on Sunday.The arms and terror paraphernalia were discovered as the IDF's 769th Brigade worked to dismantle Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure in the El-Khiam area of southern Lebanon.A video shared by the IDF shows posters of Hezbollah terrorists, including former Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, plastered on the walls of the child's bedroom.In the same house, the troops found guns, ammunition magazines, and terrorist equipment.Additional weapons, including rockets, Kalashnikov rifles, ammunition, and explosive drones, were found in other locations in the security zone. The troops also located and dismantled an explosive drone storage facility in the area.Lebanon charged 13 Hezbollah terrorists for explosives smuggling attemptThe Lebanese government is also making efforts to curb the influence of and disarm Hezbollah as the Lebanese Military Court charged 13 Hezbollah terrorists over the weekend in connection with an explosives smuggling operation.Of the thirteen men charged, two were arrested while transporting the explosives and are the only terrorists still in Lebanese custody.The explosives were discovered in October at a checkpoint in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, leading to suspicions that they may have been intended for use in a political assassination.Hezbollah claimed that the explosives were intended to be used against Israel, but Lebanese commentators said that they were the same type as materials used in a truck bombing that killed former Lebanese prime minister Rafic Hariri.Danielle Greyman-Kennard contributed to this report.

title: Facing the Middle East with Felice Friedson: Hope and Heroes
body: The psychological toll of two years in Hamas captivity, a Christian initiative to challenge European boycotts of Israeli settlements, and an effort to change how Israel is portrayed abroad lead this special post-October 7 edition of Facing the Middle East. I speak with former hostage Evyatar David and former Miss Israel Melanie Shiraz, while reporter Gabriel Colodro takes us into the West Bank.David recounts how an outing with friends to the Nova Music Festival on October 7, 2023, became a desperate escape attempt as Hamas-led attackers opened fire. David and his friend Guy were abducted; two other friends, Ron Zarfati and Idan Haramaty, were killed. He spent 738 days held in Gaza, including time in tunnels, and describes his captors' efforts to convince hostages that their families and governments had abandoned them.For David, the deaths of his friends remain the most painful memory. He recalls how an earlier hostage agreement gave him hope of returning home. When I ask what he wants people to learn, he urges them to appreciate family and ordinary freedoms that can disappear without warning. He also warns about the continuing threat of extremist violence beyond Israel.Christians visit West Bank, protest sanctions on West Bank goodsThe program next follows Christians traveling with the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem into Israeli settlements in the West Bank. In his report, Colodro accompanies visitors shopping in Samaria and Gush Etzion as a deliberate protest against restrictions on goods originating in Israeli settlements. Representatives from Ireland and Norway argue that the measures penalize communities they support. The segment examines differences between European policies, including exemptions for tourists' personal goods and proposals for criminal penalties for certain trade. Norway's government says its proposed restrictions aim to avoid sustaining settlements it considers unlawful under international law.I also speak with Shiraz, Miss Israel 2025, about campus antisemitism and her shift from data science to international outreach. She explains why arguments based on statistics alone often fail to reach people whose views are shaped by emotion, social media, and algorithms. Recalling a candid conversation with a Lebanese rideshare driver, Shiraz calls for face-to-face encounters that allow Israelis and others to see each other beyond political labels. She introduces the Israel Cultural Diplomacy Institute, intended to train people in arts, music, sports, and other cultural fields to represent Israel internationally.We're also celebrating an exciting milestone for The Media Line: the launch of our completely redesigned website, more than a year in the making. This is much more than a new look. We're introducing a new way to experience Middle East journalism, combining independent reporting with interactive educational tools that encourage critical thinking, challenge assumptions, and help readers separate fact from fiction. We're excited to unveil what we've created, and I invite you to explore the new experience and share it with others.

title: Both sides honored commitments during ceasefire in Alyoshki — human rights ombudswoman
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides fulfilled all commitments during the ceasefire in the humanitarian mission zone in Alyoshki, Kherson Region, Russian Human Rights Ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said.
"The ceasefire in the humanitarian mission zone in Alyoshki has concluded. <...> All commitments were honored by both sides. This made it possible to deliver aid to residents and ensure the safe, voluntary departure of those who chose to leave the city," she wrote on her channel on the Max messenger.
Lantratova also noted that efforts are currently underway to continue these humanitarian operations. "It is important to maintain the cooperation that has helped people and to ensure that the delivery of humanitarian supplies becomes regular," the ombudswoman added.

title: Ukraine, Türkiye considering cooperation on satellite technologies – Zelensky
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with CNN Türk following his visit to Türkiye, Ukrinform reports.
“We will also work in this area. This issue has been discussed and evaluated. You will agree that it is not an easy task,” Zelensky said in response to a question about the possibility of joint production or development of technologies with Türkiye, including satellite technologies.
The President stressed the importance of developing their own technologies for the security of both countries.
“However, security is of great importance to both states. Without our own efforts, without having our own technologies, including in the space sector, it is difficult for us to progress,” he stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, in April 2025, Türkiye put into operation its first domestically produced communications satellite, Türksat 6A, which was launched into space in July 2024 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Türkiye thus joined the group of 11 countries capable of manufacturing their own communications satellites.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

title: T-bills auction: Government exceeds target by 4.12%, interest rates take a nosedive
body: The government again exceeded its treasury bills target by 4.12%, reaching GH¢2.54 billion, as demand for treasury bills persisted. The government accepted bids of GH¢1.91 billion from investors. A little over GH¢1.5 billion of the bids were tendered for the 91-day bill, representing 59% of the total bids. The uptake was, however, about GH¢1.2 billion. The 182-day bill received bids of about GH¢423.47 million. About GH¢395 million was accepted. For the 364-day bill, about GH¢613 million of the bids were tendered. A little above GH¢292 million of bids were accepted. Meanwhile, interest rates declined across the shorter end of the yield curve, but rose on the longer end of the yield curve. The yield on the 91-day bill declined by 7.0 basis points to 4.54%. Similarly, the 182-day bill also went down to 6.26% from the previous week’6.26%. Also, the yield on the 364-day bill dropped by 15.0 basis points to 9.60%. title: Lockheed Martin examines F-16 variant tailored to Ukraine with AESA radar and European weapons
body: The potential variant comes alongside intensive discussions between Lockheed Martin and Ukrainian authorities in October over weapons supplies, maintenance and aircraft availability. Ukraine wants to improve the fleet’s capabilities while expanding the domestic support network needed to sustain regular combat operations. An active electronically scanned array radar could improve detection and tracking of small, low-flying targets, including attack drones and cruise missiles. A longer detection range could give pilots more time to respond, while the ability to track more targets simultaneously would support operations during Russian aerial attacks. Integrating European guided bombs and cruise missiles could broaden the weapons available to Ukrainian F-16 crews. Development costs, the number of aircraft involved and the weapons to be integrated first have yet to be determined. Ukraine received its first F-16s from European allies in 2024, drawing on older aircraft upgraded through the Mid-Life Update program. These fighters use mechanically scanned radars, unlike newer F-16 Block 70 aircraft equipped with AESA systems. F-16s account for about 80% of Ukrainian Air Force combat sorties, and one Ukrainian F-16 wing is credited with destroying more than 1,000 Russian Shahed drones and cruise missiles. Sustaining that workload makes maintenance capacity an important part of the discussions alongside potential radar, range and weapons improvements. Intensive flying accelerates wear on engines and airframes, while lengthy repairs reduce the number of fighters available for missions. Ukraine is seeking to spread maintenance across more locations and increase domestic industry’s role in supporting the fleet. A dispersed maintenance network could shorten aircraft downtime and reduce the risks associated with concentrating fighters and infrastructure at a few bases. Those changes would support fleet availability while limiting exposure to Russian attacks on individual facilities.

title: Two non-compliant oil tankers detonate, burn in Hormuz Strait
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – IRGC Navy said Sunday night that two oil tankers violating established regulations exploded after striking naval mines while attempting to transit an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the statement issued on Sunday night, one of the vessels is a supertanker. It is currently engulfed in flames following a powerful explosion after navigating the unauthorized path.
Both vessels had deliberately deactivated their navigation and identification systems in a bid to pass covertly through the restricted southern route, operating with the support of the terrorist US military. Both vessels came to a halt at the scene following the explosions, the statement added.
The IRGC Navy stressed that the tankers ignored repeated warnings and entered dangerous waters in clear violation of the regulations governing the strategic waterway. Responsibility for the consequences lies fully with the vessels’ owners, who chose unauthorized transit over compliance with Iranian maritime safety protocols.

title: Sand contractors seek regulatory clarity over enforcement operations at Dawa
body: The Sand and Stone Contractors Association of Ghana has called on state authorities to clarify the regulatory procedures governing sand-winning and transportation activities at Dawa and neighbouring communities. The Association says uncertainty surrounding enforcement operations, documentation requirements and the issuance of fines is creating difficulties for sand winners and tipper truck operators and requires urgent attention from the relevant institutions. In a petition signed by its Acting National Chairman, Anthony Mensah, the Association said it had approached several state institutions, including the Minerals Commission, the Ghana Military Police, the Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ), the Tema Regional Police Command and the Member of Parliament for Ningo-Prampram, Samuel Nartey George, to seek intervention. It said the concerns relate to activities affecting operators at Dawa, Sege Volivo, Tokpo and Lurta, as well as members operating from several surrounding communities. These include Dawhenya, Prampram, Afienya, Spintex Junction, Nungua, Dodowa, Adenta, Amrahia, Tsopoli, Teshie Tsui Bleoo, Tema Motorway Roundabout, Mataheko and Mobole. A major concern raised in the petition is the need for clarity regarding the authority of personnel undertaking enforcement operations and the procedures governing the issuance of receipts and notices of fines. The Association said it wanted the Minerals Commission and the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) to explain their respective mandates and the legal basis for the activities being carried out in the affected areas. It indicated that although the Minerals Commission had reportedly distanced itself from some of the operations, documents, including receipts and notices of fines, had been issued to operators. The Association said it had attached a copy of a receipt to its petition for verification and was seeking an official explanation of the circumstances surrounding its issuance. It also raised concerns about the documentation required for the transportation of sand, particularly the use of waybills. According to the Association, tipper truck drivers often find it difficult to distinguish genuine waybills from fraudulent ones and are not necessarily equipped or authorised to inspect the operational documents of sand winners. It is therefore proposing a formal education programme involving sand winners, tipper truck operators and officials of the Minerals Commission to clarify documentation requirements, regulatory responsibilities and the procedures operators are expected to follow. The Association believes such engagement would help prevent misunderstandings between operators and enforcement personnel and promote compliance with the applicable regulations. It is also calling for an urgent stakeholder meeting involving the Association, affected operators, the Minerals Commission, NAIMOS and the relevant security agencies. The proposed meeting, it said, should provide an opportunity to address outstanding concerns, clarify institutional responsibilities and agree on procedures for regulating sand-winning and transportation activities. The Association further wants operators engaged in lawful sand-winning activities to receive the necessary protection and says any complaints involving misconduct in the course of enforcement operations should be investigated and dealt with through the appropriate legal processes. It expressed concern about growing frustration among its members and warned that unresolved issues could lead to confrontations or demonstrations. However, the Association stressed that it did not support violence or unlawful conduct and maintained that its objective was to promote fairness, accountability and transparency in the sector. It said it had planned a press conference for November 19, 2026, but remained hopeful that the relevant authorities would intervene and address the concerns before then. The Association is seeking a coordinated response from the institutions involved, arguing that clearer communication, public education and stakeholder engagement are necessary to ensure that regulatory activities are properly understood and carried out. It reaffirmed its commitment to pursuing a resolution through lawful channels and urged the authorities to respond promptly to its petition.

title: Ukraine's air raid alert system hacked, Air Force says as false nuclear, chemical warnings sound
body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine's air raid alert system was hacked late Nov. 1, the Air Force said, as sirens sounded across the country and people received false alerts warning of nuclear, chemical, and street fighting threats.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground received notifications on their phones from the officially supported Air Alert app , made in collaboration between the Digital Transformation Ministry and security technology company Ajax Systems.
"Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is on its way," one of the false warnings read in Russian on the Air Alert app.
Air raid alerts also sounded in streets across the country, including Zakarpattia Oblast in western Ukraine, journalists on the ground reported.
"It is likely that the 'Air Alert' app has been compromised by the enemy. There is no radiation threat! Please stay calm and follow our updates on our (Telegram) channel," Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation claimed that the "Air Alert" app was "likely compromised."
For Kyiv residents, the Digital Transformation Ministry recommended using the "Kyiv Digital" app to stay aware of air alerts.
Several regional governors also warned that the system was hacked and advised residents that there was no threat.
"Currently, the situation in the oblast is calm. Reports indicate a cyberattack on the notification app," Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk said .
Officials also warned the cyberattack could involve a phishing operation with attached links.
"Cyberattack on the 'Air Alert' app. Do not click on the link in the message," Vinnytsia Oblast Governor Natalia Zabolotna reported .
The false alerts were then cleared about an hour later.
By midnight local time, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said while the nationwide alert system was back to operating normally, citizens should continue to monitor information from local authorities and listen for signals played on loudpseakers.
"We once again urge citizens not to click on links from unknown sources and not to spread unverified information," the Emergency Service said. At around 2 a.m. local time, the Air Alert app said that operations were gradually being restored while the display of targets was temporarily suspended. "The team is implementing additional security measures to protect the app and prevent similar incidents in the future," said the app's official Telegram channel. "We would like to reiterate that the app does not store or use personal data, so there is no threat to users."
In the early hours of Nov. 2, Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry claimed that its own mobile app had been hacked and false information had been shared with its users. The ministry said it was working to restore operations for the application.

title: True or false? How fake online reviews are concerning businesses
body:
Online reviews can help people decide what to buy, but business owners and consumer watchdogs say some are confusing customers because they’re not actually real.
For Charlotte Ashley, who runs Trident Booksellers and Cafe in Halifax, fake reviews have led customers to request items the business doesn’t even carry.
“Maybe they want menu items that we don’t serve,” said Ashley. “People are disappointed and that’s not the kind of visit that we want them to have at our business.”
Ashley pointed to one such review posted on Google that gave the business five stars but also said the supposed customer got a mushroom quesadilla that the cafe doesn’t serve.
She’s unsure what has caused the fake reviews to pop up on her business’s page or the motive behind them.
But fake reviews are far from new, with a report by the Canadian Anti-monopoly Project showing there’s a market for them on Google and Amazon.
The report says fake reviews harm three groups: consumers because they “obscure” the true quality of the service or product; honest sellers because the reviews put them “at a clear disadvantage”; and platforms if consumers lose trust in them.
“There is a substantial market for fake reviews operating kind of in plain sight and it affects customers who are looking at reviews on all sorts of platforms,” said Emily Osborne, a fellow at the project and policy researcher at the Canada Shield Institute.
Osborne said fake reviewers can be recruited in various ways, including through social media groups.
She said a third-party seller could ask reviewers to post a five-star review potentially in exchange for a free product.
Companies such as Amazon have acted to take down fake reviews, Osborne noted.
Osborne told Global News the Canadian government needs could do more to hold the platforms more accountable.
“I think there’s some space for Canadian policymakers to require better enforcement against fraud on platforms,” she said.
There are posts that exist on social media by “professional review providers,” with a list of prices provided with some offering 100 reviews for $180.
Kay Dean, a U.S.-based consumer watchdog, says the marketplace for fake reviews is “immense.”
“It’s just shocking how immense the problem is, I believe it distorts the whole small business economy globally,” said Dean, who started Fake Review Watch, a website and YouTube channel where she posts her investigations and research. Dean is a former federal prosecutor.
She said her investigations have found businesses bartering and trading reviews with each other on social media. She’s also found marketers and search engine optimization companies with “networks of profiles” that post negative reviews.
“So there’s just a variety of ways to procure fake reviews, it’s very, very easy and inexpensive,” she said.
The exact number of fake reviews online is difficult to determine. But a 2023 report by the U.K. government found 11 to 15 per cent of all reviews on e-commerce platforms for three common product categories were likely fake. Product categories typically included consumer electronics, home and kitchen, and sports and outdoors.
It also found well-written fake reviews can distort consumer decision making, with buyers 3.1 per cent more likely to purchase a product.
There are things people can do to take precautions when shopping, including using caution when “flawless” ratings are given. Experts say the best advice comes through word-of-mouth.

title: Toluwanisings’ death and social media prosecutors, By Festus Adedayo
body:
My eyes are misty as I write this. I have spent the better part of the morning listening repeatedly to one of the tracks of that gifted Yoruba gospel musician, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known on stage as Toluwanisings. The 34-year-old was nature’s human carving of an Àwòko for the listening pleasure of humanity. Toluwanisings was the nightingale, the mockingbird of sacred song. The nightingale holds a sacred placement in Yoruba avian symbolism. Àwòko is the peerless soloist of the forest, gifted with an unmatchable range of sweet cadence.
This human nightingale hailed from Ikirun, Osun State, the ancient town that houses Akinorun Grammar School, where I spent a memorable chapter of my secondary school education. Toluwanisings passed away suddenly a few weeks ago, on 14 October, after collapsing on the staircase of his Ibadan, Oyo State residence. He had just returned from an exhilarating worship concert titled In His Presence .
The palaver generated by his sudden departure is immense, disturbing, and deeply instructive. It calls to mind that timeless Swahili proverb which says, on the day a monkey is destined to be killed by a prowling wild cat, every tree it clings to becomes slippery. How does a man who sang so confidently about conquering postpartum human mockery and the conceit of hypocrites suddenly, barely a month after departing this mortal space, become the chief victim of these very wicked forces?
In that particular track that drew hot tears down my cheeks, he sang with prophetic defiance: “The machinations of the enemy will not triumph over me/Satan will never rejoice over my life/Heavens will not regret lifting me high/My sunlight will not be eclipsed by darkness/I saw Satan fall like lightning/The dragon was conquered by the power of our testimony/Satan will not celebrate the fall of a mighty man/My giant will not become a pygmy, as the Lord lives.”
I translated the above searing, tear-jerking lyrics from his verbatim Yoruba rendering that goes thus: “Ero ọta ko ni ṣe lẹ mi l’ori/Inu Satani ko ni dun l’ori aye mi…/Ọrun o ni k’abamọ p’ohun gbe mi ga…/Imọlẹ mi ko ni wọ l’okunkun.. . /Emi ri Satani to ṣubụ bi mọnamọna/A ṣegun Dragoni nipa ọrọ ẹri ẹnu wa/Satani ko ni s’ajọyọ p’alagbara ṣubu/Omiran mi o ni d’arara b’Oluwa ti ń bẹ.”
Posthumously, however, it would appear that the very machinations Toluwanisings prayed against have encircled him like the enveloping grips of a boa constrictor. The invisible demons of this world seem to be celebrating his passage, while those who should have protected his memory – including members of his immediate and extended family – have perfected plans to reduce this musical giant into a pygmy in the court of public opinion. On the day Toluwanisings passed, every road led to the imagined blood the prowling cat spilled out of the Swahili monkey. All the monkey’s renowned tree-climbing theatrical skills became effete in an instant. The most knowledgeable became the most foolish, and the most celebrated became the most vulnerable.
Toluwanisings’ death and the social media conceit that followed confirm the age-long wisdom of our forebears: if the well-known acrobatic tree-to-tree escape from its foes meets the monkey on plain, treeless ground, the creature becomes as helpless and vulnerable as any ordinary mammal. Ancient Yoruba wisdom packages this as: “Bi igi o ba sunmọ igi, ọmọ ẹdun a d’ope” – when trees fail to stand close to one another, the young monkey loses its agility and becomes a big-time fool.
Before we even examine Toluwanisings’ tragic post-death drama, we must confront the horrifying circumstances surrounding his final hours. It was a familiar Nigerian tragedy that unfolded: the gospel musician slumped in his home; medical attention was fatally delayed and ultimately denied, and Àwòko flew away with his melodious voice.
For decades, Nigeria has grappled with the twin evils of hospital emergency management – systemic negligence and outright rejection – which have consumed some of the finest minds and sweetest voices of our country. Added to these is the third evil: the notorious refusal by hospitals to treat emergency and gunshot victims without police reports. Added together, they constitute an unfeeling bureaucratic cruelty that continues to send citizens to early graves.
Reports indicate that as Toluwanisings fought for breath upon slumping, he was rushed to approximately seven to eight different hospitals across the city of Ibadan, including the apex federal tertiary institution, the University College Hospital (UCH). Each institution either rejected him outright or presented one administrative excuse after another. They passed the dying artist around in a macabre game of medical hot potato, until the Owner of the leash on the goat’s neck finally pulled it into eternity.
Predictably, social media collapsed under the weight of anger and unfeeling cross-examinations. Àwòko ’s sudden, needlessly avoidable silence provoked widespread outrage online, as netizens poured bile on Nigeria’s broken health infrastructure. They then resurrected that haunting, tragic national shibboleth: May Nigeria never happen to us.
Yet, the moment Toluwanisings’ eyes closed to open in eternity, the conversation shifted from the systemic failure that killed him to a toxic, voyeuristic dissection of his personal life. The posthumous uproar and needless media harangue attending Toluwanisings’ passing and burial sound so absurd. They bear a striking resemblance to the dark spectacle that followed the death of Ilerioluwa Oladimeji Aloba, widely known as Mohbad, in 2023.
Mohbad was just 27 years old when he died on September 12 of that year. A talented singer and songwriter too, his death detonated a complex web of controversy, ranging from allegations of Lagos music underworld bullying and assault to disputes over the paternity of his infant son, coroner’s inquests, and disgraceful family squabbles over his estate. For years, that young boy’s corpse remained trapped inside the dark coldness of the morgue, suffering endless postponements while living relatives traded insults on social media.
The Mohbad spectacle reminded me of the decades it took for the secrets of Asipa Oyo, Amuda Olorunosebi, to be covered by Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyer i – the earth’s crust. Gruesomely murdered on his Oyo Alaafin farm on November 26, 1992, with acid poured on his body by his assailants, he remained unburied for seven years, until November 26, 1999. Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyer i is not a mere descriptive phrase; it is a sacred metaphysical name the Yoruba gave to the earth and soil. To our ancestors, the earth is not a passive, inanimate natural resource or mere dirt under our feet; it is a living, conscious, spiritual entity possessing an interconnected affinity with the divine. The earth-crust is venerat ed as the ultimate, considerate concealer of the human creature’s secrets when life is done.
Instead of allowing Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ to grant Toluwanisings that sacred cover immediately after he breathed his last, his family members from Ikirun began to heap mounds of hot ash on his memory. For weeks, public attempts were made to paint him as an ungrateful child who abandoned his father , lavished his fortune on his wife’s family, and lived a hypocritical life of a wolf in a sheep’s clothing.
In the heat of this online trial, the question of where his body should be interred morphed into a bitter public war. While his widow favours a quiet, dignified burial in a modern cemetery, his father and patriarchal relatives insist on burying him either inside his newly completed Ibadan residence or beside his late mother’s grave in Ikirun – warning that otherwise, Ir ẹ l ẹ , Ikirun’s deeply venerated ancestral guardian deity and mythical god, would unleash its mortal strike. There is nil consideration for Toluwanisings’ young wife and two little girls, except their patriarchal ego and inflated manhood. The contestation s has become messy, laughable, and – pardon the word – utterly idiotic. A man who spent his life crafting melodies to heal broken hearts became, in death, a piece of bone fought over by dogs.
If we take a step back from our local grief, however, we will realize that this posthumous hubris is not unique to contemporary Nigeria. Throughout music history, the corpses and legacies of legendary artists have passed through remarkably similar, sordid corridors of greed, hypocrisy and family warfare.
Take the case of my revered musical totem, Winston McIntosh, known to the world as Peter Tosh. By the way, I ported from his friend and arch-rival, Bob Marley, to Tosh when I discovered Tosh’s boundless depth, poetry and philosophy were way out of Bob’s . S orry, I digressed. Peter was the uncompromising co-founder of The Wailers whose posthumous Grammy recognition celebrated his genius. Shot in the head during a violent home robbery on 11 September, 1987, Tosh’s death immediately triggered a chaotic funeral planning process marred by a thick confetti of familial, religious, and political conflicts.
As Tosh’s body was being prepared for interment, two different men suddenly surfaced claiming to be his biological father. One was Alfred McIntosh, backed aggressively by Tosh’s common-law wife, Marlene Brown; the other was James McIntosh, who was eventually confirmed by Tosh’s grieving mother, Alvera Coke, as his father. A fierce feud erupted over his burial site between Marlene Brown and his mother. While Brown insisted on her legal right to manage the funeral, his mother demanded that her only child be brought back to her home parish of Westmoreland. Because the Jamaican state did not legally recognise common-law marriage, the government handed the body to Tosh’s mother.
Tosh’s funeral descended into utter madness. As a devout Rastafarian who spent his life denouncing the hypocrisy of state institutions, the attempt by the Jamaican government to dominate Tosh’s official state funeral sparked protests. How could the same “Babylon” that hunted Tosh to death – whose polais-mon ( police ) cracked his skull for smoking ganja – be same mourner shedding crocodile tears at his funeral? His Rastafarian brethren thus turned the funeral into a raucous, chaotic demonstration. To compound the surreal drama, a self-proclaimed prophet marched up to the casket, unlidded it in front of the congregation and fruitlessly chanted commands for Tosh to “rise from the dead!”
Similarly, the tragic end of Apala music legend , Ayinla Omowura , in May 1980 saw a battle over the soul and body of the man who prided himself as the nightingale – a bird the Yoruba also call the Olóbùró . Culturally, the Yoruba appellation for this ancient bird is that it has 200 voices ( ẹyẹ olóbùró ní ohùn igba ), with its famed beautiful, endless repertoire of songs that come in loud, bold vocal variety. Apologies: I digressed again. Stabbed in the head with a heavy beer glass during a barroom brawl in Ago-Ika, Abeokuta, Omowura died of cranium damage. Though born a Muslim, he was notorious for ignoring daily Islamic prayer rituals. His Itoko home was a haven for traditionalists and fiery masquerades, most notably his personal masquerade named Tankurubaku. His open indulgence in cannabis and violence was also legendary.
Upon Omowura’s killing, the conservative Islamic clerics of his Itoko neighbourhood staunchly refused to administer the Salat al-Janazah (Islamic funeral prayer) on his body, declaring his lifestyle un-Islamic. It was only after community elders reminded the clerics of Omowura’s massive, anonymous financial contributions to their local mosque that the religious leaders reluctantly assented to perform the rites.
The Western world offers equally bizarre examples of squabbles over artists’ corpses. Elvis Presley and James Brown followed that trajectory, with their passages shrouded in ruckuses. When Presley, the “King of Rock and Roll,” died of cardiac arrest on August 16, 1977, he was buried in a mausoleum at Forest Hill Cemetery in Memphis. Shortly after, police arrested four men who had broken into the vault attempting to steal his corpse in order to extort millions of dollars in ransom from his estate. His body had to be exhumed and reburied in a heavily guarded, fortified garden at Graceland.
Similarly, when James Brown, the “Godfather of Soul,” died on Christmas Day in 2006, his body remained unburied for months in a temperature-controlled room while his children and his partner, Tomi Rae Hynie, waged a vicious legal battle over the validity of their marriage, control of his multi-million dollar estate, and the choice of his final sepulchre.
Perhaps the most bizarre posthumous spectacle occurred following the 1973 drug overdose death of country rock pioneer Gram Parsons. Prior to his death, Parsons and his road manager, Phil Kaufman, had made a secret pact: whichever of them died first would be cremated by the other in the high desert of Joshua Tree National Park. Thus, when Parsons died, his stepfather, Robert Parsons, attempted to hijack his body for a private burial in Louisiana to secure control over the musician’s estate. Kaufman responded by posing as a mortuary driver at Los Angeles International Airport and stole the coffin from the hangar. He then drove it out to the Joshua Tree desert, poured five gallons of petrol over the corpse, and set it ablaze. Kaufman was later arrested; however, the charge of cadaver theft against him in court couldn’t stand because it wasn’t explicitly classified as a crime under California law at the time. Kaufman was merely fined $300 for the theft of the wooden casket!
What these global cases reveal is a disturbing, universal human impulse: society is deeply, structurally unfair in its posthumous assessment and handling of artists.
When a musician is alive, we consume their talent, exploit their vulnerabilities, and demand that they serve as vessels for our inspiration, our worship, or our entertainment. But the moment breath leaves their lungs, we strip them of their human dignity. The living descend, like vultures, upon their corpses – relatives fight over property, fans trade salacious rumours, religious institutions pass sanctimonious judgments and the public turns their personal tragedy into cheap online entertainment.
Toluwanisings spent his short life crafting songs that offered solace to thousands. He sang of triumphing over mockery, of light piercing through darkness, and of giants refusing to become pygmies. Yet in death, he became temporarily trapped in the very noise, malice, and belittlement he spent his career singing against.
These are my questions for Toluwanisings’ sabre-rattling uncle, who has become the mythological social media dragon breathing out fire and brimstone over the preferred site of his burial: Does he know that, upon cessation of breath from the nostrils, the living body has no more worth than a log of wood? Why prioritize a log of wood’s welfare over that of the living?
Whether Toluwanisings is buried in the finest sepulchre on earth like Michael Jackson (whose crypt burial site at the Great Mausoleum–Holly Terrace in Forest Lawn Memorial Park cost $590,000 for the crypt title alone, out of a total private funeral cost of more than $1 million) or the modest cemetery replica of where President Umaru Yar’Adua was interred, like every man, maggots will feast on the body a few days post-interment.
Why compound the pain of a widowed young woman who would have to daily agonize as she wakes to see a cryptic grave that was once her ebullient husband? If there is a need to sell Toluwanisings’ new house, especially to finance his young kids’ education, does this uncle realize that a home used as a burial site could bring down its value? The obvious reality is that Toluwanisings’ paternal family is locked up in the ancient patriarchal view of a woman as chattel and unworthy of inheritance, especially since it is obvious that she might remarry.
Society must learn to give the departed their peace. The dead cannot defend themselves, nor can they respond to allegations whipped up by living relatives or social media prosecutors. It is time we let Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyer i do its sacred work of covering the secrets, the flaws, as well as the bones of the departed , in a modest time frame – human foibles which all the online prosecutors also possess . By doing so, we would allow the art of the dead and not their human limitations, echo into eternity.
The story of Nevada Pierre, the sensational three-year-old American soccer prodigy from Florida, is fast becoming an archetype of how qualification can, ironically, disqualify the qualified. If you l ook closely enough at the Nevada narrative, you will also tease out a sobering commentary on the shrinking boundary of human patience for natural talent and competition.
Nevada set the internet ablaze recently following a youth soccer match organized by i9 Sports in Winter Park , a game that degenerated into a dispute so heated it required police intervention. The toddler’s brilliant ball control, eclectic dribbling and total pitch dominance left the parents of opposing children visibly incensed. Complaining that the boy was “too advanced,” the disgruntled parents summoned the Winter Park Police Department. But their outrage backfired spectacularly. Rather than suppressing the prodigy, the police dispatch catapulted Nevada into global headlines, earning him an invitation to train at Eddie Johnson’s Orlando-based EJE7 Soccer Academy, the admiration of celebrity children’s entertainer , Rachel Griffin-Accurso and a wave of fan-backed GoFundMe support.
Instructive as the Nevada Pierre episode is, what commands my attention most is its central lesson: how man readily manipulates qualification for selfish ends.
A raging issue that underscores this moral deficit right here in Nigeria involves the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and its 2024/2025 recruitment exercise, where candidates who officially triumphed are now being punished for their success.
According to media reports, the NCS published the final list of successful candidates of the exercise in July 2026. The y then received formal provisional offers on the official recruitment portal, complete with instructions to fulfill specific prerequisites . These includ ed submi ssion of medical certificates of fitness from state hospitals and formally accepting the offers within a stipulated window. Trusting the sanctity of the process, several candidates resigned from their existing jobs.
Yet, when basic training commenced, these successful applicants discovered to their utter shock that their names had been systematically erased. In their place were entirely new names , individuals who allegedly never participated in the initial screening exercise.
While the Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, reportedly intervened by ordering a case-by-case review of the aggrieved applicants’ complaints, the Service continues to defend its posture with the defense that inclusion on its published shortlist does not constitute an automatic guarantee of enlistment.
What the NCS must realise is that when administrative discretion becomes a veil for organisational impunity, institutional integrity leaves through the window. Just as the aggrieved parents in Winter Park sought to police away superior talent out of spite, the arbitrary erasure of verified candidates from the Customs recruitment list signals a dangerous culture where merit is treated as a liability rather than an asset. Comptroller-General Adeniyi’s promised review must move beyond mere damage control to full restitution. A nation that off-handedly mourns its brain drain and institutional decay cannot continue to systematically disqualify its most qualified, simply to satisfy the appetite of elite man-know-man .
Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

title: Nine people killed in business jet crash in Palm Beach, USA — US Transportation Secretary
body:
NEW YORK, November 2. /TASS/. Nine people were on board a Learjet 60 business jet that crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, there are no survivors, U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced.
"Today’s plane crash in Palm Beach County is a horrific tragedy," he wrote on the social media platform X. "All 9 people on board were killed."
Duffy added that the aircraft had departed from Austin, Texas, and was en route to the Bahamas.

title: Decoupling Sovereignty Index (5): How decoupling reinforces itself, By Max Amuchie
body:
A territory can register alarming scores across multiple indicators and still leave a fundamental question unanswered: are the forces undermining state sovereignty operating independently, or have they begun reinforcing one another to create a self-sustaining alternative order?
This distinction matters. A state may experience economic extraction by armed groups, territorial insecurity and the weakening of public legitimacy simultaneously. Yet the presence of these conditions does not necessarily mean they have combined into a resilient system capable of reproducing itself despite government intervention.
The challenge is to establish not merely whether sovereignty is weakening, but whether the forces responsible for that weakening have begun to reinforce one another.
This is the problem addressed by the Convergence Indicator of the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI).
In the earlier instalments of this series, we introduced the DSI as a quantitative diagnostic instrument developed to assess the gap between a state’s formal sovereignty and the realities of authority, security, territorial control and institutional performance within its territory.
We examined its three diagnostic vectors—Money, Land and Mind—and introduced the 19 universal indicators through which the instrument seeks to make territorial decoupling systematically observable.
The indicators provide the underlying measurements. But measurements alone cannot fully explain the relationships among the conditions they describe.
Two territories might register comparable levels of insecurity yet face fundamentally different challenges. In one, the loss of state authority may be concentrated in a particular sector, leaving other institutions and territorial arrangements relatively resilient. In the other, economic extraction may finance territorial expansion, territorial control may facilitate coercive rule, and that rule may progressively displace the state’s capacity to regulate everyday life.
The second territory presents a more complex problem. Its weaknesses are not merely accumulating; they are becoming mutually reinforcing.
The DSI’s Convergence Indicator is designed to investigate this distinction.
From Separate Weaknesses to a Self-Reinforcing System
Sovereign decoupling does not necessarily follow a straight line. Weakness in one dimension of governance may remain contained, while another dimension continues to function.
A state might struggle to prevent kidnapping while retaining control over agricultural production and local dispute resolution. It might lose effective control over a rural corridor without losing the population’s confidence in its public institutions. Alternatively, it might maintain a visible security presence while failing to prevent the economic exploitation of residents.
These are different configurations of decoupling, and each may require a different policy response.
The danger intensifies when the weaknesses begin feeding into one another.
Consider a territory in which a non-state armed organisation derives revenue from kidnapping, extortion or illegal taxation. The proceeds finance recruitment, weapons, logistics and further territorial expansion. Control over territory then enables the organisation to regulate movement, influence production, restrict access to markets and impose rules on residents.
As the organisation’s practical authority grows, it may become increasingly capable of extracting resources, protecting its economic networks and punishing those who resist its demands.
Some residents may comply because they fear retaliation. Others may depend on arrangements imposed by the organisation because formal institutions cannot provide effective alternatives. Still others may adjust their behaviour simply because the organisation has become a persistent feature of the local political and economic environment.
Such compliance must not automatically be interpreted as voluntary allegiance or legitimacy. Nevertheless, it can contribute to the organisation’s capacity to maintain control.
Economic extraction finances territorial power. Territorial power enables further extraction. Coercive authority regulates behaviour, while the resulting compliance can make the organisation more difficult to displace.
Money reinforces Land, while the resulting arrangements affect the Mind vector through coercion, perceived legitimacy, competing allegiances and the population’s relationship with formal state institutions.
The three vectors begin to interact as parts of a larger system.
This is the central analytical proposition behind the Convergence Indicator: the significance of decoupling depends not only on the severity of individual weaknesses, but also on whether their interaction produces a more resilient alternative order.
If the underlying indicators are moving in different directions, the resulting pattern may represent uneven or sectoral decoupling.
The state may be losing control over a particular economic activity while retaining the ability to protect the surrounding population. It may face territorial insecurity without having lost the credibility of its institutions. It may also retain opportunities to reverse a particular weakness through a targeted intervention.
Under such circumstances, a policy response can focus on the specific source of the problem while strengthening the institutions that remain functional.
However, where adverse conditions across Money, Land and Mind increasingly reinforce one another, interventions directed at individual symptoms may have limited effects.
A military operation might disrupt an armed organisation without dismantling the economic networks that finance its return. An economic development programme might increase commercial activity without protecting traders from extortion. A public information campaign might seek to rebuild trust while residents remain exposed to coercion.
In each case, the intervention addresses a genuine problem but may leave the relationships sustaining that problem largely intact.
The Convergence Indicator is intended to help analysts distinguish between these situations.
Its purpose is not simply to establish that several indicators have high scores. Rather, it is to assess whether the underlying evidence supports a finding that adverse conditions are interacting across the three vectors in ways that intensify and sustain decoupling.
This requires more than observing simultaneous deterioration. Researchers must identify the relevant relationships, establish the direction of the indicators and apply explicit rules for determining whether the evidence supports a convergence signal.
The distinction is essential to the DSI’s credibility as a quantitative instrument. High scores across multiple indicators may suggest a serious crisis, but the claim that the crisis has become self-reinforcing requires additional analytical justification.
The Event Horizon: When Shadow Authority Becomes Resilient
The DSI uses the term Event Horizon to describe a critical condition in which a Shadow Order has become sufficiently resilient and institutionally embedded that formal state intervention can no longer easily reverse its position. The concept draws attention to a potentially consequential transition.
At an earlier stage, a non-state organisation may exploit a specific weakness in state authority. Its activities may remain geographically limited, economically dependent on particular opportunities or vulnerable to targeted disruption.
As its power expands, however, it may develop a broader system of economic extraction, territorial control and coercive regulation. These capabilities can reinforce one another, enabling the organisation to survive interventions that address only one dimension of its power.
The territory may then become increasingly difficult to recover through isolated security operations or conventional development programmes.
An Event Horizon, in this analytical sense, is not simply a point at which violence reaches a particular level. It describes the possibility that an alternative order has acquired sufficient internal resilience to reproduce the conditions supporting its authority.
The distinction between resilience and legitimacy is important. A Shadow Order may persist without enjoying popular support. Its durability may depend on coercion, economic dependence, the absence of credible alternatives or the population’s inability to resist safely.
Nor does the concept imply that recovery becomes impossible after a particular threshold has been crossed. Rather, it signals the possibility that restoration will require a more comprehensive response than interventions designed to address individual symptoms.
For the DSI to operationalise the Event Horizon concept, the methodology must specify the evidence and decision rules required to distinguish severe but reversible decoupling from a more consolidated alternative order.
The concept provides an analytical proposition to investigate, not a universally established threshold that can be assumed to apply identically across territories.
Three Convergence Signals of Particular Importance
Within the DSI’s current indicator architecture, three designated combinations carry particular analytical significance. They illustrate how relationships among indicators can help identify broader patterns of territorial and institutional breakdown.
1. M6 and L6: Agricultural Sovereignty Collapse
Agriculture is not merely an economic activity. In many vulnerable territories, it sustains household income, food availability, local markets and the productive use of land.
When agricultural livelihoods are undermined by economic pressures and territorial insecurity, the consequences can extend far beyond reduced output.
Farmers may abandon their fields because access is unsafe. Traders may be unable to transport produce. Disrupted production can reduce household income, while displacement can weaken the labour and commercial networks needed to restore agricultural activity.
Declining production may, in turn, increase economic vulnerability and deepen dependence on alternative sources of income or coercive arrangements.
The relationship between M6 and L6 is intended to flag conditions associated with the breakdown of agricultural sovereignty: a situation in which the practical capacity to sustain agricultural production and livelihoods is seriously compromised.
The analytical concern is the interaction between the relevant economic and territorial conditions, not simply the existence of agricultural decline.
2. L7, L3 and MD5: Human Sovereignty Collapse
The second designated combination concerns the conditions under which people can live, move, maintain livelihoods and exercise agency within their communities.
Where territorial insecurity and competing systems of coercion become entrenched, residents may be forced to flee, abandon productive activities or reorganise their lives around the demands of armed actors.
Others may remain physically present but lose meaningful freedom of movement, access to essential resources or the ability to make ordinary decisions without fear.
These conditions affect more than physical security. They can weaken the social and economic foundations of community life and undermine the practical relationship between residents and the institutions expected to protect them.
The designated relationship among L7, L3 and MD5 is intended to signal this broader pattern of human sovereignty collapse.
Here, human sovereignty refers to the practical conditions under which people can exercise agency and sustain ordinary life. It does not replace or negate the legal sovereignty of the state.
The distinction matters because a territory may remain internationally recognised as part of a sovereign state while its residents experience severe constraints on their everyday freedom and security.
3. L5 and MD1: Justice Sovereignty Collapse
The third combination addresses the practical authority of the state in the administration and enforcement of justice.
Where formal institutions cannot reliably protect residents, resolve disputes or enforce legal decisions, alternative arrangements may emerge.
These arrangements can be imposed by armed organisations or maintained by other authorities operating beyond the state’s effective reach. Residents may comply because the alternatives are inaccessible, because they perceive an alternative arrangement as more predictable, or because resistance carries unacceptable risks.
Predictability under these conditions should not be confused with fairness, legitimacy or voluntary acceptance.
The relationship between L5 and MD1 is intended to flag circumstances in which the state’s effective authority over justice is seriously compromised.
The consequences may extend beyond individual disputes. When residents cannot depend on formal institutions for protection or redress, the credibility of those institutions may decline further. That weakening can make it harder for the state to rebuild public confidence and restore its authority.
These three designated combinations demonstrate the intended analytical value of convergence signals: they direct attention to relationships among indicators that may reveal broader patterns of breakdown.
Their exact definitions and operational implications must be documented in the DSI methodology. The presence of a designated combination should not, without supporting evidence, be treated as conclusive proof that a particular form of collapse has occurred.
The Convergence Indicator occupies a distinct position within the DSI architecture.
The 19 universal indicators provide the underlying field measurements. The Convergence Indicator synthesises evidence about relationships among those measurements to help determine whether decoupling is sectoral, uneven or potentially self-reinforcing across the three vectors.
It therefore addresses a question that individual indicator scores cannot answer on their own: are the forces undermining state authority developing into a mutually reinforcing system?
This question has direct implications for policy.
Where the evidence points to a relatively contained weakness, targeted interventions may be appropriate. Where the evidence indicates that economic extraction, territorial control and competing authority reinforce one another, interventions may need to address those relationships together.
The practical implications will depend on the circumstances of each territory. The DSI does not presume that all forms of convergence require an identical response, nor that one score can substitute for detailed contextual analysis.
Its contribution lies in providing a structured way to examine the systemic relationships that should inform that analysis.
The instrument’s value will ultimately depend on the transparency of its scoring rules, the quality of its evidence and the results of empirical application. These requirements are particularly important if the Convergence Indicator is to support comparisons across territories or guide decisions with substantial security and development consequences.
The DSI is being developed by Sundiata Post, with its methodological work administered through the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL). The forthcoming DSI Methodology and Indicator Manual will document the technical specifications and operational guidance required to support its application by researchers and policy practitioners across Africa and the Global South.
The Convergence Indicator represents one part of that developing architecture. Its task is to make the relationships sustaining decoupling more visible and to help analysts distinguish a collection of weaknesses from a system capable of reproducing them.
Yet diagnosis alone cannot determine whether a proposed recovery programme is structurally viable.
Even when the sources of decoupling are understood, the state must still confront another question: in what order should it rebuild the conditions required for effective authority?
That is the problem addressed by the DSI’s second higher-order diagnostic.
In the next instalment, we examine the Recovery Sequencing Score and the proposition that sustainable sovereign restoration depends not only on what governments do, but also on whether the conditions necessary for recovery are established in the right order.
Max Nwabueze Amuchie is a scholar-journalist, CEO of Sundiata Post and Lead Researcher at the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL), Abuja. He developed the Insecurity Triad, the Trinity of Sovereignty Decay (TSD), the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI) and the Sundiata Post Model (SPM). He is an Expert Member & Peer Reviewer, Behavioural Sciences at ScienceOpen. Email: [email protected] . X: @MaxAmuchie

title: In Makkah, Tinubu prays that Nigeria’s diversity would lead to prosperity
body:
President Bola Tinubu has beseeched Almighty Allah to transform Nigeria’s rich diversity into a source of prosperity, unity, peace and sustainable development for the benefit of all Nigerians.
President Tinubu offered the prayer on Sunday in the holy city of Makkah, Saudi Arabia, while hosting members of his delegation for dinner.
The president expressed the hope that Nigeria’s ethnic, religious, and cultural diversity would continue to serve as a source of strength and national advancement rather than division, stressing the need for citizens to embrace mutual understanding, peaceful coexistence and a shared commitment to the country’s progress.
He prayed that Almighty Allah would bless Nigeria with enduring peace, harmony and prosperity, and grant the nation’s leaders the wisdom, courage and foresight to steer the country towards greater development and improved living conditions for its people.
“May Almighty Allah bless Nigeria, convert our diversity into prosperity as a country,” the president said.
President Tinubu also prayed for divine guidance and protection for Nigerians at home and abroad, asking Allah to strengthen the bonds of brotherhood among citizens and inspire a renewed spirit of patriotism, compassion and service to the nation.
The President noted that Nigeria’s abundant human and natural resources, coupled with the talents, creativity and enterprise of its diverse population, provided a strong foundation for building a prosperous and inclusive nation.
The dinner with members of his delegation in Makkah provided an opportunity for fellowship and reflection on Nigerians’ shared aspirations for a peaceful, united and prosperous country.
President Tinubu urged Nigerians of all faiths and backgrounds to keep working together in the national interest, expressing confidence that, with faith in Almighty Allah, unity of purpose, and collective determination, Nigeria would overcome its challenges and realise its full potential.
The Chairman of BUA, Abdulsamad Rabiu, reaffirmed President Tinubu’s commitment to peace, unity and prosperity of Nigeria.
“Today is actually the third dinner we’re having with His Excellency Mr President since we came to Makkah on Thursday night or Friday morning when Mr President arrived.
“So, we discussed, and the discussion was, you know, to always continue to pray for Nigeria, for peace, for unity and for Nigeria’s prosperity. To again, you know, thank His Excellency for his passion, for what he’s doing for Nigeria.
“And also for us, it’s quite important because, as I said, it has given us the opportunity to come and pray not only for ourselves and our families, but also for Nigeria.
“We will continue to support His Excellency in whatever capacity we can and definitely, as you all know, Mr President is very passionate about the country. He’s working very hard, and we’ll continue to support him,” he said.
Kwara State Governor and Chairman of the Nigerian Governors’ Forum, Abdulrahman AbdulRazaq, said the forum is overwhelmed by the president’s passion and commitment to achieving a united and prosperous nation.
“Only Allah can reward you; we will continue to pray for you daily and pray for Nigeria that you lead. May Allah continue to strengthen you in making the right decisions, strengthen your wisdom, your boldness, your audacity, your courage. May Allah lead you to the right path,” he said.
The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, also prayed for Almighty Allah to continue to strengthen the President in his determination to deliver governance and justice to all Nigerians irrespective of their religion or ethnic backgrounds.
The dinner was attended by Yobe State Governor Mala Buni, Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, Jigawa State Governor Mohammed Namadi, Sokoto State Governor Ahmed Aliyu, Borno State Governor Babagana Zulum, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Mohammed Pate, National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu, Chief Executive Officer of Oando Plc Wale Tinubu, Special Adviser to the President on Political Matters Ibrahim Masari, and Chief of Staff to the President Femi Gbajabiamila, among others.
