title: [New Rx] What if the Philippines leased an island for 100 years?
body: The Philippine peso recently reached a record low of ₱64.17 against the US dollar. While currency depreciation alone does not indicate economic weakness, it raises a key question: how can the Philippines strengthen investor confidence and attract long-term capital for economic transformation? During a visit to the Philippines, my father made an unusual suggestion: why not lease one island to another country for 100 years? Under this proposal, the partner country would help establish a distinct legal and institutional framework while the Philippines retains sovereignty, national defense, and responsibility for essential public services. After a century, the Philippines would inherit a thriving economic center with modern infrastructure and competitive institutions. An idea with an unexpected precedent In January 2016, then-presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte proposed leasing islands to multinational companies with autonomy to develop infrastructure and operating rules. However, my father’s proposal differs: rather than relying on private corporations, it involves a government-to-government institutional partnership. The historical comparison is Hong Kong. In 1898, China leased the New Territories to Britain for 99 years. Decades later, Hong Kong helped channel international capital, expertise, and commerce into Shenzhen and the Pearl River Delta, illustrating how a jurisdiction with distinct institutions can stimulate development far beyond its borders. Not another economic zone The Philippines already offers investment incentives and special economic zones, but these remain subject to the national administrative framework. What if one island operated under a distinct system of civil and commercial laws, an independent judiciary, taxation, and regulatory institutions? The goal would be to offer investors predictable rules, enforceable contracts, and credible institutions. Like Hong Kong, it could feature separate residency arrangements while preserving Philippine citizenship. Importantly, the foreign partner would not operate the entire government. The Philippines would continue providing healthcare, education, policing, municipal services, and defense. The partner would supply the institutional architecture: judicial expertise, regulatory standards, and independent oversight. Such an arrangement would require constitutional changes, particularly to establish an independent judiciary and a distinct immigration system. The experiment would concern institutions, not merely financial incentives. Why would Singapore be interested? Singapore’s domestic market is small, land and labor are constrained, and its companies need international expansion. Initiatives like the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone demonstrate its strategy of pairing financial and technological strengths with regional land and workforce capacity. A Philippine island could offer another variation of that strategy. Singaporean businesses could establish manufacturing facilities, logistics hubs, and research campuses operating under familiar standards. Headquarters and advanced research would remain in Singapore, while land-intensive operations locate on the island. Unlike conventional industrial parks, the arrangement would feature a separate judicial and regulatory framework supported by Singaporean institutions. Private investors could finance much of the infrastructure, limiting Singaporean taxpayer exposure while Singapore contributes institutional expertise rather than assuming territorial administration. Singapore has not expressed interest in such an arrangement, and its potential participation would require further examination. South Korea offers another possibility Alternatively, South Korea brings strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and digital governance. The partner could be any country with strong institutions, proven administrative capabilities, and no territorial ambitions. An economic engine for surrounding provinces Imagine an underdeveloped island transformed into an international commercial center with modern ports, industrial parks, and universities. The benefits would extend to surrounding provinces supplying agriculture, labor, and materials, stimulating investment across the region. Any location would require an independent feasibility study and a credible process for securing the informed consent of affected communities. Protecting sovereignty — and the foreign partner To protect Philippine sovereignty, foreign military bases and territorial claims would be prohibited. The Philippines would retain national defense and natural resource rights, while existing residents’ citizenship, property rights, and political representation would be protected. Equally important, foreign partners would need assurances against unilateral termination by future Philippine administrations. A constitutionally authorized bilateral treaty, international arbitration, compensation provisions, and political-risk insurance could reduce these risks, although no legal safeguard could entirely eliminate them. Could one island change expectations? Beyond economics, experiencing predictable permits, efficient dispute resolution, and transparent rules could raise public expectations for governance across the Philippines, encouraging broader national reforms. The island’s greatest legacy might be changing what Filipinos expect from the government. Beyond defending the peso The Philippines has pursued growth through incentives and economic zones for decades. The next experiment should focus on institutional credibility. By starting with just one island, the Philippines could create a model that delivers capital, infrastructure, and institutional learning for generations to come. After 100 years, the Philippines could inherit not only a thriving economic center but also institutions and practices worth adopting elsewhere. Speaking in Parliament in 1977 about Singapore’s need to develop its own institutional approach, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew expressed a philosophy that remains relevant far beyond its original context: “We have got to find our own style. We have got to be bold enough to experiment.” – Rappler.com Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

title: Sowore releases video of alleged attackers, alleges erased CCTV footage in Ekiti
body:
Omoyele Sowore, the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), has released a video purportedly showing individuals he identified as participants in the attack on his team in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State, last Friday.
In a post announcing the development on X, the Sahara Reporters publisher described the video as a breakthrough in identifying those involved in the attack. He, however, called for an independent investigation to establish the identities and roles of the individuals shown.
The video appears to show some men wielding cutlasses and sticks during a confrontation, while another person dressed in a black suit is seen being dragged. Several bystanders are also visible watching the incident.
Mr Sowore also alleged that CCTV recordings from Tawakalitu Restaurant, where the incident occurred on 30 October, had been erased after police officers and operatives of the State Security Service (SSS) also known as the Department of State Services (DSS), allegedly took possession of the surveillance equipment.
“The breakthrough comes amid disturbing revelations that CCTV recordings from Tawakalitu Restaurant, where the attack occurred, have reportedly been completely erased after police officers and the DSS took possession of the equipment and took it to Government House only to return it this evening without any images,” he alleged in an X post.
He further sstated that the CCTV equipment was subsequently returned to the restaurant management without the recorded footage.
“Tawakalitu Restaurant management reportedly confirmed that a DPO returned the CCTV equipment, but the recordings had been completely wiped. The management refused to identify the officer responsible for returning the equipment. This is an indication of a coordinated cover-up by the police hierarchy in Ekiti State,” he said.
The latest allegations came three days after Mr Sowore accused suspected political thugs of attacking him and members of his team in Ado-Ekiti. The Ekiti State Police Command had disputed his account, describing the incident as an “altercation” with some individuals at a restaurant.
In an earlier statement, the police command said officers rescued Mr Sowore after receiving information about the incident and that he sustained minor injuries. The command also said the Commissioner of Police, Michael Falade, had ordered a discreet investigation to establish what happened and identify those responsible.
Mr Sowore said he contacted Mr Falade, the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) of Ado-Ekiti Central Police Station, Mustapha Mohammed, and the Rapid Response Squad commander to request an update on the investigation.
He claimed the officers told him there was no complainant because he had not submitted a written statement.
Mr Sowore questioned this explanation, arguing that the police had already intervened in the incident.
“The officers claimed there was “no complainant” because I had not submitted a written statement, despite police rescuing the victims, taking them to their hospital, arresting suspects, and recovering weapons, stolen phones, and other devices,” he said.
Mr Sowore called on the police and the SSS to release the CCTV footage from the restaurant, saying it could help establish what happened during the incident.
He also demanded the removal of the state Commissioner of Police and other officers he accused of mishandling the investigation.
PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Ekiti State Police Command’s Public Relations Officer (PPRO), Sunday Abutu, by phone to seek his response to the allegations. However, he asked the reporter to call back in the afternoon.
“I will get back to you, please,” he said. “Call me around 12:00 p.m.”

title: Europe’s Coffin Makers Face “Death Knell” as Cheap Chinese Imports Surge
body: The trade tensions between the European Union and China have reached an unexpected sector: coffins. After disputes over electric vehicles, steel and other industrial goods, European coffin manufacturers are preparing a formal anti-dumping complaint with the European Commission. They argue that low-priced Chinese imports are threatening the survival of their businesses. Industry under severe pressure According to consultant Folco Ciulli, who is coordinating the complaint, the number of coffin manufacturers across Europe has fallen from roughly 120 to 90 in the past five years—meaning about one in four companies has closed. Smaller factories were hit hardest, unable to match imported prices. The remaining producers have absorbed only about half of the output lost when the others shut down. The core issue is the cost gap. European manufacturers estimate that a coffin can be produced in China for about one-third the cost of an equivalent product in Italy, even when similar timber is used. They point to lower wages, cheaper raw materials, possible state subsidies and export-related tax advantages as the main reasons. Some reports cite production costs of around €260 in Italy versus roughly €80 in China, allowing Chinese coffins to be sold in Europe for €100–110. The unexplained 30,000-coffin gap Beyond prices, producers are examining an anomaly in the Italian market. Mathematician Emiliano Ingusio, commissioned by the sector, identified a discrepancy equivalent to about 30,000 coffins a year. The figure comes from comparing domestic production, imports, exports and consumption. Because coffin demand is tightly linked to the number of deaths—which can be calculated with reasonable precision—the gap has raised questions about how some imports are being recorded. Suspected “IKEA loophole” and other practices Manufacturers suspect that some Chinese coffins enter Europe without being properly classified as finished coffins. One practice under scrutiny has been nicknamed the “IKEA loophole”: products arrive flat-packed or in pieces, declared as wooden components, and are later assembled and sold as complete coffins. Another possible method involves declaring coffins as packaging or containers for other goods. These remain suspicions rather than proven customs violations. The European Commission has noted that, under international rules, an unassembled product can still be treated as complete for customs purposes if it has the essential characteristics of the finished item. What is required for duties The newly formed coalition (which previously lacked dedicated lobby representation) has already held talks with European Commission officials and is assembling a formal file. Proving that Chinese products are cheaper is not sufficient. To obtain anti-dumping duties, manufacturers must demonstrate three things: Chinese products are sold in the EU below their normal value European producers are suffering material injury There is a clear causal link between the imports and the industry’s losses The Commission has declined to confirm specific contacts, stating that such discussions are confidential. It has pointed out that the EU already maintains more than 200 trade defence measures and launched 32 new investigations in 2025. In January, duties of 56–60% were imposed on Chinese candles. A traditional sector now in the spotlight The case illustrates how the broader EU-China trade dispute has moved beyond high-tech and heavy industry into long-established manufacturing sectors with relatively predictable demand. European coffin makers, facing a market that continues to grow with population trends but is under intense price pressure, are now seeking protection through the EU’s trade defence tools. title: Sharjah Design Centre to open in 2029 with seven labs to test and develop products
body: A new design institution featuring specialist laboratories and production facilities is set to open in Sharjah in 2029, with the aim of helping designers turn experimental ideas into commercially viable products. Sharjah Design Centre, led by Sheikha Hind bint Majid Al Qasimi, will be one of the main institutions within Sharjah Creative Quarter , a cultural district being developed near the House of Wisdom and University City of Sharjah. The plans, announced on Monday, include seven laboratories dedicated to textiles, rapid prototyping, glass, ceramics, jewellery, metal and wood. The centre will also feature private studios, co-working areas, exhibition spaces, a retail outlet, a Material Library and a Digital Archive. “Promising ideas often remain at the research stage because the infrastructure to develop and realise them is not readily accessible,” Sheikha Hind says. “Sharjah Design Centre will change that and give designers a place to research, test and realise their ideas with the expertise, resources and collaboration opportunities to take them all the way into production.” The facilities will provide designers, researchers and entrepreneurs with equipment and technical expertise, while the library and archive will document material research and information about local manufacturing capabilities. Exploring Sharjah's local materials Although the centre will not open until 2029, several research projects are already under way. Among them is Theatrum Al Kimiya, developed with Atelier LUMA, a research programme based in Arles, France. The project is investigating the potential of locally sourced and discarded materials, including salt, sand, clay, palm, shells, wool, ceramic waste and demolition waste, for use in design and construction. Researchers are also exploring mycelium, the root-like network of fungi, building on earlier studies into traditional crafts and material innovation by Sharjah's Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council. The centre is collaborating with the American University of Sharjah on material testing and certification. It is also working with the university and Sharjah Economic Department to map the emirate's manufacturing capabilities and connect designers with local industry. Its educational programme will include workshops, masterclasses, residencies and professional development opportunities for emerging designers. Part of wider creative district Sharjah Design Centre will be among several institutions housed within Sharjah Creative Quarter, which is also scheduled to open in 2029. Established by Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, and chaired by Sheikha Hoor bint Sultan Al Qasimi, the district will bring together initiatives spanning art, fashion, crafts and cultural heritage. These include Irthi Museum , Sharjah Fashion Lab, Qasimi Archives , the Sheikha Jawaher bint Mohammed Al Qasimi Collection and L'ecole, School of Jewelry Arts, supported by Van Cleef & Arpels . Sharjah Design Centre has been designed by Mexican architectural practice Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha in collaboration with Spanish architect Daniel Rossello. The building will combine traditional design principles with modern technology, incorporating rammed earth construction to reduce its environmental impact. Established by Emiri Decree in 2025, Sharjah Design Centre forms part of the emirate's broader efforts to strengthen its creative industries by connecting local talent with research, manufacturing and commercial opportunities.

title: Stuck in shelters, some migrant kids lose hope of staying in U.S.
body: One morning this summer, a 9-year-old girl from El Salvador picked through colorful markers at a Houston-area shelter for migrant children and crafted a letter to her mom."I want to be with you already," the little girl, M.R., wrote in misspelled, unpunctuated Spanish, adding hearts, a rainbow, and a large "I love you" surrounded by pink and blue dots. "I miss you a lot, mami I love you a lot mami I want to be with you."The girl had begged to leave the government-run shelter where she had been held for more than seven months, an attorney for the child said. She'd become distraught, telling her mom on the phone that she felt sad and lonely, that she desperately wanted a hug, that she was getting nosebleeds and thought she had an infection.Meanwhile, as her mother, Carmen, was going through the process to regain custody, federal immigration officials instead arrested her, sending her to a Louisiana detention center though she had a pending asylum case and no criminal record."Both of us are trapped," Carmen said in a September interview from the detention center. "She's just a helpless little girl. The process shouldn't be like this." KFF Health News is using only the mother's first name and daughter's initials, because they fear government reprisal for sharing their story.As of September, the 9-year-old was among almost 1,900 children being held at shelters overseen by the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Refugee Resettlement, which was tasked by Congress over a decade ago with looking after unaccompanied children to separate their care from immigration enforcement.Instead, the second Trump administration has reconfigured the resettlement office to aid its deportation campaign. This includes holding children rather than reuniting them with family in the United States, and often using them to ensnare family members, according to interviews with families, lawyers, and child advocates, as well as reviews of court documents. Many children in the office's care are fleeing violence or abuse in their home countries.Previously, the resettlement office attempted to prioritize the well-being of children in its care, said Jonathan White, a former federal health official who ran the office's unaccompanied children program for part of President Trump's first term. The office is legally required to place children "in the least restrictive setting" and release them "without unnecessary delay," usually to a vetted parent or other family member who is willing to care for them.Now children in the office's custody have become collateral damage as the administration seeks to advance its larger immigration policy goals, said White, a licensed clinical social worker. He said the administration is deliberately reshaping the nation's shelter system for unaccompanied minors from a child welfare program into a detention program that encourages immigrants to leave the country.Although fewer kids are now held in the office's shelters than in past years, those who remain often find themselves trapped for months with no clear way out other than to enter long-term foster care or return to the dangerous conditions they fled, attorneys said. That's because their potential guardians get detained themselves or are afraid or unable to complete the sponsorship process. Often, attorneys said, the office refuses to release the children even when sponsorship requirements are met, and they have to sue for the kids' release."When a child sees no way out of detention, voluntary departure may no longer feel like a real choice," U.S. Rep. Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.) said during an Oct. 1 news conference calling attention to the administration's changes to the unaccompanied children program.The Department of Homeland Security did not directly answer questions sent by KFF Health News but framed detentions of migrant children's sponsors by Immigration and Customs Enforcement as part of an effort to prevent kids from being harmed. A federal watchdog in 2024 found that the resettlement office didn't properly screen sponsors amid a surge of unaccompanied children during President Joe Biden's term, and news reports have documented incidents of children being exploited after their release from the agency's custody.In an unsigned email, DHS reiterated previous statements that "ICE does not separate families" and that the administration is working to locate 450,000 unaccompanied children that came during the Biden administration. It said many of the children were placed with unvetted sponsors who were smugglers and sex traffickers, a claim that has been disputed. It provided a list of 16 cases in which sponsors were arrested in connection with serious crimes, including the rape of an unaccompanied child, drug trafficking, and homicide. KFF Health News also sent questions to HHS about the case and the resettlement office's treatment of unaccompanied minors. The agency did not respond.From child welfare to detentionM.R. spent about two weeks traveling to the U.S. late last year with her older sister, wading across the Rio Grande before being detained by Border Patrol officers in Texas, according to case documents. The sisters hoped to join their mother and a brother who had fled El Salvador a few years earlier and were living in Tennessee. Gang members murdered M.R.'s father, her uncle, and a pregnant cousin, according to Carmen, who feared for her daughter's safety, too. M.R.'s maternal grandmother in El Salvador hit her and her sister with a belt and open hand while caring for them, M.R. later told a social worker.Like others arriving in the U.S. alone and without legal status, the girl and her older sister landed in a shelter thinking they would be out in days. Before Mr. Trump's second term, children typically waited in the resettlement office's custody for about a month while federal officials screened their relatives or other sponsors. M.R.'s brother, who arrived in the U.S. in 2024, said he stayed in a shelter for 11 days.The second Trump administration is arresting parents and other trusted caregivers who have come forward to get children released, has created onerous new requirements for sponsors, and has installed a former immigration official with experience in law enforcement as the head of the resettlement office. Average stays stretched to nearly six months, with some like M.R. staying much longer, even when they have qualified sponsors.Alvaro Huerta of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center said during a July news briefing that a 3-year-old remained in the resettlement office's custody for 300 days. A 6-year-old girl remained in custody for seven months, Huerta said, after her father was detained while being vetted as a sponsor and then deported. When the mother arrived at an appointment in March to reunite with the girl, he said, they were sent together to an immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas, that has drawn criticism from Democratic lawmakers, advocates, and families who have reported inhumane conditions.Immigration lawyers say the administration has undermined legal protections for migrant kids while simultaneously fast-tracking deportation. Children, including some as young as 1, are appearing before immigration judges alone because of administration disruptions to legal services. In some cases, immigration officials are detaining kids after they have been placed with sponsors and are already living in their communities. The administration has also offered children, including M.R., payments of at least $2,500 if they agree to return to their home countries voluntarily.M.R.'s sister was released when she turned 18, three weeks after her arrival. Courts have blocked the Trump administration's attempts to transfer to immigration detention people who turn 18 while in the resettlement office's custody. That left young M.R. on her own in a new country, without her mom, her twin older siblings, or other close family.Family separationIn April, Carmen went to a DNA test appointment, which she was told was the last step she needed to secure her daughter's release. KFF Health News reviewed a text confirming the appointment at a DHS office. She thought she would soon be reunited with her youngest child. By then she had already presented her tax and salary information, submitted fingerprints, and been visited at home by a social worker. She and her teens prepared the little girl's bedroom, adorning it with a Hello Kitty bed cover, "Frozen" curtains, and a lamp that projects stars and astronauts on the ceiling. They showed it to M.R. on a video call. She was excited, her brother said.Without a warrant, immigration officers detained Carmen at the appointment. The resettlement office subsequently rejected her sponsorship application, citing the detention it had helped facilitate.The girl was crushed. "She doesn't have an understanding of why she's stuck there and why the government would detain her mom instead of reuniting them," said Alexa Sendukas, managing attorney with the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, which is representing the girl. "Our government has completely failed them and has treated them in a way no human being should ever be treated."DHS declined to comment on a description of the case of Carmen and her daughter. The agency said it could comment only if it had the names, dates of birth, and noncitizen identification numbers of the people involved."When the media refuses to give names, it makes it impossible to provide details on specific cases or even verify any of this even happened or that the people even exist. If you can't do your job, we can't do ours," the agency's press office responded, without providing the name of a spokesperson as requested.Reports from the Houston-area shelter show that the girl received counseling. She was not diagnosed with any mental health conditions, though the therapist reported she was sad and cried while discussing her long shelter stay and missing her mom.Carmen, who talked to her daughter on the phone about three times a week, said the child was struggling. The girl blamed herself, Sendukas said.Every phone call, M.R. would ask her mom when she'd be released and when they'd be together again. She complained of feeling unwell. She lamented having no one to hug or comfort her, despite all the bad news she'd received, her mom said."I felt like the worst mother in the world, because I couldn't explain to my daughter what was happening, what they'd done to me," Carmen said.Situations like M.R.'s are indicative of the resettlement office's shift to prioritizing immigration enforcement over children's well-being, White said."There is no scenario ever where it's in the best interest of the child to tell them you're going to release them to their mom, and prepare them for that, and then use their planned unification as a pretext to apprehend the mom," he said.Sural Shah, part of a team of physicians with the American Academy of Pediatrics who have visited several shelters for migrant children over the past year, said many are developing mental illnesses due to prolonged shelter stays."It's heartbreaking," Shah said, adding that kids are exhibiting anxiety, depression, and stress disorders, leading them to regress developmentally, act out, and harm themselves. Some wet their beds, experience chest pains, or cry out at night. Being stuck in a shelter for months can have long-term health effects like post-traumatic stress disorder, she added.Some distressed children have also attempted suicide, said Mickey Donovan-Kaloust, legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, which has offices across Southern California.A teenage brother and sister from Venezuela who spent more than a year in a different federal shelter in Texas told KFF Health News that during their stay, they barely left the building and had to follow a rigid routine. The academic lessons they received at the shelter repeated every month, they said, and meals were the same each week. They also complained that they got reprimanded for small things like laughing too loud or having water fights.When their father was detained during his sponsorship process, the girl stopped eating for days, she said. She showed symptoms of PTSD.The boy said the experience wore him down mentally and emotionally."I was a broken kid," he said. "I didn't know whether to laugh when I got bad news, I didn't know whether to cry." An excruciating choiceIn detention, Carmen received a deportation order and faced an unthinkable choice: leave her youngest child behind in long-term foster care or return to potentially deadly conditions in El Salvador together, leaving her teens in the United States. Although gang violence is down in the country, Carmen said the people who killed her family members and threatened to kill her are still active in her old neighborhood.It's the kind of choice that immigrant families across the country are facing daily, said Jennifer Podkul, chief of global policy and advocacy at Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that represents kids in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody.In July, Carmen decided she could no longer bear her youngest daughter's distress. They asked to leave together.The mom could have appealed her deportation order but was worried about the mental health toll, Sendukas said. Carmen said her daughter told her: "I don't want to feel alone again like I did at Christmas, like I did on Mother's Day, and for your birthday. All of those days I've felt so alone. I don't want to go on like this."In mid-September, three weeks before her 10th birthday and 281 days after she arrived in the U.S., the daughter was sent with her mother to El Salvador. The child's older siblings remain in the U.S. fighting their own asylum cases without their mother. The brother dropped out of high school in Tennessee and, along with his twin sister, moved to live with a relative."I just hope other people understand that we're all fighting for something," he said. "We were fighting to be together. It wasn't a dream that hurt anyone."Jazmin Orozco Rodriguez contributed to this report.KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Apartment building damaged in Russian drone attack on Vinnytsia
body:
According to Ukrinform, Vinnytsia Deputy Mayor Roman Furman reported this on Facebook .
"One of the apartment buildings in Vinnytsia was damaged in the enemy attack on November 2. As of 10:30, windows had been blown out in ten apartments," Furman wrote.
He said a municipal council commission was working at the scene. Specialists will document the damage so residents can receive compensation under the government's eRecovery program, as well as financial assistance from the community budget.
At the same time, teams from property management companies are beginning work at the site. They will carry out urgent repairs: the damaged windows will be covered with plastic sheeting today and, if necessary, OSB boards.
Meanwhile, initial repair work is nearing completion in the Vyshenka neighborhood, which was damaged on November 1. By the evening, windows in 61 apartments had been covered. The same work has now also been completed in common areas of ten buildings.
As reported, in the early hours of November 1, drone debris damaged 17 buildings in Vinnytsia and a car was burned.

title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
body:
All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.
A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.
The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.
In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.
The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.
“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”
Hidden Behavior
Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.
“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.
Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.
This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.
Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.
“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”
Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.
One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”
DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)
Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.
“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.
Chinese Origins
Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.
The apps and domains across the network have often used generic privacy policies, free email addresses from Gmail or Outlook, and obscure developer names as part of their alleged efforts to hide their connections. Ads for the apps posted on Meta’s platforms have also used apparently false names—such as Draftmondcreldbro Duhustepre and Swaldmungsha Glasirdcroldshold—and pages with no followers. Since the start of this year, Bouchaud’s research has found tens of thousands of explicit deepfake ads linked to the network—often using similar language in their advertising copy—on Meta’s platforms.
“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.
KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.
Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.
When WIRED contacted KeLing email addresses, plus some of those listed in apps privacy policies, we received no response. However, after WIRED reached out, someone renamed some of the associated online social media channels, removed KeLing email addresses from the AI Veyra website, and removed the KeLing Technology Limited address from the first registered website.
Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.
After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.
“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.
As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.

title: Press review: Moscow and Kiev positive on Alyoshki truce as Lavrov attends G20 in US
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Russia and Ukraine conclude their Alyoshki ceasefire, while Russia’s top diplomat Sergey Lavrov takes part in the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta. Meanwhile, a power struggle over control of Poland’s Constitutional Court breaks out. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines in Russia.
The mission in Alyoshki has "successfully concluded," Russian ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said. Humanitarian aid was delivered to Alyoshki residents, and those who chose to leave the dangerous town did so. They have already been accommodated in south Russia’s Krasnodar Region, with some receiving medical assistance. The evacuees said many of them literally ate grass and lived under incessant Ukrainian aerial attacks for days over the past few days. The humanitarian ceasefire officially ended at 11:59 p.m. Moscow time (8:59 p.m. GMT) on November 1, but Lantratova did not rule out organizing new missions to help those remaining in the town leave. Washington, Kiev and Moscow have acknowledged the success of the campaign. It could create a positive backdrop for reviving trilateral peace talks, experts say.
"Our troops have accomplished all tasks as part of the humanitarian operation. The Ukrainian army was only required to keep quiet and not to open fire," military expert Viktor Litovkin told Izvestia. It was the Ukrainian army that blockaded the town by mining all roads leading to it with drones, which ultimately created a challenging humanitarian situation there, he recalled.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who mediated the ceasefire agreement, was satisfied with the results of the mission and expressed hope that it would help resolve the Ukraine conflict and "become the starting point for lasting peace."
The localized ceasefire in Alyoshki could pave the way for further humanitarian operations, Denis Denisov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, argued. According to him, another humanitarian ceasefire under international monitoring could take place at the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), which would help establish a safe zone for personnel rotation and reduce nuclear risks.
In the event of victory in the November 3 congressional election, US President Donald Trump could show greater interest in targeted humanitarian initiatives, researcher at the Institute of CIS Countries Alexander Dudchak told Izvestia.
The successful completion of the Alyoshki operation will create a positive backdrop for reviving trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, experts argue. However, the humanitarian and political tracks between Russia and Ukraine obviously run in parallel, so one should not expect any automatic progress in the peace process. Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov stressed earlier that the upcoming round of talks in Abu Dhabi following a lengthy pause will be "a trial meeting."
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to the United States for the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta showed that Washington and Moscow have been making little headway on Ukraine and have yet to tackle key issues. However, the positive sign is that America is still trying to act as a mediator, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. According to him, this is reflected in more constructive remarks from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "Against this background, Patriot supplies to Ukraine have been approved, but this should be considered in the context of long-term allied obligations. They are also trying to involve Russia in the diplomatic orbit," the expert noted. In the US understanding, Russia will remain a threat anyway, he explained, but the approach to relations with it is that risks must be reduced. The other issues, including the diesel deal announced by Trump on his Truth Social media platform on October 9, are linked to whether the Ukraine crisis will be resolved, the expert pointed out.
In this context, it cannot be said that Lavrov’s trip was related exclusively to bilateral relations between Russia and the United States, as the agenda was centered around issues facing the G20.
"However, Ukraine remains a key issue for the two countries. And no progress is in sight here. And it will be difficult for the Trump administration to pursue a constructive policy course in the next two years. In other words, the bilateral agenda remains hostage to the Ukraine crisis," Koshkin concluded. The difficulties in relations between Europe and the US do not alter the fact that Washington will have to take Brussels’ opinion on Ukraine into account, he added.
Among other things, Lavrov held talks with Rubio on the sidelines of the G20 meeting, the Russian foreign minister said at a news conference on October 30. The two top diplomats discussed "bilateral relations and interaction at multilateral venues, including the UN, the G20 and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, which is set to hold a summit in China’s Shenzhen in November soon," Lavrov said. While in Atlanta, he also held talks with his Japanese counterpart, Toshimistu Motegi, marking the first meeting with a top Japanese diplomat in several years.
Lavrov arrived in Atlanta for the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on October 30. The two-day meeting that concluded on October 31 became a key event ahead of the G20 Leaders’ Summit scheduled to be held in Miami in mid-December.
On Friday night, Poland came to the brink of a coup as a dispute broke out between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki, supported by the Law and Justice (PiS) party, over control of the Constitutional Tribunal, the republic’s supreme constitutional court.
Last weekend, Nawrocki held consultations with political forces, but a way out of the crisis is still not on the horizon as the conflicting sides continued to accuse each other of attempting a coup and abusing power. Lawyers are at a crossroads as the current situation extends beyond the existing laws, and neither solution has any legal basis. The key paradox is that the body tasked with resolving disputes is at the epicenter of the dispute.
Many Poles view the developments as a power struggle between politicians who have gone too far. "What is happening is living proof of how a serious state can start morphing into a banana republic sooner than anyone expected," Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Polish lawyer Marcin Matczak as saying. "All it takes is for politicians from the two most influential forces to decide that a violent confrontation could earn them more brownie points politically than compliance with laws," he argued. "The whole situation reflects a deeply divided society and a weak political class," the newspaper Fakt reported. According to it, "the current Polish political elites care neither about the state, nor about democracy, or about citizens."
The current situation around the Constitutional Tribunal reflects a long-standing conflict in Poland between the liberals, led by Tusk, and the country’s national-conservatives, led by PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, Dmitry Bunevich, an advisor to the director of the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, explained to Vedomosti . Both Tusk and Nawrocki are using this conflict to rally their respective electorates ahead of the upcoming elections to Sejm, scheduled for next fall. While Nawrocki has managed to strengthen his position as the leader of the right-wing camp, a snap election is unlikely; and Tusk holds a majority in the Sejm and has no interest in such a scenario, Bunevich argued.
Tusk sought to demonstrate his strength, relying, among other things, on verdicts by European courts, Stanislav Kuvaldin, researcher at the European Union Research Sector at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO RAS), said. Tusk’s actions have led to the unification of right-wing forces, including those that previously had strained relations with one another, in Poland. In this light, Nawrocki is indeed strengthening his position as he has emerged as a leader of the right-wing camp - a significant development ahead of the elections due to take place a year from now, the expert told Vedomosti. According to Kuvaldin, protests may also continue, and even if an overhauled Tribunal begins its work, half of the political parties and a large segment of Polish society will simply refuse to recognize its legitimacy.
The seven OPEC+ countries once again put adjustments to their output policy on hold, agreeing to leave their December targets unchanged at the levels set in September. Despite rising production and exports through the Strait of Hormuz, the core oil-producing countries, including Russia, continue to produce below their assigned quotas. The alliance may resume output increases in the spring of 2027, provided its forecast of growing crude demand proves accurate.
At a meeting on November 1, the seven OPEC+ countries agreed to keep their December output quotas unchanged at the levels set in September, according to the organization’s decision. As a result, production levels have remained unchanged for four consecutive months. The OPEC+ producers raised their collective oil production quotas by 188,000 barrels per day (bpd) between June and September.
The decision to maintain current oil output levels was largely expected in a situation where supply volumes remain below the established limits and the market is paying less attention to OPEC+ decisions than to how the conflict in the Middle East evolves, Open Oil Market Director General Sergey Teryoshkin told Kommersant. According to him, the current level of quotas will likely remain unchanged until the end of 2026, and future decisions will depend on when and how the Middle East conflict is resolved.
OPEC+ may resume easing its output curbs next spring, before the peak season begins, if incoming data support its forecast for oil demand in 2026-2027, Andrey Polishchuk, senior oil and gas industry analyst at Euler, argued. OPEC expects global oil consumption to increase by 200,000 bpd in 2026 and by as much as 2.6 million bpd in 2027.
The Binance hack and a record $6.3 billion heist sent Bitcoin prices tumbling to $76,000. The crypto firm was hacked after its infrastructure was compromised, experts said. This means that Russian crypto custodians will have to implement multi-layered security measures, including cold wallets, key distribution and multi-signature protocols, to safeguard client funds when full-scale trading opens on the Russian cryptocurrency market. Such security measures will require significant investment from market players, meaning only a few of them will be able to build robust infrastructure.
A major decline in Bitcoin prices began on the night of October 29 after reports of the Binance hack emerged. Binance reported a heist of about $6.3 billion. "That could potentially be the largest heist ever in the history of cryptocurrencies," Shard, a Russian platform for assessing digital asset risks, noted. The downturn was further fueled by a massive outflow from ETFs that reached $643 million on October 30.
The Binance hack shows that "neither the scale of the company nor its billions of dollars’ worth of investment in security guarantees complete protection for its assets," Alexander Peresichan, CEO of Tehnobit Systems, told Kommersant .
Should the withdrawal of funds remain blocked longer than the stated period, the risk of a large-scale client exodus will increase, Managing Director of the Investment Business Development Department at Sberbank Roman Kozhura warned in an interview with Vedomosti .
The incident will likely prompt further scrutiny of the safety of Binance’s internal systems by the US Department of Justice and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Kirill Komalenkov, director for strategic communications at Bitbanker, argued.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: [Rappler’s Best] America, your turn
body: The past week thrilled liberals and leftists across the world as elections in three polarized countries stemmed the march of the far-right in Latin America, demonstrated student power in Europe , and humbled Benjamin Netanyahu. These polls have been hard fought, but the post-election transitions will be doubly harder. Crying fraud but also facing corruption charges back home, Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate, has fled to the US into the welcoming arms of his patron, US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro can stay in America for as long as he wants, Trump said. His father, Jair, a former president, is in jail in Brazil . Running on an anti-corruption wave, Serbia’s student protest movement managed to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election, but now comes the hard part of governing. For starters, the student leaders have called for the resignation of top public officials and investigations into alleged corruption under Vucic. In Israel, the far-right continues to dominate, but did not come out solidly for Netanyahu, whose party lost the majority in parliament. Without any bloc enjoying majority numbers, however, he will likely serve as caretaker prime minister. How could Israel break an election deadlock? Here’s an explainer . And so we turn to the next logical question: what will America show the rest of the world this week? The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as Trump enters the last two years of his term. Here are things to know . If you’re a liberal and listened to pollster Nate Silver’s interview with Ezra Klein (as I did), you’d be expecting a “momentous” turnaround — a more than 70% chance for Democrats in the Senate — that could flip Congress against Trump. If the results reflect what he’s seeing in his polling, Silver said these would effectively end the Trump era . The Economist has more conservative numbers. While conceding that the “auguries are good for Democrats,” it’s putting the probability of the US Senate going to the Democrats at just 54%. But the White House is already crafting a path to govern without Congress in case Democrats win, according to a Reuters report . These are the races that will decide control of the US Senate, and the key seats that could shape the next House. The campaign period has been reminiscent of traditional tactics in Philippine elections, writes Filipino-American Oscar Quiambao in this piece . There have been concerns about Republican efforts to delay the vote counts and intimidate voters. And let’s not forget that Trump himself offered $5,000 to every American if Republicans win. There are four ways foreign policy could change if Democrats win this week. This also marks the first elections in the US where voters have been relying on chatbots to guide them. It’s a cautionary tale. A study showed almost 40% of chatbots’ replies to election-related queries contained at least one factual error. Read more . The flood of AI-driven disinformation has been unprecedented, according to this story , which cites one instance when the Democrat running for US Senate in Texas (a Republican base), James Talarico, had to take time off from campaigning due to flu. A fake video about him supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio went viral. Russia is apparently fueling fake reports about Democrats, according to an intelligence briefing that US lawmakers received. Read more . Outside the US, in Brazil, AI content bypassed election rules — a lesson for the Philippines, writes Alex Culla in this story . As Trump spent the past days doing his final push for a Republican win, his defense chief Pete Hegseth flew to Cebu for the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting. There, the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro, snubbed the Chinese defense attaché who ranked lower than him. Bea Cupin gives us a recap of the meeting in this report . On another note, we extend our deepest condolences to the family of Philip Juico, who died on October 31 after years of battling cancer. Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss: JC Punongbayan spells out what we can do as the peso continues its steep decline. Watch Shay Du’s take on it here . James Patrick Cruz shows how to track insertions in the House-approved 2027 budget. There’s pork barrel everywhere, writes JC Punongbayan . Lance Spencer Yu lists the adjustments that businesses need to make to regain customers dealing with high prices and a weak peso. Isagani de Castro Jr. tells us why 2 Valid IDs is on track to make Philippine film history. Joey Salgado writes that Dutertismo will be on the ballot in the 2028 elections — even if Sara Duterte is disqualified from running. Paterno Esmaquel II reminds us how Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla dropped the ball on fugitive Senator Bato dela Rosa. It’s Macacua: BARMM Parliament picks region’s first elected chief minister Maharlika Fund’s NGCP deal collapses nearly 2 years after Marcos’ blessing LIST: Evidence submitted by prosecution to impeach court vs Sara Duterte El Niño-ready? These infrastructures in Quezon City collect rainwater 68 GB of stolen PH gov’t data found online, says cybersecurity firm Rappler’s Best is a weekly Rappler+ exclusive newsletter of our top picks delivered straight to your inbox every Monday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe. The views expressed by the writer are his/her own and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Rappler .

title: Republicans are privately blaming Trump, even if they won’t say it out loud
body: Republicans are already privately blaming President Donald Trump as they brace for losses on Tuesday. Even as they race to distance themselves from his actions on tariffs, the unpopular Iran war and his mass deportation agenda, few have been willing to criticize him publicly — a clear sign of just how powerful Trump's grip remains on the GOP. But interviews with roughly a dozen candidates, campaign officials and lawmakers reveal they're acutely aware of who, exactly, put them on the back foot this entire cycle. "There was a point earlier this year where we really felt like we could defy history," said one House Republican, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to candidly discuss midterms dynamics. "And then Trump bombed Iran. And it was just one thing after another.” Republicans are tied or trailing in polls in numerous critical battlegrounds and expecting to lose some once-secure red seats. And Trump's unfocused closing message — including repeated comments about male candidates' physical appearances — has further frustrated an already on-edge party. “I think Jon Husted's ass and Nicki Minaj's is a great closing message,” T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist working on the South Carolina Senate race and others, said sarcastically in an interview on The Conversation with Dasha Burns . “You’ve got to take the good with the bad with Trump, unless you want to drive yourself crazy every day.” “People are gonna go after the president. The buck stops with him. His approval ratings aren't great,” he added. Privately, some Republicans are even harsher. “At least when Barack Obama was president, he only screwed his enemies, never his friends,” said a second House Republican. The White House defended its involvement in the war with Iran, tariff regime and approach to immigration enforcement. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Trump “is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” One White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the blame game “an asinine adventure” and said Trump “has obviously left it all on the field.” If the bottom falls out for the GOP on Tuesday, the quiet calls assigning him blame may turn into a public shanking as Trump nears the lame-duck stage of his presidency, Republicans refocus on how to win voters back for 2028 and jostle for their own spots in the party’s future. “I'm not sure what the Republican Party looks like in six months. Look, a lot of Republicans have held their tongues. A lot of Republicans who have real problems with the way things have gone the last two years have been good soldiers,” said a Republican strategist involved in competitive midterm races across the country. “But what happens if we lose 35 House seats and six Senate seats?” “We all know who the problem is. It’s Trump. And do we continue down a path of losing?” the strategist added. In Georgia, some Republicans have already warned that low early voting turnout in rural parts of the state could drag down their entire ticket. "If you live in rural Georgia, you're going to be disproportionately hurt by higher — especially diesel — prices,” said Jason Shepherd, the former GOP chair of suburban Cobb County. “The promise of the great Trump economy has not materialized." Top Hill Republicans have worked behind the scenes for months to try to alleviate some of the political fallout from Trump’s election year policy moves, including arguing to White House officials that Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers could lose their races if the administration didn’t reach an off-ramp from the trade war with Canada, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the matter. Eventually, Trump agreed to roll back some tariffs and add new ones in a boost to Collins. Republicans also pressed for the White House to undo some of Trump’s other controversial moves, like his executive order to import more foreign beef that has riled ranchers and farmers in red states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas. But that relief never came. "Republicans have always been aware of the historical midterm precedent, and that's why we're barnstorming the country to tout the president's achievements on cutting taxes, securing the border, and lowering drug costs,” said Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. “Any anonymous strategist who says the president is not helpful in turning out Republican voters has no idea what they're talking about, and their candidates should request a refund for their shoddy consulting services." But Trump’s actions, Republicans say, are hitting different parts of the country hard. The Iran war, they argue, was a significant blunder from Trump that has multiplied Democrats’ paths to power in both the House and Senate by driving fuel and fertilizer costs up — most notably impacting races across the Midwest. The White House’s tariffs regime has been a major concern in battlegrounds on the Canadian border like Maine and Michigan. Hardline immigration enforcement that has resulted in the deportation of thousands has hurt especially in heavily Latino border states like Arizona and Texas, and the cancelling of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Venezuelans has enraged South Florida voters. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Miami Republican, warned the president in a campaign ad earlier this year that his immigration tactics had gone too far. “Trump won Miami, and yet he went to the place that gave him the biggest support, and kind of just fucked everybody over if we're being honest.” said one Florida-based Republican operative. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Republican midterm voters are split over who they would blame if the GOP performs worse than it did in 2024: A sizable 29% blame Trump for making the GOP less popular, while 30% said it is because Trump himself is not on the ballot. Fourteen percent said it would be because the Democratic Party has become more popular, while roughly one in four said they don’t know. Some in the party question whether Trump’s last-minute campaign travel across the country and the millions of dollars his political operation has poured into battleground states will even be enough. They see him as more absorbed in protecting his legacy than making actionable policy changes to help his party stay in power. “He cares more about the ballroom than he cares about Republicans winning the midterms,” said a third Republican strategist working in battleground races. “He wants the Nobel Peace Prize, these big legacy-defining things seem to be taking up more of his attention than actually being president.” A fourth GOP operative working on midterms races has a curt message if Republicans lose big: “Thank you, Donald Trump." Dasha Burns contributed reporting.

title: 6 things to watch for on election night
body:
People walk by a sign for voting on November 1, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. Michigan has become a focal point in the upcoming midterm elections, with a close race between Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI), and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that could decide who controls the chamber. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
It can be hard to know what to focus on in midterm elections. There are so many races, from elections for governor and senator to the House and state legislatures. For a better idea of how the night might go to see which party might control Congress, here are six things to watch:
There are two states, Indiana and Kentucky, that will see results in the 6 p.m. ET hour. And then there's Florida, which is split between the Eastern and Central time zones. But most of the state is on Eastern time. So lots of House race results will be coming in during the 7 p.m. ET hour, even if statewide contests like the Senate and governors races won't be called at the earliest until 8 p.m. ET.
Some races to watch for early indicators of what might come later in the evening — Indiana's 5th Congressional District, Kentucky's 6th and Florida's 22nd and 27th. Indiana's 5th and Kentucky's 6th are seats held by Republicans that are more competitive now than at the beginning of the cycle. If these are close or tipping to Democrats, it could be a sign of low Republican turnout and a bigger Democratic wave.
Florida's 22nd is held by a Democrat but redrawn to tip in Republicans' favor. Trump won Florida's 27th by double-digits so this heavily Latino district could be an indicator of how this key subgroup votes.
Independents are a key swing group, but they are also a lower-propensity voting group in midterms.
It used to be that Republicans had to win a bigger share of independents before the Trump era. Mitt Romney, for example, won 55% of independents in 2012 but lost the presidential election. But there's been a political realignment in this country with blue-collar white voters trending toward Trump, fewer people identifying as Democrats and better-educated white voters shifting toward Democrats.
So in the decade since Trump has been on the political scene, Republicans have done well when they win at least 46% of independents. When they haven't, they've lost.
The Michigan Senate race is important for control of the Senate. If Republicans flip it, the magic number for Democrats goes from four to five, meaning Democrats would have to win five seats held by Republicans to win control of the Senate.
For Abdul El-Sayed (D) to win in Michigan, a key is going to be Black voters in Wayne County. If he runs up the score in and around Detroit, he has a path to victory, but if he doesn't, it becomes that much harder — and it's been an area of vulnerability for him.
During the Trump era, Democrats have needed 68% or more in Wayne County to win Michigan unless, like Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024, they can overperform in the suburbs.
Wayne County Democratic margins 2024 Slotkin 63% Win (11% share) 2024 Harris 62% Loss 2020 Biden 68% Win (12%) 2020 Peters 68% Win 2018 Stabenow 69% Win (15%) 2016 Clinton 66% Loss (13%)
Voters 18 to 29 see a drastic drop off in turnout between presidential and midterm elections. During presidential races since 1992, 43% of registered young voters cast ballots. But in midterms, that falls to 21%, just 1 in 5 who show up at the polls.
But they are crucial to Democratic success. In the last 20 years, when Democrats won this group by more than 20 points, they have done well, winning presidencies or making gains in midterms. The only exception was 2022, but arguably, the strong margin Democrats won with young voters that year, helped them stem what could have been a much larger Republican tide. That year, Democrats lost nine House seats, but gained a Senate seat.
Democratic margin with voters 18-29, election result 2024 +11, Trump wins presidency 2022 +28, Republicans win House, Democrats gain Senate seat 2020 +25, Biden wins presidency 2018 +35, Democrats win House 2016 +19, Trump wins presidency 2014 +11, Republicans expand House majority, win Senate 2012 +23, Obama wins re-election 2010 +17, Republicans win House 2008 +34, Obama wins presidency 2006 +22, Democrats win House
Given past polling errors in Texas that underestimated the Republican vote, there's a healthy skepticism that Democrat James Talarico's margin of error lead in polling averages is enough to win.
There was lots of enthusiasm in 2018 for Beto O'Rourke's (D) 2018 bid against an unpopular Republican senator in Ted Cruz, but Cruz still won, although by less than 3 percentage points. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and no Democrat has been elected to the Senate from Texas in 38 years.
For it to actually happen in this state Trump won by 14 points in 2024, two groups are key – Republicans and Latinos. Ken Paxton (R) is unpopular. Republican Gov. Greg Abbot is also facing a tight race, but he's thought to be in better shape than Paxton. In 2018, Cruz won about 400,000 fewer votes than Abbott, but Cruz still won by more than 200,000 votes. So watch if the difference between Abbott and Paxton is more than 400,000 for Talarico.
Voters cast their ballots in Anchorage, Alaska on November 1, 2026. Christian Moorman/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The second part of Talarico's path to victory runs through South Texas. Statewide, O'Rourke won 64% of Latinos in 2018, and they were 26% of the electorate, according to exit polls . If Talarico is north of both of those, that's how he wins the seat. Talarico would need to improve on O'Rourke's totals in these Latino-heavy counties: Cameron 63%, Hidalgo 69%, Webb 71%, Nueces 51%. As a bonus, watch the fast-growing and heavily populated Dallas suburbs – Collin 47%, Denton 46%, Tarrant 51%.
Because of the political realignment that's taken place in the Trump era, watch how people identify in exit polls.
The percentage of those saying they were Democrats hit a low in 2024 at 31%. That trend is happening as the base of the Democratic Party has become more liberal and more disaffected with their own leadership. This year, though, Democrats were among the highest in enthusiasm levels, according to the latest NPR poll , but they are likely going to have to be far higher than 31% as a share of the electorate to do well.
Democrats as a share of the electorate 2024 31% 2022 33% 2020 37% 2018 37% 2016 37% 2014 35% 2012 38% 2010 39% 2008 39%
That's quite possible given the opposition to Trump in this election is sky high – 53% of likely voters in the latest NPR poll said they strongly disapproved of the job he's doing. That is very likely to be a unifying force for the left in this election. As the saying goes, the enemy of my enemy is my friend.
Along these lines, it's going to be important to watch races like the Michigan Senate race and the contest for Michigan's 7th Congressional District, both of which have very progressive Democratic candidates trying to win in purple places. Democratic unity – and the party's ideological future – is going to be a key storyline of the 2028 presidential primary and could define the American left for years to come.
