title: How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?
body:
Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is a fluoride-free option that has some research backing its effectiveness. mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images hide caption
How you brush your teeth — and what you use to do it — matters.
Recently, dentist Dr. Jin-Ho Phark says he's noticed patients asking about fluoride-free toothpaste options. Phark is an associate professor of clinical dentistry at the Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry of University of Southern California.
"There's a lot of interest from the patients," Phark says. "I hear that also regularly from students."
One product that patients are asking about in particular is a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite. Many patients, Phark says, may have seen the products on social media, "being pushed by influencers and other people quite intensively."
The traditional fluoride toothpaste became common in the late 1950s , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when Procter & Gamble Co. released Crest nationally. Over the next few decades, oral care products with fluoride as their active ingredient became widely available around the world. These products help protect the outer layer of teeth from cavity-causing bacteria.
And dental health is important because it's related to so many systems in your body, from your heart to digestion.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
"There are these connections made between your oral health, and the bugs that you have in your mouth, and systemic health and even the composition of your gut microbiome," says Dr. Livia Tenuta , a dentist who specializes in preventing tooth decay and associate professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.
The promise of hydroxyapatite? Many of the things you care about when it comes to toothpaste: cavity protection, whitening, enamel-strengthening. But without fluoride.
Health experts widely agree that fluoride — a naturally occurring mineral — is beneficial to health. But curiosity is growing about fluoride-free options.
"There is an increasing number of people who are refusing fluoride totally, or hesitant to take it, especially for their children," says Bennett Amaechi , a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio.
That hesitancy stems from a history of skepticism about fluoride. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has blamed the fluoridation of water for a number of health problems, including arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer, IQ loss, neurodevelopmental disorders and thyroid disease.
Low levels of fluoride are generally considered safe and key to preventing cavities. Amaechi says there's no concrete evidence about potential harms of fluoride when it comes to children's IQ. And research that has found associations between fluoride and IQ has looked at very high levels of fluoride — over twice what's recommended in the U.S. water supply. The CDC previously named the addition of fluoride to public drinking water one of the top 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century , alongside vaccinations and family planning. They also say fluoride in water reduces cavities by 25% .
Still, Kennedy's criticism of fluoride seems to have made its way to toothpaste — and opened up space for products that use hydroxyapatite instead.
The hype around hydroxyapatite is, in part, due to its similarity to tooth enamel. There's also some research that suggests hydroxyapatite can help with tooth sensitivity.
Tooth enamel is mostly made of calcium and phosphate. Those minerals form the outer layer of your teeth, which protects the internal layers of tissues, nerves and blood vessels, from damage.
Your enamel is stronger than your bones, but still susceptible to damage over time from things like sugary foods and dental plaque. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars, and produce acids that eat away at the outer layer of your teeth. Tenuta says over time, that process sets the stage for tooth decay, often referred to as caries , or eventually cavities (a hole in a tooth that comes from this decay).
She says fluoride toothpaste helps protect teeth by "remineralizing" them with calcium and phosphate.
"When [fluoride is] available in our saliva, in the dental plaque that we were not very perfect in brushing, that fluoride that is left over after brushing with the fluoride toothpaste will actually bring minerals back to the tooth," Tenuta says.
Fluoride works with those minerals to form a new compound that protects teeth. It acts like a shield for your enamel. But you need to brush with fluoride toothpaste consistently. Dentists recommend twice daily to keep those minerals around in our mouths.
Hydroxyapatite is thought to work in a slightly different way. These products seem to get into tiny crevices in the tooth enamel .
Many hydroxyapatite products use a form called nano-hydroxyapatite, which has smaller particles that, in theory, can more easily penetrate pores in enamel, though research data is limited.
Amaechi, who studies hydroxyapatite use, says fluoride is extensively researched, especially in long-term studies. But he says early research on hydroxyapatite is positive.
"When it comes to remineralization and preventing caries manifestation, it is as effective as fluoride," Amaechi says.
Amaechi was an author on a 2021 study in the journal Scientific Reports, that followed 177 children for almost one year, and compared hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste. The researchers tracked tooth decay in each group, and found that both groups had similar outcomes. That study included funding from Dr. Wolff Group, a German company that owns two brands that make hydroxyapatite toothpastes.
That company contributed funding to another study , published two years later in the journal Frontiers in Public Health. Researchers found similar results after tracking 171 adults, comparing tooth decay in participants using a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to those using a fluoride toothpaste for 18 months. Both groups showed similar outcomes, suggesting that hydroxyapatite worked as well as fluoride in the study. However, the participants in the study were mostly healthy young adults without any severe oral health problems.
Tenuta says she'd want to see more long-term studies, especially in people with high risk of tooth decay.
"There are very few studies and they recruited participants of low caries risk," she says.
One shorter-term study in 2019, published in the Journal of Investigative and Clinical Dentistry, did compare a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste in 133 people who were at higher risk of caries. After a little over five months, the researchers found both toothpastes performed similarly.
Hydroxyapatite toothpastes tend to be more expensive than fluoride ones — some over a dollar more expensive per ounce.
For patients who are open to both options, "I will advise them to use fluoride because fluoride has more evidence supporting its efficacy," Amaechi says.
"I would recommend as a best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's what we have a lot of evidence behind," she says.
The American Dental Association , a professional group for dentists, said in an email to NPR they acknowledge more people are using products with forms of hydroxyapatite and that some evidence suggests those products can contribute to remineralization.
However, research on the ingredient is new, "and evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous, especially regarding clinical indications," wrote ADA Consumer Advisor spokesperson Dr. Ada Cooper.
Instead, the ADA recommends you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, floss daily and regularly visit a dentist.

title: What Vance's midterm push reveals about his potential 2028 bid
body:
US Vice President JD Vance listens to US President Donald Trump as he hosts Stephen Hubbard in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 30, 2026. ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
At a Thursday speech in Weatherford, Texas, Vice President JD Vance seemed to relish the opportunity to snipe at Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
"Now James Talarico has also said that he really has to grapple with his masculinity in addition to his whiteness," Vance said. "And you know, James, the good news is, there ain't a whole lot to grapple with," he finished to cheers from the crowd.
Vance gave the speech the same afternoon that President Trump spoke in Rock Hill, South Carolina, as part of his pre-midterm blitz of rallies. And while Vance's delivery was different from the president's – less borscht-belt comedian, more practiced politician – it contained plenty of MAGA DNA, from insulting a candidate's masculinity to promising a return of American greatness. It all gives a sense of what a Vance presidential pitch might look like once 2028 campaigns begin in earnest next year.
Vance paints a rosy picture of the America of his youth, in his speeches – in North Carolina this week , he invoked the "sense of pride and unity and fellowship" Americans had after September 11, 2001.
He added to that message in multiple speeches remembering his childhood football teams being sponsored by local small businesses.
"I distinctly remember looking in my old jerseys and seeing the names of the businesses that had sponsored those teams and realizing that most of the teams I played for, those businesses no longer existed," he said in Howell, Michigan . "They were casualties of politicians in a faraway place who didn't give a damn what happened to Michigan or Ohio, and it was us that paid the consequences."
It's a story about a Norman Rockwell vision of America corrupted by Washington elites. The story Vance tells is that his brand of populist politics can bring that back.
But it's not just about economics; Vance leans hard into the culture wars fought during the Trump years. In his stories about peewee football, Vance talks about racial harmony well before the advent of Black Lives Matter: "the children of working-class Black families and the children of working-class white families would play football together, would cheer with one another, would never worry about the color of their skin or who had more privilege," he told the crowd in North Carolina.
It amounts to a more traditional, more eloquent packaging of Trump's anti-woke MAGA message. However, Vance also is experimenting with crassness in his remarks, dropping the occasional swear word or telling the Texas crowd he was "sweating my balls off" at the podium.
The challenge for Vance right now is in promoting GOP candidates while the Republican president he serves is unpopular.
That challenge is particularly acute where the president's policies have directly caused economic woes. Vance doesn't tend to bring up the Iran War up in his stump speeches – a war that sent gas and diesel prices spiraling upward – but he does cast the gas prices caused by the Iran war as an unfortunate, recurring result of geopolitics:
"Remember in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine and gas prices skyrocketed? They skyrocketed, by the way, far higher than they are today," he told a Montana crowd . "They skyrocketed in 1979. They skyrocketed in 2001. They skyrocketed in 2007. They skyrocket every time some tin pot dictator decides to throw a tantrum."
Likewise, Vance has acknowledged the high price of beef, casting it as a problem of consolidation among meatpackers, while sidestepping that Trump's own policies have angered beef producers .
Interspersed with his campaign speeches this year have been appearances as the head of President Trump's anti-fraud task force, which has a goal of rooting out malfeasance in social safety net programs.
The task force provides Vance with both resume material and an opportunity to talk about his personal story.
"I worked as a cashier at a grocery store for a couple of years, this was my very first job, Dhillon Foods, probably 20 miles from where we're standing today," he told a crowd in Cincinnati last week. "I also had a lot of members of my family benefit from these food benefit programs provided by federal tax dollars."
Vance was first propelled onto the political scene as a result of his memoir about growing up in poor, rural southern Ohio.
His biography gives him some political tools that President Trump does not have, like the ability to talk personally about military service and economic difficulties.
However, crowds loved Trump not because of his biographical relatability but because of his bombast and unfiltered anger. The challenge for any would-be 2028 Republican candidate is figuring out how to follow Trump's singular, decade-plus-long performance, and what – if anything – can replace that in the hearts of GOP voters.

title: When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere
body:
A sign directs residents to a polling place in Dearborn, Mich., on Aug. 4. Scott Olson/Getty Images hide caption
There's one big difference, Tina Barton says, between running an election in a battleground state and a non-battleground.
It's what happens when there are mistakes.
"If a human error happens, it's easily explained in the press and it's not a story," Barton says. "You have a human error in a battleground state and all of a sudden it can become a massive conspiracy."
In 2020, she oversaw elections as city clerk of Rochester Hills, Mich. On election night, her office mistakenly sent an unofficial absentee vote file twice because the first one didn't initially appear to send.
Such mistakes happen every election cycle in a national process run by tens of thousands of human beings. A machine isn't plugged in. A poll worker sleeps through their alarm clock and doesn't open a precinct on time. Someone gets handed the wrong ballot.
In Barton's case, the issue didn't impact actual votes, and it was corrected in the tally the following day.
The chairwoman of the Republican National Committee accused her office of improperly giving votes to Democrats, and Barton received a rush of death threats, including a voicemail saying she deserved a "throat to the knife" because she had "frauded out America of a real election."
More than half a decade later, for better or worse, election officials in swing states like Michigan, Georgia and Arizona are more used to that level of pressure and scrutiny.
In this year's midterms, however, because the races that will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate are spread around the country, local officials in places like Iowa, Alaska, New York and Kansas may find themselves in the national spotlight for the first time.
Chris McGinn is executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials. In an interview with NPR earlier this year, he noted that Texas has been a reliable Republican state for the better part of 50 years , which has meant fewer competitive elections and less pressure on voting officials in federal election cycles.
A huge part of McGinn's job has been preparing clerks for the possibility that could change this year, considering the U.S. Senate race there could decide the balance of power in that chamber. The Republican nominee for that seat sought to help President Trump overturn his 2020 election loss.
"We're still in a state of not thinking it can happen to us — 'That happens in other places,'" McGinn said. "One of the things that I jokingly but realistically preach to our members is we don't want to be Florida in 2000."
On a whole, the threat environment for voting officials seems calmer than it did in the period following 2020.
Wendy Link — the supervisor of elections for Palm Beach County, Fla., a county that includes part of a toss-up congressional district this year — says her office still regularly gets "love letters," as she calls them, but she's not as worried for own safety as she has been at different points in the job.
"We get emails saying, you know, 'We're going to send our army to arrest you, you'll be spending your time in Guantanamo Bay,'" Link told NPR. "So do I love reading some of the emails? No. Do I think some of them are clearly intended to intimidate me? Yes. But am I reaching out and asking for a security detail? No."
But Barton, the former Michigan clerk, worries it could all escalate again if the midterms are close. She's now vice president of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, which helps local officials game-plan and prepare for different worst case scenarios.
"It can happen whether you're a red state or a blue state. Controversy can find you," Barton said. "All it takes is some ballot equipment going down, a problem with ballots jamming, a website going down."
Researchers who study election misinformation say most false narratives usually emerge from real events like those Barton mentioned , which are then seized on by influencers or politicians to falsely imply they're happening intentionally or at a wider scale than they actually are.
This year CSSE doubled the number of trainings the organization led when compared to 2024 — a sign of new concerns around the Trump administration's actions in elections but also an expanded understanding of what it means to be in a battleground state.
When Barton talks to officials in competitive districts, her message is simple.
"I've told them all, you better be on your game," Barton said.

title: With students scarce, college admissions offices get friendlier, less intimidating
body:
Prospective students and their families participate in a campus tour at Skidmore College in New York. Oliver Parini/The Hechinger Report hide caption
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
That's how 17-year-old high school senior Alex Zaret described the college admissions process, during a tour of the Skidmore College campus — the fourth school Zaret had visited, with another half-dozen to go.
"It is kind of a full-time job," Zaret's father, Owen, said.
He wasn't joking. With research to do, visits to make and applications and financial forms to fill out, "it's a lot, and it's a lot on top of two full-time-employed parents and a very engaged high school student," Owen Zaret said.
But even in the year or so that the family has been doing this, the Zarets have detected a subtle shift.
At first, the process seemed to be what Owen Zaret called an ivory tower approach. It signaled: "'You're lucky if you come here.' And now, I think, for a variety of reasons, that's changed. It's more like, 'We want you to be here.'"
Alex Zaret (right, in yellow) and parents listen to tour guides Lily Boardman and Fiona Salas on a campus tour. Oliver Parini/The Hechinger Report hide caption
Hurting for students, colleges are striving to transform an admissions process that has often been intimidating, secretive and stressful into an experience that's open, easier and downright friendly.
"It's one of those things that's in everybody's interest," said Marc Conner, president of Skidmore, which has been making a particular push to do this. Even though application and enrollment data show his college is not among the many others having trouble filling seats, he said, "We depend on students coming to our campuses and, when they do come, getting them to enroll."
Some universities and colleges are waiving application fees and promising additional financial aid for students who show up for campus tours. Public universities in 17 states now admit high school students who haven't even applied , according to the Education Commission of the States; more than 150 private colleges also make direct admissions offers to students who fill out the Common App, a standardized online application used by about 1,200 institutions. And the overall odds of getting accepted to college are going up .
Now Skidmore and a small number of other institutions have taken a surprising next step: enlisting faculty to help recruit new students — a role they previously left entirely to the admissions office — by meeting with and opening their labs and classrooms to prospective and admitted applicants.
"It creates a feeling of what it would be like to be seen, valued and to find a place of belonging on a campus," said Jess Ricker, the college's vice president for enrollment. And that, Ricker said, can help distinguish Skidmore from the other schools on students' lists.
Admissions leaders are looking for any advantage. Two-thirds of them had trouble meeting their enrollment targets in at least one of the last two years, according to a survey by the ratings platform Niche. Ninety-seven percent expect the competition to increase.
The reality they face: The supply of traditional-age freshmen nationwide is projected to decline by 13 percent over the next 15 years, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. The proportion of high school graduates choosing to go on to college is also down, from 70% in 2016 to 63% in 2024 , the most recent year for which the figure is available, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports.
One little-noticed result: Being accepted to college is generally easier than it has been in the past and than Americans seem to think it is.
"The majority of institutions in the United States actually accept the majority of students who apply," says Angel Pérez, CEO of the National Association for College Admission Counseling. Oliver Parini/The Hechinger Report hide caption
Nearly 8 in 10 first-year applicants for undergraduate admission to public and 7 in 10 to private colleges and universities get in, the National Association for College Admission Counseling, or NACAC, reports. That's up from 68% and 65%, respectively, about 10 years ago. Nearly 9 in 10 private, nonprofit four-year universities and colleges admit half or more of applicants, according to separate research by the conservative think tank the American Enterprise Institute.
This news has been slow to trickle down to students. More than 40% of 18- to 29-year-olds wrongly think it's harder to get into college than it was for people in their parents' generation, a Pew Research Center survey found.
"Most of the public actually doesn't understand that the majority of institutions in the United States actually accept the majority of students who apply," said Angel Pérez, NACAC's CEO.
He blamed an obsession with acceptance rates at institutions such as CalTech , Harvard , Princeton and Stanford , which each take about 1 applicant in 25.
In fact, only 33 colleges and universities in the country admit 10% or fewer of their undergraduate applicants, NACAC figures show.
The intensifying competition for them might be good for students, but it's bad for many colleges. At some, offices of admission are struggling to shake what Ricker joked is their historic reputation as "offices of rejection."
A few, including Skidmore, are appealing to the faculty for help. At Ohio Northern University, at least one member of the faculty now meets with every visiting applicant. Faculty at Washington College in Maryland sit down with visiting applicants on designated Fridays during the admissions season and at open houses.
"Presidents and vice presidents of enrollment are telling people that every interaction counts." said Rob Springall, a consultant at the executive search firm WittKieffer and former executive director of undergraduate admissions at Pennsylvania State University.
There's another reason for this that's less widely understood among consumers. As students hedge their bets by applying to more colleges than their historical counterparts — Common App users now apply to an average of more than seven schools apiece , a number that's been steadily increasing — it's getting harder for enrollment managers to predict how many they admit will actually enroll. In admissions lingo, this is called the yield.
Yield has declined from 32% in 2014 to 22% in 2024 at public and from 24% in 2014 to 18% in 2024 at private, nonprofit colleges and universities, on average, federal data shows. That's the last period for which the figures are available.
This means colleges have to admit around five times as many students as they need — and that admitted applicants need to be persuaded to follow through and put down their deposits, including the many of them who come back to take another look around.
Colleges "are realizing that everyone has to help with the recruiting process," said Leah Beth Hubbard, assistant vice president of enrollment strategies at the enrollment consulting firm The Parish Group. She advises clients to "teach everyone to smile. Teach everyone to introduce themselves and say what they do at the institution."
Coaxing faculty to do this, on top of their existing obligations, isn't always easy, campus leaders said — at least, at first.
"Some faculty didn't want to be part of it," said Johnnie Johnson, Washington College's vice president for enrollment management. "They'd say, 'You go recruit and I'll teach.'"
Like other university and college administrators, Johnson said he countered with a frank assessment of enrollment trends.
"When you put a financial figure on every student who comes in, that equates to programmatic funding. That equates to raises," he said. And faculty are seeing what happens when those numbers fall. "They have colleagues who have been at colleges that closed" or whose programs have been cut, said Johnson. "They don't want to be next."
Becca Johnson, who goes by Dr. J, is a professor and chair of psychology at Skidmore College who often meets with prospective students. "I think more information is better than less," Johnson says. Oliver Parini/The Hechinger Report hide caption
Skidmore, which has 2,719 students, hasn't experienced the problems many other small private, nonprofit colleges are confronting. It's seen its number of applications rise, not fall; unlike colleges in general, its acceptance rate is down, from 37% 10 years ago to 24% today . Yield is an above-average 24%.
Still, said Conner, the president: "Even if the school is doing all right during these times, we're still facing the same headwinds as everybody else."
Everyone from dining hall workers to groundskeepers are encouraged to be welcoming, he said.
"It helps that we're in a tough time in higher ed and they see what's happening at other schools," said Conner. "And they know a school is going to rise or fall depending on how much the community joins together."
More than three-quarters of admitted students who came to the campus last year other than for a weekend open house requested to sit in on a class or meet with a faculty member, the college says. That added up to 300 personal visits.
There's not yet data about whether those young visitors apply or enroll. But Psychology Department Chair Becca Johnson, who often meets with applicants, said she hears feedback that it makes a difference.
One mother told her, " 'You know, my student has applied to so many schools, been accepted, had a number of wonderful possible possibilities,' " Johnson recounted. " 'And you're the first person from outside of an admissions office to contact us. And that was so meaningful for them in their decision."
This story was produced by The Hechinger Report , a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education.
Edited by Nirvi Shah Audio story edited by Elissa Nadworny Audio story produced by Lauren Migaki

title: N70,000 Transport Allowance: NLC Can Negotiate Alone – Ajaero Counters Usifo
body: The National President of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), Comrade Joe Ajero, has argued that the Union has the power to negotiate alone on labour matters based on the principle of most workers representatives of the International Labour Organization (ILO). Ajaero spoke while appearing as a guest on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Monday. According to him, the Trade Union Congress (TUC) can only negotiate alongside NLC but not alone. “TUC can negotitta along with NLC but NLC can negotiate alone based on the principle of most workers representatives of the ILO”, the NLC President noted. This is coming after both labour bodies have disagreed over the₦70,000 transport intervention approved by the Federal Government for workers across all levels for six months. Ajaero stated that the TUC has no power to sit at the table to negotiate alone with the labour authorities. The labour leader argued that the Trade Congress is required to present its propositions to the NLC when engaging with the ILO. “TUC sent their negotiation alone ahead of the ILO conference but they retured it back and I had to muninuite on it. “They have to send their list here for me to forward it; that is the position of the ILO. NLC determines how TUC participates”, adding that the TUC does not submit its proposal to TUC. “It is the other way round” Ajaero stated that the Ministry of Labour and other labour authorities will not engage with the Trade Union, as it acts alone on workers’ welfare negotiations. “TUC can’t negotiate alone; if they are saying and it is implied, it does not happen. I don’t think the Ministry of Labour or the Labour Authority will allow that to happen.” Ajaero, responding to Festus position of having over 300,000 members in the federal civil service, said, “The 2005 Trade Union Amendment Act made membership of trade unions voluntary. “It is the worker that determines the union he belongs to; the Act makes “Section 40 of the Nigerian 1999 Constitution as amended was clear that every Nigerian worker has the right to belong to any trade union, political or religious institution of his choice, which gives every worker the latitude to belong to any union of their choice”. He argued that Festus saying he has a good number of workers in his union does not add up, given that only one member union of TUC belongs to the Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council,, which consists of eight union bodies, and seven of them are in NLC. He further argued that one union from TUC, which is a member of the joint body, has subjected its power to the joint body. Ajaero maintained that the Nigerian Labour Congress engaged with the federal government to secure the ₦70,000 transport intervention “We gave government an ultimatum; we were supposed to start an action. The government asked for four days and to meet with us, and we met, and they resumed sitting after four days. After the meeting, the 70k allowance came up” He asserted that minimum wage demands could not be presented when the government has not set up a negotiation committee; stating that it requires wider consultation among Labour leaders, government officials, and employers before any wage increase can happen. The post N70,000 Transport Allowance: NLC Can Negotiate Alone – Ajaero Counters Usifo appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
body: Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States , and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2. The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran , with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal. The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries. “Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said. On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged. Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump. The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.” Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action. title: U.S. Navy selects Thales subsidiary for $53.9 million remote mine-hunting systems contract
body: The modules will allow sailors to detect, locate and classify undersea mines remotely, keeping personnel and platforms farther from threats. The system combines sonar, mission-management software and remotely operated vehicle technology to support the Navy’s “Find, Fix and Finish” approach to mine countermeasures. “The ability to counter undersea mine threats remains fundamental to maritime security and naval mission success,” said Rob Geckle, CEO of Thales North America. “By advancing the Navy’s MCM capabilities, this program will help strengthen fleet readiness and support mission success in an increasingly dynamic operating environment.” The award combines technology from Thales’ international portfolio with the U.S.-based subsidiary’s experience supplying integrated undersea warfare capabilities to the Navy. Thales said the program would support unmanned mine-countermeasures operations and help move more quickly from detecting a threat to taking action. A multiview towed synthetic aperture sonar will provide high-resolution mine detection and imagery, with the aim of reducing false targets. AI-augmented automatic target recognition software will help operators process, classify, map and manage the data, shortening the search and classification process while improving confidence in the results. “This program brings together the most advanced mine warfare technologies across the Thales portfolio, with AAC’s deep experience delivering integrated undersea warfare capability to the U.S. Navy,” said Mike Carnovale, president of Advanced Acoustic Concepts. “By integrating sonar, classification software and future remote neutralization capabilities into a single operational solution, we’re helping simplify mine hunting operations and accelerate the path from detection to action for both manned and unmanned surface vessel platforms.”

title: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain
body: Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.  For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.  But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.  The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed. Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.  A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.  Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.  Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.  The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

title: First shipbuilder chosen under US Navy LSM program
body:
TOTE Services has selected Hanwha Defense USA as the first shipbuilder for the US Navy's Medium Landing Ship (LSM) program, awarding a $269 million contract for the construction of the initial vessel at Hanwha Philly Shipyard.
As vessel construction manager (VCM) for the LSM program, TOTE Services issued a competitive request for proposals (RFP) to qualified US shipyards in July 2026. Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) is the first shipbuilder selected through that process, based on its competitive pricing and acceptance of TOTE Services’ subcontract terms and conditions.
The award covers construction of one LSM, valued at $269 million, at Hanwha Philly Shipyard (HPSI), with options for three additional vessels.
The program will include up to eight new vessels under the base contract. TOTE Services continues productive contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, both directed shipyards under the VCM contract, which are expected to play a meaningful role in building the LSM fleet.
“This award shows the speed at which the VCM model can move from RFP to contract,” said Jeff Dixon , President of TOTE Services.
“Through a competitive process, we secured strong terms that benefit the government, along with build positions that allow construction to start in the fourth quarter of 2027.”
“TOTE Service’s selection of Hanwha Defense USA and Hanwha Philly Shipyard for the LSM program is a testament to the skilled union workforce, transformational investments, and experienced partnerships that make Philadelphia one of the nation’s premier shipbuilding centers,” said Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon (PA-05).
“This selection is a significant step forward for the Hanwha Philly Shipyard as it supports Navy and Marine Corps efforts to rebuild U.S. shipbuilding.”
TOTE Services’ $2.2 billion VCM contract supports the US Navy and Marine Corps’ planned 35-ship LSM fleet. The first vessel is expected to deliver in 2030.
The company will provide one accountable management structure connecting government requirements to shipyard execution across three domestic shipbuilders, helping to accelerate delivery, strengthen cost and schedule discipline, and expand the US shipbuilding industrial base.
That work includes standardizing configuration across the fleet, using block buys to secure favorable pricing, and rapidly delivering high-quality vessels.
TOTE Services previously served as VCM for the US Maritime Administration’s five-ship National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) program, overseeing shipyard selection, design, construction, testing, delivery and lifecycle logistics.
Four vessels have been delivered, while the fifth, Golden State, is scheduled for delivery in 2027.
The Medium Landing Ship award extends TOTE Services’ involvement with Hanwha Philly Shipyard, which has participated in the NSMV program and is expected to construct the first LSM under the new contract. Hanwha has also announced investments aimed at expanding the shipyard’s production capacity.

title: Muntaka calls for stronger law enforcement cooperation to tackle transnational crimes
body: The Minister for the Interior, Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak, has called for stronger cooperation and information sharing among law enforcement agencies to tackle the growing threat of transnational crimes and strengthen national and regional security. He said the increasing cross-border nature of criminal activities required security institutions to work together and improve the exchange of information to support investigations and prevent criminals from exploiting weaknesses in the security system. The minister made the call at a meeting of the West African Police Information System (WAPIS) Ghana National Committee (WANACO) at the Police Headquarters in Accra, where stakeholders discussed the progress, challenges and sustainability of the programme. He identified human trafficking, drug trafficking, cybercrime, financial crime and other organised criminal activities as some of the crimes requiring closer cooperation among law enforcement agencies, given their increasingly transnational nature. The Minister observed that criminals continued to take advantage of communication gaps and weaknesses in information exchange among security institutions, making effective collaboration essential in tackling such activities. He said law enforcement agencies must therefore strengthen their capacity to collect, manage, analyse and share criminal information in a timely, secure and lawful manner. He further explained that the effectiveness of WAPIS depended not only on modern technology and infrastructure but also on accurate criminal data, adequate resources, strong inter-agency collaboration and the retention of trained personnel. To ensure that the system achieved its intended objectives, Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak urged WANACO to strengthen its oversight and coordination role by translating its deliberations into clear decisions, defined responsibilities and measurable outcomes. He also emphasised that the sustainability of the programme required the collective commitment of all stakeholder institutions, rather than leaving its implementation solely to the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) or the WAPIS Centre. The Minister said every institution involved must take ownership of the programme and actively contribute to its effective implementation and long-term sustainability. The meeting was attended by representatives of the European Union, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the International Criminal Police Organisation (INTERPOL), and various security and law enforcement institutions.

title: Dakar 2026 YOG: Kuti bounces back with victory over Tunisian opponent
body:
Nigeria’s Matthew Kuti revived his hopes of reaching the knockout stage of the men’s singles table tennis event at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games with a 3-1 victory over Tunisia’s Youssef Aidli on Sunday.
The Nigerian recovered from an opening-day defeat to Hong Kong’s Li Ki Ho to beat Aidli 11-8, 11-8, 9-11, 11-7, keeping his campaign alive at the Dakar Expo Centre in Senegal.
Kuti, Nigeria’s deputy captain and reigning African Youth Cup champion, had endured a difficult start to his Group C campaign, losing 3-0 (11-4, 11-4, 11-3) to Li, whose attacking game proved too strong for the Nigerian.
However, he responded positively against Aidli, winning the first two games before the Tunisian reduced the deficit by taking the third. Kuti regained control in the fourth game to seal an important victory.
The result leaves the Nigerian needing one more win to secure qualification for the knockout stage, with his final group match against Italy’s Francesco Travesan scheduled for Monday.
The top two players in the four-man group will advance to the next round.
Speaking after his victory, Kuti acknowledged the quality of opposition at the Games but expressed confidence in his ability to overcome the Italian.
“It has not been easy for us here in Dakar because everybody is at their best and we are all aiming for the knockout stage. I hope I can raise my game against the Italian,” he said.
Meanwhile, Kuti and his compatriot, Favour Ojo, suffered an early exit from the mixed doubles event after losing to their Thai opponents in the round of 16 on Saturday.
Ojo also failed to progress in the women’s singles event after suffering a 3-1 defeat to Egypt’s Yara Elbadawy in her second group match.
The loss followed her opening group-stage defeat, ending her hopes of reaching the knockout rounds.
With Ojo’s campaign over, attention will now turn to Kuti’s decisive encounter against Travesan as the Nigerian seeks to keep his medal hopes alive in Dakar.

title: Marvin Senaya returns to action after 120-day injury absence
body: Ghana defender Marvin Senaya has returned to competitive football after 120 days on the sidelines with a hamstring injury. The 25-year-old made his first appearance of the 2026/27 season for AJ Auxerre on Sunday, coming off the bench in their 5-1 defeat to Strasbourg in Ligue 1. Senaya was introduced in the 63rd minute, playing 27 minutes as he began his return to action. The defender had been out since sustaining the injury during Ghana’s Round of 32 match against Colombia at the 2026 FIFA World Cup on July 3. He was forced off after just 13 minutes, bringing his tournament to an early end after featuring in all four of Ghana’s matches. Senaya subsequently underwent hamstring surgery in Paris before beginning his rehabilitation with Auxerre. His return will be welcome news for both the French club and the Black Stars as he works towards regaining full fitness. Ghana will face Somalia in a doubleheader in mid-November in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

title: Havelsan and DICON to cooperate on defence tech
body:
Turkiye’s Havelsan and the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) covering potential cooperation across defence and security technologies.
The agreement was inked during the inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) in Lagos, Nigeria, which ran from 26 to 29 October. It was announced by Havelsan on the occasion of the 103rd anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Türkiye on 29 October.
The MoU covers potential collaboration in command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (C4ISR); simulation and training; unmanned and autonomous systems; information and communication technologies; integrated security solutions; and cybersecurity.
Havelsan said the agreement would enable both organisations to explore opportunities for technological cooperation, identify mutually beneficial projects and establish the groundwork for sustainable, long-term partnerships in the defence and technology sectors.
“This important step reflects Havelsan’s commitment to expanding its international partnerships, fostering technological collaboration, and contributing to the development of advanced defence capabilities alongside its Nigerian counterparts,” Havelsan said. “We look forward to translating this shared vision into tangible projects and building a strong, enduring, and mutually beneficial partnership between Türkiye and Nigeria.”
The signing followed a Türkiye–Nigeria industrial cooperation panel on 28 October at Afridex, which examined joint development, manufacturing, investment, technology transfer and skills development.
During that discussion, Havelsan Vice President Şevket Ünal outlined the company’s approach to developing capability with local partners. “Our model is very simple: Build together, produce together, and sustain together,” Ünal said, according to a News Agency of Nigeria report.
Proforce Managing Director Ade Ogundeyin also called for collaboration between international manufacturers and Nigerian defence companies, identifying simulation, software integration, maintenance and autonomous systems as opportunities for local development.
The Havelsa-DICON agreement formed part of a wider industrial cooperation agenda at Afridex, connecting equipment requirements with the expertise, infrastructure and partnerships needed to sustain operational capability, organisers dmg events said.
Speaking to The Guardian during the exhibition, Minister of State for Defence, Dr Bello Muhammed Matawalle, said Nigeria produces more than 50 million rounds of ammunition annually against a national requirement of about 300 million. He identified investment, technology transfer and local technical expertise as priorities for expanding domestic capability.
Brigadier General (retired) Morakinyo Abiodun, a director at DICON-D7G, also outlined plans to inaugurate a military jetty at Tedi Island in Ojo, Lagos, by the end of November 2026. Speaking on the sidelines of Afridex on 27 October, he said the planned facility would support the manufacture and assembly of military equipment.
International military engagements at Afridex have addressed training, maritime security and operational cooperation. Italy’s Ministry of Defence reported that General Luciano Portolano’s meetings with Nigerian officials covered the finalisation of a bilateral defence cooperation agreement, alongside potential police training and Nigerian requirements for pilot, counter-drone and counter-IED training.
Nigeria’s Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, held engagements with international delegations, including representatives from Poland, US Africa Command and Italy, on defence technology, equipment requirements, training and operational cooperation.

title: Bank of Russia buys currency worth $149.2 mln in domestic market
body:
MOSCOW, November 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia purchased the yuan worth 12.1 bln rubles ($149.2 mln) with settlements on October 30, 2026 in the domestic market, the regulator reported on its website.
Currency sales in the internal market with settlements on October 29 also stood at 12.1 bln rubles.
The Bank of Russia is buying and selling foreign exchange in the domestic market in the currency section of the Moscow Exchange with the use of the yuan-ruble instrument.

title: Uganda commissions Russian-donated military repair facility
body:
Uganda’s President and Commander-in-Chief Yoweri Museveni has commissioned a military repair facility as part of a $53 million package of military equipment and infrastructure donated by the Russian Federation.
The Magamaga facility was commissioned on 21-22 October and is among several donations made under the framework of defence cooperation between the governments of Uganda and Russia, the Uganda People’s Defence Force (UPDF) said. Other donations include a training simulator at the Mechanised Warfare College in Karama and a command post at Kalangalo under the Special Force Command.
In October 2025, Museveni announced he had launched the Military Mechanised Major Repair Facility in Magamaga as part of Russian donations to the UPDF. The Russian ambassador to Uganda at the time said this was the first of two phases, with the second involving the construction of a maintenance and repair facility in Magamaga and a boat storage site and floating pier in Entebbe, with the work expected to be completed by September 2026.
The new vehicle repair facility has been built to the north of the building where the UPDF’s Nyoka armoured vehicles were assembled, Janes reported, adding that a floating dock for small boats has also been installed at the 15th Marine Brigade base in Entebbe. This was shown being used by at least four Russian-made BL-820 patrol boats, one of which was displayed at Magamaga in October 2025 – apparently eight boats have been delivered. A floating boom has also been installed around the dock and computer screens shown in a control room indicated the base now has a radar and electro-optical surveillance system.
Museveni also inaugurated a simulator for the BRDM-2MS armoured reconnaissance vehicle at the Mechanised Warfare College in Kalama.
He thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin and the Russian Federation for the donation, describing it as a valuable contribution to Uganda’s defence capabilities.
“The gifts, if you study them, are all to ensure the survivability of our troops so that they fight better,” Museveni said.
“The gift is a gift, but we need to do more. If the cost is affordable, we should invest and upscale,” he said. The Commander-in-Chief urged the Chief of Defence Forces, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the Chief of Joint Staff, Lieutenant General Jack Bakasumba and other senior military leaders to assess the affordability of local production and consider expanding the initiative if it proved economically viable.
Museveni said he was impressed by the speed with which troops at Kalangalo set up their barracks and an operational base, and thanked the Russians “not only for the gift, but also the example.”
The President noted that Uganda’s military ties with Russia date back to independence, with the first purchases of Russian equipment made in 1967.
“I am glad that we are back in full cooperation with our Russian friends,” he said, adding that the UPDF had pledged to keep the equipment in good condition and use it efficiently.
The Minister of Defence and Veteran Affairs, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, said the facilities reflected the value of Uganda’s long-standing bilateral relations with Russia and the benefits of continued engagement between the two countries.
“Today’s ceremony is important not only because we are commissioning new facilities, but because it reflects the value that Uganda attaches to this long-standing bilateral relationship with the Russian Federation,” he said.
Kiryowa said the assistance came at a time when security challenges and advances in military technology required reliable equipment, well-trained personnel and improved capabilities in reconnaissance, surveillance, mobility, command and control, logistics and training.
He expressed appreciation to the Russian Federation and its military technical experts for their professional expertise, technical guidance and contribution to the development of Uganda’s defence infrastructure.
The UPDF Chief of Joint Staff, Lieutenant General Bakasumba, said the donation was a significant step towards strengthening the UPDF’s technical capacity, improving the maintenance and repair of military equipment, and enhancing the operational readiness of the forces.
Bakasumba said the facilities will improve UPDF’s ability to conduct extensive equipment repairs, extend the service life of military assets and develop technical skills among personnel.
He urged commanders and technical personnel to ensure proper management, effective utilisation and regular maintenance of the facilities. “Guard this investment and ensure that it delivers the intended benefits to the UPDF and the country at large,” he said.
Speaking on behalf of the Russian delegation, Lieutenant General (Rtd) Aleksandr Kshimovskii said the event reflected mutual interest, mutual respect and long-standing relations between the two countries, as well as friendship between their leaders.
He said the scale of the military technical assistance reflected the strength of the bilateral partnership and expressed confidence that the facilities will enhance the UPDF’s technical capabilities, strengthen Uganda’s defence capacity and contribute to regional stability.
In October 2025, Museveni expressed Uganda’s gratitude to the Russian Federation while receiving an earlier consignment of military and engineering equipment under the bilateral defence cooperation framework. The UPDF said this included an “obstacle clearer” and trench digger as well as boats, workshops and a coastal station.
Photographs of the October 2025 event showed the donation included two IMR armoured engineering vehicles, which use the hull from a T-55 tank with a bulldozer blade at the front and a telescopic arm to grab and move obstacles. Also seen was a TMK-2 wheeled trench digger, two GAZ-66 trucks with shelters, two towed generators, what appeared to be a Project BL-820 boat that is used by Russian naval and security forces as well as two smaller rigid hull inflatables made by the Russian company Mnev & Co, according to Janes’ analysis.
Uganda has received a significant amount of military hardware from Russia in recent years, including Mi-28 attack helicopters, T-90 tanks, and Mi-171 transport helicopters. In 2022 Uganda commissioned a maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility for UPDF Mi-24 helicopters. It was established in collaboration with Russian company Pro-heli International.

body: In today’s Nigerian newspapers review programme, Today in the News, Vanguard leads with banks raising lending rates for the biggest borrowers despite the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) lowering interest rate.
