title: Morocco receives another six AH-64 Apaches
body:
The Royal Moroccan Air Force has taken delivery of another six Boeing AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, bringing the total of delivered aircraft to 19 out of 24 ordered.
A ribbon-cutting ceremony to mark the receipt of the latest six aircraft was held on 26 October at 1st BAFRA (1ère Base Aérienne des Forces Royales Air) in Sale, next to Rabat-Sale International Airport. Major General Matthew W Brown, commanding general of US Army Southern European Task Force, Africa SETAF-AF), joined senior leaders of the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces for the event.
“This ceremony marks a consequential moment made possible by Morocco’s commitment to its own defense capabilities and the broader security of the region,” Brown said. “The aircraft before us is the most capable attack and reconnaissance helicopter in the world.”
The Apache supports the Joint Readiness and Interoperability objectives of the 2026-2036 Defense Cooperation Roadmap, which was signed at the Pentagon in April, SETAF-AF said. Brown said US and Moroccan pilots and land forces will train together on the aircraft during future African Lion exercises.
“Integrating these platforms into the continent’s premier joint exercise will directly increase our combined readiness, making our forces stronger, and more capable of operating and fighting alongside each other,” Brown added.
He said Morocco’s leadership in regional security is “vital and deeply valued by the United States of America” and that the ribbon cutting “clearly showcases the strength of our alliance.”
“We look forward to the continued growth of this historic alliance as we strive for a future of shared security, stability, and regional peace,” he added.
Morocco was the first country to recognize the US, in 1777, and the two nations share the longest-standing treaty relationship in US history.
The Royal Moroccan Air Force received its first six Apaches, via ship, in March 2025. Deliveries were originally scheduled to take place from 2024, but were delayed.
Boeing began manufacturing Morocco’s first AH-64Es in late 2023 after receiving an order for 24 in June 2020 under a $1.3 billion deal. The company is building the new Moroccan Apaches under a contract with the US Army through the US government’s Foreign Military Sales process.
In November 2019 Morocco requested the sale of 24 new helicopters and 12 options, along with AGM-114R/L Hellfire missiles, Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System munitions, AIM-92H Stinger missiles, M261 rocket launchers, 70 mm rockets and 30 mm cannon ammunition in a potential deal worth $1.5 billion.
The AH-64E that Morocco has ordered features an improved Modernized Target Acquisition Designation System that provides day, night and all-weather target information, as well as night vision navigation capability. In addition to classifying ground and air targets, Boeing said the Longbow Fire Control Radar has been updated to operate in a maritime environment.
Morocco is one of two African nations (the other being Egypt) that operate the Apache, and the only one that operates the AH-64E. Before Apache deliveries, Morocco’s military had no dedicated attack helicopter, instead relying on two dozen Gazelles flown by both Army Aviation and the Royal Moroccan Air Force.
Morocco is also acquiring other military aviation assets from the United States, including 25 F-16C/D Block 72 fighter jets to replace the Mirage F1s it received in the 1970s, the Northrop F-5E/F Tiger IIs it received in the 1980s, and to augment and eventually replace its F-16C/Ds. Lockheed Martin flew Morocco’s first F-16 Block 72 at the beginning of October.
The Royal Moroccan Air Force flies 23 F-16C/D Block 50/52 aircraft that it received from 2011 to 2012 (one was lost over Yemen during operations as part of the Saudi-led coalition). The US Defence Security Cooperation Agency in 2019 approved the upgrade of these aircraft to the latest F-16V Block 70/72 standard at a cost of $985.2 million.
Other purchases from the US include 18 M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) launchers, M57 Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) rounds, 40 AGM-154C Joint Stand Off Weapons (JSOW), and 612 FGM-148F Javelin missiles, among others.
Morocco is aggressively modernising its air force to counter Algiers’ formidable arsenal, thanks in part to a large defence budget increase. Its defence budget jumped to $15.3 billion in 2026, a 17.7% hike year-on-year. Complementing acquisitions, Morocco is fostering a burgeoning defence industry through joint ventures, partnerships, and financial incentives.
Recent Air Force acquisitions have included four Gulfstream G550s in an ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance) configuration, and various drones including Israeli Heron, Hermes 900, Chinese Wing Loong-2 and Turkish TB2 and Akinci drones.
Morocco has already acquired numerous air defence systems from China, France, Israel, and from the United States, and worked to establish a strong multi-layered network. This network includes a plethora of long range systems (HQ-9B, Barak 8, and Patriot PAC-3), mid-range systems (SPYDER, MICA VL, and Sky Dragon 50) and short range systems (Stinger and Mistral), and is supported by various radar systems such as Ground-Master 400s purchased from France.
Similarly, the Moroccan helicopter force has been growing at a steady pace with10 H225M transport helicopters ordered in November 2025 (the first six arrived in March 2025 and the next six followed in early April this year).

title: Strengthening India’s Indigenous Navigation Capabilities
body:
By R Anil Kumar 

Bengaluru, Nov 1, 2026. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully accomplished the GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission on 30 October 2026 at 23:51 hours from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC), Sriharikota.



The GSLV-F18 launch vehicle injected the Navigation Satellite NVS-03 into a precise Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). Subsequently, first orbit manoeuvre completed on 31 October 2026 at 16:48 hours. Further manoeuvres are planned to place it in its designated geosynchronous orbital slot at 111.75° East.

The satellite is the third in India's series of five next-generation Navigation satellites and is designed to strengthen the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), enhancing India's capabilities in satellite-based navigation.

Facts to Know: A spacecraft destined for geosynchronous or geostationary orbit is generally first placed in an elliptical Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). This orbit has a low perigee (closest point to Earth) and a high apogee (farthest point from Earth). For a conventional GTO, the apogee is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's surface. Near apogee, the spacecraft fires its onboard propulsion system to raise its perigee and circularise its orbit. Additional manoeuvres may adjust its orbital inclination and position, depending on the target orbit. The propulsion system used for these orbit-raising manoeuvres is commonly called an Apogee Motor. In the case of NVS-03, the orbit-raising manoeuvre was performed using its Liquid Apogee Motor (LAM), a type of chemical rocket engine.



Key Highlights of the Mission:

 	Successful Launch: GSLV-F18 placed NVS-03 into its intended Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). This marks another milestone in India's efforts to strengthen its satellite navigation infrastructure.
 	20th GSLV Flight: The mission marks the 20th flight of India's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. It demonstrates the continued operational use of India's launch vehicle for strategic space missions.
 	Next-Generation Series Satellite: NVS-03 is the third satellite of second-generation NavIC satellites (NVS-01 to NVS-05). These satellites are designed to strengthen the coverage, accuracy and reliability of India's regional navigation system.

Satellite Navigation System:

A Satellite Navigation System is a network of satellites that provides positioning, navigation and timing information. These satellites continuously transmit signals containing their location and precise timing information. Receivers, such as smartphones, vehicles and navigation devices, use signals from multiple satellites to determine their precise location, speed and direction. These systems support several applications, including route naviiesation, aircraft and ship tracking, precision agriculture, disaster management and telecommunications. Examples include the Global Positioning System (GPS) of the United States, and Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) of India.

Enhanced Navigation Signals:

NVS-03 carries navigation payloads in the L1, L5 and S frequency bands. The inclusion of the L1 signal alongside the L5 and S signals continues to enhance NavIC's capabilities and compatibility. It supports navigation coverage across India's landmass and a region extending 1,500 km beyond its geopolitical boundary.

Using multiple frequency bands allows compatible receivers to access signals transmitted at different frequencies. It also provides options for designing receivers suited to different applications and operating conditions.

Navigation Signals and Their Frequency Bands:

Navigation signals are radio-frequency signals transmitted by navigation satellites to receivers on Earth. These signals carry precise timing information and satellite-position data. Receivers use this information to calculate their location, speed and time. Frequency bands are specific ranges of radio frequencies used to transmit these signals. Satellite navigation systems use designated portions of the radio-frequency spectrum. Different bands allow signals to be transmitted and received at different frequencies.

Indigenous Technology: NVS-03 carries an indigenously developed atomic clock alongside procured atomic clocks. These clocks provide highly precise time references for navigation signal generation. Accurate timing is essential for determining signal travel times and calculating user positions.

Wider Applications: NVS-03 strengthens India's independent Positioning, Navigation and Timing (PNT) capabilities. These capabilities support applications across transportation, maritime operations, aviation, disaster management, precision agriculture and strategic services. Read more on Strengthening India’s Space Sovereignty

Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV):

The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is a three-stage launch vehicle developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to place satellites into Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) and Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The feature that makes GSLV unique from other launch vehicles is its final stage, which uses an indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage. Additionally, the boosters used in GSLV are liquid-powered, popularly known as L-40, and use a hypergolic combination of Nitrogen Tetroxide (N₂O₄) and UH25 (a mixture of 75% Unsymmetrical Dimethylhydrazine (UDMH) and 25% Hydrazine Hydrate) Read More on GTO.

The GSLV-F18 stands approximately 50 metres tall, with a lift-off mass of around 420 tonnes. It features a 3.4-metre-diameter metallic payload fairing and successfully carried the approximately 2,250 kg NVS-03 navigation satellite.

Cryogenic Upper Stage: A cryogenic upper stage is the final stage of a launch vehicle that uses these propellants to provide the high efficiency needed to place satellites into their intended orbits. ISRO’s indigenous cryogenic upper stage used on GSLV employs liquid hydrogen (LH₂) as fuel and liquid oxygen (LOX) as oxidiser, both stored at extremely low temperatures. It replaced the Russian-supplied stage used in earlier GSLV flights, strengthening India’s self-reliance in advanced launch vehicle technology.

Understanding NavIC: India's Indigenous Navigation System

NavIC is India's regional satellite navigation system, developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

It was earlier known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS).

The system provides Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) services to users.

NavIC was originally designed with a seven-satellite constellation supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Its architecture comprises three satellites in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit. The NVS series is being deployed to augment the existing constellation and ensure continuity of navigation services.

NavIC covers the Indian landmass and a region extending approximately 1,500 km beyond India's geopolitical boundary.

The NVS series adds L1 to the legacy L5 and S signals.

Two Types of Navigation Services

NavIC provides two types of navigation services to cater to civilian and authorised strategic users.

Standard Positioning Service: (SPS): An open navigation service available to civilian users. NavIC SPS signals are interoperable with the other global navigation satellite system (GNSS) signals like GPS (USA), Glonass (Russia), Galileo (EU) and BeiDou (China).

Restricted Service (RS): An encrypted navigation service available exclusively to strategic users.

Progress of the Next-Generation Navigation Satellite Series:

The five-satellite NVS series is being developed to augment the NavIC constellation and ensure continuity of indigenous navigation services. To date, NVS-01, NVS-02, and NVS-03 have been launched, while NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in the pipeline. ISRO is working to boost the coverage, reliability and availability of NavIC services. Read more on India's Space Odyssey

NVS-01 – First Satellite of the Next/Second-Generation Series

 	GSLV-F12, the 15th flight of India’s GSLV, placed NVS-01 into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit.
 	NVS-01 was launched on 29 May 2023. It is the first satellite of the second-generation NavIC series. It is designed to ensure continuity of legacy NavIC services.
 	It carries navigation payloads in the L1, L5 and S bands.
 	Its lift-off mass is about 2,232 kg.
 	The mission life of NVS-01 is 12 years.
 	It carries an indigenously developed Rubidium atomic clock, built by the Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad.

NVS-02 – Second Satellite of the Series

 	NVS-02 was launched on 29 January 2025 aboard GSLV-F15.
 	It carries L1, L5 and S band navigation payloads, plus a C-band ranging payload.
 	NVS-02 had a lift-off mass of 2,250 kg.
 	It used a mix of indigenous and procured atomic clocks for precise time estimation.
 	After launch, orbit-raising could not be carried out because the oxidiser valves did not open. As a result, the satellite could not reach its intended orbital slot.

NVS-04 and NVS-05 – Upcoming Satellites:

NVS-04 and NVS-05 are the fourth and fifth satellites planned in the second-generation NavIC series.

Like the earlier NVS satellites, they are expected to carry the L1 signal alongside L5 and S. Both are envisaged to offer enhanced navigation capabilities.

One More Step Towards India's Space Sovereignty

The successful development and deployment of next-generation NavIC satellites mark another milestone in India's journey towards Atmanirbhar Bharat in advanced space technology. By strengthening indigenous satellite navigation capabilities, India is enhancing its ability to provide reliable positioning, navigation and timing services independently. These advancements reduce dependence on foreign satellite navigation systems for critical applications. They also strengthen India's technological capacity to design, develop and operate strategic space infrastructure. These efforts reinforce India's space sovereignty, technological self-reliance and growing role in the global space sector.

title: Sultan Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III: Twenty years of a reign shaped by destiny, By Samuel Aruwan
body:
Today, 2 November 2026, Sultan Sa’ad marks exactly twenty years on the throne. He is the Sultan with the longest reign in this century and, by commonly accepted reign dates, ranks third in length of reign in the history of the Sultanate. During 2027, he is expected to surpass Sultan Muhammadu Bello and move into second place, behind only his father.
When little Sa’ad, the prince who would become Sultan Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III, was born on Friday, 24 August 1956, to Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III and Hajiya Fadimatu Binta Abubakar, neither his father, who was 53, nor his mother nor anyone in the Sultanate could have known what Allah had written for him. No one could have foreseen that he would become a military officer, serve across Nigeria and beyond, and return decades later as the twentieth Sultan of Sokoto. As he marks twenty years on the throne, the course of that journey can be seen more clearly. The throne was not the visible destination of his childhood. That knowledge belonged to Allah alone.
If any of Sultan Abubakar III’s sons appeared close to the throne, it was Sultan Sa’ad’s much older brother, Sultan Muhammadu Maccido, who was 30 when Sultan Sa’ad Abubakar III was born. Sultan Maccido became their father’s trusted aide and one of the principal contenders when Sultan Abubakar III died in 1988. Destiny first turned elsewhere with the emergence of Sultan Ibrahim Dasuki. Eight years later, Sultan Maccido was appointed Sultan. He reigned for a decade before dying with his son, Senator Badamasi Maccido, and grandson in the ADC Airlines Flight 53 crash of 29 October 2006.
Sultan Sa’ad’s mother lived to witness his accession, a blessing denied his father and brother. Hadijatu Kubbura died months before Sultan Abubakar III became Sultan in 1938, while Sultan Maccido’s mother, Hauwa, died before his accession in 1996. Sultan Abubakar III was 35 when his paternal uncle and guardian, Sultan Hassan Dan Mu’azu, died on 31 May 1938. Still grieving both his mother and the uncle who had raised him and prayed that he would succeed, he became the seventeenth Sultan on 17 June 1938.
Sultan Sa’ad did not rise through the conventional hierarchy of palace and district titles, but he was never a stranger to the Sultanate. He witnessed at close quarters how his father administered its affairs and accompanied him on journeys to Maiduguri, Kaduna and elsewhere, observing his engagement with governments, traditional rulers, religious authorities and diverse communities. His apprenticeship began at his father’s side and continued through national service.
His entry into the Army was unexpected. After performing well in his West African School Certificate examination, he appeared destined for further study. Soldiering was not his youthful ambition, and he had not joined Barewa College’s Student Cadet Force. His direction changed after General TY Danjuma visited Sokoto and urged Sultan Abubakar III to encourage educated northern youths to join the Army after the Civil War. Deciding that the response should begin at home, Sultan Abubakar III ensured that seven eligible young men from his household applied to the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA). All sat the entrance examination, three reached the interview stage, but only Sultan Sa’ad succeeded.
He entered the NDA on 30 June 1975 as a member of the 18th Regular Combatant Course and was commissioned a second lieutenant on 17 December 1977. Posted to the Armoured Corps, he held command, operational, staff and diplomatic appointments, including service in Chad and Sierra Leone. He rose to brigadier general and served as Nigeria’s Defence Adviser to Pakistan. The prince who left Sokoto returned as a commander, peacekeeper and diplomat.
Following Sultan Maccido’s death, Sultan Sa’ad hurried from Jos to Sokoto to join the royal family in receiving condolences. Nothing publicly suggested that he was returning to seek the throne. The contenders included older traditional titleholders and public servants from distinguished branches of the ruling family. His military career had kept him outside the traditional hierarchy, making his selection surprising to many. On Thursday, 2 November 2006, the grieving younger brother was announced as Sultan.
He was formally installed and presented with the staff of office on Saturday, 3 March 2007. The ceremony drew President Olusegun Obasanjo and traditional rulers from across Nigeria. Sultan Sa’ad renewed his pledge to uphold equity, fairness and justice, moving from military command to moral leadership sustained by credibility, restraint and persuasion.
When Sultan Sa’ad ascended the throne, several revered monarchs who had interacted with Sultan Abubakar III were still reigning. They included Emir Ado Bayero of Kano, Emir Shehu Idris of Zazzau, Shehu Mustapha Umar El Kanemi of Borno, Lamido Aliyu Mustapha of Adamawa, Oegwam Oegworok Gwamna Awan, Attah Aliyu Obaje of Igala and Aku Uka Shekarau Angyu Masa Ibi Kuvyon II of Wukari. Sultan Sa’ad engaged them in his own right, while their memories of his father provided a living connection between the two reigns. Emir Ado Bayero and Shehu Mustapha were among the rulers who attended his formal installation in 2007.
Two decades later, Sultan Sa’ad occupies the senior position once held by those older monarchs. Rulers who came to their thrones after him include Emir Umar Faruq Umar of Daura, Emir Abdulmumini Kabir Usman of Katsina, Oegwam Oegworok Ufuwai Bonet, Shehu Abubakar Garbai El Kanemi of Borno, Lamido Muhammadu Barkindo Aliyu Mustapha of Adamawa, Emir Rilwanu Suleiman Adamu of Bauchi, Emir Muhammadu Sanusi II of Kano, Emir Abubakar Shehu Abubakar III of Gombe, Emir Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli of Zazzau, Attah Matthew Alaji Opaluwa of Igala and Aku Uka Manu Ishaku Ada Ali of Wukari. Sultan Sa’ad has become a dean and senior reference point among them, offering experience, institutional memory and counsel. The prince who sat among rulers who knew his father now guides a younger generation of monarchs.
What appeared unplanned was preparation by another route. Sultan Sa’ad carried an established philosophy of leadership into a new age. During the upheavals of 1966, Sultan Abubakar III shuttled between Kaduna and Lagos, consulting leaders and helping to calm the country while mourning his kinsman and counsellor, Sir Ahmadu Bello. He condemned violence, discouraged reprisals and opposed taking the law into private hands. In his broadcast of 17 June 1966, he reassured frightened communities, asked people from other provinces not to leave the North and invited those who had fled to return. He deployed his moral authority in defence of peace and national unity.
Sultan Abubakar III’s accommodation of religious difference was also evident in his dealings with Christian missions. In “ Sir Siddiq Abubakar III, 17th Sultan of Sokoto ,” Alhaji Shehu Malami devotes a section to those relations. Mukhtar Umar Bunza and Jamilu Shehu provide an example in their 2018 study, “ Sudan Interior Mission: An Evangelical Operation for a Unique Task in Northern Nigeria to 1960 .” Drawing on a colonial record preserved at the National Archives, Kaduna, they state that when Christian boys began attending the Sokoto Native Authority School, Sultan Abubakar III paid for their Bibles. The gesture, entirely consistent with his Islamic convictions, reflected his willingness to accommodate the religious needs of Christians under his authority.
His openness was equally evident across ethnic lines. In “ Indigeneity , Ethnicity and Federalism ,” published in “ Transition Without End ,” Daniel C. Bach recounts the story of Alhaji Mamman Dike, known as Deke, an Igbo man born in Asaba. Other accounts identify him as Dike Okwuosa. After bringing the first motorcar to the Native Authority workshop during the reign of Sultan Muhammadu Maiturare, from 1915 to 1924, Deke entered palace service and served successive Sultans. Sultan Abubakar III valued him because “ he could keep secrets ,” made him his most trusted servant and entrusted him with the keys to his private apartments. Deke married two Hausa women, had eleven children, remained in Sokoto throughout the Civil War and died there on 22 May 1990. His life showed how trust, loyalty and belonging could transcend ethnic origin.
The tradition continued with Sultan Muhammadu Maccido, who maintained a close friendship with Chief Joe Ifedobi, the Okosisi of Akpo. Published recollections state that Chief Ifedobi drove him to the airport shortly before his appointment as Sultan was announced in 1996. Their friendship endured until Sultan Maccido’s death in 2006.
Sultan Sa’ad has carried that inheritance into a different age. His father taught that faith, education, productive work, justice, security and social welfare belonged together, and that material progress without discipline, tolerance and humility was incomplete. Sultan Sa’ad has applied those principles in democratic Nigeria, working with Muslim and Christian leaders, governments, security authorities and communities across ethnic and regional boundaries, despite exercising no executive power.
His twenty years have spanned the administrations of Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, Goodluck Jonathan, Muhammadu Buhari and Bola Ahmed Tinubu. If Sultan Abubakar III preserved the Sultanate through colonial rule, independence, coups and eight federal administrations, Sultan Sa’ad has sustained its moral authority through terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, violence between farmers and herders, communal conflict and political division. Like his father in the 1960s, he has not been absent from Nigeria’s most difficult national conversations.
He has repeatedly condemned Boko Haram, banditry and violence committed in the name of religion. Following the killing of Deborah Samuel in Sokoto in May 2022, the Sultanate Council condemned the act as unjustifiable and demanded that the perpetrators face justice. The principle was unmistakable. No allegation permits a mob to become accuser, judge and executioner. Every grievance must be subjected to the law, irrespective of the religion of the accused or the victim.
My encounters with Sultan Sa’ad span nearly two decades. I began covering him as a journalist in 2007 at meetings of the Northern Governors’ Forum, the Northern Traditional Rulers Council and Jama’atu Nasril Islam. I also recorded and reported his BBC and VOA Hausa interviews, particularly on security. Our paths crossed again in 2015 and continued throughout my decade of service in different capacities in the Kaduna State Government. That contact revealed the consistency of his concern for peace, security, religious harmony and national unity.
His campaign for peace has also travelled abroad. I was with Sultan Sa’ad at the 2022 International Ministerial Conference on Freedom of Religion or Belief in London, where he joined religious leaders, rights advocates and government representatives in advancing religious tolerance. As President General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and joint chairman of the Nigeria Inter Religious Council, he has worked with successive leaders of the Christian Association of Nigeria. The armoured officer now influences through consultation, restraint and persuasion.
The anniversary carries a rare historical distinction. Sultan Abubakar III’s reign of more than fifty years remains the longest in Sokoto’s history, while Sultan Muhammadu Bello ruled for approximately twenty and a half years in the nineteenth century. Today, 2 November 2026, Sultan Sa’ad marks exactly twenty years on the throne. He is the Sultan with the longest reign in this century and, by commonly accepted reign dates, ranks third in length of reign in the history of the Sultanate. During 2027, he is expected to surpass Sultan Muhammadu Bello and move into second place, behind only his father.
After twenty years on the throne, Sultan Sa’ad stands at the intersection of palace and barracks, mosque and interfaith table, inherited authority and democratic citizenship. Events he did not arrange redirected his life. His father’s response to General Danjuma’s appeal took him into the Army. Military service prepared him for unforeseen responsibilities. His brother’s death brought him home to mourn, only for the kingmakers to entrust him with the Sultanate.
The child whose future only Allah knew served at home and abroad before returning to continue an old legacy in a democratic era. What seemed unplanned was destiny unfolding in its appointed time.
Samuel Aruwan is a postgraduate student at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

title: Tehran, Ashgabat emphasize strengthening all-out relations
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Iran’s Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi and his Turkmen counterpart Raşit Meredow have explored avenues for expanding bilateral, regional, and international relations.
Both sides reviewed the latest state of relations between Tehran and Ashgabat and emphasized leveraging capacities to develop cooperation in various political and economic fields.
Turning to the historical ties between the two nations, Meredow said this closeness serves as the foundation for advancing relations in the future.
He lauded expanding relations with Iran in commercial, political, and cultural fields.
He appreciated Iran’s companionship with Turkmenistan in various international arenas.
Iran’s top diplomat arrived in Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan on Monday to hold talks with the country’s high-ranking officials.
Bilateral relations, regional and international developments, and avenues to bolster political and economic cooperation between Iran and Turkmenistan are among the main topics of discussion during Araghchi’s one-day visit to this country.
Relations between Tehran and Ashgabat have continued to boost over the years, with both sides emphasizing the need to make use of existing capacities to further develop bilateral ties.

title: Horrific discovery at cemetery renews debate over fate of stray dogs in Georgia
body: Journalists and animal rights activists have discovered burial pits in Georgia’s capital Tbilisi , containing dozens of dead dogs dumped and covered with soil. Activists suspect the animals were healthy strays taken from the city streets. Judging by the condition of the bodies, veterinarians believe the dogs suffered greatly before they died. The disturbing footage sparked widespread outrage on social media. Animal rights activists have called for an immediate investigation. A large protest took place in Tbilisi on the evening of 1 November. The city authorities deny accusations that they killed healthy dogs, dismiss them as a deliberate disinformation campaign and threaten criminal charges against activists who opened the burial pits without permission. Nevertheless, Georgia’s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which concerns animal cruelty. Rabies quarantine introduced in two regions of Georgia “Don’t pass the ‘foreign agents’ bill; Georgia’s homeless animals will be left helpless.” – Animal rights activists What do we know so far about the dog burial pits discovered in Tbilisi? Why do animal rights activists distrust the city authorities and municipal services? And why has Georgia been unable to solve its stray animal problem for years? Night-time trips to Veli Cemetery Blurred photograph of one of the burial sites at Veli Cemetery in Tbilisi. As the footage filmed by activists is extremely distressing, JAMnews has deliberately chosen not to use it in this article. Under cover of darkness, a white minibus leaves Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter. Someone has removed the shelter’s logo from the vehicle. The minibus soon stops at Veli Cemetery on the outskirts of the Georgian capital. The engine keeps running, but the driver switches off the headlights. Two people get out. They wear the shelter’s uniform and latex gloves. In complete darkness, lit only by the moon, they take the bodies of dogs out of the vehicle and dump them into pits that someone has dug in advance. Why stray dogs vanish in Georgia — and why activists distrust the authorities’ answers For several months, stray dogs in Georgia have been disappearing without explanation. Animal rights activists suspect authorities are simply killing them, but state agencies deny the allegations. This continues over several nights. On one occasion, the workers dump seven dogs into a pit, while an eighth falls beside the vehicle. Despite the darkness, the footage clearly shows a man wearing gloves dragging the animal towards the burial site. On the third night, the makeshift grave is already full of dogs’ bodies, and the workers begin covering it with soil. They do this in darkness too, switching on the vehicle’s headlights only occasionally to check their progress. These images come from a report that TV Pirveli broadcast on 31 October. It documents alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Tbilisi. Someone filmed the footage with a hidden camera over several nights. According to the programme’s journalists, people regularly remove dozens of dead dogs from Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter without permission and bury them in specially dug deep pits at the cemetery. Citing their sources, the journalists also report that the shelter has a quarantine area where staff euthanise healthy animals picked up from the streets. Even before the report aired, shortly after the channel announced it, animal rights activists discovered additional burial sites near Veli Cemetery. They filmed and circulated even more disturbing footage. It shows graves filled with dogs whose eyes bulge and bodies appear twisted (JAMnews warning: the footage at this link is extremely distressing.) The activists called the police to the site. Police representatives told TV Pirveli that they would investigate the matter step by step and report their findings. Animal rights activists’ demands After the story came to light, animal rights activists drew up a petition , calling on the prosecutor’s office to launch an immediate investigation. The petition’s authors point to an increasing number of suspicious cases in which dogs have disappeared across Georgia. They want investigators to examine the burial site at Veli Cemetery, exhume the remains and commission an independent veterinary and forensic examination to establish when and how the animals died. The activists also urge prosecutors to check the microchips and other identification marks on stray animals, compare reports from members of the public about missing dogs with the remains found at the cemetery, and examine the shelter’s veterinary records on euthanasia and its accounts of drugs used for the procedure. In their view, investigators must establish who ordered the animals’ burial, the legal grounds for removing their bodies and whether the burial process complied with the law. The petition’s authors stress that the public has the right to know how many animals died, under what circumstances and whether official statistics reflect the true scale of the situation. Some people recognised among the dead dogs found at the burial site in Veli Cemetery strays they had been caring for. The image illustrates one such case: a Tbilisi resident writes on social media that a dog he looked after is lying in the pit (right-hand photo). Tbilisi City Hall denies killing animals The Animal Monitoring Agency, which operates under Tbilisi City Hall, denies the allegations. In an official statement , the agency says that “the footage broadcast by TV Pirveli shows a procedure permitted by law”. The agency claims that the burial site at Veli Cemetery holds the remains of dogs that died in Tbilisi for various reasons, including illness, road accidents and other incidents, as well as natural causes. “Across the capital, hundreds of animals die through euthanasia every year, while thousands die of natural causes,” the agency says in its statement. It categorically denies allegations of mass, deliberate killings, insisting that the information circulated by journalists and activists amounts to disinformation intended to discredit the Animal Monitoring Agency and damage its reputation. Tbilisi City Hall also says that unauthorised exhumations and the removal of remains violate the law, risk biological contamination and pose a threat to public health. On these grounds, the city authorities have threatened activists with criminal liability. “We have already asked law enforcement agencies to investigate acts of vandalism committed by a particular group and take appropriate legal action,” City Hall said. 'Don’t kill stray animals': Activists in Georgia issue joint statement Joint statement by Georgian animal welfare activists criticises stray animal programme launched by National Food Agency Signs of torture on the animals’ bodies Animal rights activists question the agency’s claims that the dogs found at Veli Cemetery died of natural causes or were humanely euthanised. Activist Keso Baramidze , who has had dozens of animals euthanised when it was genuinely necessary, says dogs usually retain a peaceful expression after euthanasia. “Sadly, dozens of animals have fallen asleep in my arms. Not one of them had an expression like the dogs found in the burial pits. They all simply looked as though they were sleeping. That is why the procedure is called ‘putting to sleep’,” she says in a social media post. Baramidze outlines several possible causes of muscle tension and facial distortion in animals after death. These include: Mechanical asphyxiation (strangulation) with a rope or wire, as well as burying an animal alive or while it still shows signs of life. This can deprive it of oxygen and cause severe agony; Improperly administered chemical euthanasia – using drugs that cause muscle paralysis or other toxic substances without adequate anaesthesia. In such cases, the animal may die while still conscious; Severe physical trauma or electric shock – a powerful blow to the head or neck, or exposure to an electric current, which can cause severe muscle spasms and body tension. “With any of these methods, when a dog dies amid extreme stress, fear, struggle and muscle exhaustion, its reserves of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) are depleted almost immediately. This causes rigor mortis to set in very early, almost instantly, within the first 10–20 minutes. “Since rigor mortis always begins in the facial and jaw muscles, any grimace caused during the animal’s death throes becomes ‘frozen’. Even while the body remains warm, the face stays contorted,” Baramidze writes, citing scientific sources from abroad. Protests and investigation On Sunday, 1 November, the day after the report aired, animal rights activists staged a protest outside the government chancellery in Tbilisi. “We demand answers. Punish the officials responsible,” they called. “Dogs tortured to death”, “Where have you taken the dogs?”, “I speak for those without a voice” read the banners held by protesters, including both activists and ordinary animal lovers. Many brought their pets to the demonstration. “What we have been saying for several months has now been confirmed. They are continuing to exterminate stray dogs instead of sterilising and vaccinating them in an effort to reduce their numbers. I hope society will now become more active. Because if there aren’t enough of us, they will obviously not stop,” said Lasha Chkhartishvili, one of the protest organisers. Protest outside the Government Chancellery on 1 November 2026. Photo: Rusudan Jakeli. “A dog tortured to death” – reads the banner at the 1 November protest. That same evening, Georgia’s Interior Ministry announced that it had opened an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which covers torture, cruel treatment and other forms of violence against animals. Not an isolated incident, but a pattern This is not the first case, nor the first footage to emerge showing alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Georgia. In mid-October, a video filmed on a mobile phone at the municipal animal shelter in the town of Gori spread across social media. It showed a filthy enclosure measuring just five to seven square metres, with a damp floor and crammed with dozens of puppies. Many of the animals looked extremely thin and malnourished. The following day, volunteers rescued the puppies from the enclosures, set up temporary shelters for them and began treating them. Social media users also launched a fundraising campaign to help the puppies and the people who had taken them in. Earlier, in April 2026, disturbing footage from Gori also emerged, apparently showing animals being burned at a crematorium. However, the Gori shelter insisted that it had cremated dead dogs or amputated body parts. Stray animals on the streets have long been a serious problem in Georgia. The streets are full of stray dogs, some of which are aggressive and pose a danger to passers-by. Yet no one knows exactly how many homeless animals live in the country. Georgia has never maintained comprehensive statistics on their numbers. Animal rights activists estimate that the population could reach hundreds of thousands. Georgia has been running a new stray animal population management programme for the past two years. In theory, it should reduce the number of stray dogs through humane methods. However, animal rights activists suspect that the authorities are trying to solve the problem through straightforward extermination. They say dogs have been disappearing from the streets in large numbers since the programme began. JAMnews reported on the situation in May 2026, when activists across Georgia raised the alarm over dogs taken from the streets and then reported missing. Some of the animals had been cared for by specific individuals, vaccinated, sterilised and identified. The World Organisation for Animal Health recommends the CNVR method – Collect, Neuter, Vaccinate and Return – in its guidelines for managing stray dog populations. When properly implemented, this approach can gradually reduce the number of animals without resorting to mass killing. Activists in Georgia also regard this as the best approach. None of them wants packs of stray dogs roaming the streets. But they insist that the authorities must tackle the problem humanely. The footage that has emerged in recent weeks has raised growing questions about the conduct of government agencies and strengthened suspicions that the authorities intend to reduce the stray animal population by killing the dogs.

title: Show HN: Zero-knowledge zero-overhead LLM routing mesh using pure web primitives
body:
bringYourOwnBrain is an open-weight local AI platform that makes running small open weight LLMs free and easy for both devs and users on WebGPU & WASM.
No servers to deploy, no API keys to hide, and no token invoices. Compute belongs to the player.
In this initial release, the player clicks "Connect Local AI". An isolated sandbox loads the lightweight Qwen2.5 0.5B (more model options are being added regularly) open model directly onto their graphics card via WebGPU (with automatic WASM CPU fallback).
Inference streams straight into your game logic at native frame rates. No user prompts ever leave the browser, and you never pay an AI API token bill.
Experience what local open-weight intelligence feels like inside standard web games.
To my knowledge, this may be the world's first physics-driven, interruptible local AI NPC(s). Shove or get shoved mid-sentence to trigger an instant canned reaction or interruption. The game is a tip of the hat to a friend / dedication to Steven J. Horst and his 'old-ass' black cat, Midnight (2026)
A minimalist vanilla JS chat room demonstrating streaming token queues, local connection states, and responsive typewriter rendering.
For convenience with testing how the browser storage cache share operates in cross-origin manner , I have provided the demo chat on multiple domains: View on ResearchSimulator.com View on PathMap.org View on Hackathon.Games
Tell us what you want to build and we can pre-build a prompt for you to make an AI powered browser game using your favorite large LLM (e.g., Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, etc). Just copy the mega-prompt into free Claude or Gemini, and generate your own physics-driven BYOB AI games.
Tell us what AI game you think would be fun and get a free guide + instant one-shot prompt to make it and play it today. Zero accounts. Zero email. 100% Free.
Drop this into any HTML page. Works in pure JavaScript, React, Canvas, Phaser, or Matter.js.
Uses WebLLM to run open weights models on Apple Silicon, Nvidia, and AMD GPUs.
If WebGPU is unavailable or disabled, the engine automatically falls back to CPU via Transformers.js with zero code changes.
Built on radical local privacy and open-source transparency.

The BYOB Web SDK and connection bridge are open-source under the Apache 2.0 License .

title: Marshal Shaposhnikov frigate to participate in Russian-Seychelles military exercise
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. The Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov has docked at the port of Victoria in the Seychelles for a business call and to take part in the first Russian-Seychelles joint anti-piracy exercise, the fleet’s press service reported.
"The Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov has arrived at the port of Victoria in the Republic of Seychelles for a business call. Russian sailors were welcomed at the port by representatives of the Russian Embassy and the Seychelles Navy command. During the ship’s stay in the Seychelles, joint Russian-Seychelles naval anti-piracy drills will be held for the first time," the press service said.
It added that protocol, cultural and sports events for sailors from both countries are also planned during the port call.

title: Kazakhstan Opens Small Modular Reactor Simulator for Nuclear Training
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan has opened a training classroom featuring a simulator of the SMR-300 small modular reactor at the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Almaty on Oct. 30 to provide practical training for specialists in the nuclear energy sector. Photo credit: Aleksandr Pavsky / Kazinform. The training complex was established under the FIRST program, in which Kazakhstan has participated since 2022, becoming the program’s first partner in Central Asia. Launched in 2019 under the U.S. Department of State , the Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology ( FIRST) program harnesses the power of the nuclear industry and innovation to expedite deployment of SMRs worldwide. According to Sayabek Sakhiev, director general of the Institute of Nuclear Physics, the facility builds on the institute’s longstanding work in training professionals for the nuclear industry, reported the Kazinform news agency. “According to the recommendations of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), specialists with higher professional education for nuclear power plants should be trained on research reactors such as the one at the Institute of Nuclear Physics,” Sakhiev said. The institute’s training centers have prepared more than 5,000 specialists for Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. The new facility is also expected to serve as a regional training center. Based on the SMR-300 simulator, the complex is designed to support educational and practical training in small modular reactor technologies. The equipment has been installed and tested, with the facility intended to help students, young professionals, engineers and researchers develop practical skills. Asset Makhambetov. Photo credit: Aleksandr Pavsky / Kazinform. Asset Makhambetov, deputy chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy, said nuclear energy was becoming a strategic area of the country’s development. “The significance of the new training complex goes far beyond equipping it with modern technology. It will help improve the knowledge of Kazakh specialists and develop their practical skills,” he said. The next stage will involve developing training programs, scenarios and practical exercises in cooperation with the simulator’s developers. More than 1,300 students studying for nuclear sector Gulzat Kobenova, vice minister of science and higher education, said 12 universities in Kazakhstan train specialists in nuclear energy, including through partnerships with research institutes and foreign universities. Gulzat Kobenova. Photo credit: Aleksandr Pavsky / Kazinform. The new classroom will support not only lessons but also research projects, master’s programs, doctoral research and scientific internships. More than 1,300 students are currently enrolled in relevant programs at Kazakh universities, 96% of whom study under state-funded educational programs, according to Kobenova. The country’s annual demand for new specialists is estimated at approximately 200 to 300 people. The Institute of Nuclear Physics is also preparing a separate classroom for senior-year students specialising in nuclear energy. The opening of the facility forms part of cooperation between Kazakhstan and the United States on the peaceful use of nuclear energy and the development of modern nuclear technologies. The post Kazakhstan Opens Small Modular Reactor Simulator for Nuclear Training appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: TRIBUTE: Chief C.O. Adebayo: Remembering a true hero one year after
body:
Some people leave lasting marks, memories, and imprints on our lives. The late Chief Cornelius Olatunji Adebayo, former university lecturer, Second Republic governor of Kwara State, Senator, former minister of communications, and later transportation, a formidable figure of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), a leading voice for Afenifere, the Middle Belt Forum, and the Movement for National Reformation (MNR), amongst others, was one such person. He lived a purposeful life, defined by integrity, humility, and commitment to lofty ideals. He walked tall, carrying himself with grace, dignity and quiet self-confidence. One year later, I’m still trying to come to terms with the reality of his passing. Chief C.O. Adebayo, popularly known as C.O., left a lasting legacy. A year after his interment, we remember an elder statesman who meant so much to many people.
If you were an itinerant journalist covering politics in the early 1990s, you might well have encountered Chief C.O. Adebayo. I first met him 34 years ago at his Ilorin GRA home. I had gone to interview him as a member of the editorial team at the Lagos-based Classique magazine. I was excited to interview him. His handshake was firm, and he radiated warmth. His smile was infectious. He did not shy away from expressing his progressive views. During the interview, he spoke with clarity, precision, eloquence and coherence, so much so that I was at home with him. He was a consummate communicator and a great repository of knowledge. So, what began 34 years back as a journalistic encounter evolved into an enduring, lifelong bond until his passing last year. I have many fond memories of him. He had great oratorical skills- always delivering his points with clarity, excellent diction and rhythm. His simplicity was disarming. He was entirely without airs. There was never a time you visited C.O. Adebayo that he wouldn’t see you off, extend his customary friendly parting handshake!
I vividly remember the last time I saw him: in 2021, four years before his passing, when I visited him in his Abuja home. I had gone to check on him upon learning that he hadn’t been quite well. That afternoon, I met him with one of his daughters. He was his usual self- straightforward, attentive and jovial. As I sat with him that day, my mind went back to decades past when he was very active politically-with a commanding personality. We spent so much time together reminiscing on certain political developments and the state of the nation. He said he was very delighted and proud to see my name among those nominated by the then President, Muhammadu Buhari, as Ambassadors-designate. He promised to visit me in Bangkok, Thailand. Even then, I suspected he might not visit because of his age and the rigours of such a long trip. He was a visionary who gave his all to several organisations, including NADECO, MNR, Afenifere , and the Middle Belt Forum.
In fact, Chief Adebayo was a thought leader, a progressive compass, and a calming presence in turbulent times. Apart from being a towering figure in NADECO’s battle for the restoration of late Chief M.K.O. Abiola’s electoral mandate, C.O. Adebayo was a pivot in Afenifere, the Middle Belt Forum, and the MNR, respectively. An inimitable hero, a voice of reason and courage, late C.O. Adebayo exemplified exceptional integrity, uncommon moral force, and an extraordinary sense of both courage and compassion. His depth of thought, word choice, and unique storytelling style set him apart. He communicated his views with a peculiar ease and poise. Throughout my association with him, beginning in the early 1990s, he always evinced great wisdom, logic, strength of character and conviction.
Chief C.O. Adebayo’s insights were always pertinent, especially his vehement opposition to military rule and his call for Nigeria’s restructuring. His decency, affable disposition, and his inclination to counsel (freely) younger professionals like myself naturally drew us very close. Thus, a sustained relationship emerged that lasted for more than three decades. He was a go-to person on happenings in the defunct Social Democratic Party (SDP). Because of our closeness, he wrote me a letter from Calabar prison, where the regime of late General Sani Abacha detained him in 1994 after his frontline role in NADECO. The Calabar prison letter was more than a personal account of his experience. It is on record that C.O. Adebayo declined a ministerial offer from the regime of late General Sani Abacha. As a journalist covering politics, C.O. Adebayo drew me close, and I became one of the media foot soldiers in the battle for June 12 and democracy. He was one of the preeminent progressive voices who greatly helped me in my early days in journalism, serving as a reservoir of information. His media-friendly disposition during those turbulent years of the Babangida and Abacha regimes also helped those of us who yearned for the news behind the news! Chief Adebayo was congenial, and, to boot, exceptionally media savvy. His depth of thought, rich sense of intellectual wit, and openness drew some of us to him, and his Lagos home became a meeting place for thoughtful political engagement.
We remember him today as a statesman who positively impacted many. He was deeply genial, with an astute, quick-witted intellect. He was an Iroko whose unwavering commitment, courage, and intellectual acuteness inspired admiration and hope. He was straightforward, pragmatic and bold. His influence spanned politics, leadership, public service, community service, the Middle Belt Forum, the Yoruba nation, Kwara and Kogi States, and more. His accomplishments were remarkable. A scholar who was a Senator and governor at a young age! He was Minister of Transportation and Communications at different times. A lecturer at the University of Ife, head of the English Department at Kwara State College of Technology, and Commissioner for Education in the old Kwara State, respectively, at an early stage. There is no doubt that C.O. Adebayo was one of our nation’s most consequential statesmen and illustrious reformists who stood on the side of the people during the tempestuous years of military dictatorship.
His voice on pressing national issues was unequivocal. At the core of his political philosophy was a call to restructure Nigeria. In an interview in 2016, he was quoted as saying: “There are nations, and I am talking about the conventional sense of the word nation, in the sense that Yorubaland is a nation. There are smaller ones, and there are bigger ones. Who wants to be together? My people in Kwara want to be part of the Yoruba nation within a federation. And so long as they have such desires, they must be addressed. And if they are not addressed, the people are not happy. They are not getting what they believe they need to stay happy within the federation…Power is too heavy in the hands of the Federal Government in Nigeria. There must be devolution. Before devolution, there must be restructuring to stem the oppression of minorities within a unit. My position remains what you’ll expect it to be.”
He added: “With all modesty, I was one of the leaders of the Middle Belt Forum, and I remain one of the leaders of the forum. I was at one point chairman of the political forum of Afenifere; I remain a very strong believer in Afenifere and of course, the Yoruba nation. I believe Kwara wants and deserves the best share of whatever this country has to offer. So, beginning at home, we were talking restructuring.…I was secretary of the National Reformation Movement. And what the NADECO was about is restructuring of Nigeria…”
He was a quintessential leader, an iconic statesman whose deeds and reputation transcended many jurisdictions. He was also a man of incredible resilience and strength, confronting various challenges with grace and courage. Born on February 24, 1941, in Igbaja, in present-day Kwara State, Adebayo attended Oke-Onigbin Provincial Secondary School before progressing to Barewa College. He graduated from Ahmadu Bello University in 1967 and later attended the University of Ghana, Legon, where he earned his Master’s degree. He was a versatile personality whose rich service record spanned academia, governance, parliament, community service, and the pro-democracy movement.
Chief C.O. Adebayo was a colossus, a torchbearer, a shining star from Oke-Onigbin, Isin Local Government in Igbomina land, Kwara State, who shone brilliantly throughout his 84 years. His accomplishments and enduring influence remain a legacy for generations to come. One year later, as we remember the iconic and heroic Chief C.O. Adebayo, widely known as C.O., I find solace in the comforting words of Clare Harner, the American poet, whose poem in 1934 entitled “Do Not Stand at My Grave and Weep,” remains soothing:
“Do not stand at my grave and weep. I am not there. I do not sleep. I am a thousand winds that blow. I am the diamond glints on snow. I am the sunlight on ripened grain. I am the gentle autumn rain when you awaken in the morning hush. I am the swift uplifting rush of quiet birds in circled flight. I am the soft stars that shine at Night. Do not stand at my grave and cry. I am not there. I did not die.”
In the blueness of our beautiful skies and oceans, and in the warmth and brightness of our tropical weather, we remember C.O. Adebayo as a patriot, a forthright public-spirited leader who was deeply committed to the restructuring of Nigeria, democracy, rule of law, and a new nation built on federalism that recognises the diversity of its peoples. His exemplary accomplishments will continue to serve as a guiding light in an era of vanishing dedication to noble ideals.
Ambassador Oma Djebah, a frontline diplomat-journalist and member of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, is a former Delta State Commissioner for Information and erstwhile Nigeria’s Ambassador to Thailand, with concurrent accreditation to the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and Myanmar.

title: Death toll from bear attacks in Russia reaches 30 in 2026 — TASS tally
body:
TOMSK, November 2. /TASS/. Bear attacks have claimed 30 lives in Russia this year, including three in the Tomsk Region, according to a TASS tally compiled from statements by regional authorities and publicly available data.
Bears entering populated areas have become a serious problem in Siberia and the Russian Far East. Their numbers in forest areas have increased significantly in recent years, while a shortage of natural food in the taiga this year has forced hungry bears to venture toward settlements, where most attacks on people occur.
Emergency services told TASS on Monday that the body of a 62-year-old man had been discovered in the Tomsk Region’s taiga with multiple injuries indicative of a bear attack. His death raised the nationwide toll to 30. The Krasnoyarsk Region has reported the highest number of fatalities, with nine deaths recorded there.

title: Finding Love In Accra Episode 3: Typing…
body: Read Also: Finding Love in Accra Episode 2: Like a Brother By the time Kojo left the restaurant, I had remembered why I used to enjoy having him around. Unfortunately, I had also noticed several new reasons. “Your brother is leaving,” Emefa said. “Will you stop calling him that?” “You introduced him.” I ignored her and opened WhatsApp. His number was still saved. Kojo Campus. Four years, and I had not even promoted him out of university. His profile picture was a photograph of him standing beside the sea. Linen shirt. Dark glasses. Smiling at whoever was behind the camera. Who took the picture? I enlarged it. “Are you listening to me?” Emefa asked. “Yes.” “What did I say?” “You said… something about work.” “I asked whether you wanted the last chicken wing.” “Then why are you still holding it?” She looked at my phone. “Oh, Lovia.” I locked the screen. “What?” “Nothing. Greet your brother for me.” That evening, I opened his chat before I removed my makeup. Our last conversation was still there. Can I take you to dinner on Saturday? Just the two of us. Four years old. No reply. Seeing it now, I felt a small, uncomfortable twist in my stomach. I had somehow remembered his kindness more clearly than my own silence. I typed: It was lovely seeing you tonight. I read it twice. Too formal. We had met in Osu, not at a shareholders’ meeting. Deleted. So you were just going to leave without asking how I’ve really been? No. Accusations already? The man had returned a bracelet. Deleted. Hey, stranger. I stared at that one. I was the reason we were strangers. Deleted. At midnight, I was in bed, on his profile again. He came online. I immediately left WhatsApp. Please don’t ask me why. Apparently, he could see me through the phone. On Monday, I decided I would message him after work. By evening, I felt Tuesday would be more appropriate. Tuesday, he posted a picture of coffee and his laptop. I nearly replied, Working hard or hardly working? Even loneliness has limits. I deleted it. Wednesday was worse. He posted a woman. I sat upright so quickly my charging cable came out. Proud of you, sis I studied her face for family resemblance. There was some around the nose. Possibly. I called Emefa. “Do men call their girlfriends ‘sis’?” “Good afternoon to you too.” “I’m asking generally.” “Then generally, leave me alone. I’m at work.” By Thursday, I was annoyed with him. He had my number. He knew where to find me. Why hadn’t he said anything? Then I scrolled up to his unanswered invitation. Fair enough. That night, I finally typed what I had been avoiding. They say it takes twenty-one days to break a habit. It’s been four years, and I still can’t get you off my mind. I paused. Had I thought about him every day for four years? No. But I had missed him in little moments. When something funny happened, and I knew he would understand. When I had good news. When I needed to talk without first making myself sound cheerful. I kept typing. I know I did you wrong by not responding to your message about the date. But you know I adore you. It hurt not having you in my life. I read it. Then I imagined him opening it beside the woman from the beach photograph. Deleted everything. On Friday, Emefa took my phone. “Just say hello.” “It’s more complicated than that.” “It is five letters.” She handed it back. At 9:43 p.m., after a week of composing messages that nobody had commissioned, I sent: Hey, Kojo. It was good seeing you the other day. Delivered. I put the phone down. Picked it up. Two blue ticks. Then: Typing… I held my breath. I was wondering whether you’d reply this time. Before I could recover, another message arrived. What did you delete last night? I looked at the empty space where my confession had been. I had deleted the words. I had forgotten WhatsApp could announce that I was typing them. To be continued.

title: El-Sayed faces pointed Israel questions as Michigan Senate race heats up
body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed faced pointed questions about his views on Israel during an interview on CBS's 60 Minutes on Monday, amid growing controversy over his stance and a closely watched race against Republican Mike Rogers.During the interview with journalist Ross Douthat, El-Sayed addressed his criticism of US policy toward Israel. He argued that Washington has spent years declaring its support for a two-state solution while simultaneously providing military assistance to parties he claims are working to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state.El-Sayed also accused Israel of committing genocide in the Gaza Strip, an allegation Israel rejects and which his Republican opponent, Rogers, has also disputed.The exchange on 60 Minutes drew particular attention ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections because of El-Sayed's previous statements about Israel and his ongoing confrontation with Rogers.Rogers has said that he supports Israel's right to defend itself and exist as a Jewish state, and accused El-Sayed of refusing to recognize Israel's right to exist. As such, Douthat opted to directly ask El-Sayed, "Does Israel have a right to exist?"In response, El-Sayed objected to repeatedly being questioned about Israel's right to exist when, he argued, no one asks him about Palestine's right to exist."Does Palestine have a right to exist?" Douthat asked."Yes," El-Sayed replied."And does Israel have a right to exist?" the interviewer continued."Yes, if there is a shared understanding..." El-Sayed began to answer, but Douthat interrupted, seeking clarification about the qualification."Just let me explain," El-Sayed said. "I believe that this is the problem with this debate. We start from where we sit rather than start from principles. I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike."El-Sayed addresses Israel's right to existHe went on to clarify his position: "If the Palestinian people decide and the Israeli people decide that they want two states for two people, and they decide that on equal terms, I'm for it. If they decide that they want one state shared in a different way, I'm for that."El-Sayed therefore answered affirmatively when asked whether Israel has a right to exist, but tied his response to an agreement between the two peoples. Unlike the traditional American position, he did not present the continued existence of two separate states as the only outcome he would support.This was not the first time the Senate candidate had avoided giving a direct, unconditional answer to the question.In an earlier CNN interview, when asked whether Israel had a right to exist, El-Sayed said Israel already exists and that he would not participate in what he described as a game of "gotcha" questions.In the latest interview, El-Sayed also sought to emphasize his commitment to the security of Jews in the United States.Asked whether he was doing enough to reassure Jewish voters in Michigan, he said that despite disagreements over Israel, he and the Jewish community agreed on many other issues.He pledged to stand alongside American Jews in defending their rights and security.Democratic divisions deepen as Stevens endorses RogersThe remarks came amid growing political tensions in Michigan, where El-Sayed and Rogers are competing for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest is considered one of the key races that could determine control of the Senate following Tuesday's elections.Earlier on Sunday evening, another dramatic development unfolded in the state's election campaign when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the primary, appeared alongside his Republican opponent, Rogers, at a church in Detroit and announced her endorsement of him.The move followed a heated dispute over a campaign advertisement produced by an independent political organization supporting El-Sayed, which drew a connection between the cost of living in the United States and American assistance to Israel.Stevens condemned the advertisement as antisemitic, while El-Sayed clarified that his campaign had not been involved in producing it and that he disapproved of its content.Stevens's decision to endorse the Republican candidate, rather than support her own party's nominee as previously planned, drew sharp criticism from senior Democrats.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer condemned the move, calling it a disgraceful betrayal.Despite the political turmoil, El-Sayed maintained a lead over his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in the polls.According to the latest RealClearPolling polling average cited in the report, the Democratic candidate had 49.3% support compared with 45.4% for Rogers, a lead of approximately four percentage points.The latest CNN poll showed a seven-point lead for El-Sayed, with 49% support compared with 42% for Rogers.A YouGov poll conducted between October 26 and 29 also showed El-Sayed ahead, with 51% compared with 47% for Rogers.However, all of these surveys were conducted before Stevens's dramatic announcement that she would endorse Rogers, meaning the impact of her decision on voters could not yet be assessed.The election is scheduled for Tuesday, with the Michigan race considered one of the most important contests in the battle for control of the Senate.US President Donald Trump, who supports Rogers, also attacked El-Sayed during the campaign, accusing him of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.El-Sayed distanced himself from the organization and argued that Republican attacks against him were also directed at his Muslim identity.Michigan is home to large Arab-American and Jewish communities, and positions on Israel, the Gaza war, and US military assistance have become central issues in the state's election campaign.With voting set for Tuesday, the exchange on 60 Minutes once again highlighted the political dispute over how the United States should approach Israel and whether a Senate candidate can support the right to self-determination of both peoples without explicitly committing to a two-state solution.At the same time, the public rift between El-Sayed and Stevens illustrated the depth of divisions within the Democratic Party over Israel, particularly in one of its most consequential races in the upcoming elections.

title: US Reportedly Seeks to Restore Russian Gas Supplies to Europe Through Ukraine
body:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is pushing to restore Russian natural gas supplies to Europe through Ukraine, potentially reversing Kyiv’s decision to end Russian gas transit nearly two years ago.
The proposal was discussed during negotiations in September as part of a potential “energy ceasefire” ahead of winter, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Monday, Nov. 2 , citing US, European, and Ukrainian officials.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
It would involve selling Russian gas through a US intermediary, allowing the arrangement to circumvent European sanctions, while creating lucrative investment opportunities for American companies.
Under the plan outlined by Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Russia’s revenues from gas sales would be deposited into an escrow account in a third country to prevent Moscow from using the money to finance its war against Ukraine.
Washington is also considering reopening the Nord Stream pipeline system as part of a broader deal to end the war, according to WSJ sources.
The proposal faces significant political resistance in Europe, where governments have spent years reducing their dependence on Russian energy following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine was historically one of the main transit routes for Russian natural gas exports to Europe. Its extensive Soviet-era pipeline network connected Russian gas fields in Siberia with European markets, supplying countries across Central and Western Europe.
The network included major pipelines such as Bratstvo (Brotherhood) and Soyuz (Union), which carried gas through Ukraine toward Slovakia and other European destinations. Gas also moved through southern Ukraine and Moldova toward the Balkans and Türkiye.
Even after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine continued transporting Russian gas to European customers under a five-year transit agreement signed by Naftogaz and Russia’s Gazprom in December 2019.
In 2024, the final full year of the arrangement, approximately 42 million cubic meters (1.48 billion cubic feet) of Russian gas flowed through Ukraine daily, equivalent to around 15 billion cubic meters annually, according to S&P Global .
Slovakia, Austria, Moldova, and other European markets continued receiving supplies through the network.
Transit ended at 7 a.m. Kyiv time on Jan. 1, 2025, when the agreement expired. Kyiv refused to negotiate a new arrangement with Moscow, arguing that continuing to facilitate Russian gas exports would generate revenue for the Kremlin while Russia continued its war against Ukraine.
The Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine confirmed that the Ukrainian gas transmission system had switched to operating without Russian transit. The decision also cost Ukraine an important source of revenue from transit fees.
The end of Russian gas transit did not mean that all Russian energy exports through Ukraine stopped.
Russian crude oil continued to move through the country via the southern branch of the Soviet-era Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline, which supplies refineries in Hungary and Slovakia.
Both countries have maintained their reliance on Russian oil and benefit from exemptions under EU sanctions.
Ukraine transported approximately 9.73 million metric tons (10.7 million US tons) of Russian crude through Druzhba in 2025, according to Ukrainian energy consultancy ExPro .
Slovakia received nearly 4.9 million tons, while Hungary received approximately 4.35 million tons.
The volumes were 14% lower than in 2024, partly because the Czech Republic stopped importing Russian oil through the pipeline in March 2025.
Druzhba also became the focus of a major dispute between Kyiv, Budapest, and Bratislava in early 2026.
Russian oil deliveries to Hungary and Slovakia were suspended on Jan. 27 after a Russian strike damaged infrastructure linked to the Druzhba pipeline near Brody in western Ukraine, according to Kyiv.
The disruption triggered a diplomatic dispute, with Hungary and Slovakia stepping up pressure on Zelensky over the halted supplies.
Budapest and Bratislava accused Kyiv of deliberately delaying the restoration of deliveries, while Ukraine maintained that the pipeline had been damaged by Russian attacks and required extensive repairs.
The dispute escalated further as the EU pushed for an independent inspection of the damaged pipeline.
Ukraine announced in April that repairs had been completed. Russian oil transit resumed on April 23 , with Hungary and Slovakia receiving renewed supplies through the pipeline.
Kyiv’s announcement also came amid efforts to unblock a €90 billion ($101 billion) EU loan for Ukraine that Budapest had been blocking.
The dispute demonstrated how dependent some European countries remain on Russian energy despite the EU’s broader efforts to reduce that dependence.
European officials and EU leadership remain skeptical of Washington’s proposal, pointing to the bloc’s commitment to phase out Russian natural gas imports.
The EU has spent years diversifying its energy supplies, increasing imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and pipeline gas from alternative suppliers.
In February 2026, the EU adopted new legislation to phase out Russian gas imports . The restrictions began taking effect in March, with transitional exemptions for certain existing contracts.
The EU’s target is to end Russian gas imports by September 2027, with a limited possible extension for some long-term contracts.
One WSJ source compared the prospect of resuming Russian gas purchases to former British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s decision to sacrifice Czechoslovakia in pursuit of an agreement with Adolf Hitler.
European opposition could nevertheless face pressure as the continent prepares for winter.
Washington reportedly believes that soaring energy prices, LNG supply shortages linked to the conflict in the Middle East, and relatively low gas storage levels could make European governments less resistant to the proposal.
The administration is reportedly presenting renewed Russian gas exports as a way to lower energy prices, generate investment opportunities for US companies, and provide Moscow with an economic incentive to negotiate an end to the war.
The Trump administration is also considering the possibility of restoring gas supplies through the Nord Stream pipeline system, which connects Russia directly to Germany under the Baltic Sea.
The first Nord Stream pipeline began operating in 2011, allowing Russia to bypass traditional transit countries, including Ukraine, and deliver gas directly to Germany.
Nord Stream 1 halted deliveries in August 2022, while Nord Stream 2, completed in 2021, never entered commercial operation. Both pipelines were badly damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022, as documented by the UN .
One senior US official told WSJ that former German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s mistake was promoting the pipeline project without first securing a broader security agreement with Russia.
The official suggested that energy cooperation should have been part of a wider arrangement addressing Moscow’s security concerns.
Restarting Nord Stream would require overcoming substantial technical, regulatory, and political obstacles. The pipeline network running through Ukraine, by contrast, could reportedly resume operations much more quickly.
The Kremlin has previously rejected the idea of an energy ceasefire with Ukraine.
Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow needed “peace, not a truce.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin has separately expressed readiness to resume gas supplies to Europe “as soon as tomorrow,” proposing that the remaining operational line of Nord Stream 2 be used.
The pipeline was never brought into commercial operation.

With over seven years of experience in TV journalism, Alisa has reported on international and Ukrainian politics, making complex stories easier to understand.
