title: Bulgaria set to elect its first female president as Russia-friendly Iliana Yotova wins runoff
body: Bulgaria’s acting president, Iliana Yotova, won the second round of the country’s presidential election on November 1. With 99.68% of ballots counted, preliminary results showed 57.6% of voters had voted for Yotova and 39.3% for her main rival, former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov. Gyurov conceded defeat. Yotova has twice served as Bulgaria’s vice president under President Rumen Radev. Radev stepped down early in January 2026 to run in parliamentary elections, and Yotova temporarily took over as president. If the results are confirmed, Yotova will become the first woman elected president in Bulgaria’s history. In the first round, neither candidate received the votes needed to win outright. Yotova took 34.76% of the vote, while Gyurov took 31.94%. Turnout was extremely low in both rounds: 23% in the first round and 27% in the second. Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in April’s parliamentary elections, backed Yotova’s candidacy. According to AP, Yotova’s victory will allow Radev’s ruling majority to retain control of the presidency. Like Radev, Yotova supports negotiations with Russia and a diplomatic settlement to the war in Ukraine. She also opposes providing military aid to Kyiv and supports lifting sanctions on Russia. Yotova supports Bulgaria remaining in the EU and NATO, and she is expected to maintain the country’s pro-European course. title: What we know about seizure of booby-trapped FPV goggles intended for Russian troops by FSB
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has reported the seizure of a mined batch of FPV drone goggles intended for the Russian military in the special military operation zone as humanitarian aid.
TASS has compiled key details about the report.
- The FSB thwarted a series of sabotage and terrorist attacks using improvised explosive devices concealed inside FPV drone goggles intended for delivery to the Russian military in the special military operation zone, which were plotted by Ukrainian special services.
- Acting on instructions from military counterintelligence, a Russian serviceman in the Volgograd Region brought two FPV goggles he had received from a volunteer to the FSB for inspection.
- Explosive ordnance specialists established that Ukrainian special services had planted improvised explosive devices in the FPV goggles instead of cooling solutions.
- As a result of the measures taken, a batch of similar improvised explosives camouflaged as FPV goggles, sent into the country via the Russian Post, has been confiscated across Russia, the FSB said.
- The explosive devices would have detonated when the FPV glasses were switched on, potentially killing servicemen, the FSB specified.
- Posing as pseudo-patriots, agents of Ukrainian special services established communication with representatives of Russian humanitarian organizations and charity foundations, using anonymous accounts on the Telegram messenger, to arrange supplies to Russian Defense Ministry units, the FSB noted.
- During these exchanges, the FSB continued, they refused to share their names, phone numbers and job information or switch to the Max messenger for calls as they communicated with volunteers to arrange the delivery of FPV goggles with homemade explosive devices, while demanding video feedback with words of gratitude from Russian fighters.
- According to the enemy’s plans, volunteers were supposed to later deliver the FPV goggles laden with improvised explosive devices to Russian drone operators taking part in combat operations against Ukrainian troops, the FSB said.
- The FSB’s investigative department in the Volgograd Region has opened a criminal case.
- Efforts to identify those responsible for the shipment are underway.
- The FSB has called on volunteer organizations to accept humanitarian aid only from reliable sources and inspect it for explosives.
- Ukrainian special services can use various items to disguise homemade explosive devices, the FSB warned.
- The agency recalled that improvised explosive devices disguised as perfume sets, power banks, music speakers, miniature souvenir statues, church utensils, car components, paving slabs and even heated insoles have previously been neutralized.

title: Nearly 800 people evacuated from Oleshky during humanitarian mission – Melania Trump
body:
According to Ukrinform, she wrote this on social media platform X .
She said the humanitarian mission to the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region was a success, with critical aid delivered to the region and nearly 800 people evacuated.
"On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire. I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations," she wrote.
The ceasefire began on October 27, 2026, and concluded on November 1, 2026, as planned, the post said.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 31, the Ukrainian delegation that had carried out the humanitarian mission to the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

title: China Rejects Ukraine Talks With Trump and Putin
body:
China has shown no interest in holding a three-way summit with Russia and the US to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said, adding that Beijing views the conflict as a European issue.
Steinmeier made the remarks in an interview with German public broadcaster ARD.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He said he had raised the possibility of a Ukraine-focused summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Beijing on Friday, Oct. 30. Steinmeier has since returned to Berlin.
Although the leaders of the three countries are expected to attend the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Xi’s response suggested that Ukraine would not be on the agenda, Steinmeier said.
“From his perspective, there is absolutely no preparation under way for a Ukraine summit involving the US, Russia, and China,” Steinmeier said.
“He (Xi) explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict in which Europeans would also have to be at the negotiating table,” he added.
Steinmeier said Xi appeared surprised when he raised the possibility of a summit focused on Ukraine, adding that “one could see the look of surprise on his face.”
The discussion comes amid reports of a possible meeting between Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit, scheduled for mid-November.
Putin has proposed a three-way meeting to discuss nuclear disarmament. Trump has expressed openness to the idea and said he would also be willing to discuss other issues, “such as Ukraine.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said on Oct. 25 that preparations had begun for a trilateral summit. Speaking to Russian state broadcaster Vesti, Ushakov said Moscow, Beijing, and Washington had agreed in principle to hold the meeting.
The summit is being planned for the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting, scheduled for Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, China.
Ushakov also described a possible meeting of Russian, US, and Ukrainian delegations in November as exploratory, saying it would have a “range-finding character.”
The prospect of a meeting between Trump, Putin, and Xi has raised questions about the role of Ukraine and European countries in discussions that could affect the future of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly said that decisions concerning Ukraine cannot be made without Kyiv’s participation.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: NATO pushes faster counter-drone defenses and AI-enabled targeting as threats evolve
body: NATO is reshaping how it develops military technology as alliance leaders warn that cheap drones, artificial intelligence, and rapidly evolving battlefield threats are compressing timelines for innovation from decades to months.The effort was on display at NATO FUSE, held in Latvia on October 29-30, where NATO's Allied Command Transformation brought together three major initiatives: the Digital Backbone eXperimentation (DiBaX), the Layered Counter-UAS Initiative (LCI-X), and Next Generation Targeting (NGT).The event brought together military organizations, operators, and industry to test concepts and gather data on what works under realistic conditions rather than serving as a procurement exercise.Speaking to Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post right before the Operation NATO FUSE drills in Latvia, Maj.-Gen. Arnoud Stallmann said repeated drone incursions and lessons emerging from modern conflicts have forced the alliance to rethink both its defenses and how quickly it adopts technology.According to Stallmann, more than 30 countries and over 100 companies are now participating in the drills in Latvia. D&T understands that while Israeli companies have participated in prior NATO events, none participated in Operation NATO FUSE."What we see nowadays is that the incursions into Poland last September were the start," said Stallmann, who is the assistant chief of staff for multi-domain capability at NATO. "We see it all the time in our nations on the eastern flank, with drones entering our airspace."But the challenge extends beyond just drones. "Simultaneously, we have a task to build a backbone; we recognized a problem that the whole targeting process in general is very labor intensive,” Stallmann said, adding that NATO commanders have identified key gaps in connectivity, digital infrastructure, and next-generation targeting that must be urgently addressed."It's a sprint," he said, pointing to funding already allocated this year and next year.Modernization pushAt the same time, NATO is confronting a strategic environment in which allied territory can no longer be assumed safe from direct threats. Small drones have emerged as a low-cost means of surveillance, disruption, and attack, creating pressure for defensive systems that are both scalable and affordable."We really need to find other solutions," Stallmann said, emphasizing the importance of developing lower-cost intercept options rather than relying on expensive air defense assets such as fighter aircraft or missile interceptors designed to defeat larger threats.Stallmann explained that NATO's current focus is on building a layered and interoperable network capable of protecting key areas while sharing data across borders and domains. And that requirement places command-and-control at the center of NATO's modernization effort.The alliance is exploring a framework in which national and industry-developed systems can plug into a common command architecture – a concept such as a mosaic of interoperable capabilities connecting air, land, and cross-border operations.But cross-border coordination remains one of the most complex challenges facing NATO's command structure, making data sharing and interoperability critical requirements for future systems.That challenge sits at the center of NATO's modernization push. DiBaX serves as a test environment where NATO, allied operators, and industry evaluate connected technologies against operational problems. NATO describes its developing digital backbone as an integrated layer of software, data networks, and infrastructure designed to allow forces to connect, share data, and operate together.This year's DiBaX experiments focused on resilient command-and-control, maintaining communications when networks are disrupted, and accelerating decision-making through the integration of data, sensors, and artificial intelligence. The event also hosted both counter-UAS and targeting experimentation.Drone threatTo address the drone threat, NATO is advancing the Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, or LCI-X, a campaign of operational experimentation designed to test, integrate, and scale counter-drone capabilities across the alliance. According to NATO, the initiative moves progressively from testing individual systems to integrating connected counter-UAS cells and linking them with NATO command-and-control networks.LCI-X has been running through a series of dedicated C-UAS events conducted in Finland and Latvia over the past year. The campaign is intended to connect sensors, effectors, and command-and-control systems while providing industry with direct operator feedback.The alliance is deliberately avoiding commitment to a single technology path."We are looking wider than just what we have in our own stock," Stallmann said, adding, "We're not advocating that we have a total solution, but we have a layered C-UAS solution.”Next-generation targetingNATO's targeting effort is advancing in parallel. The Next Generation Targeting initiative aims to create a federated framework that integrates national data through modular AI and data-management tools while retaining human authority over engagement decisions. Stallmann explained that the goal is to reduce information-to-decision timelines and improve sensor-to-shooter coordination across land, sea, air, space, and cyberspace domains. NATO says NGT is intended to complement existing command-and-control systems through federated data sharing and AI-assisted analysis. One objective cited by the program is reducing information-to-decision latency by more than 50%, while keeping human operators in control of engagement decisions.For Stallmann, the broader challenge is institutional rather than technological. For much of his career, Stallmann said military modernization followed a predictable path of incremental improvements, but the rise of AI and autonomous systems has altered that dynamic."During my first 20 years as an operator, I was seeing incremental improvements and developments. Once in a while, you get a new airplane or platform and there's a leap. But in the digital age, and with what's going on in AI, decision-advantage needs to go faster than that of the enemy."'Ramping up speed'According to Stallmann, NATO must also adopt capabilities faster than traditional procurement timelines allow."We have our innovation hubs, but we need to ramp up our speed, and we need to not introduce weapons systems that take 20 years. We need to adopt quicker and innovate quicker, because the enemy is doing that too."Stallmann explained that NATO understands that it cannot rely solely on existing inventories to solve emerging challenges. Lessons from Ukraine have demonstrated that the pace at which drone technology evolves creates the need for military organizations to adapt much more quickly than traditional procurement systems allow. Prior to his current position in NATO, Stallmann led the Directorate for Ukraine, with all Dutch efforts to support Ukraine, such as deliveries of platforms and training, combined in his team. Stallmann described the current experimentation exercises not as an endpoint but as the beginning of a continuous process of adaptation driven by operational feedback from ongoing conflicts, particularly Ukraine."The character of war is changing, and we need to adapt to that new character of war," he said.The same mindset is driving NATO investments beyond drones and digital networking. Stallmann said that the alliance is also examining emerging technologies such as quantum computing and quantum-resistant systems, which he described as a potential game changer approaching the horizon.For NATO's transformation leaders, the broader objective is cultural as much as technical. The alliance must learn to field new capabilities at a pace measured in months and years rather than decades. And FUSE might just be the critical part of a broader effort to move technologies from experimentation into operational capability. "This is not only the end point. It's the start of a learning curve; learn fast and we are going to continue," Stallmann said. "This is the beginning of a never-ending cycle."

title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said. “The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito ’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post. Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB). Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB. A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch. Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency. The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

title: [Updated] Iran says ready to reopen Hormuz in two days if US agrees to demands
body: Iran on Monday said it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US agrees to its conditions, having previously proposed a one-week timeline. “The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei. “We have stated that, if Iran’s demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period.” He said an exchange of messages was ongoing with the United States via mediators and that “everything depends” on the US side accepting the Iranian demands. “Only then can we discuss the subsequent stages.” Since the Middle East war broke out in late February, Iran has claimed control over Hormuz, a vital energy conduit for shipping. It regularly targets vessels that attempt to cross the strait without its authorisation, while the US has in retaliation imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. In September, Iran initially proposed a seven-day plan that it conveyed to the US through Qatar, which would have seen Tehran reopen Hormuz on the sixth day after the US met Iranian demands. Those demands include ending the Middle East war on all fronts, the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade. In an interview with Al Jazeera released on Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed between Iran and Oman for transit through the strait. He said the US must also remove sanctions imposed in recent months and reduce American troop numbers in the region. Washington has since August rolled out a fresh raft of sanctions, part of what it called “economic asphyxiation” of Iran. The United States and Israel have in recent days also intensified threats to renew attacks on Iran amid crucial elections in both countries. On Saturday, US President Donald Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. “Any act of aggression against Iran, any military attack against Iran, by whatever means, will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response from us,” said Baqaei during a foreign ministry briefing Monday. The post [Updated] Iran says ready to reopen Hormuz in two days if US agrees to demands appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: GoldBod generates $1.011bn in forex from gold trade in October
body: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) says it generated US$1.011 billion in foreign exchange from its artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold trading operations in October 2026. In an announcement issued on Monday, November 2, the Board said the entire amount was sold to authorised commercial banks through its GoldBod GoFX platform to support stability in the foreign exchange market. GoldBod is projecting to generate US$1.2 billion in foreign exchange from its ASM gold trade operations in November. Of this amount, US$800 million is expected to be made available to commercial banks to support foreign exchange market stability. The Board said the sales would be conducted through the GoldBod GoFX platform in accordance with its approved FX Sales and Intermediation Framework to ensure transparency, fairness and regulatory compliance. It added that it remains committed to its statutory mandate of generating foreign exchange for the country and supporting the accumulation of Ghana’s foreign reserves by the Bank of Ghana under the Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Policy (GANRAP).

title: The agentic web is here
body: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, an associate professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place for humans that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse hundreds of sites in just a few seconds, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the 1990s and early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as the sites and creators we now favor struggle to survive the shift. And as last summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents themselves could even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are great at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do. In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent never sees it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree. Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots that trawl the web. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these search crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information. But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Microsoft Excel. Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expect.” This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs. As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly humans-only web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Coexistence , he decided to put together an agent-directed version that depends primarily on text and tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them. In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents could end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their own testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had taken over an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code. That hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes. As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there. The economics of control Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote. But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy. Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google introduced AI Overviews in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that some publishers saw ad revenue decrease by about 40% between 2025 and 2026 It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment. E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, an assistant professor of operations management at the University of Toronto, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents entirely ignore items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money in an agentic economy. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up. David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy. Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Amazon and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and businesses. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees. It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When OpenClaw, the first popular personal assistant agent, exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents. When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.” Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, their AI tools automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and refuse to respond. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails. The same can’t be said for OpenClaw. “These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.” How will the human web change? When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did change it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile. Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo and MapQuest failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.” “But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.” PINGNAN LU It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance. But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed billions of people in the Global South to get online for the first time, because phones are cheaper and easier to set up than computers. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world. “There’s very clear assistive potential from people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethicis scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities. Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.” He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?” Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?” “We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”

title: Melania Trump Says 800 People Evacuated from Oleshky as Russia Uses Truce to Regroup
body:
Russian forces used the humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky to rotate troops, strengthen positions and bring in ammunition, Ukraine’s General Staff said on Monday, Nov. 2, after Melania Trump said nearly 800 people had been evacuated from the city during the truce.
In a report published Monday, Sky News said it reviewed drone footage recorded by a Ukrainian military unit monitoring Russian movements around Oleshky. The report showed Russian soldiers, military vehicles and supplies moving in the area during the ceasefire, which ran from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Sky News correspondent Stuart Ramsay was given access to the Ukrainian Marines’ drone reconnaissance command center. The broadcaster said the footage showed Russian troops and equipment moving along roads, soldiers carrying supplies and personnel entering buildings.
The report also cited Ukrainian military intelligence, which said one vehicle left a humanitarian convoy and went to supply Russian positions. Sky News said footage showed Russian soldiers carrying away boxes of food intended for civilians. The broadcaster reported that it had contacted Russia’s Defense Ministry for comment.
The General Staff’s statement did not refer to specific footage. It said Ukrainian forces had observed Russian units rotating, positions being fortified, anti-drone defenses being expanded along roads, and logistics increased, including ammunition deliveries.
“The enemy, meanwhile, used the humanitarian pause to set up its positions,” the General Staff said .
Ukraine’s military said its forces had observed the agreed truce and acted within its terms. It said humanitarian supplies reached their destination and Ukrainian citizens who wanted to leave Oleshky returned to territory controlled by Kyiv.
Melania Trump said in a Nov. 1 post on X that the mission delivered humanitarian aid and enabled the evacuation of nearly 800 people. She praised Ukraine and Russia for their “leadership and cooperation” and said she hoped the operation could help build lasting peace.
Her figure followed an earlier update on Oct. 30, when she said a convoy was prepared to evacuate more than 750 people who chose to leave. She said the convoy included 25 buses, 50 medical professionals and ambulances.
The nearly 800 figure is Trump’s reported total for the operation. It does not specify how many evacuees went to Ukrainian-controlled territory and how many chose Russia. Ukraine’s General Staff said those who wanted to leave for Ukraine had returned to territory controlled by Kyiv.
The truce was established to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and give residents a chance to leave. The city, in Russian-occupied Kherson region, had faced severe shortages of food, medicine and clean water. Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners coordinated the operation, with mediation by Trump.
Before the ceasefire began, the Institute for the Study of War warned that Russia could use the pause to rebuild its forces in the Kherson region and questioned whether residents would be able to choose their destination freely.
The ceasefire was scheduled to end at 10:59 p.m. Kyiv time on Nov. 1. Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the truce had ended after humanitarian aid was delivered and civilians who wanted to leave were evacuated. He said the Ukrainian and Russian sides had honored their commitments during the operation.
Kyiv Post previously reported that evacuees chose to travel either to Ukraine or Russia, with the Ukrainian delegation accompanying people heading to Ukrainian-controlled territory. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later said those evacuees had crossed into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Displaced people in Blue Nile forests face medicine, shelter shortages
body: Thousands of people displaced by fighting in Geissan locality in Sudan’s Blue Nile region are facing extremely difficult humanitarian conditions after being forced to seek refuge in forests, amid acute shortages of food, medicine and shelter materials, and a lack of healthcare services. The situation has driven some families to turn to herbal remedies in an attempt to treat illnesses. Thousands of residents fled from the areas of Geissan, Bakori, Al-Yas, Amsi, Madlan, Al-Madina 10 and the Umara Dalo area, only to find themselves stranded in forests and surrounding areas near Shaira, Dandan and Abu Qumai, without access to even the most necessities. Yagoub Abini, a displaced person, said they have been forced to use old plastic sheeting and construct makeshift shelters from tree fronds. “Mosquitoes and the spread of disease have compounded our suffering, and some families have between five and six members suffering from various illnesses, particularly children, women and older people,” he said. “We are yet to receive any assistance from humanitarian organizations or other agencies to help them cope with our dire circumstances.” With healthcare services unavailable and medicines difficult to obtain, fears are growing over the spread of disease among displaced people, particularly women and children. Some families have consequently resorted to using herbs and plants as alternatives to medical treatment. For her part, Inam Hussein recounted her sick daughter’s ordeal, saying the girl was vomiting and suffering from headaches and back pain. “The displaced families cannot even obtain basic medicines, including Panadol tablets, forcing us to use tree barks and leaves as remedies,” she said. “The plants are boiled in water before the resulting liquid is consumed.” According to Ayman Abdel-Karim, a local activist with the Geissan Displaced People’s Gathering, displaced families are spread across four main gathering centres: Al-Madina 10, Dandan, Shaira and Abu Qumai. “The humanitarian situation is catastrophic. The Al-Madina 10 center is hosting 562 families and a communal kitchen has been established to provide meals, but it has since stopped operating because of a lack of essential supplies,” he said. “The Dandan center is hosting 314 families but has yet to receive any humanitarian assistance from aid organizations.” “Another 312 families are sheltering at Abu Qumai, where diseases are spreading amid the absence of healthcare services,” Abdel-Karim added. He also reported cases of an illness referred to by displaced people as “sea worm,” which causes skin irritation and throat pain. Malaria is also widespread, while some displaced families have turned to herbal remedies because medicines and medical services are unavailable. At the Shaira centre, Abdel-Karim said the number of displaced people had reached approximately 1,700 families, comprising nearly 8,000 people, without sufficient humanitarian assistance to meet their needs. He appealed to humanitarian organizations and relevant authorities to intervene urgently to address the needs of displaced people and provide healthcare and essential assistance. Faced with these conditions, displaced people are appealing for urgent intervention from humanitarian organizations and relevant authorities to provide food, medicine, and shelter materials, as well as healthcare services, to save thousands of civilians stranded in the forests. The humanitarian crisis is unfolding as fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in Geissan, Kurmuk, and Wad Al-Mahi localities in the Blue Nile region, raising fears of further displacement and escalating humanitarian needs. The post Displaced people in Blue Nile forests face medicine, shelter shortages appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Saab says new CB90 CX combat boat is in production for Sweden with strike and air defence roles
body: The Combat Boat 90 Capability X is larger than its predecessors, with increased payload capacity and comprehensively updated onboard systems. Designed to operate across a wider range of sea states, it uses Saab’s Autonomous Ocean Core to support both crewed and uncrewed operations. “The future of naval operations is not just about having more platforms; it is about distributing greater combat capability across the force. As operational realities change, so does CB90,” said Anders Hellman, head of Saab’s Docksta business unit. The intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance configuration uses Saab’s Giraffe 1X radar to build situational awareness across multiple domains. The anti-ship version provides over-the-horizon strike capability against surface vessels, while the short-range air defence configuration uses an anti-aircraft autocannon. Saab said the three configurations could operate together or within a wider joint force, combining surveillance and weapons capabilities at dispersed locations. The concept expands the combat boat’s role beyond transporting troops to detecting threats, sharing information and engaging targets directly. Photo: Saab. The CB90 CX retains the characteristics of its troop-carrying predecessors while allowing a broader range of equipment to be integrated. The wider CB90 family serves in nine navies across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia Pacific and the Americas.

title: "Not the time for Russia to return" — Finnish politicians condemn sports court ruling
body:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled last week that Russian teams can return to ice hockey’s international tournaments.
Finnish politicians have roundly condemned the decision, handed down by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, which allows Russian teams to return to ice hockey’s international tournaments.
Finland's sports minister Mika Poutala (CD) told Yle on Monday that Russia's return to international sports is not welcome, adding he had discussed the issue with his Swedish counterpart, Jakob Forssmed .
"At least with Sweden, we clearly share a common view on this: that it's not the time for Russia to return to ice hockey, or to sports in general — especially not under its national colours," Poutala said.
According to the CAS ruling, Russia can once again compete in men's and women's world championships as well as in the world juniors.
The verdict overturned an exclusion handed down by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In its ruling, CAS said there was insufficient evidence to support the security concerns that IIHF had raised as a reason for Russia's exclusion.
In response, an IIHF statement noted that the federation "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions".
The decision puts particular focus on next year's men's world championship tournament in Germany, as Ukraine has also qualified.
Finland is committed to abiding by CAS decisions, meaning in practice that the Finnish team is set to also take part in the tournament. Finland are currently reigning world champions, having secured the title in dramatic fashion against this year's hosts Switzerland in May.
However, Poutala noted on Monday that Finland can decide otherwise, with the Finnish Ice Hockey Association ultimately responsible for making that call.
There is a growing swell of support among Finnish politicians for Finland to withdraw from the tournament.
Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) wrote on social media platform X on Sunday that "Russian athletes will have no business coming to Finland next year" if the war in Ukraine continues.
"I intend to advance the necessary measures in the coming days," Valtonen added in her post.
Speaker of Parliament Jussi Halla-aho (Finns) also shared his opinion in a social media post, writing on Facebook that Finland should skip the tournament if Russia is permitted to take part.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb meanwhile told Yle's Ykkösaamu programme on Saturday morning that he disagrees with the CAS decision.

title: Tinubu granted rare access inside Ka’abah, reaffirms commitment to Nigeria
body:
President Bola Tinubu has reaffirmed his commitment to Project Nigeria and his determination to build a prosperous nation, invest in the future of young Nigerians, and pursue development in line with the will of Almighty Allah and the people’s aspirations.
The president stated this on Monday while reflecting on his spiritual journey to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah, during which the Custodian of the Holy Mosques of Makkah and Madinah, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, granted him a rare privilege of leading Nigeria’s delegation to pray inside the Holy Ka’abah.
At the Ka’abah, President Tinubu offered prayers of gratitude to Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving as Nigeria’s President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces.
Sheikh Dahlulah Muthawal of Masjid al-Haram led the president into the Ka’abah.
President Tinubu thanked the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for granting him and members of his Nigerian delegation the opportunity to enter the Holy Ka’abah in Makkah and offer prayers to Almighty Allah.
The president described the honour as a historic and deeply cherished spiritual experience, reflecting the longstanding bonds of friendship, mutual respect and cooperation between Nigeria and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
“I want to say a big thank you for the faith, for the recognition. I can’t believe the fencing of the Ka’abah is in Green-White-Green, which reminds us of the Nigerian identity.
“I thank the Crown Prince and all the administrators of the holy land. I thank them for the hospitality and recognition given to me as the leader of the delegation and the country.
“We are all facing challenges and hostility around us. We will overcome them with faith in God Almighty. I’m grateful forever. I thank the king and the royal crown prince.
“It is an honour that I enjoyed, and it is gracious of them to have allowed me to enter inside the Ka’abah. This is history,” the president said.
President Tinubu said he asked Allah for wisdom and resilience to continue serving Nigerians, and expressed confidence that his prayers have been answered.
“Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. I know that prayer has been granted. Before the 2023 election, I did the same thing. I asked Allah to bless my Umrah then, and He did. And I promised that I would come back to thank Him,” the president said.
Reflecting on the message from the Holy Qur’an in Surah Aal-Imran, Verse 26, which affirms that Almighty Allah is the owner of all sovereignty, granting power and authority to whom He wills and taking them away from whom He wills, the president said power is a trust that must be exercised responsibly, with humility and in the service of the people, recognising that no position of authority is permanent and that ultimate sovereignty belongs to Almighty Allah.
“There is no other God but Almighty Allah. He is the giver and the taker. He owns power and authority. He says, ‘ If I give you, use it well. If you don’t use it in accordance with my dictates, I can take it from you and give it to another person. I am the only One who has that authority,” the president said, quoting the words of the Qur’an.
President Tinubu said faith in Allah had strengthened his conviction that his emergence as Nigeria’s leader was an extraordinary blessing that must be matched with dedicated service to the country.
“I have faith in that, and I believe extremely well that He has done me and my country a great favour. Out of many millions of people, to be the President and Commander-in-Chief is a favour that only Almighty God can do to a human being,” he stated.
President Tinubu emphasised that his commitment to Project Nigeria had become even stronger, assuring Nigerians of his resolve to pursue policies and programmes that would promote prosperity, national development and shared progress.
“My commitment to Project Nigeria is higher. I am determined to usher in prosperity and fully develop the country, consistent with the wish of Allah and the support of the people.
“It is important to put Allah first, then move on. Follow your conscience. Follow the right path that will lead Nigeria to that greatness,” the president said.
On the nation’s economic outlook, President Tinubu expressed optimism about the progress made under his watch, describing the economic foundation as solid and the country’s emergence from a difficult period as encouraging.
“The foundation is solid, and the economy has come out of the dark tunnel. This is inspiring,” he said.
He maintained, however, that nation-building requires sustained investment in young Nigerians’ future, noting that today’s leaders’ decisions will determine how future generations remember them.
“We need to build a future for our youth. If we don’t invest in their future, how do we want to be remembered as leaders 50 years from now? That’s the main thing. So this is a rare privilege to lead the country,” the president added.
President Tinubu reiterated that his administration would remain focused on strengthening the country’s economic foundations, expanding opportunities for young people and creating the conditions necessary for Nigerians to realise their potential.
The president thanked Almighty Allah for the opportunity to lead Nigeria and reaffirmed his determination to justify the confidence the Nigerian people have placed in him through purposeful leadership and an enduring commitment to national progress.
Apparently seized by emotions, Minister of Justice Lateef Fagbemi, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Ali Pate, Governors of Borno, Sokoto, Jigawa, Kaduna, Yobe and Kwara States as well as captains of industry, including Chairman of BUA Abdulsamad Rabiu and CEO of Oando Wale Tinubu, expressed gratitude to Allah and the president for allowing them to enter and pray with him in the most holy mosque and sacred ground in Islam.
Bayo Onanuga Special Adviser to the President (Information & Strategy) November 2, 2026.

title: India Signs 5 65B Deal for Eight Next-Generation Navy Corvettes
body:
India’s Ministry of Defence has signed contracts worth ₹53,866.50 crore (approximately $5.65 billion) with Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE) and Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) to build eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) for the Indian Navy.
Signed on November 2 in New Delhi, the contracts allocate five corvettes to GRSE and three to GSL.
The program marks the first time warships designed indigenously by the Indian Navy will be constructed by Defense Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) selected through a competitive process.
The multirole corvettes will feature advanced missiles, weapons and sensor suites, with capabilities spanning air, surface and sub-surface warfare. Their missions will include anti-ship and anti-submarine operations, coastal defense, littoral combat, maritime surveillance and protection of critical sea routes. The project is expected to generate approximately 72 lakh person-days of employment at shipyards and 460 lakh person-days across ancillary industries and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) over the next decade.
