title: Iranian delegation leaves Doha to review settlement proposals — news agency
body:
DOHA, November 2. /TASS/. An Iranian delegation left Doha on November 1, but its departure is not related to difficulties in the talks to settle the conflict between Washington and Tehran, Reuters reported.
According to a source familiar with the consultations' progress, a draft agreement has been circulated among participants for feedback. Another meeting may be held, the source pointed out.
On October 31, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Qatar’s Al Jazeera TV channel that the Iranian delegation had arrived in Doha to discuss mediators' proposals on Tehran's nuclear program.

title: Kimi Antonelli: How F1’s newest superstar went from rookie to record-breaker
body: In the thin air of Mexico City, Andrea Kimi Antonelli could finally exhale, weeping on the radio as he was declared Formula One world champion with four races left in the 2026 season. The Italian needed just two points to secure his first title. He finished on the podium in third place before being hoisted onto the shoulders of two of F1’s greatest drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton. Antonelli’s numbers border on the absurd. At only 20 years and 68 days, he is the youngest champion in F1 history , eclipsing the 23 years and 134 days of Sebastian Vettel in 2010. He is the first Italian to take the crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953, ending his country’s 73-year wait for a F1 drivers’ title and the first to do it in a car built outside of Italy. Transformation Mercedes built the best car of F1’s new era, but the machinery only explains so much. George Russell, in an identical car alongside Antonelli, was presumed to be the favourite for the title. And yet Antonelli arrived in Mexico 123 points ahead of his teammate, armed with nine grands prix victories, five of which came in an uninterrupted run from China to Monaco . He has held a championship lead since March following the Japanese Grand Prix . Kimi ⚡️ Antonelli #F1 #JapaneseGP pic.twitter.com/lpKpNru8Z9 — Formula 1 (@F1) March 29, 2026 The scale of his transformation has been remarkable. Last season, he showed plenty of promise, but was an error-prone rookie who finished seventh in the final standings. In Monza, Antonellii’s home race, his own team principal criticised him, calling his weekend "underwhelming". Toto Wolff now considers his progress one of the greatest surprises of his career. The art of folding a corner So what makes him so formidable? The 2026 regulations helped. This season brought new cars with narrower tyres and less downforce, giving drivers less warning before they lose grip and making the rear more prone to sliding. The most delicate moment is when a driver is still braking as they turn into a corner. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella explained that smooth, tidy driving can cost lap time as he attempted to explain Oscar Piastri’s problems this season. These cars reward aggression. Antonelli ’s instincts and daring style suit these new cars. He attacks each bend, turning late and sharply so the car swivels quickly towards the exit, trying in his own words to “fold the corner up like a handkerchief”. His hands rarely sit still, making tiny steering adjustments that help him manage slides without losing speed. The technique works best in slower corners, but he’s had to rein it in at times and adapt to suit different circuits such as Barcelona and Silverstone. Russell’s smoother, more measured style of driving, which proved so effective in the previous era, has proved harder to exploit this year. His preference for getting on the throttle earlier puts greater strain on the rear tyres, particularly with this season’s unusually high tyre pressures, and can consume more electrical energy. Antonelli’s aggressive approach helped him manage rear-tyre temperatures, while telemetry suggested he could also use less electrical energy exiting corners, preserving more battery power for the straights. The rest was all about his temperament. Wolff praised the “serenity and structure” the Italian brought to the tracks this year. That’s not to say he didn’t make mistakes; his repeated track-limit infringements are something he must address, but his pace was outstanding. Key races The first came in Shanghai in March in only the second race of the season. On the Saturday, he became the youngest pole-sitter in the sport’s history , and on the Sunday, having surrendered the lead to Lewis Hamilton at the start, wrestled it back and dictated the race. He became the first Italian to win a Grand Prix since Giancarlo Fisichella in 2006, five months before Antonelli was born. “I think it’s maybe come earlier than I thought,” Wolff admitted. In Bologna, Antonelli's mother, Veronica, watched her son weep on television. His family wept with him. Antonelli wins first F1 race - in pictures Monza in September was a masterpiece. An engine change resulted in a grid penalty, forcing him to start from 19 th at his home race. It wasn’t enough to stop him. Antonelli scythed through the field, completing 26 overtakes before reeling in Russell on older tyres and passing him three laps from the chequered flag. He became the first Italian to win the Italian Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966 and was hoisted onto the shoulders of the tifosi dressed in Ferrari red. Antonelli may be a Mercedes driver, but he was also one of them. “Kimi prodigio,” ran the headline in the following morning’s Gazzetta dello Sport . His father, whose voice had all but gone, said that he hoped for fourth or fifth, but by then Antonelli was accustomed to pulling off the spectacular. “Someone up there loves him.” Antonelli celebrated by eating pasta from the trophy. Mountain climbed 💪 #F1 #ItalianGP @MercedesAMGF1 pic.twitter.com/i7iZiiVMmq — Formula 1 (@F1) September 6, 2026 In Austin last week , Antonelli perfectly demonstrated his imperious growth. He led by more than two seconds after a single lap and was never troubled, prompting Wolff to call it “probably the best race I’ve seen”. Wolff always believed in him In early 2024, Hamilton told Wolff that he was leaving the team for Ferrari. Within five minutes, by Wolff’s own admission, he resolved that the 17-year-old who had yet to start a Formula 2 race would replace the most successful driver in history. Mercedes had been tracking Antonelli since he was 11, having been alerted to his talent by Giovanni Minardi, son of the Minardi team’s founder. Minardi first spotted him karting at age eight. Mercedes talent scout Gwen Lagrue recognised his potential, and the youngster formally joined the team’s junior programme in 2019. He went on to collect European karting crowns, Italian and German Formula 4 titles and two Formula Regional championships before being fast-tracked past Formula 3 altogether. Raw speed, Wolff likes to say, is the one quality one cannot teach. “He has that, and there are not many that have it.” His debut didn’t go as planned. In his first Mercedes practice at Monza 2024, he set the fastest time on his opening lap and then speared into the barriers at the Parabolica. The team confirmed him as Hamilton’s successor the following day. Their faith was unwavering. “Toto did everything,” said an emotional Marco Antonelli, Kimi’s father, after his son captured his first GP win in March. 'Andy' Antonelli Andrea Kimi Antonelli: Many have wondered if he was named Kimi after Kimi Raikkonen, Ferrari’s last champion, but he wasn’t. The paddock may know him as Kimi, but at home he’s Andrea or simply "Andy". Motor racing is in his blood. His father, a former touring car racer who runs his own team, took the family to a race at Magny-Cours while his wife, Veronica, was pregnant and the baby began kicking at the sound of engines roaring. His father initially hoped for a different career choice, aware of the sport’s ruthless nature, and encouraged him to pursue football instead. As Kimi later explained, motorsport “can be amazing, but at the same time, can be brutal”. He eventually gave in when it became clear that his child was determined to be a racing driver. Abu Dhabi finale While Antonelli may have mathematically secured the championship in Mexico City, the season will close at the circuit where he claimed one of his first major single-seater titles. In February 2023, aged 16, Antonelli was crowned the inaugural Formula Regional Middle East champion at Yas Marina Circuit, driving for Mumbai Falcons. Three years ago, he was regarded as a prodigy. On December 6, he will return as a champion, the youngest the sport has ever seen.

title: Gunmen kill soldier, steal weapons at Plateau checkpoint
body:
Gunmen have killed a soldier and stolen two weapons after attacking troops of Operation Enduring Peace (OPEP) at a military checkpoint in Riyom Local Government Area of Plateau State .
The attack occurred at about 8 p.m. on Saturday at Sopp Checkpoint in Ungwan Boka, where soldiers were reportedly keeping vigil.
The assailants reportedly opened fire on the troops from different directions, triggering a gun battle before escaping into the bush.
The spokesperson for OPEP, Chinonso Oteh, an army captain, confirmed the incident, describing it as a deliberate and unprovoked attack on the troops.
He said security forces had restored normalcy in the area and launched an operation to track down the attackers and recover the stolen weapons.
“It was a deliberate and unprovoked attack on troops at Sopp Checkpoint, Ungwan Boka in Riyom Local Government Area.
“Troops have restored normalcy in the area and are maintaining aggressive pursuit of the perpetrators to apprehend them and recover the carted-away weapons,” Mr Oteh said.
He added that the situation remained under control, while troops had intensified surveillance to prevent further security breaches and reassure residents of their safety.
The military spokesperson urged residents to remain calm, continue their lawful activities, and provide credible information that could help security agencies apprehend the attackers.
The incident comes amid persistent security concerns in parts of Plateau State, where communities have experienced recurring attacks, killings and kidnappings.

title: Meyer Turku christens second Finnish Border Guard patrol vessel
body:
The Finnish Border Guard’s second multipurpose offshore patrol vessel, Valpas, has been christened at Meyer Turku shipyard in Finland, marking a milestone in the construction program.
The vessel was christened by its godmother, Minister of the Interior Mari Rantanen, on October 30, 2026. The ceremony was held at the Uusikaupunki shipyard, where Meyer Turku is carrying out the vessel’s outfitting. The Finnish Border Guard was represented by its Deputy Chief, Rear Admiral Tom Hanén , and Meyer Turku by Deputy CEO Ville Saksi .
In accordance with shipbuilding tradition, the vessel’s godmother gave a speech. Following the speech, the vessel was christened traditionally by breaking a bottle of champagne against its hull.
“ Offshore patrol vessels are highly complex multipurpose vessels requiring extensive expertise and close cooperation between the customer and the entire project network. The christening of the second vessel marks an important milestone in the project. Our work continues with determination to deliver vessels that meet the Finnish Border Guard’s high requirements and serve Finland’s maritime security well into the future ” said Saksi.
“ The Finnish Border Guard’s offshore patrol vessel project has reached an important milestone now that the second vessel has also been christened. The new vessels will enter service during the coming year. Our offshore patrol vessel fleet will be modern and harmonised once the operational systems of the patrol vessel Turva have also been upgraded. Finland’s ability to respond to the challenges of the security environment at sea will be significantly enhanced, ” commented Vice Admiral Markku Hassinen , Chief of the Finnish Border Guard.
The two-vessel order represents the largest single investment in the Finnish Border Guard’s history. The vessels are intended to expand its maritime operational capabilities and readiness. The first vessel, Karhu, is scheduled for completion in summer 2027, while Valpas is expected to be completed by the end of the same year.
The Finnish Border Guard’s operational capability at sea relies to a significant extent on the continuous operation and readiness of its multipurpose offshore patrol vessels. The new low-emission and energy-efficient offshore patrol vessels will operate at sea for approximately 330 days a year.
To remind, the first vessel, Karhu, was christened in August last year.

title: Ukraine’s Air Alert app was warn of radiation, chemicals, and street fighting in Kyiv. None of it was real

Ukraine’s Air Force said there was no radiation threat and that the app had likely come under enemy influence. The developers suspended the app overnight and then began restoring it. The fake leaned on a fear Russia keeps feeding. Russia has fired the Oreshnik, its intermediate-range ballistic missile, at Ukraine three times. The most recent strike came on 24 May near Bila Tserkva, a day after Ukraine warned of a possible strike with Kyiv among likely targets. In September, a Russian lawmaker threatened a fourth launch. What users received Around 22:45, the app began sending alerts about chemical and radiation threats and street fighting in Kyiv. Some messages were in Russian. They warned of an Oreshnik strike and carried a link to a Telegram channel. A message received by users of the app in Russian: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine now! Don’t worry, the Oreshnik missile is on its way.” Screenshot from the official app Shortly after 23:00, the Air Force urged Ukrainians to stay calm and follow its own channel for updates. The app’s team said outside parties had interfered with the app without authorization. It had disabled push notifications and temporarily suspended the app. The team added that the app stores no personal data, so users face no threat. It urged them not to open links from suspicious notifications. Before 02:00 on 2 November, the developers said they were gradually bringing the app back after the cyberattack. The map again shows yellow and red danger levels, which cover drone attacks and massive drone or missile attacks, and push alerts are working. The display of targets on the map remains suspended. Sirens kept working Meanwhile, sirens and other warning systems kept working, Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry said . It advised people to turn on emergency alerts on their phones and to rely only on official Air Force channels. In the capital, alerts in the Kyiv Digital city app worked normally, the ministry added. Ajax Systems built the app in 2022 at the initiative of IT company Stfalcon, with the ministry’s support. title: Can’t keep up with COP lingo? This list has got you covered
body: This story was first published on November 14, 2025. Due to recent events, we are republishing it with updated information. If this is your first time tuning in to the United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference or COP, you might be a little lost. A meeting among world leaders on solving the climate crisis sounds simple enough. That is, until you throw in a bunch of acronyms like NDCs, NAPs, and GST, along with technical terms like carbon markets, climate debt, and concessional finance — all with an extra side of a whole lot of politics. As world leaders navigate the two-week-long conference’s complicated landscape, everyone else has to make sense of whatever it is that’s coming out of their mouths. Here’s a list of terms you need to know if you’re tuning in to COP — which you probably should be doing if you care anything about our warming world. Play Video United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) – It is a treaty adopted in 1992 to halt climate change. It has since been joined by 198 countries, and is the parent treaty of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol and 2015 Paris Agreement. The ultimate goal of all these agreements is to control greenhouse gas emissions so that we do not end up irrevocably changing our climate to a dangerous degree. Conference of the Parties (COP) – As a generic term , it refers to the decision-making body composed of the countries who agreed on an international treaty or convention. In the context of the world’s climate agreements, it is an annual summit of countries who signed the UNFCCC, where they decide how to implement their commitments to tackle climate change. During the COP, countries also meet to discuss the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement in conferences known as the CMP and CMA, respectively. 1.5ºC – A tipping point in the Earth’s temperature that triggers irreversible and self-reinforcing changes in the environment, as identified by scientists. These changes include the Amazon rainforest turning into a savanna, melting ice sheets, or dying coral reefs, among others. 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge – It is a pledge by governments to accelerate the clean energy transition by increasing the share of global final energy consumption met by electricity from almost 24% in 2023 to 35% by 2035. Action Agenda – A platform for civil society to join voluntary initiatives that will accelerate emissions reduction, boost climate resilience, and support the transition to sustainable economies. It became a part of the COP’s regular program in COP21 back in 2015 as an initiative to expand beyond government negotiations and include people who don’t negotiate during the COP but act to put agreements into practice, like businesses, investors, and local governments. Adaptation – It refers to preparations made for a warmer world with more heat waves and higher sea levels. They can include strategies like planting trees for shade or safeguarding supplies against extreme weather disruptions. Funding for these strategies is called adaptation finance . (EXPLAINER: A guide to UN climate jargon, from NDCs to ‘unabated’ emissions ) Baku Finance Goal – It is a commitment to channel $1.3 trillion to developing countries each year that will help them implement climate plans. To achieve this goal, developed countries must take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion per year for developing countries by 2035. The blueprint to achieve this is called the Baku to Belém Roadmap . Belem Action Mechanism for a Global Just Transition (BAM) – It is a proposed mechanism that will outline how governments and the private sector can put people at the heart of national and sectoral transitions to renewable energy. This includes job creation, worker training, and strategies to diversify industries into climate planning and investment. Biennial transparency reports (BTR) – Every two years, countries are required to submit a report on national inventories of their emissions, progress toward their nationally determined contributions, policies and measures, climate change impacts and adaptation, financial and technical support provided or needed, and areas for improvement. The first submission of these reports was in December 2024, which means the second submission period will fall a month after COP31 in 2026 ends. Carbon credits – The carbon crediting mechanism was established under the Paris Agreement. When countries or companies reduce greenhouse gas emissions, they earn carbon credits that they can sell to other companies. Buying these credits allows companies to comply with their own emissions reduction obligations or meet net-zero targets. The trading systems in which carbon credits are sold and bought are called carbon markets . Common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) – Based on a “ polluter pays ” principle, this idea says that wealthy countries should do more to rein in climate change because they contributed the most emissions historically to the atmosphere. Climate debt – It is the sum of damages caused by emissions from developed countries on developing countries who do not emit as much yet are the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Climate finance – Funding provided by governments, development banks, private investors, and philanthropies to help countries lower greenhouse gas emissions or adapt to climate impacts. These include renewable energy projects or protection from floods, among others. (READ: What is climate finance and why does it matter? ) Champions – A person acting as a liaison between governments and civil society on behalf of the COP president , specifically working to involve businesses, communities, financial institutions, and other actors who do not negotiate climate agreements but are essential for putting them into practice. There are two types: high-level champions and youth champions . Each champion serves a term of two years. Climate justice – An idea recognizing that those who contribute least to carbon emissions are paying the highest cost. It means holding responsible countries, corporations, and people that drive the climate crisis. Concessional finance – It refers to below market rate finance provided by major financial institutions, like development banks and multilateral funds, to developing countries to accelerate development or climate objectives. COP Truce – It is an appeal to nations to stop military operations during the month of the COP. Cover decision – A statement outlining the high-level political agreements on key issues. It embodies what the summit has achieved and the broad goals that every country has agreed to pursue. (EXPLAINER: What happens at a COP climate summit? ) Decarbonization – The process of reducing carbon emissions. Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) – It was established in Article 7 of the Paris Agreement as a goal to enhance a country’s capacity to adapt, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability to climate change. It provides a system for countries to track their adaptation progress and urge them to act on managing climate change risks. Global Implementation Accelerator (GIA) – It is a “ cooperative, facilitative, and voluntary initiative ” that aims to speed up programs to keep 1.5°C within reach and support countries in implementing their nationally determined contributions and national adaptation plans. The initiative started at COP30 in 2025 and will continue into COP31. It will focus on specific actions on the ground and the mobilization of all actors. Global stocktake (GST) – It is a periodical assessment of the collective progress in achieving the Paris Agreement. It takes place every five years, with the first-ever stocktake concluded at COP28 in 2023. This assessment informs the climate action plans of every country. Green Climate Fund – A fund established under the Paris Agreement to distribute $100 billion in annual climate finance from wealthy nations to help developing countries fund the energy transition and projects for adapting to a warmer world. High-Level Segment – A part of the COP where national leaders give back-to-back speeches in the venue’s main plenary hall. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) – It is the UNFCCC’s main scientific body , where scientists from the countries who signed the treaty work together to release reports every six to seven years detailing global scientific consensus on climate science. Just transition – A shift from fossil fuels, like coal into renewable energy sources, that looks after those who will be displaced by the energy transition, especially workers. (EXPLAINER: What is just energy transition? ) Kyoto Protocol – A treaty that entered into force in 2005 where industrialized countries agreed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with agreed individual targets. It only binds developed countries, placing a heavier burden on them because they are largely responsible for the high levels of these emissions in the atmosphere. Loss and Damage Fund – Loss and damage refers to the negative consequences of climate change, like extreme weather events, rising sea levels, prolonged heatwaves, changes in ocean conditions, and damage to agriculture. They still occur despite mitigation and adaptation efforts, so COP28 approved a fund that will provide financial assistance to nations most vulnerable and impacted by these harmful effects. The Philippines is the host of this fund’s board. Mitigation – It refers to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions to slow, if not halt, global warming. It is the main focus in the world’s transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources. Montreal Protocol – It is an international agreement that regulates the production and consumption of nearly 100 man-made chemicals that harm and deplete the ozone layer. Mutirão Decision – It is the cover decision or final agreement made between countries at the end of COP30 hosted by Brazil. It was a compromise climate deal aimed at boosting finance for poor nations coping with global warming, although it omitted any mention of the fossil fuels driving it. The term “Mutirão” originally comes from the Tupi-Guarani language of Brazil and can be translated as “collective efforts.” National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) – They are strategies developed by countries, particularly developing nations, to prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change, such as droughts, floods, and sea level rise. Their main goals are to reduce climate vulnerability, integrate adaptation into public policies, plan actions based on scientific data, and access international climate finance. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) – These are pledges by each country on their target amount for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and their plans to adapt to the impacts of climate change. They are submitted every five years to the UNFCCC secretariat, and must represent a progression compared to the previous NDC, reflecting a country’s highest possible ambition. Net zero – It means releasing no more emissions than can be recaptured by technology, tree-planting, or other means. In short, reaching net zero means greenhouse gas concentrations stop increasing. Negotiating group – Countries sending delegations are distributed into groups or blocs that work together to represent their common interests in international climate change negotiations. The Philippines is part of the Group of 77 + China — the largest alliance of developing countries that promotes the interests of the Global South — and co-founded (but eventually left) the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc. New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) – It is a global climate finance goal set from a floor of $100 billion per year. In COP29 in 2024, they came up with a $300-billion annual target, called the Baku Finance Goal . Paris Agreement – A legally binding international treaty enacted in 2016 that aims to keep the increase in global average temperature to 2ºC — but preferably 1.5ºC — above levels before the Industrial Revolution. Under the agreement, signatory countries are expected to present their action plan to align with these goals. It also provides a framework for developing countries to receive support from developed countries. (READ: Where are we now on the Paris Agreement, a decade after it was adopted? ) Paris Rulebook – These are the implementation guidelines for the Paris Agreement, laying out the tools and processes for them to fully, fairly, and effectively follow the climate plans outlined in their NDCs. It was completed in COP29. Phaseout – A gradual reduction in the production and use of fossil fuels. Santa Marta First Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) – After COP30 omitted a fossil fuel phaseout in its final decision, this conference was held in Colombia in April 2026 and convened a 57-country “ coalition of the willing ” (excluding China, Russia, the US, and India to prevent the same deadlock that occurred in the previous year’s climate summit). The conference established a voluntary TAFF coordination process and adopted the “Santa Marta Vision” meant to inform the COP31 global fossil fuel roadmap. Secretariat – The UNFCCC secretariat, also referred to as UN Climate Change , is the UN entity tasked with supporting the world’s response to climate change. It organizes and supports the COP and other negotiations, provides technical expertise and reviews climate change information reported in these negotiations, and maintains a registry for NDCs. Small Island Developing States (SIDS) – They are a distinct group of 39 states and 18 associate members of UN regional commissions located in the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the Atlantic, Indian Ocean and South China Sea. They face unique social, economic, and environmental vulnerabilities because of their remote geography, such as high import and export costs for goods, irregular international traffic volumes, and a narrow resource base. The Troika – The host countries of COP28, COP29, and COP30, who said they were collaborating to ensure continuity in organizing the annual UN climate talks. All three countries have economies that rely on fossil fuels. Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF) – It is a global fund supporting tropical forest conservation that was first announced during COP30. UAE Consensus – It is a response to the results of the first global stocktake, setting standards for a just transition and goals like tripling renewable energy, halting deforestation, and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. Unabated emissions – Describes carbon pollution not being captured by new technologies such as carbon capture and storage. – Rappler.com

title: Ukraine, Russia Hit by Hackers Sending Fake Nuclear Attack Alerts
body:
Ukraine’s Air Alert app and Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry app were both hacked within hours of each other on Nov. 1-2, sending users fake warnings of nuclear attacks, chemical threats and even street fighting in Kyiv.
The first breach targeted Ukraine’s official Air Alert app on Sunday evening, Nov. 1. Users received false warnings about radiological and chemical hazards, as well as an alleged threat of street battles in the capital.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
One notification, sent in Russian, read: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine now. Don’t worry, Oreshnik is on its way.”
The app subsequently became temporarily unavailable.
Ukraine’s Air Force dismissed the warnings as false, reporting “hostile interference” with the service. The Center for Countering Disinformation urged users not to follow third-party links or spread unverified information. The app’s developers said they were working to restore the service.
Hours later, the hackers turned their attention to Russia.
The country’s Emergency Situations Ministry reported a “massive attack” on its mobile app after users began receiving push notifications in the early hours of Monday, Nov. 2, warning that nuclear warheads had been launched toward every region of Russia.
The fake alerts claimed the warheads were carried by P1-SUN systems – Ukrainian-made FPV interceptor drones developed by defense company SkyFall to take down Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles.
Users were instructed to stockpile three weeks’ worth of food and seek shelter in basements.
The warnings soon spread beyond the mobile app, appearing on regional Emergency Situations Ministry channels on Russia’s state-backed messaging platform Max. Notifications were reported in St. Petersburg and the Moscow regions, including Belgorod, Nizhny Novgorod, Sverdlovsk and Tyumen, among others.
A similar warning also appeared on the Telegram channel of the Belgorod region’s operational headquarters.
Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said it was working to fix a “vulnerability in the mobile application” and restore normal service.
“The situation is under control. We urge the public to remain calm and trust only official sources of information,” the ministry said, directing users to its website and official social media accounts.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Reports of Dog Burials in Tbilisi Reignite Concerns Over Stray Animal Treatment
body: Animal rights activists and protesters rallied in Tbilisi on November 1 after a TV Pirveli report showed footage of dogs being buried, apparently by municipal authorities, reigniting longstanding concerns over the treatment and fate of stray animals in Georgia. Authorities deny any ill-treatment, claiming the footage depicted a “lawful” procedure. The report , aired as part of Nodar Meladze’s Saturday Night investigative program on October 30, showed dog carcasses being transported in vans at night and dumped in what appeared to be a mass grave near a cemetery in Tbilisi. Animal rights activists raised concerns that stray dogs in Georgia, including healthy ones, may be subjected to cruel practices, including mass euthanasia without legal grounds. Tbilisi City Hall, meanwhile, denied any ill-treatment, arguing that the channel had distorted the facts and that the footage depicted a lawful process of burying dogs that had died “for various reasons,” including disease, accidents, or natural causes. “Particularly outrageous is the slander that alive dogs, deliberately put to sleep, are being placed in the burial site in question, which is a complete lie and disinformation,” the City Hall said. “We call on citizens to refrain from arbitrarily opening burial sites, removing carcasses, moving them, and any similar actions.” Shortly after the report, the Interior Ministry confirmed to the media that it had launched an investigation into possible torture, cruel treatment, or other forms of violence against animals under Article 259 of Georgia’s Criminal Code. Zero Strays Georgia, a local animal rights group, outlined key demands for the authorities, including a “transparent, thorough investigation” and “an independent examination of the cause of death and whether sedation or anesthesia was used.” It also called for “full records on the animals found, including medical reports and drugs used” and “an explanation of why biothermal pits weren’t used to prevent the spread of disease.” One of the protesters said at the rally that they demanded that “all carcasses be fully removed from all burial sites,” adding that the animals should be “counted and identified, because several dogs were recognized by people who had been searching for them earlier and had not received an answer from the monitoring [service].” Addressing the rally, blogger Tornike Razmadze also called for greater public oversight of facilities holding stray animals, saying that interested groups should be allowed to enter shelters and other state facilities at any time, potentially through a pre-approved list of visitors submitted to the relevant authorities. The scrutiny follows a series of similar reports and controversies over the past months surrounding the treatment of stray dogs in Tbilisi and other parts of Georgia. These included allegations and suspicions that stray dogs were routinely taken off the streets by authorities, euthanised or even cremated, or released into the wild with little chance of survival. Officials have denied such practices, claiming that dogs were temporarily taken off the streets for veterinary procedures. In October, animal rights activists also raised concerns over conditions at a shelter in Gori, a city in eastern Georgia’s Shida Kartli region, after footage circulated online showing what appeared to be overcrowded and unsanitary conditions, with activists alleging that around 300 puppies were being kept there without adequate food or water, alongside dead animals. The Shida Kartli Stray Animal Management Agency denied the allegations, responding that the footage had been circulated “out of context” and was intended to deliberately mislead the public. The footage nevertheless prompted public outrage and efforts by animal defenders to remove dogs from the shelter. Subsequent footage showed dogs being taken out of the facility, while volunteers organized their care. One of the activists said that some of the rescued puppies were placed in a large house in Tskneti, on the outskirts of Tbilisi. Also Read: 11/01/2024 – Brutal Killing of a Dog Sparks Concerns Over Animal Rights in Georgia

title: Sheikh Mohammed launches worker-led Dh9m drive to take government services to 'new levels'
body: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, has issued a rallying call to enterprising government workers to help to develop “bold new solutions” to drive UAE progress. Sheikh Mohammed on Monday set out plans to champion the country's talent and harness their expertise under a new national campaign aimed at taking government services to “new levels”. The Annual Government Challenge, announced to coincide with the start of UAE Innovation Month, will focus on advancing the use of agentic artificial intelligence in its first edition. Sheikh Mohammed said the top nine government projects and teams would be honoured for making a “real impact” in improving services, with Dh9 million in prizes on offer across three categories. Participants will be tasked with using AI agents to redesign services, enhance decision making and raise government performance. It will be overseen by the Mohammed bin Rashid Centre for Government Innovation at the Ministry of Cabinet Affairs. "As UAE Innovates begins, we launch today the Annual Government Challenge for UAE Government employees and teams," Sheikh Mohammed said. "A new national initiative to inspire our government talent to create bold new solutions with real impact on our services, operations and projects. "The first challenge: Agentic AI. We will honour the top 9 government projects and teams. We want unconventional ideas. Solutions that make a difference. Projects that take government work to new levels.” Mohammad Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and chairman of the National Committee for the Agentic AI Project, said the Annual Government Challenge underlined the UAE's vision for a government that does not merely keep pace with the future abut anticipates and adapts to change. “Government work in the UAE is more agile and better prepared to deal with change," Mr Al Gergawi said. "In the next phase, we aim to deploy Agentic AI assistants to work alongside employees in driving development, efficiency and productivity. "Through this challenge, we are counting on our ability to combine the expertise of our people with the capabilities of technology to design a faster, more efficient and more proactive government. “Through the Annual Government Challenge, we want every government employee to be a partner in developing government, and every outstanding idea to become an opportunity to design a better service, a more efficient process or a new operating model." مع انطلاق شهر الإمارات للابتكار.. نعلن اليوم عن إطلاق "التحدي الحكومي السنوي" لموظفي وفرق عمل حكومة الإمارات.. مبادرة وطنية جديدة نريد من خلالها تحفيز الكوادر والمواهب الحكومية على ابتكار حلول جديدة وجريئة تحدث أثراً حقيقياً في خدماتنا وعملياتنا ومشاريعنا الحكومية.. ونبدأ أول… pic.twitter.com/k8U9XjB3Fn — HH Sheikh Mohammed (@HHShkMohd) November 2, 2026 AI action plan The strategy is the latest step in the UAE's long-term push to promote safe and responsible use of AI within the government. In May, the UAE unveiled plans to train 80,000 workers – from ministers to junior employees – in the use of AI agents in a bid to ensure half of government services are delivered by the emerging technology within two years. Sheikh Mohammed said at the time it would be the largest AI training programme launched by the UAE government. It focuses on raising AI capabilities in five categories, covering leadership, technical skills, specialist roles, the general workforce and additional support for trainers. A dedicated digital platform, powered by Agentic AI tools, will be developed to assist federal employees through personalised learning pathways tailored to their role and skill level. The project aims to utilise AI agents – an autonomous model of AI capable of making decisions and achieving specific goals with limited supervision – to reshape government. The AI agents will be used to redesign government policies, processes and procedures and will enable smart systems to perform tasks proactively to reduce operational costs and boost productivity and efficiency. There will be a phased introduction of the scheme in ministries and federal departments, based on continuous performance and impact assessments. This will pave the way for a wider roll-out across the federal government.

title: It’s a life blessing’ – BUA boss describes entering Holy Kaaba with President Tinubu
body:
The Chairman of BUA Group , Abdul-Samad Rabiu, has described entering the interior of the Holy Kaaba alongside President Bola Tinubu as a profound, once-in-a-lifetime spiritual milestone.
In a statement issued on Facebook, the billionaire industrialist recalled the visit to Islam’s holiest site in Makkah on Sunday, expressing humility and gratitude for being among those granted access to the sacred chamber alongside the Nigerian president.
“Some moments in life are beyond words, moments that touch the soul and remain forever engraved in the heart.
“Alhamdulillah, today I was profoundly humbled and blessed to be among those granted the extraordinary honour of entering the Holy Kaaba alongside His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR”, he posted on Facebook.
Mr Rabiu described the encounter as a defining moment of divine grace, reflecting that the privilege served as an avenue to offer fervent prayers for Nigeria’s peace, unity, and economic progress.
“In that most sacred of places, my thoughts and prayers were not only for myself and my family, but for our entire nation. May Almighty Allah accept our prayers and bless our beloved nation with lasting peace, unity, and prosperity,” he added.
“It was a once-in-a-lifetime blessing, an honour beyond measure, and a moment of divine grace that will remain etched in my heart for as long as I live.
“This deeply sacred experience was one of immense gratitude, reflection, and renewed faith in the infinite mercy and blessings of Almighty Allah. May Almighty Allah accept our prayers and bless our beloved nation with lasting peace, unity, and prosperity”, Mr Rabiu stated.
The interior of the Kaaba is one of the most exclusive and strictly regulated diplomatic and spiritual sites in the world.
Unlike general pilgrimage sites in the Grand Mosque, the Kaaba is closed to the public year-round and is unsealed only under rare, highly ceremonial circumstances.
Under Saudi protocol, the door of the Kaaba cannot be unlocked without a direct royal order issued by the King of Saudi Arabia—the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques—or the Crown Prince, Muhammad Bin Salman.
Opening the Kaaba for a visiting foreign Muslim president is regarded as the highest mark of spiritual respect and bilateral esteem the Kingdom can bestow.
Even with royal approval, Saudi authorities strictly uphold a 1,400-year-old Islamic tradition regarding physical access.
The physical custody of the Kaaba and its key remains exclusively with the Bani Shaybah (Al-Shaibi) family, in accordance with the historical decree made by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) after the conquest of Makkah.
Before the door is opened, the family’s senior custodian is formally summoned to lead the physical ceremony, accompany the dignitaries, and oversee the locking mechanism.
When the golden door is opened, the general authority for the care of the Two Holy Mosques (Makkah and Madinah) deploys a mobile ceremonial staircase to the elevated threshold.
Stringent security cordons are established across the Mataf (the circumambulation area) to maintain order.
Inside, guests typically perform voluntary prayers facing any of the four walls, followed by moments of supplication, before the door is resealed.
President Tinubu was the second Nigerian president in the Fourth Republic to enjoy the rare privilege after his predecessor, the late President Muhammadu Buhari.

title: Moscow rejected Kyiv's proposal to extend the ceasefire in Oleshky
body:
Russia has rejected a proposal by the Ukrainian side to extend the ceasefire in the Oleshky region, a senior official from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) told AFP on Sunday evening.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine put forward a proposal to extend the ceasefire agreement, but the Russians refused,” AFP quoted the unnamed Ukrainian MFA official as saying.
The agreement, which aimed to deliver humanitarian aid to the population of Oleshky and facilitate their evacuation, formally expired at midnight on Sunday.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday afternoon that residents evacuated from Oleshky have already returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory. The Ukrainian delegation, which was carrying out a humanitarian mission in Oleshky, returned along with the evacuees.
Despite the unwillingness from Russia to extend the ceasefire agreement, the whole operation should be treated as a success. The Ukrainian delegation managed to safely enter and leave Oleshky alongside evacuated civilians.

title: the lost malloc()
body:
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)
Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources . This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.
This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.
In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago . C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.
Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year ! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.
While cleaning a storage room, our staff found this tape containing UNIX v4 from Bell Labs, circa 1973
The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.
In /usr/c/c20.c:814 , from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:
Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.
The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk() , when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.
And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.
This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.
In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c . And you see two functions there:
Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m . These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But , the interfaces are different.
malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree() . What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:
So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap . What are those? From /usr/sys/systm.h:2 :
They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions ! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should . Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc() / free() .
Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...
(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)
However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.
From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:
These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:
For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.
And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree() ). Basically, it's a list of blocks ( struct map ), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.
The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17 :
... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88 , I think the first ever version of diff(1) , you find:
This is not all that much different from the previous alloc() , but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143 :
I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory ( a = alloc(...); ), then roll back the region ( area = a; )! Though they subsequently just copy it to b , so it seems like this was redundant.
Most of the code directly calls malloc() / alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:
I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:
Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38 . Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make . Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.
V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.
Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7 :
If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:
I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc() / free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.
But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:
When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:
Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.
In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991 , he writes:
In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.
Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:
The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:
and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.
He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!
This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new . Wikipedia states:
Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.
And it appeared in 1967 . Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:
[...] The symbol " new " only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.
So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!
The History of Simula , by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after . This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.
Also: The development of the SIMULA languages , by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...
It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.
Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report , you won't find a mention of new . You'll however find CREATE :
When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.
For example, the statement " CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO " allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG , and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.
Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS , by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:
In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14 , part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new() :
Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).
They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.
Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.
And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.
Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap . Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc() / free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.
That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3) :
and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15 :
Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection . Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.
Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992) , P. J. Plauger writes:
Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.
Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.
Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.
I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.
Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C . There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.
At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...
(Kindly let me know if I made some mistake :)

title: Russian forces strike regional power utility facility in Odesa region
body:
According to Ukrinform, DTEK Group reported this on Telegram .
"In the early hours of November 2, the enemy attacked a DTEK energy facility in the Odesa region. As soon as it became possible, our power engineers began repair work," the statement said.
As of this morning, power engineers had restored electricity to some consumers who lost power as a result of the attack. Emergency repair and restoration work is ongoing.

title: Iran’s nuclear program to remain peaceful while country stays in NPT — MFA
body:
TEHRAN, November 2. /TASS/. Iran remains a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and is committed to complying with all its provisions, including those concerning the peaceful nature of its nuclear program, Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
"Iran’s nuclear program is entirely peaceful and remains so. We are still a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, and as long as we remain a party, we are committed to complying with it," he told a press conference.
Baghaei pointed out it is too early to discuss resuming International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspections at Iranian nuclear facilities, as the agency’s Director General Rafael Grossi must first condemn US and Israeli attacks on the country’s nuclear infrastructure.

title: Teenager’s TikTok video prompted U.S. warning of possible Moscow terrorist attack, Russia’s FSB says
body: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said a teenager who posted a video on TikTok was the source of information about a planned terrorist attack in Moscow, a threat the U.S. Embassy had warned about the day before. The teenager has been detained. His name has not been disclosed. According to the FSB, the video showed the teenager himself dressed in tactical clothing, a balaclava, a cap, glasses, and headphones, holding “an object resembling an automatic weapon.” It also included photos taken at the Tsaritsyno museum-reserve, captioned “I found a place.” The FSB also said the teenager was subscribed to a “neo-Nazi channel” on Telegram and had searched for information about mass killings. It remains unclear which channel this refers to. The FSB “expressed gratitude” to its American counterparts for the information about the planned attack, the Russian state news agency TASS reported. The U.S. Embassy in Russia had issued a warning a day earlier about a threat of a terrorist attack on the grounds of the museum-reserve. The FSB confirmed it had received the warning from the United States and said it was reviewing the matter. The German Embassy in Moscow also issued a similar warning for its citizens. The museum-reserve closed that same day, citing “technical reasons,” and reopened the next day. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. title: Trump may pin blame for war with Iran on Pentagon chief — magazine
body:
WASHINGTON, November 2. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is looking for someone to blame for the protracted war with Iran and is questioning his advisers about the performance of Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine, The Atlantic reported, citing sources close to the US leader.
According to the magazine, Trump has focused his attention on those who assured him that the war would end quickly and well before the midterm congressional elections. Hegseth and Caine were among those who viewed the conflict’s prospects positively in its early stages.
The sources noted that the Pentagon chief is unpopular in the White House and that several of Trump’s close associates believe he is painting an overly optimistic picture of the conflict with Iran for the president. "Hegseth is good at telling the president what he wants to hear," one source told the magazine.
According to The Atlantic, as the conflict drags on, Trump is becoming increasingly convinced that it is one of the reasons for the Republican Party’s declining political standing.
On October 8, US President Donald Trump said that Washington does not intend to launch strikes against Iran before the midterm congressional elections, which will take place on November 3. On October 31, he assured that talks with Tehran were going well but expressed doubts about Iran’s good faith. When asked whether he planned to resume military action against Iran the following week, he refused to give a clear answer. According to the Axios news outlet, Trump does not intend to resume military action against Iran immediately after the midterm congressional elections, as he wants to focus on negotiations with Tehran.

title: Police arrest three over political violence in Katsina
body:
Police in Katsina State have arrested three people after a vehicle was set ablaze and political posters were burnt in Yankara, Faskari Local Government Area, on Saturday.
In a statement issued on Sunday, police spokesperson Abubakar Aliyu described the incident as suspected political thuggery.
He said investigations were continuing to determine what triggered the violence.
According to the police, a crowd blocked a road in Yankara, threw stones and burnt political posters after Governor Dikko Radda had passed through the town on his way to an All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship campaign rally in Faskari.
Mr Aliyu said the governor’s convoy passed without incident under the security arrangements put in place for the campaign.
The police said the crowd later set fire to a Toyota Sienna (commonly called Sharon) belonging to a supporter who had travelled to the rally.
The vehicle had developed a mechanical fault and was parked by the roadside after its driver left for the campaign venue.
Officers from the Faskari Police Division, working with other security agencies, dispersed the crowd and arrested three suspects: Garba Shu’aibu, 25; Salmanu Ibrahim, 18; and Nazifi Hussaini, 30. Investigators are searching for others who fled the scene.
Police Commissioner Ali Umar Fage warned political parties and their supporters against violence during election campaigns.
He urged residents to remain calm and said those found responsible would be prosecuted.
The police have not identified the vehicle’s owner, established whether those responsible were affiliated with any political party, or disclosed what triggered the road blockade.
They have also not said whether the burning of the vehicle and posters was politically motivated.
The police account follows an earlier statement by the Katsina State Government on Saturday that disputed reports linking the violence in Yankara to Mr Radda’s campaign rally.
In the statement, signed by the Governor’s Chief Press Secretary, Ibrahim Kaula Mohammed, the government said preliminary information showed the disturbance arose from a disagreement between participants in a Maulud procession and security personnel over designated routes, confusing on a public street in Yankara.
The government insisted the incident had no connection with the governor’s campaign activities or the Tinubu-Dikko campaign rally in Faskari.
It said Mr Radda passed through Yankara safely, visited the district head’s palace, inspected ongoing renovation works at the Faskari Local Government Secretariat, and later attended the rally.
The government called on security agencies to investigate the incident thoroughly and urged media organisations and the public to verify reports before sharing information that could heighten tension.
It also appealed to residents to remain calm.

title: South Korean sergeant killed on border with external wounds, as tensions with North escalate
body: A South Korean army staff sergeant died after suffering external injuries at a frontline unit in Cheorwon near the North Korean border on Monday morning, Seoul's Defense Ministry said.Military and civilian investigators were examining the exact cause and circumstances of his death, the ministry said.The death comes amid heightened tensions along the border after three South Korean soldiers were wounded in landmine explosions south of the Military Demarcation Line on September 21.It was not immediately clear whether the staff sergeant's death on Monday was related to the border tensions.South Korea's military has said the mines that caused the explosions in September were laid by North Korea as part of its efforts to fortify the border since 2024, an accusation Pyongyang has denied.This is a developing story.

title: Russia’s FSB seizes booby-trapped FPV goggles intended for Russian troops
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has reported the seizure of a mined batch of FPV drone goggles intended for the Russian military in the special military operation zone as humanitarian aid.
"The Federal Security Service thwarted a series of sabotage and terrorist attacks using improvised explosive devices concealed inside FPV drone goggles intended for delivery to the Russian military in the special military operation zone, which were plotted by Ukrainian special services," the FSB said.
According to the agency, acting on instructions from military counterintelligence, a Russian serviceman in the Volgograd Region brought two FPV goggles he had received from a volunteer to the FSB for inspection. Explosive ordnance specialists established that Ukrainian special services had planted improvised explosive devices in the FPV goggles instead of cooling solutions. "As a result of the measures taken, a batch of similar improvised explosives camouflaged as FPV goggles, sent into the country via the Russian Post, has been confiscated across Russia," the FSB said.
The explosive devices would have detonated when the FPV glasses were switched on, potentially killing servicemen, the FSB added.
"Posing as pseudo-patriots, agents of Ukrainian special services established communication with representatives of Russian humanitarian organizations and charity foundations, using anonymous accounts on the Telegram messenger," to arrange supplies to Russian Defense Ministry units, the FSB continued. During these exchanges, they refused to share their names, phone numbers and job information or switch to the Max messenger for calls as they communicated with volunteers to arrange the delivery of FPV goggles with homemade explosive devices, while demanding video feedback with words of gratitude from Russian fighters, the FSB said.
According to the enemy’s plans, volunteers were supposed to later deliver the FPV goggles laden with improvised explosive devices to Russian drone operators taking part in combat operations against Ukrainian troops, the FSB noted.
A criminal case has been opened, and efforts to identify those responsible for the shipment are underway, the FSB concluded.

body:
TEHRAN, November 2. /TASS/. The issue of transferring uranium enriched to 60% from Iran to third countries was not discussed during the exchange of messages with the United States, Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmail Baghaei has said.
