title: Poroshenko hands over 6 upgraded Aypetri EW systems to military
body:
People's Deputy and European Solidarity party leader Petro Poroshenko has handed over six modernized Aypetri counter-technical intelligence (EW/CTI) complexes to military units, which are set to take up positions on Monday, November 2, the political party's website reported on Sunday.
It is noted that the upgraded complexes operate on higher frequencies. "Starting in August, the Russians began using jet-powered Shaheds, with which they terrorize Ukraine day and night. One of the very few effective means of countering such attacks is the modernized Aypetri EW complexes. As of today, they can operate at high frequencies to prevent Russian 'Gerans' and 'Gerbers' from reaching their targets," Poroshenko stated.
According to him, the entire batch was "financed by the defense ministry of one of our friendly NATO member countries, for which we are very grateful." At the same time, the politician did not specify which country is involved.
"Production is now operating day and night. And we are very grateful to the representatives of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the manufacturing plant, and our entire team that made this possible," Poroshenko said.
As reported, since autumn 2023, Poroshenko has invested over UAH 200 million in the production of Aypetri SV systems, which have successfully passed trials and are used in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Each complex includes the counter-intelligence asset itself, a pickup truck, a charging station, a generator, and necessary electronics. In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of the same year, he announced the start of cooperation with the Ground Forces Command of the AFU regarding the supply of these complexes to the military. On September 9, 2026, the Aypetri CTI was showcased for the first time at the MSPO 2026 defense and security technology exhibition in Kielce, Poland.

title: Court orders fraudulent 'rabbi,' wife to pay NIS 830,000 to woman in exploitation settlement
body: A Petah Tikva court on Sunday approved a settlement requiring Shaul Elkariv, known as the “criminals' rabbi,” and his wife, Tova, to pay NIS 830,000 (about $264,000) to Nechama Gabai, who had sued them for NIS 1.17 million (about $372,000). The court's approval makes the settlement a binding judgment.The agreement ends an unusual lawsuit alleging a long-running pattern of exploitation, intimidation, and financial control, during which hundreds of thousands of shekels were transferred to the couple.According to the complaint, filed by attorneys Dov Weinroth and Osher Rubinger, Gabai, a mother of three struggling personally and financially, turned to Elkariv in 2021 after he was presented to her as a rabbi, a kabbalist (a practitioner of Jewish mysticism), and someone with spiritual powers who could help people in trouble.Lawsuit alleged Elkariv took advantage of Gabai in order to take moneyAs their relationship grew closer, Gabai said, Elkariv became a central figure in her life, and she came to rely on his advice and follow his instructions on personal, family, and financial matters.The lawsuit alleged that Elkariv took advantage of her trust and dependence on him to persuade her to transfer large sums of money to him and his wife.Between February and March 2022, the lawsuit says Gabai transferred a total of NIS 745,467 to the couple. Most of the money came from the sale of an apartment as part of her divorce, and the rest came from government benefits she relied on to support herself and her children.One of the most striking details in the lawsuit is how the transfers were made. According to Gabai, Elkariv went with her to the bank, told her what to do, and in some cases even introduced himself to bank employees as her father. When she expressed doubts about the transfers, the lawsuit alleged, he reassured her, claiming he had spoken with her divorce lawyer, who he said knew about the transfers and approved them.The money was transferred in several installments, according to the lawsuit: some to the Elkarivs' joint bank account, some to Tova Elkariv's personal account, and some in cash. Gabai said Elkariv presented the transfers as a way to protect her assets and keep them safe.According to the lawsuit, Gabai kept the transfers secret from her family for years. Her relatives found out only in late 2025, after she ran into financial trouble and asked them for help.The lawsuit alleged that Gabai was afraid to ask Elkariv for the money back, in part because, she claimed, he had threatened to harm her family if they interfered in his affairs.Elkariv reportedly promised to pay Gabai back, described funds paid as a loanTranscripts of conversations between Gabai and her brother, and between her family members and Elkariv, were attached to the lawsuit. According to Gabai, Elkariv admitted in those conversations that he had received the money, promised to return it, and even said he planned to take out a loan to pay it back. The lawsuit further alleged that he asked the family to sign a document describing the money as a loan. Despite those alleged promises, the money had not been returned by the time the lawsuit was filed.The lawsuit also cites an earlier case in which Elkariv sued Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu and others for defamation over publications about him. In July 2024, the Tel Aviv District Court threw out that suit. The ruling examined testimony and publications about how Elkariv presented himself and allegations that he exploited women who came to him in distress. That case is separate from Gabai's lawsuit.Gabai sought the return of NIS 745,467, plus interest and inflation adjustments that brought the total to about NIS 970,000, as well as NIS 200,000 in additional damages for the alleged harm and the severity of Elkariv's conduct. At her request, the court froze assets during the proceedings to secure her claim.The parties ultimately settled, with the Elkarivs agreeing to pay Gabai NIS 830,000.

title: Russia’s Starlink rival lost a second satellite after it apparently sat idle for 103 days
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A satellite built for Rassvet, Russia’s answer to Starlink, burned up on 30 October, Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express reported . It is the network’s second loss since launches began in March. A third stricken satellite may have been saved, though sources disagree. On 5 February, Ukraine and SpaceX blocked the Starlink terminals Russian troops had used without permission. Officially, Rassvet is a commercial internet service. If it works, though, Russian forces could get satellite links that Kyiv has no US company to ask to switch off. The EU’s 21st sanctions package targeted Rassvet in July but left its operator, Bureau 1440, off the list. A satellite that apparently never maneuvered Satellite No. 17 went up on 19 July aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket with 15 others. It apparently never fired its engine, Defense Express wrote. After 103 days, residual air drag pulled it low enough to burn. No. 23 was sinking too. On 20 October, at 220 km, Bureau 1440 managed to start lifting it, and it keeps climbing, Defense Express said. Space analyst Anatoly Zak’s launch page still lists it among satellites expected to fall, citing the Aerospace Corporation. Public tracking data from 1 November put it at about 316 km, marked active. Slow, but working Of the 30 satellites in orbit, 26 have reached about 500 km, Defense Express said. The outlet described that as a staging altitude before a joint climb to the planned 800 km. Russian telecom outlet ComNews offered another reading in July: Bureau 1440 had likely lowered the working orbit to 514 km. The company’s press office did not answer ComNews. Explore further Russia is building Starlink no foreign company can switch off. Ukraine names 49 firms behind it, and 23 face no sanctions from Kyiv’s allies at all The first loss followed the same pattern. Satellite No. 4, from the March batch, fell in early June without ever raising its orbit. The serial satellites are already in test use. At a Moscow tech forum on 7 October, Bureau 1440 showed a video call over Rassvet to Adygea, a Russian republic, according to ComNews . Its first such demo, in 2023, ran on test satellites. Flat objects on Russian Molniya-2 drones were reported as Rassvet terminals. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president, rejected that, and Defense Express concluded they are probably not. title: Researchers find way to optimize biodiesel by mixing rapeseed, linseed oil
body:
TOMSK, November 2. /TASS/. Scientists have found a way to optimize the properties of biodiesel by blending rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils in a ratio of 90%, 5%, and 5%, respectively, making it possible to produce fuel with target characteristics without chemical additives and reduces logistics costs by 10-15% compared to imported raw materials, the Russian Ministry of Education and Science told TASS.
One of the main obstacles to the commercial application of biodiesel is the influence of the raw material fatty acid composition on its properties: low-temperature performance, oxidative stability, specific heat of combustion, and viscosity. Scientists consider the pre-blending of vegetable oils prior to transesterification to be a promising approach as combining raw materials with complementary fatty acid profiles helps neutralize limitations and improve properties. However, the choice of oils is often dictated by regional availability and cost rather than properties optimization.
"Scientists from Tomsk Polytechnic University, together with colleagues, have proposed an approach that allows optimizing the physicochemical properties of oil-based biodiesel fuel and, in the long term, creating a cost-effective strategy for producing biodiesel with specified characteristics without chemical additives," the ministry noted.
The comprehensive predictive model proposed by the scientists is adapted to raw materials common in regions with a temperate continental climate, specifically rapeseed, flax, and safflower, said Vladlena Chobotova, a research engineer at the Heat and Mass Transfer Laboratory,. This approach transforms the pre-blending of oils from a simple logistical measure into a precise tool for tailoring biofuel properties to the EN 14214 standard without chemical additives.
The scientists selected unrefined rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils as raw materials due to their inherent properties, regional availability, and lower cost compared to refined counterparts. The properties of rapeseed oil allow for obtaining biodiesel with a high cetane number and oxidation capacity, linseed oil helps reduce viscosity, and safflower oil yields fuel with properties intermediate between rapeseed and linseed. Methanol and potassium hydroxide were used as the alcohol and alkaline catalysts, respectively.
In the course of their research, the scientists developed eight predictive models that link raw material composition to fuel properties. Their accuracy was confirmed by statistical verification. It was also established that blending rapeseed, linseed, and safflower oils before transesterification alters the fatty acid composition almost linearly. The yield of methyl esters was 96.8-99.2%, which complies with the EN 14214 standard. Minor fatty acids significantly affect viscosity and low-temperature properties. The optimal ratio is 90% rapeseed, 5% linseed, and 5% safflower. The algorithm can be integrated into automated raw material management systems to adjust the formulation during price and quality fluctuations. The results obtained showed that using regionally available oils reduces logistics costs by 10-15% compared to imported raw materials. At the same time, the proposed optimization model can be easily adapted to other regional oil combinations, making it promising for localized and cost-effective biodiesel production.

title: El Niño conditions threaten prolonged dry spells, food production in Ghana – GMet
body: The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) has warned that persistent El Niño conditions could expose parts of Ghana to prolonged dry spells, potentially affecting agricultural production and food security. El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a naturally occurring climate pattern involving fluctuations in sea surface temperatures and atmospheric conditions over the tropical Pacific Ocean. Its effects can influence rainfall and temperature patterns in different parts of the world. Deputy Director of Research and Applied Meteorology at GMet, Francisca Martey, said the country should expect warmer days and below-normal rainfall in the coming months as the weather phenomenon continues to influence rainfall patterns. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, November 2, she said the effects were already being experienced, with much of the country recording relatively dry conditions and limited rainfall since September. She explained that GMet’s September-October-November seasonal forecast had anticipated below-normal rainfall across most parts of the country, alongside above-normal temperatures and extended dry spells. “We’re going to have long dry spells. We’re going to have below-normal rainfall,” she said. According to her, the conditions are expected to persist into the December-January-February period, coinciding with the Harmattan season, which is typically characterised by dry air and dusty winds. “We are expecting that with this timing it will continue. The Harmattan will come in. The Harmattan will be drier,” she said. Read Also: GMet warns of hotter, drier and dustier conditions as strong El Niño develops She added that temperatures were also expected to rise during the period. “We expect that December, January, and February will be warmer,” she stated. Mrs Martey warned that the northern parts of the country could face more severe consequences because of their greater vulnerability to El Niño-related rainfall deficits and their importance to Ghana’s food production. “Although the El Niño affects the whole country, its impact is higher on the northern areas,” she said. She cautioned that prolonged dry conditions could affect water availability for farming, particularly as stored rainwater in some communities and farming areas gradually dries up. “The little rainwater that they have kept or saved would also dry up,” she said. To mitigate the potential impact on agriculture, she urged farmers to adopt climate-smart practices, particularly mulching, to help conserve soil moisture. “We are expecting that they will practise more mulching systems and climate-smart agricultural systems,” she said. She also advised farmers to remain vigilant against crop pests and diseases that could become a challenge under the prevailing weather conditions. Beyond agriculture, Mrs Martey warned that reduced rainfall across parts of West Africa could affect water resources shared by Ghana and neighbouring countries. She noted that lower rainfall in the region could have implications for the Volta River system and water availability. During the interview, she also agreed that reduced inflows into the Akosombo Dam could affect hydroelectric power generation. GMet is engaging stakeholders in agriculture, health and water resources management, as well as the general public, to raise awareness and strengthen preparedness. Mrs Martey urged Ghanaians to take precautions against the expected hot and dusty conditions, including staying hydrated and protecting themselves from dust.

title: Long road from Russian occupation: Stories of Oleshky residents
body:
Journalists representing Ukrainian and foreign media outlets spent several hours waiting for citizens who had spent over a day traveling to Ukraine from the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region. As stipulated by the humanitarian mission plan, they traveled from their hometown by bus to Anapa (Russia), then by plane to Belarus, and from there once again by bus to a meeting point in Chernihiv region.
Everything was prepared at the site for the arrival—tents set up by the State Emergency Service (SES), the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS), and charitable foundations, alongside volunteers, hot food, warm blankets, and pet food.
The first vehicle to enter the site was an SES truck, from which the barking, whining, and meowing of animals could be heard. Volunteers immediately transferred the animals, frightened and exhausted by the long journey, into a URCS truck.
"There are approximately 70 animals here. All of them will undergo rehabilitation," a volunteer from the UAnimals animal and environmental protection organization reported.
After some time, buses and an extended convoy of ambulances arrived at the site. People stepped out of the buses exclaiming, "Glory to Ukraine!", "My dears!", "We are finally home." Many wept—both men and women. Someone immediately expressed concern for their German Shepherd, checking how it endured the trip before walking over to the URCS truck. Another evacuee recounted how, while still in Oleshky, they managed to coordinate with volunteers to successfully transport dogs across the river using a drone that flew over to Mykolaiv.
Volunteers, medical personnel, and psychologists immediately began assisting the evacuees.
"We took only personal belongings, documents, and photo albums containing our entire lives. And I took my apartment keys... We have nowhere to go..." an elderly woman recounted.
Meanwhile, 72-year-old Ms. Olya, following the mandatory rehabilitation provided to all evacuees, will travel to her children in Odesa.
Every arriving individual holds a distinct story. Nearly all remain uncertain of what lies ahead, and all of them are still mentally rooted in Oleshky.
"I was left alone; my husband passed away, and my son was killed last year. I have a brother living in Vinnytsia region who is inviting me to stay. There is a family house where no one currently lives. It is difficult, but I ultimately decided to leave Oleshky. I said goodbye to my men, so to speak, because I do not know when I will be able to return to visit them at the cemetery," shared another distinguished elderly lady.
The woman noted that food conditions in Oleshky had deteriorated severely since May.
"The younger ones rode bicycles or walked to Radensk. I did not go. Even if they offered me a million, I wouldn't go. I am no longer at an age where I can ride a bicycle," the interlocutor stated.
According to her, they had recently been receiving humanitarian aid drops: "Our people dropped humanitarian aid from large drones. They called those drones 'Baba Yaga'... You do not leave the house at night—blackouts were always enforced—but you hear something drop, and in the morning you check: humanitarian aid, canned goods, stewed meat, grains, pasta... As for vegetables, we grew small amounts ourselves. But crops only grew for those who had access to water and generators."
When asked what she desired most at that moment, she replied: "Sweets. Really, really delicious ones."
An elderly man joined the conversation: "In September, I rode a bicycle 20 kilometers to get food. I hadn't ridden a bike in five years. I am already 79. It took me two hours to get there. I bought 30 to 40 kilograms of provisions. I couldn't ride back loaded like that, so I walked back from Radensk to Oleshky on foot, pushing a bicycle laden with food... It took me six hours of walking. That is how one had to survive."
He added: "And you had to walk with extreme caution because many areas are mined. I nearly lost my life there seven days ago... I was walking home, already very close, when a drone crashed into a lighting pole just a few meters from me. It fell. Smoke filled the air. Breathing was difficult. For a minute, I couldn't see anything... By some miracle, those flying concrete shards from the shattered pole missed me... That was the final straw: I realized I could no longer live there and decided to leave."
Mikhailo Paliy was met upon his return by his family—his wife and two daughters.
"We lived under Russian occupation for two years. Two years ago, when I was 14, my mother, my sister, and I left Oleshky, while my father stayed behind. We evacuated through Russian filtration checkpoints. We were subjected to a four-hour interrogation solely because we lacked Russian documents," Liza Paliy recounted.
When asked how she planned to welcome her father at home in Kyiv, Liza responded: "We bought salo and cooked borscht so he could eat proper, normal food."
"We sincerely hope these humanitarian missions will continue, and that people will be given the opportunity to leave occupied territories safely, without fear or interrogations at Russian checkpoints," the young woman emphasized.
Liza harbors a dream—to visit Crimea. In 2014, the family planned a trip to the peninsula, but the Russian occupation disrupted those plans. The dream remains undiminished. She firmly believes that following the de-occupation of Ukrainian territories, she will certainly travel to Crimea—passing through our Oleshky.

title: Dakar 2026 YOG: Nigeria’s flagbearer Nwankwo eyes 100m glory
body:
Coming to Dakar, Senegal, for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games, Team Nigeria’s Rosemary Nwankwo had two main ambitions.
The first was to join the exclusive global league of top performers known as Olympians; the second was to make the podium in her event, the girls’ 100m sprint.
However, fate added another milestone to Nwankwo’s journey when she was selected to lead Team Nigeria at the colourful spectacle and pageantry of the Dakar 2026 Opening Ceremony on Saturday.
Serving as Nigeria’s flagbearer, Nwankwo proudly led her compatriots as they marched into the packed Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio, showcasing the country’s vibrant green and white colours before thousands of spectators and a global audience.
By all accounts, Nwankwo performed excellently in an opening ceremony that marked a historic moment for the continent, with Senegal becoming the first African nation to host an Olympic sporting event.
The event officially kicked off the fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympic Games, gathering young talent from across the globe.
As one of Nigeria’s brightest medal prospects at the Games, Nwankwo carried the national flag with pride, symbolising the aspirations of the country’s 19-strong athlete contingent competing across six sports.
The young sprinter is expected to be a leading contender in athletics, particularly in the women’s 100m, where she hopes to translate her immense potential into a podium finish.
The ceremony featured a spectacular display of Senegalese culture and hospitality, with music, dance, colourful performances, and elaborate choreography setting the tone for 13 days of competition across Dakar, Diamniadio, and Saly.
One of the defining moments of the evening was the arrival of the Youth Olympic flame at the stadium, following an extraordinary 45-day journey through Senegal’s 14 administrative regions.
The flame was paraded around the stadium before lighting the official cauldron, formally ushering in the Games and symbolising the spirit of friendship, peace, and unity that underpins the Olympic movement.
The packed stadium in Diamniadio provided a fitting backdrop for the historic occasion as the Nigerian delegation dazzled in their ceremonial attire.
Nigeria will compete in athletics, boxing, road cycling, swimming, table tennis, and beach volleyball, with a contingent comprising 19 athletes—12 women and seven men.
With her formal accreditation for the Games completed and having led Team Nigeria through a spectacular Opening Ceremony, Nwankwo has already checked off major milestones. Her sole focus now shifts to achieving her final ambition: a podium finish.
As she works toward capturing a medal—an achievement that comes with financial rewards promised by the Director-General of the National Sports Commission (NSC), Bukola Olopade—millions of Nigerians are cheering and praying for her and her teammates to succeed in Dakar.

title: Tyrtulia, a headless forum with no passwords, made for the terminal
body:
I like forums. Debates, questions, answers, opinions, etc. That feeling of an asynchronous community, where answers are thought through and content lasts, is what makes the internet an interesting place. That is why I like reading them and taking part in them. But I had never designed or built one. In my spare time I started sketching one, and I ended up building my humble headless , federated forum, with simple, modern technologies and open standards.
And I learned a lot along the way. A forum looks simple, but it hides the classic problems of any server. Who can do what? How do you tell a moderator from a regular user? What happens when you have to ban someone? How do you stop someone from stealing an account? Roles, permissions, bans and security. I had to solve them one by one, and you don't learn that by reading.
The server only offers a solid, documented API. It is REST with hypermedia: the client only knows one route, GET / , and discovers everything else by following links. Underneath there are some very boring standards:
There is no web interface, no forms, no advanced authentication systems, no file handling (images, attachments, etc.), and nothing that isn't strictly needed to read and write messages.
That is why it is so light. It uses between 60 and 70 MB of RAM and about 50 MB of disk. It only needs Python and SQLite to run.
How does a client know what it can do? The server tells it with links. Look at the same request, GET / , made by a guest (simplified):
If I change a route tomorrow, no client breaks, because none of them knew it in advance. They just follow the links the server gives them.
I know there are very complete free software forums:
They are all fantastic, but they are designed to be used from a web browser. They also have an ambitious scope. That is ideal for large communities, but too much for a small, light forum.
That said, Tyrtulia doesn't give up on the browser: it can be indexed by search engines and anyone can read it on the web.
No OAuth, no OpenID, no sign-up forms. There are two ways to authenticate:
There is no registration over HTTP. If you have a Unix user on the server, you already have an account: it is created the first time you connect through the socket. From there you can add your SSH keys to log in from outside. If you don't have a user on the machine, the administrator creates an account for you with your public key from the command line. On a tilde, having a Unix user is already the invitation.
Easy to use, secure, and no passwords to steal.
The idea isn't mine. I was inspired by BBJ , a bulletin board for the terminal built for small communities or clubs (tildes, pubnixes, club servers, etc.). I took its spirit and brought it to my own ground. Still, there are important differences.
What they share is a small server built on SQLite and several text clients against a documented API.
A headless forum needs clients, no way around it.
Tyrtulia TUI is the terminal client, built with Textual.
If you know me a little, you know this package was a must: tyrtulia.el .
Tyrtulia Web is more a mirror of the content than a client. Its goal is to let search engines index the forum and let anyone read it from a browser.
It has an unstyled theme and another one that mimics my website.
You can connect to one forum or set up several. Federation happens in the clients: servers don't talk to each other or copy messages between them. Each forum is independent, with its own users, rules and moderators.
Instead of splitting them into tabs or accounts, the clients mix the threads of all of them into a single list.
Of course, you can only write in the forums where you have an account. In the rest you can only read.
I think it's a pretty cool feature, because it keeps the API code much simpler and lets you explore other forums at zero cost.
It has been fun to design and build. Of course there are more complete forums, more powerful federation systems, and even decentralized systems that leave Tyrtulia in the dust (Aether, Nostr...). But its niche is very specific: a light, closed-access, federated, indexable, secure forum with text clients. For everything else, there are better things out there.
If you feel like trying it, the installation guide is in the Tyrtulia repository .
This work is under a Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International license.
Where do I publish: HTTP, Gopher or Gemini?
I send what does not fit in the articles: full configurations, messy notes and whatever I am testing right now. No spam, no sales funnels.
Send an email to newsletter@andros.dev with the subject SUBSCRIBE and you are in.
To unsubscribe, send UNSUBSCRIBE to the same address.
Every coffee gives me a push toward the next article.

title: Emergency alert apps hacked in Russia and Ukraine, sending false warnings of nuclear threats
body: The mobile app of Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry was hit by a cyberattack, and its users received notifications claiming “nuclear warheads” had been launched “across all regions” of the country. The ministry confirmed the hack, saying “hackers managed to send fake information to the public.” It added that the cyberattack did not affect the operation of the public alert system. In Ukraine, meanwhile, hackers breached the official “Air Alert” app, which displayed notifications about radiation and chemical danger and the threat of street fighting, along with a message in Russian: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across all of Ukraine right now! Don’t worry, the Oreshnik is coming!” Ukraine’s Air Force warned that the app had likely been hacked and added that there was no radiation threat. The app itself also reported that “outside individuals carried out unauthorized interference” with its operation. Notifications were temporarily disabled. title: Monday, 2 November 2026
body: Regional Russia’s Justice Ministry has added the Tbilisi-based Ingush Cultural Centre to its list of so-called ‘undesirable’ organisations. The centre was established in Tbilisi, in May 2023. The reasons for the designation have not been disclosed. A Georgian man was detained on Saturday for crossing into South Ossetia. According to the republic’s Committee for State Security (KGB), he crossed the border unintentionally. He was subsequently returned to Tbilisi-controlled territory. The editor behind the encyclopaedia Armenians of the Black Sea Region has apologised for an article entitled ‘Abaza’. Abkhazia residents say the first volume included an offensive interpretation of the names of the Abkhaz and Abaza people, which prompted Khristofor Mkhitaryan to publish a video apology. The Abaza are closely related to the Abkhaz, and primarily reside in Karachay–Cherkessia in the North Caucasus. Armenia On Sunday, a soldier was found dead with a gunshot wound. The Defence Ministry did not provide details of the incident, stating that an investigation is ongoing. The government began issuing new biometric passports on Sunday. The consumer group Informed and Protected Consumer has found abnormalities in milk, sour cream, cottage cheese, and other cheese products tested from 11 local producers. It reported coliform bacteria in several products (most often cottage cheese, from nine producers), plus deviations in yeast, mold, and lactic acid bacteria levels in some cottage cheese samples. Azerbaijan Russia and Azerbaijan plan to introduce a luxury cruise service from Moscow to Baku. Adam Hakimov noted that one vessel is already ready for the project, while two more vessels are expected to be put into operation in the near future. Imprisoned activist Bakhtiyar Hajiyev has complained about the management and prison guards at the prison where he is being held. Independent media outlet Meydan TV has cited Hajiyev’s brother as saying he was subjected to inhumane treatment by prison staff. Georgia Animal rights activists are questioning the deaths of stray dogs after TV Pirveli aired footage showing dog carcasses being buried in a pit at the Veli Cemetery in Tbilisi. Tbilisi City Hall says the dogs had died for various reasons and denies claims of mass killing. Citizens protested outside the Georgian government administration on Sunday in Tbilisi, demanding answers over the deaths of stray dogs. The Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into possible animal cruelty. The Migration Department has said it detained 61 foreign nationals staying in the country illegally. The detainees are citizens of Thailand, Azerbaijan, Turkey, Russia, Belarus, Jordan, China, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. South Ossetia South Ossetian President Marat Kambolov discussed with a delegation from the Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia (RUDN) the transition from the previously signed memorandum of cooperation with South Ossetian State University to the implementation of specific educational projects. The North Caucasus A military court in Grozny is hearing a criminal case against Aleksandr Stepanchenko, a former senior assistant to the military prosecutor in Chechen Shali and a major in the military justice service. According to investigators, he and his accomplices arranged the falsification of military hospital certificates, on the basis of which 30 soldiers from the Sever-Akhmat regiment received compensation for injuries they had not sustained. Kabarda–Balkaria’s Supreme Court has sentenced local resident Artur Yakhshibekyan to 15 years in prison on charges of treason. According to the court, he engaged in espionage by collecting and passing on unspecified information to an unnamed foreign state for use against Russia. Alan Marzaev, a 53-year-old native of North Ossetia and former Deputy Prime Minister of Bashkortostan, has enlisted to fight in Ukraine. He was previously sentenced to 13 years in prison in a case involving extortion and corruption. A court in Daghestan has fined two women from Kaspiysk ₽2,500 ($30) each for failing to stand during the national anthem. One of the women explained that she had been holding a child on her lap, while the other said she had remained seated because she was feeling unwell. Security forces detained a doctor from Daghestan in Moscow under the pretext of checking her documents, then insulted her, removed her hijab, and kept her handcuffed at a police station, the woman’s family allege . Her relatives want authorities to open an investigation into the officers’ actions. Daghestan’s Human Rights Commissioner Zapir Alkhasov has also appealed to the Moscow Prosecutor’s Office, calling for an investigation. For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear attack after Ukraine and Russian systems hacked
body: Ukraine and Russia both reported cyber attacks on their public alert apps overnight, leading to fake announcements of air raids, nuclear attack and street fights. The alerts were cancelled within hours and clarifications issued, but led to concern among residents who received the messages. It was not clear who carried out the attack, or if the two incidents were linked. Ukraine's air raid ⁠alert app, which usually warns of incoming drone or missiles, ⁠showed Kyiv under attack, with an erroneous message ​saying ⁠ Russia's hypersonic ‌Oreshnik missile had been deployed. An alert had read: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying.” Another warned people not to go outside as there was a threat of chemical attack in Kyiv “The air alert ​app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force said on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!” Ukraine's Ministry for Digital Transformation said the app was no longer in operation, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as ​were air raid sirens. The country's Centre for Strategic Communications asked residents to disregard “strange messages”. Oleksander Merezhko, chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, told the BBC that Ukrainians were used to “practically non-stop alerts”, but suspicions had been aroused because the messages were in Russian. “It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that,” he said. The mobile ​app of Russia's Ministry of Emergencies was ​hit ‌by a cyberattack that resulted ⁠in the spread of false information to ⁠the public, state news agency Tass said. It stressed that citizens should take their information from TV and radio broadcasts, text messages and loudspeakers. The fake alert had said “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia”. The alerts occurred shortly before the end of a localised six-day ceasefire in the Kherson region, which had been reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo. The ceasefire in the town of Oleshky expired at midnight Moscow time. There was no immediate indication of any resumption of hostilities by either side. It was the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in ⁠February 2022. Ms Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire “has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity ​without the constant threat of attack”. Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the 2022 invasion, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year. Meanwhile, the ​Russian ⁠military struck ⁠a military facility ​in the ⁠Odesa region of Ukraine and ⁠hit a cargo vessel ​used ⁠for ‌military ​purposes 58km south of the Black Sea port city of Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on ​Telegram ‌on ⁠Monday. An official ​in ​Odesa ‌separately said ⁠on Telegram that ⁠a Russian attack injured four people.

title: Dallas Halloween shootings leave 4 dead, 15 injured, police say
body:
The three shootings in Deep Ellum appeared to be unrelated, police said.
Four people were killed in three apparently unrelated shootings across the Deep Ellum neighborhood in Dallas late on Halloween night, police said, adding that a suspect had been taken into custody and at least one other was being sought.
"The detectives and officers are still trying to put everything together to understand exactly what happened on each scene and to see if anything is related," Dallas Police Chief Daniel C. Comeaux said during a press conference on Sunday. "At this time, we have no information that they are related, but we're still doing an investigation to try to figure that out at this time."
Comeaux said at least 15 people had been injured in the shootings, but that number could rise as some people had transported themselves to nearby hospitals.
The first shooting began at about 12:20 a.m. near the 2600 block of Elm Street, followed less than an hour later at about 1:05 a.m. by a shooting on the 2600 block of Main Street, police said. The third began at about 1:35 a.m. on the 200 block of S. Crowdus Street.
Dallas Police sources told ABC News' Dallas–Fort Worth affiliate WFAA that at one location a man allegedly said he was going to "start shooting." At least three people were killed at that location, the source said.
Such violence "is always unacceptable in our city," Dallas Mayor Eric L. Johnson said in a statement.
"Public safety must always remain our top priority and we must continue to explore strategies to ensure that Deep Ellum can be a safe gathering place in our city," Johnson added.
Johnson and Dallas City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert both said the victims and their families would be in their thoughts.
"Dallas Police officers were on the ground and able to respond immediately. Dallas Police will continue to investigate this incident and work to bring those responsible to justice," Tolbert said in a statement. "We will share additional information as it becomes available."

title: Inside Elena Rybakina’s remarkable 2026: The stats behind her rise to world No 1
body: Elena Rybakina has secured the year-end No 1 ranking before she even attempts to defend her WTA Finals title in Indian Wells next week. The 27-year-old Rybakina is the 17th player in WTA history to secure the year-end No 1 singles ranking and the first player representing Kazakhstan, male or female, in singles or doubles to finish a season ranked No 1 in the world. Rybakina ended Aryna Sabalenka’s 99-week stay at No 1 in September by rising to the top after winning the US Open, becoming the second-oldest woman to reach No 1 for the first time. View this post on Instagram She needed to claim just one victory in Tokyo last week to make sure she would not relinquish her position at the summit until at least next year, and she did just that before withdrawing from the quarter-finals with a neck issue. “Finishing the year as world No 1 in the PIF WTA Rankings for the first time is an incredibly special moment for me,” Rybakina said in a statement released by the tour. “I'm really proud of what I've achieved this season and the consistency I've shown throughout the year. I'm now looking forward to competing at the WTA Finals and hopefully finishing the season on a high.” In Tokyo a few days ago, Rybakina spoke to the press about the lingering foot injury that almost ruled her out of the US Open . “After US Open , it was a lot of travels and of course, there were a lot of emotions spent during the tournament and I needed some time off. But at the same time, I was travelling quite a lot and was not able to practise,” she explained. “Also, my foot issue is still there; it’s on and off. Now it got better a bit, but that’s why the Beijing tournament wasn’t that successful for me [she lost her opener to world No 118 Alina Charaeva]. But after some rest and proper recovery and exercises for my body, now I feel better. So hopefully again for the final eight [the WTA Finals] I’m going to get to my best form.” Finishing the year at the 🔝 Elena Rybakina will end 2026 at the summit of the PIF WTA Rankings! She's achieved this feat for the very first time, and will be presented with the trophy during the FAGE WTA Finals Indian Wells in two weeks' time 👏 @PIF_en | #PIFWTARankings pic.twitter.com/7KRR4OSvsL — wta (@WTA) October 29, 2026 Asked about how it felt being No 1 in the world, Rybakina said: “From my side, what changed is that it’s another goal which I achieved, which is great. And now, there are other ones. But definitely I got more attention, no matter where I go, which is nice. It’s not been that long yet, but this is what I can say right now: it’s definitely more attention.” With the WTA Finals just a week away, here’s a closer look at Rybakina’s banner season, the numbers that defined her 2026 season, and what it took for her to become world No 1. Trophies galore Rybakina has captured a tour-leading four titles this campaign, including two Grand Slams at the Australian Open and US Open, along with WTA 500-level trophies on clay in Stuttgart in April and on hard courts in Ningbo last month. Ningbo was her first successful title defence at tour level. View this post on Instagram Unmatched Rybakina heads to the year-end championships in Indian Wells (which replaced Riyadh as host city) with a tour-leading 54 match wins in 2026, marking the second straight season in which she has surpassed the 50-win mark. Beating the best Rybakina didn’t just win matches; she was beating top-quality opposition. In 2026, she is 3-2 against top-two opponents, 7-3 against top-five opponents, 10-5 against top-10 opponents, and 16-7 against top-20 opponents. She beat a top-ranked Sabalenka in both Grand Slam finals she played this year. It may seem like a no-brainer that a player finishing the year as No 1 in the world would have won the majority of their matches against top players, but on the men’s side, Alexander Zverev has made it to the top of the rankings with a 0-6 record against top-five opponents and a 3-9 record against top-10 opponents in 2026. Supreme serving It’s no secret that the serve is Rybakina’s biggest weapon, and her stats certainly showcase that. She leads the tour with 438 aces in 68 matches this season. The closest player behind her on the ace leaderboard is Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, who hit 347 aces in 50 matches. Rybakina has won 74 per cent of her first-serve points throughout the season, trailing only Zheng Qinwen (74.8 per cent) among all WTA players who have contested at least five tour-level matches this campaign. She has won a remarkable 82.4 per cent of her service games in 2026, the highest rate among all WTA players who have contested more than one match. Sabalenka is close behind with 81.5 per cent. Rybakina also leads the tour in break points saved, saving 65 per cent of the break points she has faced this season. Finding consistency While there may have been brief lulls in Rybakina’s season, she has certainly been consistent enough to reach at least the quarter-finals in 13 of the 19 tournaments she has contested in 2026. She reached seven semi-finals and six finals overall, with her only losses (three) in those rounds coming against either Sabalenka or Iga Swiatek .

title: Lt Gen Ajay Ramdev, Sena Medal Assumes Appointment of Commandant, ASC Centre & College
body:
Bengaluru, Nov 2, 2026. Lt Gen Ajay Ramdev, SM assumed the appointment of Commandant, Army Service Corps (ASC) Centre & College, Bengaluru on Nov 1, 2026.
On assuming the appointment, the General Officer laid wreaths at the ASC War Memorial and the Animal Transport Memorial, a unique memorial honouring the mules and muleteers, the silent warriors who laid down their lives in service to the Nation.
The Gen Officer brings rich experience in training and leadership to ASC Centre & College, the premier establishment for training of logisticians of the Indian Armed Forces. The officer is an alumnus of the prestigious Rashtriya Indian Military College, Dehradun, National Defence Academy Pune and Army War College Mhow. He is also the Colonel Commandant of Army Service Corps. 
His mandate is to ensure that every logistician trained can sustain operations across varied terrain and multi-domain environments. His vast experience at the helm of integrated training places him well to shape a future-ready logistics force.

ASC Centre & College, Bengaluru is the Alma Mater of the Army Service Corps, the arm that sustains the Indian Army with supplies, transport and logistics support in peace and war. The establishment has made considerable strides in logistics training, including the development of Drone Training infrastructure, curated courses on integrated logistics, and cutting-edge technology such as AI-based Predictive Logistics.

Beyond professional skills, the Centre & College instils discipline, physical fitness and esprit de corps among all ranks, in keeping with the Corps motto, Seva Asmakam Dharma (Service is our Duty).

title: ECONOMY360: As Mojeed Alabi’s DevReporting delves into Local Govt finances
body:
“May your road be rough,” quipped Tai Solarin in his 1964 piece of the same title. Those words echoed through my mind for Mojeed Alabi and his DevReporting crew as I sat in the midst of the audience last Thursday in UNILAG , but, as Mr Solarin warned, those immortal lines are susceptible to misinterpretation. So, I’d return to them later.
A few years ago, I led a team of journalists on a reporting project on the Nigerian agricultural value chain, with special focus on the key drivers of post-harvest losses amid sky-high food prices. Let me confess upfront that, even as an editor and team lead on several projects, nothing delights me more than travelling to the theatre of reporting with my reporter-colleagues, navigating the intricacies of data collection and source-mapping, and interacting directly with the subjects of our investigations and research. I love field reporting—–and it was against that background that I found myself covering the South-West leg of that national project, which took me to Osun and other parts of the region.
While the project exposed me to the centrality of post-harvest losses to Nigeria’s food sustainability discourse at the time, it also opened my eyes to a far bigger problem: the collapse of governance at the local government level. From Iwo through Ile-Ogbo and Ife-Odan via Ejigbo, I travelled across Osun (as well as Oyo, Kwara, Ogun, etc.) and was depressed by the level of rot I witnessed, firsthand, at the grassroots. It was clear to me that the crisis of food sustainability (evident in post-harvest losses fueled by poor road networks, poor storage facilities, etc.) was, in part, a crisis of absent grassroots governance. Interestingly, Osun wasn’t an outlier; it was a microcosm of Nigeria, offering rare insights into what had become of local governance in our country.
Last Thursday, I was at the University of Lagos’ Faculty of Arts Theatre, where the issue of grassroots governance and its centrality to national development was, again, brought to the national radar, with Osun as a case study. The occasion was the public screening of “LG Billions in the Dark”, an investigative documentary produced by development-focused niche platform, DevReporting, founded by a dear Egbon and one of Nigeria’s most decorated development and accountability journalists, Mojeed Alabi. The documentary examines the prolonged local government leadership crisis in Osun State and its implications for public finance, accountability, and grassroots development.
The event, chaired by PREMIUM TIMES publisher and one of the continent’s most iconic journalism figures, Dapo Olorunyomi, featured human rights lawyer Femi Falana as the keynote speaker. The event was also graced by the Vice-Chancellor of the host university, Folasade Ogunsola, a professor of medical microbiology, among other big names in media, academia, and civil society.
In my years observing how things work in Nigeria’s toxic political blogosphere, I’d argue that a call for people to direct their anger towards subnational governments isn’t always wrapped in the noblest intentions. In some cases, it’s a clever halfway way to divert attention from—and take pressure off—the government at the centre. But for anyone genuinely interested in the structure of governance in contemporary Nigeria, beyond the resources ostensibly meant for Local Government administration in recent years, shining a spotlight on the grassroots has become super-important.
And Mr Falana made the point most eloquently in his keynote address, titled ‘Accountability, Resources and Citizen Voices: Building Local Governments that Work for the People’, in which he argued that Nigeria’s development challenges could not be addressed by concentrating accountability demands on the federal government while neglecting state and local authorities.
Local governments, he maintained, as the tier of government closest to citizens, should be empowered to address everyday development needs, including primary healthcare, basic education, infrastructure and economic opportunities.
If there was any doubt about the strength of Mr Falana’s hypothesis, the Osun LG documentary produced by the DevReporting team put paid to it: it’s an impressive work of accountability journalism as a vehicle for exposing the deplorable state of local infrastructure, a direct consequence of the collapse of governance at the grassroots in Osun.
Midway into the documentary, one of the Osun residents interviewed in his community deployed a comical line to describe the horrible state of road infrastructure in the community: the roads were so bad that even if a cow—as recalcitrant and stubborn as the animal can be—plies them, it would have its legs broken! The hall erupted into laughter, but beyond the comic relief lies a heartbreaking reality that everyone has come to realise: we can’t attain true development on a national scale if the grassroots remain broken.
To be sure, puritan constitutional arguments against the oft-repeated calls for local government autonomy, however defined, exist, which I have no intention of dissecting in this piece. What’s clear to me from my travels across communities in Nigeria, however, is that beyond the academic and theoretical arguments, the near-total asphyxiation of the local government system runs violently contrary to the spirit of democracy as a system of government that can deliver the greater good to the largest number of people. The current system requires a complete overhaul.
The event also featured an insightful panel discussion on local government administration, with panellists like the Chairman of Onigbongbo Local Council Development Area, Moyosore Adebanjo; former Chairman of Ijebu East Local Government, Wale Adedayo; legal counsel, Jiti Ogunye Chambers, Comfort Idika-Ogunye; Head of Tracka at BudgIT, Joshua Osiyemi; and a lecturer in the Department of Political Science at the University of Lagos, Vera Amaechi; and Azeezat Olaoluwa, West Africa Correspondent of Deutsche Welle. Mr Adedayo offered an interesting perspective on the importance of the grassroots tier of government in driving development, drawing on his experience in Ogun State.
At the event, Uncle Dapsy (as we fondly call Dapo Olorunyomi) made a brilliant allusion to the nexus between a nation’s media system and the state of development in its key sectors such as business, sports, politics, etc. There’s no better way to capture those dynamics. Stripped of all pretensions, that analogy brilliantly underscores the importance (or is it precarity?) of the responsibility that Mojeed Alabi and his Dev. Reporting team have chosen to shoulder.
Journalism, for the most part, is a thankless job—and no less thankless, and indeed, precarious, is that brand of journalism that chooses to question authorities and shine the light on key accountability concerns. Alabi and crew will need all the support they can get as they embark on that journey through dark, dark alleyways, unravelling bureaucratic mysteries and questioning financial opacity to promote transparency, accountability, and, ultimately, grassroots development.
So, I’d return to Solarin and say to Mojeed Alabi and his crew: “May your road be rough”. And as Mr Tai, the fearless social critic, warned, the road (towards journalistic demand for accountable governance, in Mojeed’s case) is designed to be rough, because all great accomplishments come with severe mental and physical trials and sacrifices. I wish Egbon Mojeed and the crew all the very best.
Oladeinde Olawoyin reports Business & Economy, Development and Lagos Metro at PREMIUM TIMES. A First Class graduate of Mass Communication from the University of Ilorin, Ilorin, he was nominated in the journalism category of The Future Awards Africa in 2017. Aside maintaining a column titled ‘SATURDAY SATIRE’, he also writes art and culture pieces on weekends. Twitter : @Ola_deinde

title: Google Trends data on "will AI replace [job]" searches for 56 jobs
body:
No one can tell you for certain which jobs AI will replace. What we can show is how worried people are. We measured how often the world asks whether AI will replace 56 jobs, how often it searches for AI built for those jobs, and whether fewer people are trying to get into them.
Worry index: how often people search whether AI will replace each job, since ChatGPT launched (November 2022 onward), on a scale where programmers = 100. Higher means more people are asking, not that the job is more at risk. Click a job for its full report.
Source: Google Trends , worldwide, Nov 2022 â Oct 2026. Grey rows: too few searches for a steady monthly signal. The percentage next to each value is the change in the last 12 months vs the 12 months before, shown only where the earlier year had data in at least 6 months.
Worldwide searches for âwill AI replaceâ in 2026 run at 2.5 times their 2023 level and peaked in the week of 8 March 2026. It's not a ChatGPT-launch spike that faded: the curve kept climbing through 2025 and 2026.
Weekly, relative to the highest week (= 100). Hover or use the arrow keys for values.
Searches asking whether AI will replace programmers peaked in March 2024, the month an AI âsoftware engineerâ called Devin was announced, and are â12% on a year ago. For teachers, doctors and lawyers, worried searches climbed to new highs in 2026.
Monthly. Programmers' average since November 2022 = 100.
âHow to become a â¦â searches are a rough signal of who wants into a job. Comparing the last 12 months with the year before ChatGPT, they fell for 19 of the 49 jobs with enough data: most of all in tech and writing. They rose for the trades.
Last 12 months vs November 2021 â October 2022. The 10 biggest rises and the 10 biggest drops.
Source: Google Trends , worldwide, weekly. Each job is compared with itself, so the percentages are comparable across jobs; the volumes are not.
For each job: searches for âAI for â¦â (and âChatGPT for â¦â) per search asking whether AI will replace it, since November 2022. Programmers come out low (2.6), probably because they search âAI for codingâ or âAI for programmingâ rather than âAI for programmersâ: these are search habits, not surveys.
Source: Google Trends . Jobs with too few worried searches are left out. âAI for customer serviceâ includes businesses shopping for AI support tools.
In 2026 searches for âAI proof jobsâ average 25.5 times their 2023 level and âjobs safe from AIâ 14.1 times. In the US, the alternatives people look up have grown too: âapprenticeshipâ +90%, âtrade schoolâ +80% and âcareer changeâ +140% on 2023.
For a decade âlearn to codeâ was the standard career advice. Since July 2023 âlearn AIâ has out-searched it in most months, and âAI courseâ now leads them all.
Monthly since 2015. 100 = the highest month for any of five learning searches, led by âAI courseâ.
Searches for âwill AI replaceâ, share of all searches in each state, highest = 100. Past five years.
Same search worldwide since 2022, highest country = 100 (very small territories left out).
Source: Google Trends . Interest is relative to all searches in each place, so small places with a few curious people can rank high.
The top searches related to âwill AI replaceâ, worldwide since 2022.
Source. All numbers come from Google Trends , collected on 31 October 2026 for November 2020 to October 2026 (worldwide unless noted). Trends reports relative interest: each chart is scaled so its highest point = 100, from a sample of Google searches.
One scale for every job. For each job we combine the common ways of asking, for example âAI replace accountantsâ, âAI replace accountantâ and âaccountants replaced by AIâ (Trends counts any search containing those words, so âwill AI replace accountantsâ and âcan AI replace an accountantâ both count). Every Trends comparison also holds the same question about programmers, so we can put all 56 jobs on one scale: a job's worry index is its searches divided by the programmers searches on the same page, with programmers' average since November 2022 = 100. âAI for â¦â searches use the same method with, for example, âAI for accountantsâ, âAI for accountantâ and âChatGPT for accountantsâ. Cybersecurity analysts, administrative assistants and customer service use two of the three phrasings, because of Trends' 100-character limit or because one phrasing already contained another.
Getting in. âHow to become a â¦â searches are measured on their own (each job against itself), weekly over five years, and compared as a percentage change between the last 12 months and November 2021 â October 2022, the year before ChatGPT.
Limits. This measures attention, not risk: a job can be widely discussed and safe, or rarely discussed and exposed. Broad job titles absorb narrower ones (âengineersâ includes searches about software engineers). Some titles share words with software (âeditorâ, âillustratorâ) or other things (âpilotâ), so we left editors, illustrators, video editors and pilots out. Jobs marked âfew searchesâ have data in fewer than 12 of the 48 months since ChatGPT; treat them as rough. Search habits vary by job and language, and the data is mostly English.
Collected by hand. Google doesn't allow bots on Trends pages, so a person opened each of the 96 Trends comparisons and saved what the page showed.
Swap teachers for any job's slug from its page address.
Nobody can say for certain, and search data can't either. What it can show is which jobs people worry about. Across 56 jobs we tracked, people most often ask whether AI will replace engineers, teachers, doctors, programmers and software engineers. Worried searches rose in the last 12 months for 30 of the 31 jobs with enough data to compare.
No list can promise that. Interest in the question is rising fast: searches for âAI proof jobsâ in 2026 run at about 25.5 times their 2023 level. In the US, searches for âapprenticeshipâ are up 90% and âtrade schoolâ 80% on 2023, and âhow to becomeâ searches for electricians (+67%), plumbers (+74%), mechanics (+71%) have risen since 2022.
Yes. Worldwide searches for âwill AI replaceâ in 2026 average 2.5 times their 2023 level, and hit their highest point in the week of 8 March 2026.
From Google Trends , November 2020 to October 2026. For each job we combine the ways people ask (âwill AI replace accountantsâ, âcan AI replace an accountantâ, âwill accountants be replaced by AIâ) and compare it, on the same Trends page, with the same question about programmers. That puts every job on one scale where programmers = 100. The details are in the methodology section.
Yes. The data is free under CC BY 4.0: download the CSV, embed the charts, and credit âScrollytelling AI Job Worry Indexâ with a link to this page.

title: Four injured in overnight Russian attack on Odesa
body:
According to Ukrinform, Serhii Lysak, head of the Odesa City Military Administration, reported this on Facebook .
"Last night, the enemy attacked Odesa. Four people were injured. They received the necessary medical assistance," he said.
Infrastructure facilities came under attack. Two residential buildings and a garage were damaged. The blast wave shattered windows in neighboring homes.
All relevant emergency services and the operational headquarters are working at the scene. Efforts to deal with the aftermath of the attack and provide assistance to those affected are ongoing, Lysak said.

title: Zverev reaches top of ATP rankings for first time, Medvedev stays fifth
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Germany’s Alexander Zverev has topped the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) rankings for the first time, according to the latest standings published on the organization’s website.
Zverev reached the semifinals in Vienna last week, bringing his points tally to 9,550. A quarterfinal appearance was enough to earn him the top spot. He surpassed Italy’s Jannik Sinner (9,450), who cut short his season due to a knee injury after holding the top ranking since April. Zverev became the 30th player to reach world No. 1.
Spain’s Carlos Alcaraz (6,100), who claimed the Vienna title last week, ranks third. American Ben Shelton (4,530) holds fourth place, followed by Russia’s Daniil Medvedev (3,860), who fell to Alcaraz in the semifinals in the Austrian capital.
Canada’s Felix Auger-Aliassime (2,875) fell out of the top 10, slipping from seventh to 13th. His drop allowed Spain’s Rafael Jodar (3,209) to break into the top 10 for the first time. Jodar became the first player in ATP history to accomplish the feat in his debut season, having begun the year outside the top 150.
Serbia’s Novak Djokovic (3,140) climbed one place and is now within reach of returning to the top 10 despite an early departure in Basel. The men’s record holder for Grand Slam singles titles competed at the Swiss tournament for the first time in 15 years but was defeated in the second round by Germany’s Jan-Lennard Struff, ranked 39th in the world.
Other Russians in the top 100 include Andrey Rublev (2,085), Karen Khachanov (1,940) and Roman Safiullin (807), who occupy 22nd, 25th and 71st places, respectively.

title: Illegally Detained Georgian Citizen Released From Tskhinvali Custody
body: A Georgian citizen who was detained by Russian occupation forces close to the Tskhinvali occupation line on October 31 has been released and returned to the Tbilisi-controlled territory, the State Security Service of Georgia (SSSG) said on November 1. According to the agency, the person was detained near the village of Bershueti, in Gori municipality. While the SSSG did not name the individual, continuing its recent practice, the Res news agency, based in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali/South Ossetia region, reported that he was Gela Berianidze, born in 1985, a resident of Bershueti. The report said he had “unintentionally crossed” the “state border” near the village of “Amdzarini,” the Ossetian name for Tsinagari, a village located in the occupied zone across Bershueti, which remains in Tbilisi-controlled territory. “All relevant instruments available to the central government were used to release Georgian citizens from illegal detention, including the ‘hotline’ mechanism managed by the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia (EUMM),” the SSSG said, adding that they “continue to work actively toward the release of all Georgian citizens held in illegal detention in the occupied territories.” In its 2025 annual report , the SSSG recorded 34 cases of detention near the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region and 40 in Abkhazia. title: Ugandan educator sees his project contributing to future of Russia-Africa relations
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Ugandan educator Daniel Omara, founder of the Chunga-Changa interactive Russian-language school, believes his project can contribute to a future built on cooperation and mutual respect, he said while speaking about his hopes for the school and relations between Uganda and Russia.
"I am very happy. I believe the future is with us right now," Omara told TASS, describing his hopes for a world in which countries can build partnerships without being told how to govern themselves.
Omara said he sees the emerging world order as multipolar, with countries able to preserve their differences and work together as equals.
"A future where our diversity is actually our strength. A future where Africa has a unique chance of creating lasting partnerships with real soulful friends, where parasitism is not going to be an element, where neocolonialism is going to disappear," he said.
He said his educational project was one way of helping shape that future and build connections between younger generations in Russia and Africa.
"I would say, [it is an] honor that with my project, I am actually taking part in shaping this future for ourselves and for our kids," he concluded.

title: Building resilience for the world's growing energy needs
body: This year has tested the resilience of the global energy system. Geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions and rising demand pressures have placed energy security firmly at the top of government and industry agendas around the world. Yet despite the volatility, energy markets have continued to supply the fuel, power and products that underpin economic growth. One reason is that resilience is built long before it is needed. In the UAE, the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline linking Habshan to Fujairah has helped maintain crude exports even when traditional shipping routes face disruption. Built in 2012 with capacity to transport up to 1.8 million barrels per day, the pipeline reflects the long-term planning and infrastructure investment increasingly viewed as essential to energy security. “The UAE is on track to deliver an even higher energy output than before,” UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei said in an interview for the Adipec 2026 Show Preview ahead of the world’s largest energy conference, which opened in Abu Dhabi today. “This resilience,” he said, “is the result of long-term planning and investments made well before they were urgently needed.” Although energy security has been one of the year’s dominant economic concerns, the sector has adapted to disruption better than expected. Nearly two-thirds of senior industry leaders (64 per cent) said performance exceeded expectations, the inaugural Adipec Global Energy Report 2026: Power Shift report reveals. Approximately 77 per cent of the 1,800 respondents remain optimistic about the decade ahead. Energy is an engine of the world economy; its endurance has kept global GDP stable, with expansion expected at 3.1 per cent this year , according to projections by the International Monetary Fund. In July, global GDP growth was estimated at 3 per cent. Growth is raising the stakes But a slew of systemic pressures is set to challenge future energy security. The sector will need to be reinforced if it is to withstand demand stresses arising from population growth, urbanisation, industrialisation and higher living standards. About 8.2 billion people rely on energy today; by 2050, that figure is expected to reach 9.6 bn . Emerging economies now drive more than 80 per cent of energy demand growth ; they will require more energy as they expand. And industry, which accounts for 37 per cent of global final energy consumption, will add further pressure as artificial intelligence is deployed more widely: data centres alone used 17 per cent more electricity in 2025 than in the previous year, for example, with electricity consumption expected to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030. In short, demand is rising across households, industry, transport and digital infrastructure simultaneously. Over the next five years, energy demand growth is expected to be around 50 per cent faster than the average seen during the previous decade. Meanwhile, geopolitical disruptions could continue affecting supply chains while the impact of extreme weather could further increase the need for cooling. The system itself is becoming more interconnected and complex. The world needs more energy and it needs that energy to be delivered reliably. The topic is expected to be a major talking point at Adipec’s Strategic Conference next week. In total, more than 1,800 speakers across 13 programmes – including two from the Technical Conference - and more than 380 sessions will examine the decisions, partnerships and capital needed to expand energy supply, accelerate infrastructure delivery and strengthen long-term system performance. The world needs a new kind of energy economy that can absorb shocks, adapt to changing conditions and continue delivering the energy required for long-term economic and societal progress. Although Middle Eastern crude exports have nearly recovered to the levels seen at the start of this year, according to data and analytics platform Kpler, maintaining this momentum will depend on strengthening the systems that support it. “We need continued investment in energy supply, and across all sources, as well as in the infrastructure that connects supply with demand,” Mr Al Kindy said. “We need greater flexibility and redundancy across energy value chains. We need technology that makes systems more intelligent and adaptive. And we need partnerships that endure not only when conditions are favourable, but when they are tested.” Resilience as an economic advantage In practical terms, resilience requires rethinking sectoral dynamics while planning for disruption. Recent events have shown that even short interruptions around corridors or digital systems can have a disproportionate impact on prices and public confidence. Operational preparedness requires diversified supplies, multiple routes to market and the flexibility to respond when conditions change. The International Energy Agency reports intensified efforts by both producer and consumer countries to diversify trade routes and energy sources. These include new supply pipelines and infrastructure as well as a greater focus on domestically available resources, ranging from renewables to nuclear, coal, and oil and gas. Energy resilience gives countries a clear economic edge , particularly those classified as low- and middle-income. Reliable supplies and robust infrastructure cut the risk of delays and costly outages. Steady and affordable energy helps industries control costs and protect output. And because a broader energy mix can help lower prices, exports are more competitively priced . Indeed, 85 per cent of those surveyed in the Adipec Global Energy Report 2026: Power Shift report say the energy sector is now more attractive to invest than it was five years ago. In the UAE, new investments include a second pipeline from west to east that is expected to be operational by 2027. Other efforts include integrating digital technologies, AI and energy storage solutions and a Dh200bn outlay to triple renewable energy capacity, expand zero-emission nuclear power and accelerate grid modernisation, Mr Al Mazrouei said. Collaboration across the world’s energy industry No company or country can build a resilient energy system on its own. True energy security for the world requires coordination among the public and private sectors with support from technology providers and investors. Meeting those challenges will require investment, technology deployment and international co-ordination. Those priorities are expected to shape discussions at Adipec 2026. More than 239,000 exhibition attendees from 170 countries are expected to attend, including ministers, chief executives, policymakers, institutional investors, technology leaders, engineers and industrial customers. Two new Strategic Conference programmes directly address the topic of resilience. The Energy Security & Resilience programme will examine preparedness for external shocks, contingency planning, infrastructure protection, supply-chain resilience, strategic reserves and recovery in a more volatile operating environment. Meanwhile, the Policy, Regulation and Governance programme will look at how governments can attract investment and accelerate infrastructure delivery while balancing national priorities with global interdependence. In total, there are 11 Strategic Conference programmes. They are complemented by the Technical Conference, with its SPE Technical and Downstream Technical programmes, which together represent the world’s largest gathering of technical energy engineers and experts. There are also dedicated platforms for the technologies and partnerships shaping resilient systems. Many of the technologies underpinning energy resilience will be showcased across the exhibition, including AI-enabled operational systems, digital infrastructure, logistics solutions, advanced energy technologies and industrial decarbonisation innovations. For example, as part of its focus on optimising all forms of energy, the event’s Low Carbon and Chemicals Zone has been redesigned to help meet the world’s need for more diversified energy pathways and cleaner industrial solutions. Meanwhile, the AI and Robotics Zone will showcase tools to improve energy performance and asset reliability. The exhibition will occupy 16 halls and four specialised industry zones that together create a platform for companies to present new technologies and establish commercial partnerships. “This extraordinary scale makes Adipec one of the world’s most influential meeting places for energy, technology, investment and international business,” said Christopher Hudson, president of DMG events, the organisers of Adipec. “The strong momentum surrounding Adipec 2026 ahead of its opening reflects the industry’s recognition of both the scale of the opportunities available and the urgent need for rapid action. By bringing policymakers, investors, technology leaders and energy producers together in Abu Dhabi, Adipec is helping to strengthen partnerships, drive innovation and support the delivery of the secure, reliable and affordable energy systems the world needs.” That scale is matched by a significant commercial impact. Last year, Adipec 2025 generated an estimated $53bn in commercial value through more than 49,000 deals, Mr Hudson said. Adipec is the world’s largest energy conference and exhibition. Hosted by Adnoc and organised by dmg events, this year’s event takes place from November 2-5 at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi. This page was produced by The National in partnership with Adipec.
