title: Iran continues to exchange messages with US through intermediaries — diplomat
body:
TEHRAN, November 2. /TASS/. The Iranian authorities continue to exchange messages with the US through intermediaries; the basis for the negotiations remains the seven-day plan previously proposed by Tehran and fleshed out in detail, Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
"Negotiations are ongoing. In any case, the issue is complex - or, more precisely, there are many complex issues - and the passage of time and the actions of the US have only added to their complexity. In our opinion, the exchange of messages continues to this day," he noted, commenting on the recent visit by Iran’s deputy foreign minister to Qatar.
Baghaei emphasized that the seven-day plan previously proposed by Tehran remains the basis for all negotiations and consultations between Iran and the US, conducted through intermediaries. This plan can be fully implemented within two days, the diplomat pointed out.

title: Sultan Turbans two sons, Murtala Dan’Iyan as Dallatun Sokoto
body: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto SOKOTO — The Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, has conferred traditional titles on two of his sons, Alhaji Murtala Abdulkadir Dan’Iyan Jarman Sokoto and 10 other distinguished Nigerians in recognition of their contributions to humanity and community development. The ceremony, held on Sunday at the Sultan’s Palace in Sokoto, also witnessed the turbaning of two biological sons of the Sultan. Alhaji Abubakar Sadiq was turbaned Sarkin Dawakin Tsakar Gida, while Alhaji Shehu Abubakar received the title of Fagacin Sokoto. The event marked the climax of a three-day programme organised by friends, associates and well-wishers of the new Dallatun Sokoto to celebrate his elevation into the traditional institution of the Sokoto Caliphate. It attracted traditional rulers, politicians, senior government officials, Islamic scholars, business executives and community leaders from within and outside Nigeria. Among those honoured were Alhaji Abubakar Hussain, who received the title of Sarkin Bai; Alhaji Aminu Isa-Buhari, Danmalikin Sokoto; Professor Mansur Ibrahim, Danmasanin Sokoto; and Professor Ishaq Oloyede, Kuliyan Sokoto. Others were Dr Peter Igoh, Kakakin Daular Usmaniya; Representative Almustapha Rabah, Bauran Sokoto; Dr Balarabe Kakale, Wakilin Makarantar Daular Usmaniya; Alhaji Bello Abbas, Wakilin Tarihin Daular Usmaniya; and Alhaji Gandi Umar, Sarkin Galmar Sarkin Musulmi. Speaking at the ceremony, the Sultan described the turbaning as a historic occasion organised by the Sultanate Council to recognise individuals whose contributions and achievements in their respective fields had distinguished them as worthy ambassadors of the Caliphate. He said the traditional institution would continue to recognise and honour sons and daughters of the Caliphate who demonstrated commitment, integrity and outstanding performance in their various endeavours. The monarch, however, reminded the new title holders that their elevation should not be regarded merely as a ceremonial honour but as a call to greater service and responsibility to their communities and society. He urged them to remain their brothers’ keepers, promote peace, unity and peaceful coexistence, and offer constructive ideas to strengthen harmonious relationships within the Caliphate, Sokoto State and Nigeria. In separate interviews after the ceremony, prominent personalities described the new Dallatun Sokoto as humble, honest and trustworthy, citing his philanthropic activities and readiness to assist people across religious, ethnic and social divides. A father figure and mentor to the new title holder, Alhaji Umarun Kwabo AA Jarman Sokoto, described him as loyal, humble and dependable, saying his commitment to the service of God and humanity had earned him the confidence of those around him. “I am optimistic that Dallatun Sokoto, Alhaji Murtala Abdulkadir Dan’Iyan Jarman Sokoto, will wear the shoes and crown in the service of God and humanity,” Kwabo said. He expressed confidence that his protégé would sustain the values of service, loyalty and compassion associated with the traditional institution. Also speaking, the Minister of Labour and Employment, Alhaji Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi, Katukan Sokoto, described the new Dallatun Sokoto as a trustworthy and loyal personality whose humanitarian activities had demonstrated his worthiness for the title. Dingyadi said the honour was well deserved, adding that his consistent commitment to philanthropy and community service had earned him widespread admiration and made his elevation a source of pride to the people of Sokoto State. The ceremony highlighted the role of the Sokoto Caliphate’s traditional institution in recognising contributions to society and encouraging service, unity and community development. The post Sultan Turbans two sons, Murtala Dan’Iyan as Dallatun Sokoto appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Samara region, reportedly striking Europe’s largest oil storage facility
body: Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Samara region overnight on November 2. Regional authorities had not officially commented on the strikes by the time of publication, but Samara’s airport suspended operations for two hours because of the drone threat. Ukrainian monitoring channels and Astra, an independent Telegram channel, cited photos and videos from eyewitnesses in reporting that the drones, according to preliminary reports, struck the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) near the settlement of Prosvet. The Samara LPDS is the largest tank farm in Europe, part of a network operated by Transneft. Four pipelines carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan connect to the station. Ukrainian military drones struck the Samara LPDS several times in October, causing fires and damaging storage tanks. title: Ugandan educator calls for more cultural exchanges between Russia, Africa
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. More opportunities for Russians and Africans to travel, learn each other’s languages and experience their cultures could help bring the two sides closer, Ugandan educator and founder of the Chunga-Changa interactive Russian-language school Daniel Omara told TASS.
He said relations between Russia and Africa had long been built on friendship of peoples, adding that educational projects could help strengthen these ties among younger generations.
"These projects and other educational projects are very important, because we build the future, we build communication, we can communicate with each other, we can take advantage of opportunities that will come in the future," he said.
Omara’s project, an interactive Russian-language school for African children, was launched in Uganda and is set to expand to other African countries. He also hopes to organize trips for African children to Russia and introduce Russian audiences to African culture and tourism.
"We are going to show this to Russians, and on the side of the Africans, we are going to be organizing a lot more tours for these kids to come to Russia, to experience the different ways of life, the food, the Russian culture is a rich culture," he said.
Omara said that education, travel and cultural exchanges could help Russians and Africans better understand one another, adding that he was happy to see closer engagement between the two sides.

title: Albert Camus' classic existential novel 'The Stranger' receives a sleek, stunning cinematic update
body: The Stranger, directed by François Ozon, just opened in theaters, and it's an interesting, atmospheric adaptation of Albert Camus novel that intelligently updates the story with a 21st-century sensibility.First and foremost, it is cinematic, combining Ozon's storytelling skill with stunning black-and-white visuals. The novel, one of the most important works of existentialist literature, is told from its anti-hero's emotionally detached, even numb, point of view.Its protagonist wrestles with questions of how to act in a godless universe where everything is absurd and meaningless, and makes a shocking choice to commit a murder that apparently means nothing to him.Ozon decides to expand on the novel's story by situating its anti-hero, Meursault, firmly in a vividly depicted time and place and deepening the roles of the people around him, since dramatizing his inner life would make for a bleak, one-note movie.Most importantly, he brings the late 1930s/early 1940s Algiers to life and shows the culture clash between the formal, Francophone community (the so-called “pieds-noirs”) and the indigenous population, some of which is shown to still be traditional and some of which is modernizing.Camus' original work sometimes seen as detached from Arab Algerian populationCamus, born and raised in the French community in Algeria, had a complex relationship to the place and to the French colonials there. He was politically active in trying to help the Algerians obtain rights and independence but also rejected the terrorism of some factions and felt that a compromise allowing French residents to continue living there was possible.His grandparents moved to Algeria, and he was the second generation born there, so his roots in the country ran deep. In recent decades, the fact that the Arab characters in the book, including the murder victim, are not named came under criticism and was seen as evidence of the colonialist French community's detachment from the Arab population.The film opens with a montage detailing life in colonialist Algeria, and much of the movie features atmospheric street scenes that make it clear that the French community there is only part of the picture. As the film focuses on Meursault (Benjamin Voisin, Lost Illusions), much of it is wordless, especially the first half.He is a handsome clerk in his late 20s in a commercial office who lives alone in a tiny apartment in Algiers. One morning, he receives a telegram informing him of his mother's death in a government-run old-age facility in a rural area.He is emotionless as he is given two days off from work and goes to the facility to observe the mourning ritual and attend her funeral. He is not interested in his mother's friends and what they have to say, or in a man who calls himself her fiancé and grieves for her.A relationship without meaningBack in Algiers, he meets Marie (Rebecca Marder, A Radiant Girl), a typist who used to work at his company, and they spend the day together at the beach and the movies, drifting into a sexual relationship. When she asks him if he loves her, he says he doesn't; that love means nothing to him.As is not uncommon, she still hangs around him, and when she asks if he wants to marry her, he says he will if she wants to, because it makes no difference to him.So, the dream of love and having a family means nothing to him, although he clearly enjoys sex. This may make him not unlike many commitment-phobic, taciturn guys. But where he differs becomes clear in his relationship with his volatile neighbor, Raymond (Pierre Lottin), who may or may not be a pimp.He has beaten his Arab girlfriend, Djemila (Hajar Bouzaouit), whom he suspects of cheating on him, and wants to lure her back to see him again so he can insult her one more time. But he needs Meursault's help to write her a letter.Meursault complies, not sympathizing with either Raymond or his mistress, in a storyline that demonstrates how the colonials could take advantage of the impoverished indigenous population. A drunken, elderly neighbor (Denis Lavant) who beats his dog also latches on to Meursault, evoking the same indifference.When Meursault commits the murder, seemingly on impulse, and is apprehended, he is as detached as he had been in all the previous scenes. He only shows real emotion, anger, when a priest comes to console him against his wishes.The trial is the core of exploring the novel's message, and the prosecutors spend more time on whether Meursault, who doesn't deny his guilt, cared about his mother's death than anything else, as his own lawyer knew they would.Not caring about the loss of one's mother is seen as a worse crime than taking the life of an Arab, and no one seems to think Meursault will pay a heavy price. In contrast to the book, the Arab characters have names, and the script is critical of the lack of concern for them on the part of the prosecutors and other characters.While this may sound heavy, the movie is engrossing from start to finish and gets across the message about the exploitation of and disregard for the Arab population effectively.My main criticism is that the film's black-and-white cinematography and Voisin and Marder's good looks combine to make some scenes seem like a perfume or cologne commercial, because we have seen so many similar images in such ads.The adaptation will make you want to reread the novel. It will also make you think. It brings to mind a quote from Pauline Kael's review of the great new wave classic Breathless by Jean-Luc Godard, also concerning a murder which evokes no feeling in the murderer, and which was doubtless influenced by The Stranger.Kael wrote, “They just don't give a damn. How do we connect with people who don't give a damn? Well, is it really so difficult? Even if they weren't all around us, they'd still be (to quote Double Indemnity) 'closer than that.'”The Stranger is a classic of modern French literature, and adapting it for the screen must have been daunting, but Ozon, an eclectic and often playful and original filmmaker who has made such movies as the Mystery Swimming Pool and the drama about sexual abuse by priests, By the Grace of God, is up to the task.

title: Trump says ‘at some point’ US will have to give Iran ‘the hammer’
body: US President Donald Trump on Sunday reiterated his threat to resume strikes against Iran, telling a campaign rally that he may have to give Tehran “the hammer” at some unspecified time. “And the only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can…But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” the 80-year-old president told supporters during a rally in Iowa ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. title: US Navy selects Thales for next-gen mine-hunting systems
body:
Thales’ US subsidiary Advanced Acoustic Concepts (AAC) has secured a $53.9 million US Navy contract to deliver two remote mine hunting (RMH) modules and associated engineering support.
The contract includes options for additional modules that could increase its total cumulative value to approximately $196.2 million.
The RMH system will support the US Navy’s Mine Countermeasures (MCM) mission by enabling sailors to remotely detect, locate and classify underwater mines while operating at safer stand-off distances.
The capability is based on the navy’s “Find, Fix and Finish” approach to mine warfare, which aims to improve the detection and neutralization of mine threats while reducing risks to personnel and naval platforms.
The Thales RMH solution combines advanced sonar, mission management software and remotely operated vehicle technology in an integrated module suite designed to meet the US Navy’s evolving mine warfare requirements.
The system includes a multiview towed synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) designed to provide high-resolution mine detection and imaging while reducing false target rates. It also incorporates AI-assisted automatic target recognition (ATR) algorithms and software applications that enable sailors to process, classify, map and manage mine-hunting data. These capabilities are intended to accelerate target detection and classification, improve decision-making, and increase confidence in target identification.
“The ability to counter undersea mine threats remains fundamental to maritime security and naval mission success,” said Rob Geckle , CEO of Thales North America.
He added that the program would strengthen the Navy’s mine countermeasure capabilities and support fleet readiness in an increasingly dynamic operating environment.
“This program brings together the most advanced mine warfare technologies across the Thales portfolio, with AAC's deep experience delivering integrated undersea warfare capability to the U.S. Navy,” said Mike Carnovale , President of Advanced Acoustic Concepts.
He added that integrating sonar, classification software and future remote neutralization capabilities into a single operational solution would simplify mine-hunting operations and accelerate the transition from detection to action for both manned and unmanned surface vessel platforms.
To remind, Thales recently opened a new sonar manufacturing facility in Rydalmere, Western Sydney, to support the design, production, integration and sustainment of undersea acoustic systems.

title: 2027: Bury differences to re-elect Tinubu, Otu – Governor’s wife tells APC women
body: …. Betta Edu: We won’t repeat 2023 mistakes By Ike Uchechukwu, Calabar The wife of Cross River State Governor, Mrs Eyoawan Bassey Otu, has urged All Progressives Congress (APC) members to put aside their grievances, reconcile and unite ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying party cohesion is crucial to securing victory for President Bola Tinubu and Governor Bassey Otu. Mrs Otu made the appeal at the weekend in Calabar during a meeting of the Women Mobilisation Directorate of the APC Campaign Council, organised ahead of the party’s rally in the state. The meeting was held at the instance of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu. Addressing the gathering, the governor’s wife urged party members to let go of past disagreements and focus on the task ahead. “Whatever has been bothering us, whatever has been our pain, let’s bury the hatchet and move on,” she said. She stressed that the party’s immediate political objective should be the re-election of Tinubu and her husband in 2027. Citing Ephesians 2, Mrs Otu urged members who felt offended or sidelined to remain committed to doing what was right, irrespective of how others treated them. “Whether they love you or not, just keep doing the right thing. At the appropriate time, the reward will come,” she said. The governor’s wife also highlighted her interventions in the health sector, disclosing that her free medical outreach had conducted more than 2,000 surgeries across 12 editions in three years. She said the 13th edition of the programme was scheduled for the following week. “My best might not be good enough for you, but I am trying my utmost best,” she said, explaining that her interventions were intended to bridge gaps in healthcare delivery while the governor focused on administration and infrastructure development. Mrs Otu urged APC women to take the campaign to their homes, churches, markets and neighbourhoods, noting that their familiarity with residents placed them in a good position to drive grassroots mobilisation. “Talk to your neighbours about APC. Your faces have been sold. They know you already,” she said. Also speaking, former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, Dr Betta Edu, who is Co-Director of the APC Women Mobilisation Directorate, declared that the party would not repeat the mistakes it made during the 2023 elections. Edu commended the First Lady for empowering women and noted the increase in female representation in the Cross River State House of Assembly. “I remember the days there was only one woman in the House,” she said. She told the women that their commitment to the party would be measured by their performance at the polling units, rather than assurances and promises. “There is only one line of authority in Cross River State. Our leader is Governor Bassey Otu, and his dear wife. What they tell me to do is what I will go and do,” she said. Edu called for intensive grassroots mobilisation through door-to-door campaigns, church gatherings, prayer meetings and market engagements. “We don’t even have up to 80 days for this election. It’s serious business. If you don’t organise up to 200 votes, know that you have failed yourself. “Let’s not repeat the mistakes of 2023. We must ensure we win all the LGAs, 18 out of 18, for President Tinubu and Governor Otu,” she said. title: Helping Mom out? How to send money to Ukraine from Canada
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Andrew's mom in Lviv suddenly needs money for a new washing machine, and Andrew has been living in Canada for five years now. So it's no surprise he started wondering about how to send money to Ukraine from Canada without overpaying on fees or waiting a week. There are plenty of options, but he needs something reliable and fast. And most importantly, his mom has to be able to pick up the money on the other end. So let's walk through it with Andrew as the example. Where does the money go, and when can mom receive it? Let's take Meest Canada, since that's who Andrew uses. They send the transfer in US dollars to PrivatBank, and the money shows up in the bank the next business day. That makes it a fast option and an easy one to understand. If Andrew sends it on Monday, his mom can receive it at the bank on Tuesday. If he sends it on Friday, she can receive it on Monday, because only business days count. That's pretty much what the best way to send money to Ukraine looks like: one bank, one currency and no surprises. You just send the transfer, and the recipient can receive the money at a branch or in the app. And the money will wait at the bank for up to 30 business days. For more detailed information, look at https://ca.meest.com/services/service/sending-money-to-ukraine . How much does sending money to Ukraine cost? The commission depends on the amount. It's the same all across Canada, so it doesn't matter whether Andrew lives in Toronto or Vancouver. Up to $100, the commission is $6. From $101 to $200, it's $10, and from $201 to $500, it's $12. For bigger amounts, it goes up to $16-22, and above $1,000 it's 2%. So for sending money to Ukraine for $300, Andrew will pay $12. Clear pricing is more useful than hunting for the cheapest option: you can see the total before you even go to the office. What do you need to bring to send money? Andrew walks into a Meest office to do a money transfer to Ukraine from Canada. He fills out a quick form with his address and phone number, then shows an ID with his date of birth. It sounds like a lot, but it's a secure setup, and the ID part is just there because of anti-money laundering rules. The one thing to get right is his mom's name. It has to match her passport exactly, so he asks her to snap a photo of that page. When he's done, he gets a 6-digit control number and a receipt. He sends the number to his mom, along with the amount and his last name, and keeps the receipt. Most people get stuck on little things, like a wrong letter in a name or an ID left at home. So before he heads out, Andrew skims the terms and conditions and checks everything one more time. No surprises that way. How does Mom get the money: at the bank or on her phone? This is probably the nicest part, because there are two methods for getting the money. The first is at a bank branch. Mom brings her passport or her PrivatBank card, gives them the transfer number, the sender's name, the amount and the currency, and gets her cash. If she doesn't have a card yet, the bank can open one for free if she wants. With it, she can receive transfers online, at ATMs and by phone. If she lives in a small town, it's a good idea to call the branch first and ask if they have enough cash on hand. Sometimes they don't have a large sum, and the payout can be delayed. The second way is online, on her phone: Open Privat24 Go to the "Service" menu Choose "International transfers" Pick Meest and enter the transfer number Andrew's mom went with the app. She says it beats standing in line. So that's the whole process, an easy way to send money from Canada to Ukraine: a form, a number and a bank. You can explain the whole thing to your mom over the phone. By the way, Meest Canada has other services too, so you can send not only money but also parcels, pretty much anywhere in the world.

title: Shelters for Neptune launchers, dry cargo ship hit: strikes by Russian Armed Forces
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. Overnight, Russian forces launched attacks against port infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian armed forces and seagoing vessels, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
According to the ministry, the strikes destroyed a shelter and storage facility for Neptune missile launchers in the Odessa Region.
In addition, a dry cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces was struck at sea south of Odessa.
TASS has put together the key details about the targets of the strikes.
- Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces continued striking port infrastructure facilities used in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces with unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as seagoing vessels involved in transporting military cargo.
- According to the ministry, a shelter and storage facility for the launchers of Neptune anti-ship missile systems was hit near the Tuzly settlement in the Odessa Region.
- In addition, a dry cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces was struck in international waters 58 km south of Odessa.
- Geran attack drones hit an arms depot, a logistics center involved in the transportation of military cargo, a production building at the Ukrspetssvyaz plant, and an electric locomotive on a railway line.
- The ministry added that the destruction of strategic facilities substantially diminishes the Ukrainian armed forces’ ability to conduct combat operations.
- The ministry also published footage showing the Varyag unmanned systems brigade striking Ukrainian field fuel storage facilities in the Krasny Liman area.
- Emergency power outages have been imposed in Kiev and the Kiev Region, the Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK reported on its Telegram channel.
- The reason for the outages was not specified.
- Public electric transit in Kiev has been suspended because of a power failure in the grid, the municipal utility Kievpastrans reported on Telegram.
- Kiev's funicular service has also been suspended.
- Emergency scheduled power outages have been introduced in the Sumy Region in northern Ukraine, according to the Sumyoblenergo company.
- The outages were caused by damage to power infrastructure in the region.
- Emergency power outages remain in force in several regions of Ukraine due to the difficult situation in the power grid, Ukrenergo later reported on Telegram.
- The number of regions affected was not specified.

title: Ukraine’s and Russia’s ombudsmen agree to keep working on regular humanitarian missions after the Oleshky evacuation
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s and Russia’s human rights commissioners have agreed to keep working on regular humanitarian missions after the evacuation from occupied Oleshky, Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on 31 October. A day later, the ceasefire that made the evacuation possible ended. Without a new truce, the people left behind are back where they were. In July, the Institute for the Study of War concluded that Russia was effectively blockading Oleshky, which lies across the Dnipro from Ukrainian-held Kherson. In May, journalist Zarina Zabrisky said the existing route out, through occupied Crimea, Russia, and Belarus, did not work: only three of 20 people who recently tried it got through. Oleshky as a first step Lubinets wrote that he and Russian ombudsman Yana Lantratova had agreed to continue work on regular missions. He said Oleshky should be the first step, since people living near the front line need constant support. Lantratova claimed the same day that the sides had agreed to hold regular missions. The truce had been coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump. On 1 November, Lubinets said both sides had kept their commitments. He added that the two were working through the possibilities of continuing such steps. Who stayed behind On 30 October, Lubinets wrote that some buses were heading to Ukraine and others to Russia. About 700 to 1,000 people may remain in Oleshky, The Insider correspondent Tatiana Popova estimated on 31 October. Many feared a provocation or did not want to leave their homes. Meanwhile, Ukrainian troops used the truce to evacuate 167 civilians, 22 of them children, from Ukrainian-held riverside settlements that came under daily Russian shelling, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on 1 November. Bodies moved to Henichesk On 1 November, Ukrainian journalist Oleh Baturin wrote that Henichesk residents had told him dozens of civilians’ bodies were brought there from Oleshky. Volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova confirmed it, he said. By her data, 47 bodies had been kept in the basements of Oleshky’s hospital since May. How these people died remains unknown. In September, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Oleshky’s Ukrainian military administration in exile, said more than 100 bodies lay in the basement of the hospital, which had had no electricity for four years. title: Bulgaria Elects Moscow-Friendly Iotova as Black Sea Attacks Raise Security Fears
body:
Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, won a presidential runoff vote on Sunday.
The race for the largely ceremonial post had pitted Iotova, an ally of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Iotova gained between 57.4 percent and 58.2 percent of the vote, according to estimates from several polling institutes, well ahead of Gyurov, who garnered between 38.6 percent and 39.6 percent.
Flanked by Radev, a jubilant Iotova declared victory, saying her message had focused on “incomes, peace and the challenges that lie ahead”.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Iotova.
“From security and defence to our competitiveness and energy independence, I look forward to continuing our joint work. For a strong Bulgaria in a strong Europe,” she said on X.
The election was held against a backdrop of a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea that have raised security concerns
Several vessels were struck in the Black Sea off Bulgaria in October, leaving 21 people missing, in what is thought to be spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
While centre-left Radev has said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
“Today, the Bulgarian people have chosen the future over the past,” said Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow.
“They have opted for normalcy and a stable, clear path forward.”
Iotova, 62, took over the post of president earlier this year from Radev, who stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
Sunday’s vote means she is set to become the first elected woman president in the country of 6.4 million people.
Gyurov, 50 and a former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, told reporters that he accepted “the results as they are.
“We have laid a solid foundation upon which we can build,” he added, emphasising the importance of seeking unity.
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Moscow.
“The sensitive chord of fear regarding war was exploited. Even today, Iotova presented herself as the ‘president of peace,’” sociologist Boryana Dimitrova of the Alpha Research institute told AFP.
For Radev and his allies the election was “crucial for the stability of their hold on power”, she added.
After voting in Sofia, Iotova said she wanted “Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe” and remain “sovereign in its decisions”.
A longtime ally of Radev, she supports Bulgaria’s EU and NATO membership while arguing that peace in Ukraine can be achieved only through negotiations.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Gyurov said after voting that he had voted for a “secure, stable and European Bulgaria”.
The first round -- where Iotova narrowly won over Gyurov -- recorded a record low turnout of 23 percent. Turnout in the second round was projected to be around 27 percent.
Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round because he expected a runoff.
He said he voted for “the lesser evil”, as neither candidate matched his “vision of democracy”.

title: United CEO says Boom supersonic airliner won't be ready this decade
body:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby no longer expects Boom Supersonic 's Overture airliner to enter service before the end of the decade, casting doubt on a timeline that has already changed significantly since the airline became one of the project's first major customers.
"It's not going to happen in '29 — it's going to take longer," Kirby said in an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast.
His assessment is significant because United was the first US airline to commit to the Overture. In 2021, the carrier announced an agreement for 15 aircraft, subject to safety, operating and sustainability requirements, with options for another 35.
Kirby did not dismiss the program and praised Boom founder and CEO Blake Scholl and the company's ability to adapt. But he acknowledged the scale of the challenge still ahead.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
"They've got a lot of hurdles to overcome," he said, adding that there is no guarantee Boom will overcome all of them. In March, Kirby had already estimated the chances of the Overture reaching commercial service at "50-50."
When United announced its agreement in June 2021, Boom expected the Overture to roll out in 2025, make its first flight in 2026 and carry passengers by 2029.
The schedule changed after the aircraft itself underwent a major redesign and Boom decided to develop a new engine specifically for the program. In December 2022, when the company unveiled the Symphony engine, it projected production would begin in 2024, followed by rollout in 2026, first flight in 2027 and certification in 2029.
Nearly four years later, no Overture prototype has been completed.
Boom did achieve an important milestone with the XB-1 demonstrator . The aircraft first flew in March 2024 and exceeded the speed of sound for the first time in January 2025, demonstrating that the company could design, build and fly a supersonic aircraft.
But the XB-1 is not a prototype of the Overture. The commercial aircraft is considerably larger, has a different configuration and will require certification for airline service.
One of its biggest challenges remains propulsion. After Rolls-Royce ended its involvement with Boom, the company announced the purpose-built Symphony turbofan in 2022. Boom now has to develop and certify a new commercial aircraft and a new engine before the Overture can enter service.
That challenge has also created an unexpected business opportunity.
Boom is adapting technology developed for Symphony to produce Superpower, a 42 MW natural gas turbine aimed at supplying electricity to AI data centers. In October, the company unveiled a nearly 200,000-square-foot factory in Centennial, Colorado, dedicated to turbine production.
Boom has also completed Sprint Core, its first experimental turbine core. The hardware incorporates the compressor, combustor and high-pressure turbine and will provide technology for both Superpower and Symphony. Its first firing is planned before Thanksgiving.
The company expects the first Superpower customer deliveries in mid-2027 and plans to reach production of 25 turbines annually in 2028 and 50 in 2029.
Rather than presenting the energy business as a diversion from Overture, Scholl says revenue and profits from Superpower can help finance development of the supersonic aircraft. The two programs also share technology and manufacturing capabilities.
Kirby highlighted the move as an example of Boom's ability to pivot, specifically mentioning the company's decision to produce turbines for data centers.
The contrast with the Overture production infrastructure is notable.
Boom completed its Overture Superfactory at Piedmont Triad International Airport in Greensboro, North Carolina, in 2024. The facility was designed to assemble as many as 33 aircraft per year, with plans for a second line that could eventually double capacity.
At the time, the company expected aircraft production to begin that year. More than two years after the building was completed, however, there is still no Overture prototype to assemble.

title: Adesina, Sanusi, Otti to lead African prosperity talks
body: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja Former President of the African Development Bank, Dr Akinwumi Adesina; Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi II; and Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, are among prominent African leaders expected to attend a conference in Abuja on November 3 to discuss strategies for building a prosperous, resilient and inclusive African economy. The second edition of the Oxford Global Think Tank Leadership Conference will bring together leaders from government, business, technology, finance and civil society to examine leadership, institutional reforms, technological innovation and investment opportunities capable of driving sustainable economic growth across the continent. According to a statement issued on Monday by the Conference Media Adviser, Comrade Chris Isiguzo, Adesina, who is also Executive Chairman of the Global Africa Investment Summit, will deliver the keynote address. Sanusi and the Founder of ANAP Foundation, Atedo Peterside, will serve as co-chairs of the conference. The event, themed, “Leadership for a Prosperous Future,” will examine major issues shaping Africa’s development, including the growing influence of artificial intelligence, changing global power relations, demographic shifts and emerging economic challenges. Other personalities expected at the conference include the Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr Bosun Tijani; Minister of Women Affairs, Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim; Executive Vice President of Afreximbank, Dr Kanayo Awani; Director-General of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Dr Emomotimi Agama; and Chief Executive Officer of Flutterwave, Gbenga Agboola. The discussions will focus on three key areas: resilience, innovation and dynamism. Participants are expected to explore ways of strengthening African institutions, mobilising investment capital, improving productivity and expanding economic opportunities across different sectors. The conference will also feature discussions on artificial intelligence, the unveiling of an AI report and the launch of an AI Virtual Centre. An exhibition showcasing emerging technologies and their potential applications in Africa’s development will also form part of the programme. The organisers said the conference was designed to move beyond discussions of Africa’s economic potential to identifying practical steps and partnerships that could strengthen institutions, improve productive capacity and promote inclusive economic growth. “Africa’s future will be shaped by the quality of leadership and the choices its institutions and leaders make today,” the organisers said. The conference, hosted by the Oxford Global Think Tank, founded by Ms Arunma Oteh, will hold at the Congress Hall of Transcorp Hilton Hotel, Abuja, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., followed by a cocktail reception. The Oxford Global Think Tank is an independent, non-governmental and non-partisan organisation focused on research and dialogue on development, as well as supporting public and private sector leaders in developing policy ideas and strengthening institutions.
