title: Russian Drone Attacks Kill 1, Injure Dozens, Cut Power and Water Supplies
body:
Russian drone attacks across Ukraine overnight on Nov. 1-2 killed one person and injured dozens others, including five in the Odesa region and 27 in the Kharkiv region, while damaging residential, energy, and other civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 193 strike drones from 6 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1. Ukrainian air defenses intercepted or suppressed 154 of them, including 58 Shahed-type drones, 75 of which were jet-powered.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Russian drones struck 26 locations, while debris from intercepted unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) fell at nine others, according to preliminary data as of 8 a.m. on Monday, Nov. 2.
The attacks involved Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered models, as well as Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoys. Ukrainian forces used aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned units, and mobile fire groups to counter the attack.
At least five people were injured in a Russian attack on the Odesa region overnight, regional governor Oleh Kiper reported on Telegram .
The strikes damaged civilian, residential, and energy infrastructure, including warehouse and administrative buildings and private homes. A bakery building was destroyed, while an energy facility belonging to DTEK Odesa Grids was also hit.
Power supply has been restored to some consumers, while emergency repair work is ongoing, Kiper said.
In the city of Odesa, four people were injured, according to Serhiy Lysak, head of the City Military Administration (MVA). The attack damaged two residential buildings and a garage, while the blast wave shattered windows in neighboring homes.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) later clarified that four of the five people injured in the region were hurt in the city of Odesa.
“Large-scale fires broke out in Odesa after strikes hit warehouse facilities. A gas pipeline, a residential building, and a garage were damaged,” the report said.
According to the DSNS, a bakery in the southern part of the region was destroyed by a fire, while warehouses also caught fire. In another area, an administrative building, residential homes, kiosks, and a bus station building were damaged.
More than 150 rescuers have been deployed to deal with the aftermath of the attack. Rescue operations are ongoing.
Twelve people, including a child, were injured in a Russian drone attack on the village of Vashyshcheve in the Kharkiv region on Sunday evening, the DSNS reported .
One drone struck the roof of a five-story residential building, damaging apartments and floor slabs. Firefighters rescued two residents who had become trapped in an apartment on the top floor.
Fires also broke out at a private enterprise, damaging greenhouses, hay, and a refrigeration unit. DSNS crews and a local fire brigade worked to contain the aftermath.
Separately, a Russian strike hit a four-story residential building in Izium on Monday morning, setting cars on fire and reportedly sparking a fire at a post office branch, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said, citing preliminary information.
One person was killed, and at least three others required medical attention, Syniehubov reported . However, the Izium MVA later clarified that 15 people had sought medical assistance following the attack.
The strike also damaged high-voltage power lines, leaving the entire city without electricity, according to the MVA.
“Nov. 2, between 08:50 and 09:10 a.m., the enemy launched a series of airstrikes on the city of Izium using guided aerial bombs (KABs),” the statement said.
A Russian strike on Sunday evening hit a transport facility in the Kropyvnytskyi district of the Kirovohrad region, triggering a large fire, regional governor Andriy Raykovych reported.
DSNS crews worked under the threat of follow-up strikes to extinguish the blaze. The fire was brought under control by Monday morning, and no casualties were reported.
Russia’s overnight strikes also placed additional pressure on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo, the state-owned grid operator, said emergency power outages had been introduced in some regions because of the difficult situation in the power system. Previously announced outage schedules were temporarily suspended in areas affected by the emergency cuts.
Energy workers were carrying out repairs, and the outages were expected to be lifted once the grid stabilized.
The city of Bila Tserkva in the Kyiv region also lost its water supply on Monday morning after a Russian drone attack damaged an infrastructure facility, the local utility company Bila Tserkvavoda reported . Residents were advised to stock up on water, with no estimate yet available for when supplies would be restored.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: 2026 set to be the world’s second-hottest year on record as El Niño drives August to an all-time high
body: The world has been hotter in the first ten months of 2026 than in any other year on record except 2024, a JoyNews Research analysis of global temperature data shows. Between 1 January and 26 October, the average air temperature at the Earth’s surface was 15.30°C . That is 0.64°C higher than the average for the same days between 1991 and 2020, the period scientists use as today’s “normal.” Only 2024 was warmer over the same days, at 0.71°C above normal. 2026 is ahead of 2025 (0.59°C) and 2023 (0.55°C). The figures come from ERA5, a day-by-day record of the world’s weather produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. JoyNews Research analysed every day from 1 January 1940 to 26 October 2026, a total of 31,711 days. The analysis comes days before world leaders meet in Antalya, Türkiye, for the COP31 climate summit, which runs from 9 to 20 November. Figure 1: The ten warmest years over 1 January to 26 October. Each bar compares the same days of the year What does 0.64°C mean? A rise of less than one degree can sound small. Ghanaians feel bigger swings between morning and afternoon on any ordinary day. But this figure is different. It is an average for the whole planet: every country, every ocean, day and night, for ten months. Moving that average even by a few tenths of a degree takes a huge amount of extra heat. That heat shows up locally as hotter days, more intense downpours, and longer dry spells. Scientists call the difference from normal an “anomaly.” Throughout this article, an anomaly of +0.64°C simply means 0.64°C warmer than the 1991–2020 average for that time of year. A slow start, then a sharp turn 2026 did not start as a record year. From January to April, it ranked only fourth or fifth for the time of year, at about 0.53°C above normal. Then it climbed. May and June were the second-warmest on record. By August it was first. Between August and October, temperatures averaged 0.85°C above normal , a jump of 0.32°C on the first four months of the year. The turn matches the arrival of El Niño. This is a natural pattern in which the surface of the Pacific Ocean near the equator becomes unusually warm and releases extra heat into the air, raising temperatures around the world. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said on 8 October that El Niño conditions were present, with a key Pacific temperature index at 2.1°C above normal. It gave a more than 83% chance of a strong to very strong event lasting into early 2027. Figure 2: Each month of 2026 compared with normal. The number inside each bar is that month’s rank out of 87 years. August: the hottest month ever measured August 2026 was the warmest August on record, at 0.84°C above normal . It beat the previous record, shared by 2024 and 2023, by 0.13°C, a wide margin for a global average. In plain temperature terms, August averaged 16.96°C. That equals July 2023 as the hottest month in the entire record. Copernicus, the EU climate service, reached the same finding in its own monthly report, describing August as the joint-hottest month on record. September was the second-warmest September, behind only 2023. October is running just 0.01°C ahead of the same days in 2023, too close to call until the month’s final figures are in. 65 days, those broke records A record day is one that was hotter than the same date in every year since 1940. So far in 2026, there have been 65 of them. Twenty-four of those came in August alone, more than in the whole first half of the year. From 8 August to 8 September, every single day set a new record for its date: 32 days in a row. Even on days that did not set records, 2026 was rarely far behind. Seven in every ten days this year (206 of 299) ranked in the top three for their date. Figure 3: Days in 2026 that were the hottest ever measured for their date, by month. The single hottest day of 2026 was 14 August, at 17.05°C . It is the 12th-hottest day on record; the 11 days above it all fell in July and August of 2023 and 2024. Before 2023, the world’s average temperature had never reached 17°C on any day. In 2026, it has done so on 18 days, the same as in 2024. Figure 4: Every year since 1940 plotted day by day. Grey lines are 1940 to 2022; the coloured lines are the four most recent years. Can 2026 overtake 2024? Almost certainly not. For 2026 to beat 2024 over the full year, the remaining 66 days would have to average 1.08°C above normal . No year in the record has averaged more than 0.84°C over late October to December, and that was 2023, also an El Niño year. JoyNews Research projected the rest of the year using how late-October temperatures have carried into November and December in every year since 1979. Both methods point to a full-year figure of about 0.67°C above normal , within a range of 0.63°C to 0.72°C. Every scenario puts 2026 in second place. It would also mean the four hottest years ever measured are the last four: 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Figure 5: Every year since 1940 compared with the 1991–2020 average. Blue years were cooler than that average; 2026 is a projection, with its likely range. What about the 1.5°C limit? Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries agreed to try to keep global warming to 1.5°C above “pre-industrial” levels, the average for 1850 to 1900, before large-scale burning of coal, oil and gas. On that scale, 2026 is on course to end at about 1.55°C . Copernicus puts 2024 at 1.60°C and 2025 at 1.47°C. This does not mean the Paris limit has been broken. That limit is measured as an average over 20 years, not a single year. But the world is now regularly having years at or above the line, and Copernicus expects the current El Niño to last into 2027. Warming is speeding up Over the full record, the world has warmed by about 0.14°C every ten years since 1940. Since 1979, the rate has been 0.21°C per decade. Since 2000 it has reached 0.29°C per decade, roughly double the long-run pace. What it means for Ghana The figures in this analysis are global averages and do not describe conditions in any single country. But the same El Niño is shaping Ghana’s weather. In its outlook for the September to November minor rainy season, the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) forecast warmer-than-normal temperatures across most of the country and below-normal to normal rainfall in most areas. It advised farmers to prepare for long dry spells by harvesting rainwater and using drought-tolerant and early-maturing crop varieties, while warning that flash floods remain possible in low-lying areas. The numbers leave little doubt about the direction of travel. The question for COP31, and for Ghana, is how fast the world can prepare for a climate in which a year like 2026 is no longer unusual.

title: Airbus, Wits and ISAE-SUPAERO Sign Four-Year Aerospace Skills Pact
body: Airbus Southern Africa, the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits) in Johannesburg and France’s Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-SUPAERO) signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on 17 September 2026 to align South African aerospace engineering training with French standards. The agreement targets a long-standing gap: too few locally trained engineers for an industry that Airbus, defence primes and their suppliers all need to staff. The signing was attended by Benjamin Cabouat, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of France in South Africa, according to Wits . What the Three Partners Agreed Wits and ISAE-SUPAERO will map their aerospace engineering courses against each other and close the gaps they find. The two universities will also audit academic credits, so that French programmes meet South African qualification standards before any students move between them. A reciprocal faculty exchange will connect Johannesburg with Toulouse, where ISAE-SUPAERO is based. Lecturers from each side will work together on aerospace design methods. The partners say this should lay the groundwork for regular student and staff exchanges. Qualifying Wits students will gain a route into ISAE-SUPAERO’s specialised Master’s programmes and its advanced research facilities in France. Airbus plays the industrial role. The company will run general aviation awareness events, offer design-thinking mentorship to Wits students and study whether to launch undergraduate aviation courses focused on aircraft operations. Airbus described the undergraduate courses as potential, not committed. Each institution will field an operational team and an executive team. They will review progress at regular intervals through the four-year term. Who Said What Nam-Binh Hoang, Airbus Country Representative in South Africa, said the deal connects academic work with industry needs. “We are building a sustainable talent pipeline that supports both local innovation and global aerospace standards,” he said. Professor Lynn Morris, Deputy Vice-Chancellor: Research and Innovation at Wits, said the agreement “enhances our capability to deliver world-class engineering education” and gives students access to advanced aerospace modules, international exposure and research tied to industry demand. Marie-Hélène Baroux, President of ISAE-SUPAERO, said her institute was proud to “welcome top South African talent into our specialised Master’s programmes.” ISAE-SUPAERO describes itself as the world’s first dedicated aeronautical school, founded in 1909, and the University of Colorado Boulder signed its own MoU with the institute in July 2026. Why a Skills Deal Matters to Defence Readers Airbus has worked in South Africa for two decades and depends on a steady supply of engineers and technicians. Aerospace programmes rise or fall on engineers. Design offices, maintenance hangars and test ranges all draw from the same small pool of graduates, and South Africa competes for them with Europe, the Gulf and North America. The South African Air Force feels that shortage directly: its helicopter fleet’s availability problems drove Airbus and Denel to sign a support pact at the Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) exhibition the same week. Airbus has worked in South Africa for two decades. A 2014 industry report quoted an Airbus executive saying the company had committed R4 billion in work packages and research projects to the country since 2005. The Wits deal does not build hardware. It builds the people who would design and certify it. French curricula are tied to European certification practice, so a Wits graduate who completes the pathway should arrive at an Airbus programme already trained in its methods. The MoU is not a contract. Public statements set no budget, no student numbers and no funding source, and do not say who pays for travel, tuition or staff time. Agreements of this kind are quick to sign and slow to deliver. Airbus signed a framework MoU with the government of Côte d’Ivoire in June 2018 to support that country’s aerospace sector, a comparable continental arrangement. The fairer test for Wits is what the partnership has produced by the end of its term in 2030, in graduates placed and exchanges completed. A Second Airbus Training Deal in the Same Week ALT Academy and Airbus sign a memorandum of understanding on aircraft maintenance training at AAD 2026. The Wits signing came a day after another Airbus training agreement at AAD 2026 at Air Force Base Waterkloof in the City of Tshwane. On 16 September 2026, Airbus and ALT Academy, a flight training provider based in Kempton Park, signed an MoU to explore joint aircraft maintenance training . Ryan van Wijk, chief executive of ALT Academy, signed for his organisation. Timo Eckardt, head of customer support for Airbus Africa, signed for Airbus. The two sides will decide which courses and learning tools to develop together, with the aim of narrowing the distance between classroom teaching and what operators need in the hangar. “This partnership is an important step in our commitment to building practical, high-quality maintenance training capacity in South Africa,” Van Wijk said. ALT Academy already teaches Airbus A320 and Boeing 737 simulator courses and has moved into early-stage, or “ab initio,” pilot training. Maintenance is a defence concern as much as a civil one. Air forces that operate Airbus airframes, such as the Angolan C295 shown at AAD , depend on the same pool of licensed technicians that airlines recruit from. Airbus is also expanding its African maintenance footprint beyond training. Mickaël Bertrand, Managing Director of Airbus Helicopters Morocco, told Morocco World News at the Marrakech Air Show that Airbus will open a helicopter maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) subsidiary in Morocco in the coming months. He said it will serve Morocco first and is designed to cover West Africa. From Signed Paper to Students in Toulouse The first test of the Wits agreement is the curriculum gap analysis, which should show how far the two programmes differ. The credit audit that follows will decide whether the first students can transfer. Airbus has yet to say whether it will approve the undergraduate aviation courses. A decision on those, and the naming of the first Wits students bound for Toulouse, would show whether the MoU becomes a working programme.

title: EU Extends Operation Irini to 2029, Adds Russian Shadow Fleet Task
body: The Council of the European Union (EU) extended its Mediterranean naval mission, Operation Irini, to 31 March 2029 on 9 October 2026. The renewal adds three tasks: constraining Russia’s shadow fleet, improving maritime domain awareness and protecting critical maritime infrastructure. Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2243, adopted under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), moved the end date from 31 March 2027. The Council set common costs for 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029 at €16.88 million. The previous two-year period carried €16.35 million, so the budget rises by about 3 percent, according to the published decision . Irini, formally European Union Naval Force Mediterranean (EUNAVFOR MED) Irini, launched on 31 March 2020 under Council Decision 2020/472. The name is Greek for peace. It replaced Operation Sophia, which ended on 20 March 2020, and its first job was to enforce the United Nations (UN) arms embargo on Libya. A Berlin conference in January 2020 set the case for the operation by calling for effective implementation of the UN arms embargo. The Foreign Affairs Council decided on 17 February 2020 to launch Irini. Its original task list had four items: countering illegal arms trafficking, gathering information on oil smuggling, disrupting the human smuggling business model through information gathering, and training Libyan institutions responsible for law enforcement and search and rescue at sea. What the Mandate Changes The refurbished Libyan patrol vessel Al-Kifah (LCG-206). Training Libyan maritime institutions remains part of Irini’s work. The mandate now rests on three roles. Irini protects and deters in defence of EU interests in the Mediterranean, supports UN Security Council resolutions on Libya, and builds partnerships through training and naval diplomacy. The Libya work stays. Irini will keep exposing embargo violations and monitoring illicit Libyan petroleum exports, continue aerial patrols over the high seas to detect human smuggling and trafficking, and keep training Libyan maritime law enforcement and search and rescue institutions. The decision also opens a platform for maritime security cooperation that could include Egypt, Tunisia and Lebanon, and the operation says it stays ready to scale up if conditions in Libya change. The shadow fleet is the network of ageing tankers that carry Russian oil outside normal ownership and insurance rules. The decision says Irini “shall contribute to constraining Russia’s ‘shadow fleet'” through a whole-of-route approach. It defines the term through an International Maritime Organization (IMO) resolution and ties the task to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Maritime domain awareness means a shared picture of who and what is at sea. The March 2025 extension had already added a maritime situational awareness task, so the new text builds on it. The infrastructure task covers pipelines and cables, including trials of new technology. Libya Security Monitor reported in May that the change should let Irini protect pipelines and a submarine communications cable. No New Boarding Powers The shadow fleet task brings no new inspection power. UNCLOS already lets a warship visit a ship suspected of having no nationality, which reaches false-flagged tankers. Libya Security Monitor says boardings with detentions have so far been national operations by Britain and France. The legal ground has also shifted. The UN Security Council authority to inspect ships on the high seas off Libya, Resolution 2292 (2016), lapsed on 25 May 2026. A six-month technical extension under Resolution 2804 had run since 25 November 2025. Libya Security Monitor reported that nobody requested a renewal . It appears Greece and France, who drafted the original resolution, chose not to ask. The EU said Irini would carry on under its own Council mandate. The new Libya article speaks of reporting and deterring arms trafficking. Every task reports to the EU’s Political and Security Committee (PSC), which may consider follow-on measures. Ships and Commanders Helicopters smuggled to Benghazi in eastern Libya, one of many alleged breaches of the UN arms embargo that Irini reports on. Rear Admiral Marco Casapieri of the Italian Navy is the Operation Commander. Italy and Greece swap the Force Commander post, which controls ships and aircraft at sea, every six months. On 1 October 2026 at Taranto, Commodore Stavros Polydorou of the Hellenic Navy took over from Rear Admiral Andrea Bielli of the Italian Navy. The force now sails with the Greek frigate HS Navarinon as flagship. Greek City Times reports three Greek ships, Navarinon, Nearchos and Kimon, plus two Italian warships. Agenzia Nova describes Navarinon as an Elli-class frigate, 130.5 metres long and about 3,530 tonnes. She has served in the Greek fleet since 1995 after earlier Dutch service. Irini has always been small. Its own October 2023 figures counted two naval units, six aircraft and over 600 personnel. The embargo work has produced seizures. In July 2022 the Italian frigate ITS Grecale searched the cargo ship Victory Roro, and military vehicles were seized . On 11 October 2022 Irini stopped the Dutch-flagged Meerdijk off Libya; later reports counted 41 UAE-built BATT UMG armoured vehicles aboard . Armour still reaches Libya by other routes: dozens of Turkish-made BMC Amazon vehicles appeared with eastern Libyan forces in October. Stretching Thin Hulls Across the Central Mediterranean Each new task draws on the same hulls and aircraft. A frigate watching tankers or cables is not watching embargo traffic. That trade-off is Military Africa’s analysis, not a reported finding. The EU keeps a standing naval presence in the central Mediterranean with a legal basis that no longer depends on a UN renewal. On the shadow fleet, Irini starts as a watcher and reporter. Anything beyond that would rest on flag-state consent, a stateless-ship finding or a new PSC measure. The practical question for defence planners is assets. In an early interview, the first Operation Commander, Rear Admiral Fabio Agostini of the Italian Navy, said the operation needed continuous availability of air-defence warships, airborne early warning aircraft and surveillance assets. A wider mandate makes that need larger, not smaller. The next marker is 1 April 2027, when the new budget period starts and Italy is due to take back the Force Commander post.

title: Nigeria’s Army Chief Tours Rwandan Arms Maker, Urges Local Production
body: Nigeria’s Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, toured the Rwanda Engineering and Manufacturing Corporation (REMCO) in Kigali on 21 October 2026 and called on African states to build their own defence industries. The tour formed part of an official visit to Rwanda from 18 to 23 October. Shaibu said African countries should invest in research and development, grow local technical skills and form cross-border industrial partnerships to answer their own security problems. REMCO Chief Executive Emile Rugambajye received the delegation at the state-owned plant in the Kigali Special Economic Zone. According to a statement from Colonel Appolonia Anele, Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Shaibu reviewed the company’s precision engineering, machining, metal casting and machinery fabrication work. Press reports say REMCO displayed sniper rifles, assault rifles, machine guns, pistols and armoured vehicles at the inaugural International Security Conference on Africa, held in Kigali during the visit. Talks With Rwandan Leaders Rwanda Defence Force soldiers. Nigeria and Rwanda have committed to implementing existing training and staff exchange agreements. Earlier in the week, Shaibu called on Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) Chief of Defence Staff General Mubarakh Muganga. He then held bilateral talks with RDF Army Chief of Staff Major General Vincent Nyakarundi. Shaibu said both armies had committed to implementing existing memoranda of understanding on military training and on the exchange of directing staff and logistics personnel. He also reaffirmed Nigerian Army support for specialised training, joint exercises and defence technology cooperation with the RDF. The Nigerian Army has been widening such ties this year, from a training and intelligence-sharing agreement with Jordan to an offer of counter-terrorism and drone warfare training to Bangladesh . The delegation also visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial and the Campaign Against Genocide Museum. The Army statement said Shaibu praised Rwanda’s rebuilding since 1994 and argued that discipline, leadership and national resolve remain central to countering insecurity across Africa. On 22 October, President Paul Kagame received Shaibu at Urugwiro Village, his office in Kigali, to discuss ways of strengthening defence cooperation between the two countries, The New Times reported . The Nigerian Army also reported separate meetings with Rwanda’s Minister of Defence. What REMCO Brings Small arms produced by the Rwanda Engineering and Manufacturing Corporation (REMCO) in Kigali. REMCO was founded in 2018. It specialises in engineering, metal casting, fabrication and the production of machinery, equipment and spare parts. Reports also say it makes small arms in collaboration with Israel Weapon Industries (IWI), the Israeli firearms maker. The Nigerian Army’s case for local manufacturing is practical. Shaibu said domestic production improves equipment availability, meaning the share of a fleet fit for use on a given day. It also shortens maintenance supply chains and cuts exposure to disruption in global defence supply networks. He said he wants technical exchanges, joint research, knowledge transfer and manufacturing partnerships to strengthen Nigeria’s own production, equipment maintenance and technical support. The Army tied the visit to the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON), the state arms maker, which hosted the first AFRIDEX exhibition in Lagos days after Shaibu returned home and has already paired with private firms on projects such as an indigenous counter-drone system with UNICCON . The Army has also opened a joint service centre with China’s NORINCO in Bauchi to keep imported armour running. The Import Picture The push follows a period of heavy buying. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) reported in March 2026 that arms imports to sub-Saharan Africa rose 13 per cent between 2016 to 2020 and 2021 to 2025. Imports across the whole continent fell 41 per cent over the same span, driven largely by a 78 per cent drop in Algeria. Nigeria took 16 per cent of the sub-region’s imports, the largest share. Senegal took 8.8 per cent and Mali 8.0 per cent. SIPRI counts only major systems such as aircraft, armoured vehicles, missiles and ships, so small arms like those REMCO makes sit outside its totals. Nigeria’s own buying shows the dependence. ADF Magazine, citing Business Insider Africa, reports a $346 million United States arms sale package to Nigeria and a $1.38 billion contract for aircraft and helicopters from Italy and the United States. Bell has just started building Nigeria’s 12 AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters in Texas. Nigeria is not alone in looking for shorter supply lines. Senegal has opened its first military vehicle assembly plant at Diamniadio, according to Seneweb, Mali has been widening its list of suppliers, and Abuja itself has asked the Czech Republic for help with an ammunition line . That gap matters for the Nigerian argument. Local plants can realistically cover small arms, ammunition, spare parts and repair work first. Aircraft, ships and advanced armour will stay import-heavy for years, and even licensed local assembly often depends on foreign-made components, a dependence Military Africa examined in who really controls Africa’s weapons . Scale is the other constraint. Rwanda’s own army is small, so REMCO needs export orders to keep production lines busy. Nigeria has a far larger requirement and an existing industrial base in DICON, which gives it more room to absorb output but also more capacity to compete with a Rwandan supplier. From Kigali Talks to Shared Production Lines No contract, joint venture or technology-transfer deal has been announced. The visit produced commitments to carry out existing memoranda and an expressed interest in manufacturing cooperation, not a signed programme. For the Nigerian Army, the likely gain is in sustainment. Spare parts and repair capacity decide how many weapons and vehicles stay ready during a long counter-insurgency campaign. A partner that can machine and cast parts to order could help close that gap, if its quality control meets Nigerian military standards. The Army statement framed the engagement as part of joint efforts against terrorism, violent extremism and cross-border threats. Industrial cooperation is a slower track than training, but it is the one that can reduce import reliance. The next signs to watch are whether the Nigerian Army sends a DICON technical team to Kigali, whether the two sides name a joint maintenance or research project, and whether the training and staff exchanges begin before the end of the year.

title: 2027: INEC lists 35 candidates for Taraba Senate elections
body:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has listed 35 candidates to contest the three senatorial seats in Taraba State in the 2027 general elections.
The candidates, representing various political parties, will contest for Taraba North, Taraba Central, and Taraba South senatorial districts in the National Assembly election scheduled for 16 January 2027.
The final list, signed by INEC Secretary, Rose Oriaran-Anthony, shows that Taraba Central has the highest number of candidates with 14, followed by Taraba North with 11, and Taraba South with 10.
In Taraba South, the incumbent senator, David Jimkuta of the All Progressives Congress (APC), will face nine others.
They include Jauro Ibrahim of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Aliyu Yusuf of Accord, Afiniki Yarima of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Akaangee Bosha of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), and Ezekiel Ambo of the Labour Party (LP).
Others are Istifanus Mik of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Adi Ashumate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Bako Samalia of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and Ismaila Yahuza of the Young Progressives Party (YPP).
In Taraba Central, APC candidate and incumbent senator, Haruna Manu, will face 13 challengers.
The challengers include Falack Victor of Accord, Yaroojee Lawan of the African Action Congress (AAC), Ahmadu Salim of the ADC, Adamu Gassol of APGA, and Danladi Stephen of APM.
Others are Yubuin Samuel of LP, Baban Babangida of the National Rescue Movement (NRM), Nyan-Ganji Gills of NDC, Iliyasu Goje of PDP, Barak Maikidi of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Jibir Suleiman of SDP, Ahmad Kiyari of YPP and Ibrahim Hamidu of the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP).
For Taraba North, APC candidate Shuaibu Lau will contest against 10 other candidates.
They include Maigari Bello of ADC, Anthony Zawati of Accord, Ali Sani of APGA, Mathias Dame of LP and Anthony Lawrence of NRM.
The other candidates are Bandawa Anfani of NDC, Bubajoda Mafindi of PDP, Abdullahi Aminu of PRP, Usman Shekara of SDP and Musa Tukur of YPP.
The senatorial contests come amid significant political realignments in Taraba State following the defection of Governor Agbu Kefas and two of the three serving senators from the PDP to the APC.
The defections have strengthened the APC’s position ahead of the elections, with the party seeking to consolidate its control of the state’s three senatorial seats.
The opposition parties, meanwhile, face the task of rebuilding their political structures and mobilising support to challenge the ruling party.
The January 2027 election is expected to test the political strength of the APC following its recent expansion in the state, as well as the ability of opposition parties to regain ground.

title: 2026 ASEAN Summit: Road closures, alternative routes in Metro Manila
body: MANILA, Philippines – Several roads in Pasay City will be closed to motorists during the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit from Monday, November 16, to Wednesday, November 18. The affected roads are mostly near the Philippine International Convention Center, one of the summit’s venues, and the Cultural Center of the Philippines. The following roads will be affected by the closures: Pedro Bukaneg Street Vicente Sotto Street Buendia Avenue corner Magdalene Jalandoni Street Diosdado Macapagal Boulevard J.W. Diokno Boulevard corner Atang Dela Rama Street Atang Dela Rama Street The Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said security checkpoints will be set up in the area from October 24 to November 8. The public may still enter during this period, subject to security screening and verification. From November 9 to 18, the area will be closed to the public. Only authorized personnel and vehicles with valid access credentials will be allowed entry. Alternative routes Motorists may take the following alternative routes to avoid the affected roads: For northbound traffic For motorists traveling along Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard toward Roxas Boulevard: 1. Turn right to Seaside Boulevard. 2. Turn right to Macapagal Boulevard. 3. Turn left to EDSA. 4. Turn left to Roxas Boulevard. For southbound traffic For motorists traveling along Roxas Boulevard toward Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard: 1. Turn right to EDSA. 2. Turn right to Diokno Boulevard. 3. Turn right to Macapagal Boulevard. The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) also temporarily suspended the issuance of permits for fun runs, motorcades, and other public activities from October 24 to November 20, 2026, in the cities of Manila, Pasay, Parañaque, Makati, and Taguig. Roxas Boulevard may also be affected by traffic caused by the ASEAN event, Manila Mayor Isko Moreno said. Moreno said some events will also be held in some parts of the city. To ease traffic congestion, Malacañang declared November 16 to November 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila. Other cities in Metro Manila have yet to release a traffic advisory for ASEAN. This story will be updated as information becomes available. Security measures The MMDA will be deploying 2,955 personnel for the summit. The Philippine National Police, meanwhile, will deploy 13,868 cops to ensure the security of delegates. In Makati, the city government banned the use of drones for the whole month of November, as part of safety and security measures for the summit. – Rappler.com

title: LP chieftain Arabambi sues CCB over Obi’s asset declaration
body: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri ABUJA – A chieftain of the Labour Party (LP), Chief Abayomi Arabambi, has dragged the Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB) to court over its alleged refusal to release the certified true copy of the asset declaration form submitted by the presidential candidate of the National Democratic Party (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi. Also listed as 2nd to 4th Respondents in the suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/2504/2026 and filed before the Federal High Court in Abuja, are the Chairman of the CCB, the Senate President, and the Speaker of the House of Representatives. The plaintiff, through his team of lawyers led by Mr. Oshoke Asimegbe, told the court that, in two separate letters dated August 31 and October 8, 2026, he requested the CCB, in line with the provisions of the Freedom of Information Act, 2011, to furnish him with details of the assets declared by the NDC candidate. According to the plaintiff, he specifically asked for the asset declaration particulars and all documents attached to the Asset Declaration Form that Obi submitted to the CCB in 2006, before he was sworn in as Governor of Anambra State, and in 2014, when he left office. Obi served as governor under the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) from March 17, 2006 to March 17, 2014. Arabambi, who described himself as a Nigerian citizen and a registered voter in Ogun State, said the legal action is predicated on his rights under the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which he said were breached by the CCB’s refusal to accede to his FOI request. He is praying the court for a declaration that his letters, which were duly received by the CCB, constitute a valid request for access to the information and official records he sought pursuant to the FOI Act, 2011. The applicant further wants a declaration that both the Senate President and the Speaker of the House of Representatives (3rd and 4th Respondents) are under a constitutional obligation to stipulate the terms and conditions for access to the official documents he requested, and that “the refusal and failure of the 3rd and 4th Respondents to set any terms and conditions for the release of the requested documents despite the Applicant’s letters to the 3rd and 4th Respondents dated 31st August, 2026 and October, 2026 is a refusal and a dereliction to perform a legal duty.” He also seeks: “A declaration that the refusal and failure of the 3rd and 4th Respondents to set any terms and conditions for the release of the official documents requested by the Applicant vide the Applicant’s letters to the 1st and 2nd Respondents dated 31st August, 2026 and October, 2026, despite the Applicant’s letters dated 31st August, 2026 and 8th October, 2026 to the 3rd and 4th Respondents, make the Respondents, and particularly the 1st and 2nd Respondents, under a legal obligation to grant the Applicant access to the requested official documents, as the law makes no room for vacuum or lacuna. “A declaration that the reasons adduced by the 1st and 2nd Respondents vide their letter dated 17th September, 2026, but received on 25th September, 2026, as the reasons for refusing the Applicant’s request for access to the certified true copies of the Asset Declaration Forms of Peter Obi Gregory are unlawful and invalid, and contrary to the spirit and letters of the Freedom of Information Act, 2011 and the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, as amended. “An order of Mandamus compelling the 1st and 2nd Respondents to forthwith release the requested documents to the Applicant in performance of their statutory/public duty by granting the Applicant access to the information and certified true copies of the records/documents requested in the Applicant’s letters of 31st August, 2026 and 8th October, 2026. “An order of Mandamus compelling the 1st and 2nd Respondents to furnish the Applicant with certified true copies of all the Asset Declaration Forms of Mr. Peter Obi Gregory that he submitted to the 1st and 2nd Respondents, as captured in the Applicant’s letters of 31st August, 2026 and 8th October, 2026. “An order of Mandamus compelling the 1st and 2nd Respondents to furnish the Applicant with certified true copies of all the documents attached to the Asset Declaration Forms of Peter Obi Gregory, which he submitted to the 1st and 2nd Respondents in 2006 and 2014, prior to when he was sworn in as Governor of Anambra State and when he left office as Governor of Anambra State in 2014. “An order of Mandamus compelling the 3rd and 4th Respondents to forthwith set out terms and conditions to guide the public on how to apply for disclosure of information from asset declaration forms deposited with the Respondents.” Likewise, he seeks “an order of court pursuant to section 25 of the Freedom of Information Act, 2011 directing the disclosure of the requested information where this Honourable Court finds that the Respondents are not authorized to deny access, having no reasonable grounds for denying access, or that the public interest in disclosure outweighs the interest served by withholding it.” Meanwhile, no date has been fixed for the hearing of the matter. title: Australia unveils secretive Ghost Shark underwater drone payloads
body: CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — Australian military officials have been furtive about how they will use Anduril-developed Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicles – or XLAUVs. However, they recently lifted the lid on some payloads the Royal Australian Navy is fielding. In an official unveiling at Anduril Australia’s manufacturing center in Sydney on Oct. 19, three Ghost Shark payloads were revealed. One entailed sea mines, another was a swarm of Altius-600 loitering munitions, and the third was logistics supply caches. In other words: Two of the three payloads comprise kinetic effectors to give the Ghost Shark greater bite. This means a single XLAUV can clandestinely deploy a dozen sea mines, perhaps in maritime chokepoints during a conflict. Meanwhile, Anduril’s Altius weapons can perform both surveillance and strike. Regarding the supply caches, an official said, “Let’s just say, people can use their imagination about the sort of forces that would use these on deployment.” The Department of Defence said in a press release: “The modular design of these platforms allows them to operate a range of different payloads, customized to the required mission.” Other payloads are being developed for the Ghost Shark, likely involving lightweight and heavyweight torpedoes, as well as electronic warfare. Ghost Sharks can deploy from shipping containers, off the stern of relatively small ships or from wharves, Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy explained. “It places question marks in adversaries’ minds,” he said. With Australia having to wait years for nuclear-powered submarines to arrive, autonomous underwater systems like the Ghost Shark can fill capability gaps as six aging Collins-class diesel-electric submarines continue to plod along. Anduril Australia opened its factory less than a year ago, and “Ghost Sharks capable of a range of complex missions operating far from our shores are now rolling off the line at an increasing rate into the hands of the Australian navy,” Conroy said. Canberra is spending A$1.7 billion (US$1.2 billion) on its fleet of Ghost Sharks. This amounts to “dozens and dozens” of XLAUVs, but Australia is not saying how many exactly. The Royal Australian Navy is also fielding the smaller Speartooth XLAUV from Australian firm C2 Robotics. Navy Chief Vice Adm. Matt Buckley said: “In terms of our platforms themselves, of course they must continue to evolve, and the evolution of modular payloads that we can fit to uncrewed vessels like the Ghost Shark … creates enormous flexibility for us and allows us to adapt these systems to future missions and future requirements.” He added: “Our purpose is clear – we need to deliver capability at the speed of relevance, strengthen our ability to conduct undersea warfare and seabed operations, contribute to sea denial and help protect our critical undersea infrastructure.” The Ghost Shark and its payloads have participated in the past few Maritime Big Play Pacific events, including one in San Diego in October. The first Ghost Shark was handed over to the Australian Navy for testing and acceptance in early 2026.

title: Drones attack Samara oil pumping station in Russia – media
body:
That is according to the Telegram channel Astra , Ukrinform reports.
"The Samara LPDS near the settlement of Prosvet was likely attacked: black smoke is rising from the direction of one of Europe's largest tank farms," the report said.
The Samara LPDS is a major critical infrastructure facility in Russia's main oil pipeline transportation system, located in the Samara region. Local authorities have not officially reported an attack on the facility, but residents confirmed hearing explosions and seeing a column of smoke rising from the direction of the station.
Overnight, Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a drone attack without specifying the locations: "An attack by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on our territory is being repelled. Air defense systems and mobile fire groups are operating."
A photograph sent to Astra by readers also shows smoke rising from the direction of the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station. The image was verified by an Astra OSINT analyst, who established that it was taken from the New Bridge in Samara.
The facility is one of Europe's largest tank farms. The station has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of more than 1.6 million cubic meters of oil.
The facility has been attacked several times before in October. Strikes and large-scale fires were recorded on October 2, 7, 10 and 11, 2026. In particular, the destruction of four RVS-50000 storage tanks and a major fire at the station were confirmed on October 7.

title: Kazakhstan’s Samodelkina Finishes Fifth at Skate Canada Grand Prix
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina finished fifth at the Skate Canada Grand Prix, scoring a total of 206.89 points across the short and free programs. Sofya Samodelkina. Photo credit: NOC. Samodelkina earned 71.84 points for her short program and 135.05 for her free skate, securing a place in the top five among 12 competitors. Japan’s Mao Shimada won the event with 235.44 points, followed by Estonia’s Nina Petrykina with 221.07. American Isabeau Levito took third place with 212.22, while Japan’s Saki Miyake finished fourth with 210.09. Samodelkina, 19, has been training in the United States since 2025 under renowned coach Rafael Arutyunyan. She won bronze at the Denis Ten Memorial in Almaty earlier this season. In a recent online meeting with Kazakh journalists, Samodelkina said her daily routine largely revolves around training, which typically takes six to seven hours a day, including three to three and a half hours on the ice, with the remaining time devoted to physical conditioning, running and walking, reported the Kazinform news agency. She said Arutyunyan’s experience and attention to detail have changed her understanding of figure skating, including how seemingly small technical issues can affect a jump. According to Samodelkina, one of the defining features of his coaching is his ability to identify details other coaches might overlook. “You can skate a program perfectly cleanly, and he will point out three things that need to be improved completely. So when a coach like that says ‘well done,’ it means you really have done well,” she said. Samodelkina also cited American figure skater Nathan Chen, the 2022 Olympic champion and another of Arutyunyan’s students, as an example of the coach’s influence. “He worked with Rafael Vladimirovich for 12 years, and I don’t have that much time anymore. Rafael Vladimirovich always says: he learned this in 12 years, and your task is to learn it in two years, otherwise you won’t make it in time,” she said. Samodelkina said she hopes to continue competing through the 2030 Winter Olympics. “I will definitely keep skating for another four years, and then we’ll see,” she said. Learning Kazakh and staying connected to home Despite her demanding schedule in California, Samodelkina said returning to Kazakhstan gives her an opportunity to relax, spend time with loved ones and feel at home. She described California primarily as a place for training, with much of her routine limited to travelling to the rink, practising and returning home. The skater said she has seen little of California during her two years there because of her training commitments. She usually spends time at home only between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. and rarely gets the chance to go out with friends. Samodelkina is also studying Kazakh through online lessons. She said representing Kazakhstan at international competitions and carrying the country’s flag have encouraged her to learn more about its language and culture. Learning the language has not always been easy, she acknowledged, particularly because of differences in pronunciation and sounds that do not exist in Russian. Nevertheless, she continues to study and enjoys using Kazakh to greet supporters and thank them for their encouragement. Following the Grand Prix events, Samodelkina is expected to return to Kazakhstan to perform in the ice show “Alice in Wonderland on Ice” in Almaty on Dec. 26. She may also compete at the Four Continents Figure Skating Championships, scheduled to take place in Almaty in February 2027. title: Rafale M Conducts Maiden Trials onboard Indian Aircraft Carrier INS Vikrant
body: The maiden landing of the French Rafale M fighter on INS Vikrant occurred on October 29, 2026. The landing was successful in the maiden attempt and marks the first steps towards operationalisation of the aircraft in the Indian Navy. The Indian Ministry of Defence had signed a $7.5 billion deal in April 2025 to procure 26 Dassault Rafale for the Indian Navy. This includes 22 Rafale M fighters and four Rafale DH trainer aircraft. The four twin seat trainers are not carrier capable since the Marine version does not have a twin seat trainer. Deliveries are scheduled to commence in 2029. A Rafale M equipped with the India-specific modifications was to be readied for trials in 2026. By mid-October, a Rafale aircraft was spotted flying near INS Hansa in Goa, which also hosts India’s Shore Based Test Facility (SBTF) for testing carrier-borne aircraft. After SBTF tests, the carrier operation was attempted on India’s indigenous aircraft carrier Vikrant . The specific aircraft being tested is understood to be from the Marine Nationale fleet. Rafale M landing on INS Vikrant . Indian Navy photo Naval News understands that the fleet will feature detachable missile rails at the tip of the wings. This was a core concern since the delta wings of the Rafale M are not foldable and the wingspan exceeds the dimensions of the aircraft elevators onboard INS Vikrant . It is being reported that some small modifications are required for the elevators and some specialised systems are being installed to accommodate the fighters. Similar modifications will be required for INS Vikramaditya as well in order to operate the Rafale M. With the development proposal for a Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF) not seeing progress, the possibility of the Navy opting for further Rafale Marine aircraft in the future cannot be ruled out. The stated requirement for fighters, split between INS Vikrant and Vikramaditya , was 57 before it was trimmed to 26. Rafale M and Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet were the competitors to complement and replace the MiG-29K/KUB fighters currently used by the two carriers. The Rafale M was chosen after both fighters underwent extensive trials in the SBTF in 2022. The choice of Rafale allows commonality with the Indian Air Force (IAF) inventory of 36 aircraft. IAF is expected to order 114 more Rafales, 90 of which will be made in India. Any additional Rafale M ordered can also be expected to be Made in India. The Rafale M procurement agreement also necessitates Transfer of Technology for integration of indigenous weapons in India. Dassault had also agreed to set up of a fuselage production facility which is being developed by Tata Advanced Systems with a capacity of two fuselages each month from FY2028. It will cater to global requirements as well. Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul facilities are being established by Dassault for airframe support and Safran for the M88 engines. The Rafale M agreement has thus placed India in the global supply chain of the Rafale. TEDBF as well as LCA (Navy) were part of the vision document Technology Perspective Capability Roadmap ( TPCR) 2025 . Naval News had reported earlier that the induction of the LCA (Navy) has been sought by many, including sections within the Navy, due to its suitability as a trainer aircraft for carrier-borne fighters. The LCA Navy prototypes have conducted multiple trials onboard both aircraft carriers in recent years. An LCA Navy fighter flies over INS Vikrant . Indian Navy picture. title: Russia-friendly Yotova wins Bulgaria's presidential runoff
body:
Bulgaria's acting president, Iliana Yotova, has secured a decisive victory in the second round of the country's presidential election, the Bulgarian National Television (BNT) reported on Nov. 2, citing the central election commission.
Yotova, who opposes military aid for Ukraine and calls for a dialogue with Moscow , won 57.58% of the Nov. 1 vote, with 99.95% of the polling station protocols processed .
The ticket of her pro-Ukraine, pro-Western opponent, former Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, lost with a significant margin, securing 39.47% of the votes.
Yotova had served as Bulgaria 's acting president since January, when her ally, a Kremlin-friendly then-president, Rumen Radev, resigned to lead his party to parliamentary election victory in April and secure the premiership.
The Balkan country's presidents serve five-year terms in what is mostly a ceremonial role, though they can appoint interim governments and veto laws. The veto can be overridden by a parliamentary majority.
Bulgaria, a NATO and EU country, lies at the eastern flank of both blocs and increasingly feels the spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war as alleged Russian drones hit several merchant vessels near its coast in October.
"This is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted," Gyurov said , conceding defeat.
Yotova declared her victory after initial projections showed her in the lead, saying her message had centered around "incomes, peace, and the challenges that lie ahead."
"Congratulations to (Iliana Yotova) on her victory in the presidential elections," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"From security and defense to our competitiveness and energy independence, I look forward to continuing our joint work."
The runoff was marked by a low turnout of about 27-29%, only a few percentage points higher than the record low of 23% in the first round held on Oct. 25.
Yotova's victory signals a strengthening of Radev's Ukraine-skeptic foreign policy. The Bulgarian prime minister has ended military support for Kyiv from Bulgarian army stocks and exited the French- and U.K.-led Coalition of the Willing.
The current Sofia leadership has also been reluctant to openly blame Russia for recent drone attacks on merchant vessels near the Bulgarian coast, even as Kyiv pointed fingers at Moscow.

title: Russia’s Admiral Golovko frigate sets sail for long-distance deployment — Northern Fleet
body:
MOSCOW, 2 November. /TASS/. The Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet frigate Admiral Golovko, carrying Zircon hypersonic missiles, has set out on a long-distance deployment and is heading for the Atlantic, the fleet’s press service reported.
"The Northern Fleet frigate Admiral Golovko has left the roadstead of Severomorsk and set out on a long-distance deployment, heading for the Atlantic," the press service said.
According to the press service, over the next few months the frigate’s crew will carry out long-distance deployment tasks in various areas of the world’s ocean, primarily flag-showing and ensuring a naval presence in operationally important areas of the distant ocean zone.
"The crew is fully prepared to carry out the assigned mission. The ship has undergone a full course of preparation and is ready for missions in the distant ocean zone," emphasized Captain 1st Rank Andrey Slavin, commander of the Admiral Golovko frigate.
Before setting sail from the Northern Fleet’s main base in Severomorsk, a ceremonial gathering was held on board the frigate, during which Captain 1st Rank Maxim Yemelyanenko, deputy commander of the missile ship force, addressed the sailors, wishing them success in carrying out their assigned tasks.
The Admiral Golovko is one of the newest Project 22350 frigates, which was commissioned into the Navy on 25 December 2023. It is equipped with long-range precision-guided missiles, including Zircon hypersonic missiles.
Between 2024 and 2025, it took part on numerous occasions in various Russian Navy exercises involving the practical use of all types of weaponry. In 2025, the frigate embarked on its first long-distance deployment and took part in the Russian-Egyptian Friendship Bridge 2025 exercise, and, for the first time in the history of the Russian Navy, together with the frigate Admiral Gorshkov, launched hypersonic missiles against a maritime target in the Mediterranean Sea during the exercise.

title: Virtual Reality series' production begins in Arkhangelsk
body:
ARKHANGELSK, November 2. /TASS/. Filming of the 15 Miles of Light Virtual Reality (VR) series, telling five stories of the northern seas, lighthouses and expeditions, began in the Arkhangelsk Region. The project's scripts, filed from different regions and even countries, were selected in a competition, the project's leader Tamara Statikova told TASS.
"Right now, the project is approaching the filming - we are looking forward to a few busy days at the theater, museum and educational venues in Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk: the Arkhangelsk Viktor Panov Youth Theater, the Severodvinsk Drama Theater, the Arkhangelsk College of Culture and Art, and the Northern Maritime Museum. We are working closely with the Arkhangelsk branch of the Russian Theater Society, which supports the project and helps organize the filming process," the project's leader said.
Experts of the Northern Maritime Museum have selected five true stories about events that happened at lighthouses and at sea. "The Tragedy at the Lighthouse" is a story about how caretakers at the Zhuzhmuy Lighthouse in the White Sea died in the winter of 1873. "The Navigator of Polar Seas" tells about one of the most important professions on any ship - about those responsible for passage planning. The third topic, "Dead Man's Chest," offers a look at the history of a particular person through marine life and objects. "The Race for the Arctic. Georgy Sedov" invites the audience to speculate about the author of the expedition to the North Pole. "Why the Svyatogor Was Sunk" is a story about the most powerful icebreaker of the early 20th century.
Each of the five stories will be different from others. In one episode, the viewer will take the place of Georgy Sedov and will hear uncomfortable questions about his expedition. Another episode will be a film about a tragedy at the lighthouse: the viewer will see how the expert commission that arrived at the scene discovered the dead team. "It is important for us not just to retell historical events, but to find ways of telling stories so that the viewer could have a feeling of being inside the event," the project's leader added.
According to her, The 15 Miles of Light is also a training program for the regional film industry and an opportunity for local residents to gain new skills. "We want students to gain real production skills, learn modern technologies and try professions that are in demand in the film industry. One of important objectives that the project has is to train regional specialists, expand their competencies and create conditions for creative industries' development in the North," she said. "We hope the gained experience would not to remain inside one laboratory, we hope it will become the basis for new creative teams and projects in the Arkhangelsk Region."
The VR series will become part of the Northern Maritime Museum's permanent exhibition. Actors from the Arkhangelsk Lomonosov Drama Theater, the Viktor Panov Youth Theater, and the Severodvinsk Drama Theater will take part in the film's episodes.

title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
body: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. TL;DR Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b , with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported). Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results. Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it. What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology? It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. Here are the five jobs: Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models. Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage. Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API. Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. How does Auto Ontology work? The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){var d=e.data;if(d&&d.id==="mtp-aoe-2611"&&d.mtpEmbedHeight){var f=document.getElementById("mtp-aoe-frame");if(f)f.style.height=d.mtpEmbedHeight+"px";}}); What does the MCP server expose? The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. ask_question returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. check_readiness confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist. There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions. How is it benchmarked? NVIDIA ships a separate harness, auto-ontology-eval . It runs 2 arms in NeMo Gym: a schema-only LLM control and the ontology-grounded agent. Scoring is deterministic execution match, with no LLM judge. Bundled datasets include BIRD Dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) and Mini-Dev (500 questions). FDABench-Lite adds 169 questions, and BEAVER defaults to a 100-question sample. The harness repo adds 2 limitations. Optional few-shot exemplars and value anchors go to the ontology arm only. A delta measured with them covers those inputs, not grounding alone. Its tested configuration also routes both arms through a Claude model on NVIDIA’s inference gateway. How does it compare with other semantic layers? Feature NVIDIA Auto Ontology Wren AI Cube Core dbt MetricFlow License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 core (open core) Apache 2.0 backend, MIT client Apache 2.0 (v0.209.0+) How the layer is built Generated from metadata, then certified Agent-assisted context files in Git Defined in code Defined in code in a dbt project Agent interface MCP, CLI, REST API MCP, CLI, SDKs SQL, REST, GraphQL APIs Python library and CLI Data sources Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, DuckDB 22+ All SQL data sources Via dbt adapters Default models Nemotron via NVIDIA NIM Not disclosed Not applicable Not applicable Deployment and availability Local setup is docker compose up -d --build after filling in .env . Kubernetes users get a Helm chart and a DEPLOYMENT.md guide. NVIDIA team also publishes the backend as an NGC container . An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com covers the default models. Key Takeaways Auto Ontology generates a starting semantic layer from enterprise metadata. Agents query it through 9 read-only MCP tools, plus CLI and API. NVIDIA reports 90% faster ontology creation in its own testing. No text-to-SQL accuracy scores are published yet. Defaults to Nemotron on NIM, but accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Check out the GitHub repo , the eval harness and the MCP docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter .
