title: UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
body:
FILE - A Sahrawi refugee boy stands in the shadow in the Boujdour refugee camp, Oct. 11, 2021. Bernat Armangue/AP hide caption
CASABLANCA, Morocco — The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory's future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa's northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
"This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period," Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. "A smaller team reporting to the United Nations' Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.
Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force's mandate.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute.''
The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision.'' The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the ''excessive bias'' of the U.S. draft resolution.
The U.N. classifies Western Sahara as a "non-self-governing territory," while critics of Morocco's control describe it as Africa's last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the "free zone" that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.
After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.
Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco's foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco's diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.
The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.
A U.N.-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.
The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain's colonial census to determine voter eligibility.
Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.
As the mission ends, the U.N. secretary-general ''calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara,'' Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."
The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the U.N. said last month.
Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.

title: Elbit Systems Awarded Approximately $170 Million Contract to Establish and Operate an Advanced Training and Simulation Center for the IDF Artillery Corps
body:
Haifa, Israel. Elbit Systems Ltd. announced on November 2, 2026 that it was awarded a contract valued at approximately $170 million by the Israel Ministry of Defense (IMOD) to establish and operate an advanced training and simulation center for the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) Artillery Corps. The contract will be performed over a period of 15 years.



The new center is intended to support the operational integration of the “ROEM” (SIGMA) self-propelled artillery system and the “LAHAV” (PULS™) precision rocket launcher system into the IDF Artillery Corps.

Under the contract, Elbit Systems will develop and deliver an advanced training infrastructure, including mission and driving simulators, training classrooms and dedicated facilities. The solution will feature simulation technologies, automation capabilities, AI-based functionalities and innovative driver training solutions. Elbit Systems will also provide training, maintenance and support services throughout the contract period.

The project is intended to enhance the operational readiness and proficiency of IDF artillery personnel, shorten qualification and training timelines, and improve training efficiency while reducing resource consumption and wear on operational platforms.



Boaz Cohen, General Manager of Elbit Systems Land & Armaments: "We are proud to support the IDF Artillery Corps with advanced training and simulation solutions for the ROEM and LAHAV systems, key components of the IDF’s next-generation land firepower array. This project further demonstrates Elbit Systems’ ability to deliver integrated and networked training solutions that combine advanced infrastructure, immersive simulation technologies and long-term partnership, enabling forces to maximize the operational potential of these advanced platforms."

title: Kwara United throw away lead in 2-1 defeat to Bendel Insurance
body: Kwara United FC suffered a disappointing 2-1 defeat to visiting Bendel Insurance in their NPFL Matchday 11 encounter at the Rashidi Yekini Mainbowl of the George Innih Stadium, Ilorin, on Sunday. Both sides began the encounter cautiously, adopting a measured approach as they sought to establish control and create scoring opportunities. Aliyu Ferinyaro and Uche Jaguar came close to breaking the deadlock for the Harmony Boys in the first half, but their efforts were thwarted by the resilient defensive line of the Benin Arsenal. Kwara United were forced into an early substitution in the 17th minute when Anthony Nnamdi, who sustained a knock, was replaced by Mighty Emmanuel. 2027: God has granted my request to continue – Tinubu Fresh woes for pupils in Niger In spite of the efforts of both teams, the first half ended goalless. The hosts returned from the break with renewed determination and were rewarded in the 49th minute when Stephen Gideon put Kwara United ahead. Ferinyaro unleashed a shot that was parried by the Bendel Insurance goalkeeper, allowing Gideon to react quickly and slot home the rebound. However, the celebrations were short-lived as Kayode Oke restored parity for the visitors in the 52nd minute, capitalising on a poorly marked loose ball. Bendel Insurance completed their comeback just three minutes later, with Chinedu Nwosu scoring in the 55th minute to hand the Benin-based side a 2-1 lead. Kwara United subsequently intensified their efforts to find an equaliser, with further tactical substitutions introduced to change the course of the game. title: OPEC+ Countries Agree to Keep Oil Production Levels Unchanged in December
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Seven OPEC+ countries, including Kazakhstan, have agreed to maintain oil production levels in December 2026 at the levels set for September, according to a statement published by the organization. Photo credit: ixbroker.com Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman held an online meeting on Nov. 1 to review developments in the global oil market and its outlook. The seven countries had previously announced additional voluntary production adjustments in April and November 2023. Following the meeting, participants agreed to maintain their September 2026 production levels for December, according to the table published in the organization’s statement. The countries also reaffirmed their commitment to fully comply with the terms of the Declaration of Cooperation, which underpins coordination among OPEC+ members. The seven countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review global oil market conditions. Their next meeting is scheduled for Nov. 29. The post OPEC+ Countries Agree to Keep Oil Production Levels Unchanged in December appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Military, Police and civilian peacekeepers share how peace is more sustainable when we invest in women
body:
By R Anil Kumar

UN, Nov 1, 2026. The meaningful participation of women across all levels of UN peacekeeping is integral to more inclusive and effective peace operations. From community-facing work to strategic leadership, building lasting peace hinges on investing in women peacekeepers.



Women are deployed as police, military and civilian personnel within peacekeeping missions. They work across all areas, from the protection of civilians to political and civil affairs, planning, logistics or strategic communications.

As of June 2026, women represented 33 per cent of civilian personnel and 28 per cent of Heads and Deputy Heads of Mission in United Nations peacekeeping missions. Through the Uniformed Gender Parity Strategy, the participation of uniformed women in peacekeeping operations has doubled, from less than 5% in 2018 to more than 10% in 2026.

In a recent panel discussion held on the eve of the UN General Assembly’s High Level Week, Colonel Gissel Sosa, Lieutenant Colonel Glory Athumani Mkwizu and McCall Carter reflected on how, in their experience under the blue flag, women peacekeepers had “the power to empower”.

International Peace Day 2026 discussion on “Women Peacekeepers: 

"[Women] do the same task as men . We can do the same activities, like community policing, in operations, in command, or in capacity building and development,” said Colonel Gissel Sosa, Chief of the Mission Management and Support Section (MMSS) in the UN Police Division. “But the difference is in how the community trusts us—women are very important in the field. The visibility of policewomen, of course, that gives a different perspective for communities."

Colonel Sosa discusses gender issues with Community representatives at the Jean Marie Vincent internally displaced persons site in the Haitian capital, Port au Prince. Colonel Gissel Sosa

The Uruguayan peacekeeper also highlighted the importance of teaching men and boys the value of women in policing. Reflecting on her time in Haiti where she was deployed in 2011 and 2012, Colonel Sosa stressed that “I think that it's very important that the presence of policewomen in those fields and, of course that, the visibility of women in the context is one important tool that we can give to our missions when we are deployed."

She also encouraged women to consider serving: “I think they need your expertise in the field and having the visibility of women police officers is really important and we have many proofs of that." she concluded.

Colonel Sosa engages with community members at an Internal Displaced Persons site in Croix-des-Bouquets, Haiti. Colonel Gissel Sosa

In her role as Peacekeeping Training Coordinator at the Tanzania Peacekeeping Training Centre, Lieutenant Colonel Glory Athumani Mkwizu knows the importance of including women not just because of quotas, but also as equal stakeholders at the table. “Women shouldn't only be taken as the beneficials of peace but rather as partners in peace processes and peacebuilding,” she said.

"Our presence is very crucial because most of the victims of conflict are women, children and girls they are more comfortable when they see us, to access us." said Lt Col Mkwizu who currently serves with the Office of Military Affairs.

Throughout her career with the Tanzania Peoples Defence Forces, Lt Col Mkwizu observed that "[women] feel more free to talk to us and they see women as easy communicators understanding them and less threatening. That's why we're really encouraging the presence of female in peacekeeping operations."

Lieutenant Colonel Glory Athumani Mkwizu (right) speaking at the “Women Peacekeepers: The Power to Empower” event at the SDG Media Zone. Stephanie Lemesianou/ UN Peacekeeping

A lawyer and rule of law professional with more than 15 years of experience across the UN system, McCall Carter serves as a Judicial Affairs Officer with the Justice and Corrections Service in the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office at UN Headquarters. Before that, she spent 12 years working in different legal and rule of law capacities, including as a civilian peacekeeper, in the Netherlands, Tanzania, Liberia and most recently with the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS).

McCall stressed “the importance of the visible presence of women peacekeepers.” She ensured that the audience heard her clearly, stating “my colleagues have been told repeatedly by local women that seeing female peacekeepers and national justice personnel working alongside the men made them believe that they have the ability to pursue professional roles, leadership positions and independent futures themselves."

McCall Carter (middle) observes a Joint Special Mobile Court hearing in Gette, Western Bahr el Ghazal State, July 2022. McCall Carter

Closing the panel discussion, McCall shared the importance of all components working together for lasting peace: "Peace cannot come from military or police force alone. The work that civilian peacekeepers and women civilian peacekeepers in particular do is really crucial to ending conflict and helping countries transition from conflict to peace."

McCall Carter (left) poses with a state official and UNMISS Civil Affairs colleague on the eve of a pre-migration conference in Yirol, South Sudan, November 2019. McCall Carter

Women peacekeepers help build trust, expand community engagement and empower local women to shape peace and political processes. Ensuring their safety, equal opportunities and professional advancement is not just a matter of equity, it is a prerequisite for more effective and sustainable peace.

title: At Least 19 Killed As Venezuela Army Attacks Colombian Rebel Camp
body: At least 19 people were killed in the Venezuelan army’s recent attack on a Colombian guerrilla group’s camp inside Venezuela, an NGO and source close to the operation said Sunday. The FundaRedes NGO — which monitors rights violations in Venezuela’s border states — initially reported nine deaths in the attack early Friday morning in the western state of Apure. Juan Francisco Garcia, a coordinator with the group, told AFP on Sunday that “another 10 bodies” had been transported to the state capital San Fernando the day after the attack. The attack targeted a camp of the National Liberation Army, a Colombian guerrilla group known by its Spanish initials, ELN. Video shared by FundaRedes showed bodies lying on the ground, trees knocked down and the ruins of what appeared to be a campsite. A Venezuelan military source close to the operation, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the attack had been supported by US intelligence. “We had help from the CIA and the FBI. This was an order from the United States,” the source said. Requests for comment from the US State Department and Venezuelan government were not immediately answered. The strikes were carried out by drones and attack helicopters targeting the camp, which was located in a rural, forested area in the southwest of Apure, the military source said. The attack took the guerrillas by surprise — they had no time to react, the source said, noting that most of the people killed were Venezuelan nationals. ‘More Camps’ After the attack, bodies were initially transported to the town of Puerto Paez, which lies across a river from Colombia. “Several of the bodies were completely mangled. Even as they were being taken to San Fernando, they still smelled of burnt flesh,” a resident of Puerto Paez told AFP. Several armed groups engage in drug trafficking, illegal mining and smuggling along Venezuela and Colombia’s porous 2,200-kilometer (1,367-mile) border, including dissident members of the now-defunct FARC and the ELN. The ELN has been among the most powerful rebel groups in Latin America since the FARC guerrilla army signed a peace accord with the Bogota government in 2016. The military operation along the border may represent the latest shift in Venezuelan policy since the US ouster of Nicolas Maduro in January. Venezuela’s government has since been led by Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro’s former deputy who has won vocal support from US President Donald Trump for bending to his administration’s demands. Colombia has for years accused Venezuela’s leftist government of turning a blind eye to Colombian rebel groups in border areas. Human rights advocate and military affairs expert Rocio San Miguel said the Friday attack reflects a “change in doctrine” within the Venezuelan military. The military source told AFP that Venezuelan forces were “going to continue combing through the area because we believe there are more camps.” The operation also comes as Colombia’s newly elected hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, ramps up a violent crackdown on the ELN and drug trafficking groups in his country. Colombia has joined over a dozen other Latin American and Caribbean nations in a US-led regional effort to combat drug trafficking and organized crime across the region. AFP The post At Least 19 Killed As Venezuela Army Attacks Colombian Rebel Camp appeared first on Channels Television .

title: IN BRIEF: What is known about results of Bulgarian presidential election
body:
SOFIA, November 2. /TASS/. Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission has released the official vote count for the second round of the presidential election.
Presidential and vice-presidential candidates Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev received 57.581% of the vote, while Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev received 39.467%.
Yotova became the first female politician to be elected to the highest office in Bulgaria.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the election results.
- Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission has released the official vote count for the second round of the presidential election.
- According to the commission’s website, presidential and vice-presidential candidates Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev received 57.581% of the vote.
- More than 1,093,000 people voted for them.
- Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev trailed by more than 18%, receiving 39.467% of the vote.
- A total of 2.952% of voters (about 56,000 people) did not support either candidate.
- The vote count for the second round of the election is nearing completion, and the remaining 0.05% of ballots will not affect the final results.
- The official election results and voter turnout data will be presented by the Central Election Commission no later than November 4, following a re-verification.
- Yotova and Valchev will take office as Bulgaria’s president-elect and vice president-elect for a five-year term on January 22, 2027.
- According to polls, nearly 26.8% of eligible voters participated in the election.
- Voter turnout in the first round was 22.98%.
- The Bulgarian Interior Ministry reported that no serious violations were recorded during the election.
- Iliana Yotova thanked all Bulgarian voters who participated in the election, especially the Progressive Bulgaria party, the Bulgarian Socialist Party, the VMRO-Bulgarian National Movement, and other organizations that provided active support, particularly in the lead-up to the second round, which helped secure a significant victory.
- "I will be a worthy president," Yotova said.
- Bulgarian presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov conceded defeat in the second round of the presidential election.
- Prime Minister Rumen Radev, leader of the Progressive Bulgaria political party, congratulated Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev on their victory in the elections for the country’s president and vice president.
- According to him, "for us, these elections confirm that we are on the right track and encourage us to pursue even more active and decisive reforms."

title: Drones Target Russia’s Samara Oil Hub, Sparking Fire at Pipeline Facility
body:
Drones targeted Russia ’s Samara region early on Monday, Nov. 2, with a likely strike on the Samara Linear Production-Dispatch Station (LPDS) near the settlement of Prosvet, where a fire was reported.
OSINT accounts and Telegram channels reported the attack, sharing footage showing smoke rising from the facility. Kyiv Post could not independently verify the footage or confirm the extent of the damage.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Russian monitoring channels reported a drone threat in the region at around 3 a.m. local time. Some channels also said workers had been evacuated from several warehouse facilities in the city of Samara as a precaution.
By around 5 a.m., OSINT channels were reporting an attack on the LPDS. Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that air defenses and mobile fire groups were responding to a drone attack but did not identify the locations targeted.
“There is a repulse of the attack of the Armed Forces on our territory. Air defense, mobile fire groups are working,” he wrote.
The Russian outlet Astra reported that smoke was visible near the station and cited local residents who said they had heard explosions. Astra said an image submitted by its readers showing the smoke had been verified by its OSINT analyst and was taken from Samara’s New Bridge.
Separately, the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported explosions in Russian-occupied Luhansk early on Monday, Nov. 2.
At around 3:18 a.m., the channel said drones were attacking the city. It later reported that a local telecommunications company had previously been targeted, but provided no further details.
The Samara LPDS is a major facility in Russia’s oil pipeline network, handling the receipt, storage and onward transportation of crude oil. According to Astra, it has 71 storage tanks with a combined capacity of more than 1.6 million cubic meters (56 million cubic feet), making it one of Europe’s largest tank farms.
The facility was reportedly targeted several times in October 2026, with strikes and fires reported on Oct. 2, 7, 10, and 11. Astra said four RVS-50000 storage tanks were destroyed in the Oct. 7 attack, which also caused a large fire.
The latest reported strike would mark another attack on the facility within a month.
Russia’s defense ministry said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 212 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight.
According to the ministry, the drones were downed over 17 Russian regions, including Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Voronezh, Pskov, Oryol, Lipetsk, Saratov, Samara, Ryazan, Tambov, and Rostov, as well as the Moscow region and Krasnodar region.
The ministry also claimed interceptions over Russian-occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
Ukraine has not commented on its alleged involvement in the attacks.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: MURIC Demands Suspension of Law School Exams Over Hijab Ban, Threatens Protest
body: The Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) has called for the suspension of examinations at all Nigerian Law School campuses following alleged harassment, intimidation and exclusion of female Muslim students wearing hijab from examination halls. The Islamic human rights organisation also demanded an investigation into the incidents, which reportedly occurred during the final examinations for candidates seeking admission to the Nigerian Bar on Saturday, October 31, 2026. MURIC warned that it would mobilise parents, Muslim youths and other stakeholders for peaceful protests across Law School campuses nationwide if its demands were not met. The Nigerian Law School had not responded to the allegations in the statement at the time of writing. 2027: God has granted my request to continue – Tinubu Turn Nigeria’s diversity into prosperity, Tinubu tells citizens The organisation’s position was contained in a press statement issued on Sunday by its Founder and Executive Director, Professor Ishaq Akintola. According to Akintola, several hijab-wearing female candidates were allegedly prevented from entering examination halls in different parts of the country because of their religious attire. He said some candidates were reportedly made to stand outside examination halls for about an hour and were only allowed to enter after removing their hijabs. “There was harassment and intimidation of hijab-wearing female Muslim students in some Law School examination halls across the country yesterday, Saturday, October 31, 2026,” Akintola said. “Hijabites who came hoping to sit for their call-to-bar final examinations were disallowed from entering the examination halls. In some places, they were forced to remain standing outside for about one hour until they removed their hijabs before they were allowed to enter and start the examination.” The MURIC director said the organisation received numerous telephone calls, text messages and online messages from distressed candidates, their parents and concerned Muslims during the incidents. “While this was going on, our office was inundated with telephone calls, text messages and chats. We heard the cries of traumatised candidates, the lamentations of distressed parents hundreds of kilometres away from the examination centres and the agitation of concerned Muslims around the country,” he said. Describing the alleged incidents as an infringement on the candidates’ rights, Akintola said the organisation strongly condemned what it considered an unjustifiable disruption of their educational and professional pursuits. “MURIC strongly condemns the wanton disruption of the lawful educational pursuit of innocent Muslim ladies. It is crude, irrational and sadistic,” he said. The organisation expressed particular concern that “it is the Law School, the bastion of law education and the centre of legal excellence, that is involved in the denigration of court pronouncements.” He cited Section 38(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, which guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to manifest and propagate religious beliefs. MURIC also referenced the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Lagos State Government & Ors v. Asiyat Abdulkareem, which it said affirmed that banning or restricting the hijab amounted to discrimination. The organisation further argued that the alleged treatment of the candidates violated Section 42 of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom from discrimination. Akintola also cited Section 34(1)(a), which protects the dignity of the human person and prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. “The forceful undressing of our daughters at Law School examination centres in Nigeria is an open contravention of Section 34(a), which upholds the dignity of the human person by declaring authoritatively, unequivocally and emphatically that no person shall be subject to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment,” he said.

title: Blaize GSP [Graph Streaming Processor] Streams AI Graphs at the Edge
body:
Blaize built its Graph Streaming Processor around a deceptively simple insight: Neural networks are graphs, so run them as graphs. The GSP’s on-chip hardware scheduler streams the computational graph depth-first through 16 cores, keeping intermediate data in cache rather than round-tripping to external DRAM. The result is 16 TOPS at 7 W on Samsung 14 nm—and a software stack that hides all of that complexity from the developer. The GSP2, targeting 1,600 TOPS on 5 nm for automotive ADAS, extends the same architecture to a far larger stage.
Blaize, founded in 2011 in El Dorado Hills, California—originally as ThinCI—spent nearly a decade developing a processor architecture it calls the Graph Streaming Processor, or GSP. The commercial product, code-named El Cano, arrived in 2020 on Samsung 14 nm. It was Blaize’s second silicon effort; a 28 nm test chip preceded it in 2017, providing the memory characterization data that shaped the production design.
The GSP’s defining characteristic is graph-native execution. Conventional AI accelerators receive a neural network, decompose it into matrix operations, and execute those operations sequentially or in batches—a process that requires repeatedly staging intermediate results through external DRAM. The GSP treats the neural network as what it actually is: a directed graph. The hardware scheduler reads a metamap of the computational graph generated at compile time by the NetDeploy tool, then distributes subtasks across the 16 cores autonomously, depth-first.
Depth-first scheduling means that as soon as a layer produces intermediate results, the next layer begins consuming them —from cache, not from DRAM. Intermediate activations never leave the chip. The 4 Mb on-chip memory hierarchy, structured as a single unified address space, holds the working data for the active graph traversal. The cores themselves never manage scheduling; the scheduler holds that authority entirely. This inversion—schedulers in charge, cores as execution resources—is the central architectural decision that distinguishes the GSP from VLIW and GPU compute models.
Each of the 16 cores is an array of 4-bit load-store execution units that combine at runtime to handle operations from INT8 up to FP16. A 2D register file with a contiguous address space feeds data to execution pipelines. The hardware supports task-level, thread-level, data-level, and instruction-level parallelism simultaneously, allowing multiple independent graphs or graph segments to run concurrently across the chip.
Figure 1. The GSP processor block diagram. (Source: Blaize)
The architecture also deliberately conceals microarchitectural detail from software. The SIMD vector width, pipeline depth, and core granularity do not surface to the programmer. NetDeploy handles quantization, graph optimization, and partitioning—including cascading a single model across multiple chips or cards using seven available scheduling mechanisms. A model compiled for one GSP configuration requires no code changes to run on a scaled-out multi-card deployment.
El Cano delivers 16 TOPS at INT8, 32 TOPS at INT4, and 2 TOPS at FP64, all within a 7 W TDP. Samsung 14 nm fabrication keeps die cost low—Blaize’s VP of Strategic Business Development Richard Terrill noted at launch that the chip has “not lots of on-chip memory,” deliberately keeping die area and cost accessible for industrial and aftermarket automotive deployments.
Three hardware products build on El Cano. The P1600 SoM (System on Module) integrates 16 GSP cores with dual Arm Cortex-A53 CPUs, H.264/H.265 video encode and decode, and camera sensor interfaces. The X1600E PCIe card targets edge server deployments at $299. The X1600P PCIe card targets higher-throughput installations at $999. All three run the Blaize AI Software Suite.
The software stack operates at two levels. Blaize AI Studio provides a no-code visual interface for building and deploying AI applications—targeted at system integrators and domain experts who are not ML engineers. Picasso SDK provides full OpenCL C++ access for developers who need direct hardware control. NetDeploy sits underneath both, handling model conversion from TensorFlow and other frameworks, quantization-aware optimization, and multi-device graph partitioning.
El Cano targets industrial edge AI, smart cameras, and automotive prototyping in commercial grade. The automotive production part follows as the GSP2—Blaize’s next-generation SoC extending the graph-streaming architecture to Samsung 5 nm, targeting 1,600 TOPS for ADAS sensor fusion and perception. Blaize’s 2025 10-K filing places GSP2 production availability no earlier than 2028. DENSO and Mercedes-Benz have collectively paid $32 million in engineering fees against anticipated GSP2 delivery, signaling Tier 1 automotive intent.
Blaize went public in January 2025 via SPAC merger as Blaize Holdings on Nasdaq (BZAI), at a $1.2 billion valuation. The 2025 10-K flagged going-concern doubt, with a $103.8 million operating loss driven heavily by low-margin third-party GPU hardware resale. GSP2’s production timeline and the company’s ability to fund that roadmap represent the central financial risk for enterprise and automotive customers evaluating Blaize as a long-term silicon partner.
El Cano’s industrial-grade process qualification and multi-sensor support make it practical for deployment environments that consumer-grade edge silicon cannot handle. Current application areas include surround-view automotive ADAS at Level 2+, retail analytics and loss prevention, industrial inspection on factory lines, and smart city camera systems. The GSP’s ability to run multiple independent neural networks simultaneously on one chip—processing camera, radar, and lidar streams concurrently—makes it particularly relevant to sensor fusion workloads where a single-model accelerator forces sequential processing.
Blaize’s graph-streaming architecture solves a real problem—off-chip memory bandwidth as the binding constraint in edge AI inference—with a hardware scheduler approach that keeps intermediate data on-chip and hides microarchitectural complexity from software developers. El Cano validated that approach in production silicon at 7 W. The gap between El Cano’s 16 TOPS and GSP2’s 1,600 TOPS target reflects the full ambition of the automotive ADAS opportunity Blaize is pursuing. Whether the company’s financial position supports the development cycle that gap requires is the open question for customers making long-cycle design commitments now.
The GSP architecture is technically differentiated—graph-native scheduling with depth-first execution and unified on-chip memory genuinely reduces the DRAM bandwidth problem that constrains most edge AI accelerators. El Cano proved it works. The risk is entirely financial: a $103.8 million operating loss, a 2028 GSP2 timeline, and going-concern language in the 10-K create real supplier continuity risk for automotive programs with five-year design cycles.
The GSP’s graph-native execution model marks an inflection point in edge AI architecture thinking—the recognition that mapping neural networks onto matrix-multiply hardware wastes cycles on a representation mismatch, and that building the hardware around the graph eliminates that waste at the source. That inflection point is visible across the industry: dataflow and graph-native architectures from Blaize, Tenstorrent, and SambaNova all reflect the same conclusion. The question is no longer whether graph-native execution outperforms matrix-centric designs at the edge—it does. The question is which company survives to scale it.
The DENSO and Mercedes-Benz design win signals, and—critically—the financial risk assessment that any procurement team must factor into a long-cycle platform decision involving Blaize hardware.
Blaze’s GSP is one of the 152 AI processors in our AI Processor Tracking Service , which also lists performance and other specifications for 291 products.

title: INS Trishul docks in Greece to bolster maritime ties with Hellenic Navy
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan

New Delhi. Indian Naval Ship (INS) Trishul arrived at Souda Bay, Greece, on October 31 marking a key port call during its ongoing deployment to the Mediterranean Sea.



The visit is structured to deepen maritime cooperation and reinforce professional ties between the Indian Navy and the Hellenic Navy. During the port call, INS Trishul’s crew will engage in high-level discussions with senior officials from both the Hellenic Navy and the Indian Embassy in Athens, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Defence.



The itinerary features a broad range of joint engagements, including professional exchanges, cross-deck visits, and cultural exchanges. Additionally, the Indian naval personnel will tour facilities at Naval Support Activity (NSA) Souda Bay and the NATO Maritime Interdiction Operational Training Centre (NMIOTC).



As part of the visit’s ceremonial and commemorative events, the crew is scheduled to pay homage at the Souda Bay War Cemetery. The vessel will also host open-ship hours, allowing visitors to board and tour the warship during its stay in Greece.

title: Putin will not stop. Navalny's former ally warns Europe
body:
A ceasefire in Ukraine would not end Russia’s confrontation with Europe, warns Ivan Zhdanov, one of Alexei Navalny’s closest associates and former director of the Anti-Corruption Foundation. In an interview with Defence24.com, he discusses the divisions within the Russian opposition, Moscow’s calculations over negotiations with Ukraine, the Kremlin’s fear of another mobilisation and the growing threat of Russian attacks against European countries. He also explains why a future Russia must undergo fundamental political change rather than simply replace Vladimir Putin.
The Russian opposition reaches tens of millions of people through independent media, but remains divided over how to challenge the Kremlin. Zhdanov argues that Putin is exploiting high oil prices, political instability in Europe and Ukraine’s dependence on American assistance to prolong the war. He also warns that Russia could intensify sabotage and other attacks across Europe following a ceasefire, while stressing that Russian society still has the potential to influence the country’s political future.
Aleksander Olech, Defence24.com: How do you assess the current condition of the Russian opposition abroad? Is it still possible to speak about one opposition, or rather about several separate political environments?
Ivan Zhdanov: There is no single Russian opposition today, and I will not pretend that there is. Different opposition groups differ in both their audiences and their activities, from media work to human rights.
They also differ in how radical they are. There are those who call on people to go to the polls and use every legal opportunity. There are those who see this as playing by the Kremlin’s rules and support armed struggle. Nobody today knows a working recipe for defeating a modern dictatorship like Putin’s.
One can say for certain that we have an audience: the regular viewers of opposition YouTube channels alone number in the tens of millions. But nobody has the key that would turn viewers into people ready to act. Perhaps this is because, under repression, people in Russia cannot turn individual action into mass action. In these conditions, diversity remains fragmentation. But the potential for sudden change and mass protest is there: it lies in the millions of people in Russia who watch us every day, bypassing censorship.
Do you see any realistic possibility of creating a common minimum programme for the Russian opposition — perhaps even a kind of ten-point declaration defining what different groups can agree on despite their divisions?
On 20 February 2023, almost a year before his death, Alexei Navalny published his “15 theses of a Russian citizen who wishes his country well”. They include the demand to end the war, the recognition of Ukraine’s borders as defined in 1991, including Crimea, and compensation that Russia must pay Ukraine for the damage caused by the war. The main thing, of course, is that Putin’s regime must be dismantled and Russia must become a parliamentary republic with rotation of power, independent courts and federalism; Russia must be part of Europe and follow the European path.
I am sure that almost everyone who calls themselves the Russian democratic opposition today could sign up to these points. There are no serious contradictions in them.
The problem is not the text. Over the years of emigration, a huge amount of internal struggle has built up: for attention, for resources, for the right to speak on behalf of everyone. Even attempts to create a common platform become a reason for a new quarrel. In January, PACE launched a platform for dialogue with Russian democratic forces, and the arguments about who would be on it turned out to be louder than anything it has actually done. There is no dispute about principles at all. There is a dispute between personalities and groups.
What, in your view, should be the main political objective of the Russian opposition today: influencing Russian society, preparing for a future political transition, supporting Ukraine, or maintaining international pressure on the Kremlin?
Each group chooses its own objective, and these objectives often compete with each other. Some try to reach a large audience inside Russia. Others build a “platform for the future”: constitutions, reforms, plans for a transition period. This idea is sweet and attractive: it is pleasant to dream about Russia after Putin. Answering the question of how to fight Putin now is much harder: it is unattractive, dangerous and brings almost no visible results. So many people build castles in the air, although nobody can explain what to do today. I myself chose the first, reaching the audience inside Russia, along with full support for Ukraine, Europe and anti-war Russians.
Support for Ukraine is very important. For me, Ukraine’s right to defend itself is not up for discussion, and I am in favour of Ukraine receiving weapons. But many in the opposition stay silent about this: direct support for military action means taking the side of armed resistance, including against Russian soldiers. They believe that Russians themselves will not forgive them for this: millions of families have someone who fought or died. It is commonly accepted that a politician who plans to return to Russia should be afraid of this step. But it seems to me that this war can end only when Putin feels it is impossible to continue it. And that will be in the interests of Russians too. People will stop dying both in Russia and in Ukraine.
As for international pressure and sanctions, yes, absolutely. Here the opposition, and Russian-speaking people in Europe in general, are genuinely useful: we know the language, the people and the regime’s schemes, we know where its money is and who helps it get around sanctions, and we can prove it. But even here our influence is limited: we are listened to only from time to time.
How do you assess the prospect of Russian-Ukrainian negotiations, especially if the United States becomes more directly involved in shaping the process?
The chances of a real agreement are low right now. Putin uses negotiations as a breathing space and as a way to continue the war by other means. And circumstances are working out well for him.
First, oil. Because of the war around Iran, oil costs more than $100 a barrel, almost twice as much as a year ago. Even Russian Urals, with all its discounts, sells for more than $100, while this year’s budget assumed a price of $59. Putin’s success and popular support are largely based on the fact that, after the hard 1990s, the oil price gave Russians a certain level of prosperity, which Putin linked to his own rule. Such prices make it possible to continue the war. The diesel deal with Trump gives him even more opportunities.
Until now, Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries had been eating up part of this money: in the summer, the Kremlin’s oil revenues were about a third lower than they should have been at such prices. That is why it matters so much to Putin that the Americans are now demanding that Ukraine stop its strikes on refineries.
Second, Ukraine’s domestic politics. There was a crisis with the defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, there are corruption scandals, and there are demands for Zelenskyy to hold new elections. Putin sees his chance in this: to keep pressing and wait until his opponent weakens from within.
Third, a bet on instability in Europe. Europe is now Ukraine’s main support. Any political crisis in European countries, any success for those who propose to “come to terms with Moscow” benefits Putin. He is in no hurry: he only needs to wait until supporting Ukraine becomes too costly politically for European governments.
Trump is pressing Ukraine specifically because Ukraine depends on his help. He has no real influence over Russia. If the pressure falls mainly on Ukraine and not on Russia, the result will not be peace but a pause before the next war.
But there is another side to this. In almost five years of war, Putin has not achieved any of the goals he started it with, and he seems to have realised himself that he will not win on the battlefield. That is why he needs the negotiating table so badly: to win time there, and the chance to advance further.
From the perspective of the Russian opposition, what would constitute an acceptable framework for negotiations? Where do you see the biggest danger of an agreement that ends the fighting without resolving the underlying conflict?
First, about who is at the table. The Russian opposition and Europe have the same problem right now: they are not invited to the negotiations and are not considered participants. The talks are between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
For us, the problem with any deal is that Putin stays in power. And under Putin nothing can change in Russia: neither war as a way of solving problems, nor repression inside the country. So the danger of a deal that stops the fighting but does not resolve the conflict is obvious: Putin will not stop. He will get a breathing space, rebuild the army and carry on. And the pressure on Europe will only grow.
I do not like the word “hybrid”: it makes what is happening sound softer than it is. These are attacks on factories and railways, arson, murders, bribery, attempts to destabilise entire countries. After a ceasefire in Ukraine, the Kremlin will have both people and money freed up for them. The Kremlin increasingly looks for people to carry out these attacks via Telegram, for small sums, including among Russian speakers. So Russian-speaking people in Europe can become part of the defence: we read the same channels and understand the language in which they recruit.
How much influence does Russian society still have over the future direction of the country? Do you see any signs that public attitudes towards the war, mobilisation or the economic situation could eventually translate into political pressure?
It still has influence, more than it seems from the outside, although not through elections. The best example is mobilisation. In autumn 2022, after the “partial” mobilisation, hundreds of thousands of people left the country. Since then the Kremlin has not dared to launch a second wave and keeps denying the rumours about it. Instead of conscription there are contracts and huge payments, in some regions up to 3 million roubles for signing.
But this resource is running out too. This year about a fifth fewer contracts are being signed than a year ago. The Kremlin is still paying the money, there are fewer and fewer volunteers, and yet it still does not announce mobilisation. So what stops it is the possible reaction of society.
Independent media and popular channels have spent years explaining to people how to avoid mobilisation, where to get legal help and what awaits them at the front. Society itself does not want to be forcibly conscripted, and the opposition supports and amplifies this mood: one works together with the other. Together, to a large extent, they prevented a second mobilisation.
The Kremlin takes this into account. It has a good system for monitoring public sentiment: closed polls, social media monitoring, reports from the regions. It also watches the economy: prices, wages, business. That is why everything unpleasant is done gradually, in small steps, so that there is never a point where discontent turns into protest. Public sentiment is a real constraint on the authorities. It can be turned into political pressure, but that requires organisation, which does not exist at the moment.
Looking beyond the war, what should Western governments understand about a possible post-Putin Russia? What mistakes should Europe and the United States avoid if a political transition eventually begins?
First, respond as firmly as possible. After Georgia in 2008 and Crimea in 2014, Europe responded cautiously and agreed to build Nord Stream 2. The Kremlin understood this as permission to go further. Every attack must get a lightning-fast response.
Turkey is a good example. In November 2015, it shot down a Russian Su-24 bomber that had violated the Turkish border. Putin promised that Turkey “would not get away with tomatoes”, and in the end it all came down to tomatoes: a ban on Turkish vegetables, charter flights and construction work. Six months later most of the restrictions were lifted. Putin backs down when he sees strength.
Second, strengthen borders and your own independence: military, energy, information. Even if power changes in Moscow, Europe must be strong on its own.
At the same time, it would be a mistake to isolate Russia. It is impossible anyway. Russia is historically close to Europe and sees it as the source of its culture and civilisation. If after Putin Europe keeps its borders closed and its sanctions permanent, the next dictator will easily explain to people that the West wanted not change in Russia but its humiliation. Europe has two German lessons: isolation and humiliation after 1918 bred revanchism, while bringing Germany into Europe after 1945, together with denazification, produced democracy.
The bridge to such a Russia will be the people whom the war pushed out into Europe. Hundreds of thousands of Russians work here, pay taxes and send their children to European schools. Those of them who are helping Europe defend itself today will tomorrow be the partners it understands best in Moscow. Those who return should be people for whom independent courts, a free press and respect for neighbours’ borders have become normal life: they have seen it with their own eyes.
Relations with a future Russia should be built on mutually beneficial terms, but the benefits must come in exchange for real change. And total lustration must become a condition for that future. The people who built this system and waged this war must not remain in power. A person from Putin’s circle who promises peace and a market economy will not mean a transition if the courts, the security services and the propaganda stay the same. Nothing will change that way.
And one last thing. Regimes like this seem eternal until their very last day. Assad’s regime in Syria collapsed in twelve days, and Prigozhin’s mutiny in 2023 showed how few people Putin has who are ready to fight for him. Russia after Putin is closer than it seems. And our common task is not to let it remain the same as it was under Putin.
Ivan Zhdanov is a Russian lawyer and politician based in Vilnius. He leads the Progress movement, which brings together Russian anti-war media, bloggers and civic projects, and hosts a popular YouTube show about Russian politics. He is a former director of the Anti-Corruption Foundation and one of Alexei Navalny’s closest associates.

title: European LNG imports reach maximum over five months
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. In October 2026, Europe imported its highest volume of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in the last five months due to the need to accelerate the replenishment of storage reserves ahead of winter, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
In October, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system amounted to about 11.1 bln cubic meters, turning out to be 4% higher than in September and 12% less compared to October 2025.
Based on the results for January-October 2026, LNG inflows from terminals into the European gas transmission system slowed down and stood at about 112 bln cubic meters, which is already 4% less than in the same period of 2025.
LNG supplies over the 10 months hold the first place by share among Europe's gas sources at 42.4%, according to data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG) as of October 30, 2026. In second place, with a share of 38.4%, are supplies from the North Sea (mainly Norwegian gas); in third place, with 9.6%, are gas supplies from North Africa; and in fourth place, with 5.9%, are supplies from the East (Russian gas, pipeline supplies via Ukraine, as well as the withdrawal by European companies of their own gas from Ukraine's underground gas storage facilities). Gas supplies from Azerbaijan accounted for 3.6%.

title: Sabanis and Makropoulos Jump Seven Places on Greek Airplay Chart
body: Nikos Oikonomopoulos tops Greek Airplay Chart week 44 with “Enoho Kormi”, as Giorgos Sabanis and Nikos Makropoulos jump seven places. The Official IFPI Airplay Chart powered by MediaInspector publishes the weekly Top 20 of Greek-repertoire songs on AirplayChart.gr . Greek Airplay Chart week 44 covers 26 October to 1 November 2026. “Enoho Kormi” was also No. 1 in weeks 42 and 43, as Greek City Times reported last week. Heaven Music put out the song as a single on 30 June 2026, according to its Spotify listing . Away from the radio, Oikonomopoulos took his 20-year anniversary tour to the Sydney Lyric Theatre on 31 October. There, Archbishop Makarios of Australia met the singer and congratulated him on 20 years in music. Below him, APON moves up one place to No. 2 in Greek Airplay Chart week 44 with “Kantada”. The song comes from his 2026 album “Ixogenia” on Panik Records, and Greek City Times covered its music video in June. As a result, Thodoris Ferris slips to No. 3 with “Eipes”, a single that Panik Platinum issued on 5 December 2025. Biggest climbers on Greek Airplay Chart week 44 Giorgos Sabanis and Nikos Makropoulos are the biggest climbers this week. Their duet “Xartines Agapes” jumps seven places in Greek Airplay Chart week 44, from No. 14 to No. 7. Panik Records issued the single on 5 October 2026, according to its Apple Music listing . Sabanis also has “Ti Thelo Ego Me Sena” at No. 9, giving him two songs in the Top 10. Katerina Lioliou climbs two places to No. 4 with “Pagkosmia Mera Tou Psefti”. Panik Platinum put out the song on 4 September 2026, and it also appears on her album “2100 – Gen Eta (Part A)”. In addition, Lioliou and Sakis Rouvas opened a joint winter season at the Athens club Enastron on 30 October. Further down the IFPI list, Panos Kiamos rises two places to No. 15 with “Anoixti Akroasi”. Konstantinos Argiros gains two as well, since “Revma” moves from No. 19 to No. 17. Higher up, Ioulia Kallimani gains one place to No. 6, while Anna Vissi’s “Aigaio” rises to No. 11. PAN PAN and Kalliopi Mitropoulou then climb from No. 20 to No. 19 with “Anisopedi Disko”. Ioulia Karapataki returns to the Top 20 of Greek Airplay Chart week 44 with “Takounia Gia Karfia”, up from No. 21 to No. 20. The song was at No. 20 in week 42, before it slipped just outside the Top 20 last week. Apple Music lists the track, with Orestis Ntantos, on a 2022 EP from Cobalt Music. Falls and exits on the chart this week By comparison, Vissi’s “Oxi Giati” and Natasa Theodoridou’s “Fortigo” share the largest fall in Greek Airplay Chart week 44, at four places each. Vissi drops from No. 4 to No. 8, whereas Theodoridou slips from No. 8 to No. 12. Dimitris Bakoulis and Mariana Katsimicha fall two places to No. 13 with a live recording of “To Vals ton Oneiron”. Christos Mastoras also drops two, because “Margarita” moves from No. 16 to No. 18. Lioliou’s “Logariasmos” and Oikonomopoulos’s “Me Liga Logia” each lose one place, to No. 16 and No. 14. In contrast, Christos Menidiatis holds No. 5 on the IFPI chart with “O,ti Pio Omorfo”, and Petros Iakovidis stays at No. 10 with “Pagkosmio Fainomeno”. Only one song leaves the Top 20 in Greek Airplay Chart week 44. Antonis Remos’s “Deutera” was at No. 18 last week, and Greek City Times covered the song’s music video in December 2025. Still, four acts have two songs each on the chart: Oikonomopoulos, Vissi, Lioliou and Sabanis. title: Spot electricity prices jump on Monday
body:
Prices are impacted by reduced hydropower reserves in the Nordics and the ongoing crisis in the Middle East.
Households on spot price electricity contracts in Finland will see hourly rates climb to almost 50 cents per kilowatt-hour by mid-morning.
Prices will stay at this level for much of the day, reaching a peak of nearly 51 cents between 5 and 6pm. They will only fall back below 20 cents late in the evening.
The jump is sharp compared with the weekend, when hourly prices remained under 20 cents.
The average price for Monday, including value-added tax, is just under 26 cents per kilowatt-hour.
Forecasters had warned that spot prices would be higher than in recent years this autumn and winter, pointing to reduced hydropower reserves in the Nordic countries and the ongoing crisis in the Middle East.
Large Finnish companies meanwhile believe data centre investments will significantly increase competition for electricity.
In a survey by OP Financial Group, more than 80 percent of respondents said Finland's energy policy must treat companies investing in data centres and traditional industrial firms equally.

title: Nine Dead In Small Plane Crash Near Trump’s Florida Home
body: A Learjet plummeted into a neighborhood in southern Florida miles from US President Donald Trump’s resort home on Sunday, killing all nine people on board, officials said. Several unverified clips posted to social media depicting the deadly crash showed an aircraft nearly vertical, slamming at high speed into the ground, creating a large fireball and leaving a flaming crater near a busy roadside. “Today’s plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement, confirming that all nine people on the aircraft were killed. Duffy said the plane, a Learjet 60, had departed from Austin, Texas and was headed for the Bahamas. The crash occurred near Cresthaven, a neighborhood in Palm Beach County that is less than seven miles (11 kilometers) from Trump’s resort home Mar-a-Lago. “Obviously this is a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters near the scene. “It looked like a missile going down,” he said, adding there were no reports of anyone on the ground being injured. Trump had been at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday but departed from the nearby and newly renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport shortly after he boarded Air Force One at 11:55 am (1655 GMT), about an hour before the crash of the Learjet aircraft. The plane came down near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said, noting about 600 residents were evacuated and relocated to shelters. “The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate” the crash, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. Storms had been reported in the area. Trump carried an umbrella as he boarded Air Force One. In an audio recording posted to air traffic website liveatc.net, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting “moderate turbulence” and saying the crew was “managing the ice.” The person said the plane was “picking up precipitation” and needed “to climb” shortly before saying: “Mayday, mayday, we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute.” Seconds later, the person said they were “declaring an emergency” as the plane descended 20,000 feet per minute. “We’re going to crash into the ground,” the person said, shortly before communications stopped. AFP The post Nine Dead In Small Plane Crash Near Trump’s Florida Home appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Air Marshal Mehtab Singh Deswal Takes Over as Head of IAF’s Eastern Air Command
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan
New Delhi. Air Marshal Mehtab Singh Deswal, AVSM, VM, on November 1, 2026, assumed charge as the Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief (AOC-in-C) of the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) Eastern Air Command (EAC).

Commissioned into the IAF’s flying branch as a fighter pilot on June 14, 1989, Air Marshal Deswal has over 3,200 hours of flying experience on various fighter aircraft. A specialist in strike operations and air defence roles, he is also a qualified Pilot Attack Instructor.

An alumnus of the National Defence Academy (NDA) and the National Defence College, Air Marshal Deswal has held several important operational and staff appointments during his distinguished career. These include commanding two operational flying bases as Air Officer Commanding and serving as the Commanding Officer of a fighter squadron.

He has also served as Air Attaché at the Embassy of India in Pakistan, providing him with diplomatic and strategic exposure in addition to his extensive operational experience. At Air Headquarters, he held the appointment of Director General (Weapon Systems).
Immediately before taking over as the head of the Eastern Air Command, Air Marshal Deswal was serving as the Senior Air Staff Officer (SASO) at Headquarters South Western Air Command (SWAC).

In recognition of his distinguished service to the IAF, he has been conferred the Ati Vishisht Seva Medal (AVSM) and the Vayu Sena Medal (VM).

title: Greece Moves to Spread Old Tax and EFKA Debts Over 120 Instalments
body: Greeks who owe money to the tax office or to social security funds could soon get up to 10 years to pay it back, under provisions tabled in Parliament by the Ministry of National Economy and Finance. The bill raises the number of monthly instalments in the special debt-settlement scheme for the Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) and e-EFKA/KEAO from 72 to as many as 120, Naftemporiki and in.gr reported. It also widens the range of debts that can be included and extends the deadline for applications to 30 June 2027. Naftemporiki reported that the omnibus bill is due to be voted on in November, while in.gr said the AADE application platform is expected to open by mid-November. Until the law passes, the details below remain subject to change. Who can apply According to Article 35 of the bill, as reported by in.gr, the scheme covers confirmed debts to the tax administration that fell overdue by 31 December 2024, provided they were not already under a payment arrangement on 30 September 2026 and have not been placed in another arrangement before the application is made. To join, taxpayers must, on the day they apply: have paid off or legally settled their other overdue debts, for example through AADE’s standing 24- or 48-instalment scheme (in.gr reported that debts arising from 1 January 2025 must be settled within one month of joining); have filed all income tax returns for the past five years; have no final conviction for tax evasion or smuggling. All eligible debts that are not suspended must be included, while including suspended debts is optional, in.gr reported. Some debts are excluded, including amounts owed from the recovery of state aid under European decisions. What it costs The minimum instalment remains â‚¬30 a month and the annual interest rate is fixed at 5.84%, with a 15% surcharge for late payment, according to in.gr. Kathimerini reported that monthly payments could be up to 40% lower than under the current 72-instalment scheme. But more instalments also mean more interest. In an example published by in.gr, a â‚¬12,000 debt spread over 120 instalments costs about â‚¬132 a month, but â‚¬15,872 in total. Over 72 instalments, the monthly payment rises to â‚¬198, while the total falls to â‚¬14,254. Switching from 72 to 120 instalments Taxpayers already in the 72-instalment scheme can move the remaining balance to the new one, as long as their current arrangement is still active. The switch is optional, and those who stay put keep their existing terms. Naftemporiki said about 35,000 debtors could benefit. The move will not happen automatically. According to Ta Nea, people with an active arrangement will need to file a new online application on the AADE platform once it opens, so their balance can be recalculated. How to apply and pay Applications are made online. Entry into the scheme is confirmed only when the first instalment is paid, within three working days of the application. Later instalments are due by the last working day of each month. In.gr said more than one million households and businesses could use the scheme. Those who keep up their payments can obtain a tax clearance certificate, while criminal prosecution for unpaid debts to the State and enforced collection measures are suspended. However, the State keeps the right to register a mortgage, to offset amounts it owes the taxpayer, and to refuse a clearance certificate for a property transfer when the debt is not secured. How the arrangement can be lost The arrangement is cancelled if the debtor: misses two consecutive monthly instalments, or pays the last two more than two months late; fails to settle other overdue debts within one month of joining; fails to pay or settle new tax debts within three months of their due date. In that case, the unpaid balance becomes due immediately and enforced collection resumes. Social security debts Debts to e-EFKA and other social security bodies for periods up to 31 December 2024 can also be spread over as many as 120 monthly instalments. Applications will be made mainly online through KEAO, the Centre for the Collection of Social Security Debts, and the first instalment is due by the last working day of the month in which the application is made, in.gr reported. Debtors who keep to the terms will be able to obtain a social security clearance certificate, and enforcement measures will be suspended. The arrangement is lost after two consecutive missed payments or if other social security debts are not settled. People with an active 72-instalment arrangement for these debts can also switch. title: Belgian Prime Minister may resign on Monday — newspaper
body:
BRUSSELS, November 2. /TASS/. Prime Minister of Belgium Bart De Wever may resign after the meeting with King Philippe on Monday, De Standaard newspaper reports, citing a source.

According to the news outlet, the Belgian government "is in a deep crisis." It is not yet clear whether the king consents to the resignation of the prime minister or gives more time to settle the crisis, the newspaper added.
