title: Police Hunt Suspect After Murder Of Woman In Akwa Ibom
body: Akwa Ibom State Police Command has launched an intensive investigation and a manhunt following the murder of Unwana Okon, a resident of Ndot Village in Oruk Anam Local Government Area. The incident was reported around 3.30 pm on Sunday by the victim’s brother, Eno, who told police that his sister had received a telephone call from an unidentified person inviting her to Mbiaikot village to buy African wild spinach (Gnetum Africanum), popularly called afang leaves. ‎According to the report, Unwana went to the village after receiving the invitation. She was later found murdered. Her mobile phone and an undisclosed sum of money were reportedly taken. ‎Police operatives have begun investigating the circumstances of the killing and working to identify those responsible. ‎The Commissioner of Police, Baba Azare, has ordered a comprehensive investigation. He has also directed that the case be transferred immediately from the Divisional Police Headquarters to the Command’s Violence Crime Response Unit (VCRU) for a thorough and coordinated investigation. The aim, the Command explained, is to identify, arrest and prosecute anyone found culpable. ‎The Command also condemned the killing, saying it will deploy all available operational and investigative resources to bring those responsible to justice. ‎Police urge residents of Oruk Anam and neighbouring communities to remain vigilant and report suspicious activity or any information that could assist the investigation. Anyone with credible information should contact their nearest police station or use the command’s established communication channels. ‎The command reaffirmed its commitment to protecting lives and property and tackling crime across the state. ‎The statement was signed by DSP Timfon John, Police Public Relations Officer, for the Commissioner of Police, Akwa Ibom State Police Command, on Sunday night. The post Police Hunt Suspect After Murder Of Woman In Akwa Ibom appeared first on Channels Television .

title: What the US midterms could mean for Ukraine
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Mississippi, U.S. on Oct. 26, 2026. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
For months, Ukraine has faced mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, as he seeks to secure political gains ahead of the November midterm elections.
With both chambers of Congress at stake on Nov. 3, the key question is how heavily Republicans will lose — and whether the scale of any setback will be enough to shift Washington's foreign policy.
The vote comes at a low point in U.S.-Ukraine relations.
Trump drew fire from U.S. lawmakers, Kyiv, and European capitals for allowing Russian diesel into the U.S. and easing sanctions on Russia, running counter to the West's long-standing strategy for ending the war in Ukraine.
And while Moscow avoids pressure, Kyiv is pressed to end its strikes against Russian refineries while grappling with disruptions in intelligence support and Patriot air defense shipments.
A Democratic victory might give Ukraine a sympathetic Congress and offer greater scrutiny over Trump's foreign policy pivots. However, experts who spoke with the Kyiv Independent say that the U.S. president would ultimately keep firm control over his country's foreign policy.
This week, U.S. voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, where Democrats are widely expected to win a majority for the first time since 2020.
The Democratic Party faces steeper — but not insurmountable — odds in the Senate, where only about one-third of the 100 seats are up for a vote, with a mere seven considered toss-ups .
Even if the Democratic Party ends up with 51 Senate seats needed for a majority, they would still need the Republican Party to overcome a filibuster, a U.S. policy where 60 votes are needed in the Senate to pass crucial legislation.
For Kyiv, that is not the end of the road, however.
U.S. senators have shown they can build a bipartisan majority around support for Ukraine, most recently in August, when they passed the Lindsey Graham Act — spearheaded by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — with 86 votes.
But this bipartisan consensus cannot be taken for granted when it comes to Republican lawmakers challenging Trump.
"In today's highly polarized political environment, most lawmakers hesitate to oppose a president of their own party, even when they disagree with his policy choices," James M. Lindsay, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, told the Kyiv Independent.
Should Democrats muster enough support to push through a bill on assistance for Ukraine or tougher sanctions against Russia, Trump wields powerful veto rights.
Only a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers can override it, and that number is something Democrats are unlikely to whip up.
"Congress has a poor track record in overturning presidential vetoes, especially in foreign affairs," Lindsay notes.
Still, a Congressional majority would hold some leverage.
Lawmakers could include measures supporting Ukraine in "must-pass" legislation, such as defense appropriations bills or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
Congress would then "dare Trump to veto it," said Daniel Hamilton, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "He is unlikely to do so, since the overall bill funds the Defense Department."
But even when the bill leaves the desk with a presidential signature, there comes another obstacle — the chance of Trump simply ignoring it afterward.
A sweeping Russia sanctions bill, championed by the late Senator Graham, was passed with great fanfare and signed into law by the president in September.
Yet, Trump has not toughened up on Russia since — quite the opposite.
On Oct. 16, the president issued a broad waiver of Graham's sanctions, days after his Treasury lifted restrictions on Russian diesel purchases.
This was not the first time the administration had sidestepped Congress on Ukraine matters either.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon delayed $400 million in military assistance under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) for months, even though Congress had already authorized it.
This illustrates the limits of Congress's power: passing a law does not guarantee that the executive will carry it out as lawmakers intended.
Ironically, Congress was quite capable of disrupting the White House's Ukraine course during the Biden administration.
The Republican-led House famously blocked a massive aid bill from late 2023 until 2024, leading to a critical ammunition "hunger" among Ukrainian forces.
But this dynamic would not translate to a clash between Trump and a Democratic-led House. For the Ukraine policy he is pursuing, Trump does not need congressional consent, Lindsay said.
"Some presidential powers, such as when to negotiate, whom to negotiate with, and what to negotiate over, are beyond Congress's power to direct, restrain, or regulate."
It was Trump who — to the chagrin of many pro-Ukraine lawmakers — publicly humiliated President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025 and who pulled Russia out of diplomatic isolation by hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska a few months later.
"A Democratic House or Congress may bristle at President Donald Trump's diplomacy with Russia, but it cannot compel him to change it," Lindsay said.
A Democratic victory would not upend Trump's policy, but could boost Ukraine's voice on Capitol Hill.
If House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries replaces Mike Johnson as speaker, Republican skeptics could no longer keep pro-Ukraine legislation off the floor, as they did with Biden's aid bill.
Majorities in one or both chambers would also give Democrats leadership of committees and allow them to subpoena executive officials.
According to Hamilton, Democrats may use this power to investigate SpaceX founder Elon Musk , U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, or Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Musk is allegedly responsible for the temporary throttling of Starlink services in Ukraine, Hegseth is said to be delaying shipments of Patriot missiles, and the U.S. peace envoys have faced scrutiny for at times pushing peace deals favorable to Moscow.
A House majority would also allow Democrats to impeach executive officials, including, for the third time, Trump. This would not guarantee a conviction and removal — a supermajority of senators is needed for that.
Lawmakers who spoke to the Kyiv Independent see the midterm election as a chance to set the legislative agenda on Ukraine and to scrutinize Trump's policies more closely.
"We will use every legislative and oversight tool available to hold this administration accountable and ensure Ukraine receives the security assistance it needs to defend itself," said Mike Levin, a Democratic representative for California's 49th congressional district.
Backchannel deals with the Kremlin, and any disruptions to intelligence sharing or Ukraine's Starlink terminals would face "rigorous oversight" if Democrats win House committee gavels, he told the Kyiv Independent.
Gregory Meeks, a Democratic representative and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, pledged to work with lawmakers from both parties to push through legislation to "compel the Trump administration to deliver to Ukraine the security, economic, and intelligence support it needs to defend its people from Putin's brutal and illegal invasion."
In his statement for the Kyiv Independent, Meeks further committed to "fixing" the Graham Act, "including by denying President Trump the ability to unilaterally import Russian energy and undermine U.S. national security interests."
Nevertheless, Ukraine is unlikely to be front and center in Democrats' focus after the midterms.
The party's 100-day post-victory plan focuses on issues most pressing for U.S. voters, such as the cost of living and restraining Trump's war against Iran, which has driven up inflation and fuel prices.
Ukraine is far from the top of the agenda.
And even with his back against the wall in the legislature, the president will still have a bite on the international scene.
"Historically, most presidents in this situation have turned to foreign policy, and so Trump is likely to be even more outrageous in some of his initiatives than before, perhaps including working with Putin and (Chinese President) Xi (Jinping) at the expense of Ukraine and Europe," Hamilton said.
"A Democratic Congress would do what it could to block that; how such battles unfold will depend on the specific issues."
Lindsay also argues that Trump appears unconcerned about how unpopular his foreign policy maneuvers are, be it the Russian diesel deal or the sanctions waiver.
And since he cannot run for another term, he has even less incentive to temper his policy, the expert added.
"Those are not decisions of a president who is following the political winds."
Hi, this is Martin, the author of this article.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the U.S. has been Ukraine's first and foremost ally. American weapons, intelligence, and sanctions have helped Ukraine hold the line.
This alliance now looks fragile. But Ukraine and the U.S. have shown they can weather political storms because their support has never rested on a single president. It rested on lawmakers, voters, and ordinary people who decided that helping Ukraine mattered.
If you believe in the work we do here in Ukraine and want to see more reporting like this, please consider supporting us by joining the Kyiv Independent community .
Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia. His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

title: Israeli forces shell towns in southern Lebanon
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Israeli forces have shelled the towns of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun, and fired machine guns at the Al-Hujair and Al-Salouqi valleys, in the Tyre district.
Israeli forces have shelled the towns of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun, and fired machine guns at the Al-Hujair and Al-Salouqi valleys, in the Tyre district, according to the National News Agency.

title: From Charlemagne to the Kitchen Boy: Reading the Hamburg Rathaus
body:
The Hamburg Rathaus tells the story of its city in more than a hundred small details, and this is my walk through them.
The Rathaus was one of the first things I photographed in Hamburg. The picture is still in my camera roll, taken on 6 July 2017, five days after I arrived for an internship. Like most visitors, I was impressed by its size and its tower, but what I kept coming back to was the roof. Why was it turquoise, and why were so many other roofs in the city the same colour?
The answer turned out to be chemistry. The roof is copper, and copper slowly reacts with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air. Over the decades this forms a green layer called patina, so the roof I was looking at wasn't the colour the builders had seen.
That was the first time the Rathaus made me curious, but not the last. On a city tour with Robin and the Tour Guides , our guide pointed out the emperors on the façade, the Phoenix and the Hanseatic coats of arms. We only heard a little about each, but it was enough to make me look at the building differently.
Later, I decided to build a digital 3D model of the Rathaus, which meant photographing it from every side. Zooming in, I kept finding faces, figures and coats of arms I had never noticed from the square. Reading about them one by one, I realised the Rathaus can be read like a book about Hamburg's history.
In this article, I'd like to take you around the building and share what I found.
The Rathaus we see today isn't Hamburg's first. It's probably the sixth, and fire runs through the story of the ones before it. An early Rathaus, built after the old town and the new merchant town joined in 1216, was most likely lost in the city fire of 1284. Around 1290, a bigger brick Rathaus was built next to the Trostbrücke, and it stood there for more than 550 years.
Then, in the night of 5 May 1842, the Great Fire broke out. The flames spread quickly through the narrow streets, and on the morning of 6 May the people of Hamburg blew up their own Rathaus with 800 pounds of gunpowder, hoping to stop the fire. It didn't work, and the fire went on for days. Today the Haus der Patriotischen Gesellschaft stands where the old Rathaus once was.
It took 55 years until Hamburg had a new Rathaus. The foundation stone was laid on 6 May 1886, exactly 44 years after the old one was blown up, and the building opened in 1897. Its front is 111 metres wide, and its tower is 112 metres high, almost exactly as tall as the building is wide.
The fire is remembered right on its front. High on the tower, between the clock and Hamburg's coat of arms, sits a Phoenix, the bird that rises again from its own ashes, with wings more than 2 metres wide. Below it, a gilded medallion shows the old Rathaus and the word "Resurgam", meaning "I will rise again". In 1892, exactly 50 years after the fire, the Phoenix was pulled to the Rathaus by four black horses.
In the summer of 1943, the bombing raids of Operation Gomorrah destroyed large parts of Hamburg. This time the Rathaus was spared. It was one of the few historic buildings in the centre to survive, and that's why we can still read every detail on its façade today.
Above the main entrance, two emperors stand on either side of the balcony: Charlemagne on the left and Friedrich I Barbarossa on the right. Between them, in the background, Hammonia looks down from a golden mosaic made in 1896, holding out a wreath. She is the goddess who stands for Hamburg, much like Britannia does for Britain, and she represents the city's values: freedom, peace, trade and prosperity.
It might seem strange that a city so proud of its freedom puts emperors on its town hall. But Hamburg never had a king of its own. Over the centuries, the Dukes of Saxony, the Counts of Holstein and later the Kings of Denmark all claimed power over the city, and Hamburg's answer was always the same: it answered only to the emperor, the head of the Holy Roman Empire. When Denmark claimed Hamburg in 1618, the city added emperor statues to its old Rathaus to make that point, and the new Rathaus carries on the tradition.
Around them are a few more details. Above Charlemagne is a small coat of arms with a black eagle on gold, the eagle of the empire. Above Barbarossa are three black lions on gold, the arms of his family, the Staufer. And on the columns next to the statues are the letters SPQH, short for Senatus Populusque Hamburgensis, "the Senate and the People of Hamburg". It's a copy of the SPQR of ancient Rome, and a reminder that even standing next to the emperors, the city was run by its own citizens.
Charlemagne (768–814) is where Hamburg's story begins. He was crowned emperor in 800, and in his time the area around the Alster and the Elbe came under Frankish rule. According to old stories, he also started the first church here. So it makes sense that the whole line of emperors starts with him.
Barbarossa (1152–1190) is there for a very different reason. On 7 May 1189, he is said to have given Hamburg the right to sail down the Elbe to the North Sea without paying any tolls. This is seen as the birth of the port, and the city still celebrates it every May with the Hafengeburtstag, the harbour's birthday.
The twist is that the document is a fake. Count Adolf III, who ruled Hamburg at the time and joined Barbarossa on his crusade, most likely did get some kind of promise from him. But Barbarossa died on the crusade, and there was no written proof. Decades later, the people of Hamburg wrote the charter themselves, with everything they wanted in it, and got it sealed with the seal of Barbarossa's grandson, Friedrich II. Historians have known this since 1907, but the city celebrates anyway. I find it funny that one of the biggest ports in the world partly owes its start to a clever trick.
The other 18 rulers stand in the niches between the first-floor windows, and Charlemagne and Barbarossa split them in time. Charlemagne leads the older rulers on the left, and from him the line moves forward in time until Lothar III, who died in 1137. Barbarossa, who became king 15 years later, leads the newer ones on the right, and from him the line continues all the way to Franz II, the last emperor, in 1806. Strictly speaking, not all of them belong to the Holy Roman Empire: the first five ruled before the empire began in 962, in the Frankish empire, but in the 1890s they were seen as the start of the same line.
When I was photographing them, I noticed that the emperors stand behind thin nets. At first they made them look a bit trapped, but I guess the nets are there to keep the pigeons away. These men once ruled large parts of Europe, and today they need protecting from the pigeons on the Rathausmarkt.
Hamburg gave Charlemagne and Barbarossa the place of honour, right above the main entrance. But above the emperors, the builders placed what mattered even more to them: Hamburg's own coat of arms and the four civic virtues.
The coat of arms shows a white castle with three towers on red, with a cross and two stars above it, held up by two stone lions. You don't often see the coat of arms in this full form, with the lions and the helmet on top. The last time I saw it was embossed at the top of a letter I received from the Mayor of Hamburg, congratulating me on becoming a German citizen and on choosing Hamburg as my home. The interesting thing is that the letter talks about freedom, tolerance and trade, almost the same values Hammonia stands for.
Below it sit four bronze women, the virtues that, according to the builders, every Hamburg citizen should have. Courage wears a winged helmet and holds a sword, Piety raises a large cross, Unity has a sword lying across her lap, and Wisdom holds up a torch, standing for knowledge and good judgement.
Between them, in gold letters, runs the city's motto: "Libertatem quam peperere maiores digne studeat servare posteritas". It means "May the young generation be worthy of keeping the freedom that the old generation won." It sums up the whole building in one sentence: Hamburg is a free city, and its citizens have to look after that freedom.
Above Charlemagne and Barbarossa sit the virtues. Above the other 18 emperors, the builders went a step further and placed the citizens themselves. Over each of the 28 first-floor windows is a small triangular gable with a stone bust of a profession, from fisherman and baker to judge and banker. So along the whole façade, the people who made the city work sit higher than the rulers of the empire.
All 28 busts were made by the sculptor Aloys Denoth, and half of them were modelled on real people, from craftsmen to some of the best-known names of Hamburg at the time:
The other half show the everyday trades of the city: the fisherman, skipper and merchant, the tailor, baker, butcher, farmer and gardener, the shipbuilder, carpenter and mason, the pastor, a brewer or innkeeper with a cigar, and the chimneysweep.
What surprised me most is how detailed they are. The baker holds a cake, the butcher has a pig's head, and the judge holds a law book. The sad part is that you can hardly see any of this with the naked eye. This is where you need a phone with a good camera: at 4x zoom, you can see what each of them is holding.
Between the busts of the citizens and the emperors below them, each of the 28 gables carries a small coat of arms. Each one stands for a city of the Hanseatic League, or for a city that traded closely with it. Together they run around the building, from the Große Johannisstraße side, along the Rathausmarkt, to the Alter Wall side.
The Hanseatic League, or simply the Hanse, was a network of merchant towns that worked together to protect their trade. From the 13th to the 17th century it connected around 200 towns, from the Netherlands to the Baltic, with Lübeck as its leading city. The Hanse is so interesting that it would need its own article, but you can still see its traces in Hamburg today. The city's official name is the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, and that's why Hamburg's number plates start with HH, for Hansestadt Hamburg.
Two of the coats of arms are bigger than the others: Lübeck on the left side of the front and Bremen on the right. They sit below the two most important busts, the president of the city parliament and the mayor, and it's probably no accident. Lübeck was the leading city of the Hanse, and when the league slowly faded away, Lübeck, Bremen and Hamburg were the last three cities that kept its name. Like Hamburg, they still call themselves Hanseatic cities, and their number plates still start with HL and HB.
Not every city on the façade was a full member. Amsterdam and Utrecht, for example, were trading partners rather than members. Florence is far from the North Sea, but its bankers, like the Medici, had offices across Europe, including in Bruges, one of the Hanse's main trading posts. A few of the coats of arms are not fully confirmed, Florence among them.
Here are all 28, grouped by where the cities are:
Below the balcony that runs under the emperors, above the arched ground-floor windows, there is another set of coats of arms carved into the stone. These belong to Hamburg's own families. Until 1919, Hamburg was run by a Senate made up of men from the city's richest and most powerful families. They were chosen for life, not by a public vote, and 29 of these families have their coats of arms here.
You might not know their faces, but you probably know their names, because many of them live on in the city's streets, squares and parks:
The others are the Abendroth, Bartels, Chapeaurouge, Geffcken, Kähler, Kunhardt, Lehmann, Merck, Möring, Moller, O'Swald, Roosen, Roscher, Schemmann, Schröder, Stahmer and Stammann families.
Hayns Park is one of my favourite parks for a walk on a nice day. I usually go there after stopping by the French café Éclair au Café . I had always wondered where the park's name came from, and now I know.
Higher than anything else except the tower, nine saints stand on top of the large roof gables. Two of them hold the front corners facing the Rathausmarkt, St. Michael on the Große Johannisstraße side and St. Catherine on the Alter Wall side, and the others are spread around the sides and the courtyard. They are also the hardest figures on the building to see. From the ground they are just small shapes against the sky, and only at 8x zoom do they turn into figures with faces and the objects they hold.
Hamburg had been Protestant for more than 350 years when the Rathaus was built, so the saints aren't there to be prayed to. They stand for places. For centuries the city was divided into parishes, areas that each belonged to one church, and these parishes were also the basis of its politics: citizens met, voted and paid their taxes by parish. So the nine saints are really a map of old Hamburg.
Five of them stand for the city's five main churches, which you can still visit today: St. Peter for St. Petri, Hamburg's oldest parish church; St. Nicholas for St. Nikolai, the church of the merchants and sailors, whose ruined tower is now a memorial to the victims of war; St. Catherine for St. Katharinen by the harbour; St. James for St. Jacobi; and St. Michael for St. Michaelis, the "Michel", Hamburg's best-known church.
The one that surprised me most was St. Michael. I know the Michel well: I've passed it many times and even lived close by for more than a year. But I had never imagined the saint behind the name, an archangel with big wings.
Two more stand for the old suburbs outside the city walls, St. Pauli and St. Georg. Both are still districts today, and it's interesting how far they have moved from the saints who gave them their names. St. Pauli, named after the apostle Paul, is known for the Reeperbahn and its nightlife, and St. Georg, named after the knight who killed the dragon, is known as the heart of Hamburg's gay scene.
The last two stand for monasteries that are long gone: St. Mary Magdalene for the monastery that stood where the stock exchange is today, and St. John for the St. Johannis monastery near today's Rathaus, which still gives its name to the Große Johannisstraße.
The Rathaus is home to two different bodies: the Bürgerschaft, the city parliament, and the Senate, the city government. The parliament sits in the wing on the Große Johannisstraße side, and the Senate in the wing on the Alter Wall side. The figures on the two side façades show what each of them is about.
On the parliament side stand two orators, both made by the sculptor Friedrich Offermann. One is a young man in a Roman robe with the words "Plus ultra", meaning "More beyond". He stands for progress. The other is an old man with a book and a document and the words "Parta tueri", meaning "To protect what has been gained". He stands for conservatism. Together they show the two sides of every debate in a parliament: moving forward and keeping what already works.
On the Senate side sits Justitia, the figure of justice, also by Offermann. Today we would expect justice to sit with a court, not with the government. But until 1860, the Senate was not only Hamburg's government but also its highest court, so justice belonged right there.
Behind the Rathaus is a courtyard it shares with the stock exchange, open to everyone from the Große Johannisstraße and the Alter Wall. It's much quieter than the Rathausmarkt, and the figures here tell an older story.
In niches about 12 metres up stand six men who shaped Hamburg long before it became a free city: three archbishops, who made it a centre of the church, and three rulers, who helped it become a trading town. Some of them we already met through the emperors on the front.
Higher up, on four smaller gables, stand bronze shield-bearers, most of them in 16th-century armour, each holding a halberd and a shield. The round medallions below them carry four names: Bruegge, Nowgorod, London and Bergen. These are not member cities but the Hanse's four big trading posts abroad, called Kontore. In each of them, Hanseatic merchants had their own rules and trading rights, and everywhere except Bruges, their own walled quarter with warehouses and living quarters.
In the left corner of the courtyard is a doorway that was meant for weddings. Above it sits Hymen, the god of marriage, with two torches, and on either side stand Adam with a dog and Eve with an apple and the snake. The figures were made in 1896 for a wedding office that was supposed to move into the Rathaus, but it never did, so the gate has never been used for a single wedding. Couples can marry in the Rathaus today, in the Phoenix Hall once a month, just not through this door.
In the right corner, above the kitchen window, sits a small carved kitchen boy, licking a spoon and holding a fork. It's one of the smallest details on the whole building and very easy to walk past.
In the middle of the courtyard stands the Hygieia fountain. It was built in 1895–1896 to remember the cholera epidemic of 1892, when more than 8.000 people in Hamburg died, mostly because of unclean drinking water. The first plan was to show Mercury, the god of trade, but after the epidemic the city chose Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health, instead.
Hygieia stands at the top, holding a small bowl of clean water, with a dragon at her feet that stands for the defeated cholera. Around the basin below sit six bronze figures showing how people use water, such as a man with a ship for shipping, a man with a fish for fishing and a woman with a jug for drinking water.
The best detail is hidden in the base. Between the figures hang bronze faces, each above an arched opening with a grille. These openings are the air intakes of the Rathaus ventilation system: air was drawn in over the water, which helped cool the building. So the fountain is not only a memorial, but also part of the building's air conditioning.
Standing in the courtyard, I always imagine it busy with senators and merchants, talking next to the fountain between a meeting in the Rathaus and a deal at the stock exchange. You have to admire how transparent the city is: the government and the stock exchange share one courtyard, so at least nobody can say they didn't know whose interests the decisions were made for.
Even after all this, there are many details I haven't covered, and I haven't even gone inside: the Rathaus has 647 rooms, and its halls and staircases are full of paintings and carvings that would need an article of their own.
I'm not sure there is another town hall in Germany that tells the story of its city in this much detail, from the emperors and saints to the fishermen, bakers and a kitchen boy licking a spoon. Almost every figure was chosen for a reason, and many of them point to something you can still see in Hamburg today.
While researching this article, one book kept coming up again and again: Das Hamburger Rathaus by Heinz-Jürgen Brandt, from 1957, which describes the building's history, architecture and decoration in detail. When I tried to buy it, I found out it's no longer in print, and in the end I ordered a second-hand copy for a much higher price, which I'm really looking forward to reading. There is a newer book, Das Hamburger Rathaus: 125 Jahre – 125 Geschichten by Rita Bake and Michael Zapf, published for the building's 125th birthday in 2022, but I'm not sure it covers the façade in as much detail as the old one.
This wasn't the first time I've had this problem. Whenever I want to go deeper into a part of Hamburg's history, the best books are often out of print, and second-hand shops are the only way to find them. When I first wanted to learn about the city's history, I couldn't even find a single book written in English.
I'm not sure the city is aware of this, but I believe that if these stories aren't told, they will slowly get lost. And if people don't know the stories behind the places they pass every day, they probably won't feel as connected to their city. This article is my small attempt to keep some of them alive.

title: Situation in Russia stable despite special op challenges — Security Council
body:
MOSCOW, November 2. /TASS/. The security situation in Russia remains stable despite continuing challenges and threats related to the special military operation, the press service of the Russian Security Council’s staff told TASS.
"An analysis of key crime indicators for January-September 2026 by the Russian Security Council’s staff shows that the overall security situation in the country remains stable despite persistent challenges and threats related to the special military operation," the press service said.
The number of criminal offenses fell by 16.3% in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the report noted.
"The decline was primarily driven by a reduction in property crimes, down 16%, including thefts, down 8.9%, and fraud cases, down 23.8%. The number of serious and particularly serious crimes fell by 21.7%, while their share of all recorded offenses decreased from 35.5% to 33.2%," it added.
"Serious and particularly serious crimes against people also declined, including an 11.9% drop in murders and an 18% decrease in cases of intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm. A downward trend was also recorded in crimes committed using IT or involving computer data, with their number falling by 31.5%," the Security Council concluded.

title: Russia used humanitarian pause in Oleshky to fortify its positions – General Staff
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces reported this on Facebook .
"Ukraine's Defense Forces ensured a ceasefire in the Kherson region. During the ceasefire introduced to allow a humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of Ukraine's Defense Forces ensured compliance with the ceasefire and acted strictly within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said.
As a result, humanitarian aid was delivered to its intended destinations, and Ukrainian men and women who wished to leave Oleshky returned to Ukrainian government-controlled territory.
"The enemy, meanwhile, used the humanitarian pause to reinforce its positions. During the ceasefire, we recorded the rotation of Russian units, the fortification of positions, the expansion of anti-drone defenses along roads, and increased logistical activity, including the delivery of ammunition," the General Staff said.
As reported, from October 27 to November 1, Ukraine introduced a ceasefire in a designated area to allow a humanitarian operation in Oleshky.

title: ANA @45: Towards a National Renaissance
body: I had my first experience as a panellist at the 45th Association of Nigerian Authors’ Conference and Convention, and what an incredible experience it was. The invitation from the amiable President of ANA, Associate Professor Usman Oladipo Akanbi, to serve as a panellist came unexpectedly. My path first crossed with that of the ANA President when I was working in Kwara State. It was my friend, Adamu Danjuma, who recently completed his PhD programme at the University of Alabama, USA, who introduced me to him when I was looking for a venue to launch my first published book, ‘We Are All Guilty’, a drama I wrote in 2016 as an undergraduate. Dr Akanbi not only offered me his late father’s foundation as a free venue for the book launch but also supported me by inviting dignitaries, including the erudite lawyer Yusuf Ali, SAN, who served as the chief launcher and made a generous donation. My relationship with the ANA President has gone beyond the book launch stage, and I am now more like a family member to him. So, when he called to inform me that the retired Commissioner of Police, CP Emmanuel Ojukwu, a man I hold in high esteem, had withdrawn at the last minute due to unforeseen circumstances, he asked me to replace him. I had to take up the gauntlet. The theme of this year’s convention was Literature, National Security and the Place of Nigeria in the World. The session was moderated by the great Okoh Diego Okenyodo. Although I first saw Mr Okoh Diego in Ibadan during a conference organised by my late boss, IGP Solomon Arase (rtd.), who was then the Chairman of the Police Service Commission, I did not approach him to introduce myself as the media aide to the late IGP Arase. Perhaps that was why he only mentioned that I had worked with IGP Kayode Egbetokun and was equally working with the current IGP, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, without mentioning that I had once served as media aide to the late IGP Solomon Arase (rtd.). Now, back to the main talking point. I felt jittery as soon as I climbed the stage and walked past the moderator and the keynote speaker, Professor Mahfouz Adedimeji, whom I sat close to. The Professor delivered an explosive speech. The part that appealed to me most was his discussion of the single-story narrative. The representative of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation also spoke exceptionally well. It was a gathering of literary oracles, great men and women who have paid their dues in the literary world. The theme of the conference was quite instructive, timely and, at the same time, long overdue, as I stated in my submission. It reminded me of Chinua Achebe’s famous observation in Morning Yet on Creation Day. Achebe argued that an African creative writer who tries to avoid the big social and political issues of contemporary Africa will end up being completely irrelevant, like the absurd man in the proverb who leaves his burning house to pursue a rat fleeing from the flames. This quotation remains germane to our understanding of the responsibility of an African writer. Writers, anywhere in the world, are the conscience of the societies in which they live. They serve as watchdogs. At a time when the country is grappling with a myriad of challenges, writers cannot afford to be indifferent. As Haile Selassie said, “Throughout history, it has been the inaction of those who could have acted; the indifference of those who should have known better; the silence of the voice of justice when it mattered most; that has made it possible for evil to triumph.” If you look at the generation of writers represented by Professors Chinua Achebe and Wole Soyinka, you will find that they spoke truth to power without fear or favour. They even suffered undue persecution as a result. Unfortunately, the current generation of writers has not done enough, and this has allowed the very evil Haile Selassie warned against to triumph. The moderator asked me about the inaccessibility of literature to ordinary Nigerians and whether the government was to blame. I answered that it was not really the government’s fault because we now live in a digital age. What we should be concerned about is the dying reading culture and the misplaced priorities of the average Nigerian. I gave the example of Big Brother Naija (BBNaija) and the Nigerian Prize for Literature, organised by Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), to illustrate how citizens often prioritise BBNaija over literary excellence. While reality television attracts enormous public attention, the Nigerian Prize for Literature does not always receive comparable recognition. The government, in turn, has chosen to play to the gallery rather than do enough to promote a reading culture and take literary development seriously. The final question was what I would do to make the government take literary institutions seriously. My answer was simple: I would do my best to ensure that the government prioritised literary institutions. I concluded by saying that the government knows what to do. In a country with a ministry responsible for the creative economy, writers should not have to beg for a place at the table. In fact, a writers’ body like ANA should not have to seek government patronage. Doing so risks compromising its independence, and the vision of its founding fathers could be defeated in the process. Talking about the place of Nigeria in the world, it is no news that the country has lost some of its pride of place among the comity of nations. However, as writers and citizens, we have a role to play in ensuring that the single-story narrative of corruption, insecurity, 419 and other vices associated with Nigeria does not overshadow the country’s positive attributes. No country is perfect. Even first-world countries have their dirty linen, but they don’t wash it in public, just as we do ours. As writers, we must tell the Nigerian story in its entirety, acknowledging our challenges without allowing them to overshadow the good things about our country. That said, one must commend the current ANA President for the great work he has done since taking over the mantle of leadership. He came in at a time when the Association was struggling to find its footing amid warring factions. He seems to have steadied the ship by building bridges across the board, even though there are still some discordant tones from within. The important thing is to sustain the progress made, strengthen the Association and ensure that personal differences do not overshadow the collective purpose for which ANA was established. Despite the challenges, I believe the future of ANA is bright if the current leadership continues to build on the progress it has made. Differences are inevitable in any institution, but what matters is the ability to resolve them in the collective interest of the Association. ANA must remain a platform where writers can disagree without losing sight of the greater responsibility they owe society. Ultimately, a national renaissance cannot happen without a literary renaissance. A nation that neglects its writers risks losing an important part of its conscience, history and identity. Literature does more than entertain; it questions power, challenges injustice, preserves our collective memory and inspires future generations to imagine a better society. As Chinua Achebe reminded us, African writers cannot afford to turn away from the realities of their societies. The question, therefore, is not whether literature has a place in Nigeria’s national development, but whether we are ready to give it the place it deserves. Isah can be reached via Lawcadet1@gmail.com

title: Salisbury Panigiri Draws 1,000 People to St Dimitrios Parish
body: More than 1,000 people attended the Salisbury Panigiri at St Dimitrios Greek Orthodox Parish in Salisbury on Sunday 25 October, the parish said. The festival, billed as Salisbury’s Premier Greek Festival, marked the feast of St Dimitrios on 26 October. It was also the third year in a row since the parish revived the Salisbury Panigiri in 2024. Before the festivities, more than 500 people attended Matins and the Divine Liturgy, according to the parish. Afterwards, Band Kosmos played through the afternoon while six dance groups performed under the Salisbury Panigiri marquee. Parish priest Fr Michael Psaromatis said the day showed a community choosing unity. “This generation of Australian Hellenes is choosing to concentrate on what unites us, rather than what has divided us,” he said. He also spoke about the parish’s place in the wider area. “We are proud to share our Orthodox Christian Faith and Greek traditions with Salisbury. We also want to be known as neighbours who can be relied upon,” Fr Michael said. Leaders at the Salisbury Panigiri The Divine Liturgy at St Dimitrios Greek Orthodox Parish, Salisbury, on Sunday 25 October 2026. Photo: Supplied Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis attended on behalf of Premier Peter Malinauskas. In addition, Minister Michael Brown, Zoe Bettison MP, John Fulbrook MP and Tony Zappia MP attended. So did Aria Bolkus, State Member for Colton. Deputy Mayor Chad Buchanan represented the City of Salisbury on behalf of Mayor Gillian Aldridge, who is mourning the sudden death of her daughter. He spoke of council grant funding for the parish’s narthex refurbishment and air conditioning. The South Australian Government also gave the Salisbury Panigiri a $25,000 grant, the parish said. Fr Michael represented Archbishop Makarios and Bishop Silouan, who were overseas for the 35th anniversary of Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew’s patriarchate. Meanwhile, dancers from the Pontian Brotherhood of SA, St George College and the GOCSA Dance Academy performed. The Cretan Association of SA, Cyprus Dance Group SA and the Messinian Greek Dance School of SA also took part. Parish mission work Festival-goers at St Dimitrios Greek Orthodox Parish, Salisbury, on Sunday 25 October 2026. Photo: Supplied The parish also used the Salisbury Panigiri to highlight its outreach work. In July, a team of six spent five days in Fiji and visited more than 300 families. They handed out more than 300 aid packs, up from 150 the year before. Closer to home, the parish supports Pacific workers in South Australia under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme . That evening, Fr Stavros Psaromatis led Great Vespers. Fr John Psalios of St Spyridon Church, Unley, gave the homily, quoting St John Chrysostom: “For to honour a martyr is to imitate him.” On Monday’s feast day, worshippers joined a procession of the icon and a festal lunch after the Divine Liturgy. Greek City Times has explained why the village festival is a unique Greek summer tradition . At the Salisbury Panigiri, Fr Michael closed with an invitation to the crowd. “Enjoy today, and make room at your table for someone new,” he said. title: Kogi: Troops kill 2 suspected bandits
body: The Joint Task Force, Operation WHIRL STROKE, has killed two suspected bandits in Kabba-Bunu and Lokoja local government areas of Kogi State. The Acting Media Information Officer, Headquarters JTF Operation WHIRL STROKE, Lt. Ahmad Zubairu Zubairu, disclosed this in a statement issued to newsmen on Sunday. According to him, troops of Sector 3 of the JTF conducted the operation on Saturday, October 31, 2026, against suspected terrorists following an intelligence-led ambush along the Adankolo–Apata Road. “Acting on the intelligence, troops laid an ambush at suspected bandits’ supply route. The troops subsequently made contact with the suspected criminals who were subdued and forced to flee,” the statement read. It added: “At about 0900 hours on the same day during exploitation, troops received information regarding the discovery of suspected bandits’ bodies towards Adankolo Forest. “On arrival at the location, troops found corpses of the two suspected bandits and recovered one locally made pistol, one cartridge and one empty case of 7.62mm special ammunition.” Meanwhile, the Force Commander, Joint Task Force Operation WHIRL STROKE and General Officer Commanding 5 Division, Nigerian Army, Major General Moses Gara, urged members of the public to continue supporting security agencies by providing timely and credible information on suspicious activities, stressing that security remains everybody’s responsibility.

title: 130,000 children to receive fresh polio vaccination in Adamawa
body: The Adamawa State Government, in partnership with development partners, will conduct a special polio vaccination exercise in two local government areas, targeting a total of 130,000 children. Director, Disease Control and Immunisation of the State Primary Health Care Development Agency (ADSPHCDA), Dr James Jacob Vassumu, disclosed the position at a media dialogue on Friday in Yola. He stressed that the Agency, in conjunction with its development partners, has scheduled the special vaccination for November 5th to 12th, targeting 130,000 children in Gombi and Fufore LGAs. Dr Vassumu stated that the proposed exercise was carefully planned to strengthen immunity in the targeted communities of the two local councils as part of activities for the November 2026 National Plus Days Immunization Campaign. Vassumu said that the history of polio virus circulation, disease surveillance records, and assessment of immunisation coverage informed the choice of the exercise in Gombi and Fufore councils. He explained that the vaccination exercise will focus on children from zero to 59 months of age, with special emphasis on those living in hard-to-reach communities where routine immunisation coverage remains inadequate.

title: Blasts, missile attacks shake southern Saudi Arabia
body:
TEHRAN, Nov. 02 (MNA) – Media reports say explosions were heard in Khamis Mushait and Abha, while Najran in southern Saudi Arabia was targeted by missile attacks.
Media sources reported explosions in the Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha.
Najran in southern Saudi Arabia was targeted by missile attacks, according to published reports.
The reports did not specify the cause of the explosions or provide details on possible casualties or damage.

title: FG pays N13.87bn pension arrears to 18,822 retirees
body: The Pension Transitional Arrangement Directorate (PTAD) has paid N13.87bn in outstanding pension increment arrears to 18,822 retirees under the Defined Benefit Scheme (DBS). The beneficiaries include pensioners of the defunct Power Holding Company of Nigeria (PHCN) and five other government-linked organisations. The payments followed the implementation of pension increases of 13.8 per cent and 20.55 per cent, with some retirees receiving arrears accumulated over five years. This was disclosed in a statement issued yesterday by PTAD’s Head of Corporate Communications, Olugbenga Ajayi. The statement said the payments covered pension adjustments approved by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission. It stated that the directorate disbursed a total of N13,873,565,547.52 to the 18,822 pensioners. A breakdown of the payments showed that N9.42bn was paid to 7,391 pensioners of the defunct PHCN as arrears from a 13.8 per cent pension increase. The payments covered 65 months, from June 1, 2021, to October 31, 2026. The PHCN pensioners received about 67.9 per cent of the total amount disbursed, although they accounted for 39.3 per cent of the beneficiaries. PTAD also paid N4.46bn to 11,431 pensioners from five defunct organisations to settle 22 months of arrears arising from a 20.55 per cent pension increase. The affected organisations are Peoples Bank of Nigeria, Assurance Bank, NICON Insurance, Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation and NITEL/MTEL. The arrears covered the period from January 1, 2025, to October 31, 2026. The statement said the two pension increases were approved by the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission in a circular dated January 14, 2026. PTAD said the payments were part of its efforts to clear outstanding pension obligations and improve the welfare of retirees who served in government establishments.

title: Turn Nigeria’s diversity into prosperity, Tinubu tells citizens
body: President Bola Tinubu has urged Nigerians to embrace unity, peaceful coexistence and mutual understanding, irrespective of their ethnic, religious and cultural differences. Tinubu made the appeal on Sunday in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, while hosting members of his delegation to a dinner. He prayed to Almighty Allah to transform Nigeria’s diversity into a source of prosperity, unity, peace and sustainable development. “May Almighty Allah bless Nigeria, convert our diversity into prosperity as a country,” he said. The President also sought divine guidance for the country’s leaders and protection for Nigerians at home and abroad. He called for stronger bonds of brotherhood, patriotism and compassion, expressing confidence in the ability of Nigerians to overcome the country’s challenges through collective efforts. Tinubu said Nigeria’s abundant human and natural resources, coupled with the talents and enterprise of its diverse population, provided a strong foundation for inclusive growth. Speaking at the dinner, Kwara State Governor and Chairman of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum (NGF), AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, commended Tinubu’s commitment to national development. He pledged the governors’ continued prayers for the President and Nigeria, seeking divine guidance and strength for the administration. “Only Allah can reward you; we will continue to pray for you daily and pray for Nigeria that you lead. “May Allah continue to strengthen you in making the right decisions, strengthen your wisdom, your boldness, your audacity and your courage. “May Allah lead you to the right path,” AbdulRazaq said. The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi (SAN), also prayed for divine strength for Tinubu. He sought Allah’s guidance to enable the President to deliver justice and good governance to all Nigerians.

title: Zelensky: Ready to Meet Putin in Turkey, Rules Out Concessions
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was ready to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Turkey, expressing hope that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan could help arrange the talks.
In an interview with CNN Türk , Zelensky described direct negotiations at the presidential level as necessary, arguing that previous contacts between the two sides had failed to end Russia’s war against Ukraine .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We are ready for this meeting in Turkey. I know that President Erdoğan has his own ties with Putin. That is why we support holding a meeting in Turkey,” Zelensky said.
He argued that a face-to-face meeting could help resolve issues that have remained unsettled in negotiations between the countries’ delegations and technical working groups.
“That is precisely why I want to meet with him – as the person who makes the decisions,” Zelensky said.
He said a ceasefire along the front line and a mechanism to monitor compliance with any agreements should be among the main topics of a potential meeting.
He also said the leaders should discuss security guarantees, Ukraine’s reconstruction and the status of occupied territories. However, Zelensky ruled out accepting Putin’s demands that Ukraine hand over the Donbas or recognize Crimea as Russian territory, saying such concessions would violate the Ukrainian Constitution.
Zelensky also addressed the possibility of attending the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December, saying Ukraine had not yet received an official invitation from Washington.
He said there had been signals that US President Donald Trump might invite Ukraine, potentially alongside an initiative aimed at ending the war.
“The discussion touched upon the possibility that President Trump might invite us to the G20 summit and perhaps put forward an initiative aimed at ending the war. Naturally, if Trump extends an official invitation, we will welcome it,” Zelensky said.
The US invited Putin to the summit in September, raising the possibility of a meeting between the Russian leader and Trump. The Kremlin had previously rejected Zelensky’s proposal to meet Putin on the sidelines of the gathering.
On Saturday, Oct. 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington might invite Zelensky if his participation could help produce positive results. Trump also did not rule out the possibility on Nov. 1.
Zelensky stressed that any negotiations over ending the war must include Ukraine, rejecting the idea that other countries could decide its future without Kyiv’s involvement.
“It is impossible. You cannot decide Ukraine’s fate without Ukraine. That would be unfair and would lead nowhere. It is illogical to negotiate the fate of a country without the country itself being present,” he said.
He added that similar attempts by other leaders in the past had failed to produce results.
Zelensky also pointed to Russia’s failure to achieve its initial military objectives, despite its claims that it could conquer Ukraine within days.
“Russia, for instance, considered itself a great power and claimed it would conquer Ukraine in three days. We are now entering the fifth year of the war. For five years, Russia has been unable to conquer Ukraine,” he said.
He added that no third country had the right to negotiate matters of Ukrainian sovereignty without Ukraine’s direct participation.

title: Kaduna boosts school enrolment to 2.57m in 2025 – Uba Sani
body: Kaduna State has increased basic school enrolment from 2.17 million in 2022 to more than 2.57 million in 2025, Governor Uba Sani has said. The governor disclosed this through his deputy, Dr Hadiza Balarabe, at the close-out event of the UK-funded Partnership for Learning for All in Nigerian Education (PLANE) programme in Kaduna. He said the achievement reflected the state government’s commitment to expanding access to education and ensuring that more children had the opportunity to acquire basic education. Sani called on state governments to sustain the gains recorded under PLANE, stressing that the programme’s closure should not lead to a reversal of progress in education. “PLANE has done its part. It is now up to us, the state governments, to keep the progress going and to make sure that every child in our respective states has the opportunity to go to school and learn,” he said. The governor said the programme had made significant contributions to improving access to education, particularly for vulnerable children and those affected by emergencies. He urged stakeholders to continue investing in education and strengthening systems that would improve school enrolment, attendance and learning outcomes. The British High Commissioner to Nigeria, Pete Vowles, said PLANE had reached more than two million children and supported the training of over 25,000 teachers and facilitators across northern Nigeria since its launch in 2019. He said the programme had strengthened education policies, systems and institutions at federal and state levels.

title: Feature| Child marriage: ‘I was forced into marriage at the age of 14’
body: Married at 14 in exchange for cows, Nyanbuot is now a mother and is six months pregnant with her second child. Despite South Sudan’s laws protecting girls from early and forced marriage, she is still struggling to reclaim the future she once imagined. At 14, Nyanbuot was dreaming of becoming a doctor. She was in Primary Seven, studying in Kenya and imagining a future in which she could help pregnant women and mothers facing health challenges. But in January 2024, her life took a different turn. Without her knowledge or consent, she says, her relatives arranged her marriage to a man she had never met, in exchange for cows and other wealth. Now 17, Nyanbuot is a mother and is six months pregnant with her second child. Her education has been interrupted, her ambition of becoming a medical doctor put on hold, and her daily life shaped by responsibilities she says she was far too young to bear. “My family just decided to marry me off because of the cows. So, I was married into a family and to a man I had never met or seen in my life,” she said. The marriage was arranged while Nyanbuot was studying in Kenya. She said her relatives called her home during the Christmas period, assuring her that everything was fine. She had no idea that plans for her marriage had already been made. When she arrived in Rumbek, Lakes State, she discovered that her family had other intentions. “I was studying in Kenya, not in South Sudan. People just informed me during Christmas time that I should come back and see the family. When I came, I stayed for only two days before they married me off immediately,” she said. A childhood interrupted For Nyanbuot, the transition from schoolgirl to wife was overwhelming. She said her first pregnancy was particularly difficult, as she struggled to cope with household duties while carrying a child and adjusting to a husband she barely knew. “I am not feeling okay because this is a very new life to me. Imagine, someone who is a child like me is also carrying another child,” she said. “It was really very hard in the past months when I was pregnant. I struggled to cook while I was also pregnant. Sometimes, he could beat me, and I could not talk to him because he was someone I did not love.” She said that when she tried to turn to her parents for help, they also beat her rather than offering support. Leaving the marriage, she added, was not a straightforward option. Her family had received cows in exchange for her, and she feared that her relatives, particularly her brothers who owned the animals, would refuse to take her back. “My brothers, who received the cows, would not be happy to accept me back from the marriage. They could also chase me back to the man. So, my life was very hard,” she said. Her concerns are compounded by the demands of raising a young child in a household where, she said, her husband struggles to provide for the family. “I sometimes wonder why my family members put me into this difficult life because I am suffering, and my little child is also suffering. This man does not have anything apart from the cows he gave to my parents,” she said. Now six months pregnant again, Nyanbuot faces the prospect of raising two children while still trying to understand and cope with a life she says she never chose. A wider concern Nyanbuot’s experience is not isolated. Forced and early marriage, often linked to the payment of cattle as bride wealth, has been documented in Lakes State, where girls have also faced violence for resisting family-arranged unions. In April 2019, a 20-year-old girl was beaten to death in Yirol after refusing to marry a man selected by her family. The suitor had offered 40 cows to the family. In May 2020, a 20-year-old woman was beaten to death by her brothers in Rumbek Centre after rejecting a marriage arranged by her family. In February 2025, a girl was hospitalised in Rumbek after her brothers beat her for refusing a marriage partner chosen by her family. A 2023 briefing by Saferworld on gender-based violence in Lakes State also identified forced marriage as a serious concern affecting girls. The cases highlight the risks faced by girls who resist marriages arranged by relatives, particularly where cattle payments influence family decisions. Law protects girls South Sudan has legal provisions intended to protect girls from early and forced marriage, violence and practices that undermine their dignity, health and education. Yet Nyanbuot’s experience raises questions about how effectively those protections are being implemented in communities. Article 15 of the Transitional Constitution of South Sudan provides that no marriage shall be entered into without the free and full consent of the man and woman intending to marry. Article 17 defines a child as anyone below the age of 18 and guarantees children protection from harmful cultural practices affecting their health, welfare or dignity. It also requires the best interests of the child to be the primary consideration in decisions concerning children. The Child Act 2008 provides more specific safeguards. Section 23 guarantees every child protection from early marriage and cultural or traditional practices likely to harm their health, welfare, dignity or physical and psychological development. Section 26(1) specifically protects girls from sexual abuse, exploitation and gender-based violence, including early and forced marriage. The same section guarantees girls equal access to education and training. It also states that no girl should be expelled from school because of pregnancy or motherhood or prevented from continuing her education after one year of lactation. South Sudan’s legal framework therefore recognises children’s rights to protection, education and development. But the existence of these provisions has not necessarily translated into effective protection for girls facing pressure from their families and communities. Still dreaming of school Despite the difficulties, Nyanbuot has not abandoned the ambition she held as a schoolgirl. She wants to return to the classroom, complete her education and eventually become a doctor. She hopes to help pregnant women and mothers facing health challenges, drawing on some of the difficulties she has experienced herself. “Yes, I still have hope of going back to school because I had a good dream of becoming a doctor. But now I am just at home. I want to become educated so that my children can have an educated mother in the family and so that I can also help pregnant mothers,” she said. She said her husband had previously agreed, following discussions with some of her maternal uncles, to allow her to resume her studies and complete Primary Eight. But that agreement did not last. When she raised the matter again, she said, her husband refused to let her return to school, questioning the value of education for a married woman. “When I tried to tell him to let me go back to school because he had agreed the previous time, he refused and asked me what the benefit of education was. He told me that I was now his wife and had no decision to make unless he decided. So, he refused to take me back to school,” she said. Returning to education would also require practical and financial support. With a young child to care for and another on the way, she said she needed a way to earn an income while pursuing her studies. She is particularly interested in vocational training, especially tailoring, which she hopes would enable her to establish a small business. “I would want life skills training and vocational training, such as tailoring, so that I can start a small business. I will be able to provide food for my child, buy medicine and also meet my own needs, including scholastic materials, as I continue with my studies,” she said. Without an independent source of income, she fears that returning to school would leave her struggling to meet her children’s needs. Rethinking marriage tradition Nyanbuot’s ambitions now extend beyond rebuilding her own life. She wants to help prevent other girls from experiencing what happened to her. She believes traditional leaders, particularly chiefs, could play an important role in challenging early and forced marriages in Lakes State because of the influence they wield within communities. “If I am given an opportunity to serve my community, I would talk to the elders, especially the chiefs. These are people who are always respected, and their voices are heard in the community. I would engage them so that they can take action against anyone who tries to marry off a schoolgirl,” she said. Looking back, she said fear had prevented her from reporting her own situation. She worried that seeking assistance from a human rights organisation or the police would cause her parents to disown her. “During my time, I was afraid that if I reported myself to an NGO supporting girls’ education or the police, my parents would disown me. But now I have seen that these organisations are helping girls facing forced marriage,” she said. Traditional leaders face challenges Majak Deng Mabok, Executive Chief of Ayen Paciec Boma in Maleng-agok Payam, Rumbek East County, spoke to Radio Tamazuj about the issue. He said traditional authorities were working to discourage early and forced marriages through community awareness campaigns and dialogue with families. But he acknowledged that identifying and addressing cases remained difficult, partly because many girls did not report marriages arranged against their wishes. “Most victims of forced marriage do not come to us or show up to tell us that they are victims,” he said. Majak Deng Mabok, Executive Chief of Ayen Paciec Boma in Maleng-agok Payam, Rumbek East County (Photo: Radio Tamazuj) Majak said traditional authorities had recorded three cases of forced marriage this year. One had been successfully addressed, while two remained unresolved after families insisted on making their own decisions. He said customary courts engaged parents and encouraged them to give girls time to grow up and complete their education before marriage. “Even if both parents agree to marry the girl, we still give her time, at least one year, to grow to the marriageable age of 18 years,” he said. He added that traditional leaders could intervene through dialogue with families and, where parents refused to heed their advice, order the arrest of those involved in arranging forced marriages. However, he said their ability to act is limited when girls don’t personally come forward to challenge the arrangements. “It would have been good if a victim came and said, ‘I don’t want this marriage.’ Then the customary court would intervene by any means. There are ways for the traditional court to intervene, including holding dialogue with both parents,” he said. Majak’s account highlights the importance of reporting and community intervention, but Nyanbuot’s experience illustrates the difficulties girls can face when the very families expected to protect them are involved in arranging their marriages. For her, the consequences have been far-reaching: an interrupted education, an early pregnancy, domestic responsibilities and a struggle to secure independence. Yet she continues to imagine a different future, one in which she can return to school, support her children and perhaps one day fulfil her ambition of becoming a doctor. Her message to parents is simple: give girls the chance to grow up and decide their own futures. “I want parents to allow their daughters to continue their education and reach an appropriate age before getting married,” she said. Note: This feature story is part of a series amplifying the voices of girls across South Sudan, sharing their personal experiences, challenges, hopes and aspirations, and highlighting the issues affecting their rights, safety and future. title: Inside the world of Filipino embalmers
body: First of two parts For 19 years now, 48-year-old Joycel Regalado has made a living by facing death. She works on the remains of the departed, making sure that the memory of a beloved who has gone ahead of grieving family members is preserved. It is a final act of honoring that memory, of bringing comfort to the afflicted. She had not always been interested in this kind of service — mortuary science, or the study of managing deceased human bodies. The closest she had been to it was helping with the processing of death certificates for the funeral services business of her relatives. They persuaded her to get a license for embalmers so she could help in the business. At age 23, she enrolled in an accredited Department of Health training program for embalmers and undertakers. On her first try, she passed the licensure exam and decided to head to Manila to try her luck. She left Bacolod to prove to her family that she wasn’t meant for just paperwork, and that she was actually capable of doing the work itself. Joycel ended up with Arlington Memorial Chapels along Gregorio Araneta Avenue in Quezon City, armed with the necessary guts to do the job of respectfully handling the dead. As senior embalmer at Arlington today, she has done services for more than a decade already, multiple times daily. She still remembers her first time working on the remains of a baby. Already wearing her protective gear, she couldn’t help but weep with the bereaved family as she felt their anguish. “Mahirap kasi nanay din ako.… [Pero] kahit umiiyak, gagawin ko…Iniisip ko na lang na kailangan ko itong gawin para ma-preserve din yung baby [at] makita siya ng mommy niya, ng pamilya niya,” she recalled. (It was difficult because I am also a mother…. But even if I was crying, I did my job…I was thinking that I needed to do it to preserve the baby so the mother and family could still see the body.) The task is not that different, day in and day out. She receives the body from the hospital, washes it thoroughly, sets the features of the face, drains the blood and injects formalin — the chemical that preserves the body — into the arteries. Organs are drained and formalin is injected into the body cavities to preserve the organs. She double checks where fluids could leak from incisions in veins and arteries then stitches parts of the body. After she washes and dries the body, she grooms it, using a photograph of the deceased as her guide. Light cosmetics are applied to restore skin tone before the body is dressed in clothes provided by the family. It is finally put in a casket for viewing. COVER. Joycel Regalado prepares clothes and grooming tools for a deceased older woman she has embalmed. Jake Gomez/Rappler The entire process takes an average of two to four hours, in some cases possibly longer, depending on the body’s condition. ‘Nasanay na ako’ 47-year-old, on-call embalmer RJ Cabillan has been in practice longer than Joycel. For him, it’s been almost 25 years of constantly seeing the dead at multiple funeral homes every week. “Hindi na bago sa akin ’yung mga body, mga katawan ng pasyente, mga namamatayan. Kasi wala na, nasanay na ako,” he said. (The bodies of patients and relatives of people who have passed away are nothing new to me. I’ve simply gotten used to it.) MORGUE. Embalmer RJ Cabillan shows some of the tools he regularly uses at Belmont Funeral Service – a trocar needle and an aspirating syringe, used to drain the body of fluids. Eirene Manatlao/Rappler He had grown accustomed to being around bodies of the deceased since he had been accompanying his father — also an on-call embalmer — to work as early as age 9 or 10. By age 13, RJ began assisting his father in embalming the dead. “ That’s how I acquired the skills and eventually entered the field of embalming,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino. After finishing high school, he first took on a construction job. But after he got weary of contractual setups, his father persuaded him to return to the embalming business. He did in 2001, and has never looked back since. RJ found his way to Belmont Funeral Services in Novaliches, Quezon City, where he’s been working as resident embalmer for four years. Like Joycel, RJ could not help tearing up while also embalming a baby. The experience, he said, reminded him of a personal tragedy — when three of his children passed away about two years apart, owing to pregnancy complications. “Mapapaluha ka rin kahit anong tigas mo…Hindi mo maiiwasan ’yun.” (No matter how tough you are, you can’t help but end up in tears…There’s no avoiding it.) No matter how difficult it was, RJ said he had to keep doing his job and pushing forward. Comparisons Years of experience have desensitized both Joycel and RJ to the sensory demands and anxieties of mortuary work. Although both share the same job description as an embalmer, their daily routines differ based on the clientele they serve: Joycel works at a high-end facility, while RJ provides embalming services to low- and middle-income funeral homes. As an in-house embalmer at Arlington, Joycel has a fixed shift schedule and focuses only on her areas of responsibility. RJ, for his part, waits for calls from four of the funeral homes he also serves. Joycel has a fixed salary. Pay for senior embalmers can range from P25,000 to P30,000, depending on experience, on top of which is a benefits package that includes a rice subsidy, clothing and footwear allowance, routine medical checkups, and job-related hazard vaccinations. They have comprehensive machines, equipment, and a broader range of amenities. EQUIPMENT. Regalado uses an arterial injection pump (white equipment), along with other tools, to pump formalin through the arteries. Jake Gomez/Rappler RJ, on the other hand, charges P1,000 per body for his services. There have been times when he has had to manually pump formalin because of the absence of automated machinery. MANUAL. Cabillan uses syringes and needles to manually pump formalin and drain bodily fluids. Eirene Manatlao/Rappler Compared to other countries, their pay is extremely low, considering the hazards of the job. Joycel recalled preparing a corpse that had live worms in its legs. After an extremely repulsive experience, RJ now declines to embalm decomposed bodies. Both work on four to six bodies a day, depending on the month. Joycel said work gets heavier during the hotter seasons. Their counterparts in the US are paid much higher. In 2025, embalmers in the US received an average annual salary of P3.7 million* or around P300,000 a month. Unusual work Not many appreciate the work that embalmers do. Joycel said she has been asked, “Out of all the jobs out there, why is that your job?” While embalming was once belittled as an occupation, Joycel said she aims to challenge that perception, emphasizing that embalmers complete formal studies and earn professional licenses. When RJ was once asked how he is able to handle bodies of the deceased at work every day, he replied, “For me, that’s just normal. Given how long I’ve had this experience, I’m no longer afraid.” Joycel asked: “ Kung wala kami, sino ang mag-aayos ng patay?” (If we weren’t here, who would take care of the dead?) She takes pride in her work. “Embalmers are still needed; embalmers are still in demand,” she said. Valuing life Her job has taught Joycel to value her time with the living. “I realized that life is not just about work. I need to set aside time and balance for my family’s well-being, as well as for how I interact with others. Be kind, be understanding. Be good, and do good,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino. RJ echoed the importance of time with family, adding that accepting death as a part of life is a better way to look at things. “Because we’ll arrive at the same outcome at some point in our lives,” he said. For Joycel, her job as an embalmer is her ultimate good deed. “What we do for the deceased…We bring comfort to their families. We help lighten their [spirits]. That’s the only way I look at it.” (To be concluded) – Rappler.com NEXT: Filipino embalmers — last caretakers of the dead, seldom cared for *$1 = P63.74 as of October 30,2026
