title: F/OSS Comics #13: BSD Unix, Part 3 – The Beginning of BSD Unix
body:
When Ken Thompson returned to Bell Labs in 1976, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley began exploring the Unix kernel themselves.
Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel.
Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler.
Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape.
In early 1977, Bill Joy put together the Berkeley Software Distribution, or BSD, bundling the Pascal system with ex, a line editor developed from em. Early BSD was not a standalone operating system: it was a collection of software to install on an existing Unix system. About thirty copies were sent out over the following year. [1]
At the time, an AT&T Unix source license was needed to get BSD. Berkeley charged only for the tape and distribution. [2]
If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage.
Berkeley already had a tradition of sharing research software. BSD carried it on. Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, hippie culture, and antiwar activism are also said to have influenced Joy's decision to charge so little. [2]
Universities and research institutions could obtain Unix, including its source code, for a modest licensing fee. This also helped the system spread. [2] [6]
We have Unix, but the antitrust agreement bars us from the computer business... We can't sell it as a product, either.
After the first BSD distribution, Joy improved the Pascal system based on user feedback. He bundled it with vi (ex's visual mode), the C shell, and other tools to form the Second Berkeley Software Distribution, or 2BSD. Nearly seventy-five tapes were shipped over the following year. [1] [5]
Joy did more than fix bugs. He handled every distribution request, copied BSD onto tapes, and mailed them out himself.
Professor Fateman's group is getting a VAX. It's 32-bit, with a whole megabyte of memory.
They've already got VAX Unix from Bell Labs. It's called 32/V.
My adviser asked me to add virtual memory to VAX Unix. Could you look over the code?
Babaoglu was a Berkeley graduate student working with Professor Domenico Ferrari. Joy helped him integrate the virtual-memory code into 32/V and debug it. [1] [4]
At the time, 32/V did not use the VAX hardware's virtual-memory capabilities. A program's address space was limited by physical memory, but Professor Richard Fateman's work on the computer algebra system Macsyma needed more. Virtual memory uses disk storage to give programs an address space larger than physical memory. [1]
Macsyma, developed at MIT beginning in the late 1960s, worked with symbolic expressions. It could factor expressions, compute derivatives, and perform integration.
Debugging continued through the holidays at the end of 1978.
Might as well debug this while fewer people are using the VAX.
By January 1979, most of the bugs had been fixed. [1]
Joy ported ex, vi, the C shell, and other 2BSD tools to the VAX, while Peter Kessler and Marshall Kirk McKusick ported the Pascal system. These programs were bundled with the standard 32/V utilities and the virtual-memory kernel that Babaoglu and Joy had integrated and debugged. The result was 3BSD, which began shipping in December 1979. [1]
Since 1969, ARPANET had linked research institutions funded by DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. [3] But these institutions used different computers and operating systems, so they often couldn't share software. Porting the existing software to new machines was also costly. DARPA became interested in Unix's portability, and took notice of Berkeley's successful distribution of 3BSD to research institutions. [1]

title: Stevens endorses Rogers amid rift with El-Sayed
body: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday amid a rift with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed that has come front and center in the final sprint to Election Day. "Our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video posted on social media Sunday. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."Stevens appeared alongside Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday. Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in August, where she was heavily supported by the Senate Democrats' campaign arm, called on El-Sayed last week to condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. military aid to Israel to rising grocery prices, which she characterized as antisemitic. El-Sayed accused Stevens of "relitigating a primary that ended three months ago," although he has also clarified that the ad "was not made by me" and said he disagrees with its contents.El-Sayed pushed to return the attention to the issues facing Michigan voters as he takes on the GOP candidate, Rogers. But Rogers praised Stevens on Friday for calling on El-Sayed to denounce the ad, and for expressing concerns raised by Michigan Jewish voters. "Representative Haley Stevens is a courageous leader who deserves the respect of every Michigan voter," Rogers said in a post on X. "She has conducted herself with nothing but class since the Democratic primary, a primary where a majority of voters did not vote for her party's nominee."Speaking to reporters after he appeared with Stevens at the Detroit church Sunday, Rogers said he was honored to receive her support."This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else," Rogers said. Rogers said he got the call Sunday morning from Stevens, and the two decided to appear together at the church. He said he and Stevens talked about what was better for the future of the state. And he noted that Stevens reminded him at the end of their call that she remains a Democrat. Responding to the endorsement on Sunday, El-Sayed said, "I actually don't think about Haley Stevens.""This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones who are talking about."Stevens said she's "not trying to harm" the Democratic Party with the move, insisting that she isn't "turning her back on Democrats."  "It is this one vote," she said. "And I will tell you why: Because when you see hate, when you see us standing with Hasan Piker, and repeated hate, it's not acceptable.""That's it. It's my personal and private decision," Stevens said. "It's a Michigan moment, and everyone is entitled to their opinion."Stevens said she "meant it" when she previously endorsed El-Sayed. But she added, "He chose to close his campaign by saying I wasn't welcome."The appearance with Rogers came after Stevens had been expected to appear with El-Sayed at a unity event Sunday alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. But El-Sayed said Saturday, "I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign."Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, said last week that he is voting for Rogers. Democrats stunned by reversal, Trump praises StevensAfter Stevens endorsed Rogers, top Democrats expressed their continued support for El-Sayed's candidacy, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer."Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said in a statement. In a post on X, Schumer called it a "despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens."Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan said Michiganders "want leaders focused on making their lives more affordable.""That's what they're talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens' continued efforts to get attention," she said in a statement. "  If we are going to fight to improve the lives of working men and women in Michigan, we must stay focused on electing Democrats up and down the ballot, and that includes electing Abdul El-Sayed as Michigan's next senator." Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel posted on social media that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."President Trump praised Stevens for backing Rogers."Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did."He told reporters later: "That was a big move, I think. Nobody expected that, but it's a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country. So I thought that was fantastic."Appearing with Mr. Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said  he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers and "encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth."More broadly, Republicans cited the move as they billed El-Sayed as too liberal for the state. "Democrats who feel Abdul has abandoned them have a home with Mike, who is building a winning coalition of Democrats, Independents, and Republicans to save Michigan from El-Sayed's radical, terrorist-sympathizing agenda," Republican National Committee spokesman Hunter Lovell said in a statement. "The center of Michigan politics has moved, and Abdul is on the wrong side of it."Stevens defends endorsing RogersStevens on Sunday night gave her first interview since she endorsed Rogers, telling CNN's Anderson Cooper she felt like there was a "weight off my shoulders."During their 15-minute interview, Cooper repeatedly asked Stevens why she changed her mind after she reportedly told her colleague Rep. Debbie Dingell in a phone conversation Saturday night that she was not going to endorse Rogers. Stevens confirmed the conversation took place but never gave Cooper a direct answer about what changed her mind. She told him, "That's just where I landed with this. I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and, you know, focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."Asked again what changed her mind, Stevens replied, "I was there and just, you know, alone with my thoughts. I was writing things out, and look, this level of anger and the things that we are seeing — look, we all want Democrats to win. I'm a really proud Democrat. And by the way, Abdul's got every other Democrat with him. He just doesn't have me and a few other people who love this party.""Nothing with me changed, Anderson," said Stevens, who had previously endorsed El-Sayed.Stevens cited El-Sayed's alliance with left-wing streamer and political commentator Hasan Piker and a controversial ad from Rebellion PAC that tied the war in Gaza to increased costs at home. It shows a couple in a grocery store shopping for food for their children, and the woman instructs her husband to put the eggs back. The children still "like eggs," she tells him. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." El-Sayed said his campaign had nothing to do with the ad."That ad was very painful," Stevens said. "There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they're just being told, 'Hey, this is a party you don't belong in, or this is a campaign you don't belong in.'"Stevens told Cooper she "absolutely" wants Democrats to take control of the Senate after Election Day and that it's essential for Democrats to retain the seat in Michigan to take control of the Senate.Cooper pointed out that in August, Stevens had posted on social media that Rogers would be "another rubber stamp for Donald Trump's dangerous agenda. We can't afford to give MAGA another Senate seat in November." He asked Stevens, "Why is it OK now ... why can you afford to give MAGA another Senate seat in November?" Stevens replied, "Well, why is it OK to have the Democratic Party and a top nominee injecting ... this type of anger and lack of kindness?"Cooper asked if she was referring to being disinvited from a planned joint appearance with El-Sayed Sunday."Anderson, I was just trying to help this campaign and stand up for people who feel hurt," Stevens replied. Cooper interviewed Dingell following Stevens' appearance, and Dingell described the back-and-forth between the CNN host and her colleague as "one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.""I'm very concerned that this has all become a distraction," Dingell said.Stevens' team resigns after endorsementAhead of Stevens' endorsement of Rogers and her appearance on Sunday, her longtime chief of staff resigned, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon.In a statement first shared by CNN, Stevens' former chief of staff Justin German said he and the team are "shocked and heartbroken" by her decision to support Rogers and that they are "wholeheartedly supporting" El-Sayed for Senate."This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines," German wrote. "Those of us who are Michigan voters are supporting Democrats up and down the ballot and have been working all season to elect strong Democratic majorities to the House and Senate — we will continue to do so.""Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens," an automated email reply from Stevens' former communications director, Logan Basch, reads.Joetta Appiah, Stevens' former press secretary and campaign spokesperson, said in a statement that Stevens is "walking back on everything her campaign stood for.""Michiganders deserve better, and they need to stay focused on what matters, which is electing Abdul to the Senate to stand up to Donald Trump, hold his administration accountable, and fight to lower costs for Michiganders," Appiah said. "We cannot let this distract us from Tuesday."60 MINUTES will feature Ross Douthat's exclusive interviews with Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers.

title: Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA
body:
The jet departed from Austin, Texas, for the Bahamas, the FAA said.
A Learjet believed to be carrying nine people crashed on Sunday afternoon in Palm Beach County, Florida, after making a rapid dive of about 350 feet per second, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The plane, a 22-year-old twin-engine Learjet 60, crashed after taking off from Austin, Texas, and was headed to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas, according to the FAA.
The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, the FAA said.
Photos and videos online showed a jet hitting the ground nose-first and bursting into a fireball. The impact of the crash left a crater near a shopping center.
The jet crashed near Military Trail, between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue, in the Greenacres community of Palm Beach County, authorities said.
There was no immediate word from authorities on deaths and injuries.
The plane went from 35,250 feet to 8,750 feet in a little over a minute, or roughly 350 feet per second, before it slammed into the ground, according to the FAA.
"Obviously, this was a cataclysmic plane crash," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said during a press briefing on Sunday. "It looked like a missile going down. It left a big crater on the side of the road."
"I think people will recognize this as a major tragedy," he said.
According to records, the plane belongs to a private company and has been used as a rental in the past.

title: Ukrainian Film Festival kicks off in Poland on Nov 2, with 50 films to be screened in 12 cities
body:
Beata Bieronska-Lach, director of the Ukraine! Film Festival, announced this in an interview with Ukrinform.
According to her, despite the full-scale war, Ukraine's film industry continues to develop, particularly thanks to international cooperation and foreign funding.
"Every year, I worry about whether we will have enough Ukrainian films and whether there will be anything to screen. I fear that film production might grind to a halt under wartime conditions... However, my concerns have proved unfounded: Ukrainian films are being made. If not directly in Ukraine, then through numerous international co-productions. Ukrainian filmmakers have started looking for funding abroad, and they are succeeding. There are many funds that finance Ukrainian cinema," Bieronska-Lach said.
She said that this year's festival program will include Polish-Ukrainian and German-Ukrainian co-productions. The competition program will feature eight full-length fiction films, nine documentaries and 23 short films. Screenings of children's films and a separate section dedicated to Belarusian cinema are also planned.
The festival director noted that after the screenings in Warsaw, the festival will continue in 11 other cities: Krakow, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Lublin, Gliwice, Lodz, Rzeszow, Plock, Bielsko-Biala, Zielona Gora and Poznan. The screenings will run until mid-December.
The organizer said the festival's geographical reach is changing. This year, screenings will not take place in Torun because the institution that previously hosted the event is undergoing restructuring. At the same time, new cities and organizations are joining the festival.
"Overall, the cities and cinemas that hosted the festival in previous years want to continue working with us. At the same time, new institutions are emerging and approaching us on their own initiative because they want to screen Ukrainian films," Bieronnska-Lach said.
According to her, these are most often Polish organizations, foundations or cinemas seeking to respond to demand from local communities. In cities with large Ukrainian communities, such screenings make it possible to organize joint cultural events for Ukrainians and Poles and promote integration within local communities.
The festival director said that Bielsko-Biala and Zielona Gora are the new venues this year. According to her, the cities themselves expressed interest in joining the event.
Bieronnska-Lach also noted that Polish cinemas continue to show interest in Ukrainian films. Last year, she feared that amid some cooling in Ukrainian-Polish relations, cinemas would gradually lose interest and withdraw from screenings, sometimes suggesting postponing them until the following year.
"Instead, we can see today that interest remains, which means the films will be screened in various cities," Bieronnska-Lach said.

title: Fact-checking El-Sayed and Rogers on 60 Minutes
body: With 48 hours to go before polls close in Michigan, few midterm races in the country have captured as much attention as the contest playing out between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.Rogers is seeking to become Michigan's first Republican U.S. senator in 25 years, as Democrats try to hold onto the seat. The contest has become increasingly tense in recent days, with El-Sayed engaged in a public rift with his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, who he beat by fewer than 15,000 votes.In a stunning turn, Stevens, who had been expected to appear alongside El-Sayed at a campaign event, instead appeared with Rogers Sunday at a Detroit church service – and endorsed him for Senate. "I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted Sunday on social media. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, called Stevens' move a "despicable betrayal."It was only the latest turn in a hotly contested, closely watched race, which is why we led tonight's 60 Minutes broadcast with this story. Correspondent Ross Douthat sat down with both candidates as they made their cases to Michigan voters: on the economy, healthcare, Israel and other issues that have come to define the race.The contest is close and contentious. On the campaign trail, President Trump has been throwing his support behind Rogers and disparaging El-Sayed as a "jihadist."Along with the broadcast segment, we decided to post extended interviews with El-Sayed and Rogers. We're doing so for a simple reason: these conversations are in the public interest. And we owe our viewers as much transparency as possible—especially in a race of such consequence.60 Minutes sat down with each candidate for more than an hour in late October. In their interviews, both candidates made several claims that were false, misleading or unsupported by our reporting. We believe it is important to share those claims and provide the facts and context viewers need to evaluate them:Rogers claims El-Sayed wrote a letter supporting Muslim BrotherhoodRogers claimed that El-Sayed "wrote a letter in support for the Muslim Brotherhood … when they took over Egypt in 20 — whatever that was, 2012 and 2013 — that I think is very, very concerning. And, again, it's not about how he prays. It is his ideology. It's the way he thinks."Our reporting shows that after the Arab Spring, El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian-Americans who signed a letter addressed to Egypt's new democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, who was a senior leader of the Muslim Brotherhood. The letter urged Morsi to take action against allies of the country's previous authoritarian leader. At the time, the United States had not designated the organization as a terrorist group. Earlier this year, the Trump administration called branches of the organization terrorist entities.El-Sayed denies any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and has publicly disavowed the group.  El-Sayed claims Michigan utility DTE "buys off almost every politician in our state"When asked to give an example of a monopoly that has held power over an extended period of time, El-Sayed named DTE, saying, "They have raised our rates faster than in 46 other states over the past 20 years. They buy off almost every politician in our state, so that, you know, they all look the other way and they just make money hand over fist."DTE and its political action committee have made extensive, publicly reported contributions to Michigan politicians, including a large majority of state legislators, but 60 Minutes found no evidence that DTE made improper payments in exchange for votes or regulatory decisions. El-Sayed claims Rogers "made 14 million bucks" after leaving CongressEl-Sayed said "the rules of our game in politics are about taking corporate money to do corporate bidding and then make money on the back end of the same corporations you're regulating" and suggested his opponent has "played that game.""He made 14 million bucks and moved to Florida, bought a mansion and two yachts, and he's watching Donald Trump play that game and make billions," El-Sayed claimed.Financial disclosures show Rogers' household net worth rose substantially after he left office in 2015, to an estimated $7 million to $14 million or more, but those figures reflect net worth, not earnings, and 60 Minutes was unable to verify that Rogers made $14 million.  As for the yachts, Rogers registered two boats in Maryland (32 feet and 39 feet, respectively) and sold one before registering the other.Rogers calls El-Sayed a Democratic socialistRogers called his opponent "a very gifted Democrat Socialist of America." While El-Sayed has campaigned with some prominent Democratic socialists, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, nor has the group officially endorsed him.When Douthat asked El-Sayed, "Were you ever a socialist," the candidate responded: "No. I'm a capitalist." Rogers says El-Sayed wants to defund the policeWhile expounding on El-Sayed as a Democratic socialist, Rogers said: "If you look at his issue set, defund the police, let people out of prison, all of the things that are associated with that Democrat socialist, big government — government taking over private health care, you lose your private health insurance, that's all DSA."It's true that El-Sayed called for defunding the police back in 2020 following the killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. El-Sayed recently called it "a pretty dumb and unnuanced slogan" but said "that was the conversation that was happening." Most recently while campaigning for the Senate, El-Sayed has called for increased funding for police recruitment, retention and retirement.Watch: Extended interview with El-SayedWatch: Extended interview with Rogers

title: Victor Wembanyama navigates uncharted territory on the court
body: San Antonio Spurs star center Victor Wembanyama says there's no blueprint for how to play the game with his unique combination of size and skill.At 7-foot-4, the 22-year-old reigning Defensive Player of the Year gave insight into how he trains and envisions his career. "I think the key is being comfortable not knowing, being comfortable finding out my own answers," he said, adding, "I am comfortable not knowing my answers. I am comfortable walking through the fog."Wembanyama reflects on Spurs' 4–1 series loss to the New York KnicksWembanyama says he felt like his head was poking through that fog last season when the Spurs were on a winning streak. "Last year, there was this, I think the month of February, we didn't lose a single game," he said. "[These are the] moments where everything clicks, you know."The Spurs kept clicking through the spring. The team beat the Oklahoma City Thunder in the Western Conference finals. But then, despite being favored in the Finals, San Antonio lost in five games to the New York Knicks. Wembanyama, by his own admission, was far from his best.He was portrayed as a villain in the Finals, but he said that didn't bother him."It showed my limits more than anything else," he said. "Going out there, you need to play basketball. You don't need to beat the s**t out of people — if you want to win, at least.""A winner's franchise"That self-awareness comes from someone just starting his fourth NBA season. Wembanyama was a teen in France when he first appeared on scouts' radars. He was the most anticipated rookie since LeBron James 20 years earlier. It was a given he would be the top pick in the 2023 draft.The draft pick brought him from the Paris suburbs to one of the NBA's smallest markets. For Wembanyama, it was the perfect pairing of player and franchise. "The franchise with the greatest coach of all time, the franchise with a big French history as well," he said. "And yeah, just winning. A winner's franchise, you know?"Wembanyama is talking about Gregg Popovich, who retired from coaching in 2025, but not before leading the Spurs to five NBA titles. Wembanyama says Popovich taught him about humility."He often said something when we were in film, 'After a win, you're rarely as good as you thought you were, and after a loss you're rarely as bad as you thought you were,'" Wembanyama said.The key to Wemby's careerAfter a blood clot in his shoulder shut down his second season, Wembanyama doubled down on his conditioning. Wembanyama says because big men have often had problems with their feet, he is preoccupied with strengthening his. "I also find more and more that feet are responsible for so much more that goes on," Wembanyama said. "It's funny, because I was just talking to a rookie. I went to practice barefoot, and he sees me walking without shoes, and he's like, 'I didn't know you could just not wear shoes.'"Wembanyama's an evangelist for going barefoot."I try to walk barefoot as much as I can, and wear minimalistic shoes," he said.Shoes that don't respect the natural shape of the foot, he said, don't do anything to strengthen the feet. "If you got a good foot strength, which brings a good foot posture, everything else can develop the right way: knee, hip and back, everything," Wembanyama said.Lessons from monks and chess players Wembanyama says curiosity is his defining trait. In the summer of 2025, he went to China where he learned kung fu and meditation from Shaolin monks."It was hard because they push you to the next level," Wembanyama said. He could lock in and meditate for around a half hour, "and then an hour and a half wondering, 'How much longer is it going to go on for?'"Wembanyama says you could call what he does at the free throw line meditation. When asked what's going through his mind, he says "nothing for a second and then focusing on making the shot"His curiosity has also led him to develop his game as a chess player. Wembanyama says there is overlap between basketball and chess. "I find that chess is a lot about decision-making," he said. "And that looks like basketball a lot, at least in theory. Because there are some theoretical good moves."A Frenchman in TexasThis past summer, Wembanyama returned to France where he runs an annual tournament that combines chess with basketball. On the same trip home, he hosted his Spurs teammates. "I wanted to show them, you know, the refinement at times, but also how I would take care of them, you know? Because it really matters to me," he said. "But it did more for me than for them that they came."When asked what he tells people back home when they ask him what it's like to live in the U.S., Wembanyama rejects the premise of the question."My answer is always, 'Well, I don't know, because I don't live a normal life in the U.S.' I live the life of an athlete, of a rich person, you know, the life of somebody that's going to have everything taken care of, you know, no matter what I do, really," he said. "It's not the life of the regular American. But it's the best country to be an athlete in."

title: Democratic Rep. Stevens endorses GOP candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan US Senate race
body:
Stevens and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed have feuded publicly recently.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan's race for the U.S. Senate against Democratic nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, she said Sunday – a stunning move after Stevens had previously said she would support El-Sayed.
“Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today. I don't belong in Abdul's campaign,” Stevens said in part in a video posted on social media on Sunday .
El-Sayed and Stevens faced off in an acrimonious primary, but had seemingly mended fences afterward. However, in recent days a new dispute spilled out into the open after Stevens had asked El-Sayed to disavow an ad from an outside group that she said was antisemitic. Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, has also said he plans to vote for Mike Rogers, and attended an event with Mike Rogers and Sen. Ted Cruz last week.
In a joint press conference after the endorsement, Stevens defended the decision as one that is right for Michigan, adding that it was about standing "with country."
Stevens said that “90% of the votes I'm going to cast are going to be for Democrats. My vote for Senate, I am just one vote, as is every Michigander. My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers. And I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country."
She said El-Sayed boxed her out of his campaign. "I did endorse the Democratic nominee, and he chose to close his campaign by saying I wasn't welcome… This is about looking in the mirror about how real Democrats for Rogers are."
Stevens also attended a Black church service on Sunday in Detroit with Rogers. A Rogers campaign representative posted a photo on X Sunday morning of Stevens and Rogers standing side-by-side at the service.
As recently as last week, Stevens told CNN that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying "Of course I'm voting, you know, for our Democratic nominee for Senate. I'm voting for the Democratic ticket."
El-Sayed attended a Black church service at a different church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens had been previously expected to appear with him, but the joint appearance was thrown into doubt after the newfound dispute broke out into the open.
"At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," El-Sayed said of her endorsement Sunday in remarks to the press after the service, alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C), who attended the service with him.
“So I have a sense that you all are here today because of the decisions of somebody who's not here right now. Am I right about that?" El-Sayed said. "But I'm just going to tell you, this is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about,” he went on, bringing up gas prices, grocery costs, and air and water quality as examples of issues Michigan voters are dealing with.
President Donald Trump lavished praise on Stevens in a social media post Sunday for endorsing Rogers, saying in part that Stevens showed “great and almost unprecedented loyalty” to Michigan in doing so.
But Stevens' fellow Democrats were swift to condemn her endorsement.
"This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York wrote in a post on X . "Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors."
“We are dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt," Democratic National Committee Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins said in a statement released by the Michigan Democratic Party. "Congresswoman Stevens has lost her way, and Michiganders know that Mike Rogers is a shill for Trump and has failed Michigan. We are ready to elect Abdul on Tuesday.”
"Michiganders ... want leaders focused on making their lives more affordable. That's what they're talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens' continued efforts to get attention,” Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell wrote in a statement on X , adding, "we must stay focused on electing Democrats up and down the ballot, and that includes electing Abdul El-Sayed as Michigan's next Senator."
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says
body:
"We are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Murphy's chief of staff said.
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff said in a statement on Sunday.
The 53-year-old Democrat was taken to a hospital on Saturday after he started to feel numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game, said Allison Herwitt, Murphy's chief of staff.
Upon examining Murphy, doctors determined he had suffered a stroke, Herwitt said, adding that the senator has been transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore.
"The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said.
No further information was released about Murphy's condition.
For the past several weeks, Murphy has been traveling the country campaigning for Democratic candidates in Tuesday's midterm elections. He was scheduled to appear Sunday with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, according to the New Hampshire Democratic Party.
In 2024, Murphy won his third term to serve Connecticut in the U.S. Senate and has been viewed by some Democratic party officials as a possible candidate for president in 2028.
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont released a statement on social media on Sunday saying he and his wife, Annie, are keeping Murphy and is family "in our prayers."
"Just two days ago, I was with Senator Chris Murphy doing what he loves most: Encouraging Connecticut residents to make their voices heard and vote on Tuesday," Lamont said. "There is no stronger advocate for our democracy. And no one who fights harder for the people of this state. Chris is a great friend to Connecticut and to me personally."
"I am sure that he will be walking across the state again very soon. And we will all be cheering him on," Lamont added.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
