title: Türkiye-South Korea Comparison in Submarine Construction: Same Starting Point, Different Outcomes
body:
Türkiye’s submarine journey dates back 140 years, to the Golden Horn and Taşkızak Shipyard. Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command, meanwhile, has been building submarines for the Turkish Naval Forces for nearly 50 years through models based on foreign designs, technical assistance, material packages and technology transfer. The accumulated know-how, trained workforce and production infrastructure acquired throughout this process have today created a substantial technological foundation extending to Türkiye’s national submarine project, MİLDEN.
South Korea entered submarine construction roughly 15 years after Türkiye, under the KSS-I Program launched with Germany in 1987. Seoul, however, treated licensed production not merely as a platform procurement method, but as a long-term instrument for developing domestic industrial and technological capabilities.
Experience gained through the Chang Bogo and Son Won-il Classes was transformed into an indigenous design and system-development capability with KSS-III, while South Korea also became a submarine-exporting country within a relatively short period.
The submarine construction journeys of Türkiye and South Korea therefore offer a striking comparison. Although both countries began with German designs and technology transfer, they followed different paths in terms of industrialization models, the manner in which shipyards were integrated into the programs, the time required to transition to design capability, and export objectives.
Today, Türkiye is continuing its transition to a fully indigenous and national submarine design with MİLDEN, drawing on the substantial accumulation of knowledge in engineering, design and planning gained through the AY, PREVEZE, GÜR and REİS Class submarine projects, together with a skilled workforce developed at factory level. South Korea, meanwhile, has demonstrated an indigenous design capability through KSS-III and has moved beyond conventional submarine technology by placing the development of a nuclear-powered submarine on its agenda.
The history of Turkish submarining began exactly 140 years ago, on 6 September 1886, when the Nordenfelt Class submarine ABDÜLHAMİD was launched at Taşkızak Shipyard on the Golden Horn, where its final assembly had been carried out. Under an agreement signed on 23 January 1886 between the Ottoman Ministry of the Navy and the Swedish Nordenfelt Company, two steam-powered submarines built in the United Kingdom were transported to Istanbul in sections and assembled at Taşkızak Shipyard.
These two platforms, named ABDÜLHAMİD (Nordenfelt 2) and later ABDÜLMECİD (Nordenfelt 3), became the first submarines of the Ottoman Navy.
Efforts to develop submarine construction capability in Türkiye continued during the Republican era. Of the diesel-electric AY Class submarines ordered from the German Krupp Germaniawerft company in 1936, ATILAY and YILDIRAY were built in Türkiye at Taşkızak Shipyard. These submarines were a version of the German Type IX Class customized for Türkiye and were equipped with German D.W.K. torpedoes.
YILDIRAY became the first submarine in Turkish submarine history whose construction was completed entirely by Turkish workers. The harbor and sea trials of YILDIRAY were also conducted without any foreign specialists, and the submarine entered service in 1946.
The Beginning of the Submarine Construction Era at Gölcük
Under U.S. military assistance, the Turkish Naval Forces maintained their submarine strength with 11 FLEET Class submarines between 1948 and 1960, followed in the 1970s by 10 GUPPY Class submarines that replaced the FLEET Class. However, because these submarines had quite limited speed and diving-depth performance, and were assessed as likely to become inadequate against the evolving threat environment, studies were initiated toward the end of the 1960s to identify a new submarine type suited to Türkiye’s requirements.
Following the evaluations, the 1,000-ton Type 209/1200 Class of the German company Howaldtswerke-Deutsche Werft (HDW, now TKMS) was selected because of its high underwater speed and maneuverability, as well as a significantly greater diving depth than the existing submarines.
Of the six AY Class Type 209/1200 submarines procured under four separate contracts signed with HDW using German NATO Defense Aid funds, three were built at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command with material packages and know-how support supplied by HDW, and entered service between 1981 and 1989.
When the first contract covering the construction of two submarines at HDW’s shipyard in Germany was signed in 1972 for the type designated the AY Class, on-the-job training was also included because construction activities were planned to be transferred to Türkiye at a later stage of the program. Training of Turkish Naval Forces personnel at HDW Shipyard began in 1973.
Under the second contract signed at the end of 1974, one submarine was built at HDW Shipyard in Kiel and the other at Gölcük Shipyard. Drawing on more than a century of operational experience and accumulated knowledge within the Turkish Submarine Fleet, the sonar and fire-control system configuration of the submarines in this second package was modified.
The fire-control system, manufactured in accordance with requirements defined by the Turkish Naval Forces, which played an active role in the system design, was later also selected by other countries for submarines of this type.
The fifth AY Class submarine was also built at Gölcük Shipyard under the third contract signed using German NATO Defense Aid funds. With the fourth contract signed in early 1985, construction of the sixth submarine began in July 1985.
TCG Yıldıray (S-350), for which the first frame welding at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command was carried out in 1975 and construction began in 1976, became the first submarine built in Türkiye. Construction of TCG Yıldıray, the fourth submarine of the program, was completed in 42 months as planned, and the submarine entered service on 6 January 1981. Approximately 200,000 man-days of labor were expended during construction, while certain construction and outfitting materials were procured from the domestic market.
For TCG Dolunay, the third AY Class and sixth submarine built at Gölcük Shipyard, the labor requirement was reduced to approximately 150,000 man-days.
Beginning with TCG Yıldıray, submarine pressure hulls were manufactured entirely at Gölcük Shipyard, with only diesel engines, electronic equipment and other systems used during outfitting being supplied from Germany. It can be said that the Turkish Naval Forces learned modern submarine operations through the AY Class submarines.
Personnel sent to Germany for training under the project further consolidated the instruction and knowledge they had received from instructors with combat experience by serving aboard submarines. As a result, the Turkish Naval Forces accumulated significantly more user-experience-based knowledge on the AY Class than HDW itself. Although the shipyard possessed design expertise, the Type 209 Class did not enter service with the German Navy, meaning HDW lacked the operational user experience needed to identify shortcomings and potential deficiencies in the design.
Consequently, the Turkish Naval Forces made a significant contribution to the development of the Type 209 Class through the feedback it provided. The evolution of the Turkish Naval Forces’ submarine expertise can also be seen in the technical requirement documents prepared for the AY, PREVEZE and GÜR Class submarines.
While the specification prepared for the AY Class consisted of only four pages, the PREVEZE Class specification expanded to 100 pages, and for the GÜR Class the specification grew to four volumes. Although the submarines appear very similar externally, Turkish Naval Forces engineers implemented 1,700 improvements on the GÜR Class compared with the PREVEZE Class.
Capabilities Mature with PREVEZE and GÜR
Türkiye continued its cooperation with HDW after the AY Class through the PREVEZE Class Type 209/1400 submarines. Four PREVEZE Class submarines - TCG Preveze, TCG Sakarya, TCG 18 Mart and TCG Anafartalar - were built at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command under two separate contracts and entered the Submarine Fleet inventory between 1994 and 1999.
Under the first contract signed on 17 November 1987, TCG Preveze and TCG Sakarya were constructed, with German NATO Defense Aid funds contributing to project financing.
Construction of the first submarine, TCG Preveze (S-353), began on 11 September 1989, and a total of 220,000 man-days of labor were used during construction. The single-hull, compartmented PREVEZE Class (Type 209/1400) submarines had pressure hulls consisting of six main sections and a total of 119 frames. TCG Preveze (S-353), the first submarine of the class, was launched after 199,000 man-days of direct construction effort, within a total labor expenditure of 220,000 man-days, while the corresponding figure for the second boat, TCG Sakarya (S-354), was reduced to 165,000 man-days.
During the construction of TCG Preveze, a circular welding-error tolerance of 6 mm and a pressure-hull roundness accuracy of 1/1,000 were achieved. Construction of the PREVEZE Class submarines involved 17,271 material items and 11,843 technical drawings.
For the PREVEZE Class pressure hull, 250 tons of HY-80 steel plate were used, along with 28 tons of fiberglass material for the fairwater and external hull structures, 34 tons of welding electrodes, 15 tons of paint and five tons of insulation material. During outfitting, 3,617 pipe components were fabricated for 50 separate piping systems; 8.5 km of piping and a total of 37 km of cable were installed, and 563 different items of equipment and systems were integrated into the submarine.
TCG 18 Mart and TCG Anafartalar were built under a contract worth 460 million Deutsche Mark (DM) signed on 16 June 1993. Of the contract value, DM 440 million was covered from the national budget and DM 20 million through German NATO Defense Aid.
German NATO Defense Aid played an important role in the development of Türkiye’s submarine construction capability. From 1964 through the end of 1994, the Federal Republic of Germany provided grant defense assistance worth approximately DM 4.74 billion in 18 separate tranches. Initially used primarily for Turkish Land Forces requirements, these resources were later extended to naval and air force projects.
Funds allocated to the Naval Forces were used in projects conducted with German shipyards for the MEKO Class frigates, AY and PREVEZE Class submarines, and DOĞAN Class fast attack craft.
The next major step in Türkiye’s submarine construction capability was the GÜR Class. The 1,400-ton GÜR Class Type 209/1400 Mod submarine project was launched to improve the quality and quantity of the underwater strike force. On 22 July 1998, the Ministry of National Defense and HDW signed a contract worth a total of DM 996 million for four submarines to be built at Gölcük Shipyard, including material packages, logistics support and the procurement of new systems. The project was financed entirely through the national budget.
Possessing more advanced capabilities than the PREVEZE Class and capable of firing the DM2A4 heavyweight torpedo, the four GÜR Class submarines - TCG Gür (S-357), TCG Çanakkale (S-358), TCG Burakreis (S-359) and TCG I. İnönü (S-360) - entered service between 2005 and 2008.
Construction of the single-hull, compartmented GÜR Class (Type 209/1400 Mod) submarines, whose pressure hulls consist of six main sections and a total of 119 frames, required approximately 180,000 man-days of labor, more than 17,000 material items and around 13,000 technical drawings.
Approximately 250 tons of HY-80 steel and 31 tons of welding electrodes were used to construct the pressure hulls of the GÜR Class submarines. Around 9 km of piping and 36.5 km of cable were installed, five tons of insulation and 15 tons of paint were used, and some 600 items of equipment of varying sizes were fitted to each submarine during the outfitting phase.
On TCG I. İnönü (S-360), the last GÜR Class submarine, the pressure-hull section containing the torpedo tubes (Section 42, the bow section) was constructed at GÜRDESAN by Turkish engineers and workers. Thus, the bow section containing the torpedo tubes - one of the most critical parts of submarine construction - was manufactured domestically for the first time.
Beginning with the GÜR Class, the Turkish Naval Forces Command formally set the objective of a national submarine design. In this context, training in submarine concept design and on-the-job practices was received, and subsequent contracts were shaped according to the results of that training. The REİS Class Submarine Contract was also developed following this process, creating a significant body of knowledge in support of the national submarine design objective.
Under the New Type Submarine Project contract signed on 2 July 2009 between the Secretariat of Defense Industries (SSB) and the German TKMS Joint Venture, formerly the HDW-MFI Joint Venture, construction of six REİS Class Type 214TN submarines with fuel-cell/AIP capability began at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command. TKMS (Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems) provides technical assistance, material packages and technology transfer under the project.
The first submarine of the class, TCG Pirireis (S-330), entered the Turkish Naval Forces inventory on 17 October 2024, followed by the second, TCG Hızırreis (S-331), on 27 November 2025. Construction and test activities are continuing for MURATREİS (S-332), AYDINREİS (S-333), SEYDİALİREİS (S-334) and SELMANREİS (S-335), while completion of the provisional acceptance process for the third submarine, MURATREİS, is expected.
At the beginning of the project, the first submarine had been planned to enter service in 2015.
However, the program experienced delays because the contract signed in 2009 did not enter into force until 22 June 2011; there were delays in securing the financing credit; TKMS delayed the delivery and shipment of construction and outfitting materials used for submarine production as a result of what the article describes as an undeclared embargo imposed by the German Government; and modifications were made to the Type 214 design in line with the Turkish Naval Forces’ operational requirements.
Five major design problems identified in the original design were corrected, while the submarine was lengthened twice, increasing the hull length by a total of 2.05 m. The modification was designed entirely by engineers of the Design Project Office (DPO) to improve the submarine’s dynamic and static stability and to eliminate the risk of capsizing associated with stability problems reportedly experienced during surfaced operations in high seas by other Type 214 users, including the Portuguese, South Korean and Greek navies.
It has also been claimed that the Type 218SG submarines built in Germany for the Republic of Singapore Navy, with an overall length of 70 m, a surfaced displacement of approximately 2,000 tons and a submerged displacement of 2,200 tons, experienced a similar rolling problem and that first submarine heeled to 67 degrees in rough seas during sea trials in Germany. During sea trials of TCG Pirireis, the first REİS Class submarine, the stability and rolling problems associated with standard Type 214 submarines were not encountered.
This indicates that the improvement implemented by Turkish engineers achieved its intended result. In addition, various subsystem modifications were introduced to allow the REİS Class to operate in warmer waters. Owing to the delays and design-improvement work, construction of the first submarine, originally planned for 2013, began on 28 September 2015, with the first welding ceremony held on 8 October 2015.
Each single-hull, compartmented REİS Class submarine, with approximately 100 structural frames, requires a total of 180,000 man-days of labor. During construction, the non-pressure aft diving tanks are manufactured first, followed by the frames that constitute the initial stage of pressure-hull construction. The main blocks designated Section 10, Section 20, Section 30, Section 40 and Section 50 are then constructed.
For the first two submarines, the section containing the torpedo tubes was manufactured by the project’s German prime contractor, ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS). The Section 50 units used on submarines three, four, five and six are being produced in Türkiye at GÜRDESAN Shipyard. Another major section built in Türkiye for the first time under the project at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command is the aft spherical bulkhead forming the submarine’s rear dome.
A submarine is an inherently complex system in which a large number of high-technology subsystems must operate together within an extremely confined space. Consequently, tolerance for construction errors is far lower than in surface-ship construction. All welding performed during pressure-hull construction is subject to radiographic X-ray inspection.
For the REİS Class submarines, the circular welding-error tolerance is +/-9 mm, while a roundness accuracy of 1/2,000 has been achieved in welding-quality measurements. Under the applicable standards, 3/2,000 would be sufficient. The resulting increase in welding quality has provided the Type 214TN submarines with an additional margin above standard requirements in both diving depth and survivability at depth.
Today, the Turkish Submarine Fleet operates a total of 12 submarines: two AY, four PREVEZE, four GÜR and two REİS Class boats. With 140 years of history, accumulated expertise and operational competence, the Turkish Submarine Fleet ranks among the world’s established and respected submarine forces.
Three submarines from Sweden and France entered service during the Ottoman era, while a total of 50 submarines from five countries - the Netherlands, Italy, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States - entered the inventory during the Republican era. The total number of submarines to have entered Turkish service therefore reached 53. Final assembly and construction of 16 of these submarines were carried out in Türkiye.
While 39 submarines were retired after completing their service lives, TCG Atılay and TCG Dumlupınar were lost in July 1942 and April 1953 as a result of accidents involving a mine strike and a collision with a cargo ship, respectively. Twelve submarines remain in active service.
On 17 April 2026, the Turkish flag was raised on MURATREİS, the third REİS Class submarine, which is the 17th submarine built in Türkiye and will become the 54th submarine to enter the inventory. The submarine conducted its first sea sortie on 20 April.
Over the nearly 50-year period since 1976, Türkiye has built a total of 14 submarines at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command under German HDW/TKMS license, with technical and logistics support, material packages and technology transfer provided from Germany: three AY, four PREVEZE, four GÜR and three REİS Class submarines. Construction of three additional REİS Class submarines is continuing.
The most important stage reached through this long construction experience is MİLDEN. Construction of the first test block for the fully indigenous and nationally designed National Submarine began with the first welding ceremony held at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command on 16 December 2024. The Test Block was displayed to visitors during the TEKNOFEST Blue Homeland event held at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command on 20-23 August 2026. The first submarine of the MİLDEN Class, which will be Türkiye’s first nationally designed and indigenous submarine, has been named ATILAY.
ATILAY will be the 21st submarine built in Türkiye and the 58th submarine to enter service with the Turkish Naval Forces.
Why Is Building a Submarine So Difficult?
Submarine construction is not simply a matter of using an existing shipyard infrastructure. In addition to extensive know-how and a highly trained workforce, it requires major facility investments and the procurement and installation of costly equipment such as main-block assembly and welding stations.
Even the ground structure of a Submarine Construction/Manufacturing Facility requires substantial fixed gravel/concrete infrastructure investment. Furthermore, submarine construction and assembly activities, specifically welding the plates that form the pressure hull and joining the blocks, require the installation of high-cost, semi-automated modern machinery and stations. These include the Main Block Assembly and Welding Station, Pressure Hull Welding Station, Sub-Block Joining Station, Robotic Frame Welding Station (RFWS), Sub-Block Assembly Jig, Bevel Jig, Web-Flange Assembly/Frame Fabrication Station, Frame Handling Fixture, Frame Assembly and Tack-Welding Fixture (OCTOPUS), Frame-to-Hull-Plate Welding Station, and Continuous Frame Welding Station.
For this reason, it is not easy for a private-sector shipyard to enter the field solely to ‘build submarines’ while assuming the required investment cost. One of the main reasons submarine construction activities in Türkiye have not yet been fully integrated into or transferred to the private sector is this very high infrastructure cost.
Indeed, even after the 17 August 1999 Gölcük Earthquake, when transferring certain activities from Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command to Istanbul Naval Shipyard Command was considered, it was not possible to relocate Gölcük’s fixed gravel/concrete infrastructure and submarine construction facility.
Accordingly, Türkiye’s most comprehensive capability for building a submarine remains at the Ministry of National Defense’s Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command. Having built submarines for nearly 50 years, Gölcük Shipyard continues to serve not only as a strong institutional culture center but also as an important source of knowledge and personnel for the Turkish submarine ecosystem. Many personnel now employed by civilian companies and actively involved in the submarine ecosystem also have backgrounds at Gölcük Shipyard.
South Korea’s Submarine Journey: From German Design to Indigenous Design
Türkiye began developing a modern submarine construction capability through the AY Class Submarine Project signed with HDW in 1972 for the procurement of six Type 209/1200 submarines. South Korea entered the same process roughly 15 years later through the KSS-I Program launched in cooperation with HDW in 1987.
The KSS-I Program covered the procurement of nine Chang Bogo Class Type 209/1200 submarines in three separate batches of three boats each. These diesel-electric submarines were 56 m long and displaced 1,100 tons surfaced and 1,285 tons submerged. The three submarines in the first batch were delivered in 1992, 1994 and 1995.
Unlike in Türkiye, South Korea’s naval submarine requirement was met by the Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) shipyard in Ulsan and Daewoo Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering (DSME, now Hanwha Ocean) in Okpo. DSME/Hanwha Ocean built eight Chang Bogo Class submarines under HDW license within the KSS-I Program.
A notable feature of the KSS-I Program was the gradual transfer of the production method to South Korea. The first submarine was built at HDW Shipyard in Kiel. Kits for the next two submarines were manufactured in Germany, shipped to South Korea and finally assembled at DSME’s Okpo shipyard. The remaining six submarines procured under Batch II and Batch III were built almost entirely at DSME Shipyard.
Another major distinction between the South Korean and Turkish models was the financing structure. All South Korean submarine programs were supported through the national defense budget. Funding was provided through defense budgets approved by the National Assembly, while procurement processes were managed by the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA).
This ensured that the large budgets allocated to submarine projects flowed back into domestic shipyards, engineering companies and production infrastructure.
This approach enabled South Korea to treat submarine programs not simply as military platform procurement projects, but as long-term industrial-policy and technology-development programs.
The Same German Shipyard, Different Strategies
While Türkiye was conducting the PREVEZE Class Submarine Program, South Korea was also sending personnel to HDW’s shipyard in Kiel for training under the Chang Bogo Program. During this period, Turkish and South Korean naval personnel had the opportunity to work together in Kiel. South Korean personnel were also observed seeking knowledge from their Turkish counterparts, who at that time had greater experience in submarine construction.
South Korea, however, did not limit itself to technology transfer from Germany. To build up expertise in submarine design and construction, it sent design teams to four or five different countries for training, creating a broader learning process aimed at improving national design and construction competence.
Türkiye’s continuation of the package-project model with Germany for a much longer period became an important point of divergence in the development of the two countries’ submarine construction capabilities. In Türkiye, the model whereby kits pre-manufactured at HDW Shipyard were shipped to Gölcük Shipyard for final assembly continued into the REİS Project.
Beginning with TCG Yıldıray, pressure hulls were built in Türkiye, while Germany supplied only diesel engines, electronic equipment and other systems used during outfitting, including periscopes, masts and the sonar suite.
South Korea completed this transition in a much shorter period. After construction of the nine Chang Bogo Class submarines - the first built entirely in Germany, the second and third assembled in South Korea from modules supplied by HDW, and the pressure hulls of the remaining six built in South Korea - Seoul ordered three KSS-II Batch I Son Won-il Class submarines in December 2000. Following that order, with the first submarine of the class entering service in June 2006, South Korea launched the indigenous KSS-III Program in 2007.
In December 2008, a contract was signed with HDW for an additional six KSS-II Batch II Son Won-il Class submarines. The three submarines built under KSS-III Batch I entered service between 2021 and 2024, while the first of the three Batch II submarines was launched in October 2025 and is expected to be delivered in 2027.
From Chang Bogo to Operational Proficiency
ROKS Chang Bogo (SS-061), the first KSS-I Chang Bogo Class submarine, formed the foundation of South Korea’s submarine fleet. With the entry of these submarines into service, South Korea became the 43rd country in the world to operate submarines.
From its commissioning on 14 October 1992 until its decommissioning on 31 December 2025, ROKS Chang Bogo accumulated 12,131 operational days during 34 years of service. Over that period, it sailed approximately 342,000 nautical miles, or 633,606 km - equivalent to circling the Earth roughly 16 times.
South Korea’s submarine operational capability also attracted attention during the 2004 Rim of the Pacific Exercise (RIMPAC). Chang Bogo reportedly conducted 40 simulated torpedo attacks against more than 30 ships, including U.S. aircraft carriers, without being detected. Open sources state that ROKS Chang Bogo virtually sank 15 ships during the exercise, including the U.S. Navy nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS John C. Stennis and escorting units.
South Korea modernized its KSS-I Batch II and Batch III submarines over time. Under modernization agreements signed with prime contractor DSME/Hanwha Ocean in 2014 and 2020, the submarines received an indigenously developed integrated Combat Management System (CMS) from LIG Nex1, improved target-detection and tracking capability, a towed-array sonar and various other systems.
KSS-II: Moving Beyond Licensed Production
Following the Type 209/1200-based Chang Bogo Program, South Korea transitioned to the Type 214-based KSS-II Program. Under two separate contracts signed in December 2000 and December 2008, construction of a total of nine Type 214 Son Won-il Class submarines was planned.
The first three submarines and boats 5, 7 and 9 of the second batch were built at HHI Shipyard, while boats 4, 6 and 8 of the second batch were built at DSME/Hanwha Ocean. The submarines entered service between December 2007 and January 2020. The final submarine of the program, ROKS Shin Dol-Seok, was commissioned on 31 January 2020.
South Korea is also continuing modernization work to improve the capabilities of its KSS-II submarines. In July 2025, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) was selected as the preferred bidder for the KSS-II Type 214 Mid-Life Upgrade (MLU) program managed by DAPA.
Worth approximately KRW 500 billion, or around USD 360 million, the program covers performance and capability enhancements for the first three submarines acquired under the KSS-II procurement program.
The modernization is planned to include improvements to the CMS, towed-array sonar (TAS), mine-avoidance sonar and floating antenna system of the first three KSS-II Batch I submarines.
KSS-III: South Korea’s Transition to Indigenous Design
The real turning point in South Korea’s submarine journey was the KSS-III Program. DSME/Hanwha Ocean, which had previously built eight Chang Bogo Class submarines under HDW license through KSS-I, this time joined HHI in developing the new-generation KSS-III ocean-going submarine based on an indigenous design.
The KSS-III Program was formally launched in 2007 after approval at South Korea’s 16th Defense Acquisition Program Development Meeting. Preliminary design studies and initial concept-development activities for the program, however, are reported to date back to 2004.
Also known as the Ahn Changho Class, KSS-III elevated the Republic of Korea Navy to a different level in conventional submarines. In terms of size, KSS-III reached a level generally associated with nuclear-powered submarines, with only a limited number of conventional submarine classes - such as Australia’s Collins Class and Japan’s current Taigei and Soryu Classes - being comparable. It also achieved a significant degree of domestic content. According to DSME, 76 percent of all KSS-III components were produced in South Korea.
Under KSS-III Batch I, construction of the first two submarines was awarded to DSME/Hanwha Ocean and the third to HHI Shipyard. Under Batch II, separate contracts were signed with DSME for all three submarines, which will be longer and heavier and feature lithium-ion battery sets and 10 VLS cells for ballistic missiles. Batch I submarines have six ballistic-missile VLS cells.
One of the clearest indicators of South Korea’s achieved capability was the submarine export order it received from Indonesia in 2011. Competing against offers from Russia, France and Türkiye/Germany, South Korea won Indonesia’s tender for three 1,400-ton Improved Chang Bogo Class submarines.
South Korea’s submarine relationship with Indonesia had in fact begun earlier, when DSME won the modernization and comprehensive maintenance contract for KRI Cakra (401), a submarine built by HDW in Germany and commissioned into the Indonesian Navy in March 1981. Work began in 2004 and was completed in 2005. Modernization of sister ship KRI Nanggala (402) was delayed because of financial problems in Indonesia and was eventually completed in early 2012.
Under the USD 1.1 billion contract signed with Indonesia in December 2011, the first two submarines, KRI Nagapasa and KRI Ardadedali, were built by DSME in South Korea and delivered in 2017 and 2018. Final assembly of the third submarine, KRI Alugoro (405), was conducted at PT PAL Shipyard in Surabaya, Indonesia, and the submarine entered service in April 2021.
The project was particularly significant because South Korea transferred to another country the technology-transfer model that it had previously received from Germany. In other words, within roughly 24 years of beginning its submarine journey in 1987, South Korea had evolved from a country conducting licensed production through technology transfer into a submarine manufacturer capable of providing technology transfer for indigenous design solutions.
By the 2020s, the KSS-III Program had crystallized South Korea’s transition from licensed production and construction based on foreign designs to an indigenous design and system-development capability. Today, South Korea has transformed the journey that began in 1987 into an advanced submarine program developing 3,000-ton-class boats capable of carrying ballistic missiles and submitting bids in countries including the Philippines, India, Canada, Poland and Greece.
The country has also initiated development of the nuclear-powered Chang Bogo-N submarine.
From Conventional Submarines to Nuclear Propulsion
Through the Chang Bogo-N Program, which targets the mid-2030s, South Korea is preparing the legal and strategic framework for developing nuclear-powered attack submarines armed with conventional weapons and using low-enriched uranium.
South Korean shipbuilders such as Hanwha Ocean and Hyundai Heavy Industries possess experience in the infrastructure and ongoing validation and technology studies that could enable this transition. The Chang Bogo-N Program represents the next stage in South Korea’s submarine development: the ambition to move from conventional submarine design and construction capability to the development of nuclear-powered submarines.
A New Phase in Indonesia and a New Competitor for South Korea
South Korea’s submarine cooperation with Indonesia did not end with the Nagapasa Class. In April 2019, a new contract was signed for the construction of three additional Nagapasa Class submarines. Under the agreement, pre-manufactured kits for the first submarine were to be shipped from DSME to Indonesia for final assembly at PT PAL Shipyard, while the other two submarines were planned to be built almost entirely at PT PAL.
However, the contract remained ineffective for a prolonged period because of problems between South Korea and Indonesia. As a result, Indonesia chose to meet its submarine requirement through the Scorpene Evolved submarines proposed by France’s Naval Group.
Under the Scorpene for the Republic of Indonesia (SRI) project, which aims to establish a submarine design and construction ecosystem in the country, Indonesia began construction of the first of two ordered Scorpene Evolved submarines with a steel-cutting ceremony held at PT PAL Indonesia Shipyard in Surabaya on 7 August 2026. The two submarines, with a submerged displacement of 2,800 tons, are planned to be completed within seven to eight years.
Two Countries, Two Different Industrialization Approaches
The submarine construction journeys of Türkiye and South Korea are highly similar in terms of their starting points. Both countries developed modern submarine construction capabilities through German HDW designs and technology transfer. Both initially built foreign designs under licensed-production or package-project models and gradually increased their domestic capabilities. Beyond that point, however, their trajectories diverged.
Türkiye has built submarines based on German designs at Gölcük Naval Shipyard Command for nearly 50 years, accumulating significant operational, technical and human-resource expertise in the process. The AY, PREVEZE, GÜR and REİS Classes represent successive stages of this capability development. The MİLDEN Project is the most critical step in Türkiye’s long-running effort to transition to an indigenous submarine design and construction capability.
When the striking similarities in the starting points of the two countries’ submarine journeys and the different development models they subsequently pursued are examined, an inevitable question arises: If Türkiye had been able to take its submarine construction capability beyond the boundaries of military shipyards and expand it into civilian shipyards at an earlier stage, could it have reached a level comparable with South Korea today in indigenous submarine design and construction?
South Korea, by contrast, advanced the licensed-production process that began with HDW in a shorter period and in a manner designed to increase the production capabilities of domestic shipyards. The process that started with Chang Bogo continued with Son Won-il and reached the indigenous-design level with KSS-III. South Korea also converted these capabilities into export projects and, as demonstrated by the Indonesian example, became a country providing technology transfer.
Accordingly, the fundamental difference between the two countries’ stories is not simply ‘how many submarines were built,’ but how those construction activities were linked to industrial policy, design competence, indigenous system development and export objectives.
The indigenous design and system-development capability Türkiye now seeks through MİLDEN is being built on more than half a century of submarine construction experience at Gölcük. South Korea, starting from a similar point, has largely completed its transition from licensed production to indigenous design through KSS-III and has now moved beyond conventional submarine technology by placing the development of a nuclear-powered submarine on its agenda.
From this perspective, the submarine journeys of Türkiye and South Korea offer a noteworthy comparison of the outcomes produced by two countries that began from similar technological starting points but pursued different industrialization and capability-development models.

title: Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
body:
Route diversion: An election campaign poster for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with US President Donald Trump, reads in Hebrew 'We Have One Chance To Win' is seen on the back of a bus in Jerusalem. Image: UPI / Alamy Stock
Benjamin Netanyahuâs interest in cryptocurrency reveals both the continuing power of financial sanctions and the current limits of technological attempts to circumvent them.
Thanks to the widely reported efforts of the Russian Federation, it is no longer fantasy that cryptocurrency and blockchain-based payment systems can help sanctioned actors move money, circumvent restrictions and sustain particular commercial relationships. But importantly, while crypto might facilitate payments, its use cannot replicate the broader economic benefits of access to the international financial system. Governments considering crypto as protection against financial isolation risk confusing the ability to transfer value with the ability to participate in the global economy.
While Russiaâs experience provides the principal case study of both the possibilities and limitations of alternative financial arrangements, the recent Israeli debate, in the days before the 27 October election, provides a particularly revealing illustration of how these considerations are spreading. Appearing on Israelâs Channel 10 TV station , Netanyahu said he was preparing for the possibility that sanctions would be applied against Israel. This is not speculation. In September, the UK and other Western governments announced their intention to apply sanctions and trade measures against certain elements of the Israeli economy in response to, in the words of UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, the unlawful occupation of the Palestinian Territories, specifically against âthose who finance or facilitate illegal settlementsâ.
In particular, he noted that âThere could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks, so you need to set up a bypass economyâ using currencies â including cryptocurrency â that can bypass sanctions, revealing in conclusion that âwe are also working on thatâ.
His comments were met with criticism by the Bank of Israel that suggested he would do better to focus on policies that did not require such measures, noting that âThe right course for Israelâs economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.â An open letter signed by more than 100 economists also poured scorn on Netanyahuâs actions, saying that he is âknowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightestâ.
His political opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, likewise ridiculed the plan as âmadnessâ, calling it the âBibiCoin policyâ and predicting it would encourage Israeli companies to move abroad and threaten national security.
Regardless of the merit of the idea, it is striking in itself that a sophisticated, internationally integrated economy such as Israel is contemplating alternative financial arrangements in anticipation of possible sanctions. The fact that its leadership apparently regards sanctions as a credible economic threat will not have escaped notice in those countries â including the UK â that have threatened sanctions in response to the further expansion of Israelâs illegal settlements. Sanctions may not change Israelâs behaviour towards settlements in the occupied territories, but the threat of application certainly has the potential to cause disruption.
Zooming out from the specifics of Israel, Netanyahuâs comments pose an important question: have crypto and the blockchain matured sufficiently to allow a country to pre-emptively crypto-proof itself against sanctions? The attraction is alluring, particularly when a government anticipates looming financial isolation. If conventional banking relationships are likely to be interrupted, why not build an alternative system that cannot be so easily disrupted?
The experience of other sanctioned countries such as Russia, Iran and other actors that have already explored alternative financial systems is that while tactical advantage might be secured, running an entire economy â particularly as developed as Israelâs â through the so-called âcryptoverseâ remains out of reach, even for such a technically sophisticated country. Accessing sufficient crypto liquidity, identifying the necessary range of trading partners who will deal in crypto, and rewiring an economy to accommodate such a move are all immense (and mostly insurmountable) challenges.
Bibiâs vision rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes financial sanctions powerful for a globally integrated economy: the ability to move money is not the same as the ability to participate in the international economy.
This might seem like an obvious question, but much of the rhetoric on sanctions â particularly from political leaders â is misguided and aspirational, and it is thus important to ensure expectations are correctly set.
Help your search results show more from RUSI. Adding RUSI as a preferred source on Google means our analysis appears more prominently.
Sanctions do not switch off the targetâs economy. Consider the extent to which â and the way in which â Russiaâs economy has continued to function. But sanctions do force an economy to reshape and rewire, adding friction and cost, and forcing the countryâs leadership to make choices. Thus, while banks are required to stop processing payments, the core power of sanctions stems from their ability to restrict access to the complex network of global institutions, services, markets and commercial relationships that allow a developed economy like Israel to function.
The plumbing of the international commerce that enables an economy and its exporters and importers to function includes correspondent banking, trade finance, credit, insurance, investment, reserve management and the engagement of trusted finance and trade counterparties. Sanctions create legal, regulatory, reputational and commercial risks that affect all these relationships â and secondary sanctions and the prospect of losing access to major markets amplify these risks and the resulting effects.
In short, running a nationâs economy depends on far more than merely enabling payments settlement.
It would be wrong to dismiss the use of cryptocurrency outright. Russia has very effectively developed crypto-based payment systems that allow it to pay for the procurement of the critical high-priority list items it needs to wage its illegal war of aggression in Ukraine. It is thus important to recognise these advantages to understand both the appeal (even if misplaced) and the limitations of the greater adoption of crypto in the face of sanctions.
Let us start with the legitimate appeal. Crypto can enable cross-border value transfers without relying on traditional correspondent banking arrangements; stablecoins, such as USDT from Tether, can provide a relatively convenient means of transferring dollar-denominated value; and peer-to-peer transactions, decentralised systems and intermediaries operating in permissive jurisdictions can make sanctions enforcement more difficult. All of these features will seem alluring to a political leader faced with the impact of major financial restrictions stemming from broadly arrayed sanctions.
Receive a monthly newsletter and emails about upcoming events hosted by the Centre for Finance and Security Research Group
Get a weekly round-up of the latest commentary and research straight into your inbox.
Russiaâs development and use of alternative financial systems, most famously the A7 payment platform, which has been openly backed by Vladimir Putin, demonstrates that such mechanisms are not merely theoretical. In short, crypto can support specific transactions, intermediary networks and sanctions-circumvention operations.
But can crypto support the operation of an entire economy, particularly one as large ( the 25th largest in the world ), networked, and exposed to the West, as Israelâs?
Three fundamental â and existential â challenges exist. First, liquidity, scale and reliable conversion will present material constraints. There simply is not enough capacity in the cryptoverse to accommodate any but the smallest economies. Second, stablecoins introduce meaningful risk dependencies (just look at the 29 October Binance hack) that the traditional financial system has spent decades addressing. And third, crypto might provide an alternative payment mechanism for an individual transaction, but providing an alternative market for a countryâs exports is another question entirely, which would require a rewiring of counterparty nationsâ payment systems to accommodate such a transformation.
As widely studied and reported, Russia provides the most instructive contemporary example of the distinction between circumventing particular restrictions and replacing the entire basis on which a country interacts with the international financial system.
Since triggering wide-ranging financial sanctions and economic restrictions on itself as a result of the Kremlinâs 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has made considerable strategic investment in developing alternative payments infrastructure, including bilateral settlement arrangements (with Iran) and broader mechanisms designed to reduce dependence on Western financial institutions and markets.
Cryptoassets have become elements of this effort â but not uniquely. Russia has also relied on third countries for trade circumvention, opaque corporate structures and ledger systems for offshore payments, and a range of other obfuscation and evasion tactics.
The breadth and complexity of this range of arrangements demonstrate the need for adaptability and the extent to which sanctions evasion requires an array of tools.
The result? Russia has maintained substantial international trade despite sanctions, but the mechanisms it has needed to use are often more costly, less efficient, more time-consuming and more risky than those it used previously. Is that what Israel wants?
Thus far, the focus has been on what the government of a country targeted by sanctions can do â what it can almost certainly not do is compel the rest of the world to sign up to the same mission. For example, is a foreign supplier going to have confidence that it will receive the same trusted value via a new blockchain-based âcurrencyâ; and are third-country facilitators of such a scheme (for example banks converting stablecoins into local currency) going to be willing to run the risk that they too may become subject to sanction as a result? Financial sovereignty is inextricably linked to the willingness of other economic actors to trust, accept and use the proposed system.
So, can Bibi use the blockchain to set up a bypass economy? In short, no. Could certain payments be moved from the traditional banking system onto the blockchain? Yes â this is what Russia has done to pay for many of the critical components it needs for its military. But that does not isolate those payments or those that facilitate them from further sanction and disruption. The only way to do that is to follow the advice of the Israeli central bank and âfocus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economyâ.
More broadly, governments considering the adoption of crypto as insurance against sanctions should recognise what they are proposing. Crypto may offer a means of moving money when conventional routes are closed, but it cannot guarantee that anyone will want to receive that money, provide credit, insure a shipment or invest in the economy. Building an alternative payments system is not the same as building an alternative means of engaging with the international economy.

title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
body:
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:
Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.
Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories.
But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today:
Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.
This is a note by Simon Willison, posted on 1st November 2026 .
