title: Understanding Org's LaTeX previews
body:
TL;DR : LaTeX in Org mode now go whoosh , all pretty like. Install the development branch of Org mode to use it.
After grumbling about the inadequacy of LaTeX previews in Emacs – and specifically Org mode – for over a decade, Tecosaur and I decided to take the leap and rewrite the feature from the ground up. The result is a preview system for LaTeX math that can provide near-WYSIWYG feedback but retains the properties we expect in the Emacs environment: text-first, extensible and composable.
It’s not much code, but it contains many moving pieces and makes contact with several corners of Emacs. Now that the feature is part of Org mode, I thought I would take this opportunity to document how it works from the ground up, and use it as a launchpad to explain relevant aspects of Emacs’ event loop and its unofficial package API Emacs doesn’t really have a “package API”, since you build Emacs packages from the same elements as Emacs itself. .
This article is not an exhaustive demo of all the shiny new features, although there are a few videos peppered throughout. It’s also not the user manual (not yet updated on orgmode.org) or a tutorial (see Tecosaur’s This Month in Org writeup).
Instead, it aims to provide an overview of the goals and design of the library, along with some explainers of relevant aspects of the Emacs API and tips to write your own features. This write-up is for you if you are interested in
This is a feature included with Org mode to preview LaTeX math snippets as images in Emacs buffers. The contents of LaTeX fragments and environments in Org mode are replaced with rendered images.
It has existed for decades at this point, but in a form that I consider barely usable; this rewrite overhauls the code base and adds a number of quality-of-life features. There is a 13 minute demo that can give you a good idea of the new capabilities of Org mode:
The rest of this article is mostly about how it works, and briefly why. As such, it has a “fractal” level of detail. There is information intended
To that end, many details are tucked away in blocks like the following. You can safely ignore them in favor of the top-level headings, images and video demos.
Blocks like this describe the concrete implementation of aspects of the code.
This is probably only interesting if you are looking to dive into the code itself, or if you are looking to write a similar package.
Blocks like this are for additional notes on aspects of Emacs’ API, including the odd code snippets.
Blocks like this describe other Org features relevant to LaTeX preview generation.
Blocks like this describe CLI commands associated with this process, or their output.
LaTeX was not built with the aim of minimizing latency. Having to start multiple new processes even for a one-character change places a hard cap on what’s possible in terms of real-time feedback. Implementing an equivalent preview feature for a system designed for modern computers, like Typst, is trivial in comparison.
Moreover, as popular as Org mode is, it’s a small player in the space of markup languages. The fraction of Org and LaTeX users who would prefer to use Org mode to write LaTeX is smaller still. And while Org attempts to integrate well with LaTeX, navigating the mishmash of Org and LaTeX syntax presents an extra learning curve on top of learning to use the two markup languages individually.
But it also has a few things going for it.
First, LaTeX is ubiquitous, and Org mode is a far more convenient format for writing than raw LaTeX. There is significantly less visual noise (think Markdown vs HTML), and Org provides an escape hatch for adding LaTeX verbatim. Org’s simple interface for shuffling text around, monitoring task progress and executing code blocks makes it easy for eventual LaTeX documents to begin as Org files. Since everything in Emacs composes with everything else, your system for (say) fast LaTeX input transfers over to Org mode seamlessly.
Second, the fact that Org is versatile as a publishing tool implies that some benefits of better LaTeX support transfer over to other formats too, like equations in HTML or ODT exports.
There is a wide swath of applications built on Org mode that benefit from LaTeX math input, such as Org Roam and Org Noter. For these applications converting Org documents to LaTeX is not the goal, as they are not primarily publication tools: they stick around as private digital archives, and better LaTeX support is a bonus to the user’s expressivity.
Real-time feedback when editing LaTeX snippets is a categorical improvement to the user’s experience. I did not realize this when I started work on org-latex-preview , but now I wouldn’t want to LaTeX without it. It baffles me that web LaTeX editors (Overleaf etc) don’t provide this out of the box, especially as they target novice LaTeX users. .
Finally, we can keep Org mode out of the picture: org-latex-preview can technically work anywhere in Emacs, and in every major-mode. it’s just not there yet (See below ) .
But perhaps the most germane reason is that Emacs users don’t shy away from settling comfortably into tiny, cramped and poorly insulated niches. Comes with the territory!
Emacs users are closely acquainted with its frequent unresponsiveness. You’re never more than one minor-mode or mode line indicator away from causing Emacs to block or lag. While it’s not a big ask to wait a second for the result of an action you initiate, the unresponsiveness often manifests as short random freezes, which is unacceptable. But there’s more. Beyond the annoyance and inconvenience, poor responsiveness denies us an entire class of uses: real-time feedback is everything for interactive applications.
Owing to both its design and age, Emacs is not very well suited for asynchronous applications. Certain patterns of asynchronous usage are viable (see below), but concurrency support is limited and parallelism is absent: no worker threads, channels, async-io, or anything of the like.
I lied. In addition to Elisp threads, there exist prototype libraries for async-io ( Chris Wellons ) and channels/CSP ( Andrey Listopadov ) based on Emacs’ generators library , which in turn is implemented using continuation passing. But generators as provided by this library do not have anywhere near the level of robustness or support you need to build actual applications: no introspection, error handling or debugging support, poor performance, and just overall jankiness. I’ve tried and lived to regret it – Elfeed Tube is a real mess.
The Futur package is another promising swing at an async-io style interface, but it’s new and I haven’t been able to try it yet.
In any event, a more responsive org-latex-preview would require parallelism and not just concurrency. There is John Wiegley’s async library (and packages inspired by it, like session-async ) that spawn a child Emacs that runs in parallel, but communication is limited and the overhead is sizeable, so this is a bit of a bludgeon.
The upshot is this: we want org-latex-preview to be as asynchronous as possible within Emacs’ effectively single-threaded event loop model. The goal is to minimize how long the user has to wait, in terms of both the overall run time and the fraction of that for which Emacs is unresponsive. We end up having to trade these off against each other.
A close second concern is preview generation speed. This is desirable both in the large and the small. Previewing upwards of a hundred LaTeX math fragments in a math-heavy Org document used to be an exercise in patience. Now it takes about one second, and can be much faster with some trade-offs.
Figure 1: LaTeX preview generation times under the slowest settings. The vertical axis is time, and along each vertical line the red chunks correspond to intervals for which Emacs is blocked. We still manage to process a file with 250 LaTeX fragments in about a second with minimal impact on Emacs’ responsiveness.
Speeding up bulk generation is at most a boost in convenience. You don’t regenerate a large buffer’s worth of previews more than once every few sessions, and the resulting images are cached anyway. The more interesting aspect is that speed enables a close to real-time feedback loop that wasn’t available before. This is especially useful when you’re deep inside a messy structure like an array:
No more counting field separators. No more exiting, regenerating and re-examining snippets. It’s the best parts of WYSIWYG and visible markup, together.
Even in the niche of academic types who use Org mode with LaTeX, there are very different orientations. There’s Org the transient format, where an Org document starts out as a rough sketch, a thought bubble translated to the screen, and soon transitions into a TeX file that becomes the source of truth. There’s Org the intermediate publication format, where the document lives as an Org file, but its value is in the web page or PDF document it eventually becomes. For the adherents of this style the appearance of the Org document is irrelevant.
Finally, there’s the class of uses described above , where the desired output is the Org document itself, or a cross-linked collection of them. These are folks who care about the aesthetics of Org documents and often suffer a thousand cuts in trying to make Emacs look “modern”.
One of the objectives of org-latex-preview is to ease their self-imposed burden somewhat: LaTeX previews should blend in perfectly with the surrounding text. This means
Getting the fonts to match is possible too, but requires some degree of compromise on the part of the user You could start by using the variable-pitch Latin Modern font in your Org documents. .
Each of these is a long-standing issue with LaTeX previews in Org, and Stack Overflow and the usual haunts have decades of discussions on how to fix them, with band-aid after band-aid proposed as solutions. We took an elephant gun to this problem, starting by throwing out the giant mess that was Org’s accreted LaTeX preview code of the past two decades.
Here’s a demo of theme-aware LaTeX preview colors:
Finally, there are a few features we picked up along the way because they came free.
Recording compilation errors was a simple matter since we scan the LaTeX output anyway.
Consistent equation numbering was expensive in the past because numbering changes can propagate across the document, and parsing the Org document and LaTeX fragment compilation were both slow. Recent changes to Org have made the former a non-issue (see the parsing section below ), and the performance scaling of our bulk LaTeX runs has fixed the latter.
There are several more minor features along for the ride, such as improvements to editing LaTeX with org-edit-special ( C-c ' ).
As mentioned in the introduction, the LaTeX preview system draws on a few different facets of the Emacs API: mainly async process interaction (the “backend”) and overlays (the UI or “frontend”). The live-updating behavior leans heavily on hooks and timers, and we join these pieces together with very simple Lispy data structures, like alists and plists.
We also (naturally) use a few Org mode specific APIs, including ones developed by us for this purpose. We cover these further below as we encounter them.
If you are designing an Emacs application that interacts with the outside world, it helps to start with a mental picture of Emacs’ event loop. To a first approximation, the main loop does only four things:
Together these two connect the user and Emacs. If the main loop did only these two things Emacs would still qualify for the title of “Lisp evaluator masquerading as a text editor”, but it wouldn’t be nearly as useful. For that we need it to
The last event loop function combines the above three, but across time:
This design explains why timers in Emacs are not reliable in the absolute sense. The timer runs not when it’s ripe, but when it’s ripe and when the main loop gets around to it. Nevertheless, scheduling code provides a much-needed degree of flexibility to a rigidly ordered task list.
The way these four tasks are actually organized in the main loop code is less pleasing:
Also, Emacs is obviously doing things outside of the event loop as well. Font caches are compacted, Emacs is responding to the compositor and some OS signals, interacting with dynamic modules, and so on. In the currently experimental MPS branch, some garbage collection activities also occur in the background. These are invisible to the Lisp evaluator and thus out of scope when learning to build an Elisp package.
This design suggests that Emacs can only do one thing at a time As of Emacs 31 , so that designing a responsive application is a steep ask. But the situation is more nuanced:
Yes, the Lisp evaluator holds a global interpreter lock. At any point in time Emacs is doing exactly one of the following: painting the screen (redisplay), updating syntax highlighting (fontification), running hook functions or timers, responding to window changes, handling keyboard input, and – crucially for us – interacting with subprocesses. Every action is thus blocking .
The only asynchronous interaction possible is by starting an OS-level subprocess Another lie, since we have dynamic modules, covered below . . Emacs continues to run independently from the subprocess, but it still has to handle its STDOUT and STDERR streams and respond to process signals. When it is doing this, it cannot pay attention to your input or anything else. Again, Emacs can only do one thing at a time.
There are multiple commands to start an asynchronous subprocess from Emacs (see M-x shortdoc process ), but start-process covers most common use cases.
Processes are (optionally) associated with a buffer where process output is inserted. To send a subprocess some input, there’s process-send-string and process-send-region . Responding to process output and signals is the responsibility of process filters and sentinels ( next block ). kill-process does what you’d expect. All of these functions take the process object that start-process returns as an argument.
Except for some fiddly details , that’s essentially all there is to the process interaction API. There are several variants of start-process available – the synchronous call-process , the shell versions start-process-shell-command and call-process-shell-command , and so on. The only one that does something different is the primitive make-process , which is a more extensive version that can (additionally) create network processes, send data through TCP or Unix sockets and so on.
Emacs will try to prioritize user input events. To do this it can delay tasks like reading from subprcesses if necessary. Idle timers are another example of this. Some actions are thus delayable , but they block Emacs when they (eventually) run. There might be a penalty to pay afterwards, for instance when there’s more subprocess output to process as a result of delaying the task.
By default, Emacs inserts the output from a subprocess into the process buffer, or ignores it if there is no process buffer. (Crucially, it still has to read the output from the process pipe.) This is good enough for simple tasks. To use or transform subprocess output in more specialized ways, you can write an elisp function that is used as a process filter . It is called whenever Emacs reads new process output. In the language of shell commands, I think of process filters like this:
Process filters can be tricky to write if you want to parse structured process output, because the amount of data that Emacs reads from the pipe can be arbitrary. Unless latency is a concern, it’s often preferable to work with process sentinels for this reason. Sentinels are the second tool Emacs makes available for reacting to processes. A process sentinel is an elisp function (callback) called whenever the process changes state or raises a signal, including when it terminates. Practically speaking, I think of them like this:
They are typically used for cleaning up after the process, and updating Emacs’ state depending on how the subprocess ends. But you can use them to access the process buffer containing all the process output, and thus do whatever you would in the filter.
Filters and sentinels can be attached to a subprocess object created with start-process using set-process-filter and set-process-sentinel respectively.
Many blocking operations can be interrupted by signaling a quit : this is what pressing C-g does, with some variations, in most contexts. Crucially for us, however, quitting is suppressed when Emacs is handling subprocess output or signals This is to keep your C-g from doing something unpredictable to “background” code that you didn’t initiate. . If Emacs is blocked because it’s reading a large data dump… well, tough luck.
keyboard-quit ( C-g ) is a specific input that interrupts any code, with a few exceptions.
The obverse of this is to wrap code in a while-no-input clause – now any input will interrupt the processing of this specific block. This can be used to do background processing in small chunks without making Emacs unresponsive, but there are subtleties involved that I’m not familiar with.
Despite these carveouts, a package that interacts heavily with external processes faces a latency-throughput tradeoff. The more time Emacs spends starting processes and managing their output, the less attention it can pay to your input. Designing Org’s LaTeX preview thus involves finding an acceptable balance.
Figure 2: (Top) Emacs dealing with a “fat” high-throughput process, where it spends a chunk of time reading subprocess output. The time between reading your input and running the resulting command is thus longer than (bottom) the “thin” low-throughput case.
It is significantly easier to write a large Emacs library than an equally versatile plugin for most plugin systems built around multi-threaded GUI applications. I say this as a non-programmer who has only succeeded at the former. We lean on the interpreter lock in many ways, choosing simple data structures and control flow that wouldn’t work if Emacs was multi-threaded. But most of Emacs wouldn’t work if Emacs was multi-threaded, anyway. In for a penny…
Overlays are a way to alter the appearance or behavior of regions of buffer text without modifying the text itself. Displaying images is one of their most common uses: LaTeX preview images are overlaid on top of the source fragments.
Once you have the preview images in hand, placing them in overlays and managing their state is essentially all the LaTeX preview code does.
In fact, overlays account for much of the display trickery in Emacs: Images over text? Overlays. “Virtual text” like in whitespace-mode ? Overlays. Inline results of code evaluation: overlays. Multiple cursors ? Those are overlays. Emacs has only one cursor.
For a quick look into the overlay API, run M-x shortdoc overlay .
The even shorter version: We can create an overlay ov from buffer position BEG to END with
To avoid creating garbage, it is preferable to reuse overlays when possible instead of throwing them away with (delete-overlay ov) and starting over. move-overlay can move them to other buffers too.
The only other tricky question is what happens to the overlay when text is inserted at its left or right boundaries. Does it expand to contain the text? This is left as an exercise for the reader.
These alterations are specified by adding or modifying the overlay’s “properties”. Like symbol properties , overlay properties are a way to store arbitrary information along with the overlay, and org-latex-preview uses them to keep track of state, such as whether the preview image is out of date because the LaTeX fragment has been edited, and to store LaTeX compilation errors for the corresponding fragment.
To set and retrieve overlay properties, we can use
where the property prop is any elisp symbol. There is also an overlay-properties function to access the full list. Once again, M-x shortdoc overlay has us covered.
Some properties have special meanings as interpreted by Emacs’ display engine. display , the most common property, changes how the overlay region appears on screen, and this is typically set to the image we want to see in place of the text.
But several more interesting modifications are possible with overlays, such as changing the face (font+style) of the underlying text, making it invisible, making it intangible to the cursor, or specifying keymaps that are activated when the cursor is within the bounds of the overlay.
The only other detail we need is the list of overlay properties that Emacs considers special. The display property can be used to show an image instead of the text “below” (or “under”) the overlay, for example:
The face property can change the display of the text. Here we dim the text the overlay covers:
Here are a few more interesting uses of other special overlay properties.
Send a message if the text under the overlay changes:
You can use this to set up a “watcher” – perhaps run a process when a region inside a buffer changes If you want to set up a watcher on the contents of the entire buffer as opposed to a piece of it, you should avoid overlays and look at the hook after-change-functions instead. Be warned: it’s easy to slow down Emacs to a crawl this way if you’re not careful. ! This is not hypothetical: preview-latex does this to re-dump the LaTeX preamble of TeX files (in the background) as you edit them.
Add a highlight and tooltip (“hover text”) when the mouse is on the overlay:
Open the displayed image externally when pressing RET with the cursor on it:
This works by defining a keymap overlay property with the required function. (On non-Linux systems, you will want to change "xdg-open" to an equivalent command-line utility.)
This image stays centered as you resize the window:
This one needs a little explanation: The before-string overlay property displays an object before the overlay itself. The object we choose to display is some propertized text with a display text-property . The display text-property provides the means to insert spaces of specified widths , and a symbolic way to refer to the text margins, window center and horizontal window boundary positions. Combining the two gives us (consistently) centered images in Emacs.
In its basic form, the LaTeX preview feature involves no reactive behavior: there is one command to overlay preview images on LaTeX fragments, another to clear those overlays, and nothing else.
But this is a far cry from our goal of real-time feedback. For LaTeX previews to be automatically generated and updated as we type, we need both timers and hooks .
Hooks are variables provided by Emacs where we can register code to run at certain points. In this case, we want to react primarily to two kinds of user inputs:
In turn, org-latex-preview exposes hooks of its own for consumers to run additional processing. These fire when LaTeX subprocesses finish, when overlays are created, and so on.
Timers are complementary to hooks, used to space out or limit the consequences of hooks firing. They are used
Besides basic Elisp data structures, that’s everything we need from Emacs to implement non-blocking, fast LaTeX previews. Assuming you have a handle on what org-latex-preview does, we can start peering into the how.
Here is a high-level overview of the control flow of LaTeX preview generation:
Figure 3: Control flow for Org mode’s LaTeX preview system.
This is a rough picture of how LaTeX previews are generated in Org mode, subdivided into tasks The made-up term “task” corresponds to a handful of functions devoted, in our heads, to one purpose. . Each action belongs to one of three categories:
When a LaTeX preview command is issued, the first chunk of processing (the PREPARE block)
It then starts a two step process chain (the RUN block) that runs asynchronously. The end result of a successful run is a preview image or series of images.
The PROCESS FILTERS block: From this point on until either process ends, Emacs checks in periodically through the associated process filter, acting on the STDOUT to capture various bits of preview metadata. It also keeps track of images that have finished processing, and (synchronously) caches them and adds them to the overlays in the buffer for these fragments. This continuous update is doubly useful:
The POSTPROCESS block: After the subprocesses have finished, Emacs runs their process sentinels, which clean up the detritus of this process chain, or reset the buffer if the preview run failed.
This figure shows the same process but with an emphasis on disk I/O. The primary chain is TeX file → DVI/PDF output file → SVG/PNG preview images .
Of the file categories involved in the process, we care about two: the “format dump file” produced by precompilation, and the preview images. Both are cached and persisted across Emacs sessions. All other produced files are deleted by the POSTPROCESS block.
Displaying previews that are color-, alignment- and size-aware, along with associated information like errors, requires a considerable amount of bookkeeping. Since this information arrives piecemeal and processing happens asynchronously in chunks, we also need some way of storing and passing along this context. There are perhaps clever ways to do this, but we use a straightforward solution – a (dynamic) global plist that associates each active process chain with its data (see org-async below).
All of the data generated and required for the many tasks in our process chain are captured in a single mutable container, referred to here – for convenience – as “Extended Info” ( extended-info ). This data includes
“Extended Info” is implemented as a plist (property list). Actually, almost every compound data structure org-latex-preview uses is either an alist or a plist, which is just a linked-list under the hood. extended-info is also a tree since a few of its members are plists themselves ( see below ).
We used property lists at first since they’re mutable and schema-less, and the design of the library was very fluid. Unfortunately we are now well past the point where we could switch to something more structured like cl-defstruct , so plists it is.
If it’s any consolation, most of Org works with large property lists too. Org’s export system passes around a big plist bucket for communication in much the same way we do here. Access can get expensive as they grow, but at least passing them around is cheap. It’s… not much of a consolation.
plists have one other coincidental(?) advantage: You can splice them in as arguments to a cl-defun .
which is just a list with the name of the function followed by… a plist. So we can build up the plist programmatically and use it directly as foo ’s argument list:
’tis a silly thing but oh, so satisfying. In fact, this is a convenient way to feed a job spec to org-async ( see below ).
The setup functions in the PREPARE block initialize this bucket with data from parsing the buffer – i.e., LaTeX fragment locations, equation numbers, etc. From then on, each task updates extended-info with progressively more information. The structure of extended-info and this flow of information into it is visualized in this “data flow” diagram:
Contained in “Extended Info”: “Processing Info” contains information about and relevant to the external process (LaTeX and the image converter). “Fragment” is a list of metadata for fragments to be previewed, including the overlays that will eventually display the preview images. All of this preview metadata is obtained from the outputs of the latex and image converter runs via the process filters.
Note that Emacs’ interpreter lock precludes data races and other concurrency issues, since only one function modifies extended-info at a time.
The above chart only captures the flow of data in one direction: from the sources of computation into the extended-info container. Tasks that don’t modify extended-info still need to read it to do their jobs. For example,
Most functions in the process chain are passed extended-info , or a subset thereof, as an argument.
Once again, we get away with it because there are no concurrency problems when there is no concurrency. This design pattern of passing around a single heap-allocated container across setup functions and callbacks works for all kinds of applications in Emacs. This is exactly how Org’s (synchronous) export system manages information as well.
This is where we get into the weeds. If you’re here for the bird’s eye view, you can skip ahead to Live previews now.
This is the Collect LaTeX Fragments task in the control flow diagram .
Org’s syntax is extensive , and parsing Org files used to involve a giant mess of regular expressions. Thankfully the mess is now handled by the org-element library, which provides a simple and powerful API for querying or acting on Org’s AST. A fair amount of work has gone into making it perform well under the constraints of Emacs’ single-threaded event loop Besides caching its state, it uses timers to schedule parsing work outside of the times the user is interacting with Emacs. .
Crucially for us, Org has first-class support for LaTeX environments and fragments, and this greatly simplifies parsing and metadata handling. This support is what makes using LaTeX in Org a pleasant experience in the first place.
Added in late 2021, the org-element library greatly simplifies the process of working with Org documents.
I have a minimal working knowledge of the library, so this block covers only the aspects of org-element that we use in org-latex-preview .
Org’s syntax distinguishes between “elements” and “objects”, where anything “larger” than a paragraph is an element, and any syntax that could be contained within a paragraph is an object Incidentally, the default mark-paragraph binding runs org-mark-element in Org mode, which selects the smallest logical element is at point instead. Try M-h at different locations in an Org buffer to see what element you’re on! .
This distinction matters to us because LaTeX text to be previewed can be either. As you might expect, inline math ( $...$ or \(...\) ) is an object, and LaTeX environments ( \begin{foo}...\end{foo} ) are elements, and they differ in the way we must display the preview images.
Every node in the AST as parsed by org-element is made available as a plist whose keys are properties of the element. These properties include the start and end positions of the element and its contents ( :begin , :end and :contents ), as well as metadata like properties and keywords. For example, every element can be named with a #+name: keyword.
These are the only things we need from org-element as far as parsing goes.
The objective of the parsing step is to find the bounds of LaTeX fragments in the buffer (or in some region). In principle, we could do this with org-element :
But this would be too slow, and would allocate far more memory than we need. Instead, we use a simple regexp scan of the buffer to find the bounds of LaTeX fragments and environments, and org-element only to gather specific metadata about these elements.
This is the Create preamble task in the control flow diagram .
Many editor plugins (and web apps) implement LaTeX previews, usually via MathJax or KaTeX . KaTeX is fast, and both function well for web pages with limited needs. But they implement ersatz support for a limited number of LaTeX packages, and cannot consume an actual “full-fat” LaTeX preamble of the kind you might use when writing a research paper. There is no \usepackage{} macro or TikZ support, for example.
By comparison, org-latex-preview is backed by a full LaTeX engine and LaTeX distribution, so nothing is off the table. Of course, this means we need a way to construct the preamble and feed it to the LaTeX engine.
In addition to Emacs-wide settings (like org-latex-preview-preamble and org-latex-packages-alist ), document-specific LaTeX headers can be specified with the #+latex_header: directive:
The combined preamble must be constructed when exporting the Org document to LaTeX, and this machinery lives in the ox-latex library. org-latex-preview simply calls into it for the preamble. Among other benefits, this means the preamble used for the preview run is identical to the one used for LaTeX exports unless you want them to differ, because of course Org provides ways to do that , so these truly are previews .
The ox library and its children, like ox-latex provide an interface to convert Org documents to any other format, like Pandoc does.
While the specifics (like collating a LaTeX preamble) are output-format dependent, the basic method is uniform and simple. An exporter maps each Org syntax element and object to a function that creates the equivalent in the output format, like image links to HTML img tags, or #+begin_quote ... #+end_quote blocks to HTML blockquotes elements. The fact that the Org syntax supports LaTeX environments natively helps with LaTeX exports.
Of course, when a clean mapping like this is not possible, you can work on the buffer directly and rip out and replace raw text. Emacs, huh.
This does make ox-latex one of the few dependencies of org-latex-preview , which is regrettable given the larger aim of providing LaTeX previews across Emacs .
This is the Precompile LaTeX preamble task in the control flow diagram .
To process a preamble, the LaTeX engine needs to tokenize and execute tens of thousands of lines of macro source. For a complex preamble, the kind you would use for a book, this can take several seconds on a modern processor.
Since org-latex-preview aims to provide close to real-time feedback as you type, we resort to a trick from the 1990s: we serialize the entire engine state – the string pool, macro bodies as token lists, font data, engine execution parameters and so on – into a single binary memory image. This process, called format dumping or precompilation , was automated for document preambles by David Carlisle’s mylatex.ltx , modernized as the mylatexformat package by Florent Chervet.
The upshot is that precompilation saves a significant amount of LaTeX startup time, reducing and (almost) flattening it across all preamble sizes.
Precompilation relies on a number of hacks and only works because pdftex has changed little for decades. Unfortunately, precompilation is not supported at all by xelatex and only partially by lualatex preambles that load OpenType fonts or Lua code are unsupported , so org-latex-preview is slow with the Unicode engines.
Under a different LaTeX preview architecture , none of this would be needed. But it’s what we have so far: a very 90s solution for a very 90s editor.
And speaking of being stuck with an old architecture, depending on pdflatex implies that we have to create and feed it a TeX file for each batch of previews pdflatex and friends do accept input via STDIN, but this did not work out for finicky reasons. .
This is the Create TeX file task in the control flow diagram .
As you might expect, the generated TeX file contains a reference to the precompiled dump file and a listing of all the LaTeX fragments to be previewed. Instead of placing them into the document separated by something like \pagebreak , we place them inside \begin{preview} and \end{preview} blocks provided by the preview.sty CTAN package.
preview.sty is authored by David Kastrup, who also wrote the Emacs-side preview.el package that’s part of AUCTeX. preview.el was the inspiration for org-latex-preview – it was clear at least that previews in Org mode could be much, much faster.
preview.sty does three critical things for us:
These modifications were technically doable through a combination of other packages (Org’s old implementation used the tightpage option of the preview machinery), but in cumbersome and error-prone ways.
This makes preview.sty an external dependency of org-latex-preview . Fortunately this package is included by default even with minimal installs of all common LaTeX distributions.
The pipeline from the LaTeX fragment text in the TeX file to images suitable for preview consists of two steps. A LaTeX engine (pdflatex, xelatex or lualatex) produces DVI, XDV or PDF output, which is fed to an image converter (dvisvgm, dvipng or imagemagick) to produce PNG or SVG images. This is the RUN block of the control flow diagram .
This involves a fair bit of bookkeeping, and Emacs’ callback-based async process management (via “process sentinels” and “process filters”) isn’t the most ergonomic tool for this. In the absence of reliable async-io support, we use org-async , a declarative process chain manager now bundled with Org mode.
Because we need to run a chain of processes with different callback behaviors depending on the exit statuses, org-latex-preview uses org-async , a process queue manager that wraps Emacs’ start-process , process filter and process sentinel API. It handles a lot of the bookkeeping for us, providing for
The global variable that keeps track of the context data between async calls is managed by org-async .
The following code might be out of date, please refer to the Org manual.
An example of an org-async job spec might look like the following (simplified for clarity):
org-async-call also provides other conveniences like timeouts, retries and concurrent subprocess limits.
An example of this bookkeeping is that the pipeline isn’t always serial. When generating PNG images with dvipng, we start LaTeX and dvipng in parallel. Dvipng processes pages of the DVI file as they appear, while the LaTeX process is still churning them out. (Generating PNG preview images for a large Org buffer is much faster than the other routes.)
On the other side of the process invocation are the “process filters”, which are callbacks called by the event loop whenever Emacs reads chunks of subprocess output. This is the PROCESS FILTERS block in the control flow diagram .
Following the shell metaphor for process filters , a simple way to think of a process filter for an Emacs subprocess is as a sink at the end of a Unix pipe:
In the LaTeX preview case, the picture is a little more complex as there are multiple processes:
The analogy is different for each of the image converters. Since dvipng runs in parallel with LaTeX , for example:
In org-latex-preview ’s process filters we look for the output (DVI or image) file paths, but also a variety of metadata that preview.sty and dvisvgm emit. This includes geometry information like the width, height and baseline alignment of the image, and any compilation errors.
The printed information is cryptic. Here’s what the numbers mean.
The preview.sty manual provides more details and documents other options.
“Whenever Emacs reads chunks of subprocess output…”
This phrasing omits some important but fiddly details about how often and how much output is read at a time, in much the same way as the Unix pipe | symbol does.
While the event loop is switching between its four main tasks continuously, there are (only) a couple of knobs available at the Elisp level to manage how Emacs reads subprocess output.
Trying to optimize this for org-latex-preview has proved to be… difficult. The rates and sizes of output emitted varies significantly between different LaTeX engines and image converters:
Figure 4: Intervals for which Emacs is blocked when previewing using SVG and PNG images. The vertical axis is time, and the solid chunks are periods where Emacs is unresponsive.
They differ even between different versions of the same program across Texlive versions:
Figure 5: A time-aligned flamegraph profile showing process filter calls for the LaTeX and image converter processes when using Texlive 2022 and 2023. In the aggregate, the LaTeX and dvisvgm binaries shipped with Texlive 2023 aren’t faster or slower than the former. They just have a different profile across time to which it is difficult to adjust.
org-latex-preview settles for a broadly acceptable set of defaults in this regard.
But the main reason we use process filters here is that we can place images in the buffer as they are generated (and read in from the process STDOUT by the event loop), and don’t have to wait for the LaTeX or image converter processes to end.
The unfortunate result of being forced to do file I/O at each step of the pipeline is that we are left with a trail of intermediate files that need to be swept away Instead of, say, a block of shared memory that can simply be freed. . This is the POSTPROCESS block in the control flow diagram , accomplished in the “process sentinels”.
A process sentinel is a callback invoked by the event loop when the process changes status. In principle this includes any status change (exit, signal, stop/continue), but in practice we only care about it after the process exits.
Clearing the intermediate detritus of the compilation is not an urgent task, so org-latex-preview ’s process sentinels actually schedule this on an idle timer. Their other major function in this design is to diagnose process failures and restart the job when the cause looks transient.
This is the Cache images and metadata task in the control flow diagram .
LaTeX preview generation is an order of magnitude (or two) faster than what Org did before, so caching preview images might seem like a secondary concern. But org-latex-preview still caches images, for a few reasons:
In addition to the text of the LaTeX fragment itself, preview images are specific to the LaTeX preview pipeline configuration, the preamble, the Emacs theme and even the fragment’s position in the buffer when equation numbering is turned on. To cache previews reproducibly, all of these inputs are hashed together as the key to the cached image.
While you can specify where the preview images should be cached relative to the document, org-latex-preview defaults to using org-persist , a general-purpose caching library that is part of Org mode. org-persist is used for various caching duties by Org mode, such as resources fetched from the Internet and the partial syntax trees of parsed Org buffers.
Caching LaTeX preview images actually involves more than copying a file somewhere and serializing a hash table to disk. We also need to store, as Elisp data, the image display geometry information, including the baseline alignment height. The org-persist API supports caching different container kinds for exactly this purpose.
Finally, with sufficient time (or a large enough corpus) the cache of LaTeX images can grow to gigabytes in size, so cache entries are set to expire after a month, another function served by org-persist ’s built-in garbage collection.
This covers the in-buffer UI and affordances of org-latex-preview , indicated by the Create overlays and Place LaTeX previews blocks in the control flow diagram .
Beyond what is covered in displaying images over text , displaying the image itself is simple: the image just needs to be resized and aligned according to the recorded geometry. The overlays themselves are set up before starting the LaTeX run, and a series of overlay properties are set or unset over the course of the process.
These are basic but (hopefully) intuitive indicators of the state of the preview.
The breakdown provided so far does not explain the claims we made in the objectives section, like real-time (or at least fast) feedback as you type. As seen in the demos above, there is one more element to making the previews appear “live” and reactive to cursor movement or buffer edits.
All of these are achieved using hooks, which is ultimately the only mechanism we have to trigger reactive behavior in Emacs. The hide/show behavior involves tracking the cursor position via pre-command-hook and post-command-hook (made buffer-local). Buffer edits are tracked via after-change-functions , but with several fast-fail heuristics to avoid slowing down Emacs The difficulty of identifying, in real time, $ and $$ as LaTeX delimiter starts, delimiter ends, or as actual dollar signs is why live previews require the unambiguous \(...\) and \[...\] delimiters, even though the dollars are supported in non-live usage. . The list goes on, since we need to track Org’s folding states, as well as changes in other buffers when using org-edit-special .
The other strategy we’re forced to employ, given the event loop’s limitations, is to throttle and debounce pipeline calls, batching edits and avoiding race conditions between in-flight LaTeX runs – the interpreter lock protects Elisp state, but independent subprocesses will happily interleave and clobber each other’s output.
Finally, this feature is the source of dozens of edge cases, such as editing fragments inside folded regions (during global text replacement, say), or the many invalid intermediate states of a LaTeX fragment causing the preview to fail repeatedly. Knocking down these bugs while keeping this path fast was a substantial portion of the effort over the years this library was developed Now that it’s part of Org mode and seeing more widespread use, there are no doubt several more edge cases waiting to be reported! .
A proof of concept: the design of org-latex-preview makes it possible to preview LaTeX outside of Org mode. Here’s an example previewing LaTeX-formatted comments in a prog buffer (Clojure, here):
In fact, you can use the same code to preview LaTeX fragments literally anywhere in Emacs, including, delightfully, the Emacs calculator. This (18 minute) demo runs through a bunch of contexts outside of Org mode showcasing live LaTeX previews:
While this feature exists only as a prototype, it’s simple to implement and extend. To see why, let’s look again at the preview process breakdown . All tasks here are agnostic of Org mode save for two:
To use LaTeX previews outside of Org mode, we only need providers for these two tasks:
A parser that can identify the boundaries of LaTeX fragments in the buffer Technically you could reuse org-element in non-Org buffers for this, but there will be many false negatives and occasional false positives. . This does not need to be a full-fledged parser – just a regexp scan of the buffer looking for \begin{ or \[ can suffice. This is how the above demos were created.
A LaTeX preamble generator appropriate for the buffer. This can just be a constant string (instead of a function) that includes a reasonable set of LaTeX packages. I used Org’s default LaTeX preamble string everywhere in the above demos.
This description might be out of date, please refer to the Org manual.
org-latex-preview tries to separate these independent concerns by providing the function org-latex-preview-place , that generates previews anywhere in Emacs given the above information. Previewing LaTeX fragments is as simple as:
where entries encodes the start and end positions of the fragments, and preamble is the LaTeX preamble to use.
The positions in entries would be obtained from your parser for the major mode. For preamble you can just reuse or tweak org-latex-preview-preamble in a pinch. See the function documentation for more details.
Requiring the org-latex-preview library will in turn load a few Org libraries ( org-element , org-persist , ox and org-macs ), but it does not load all of Org. We tried hard to keep from loading the 16,000-line behemoth that is org.el .
As of late 2026, abstracting the library from its major-mode adapters remains on the TODO list.
When we started org-latex-preview in 2021, live-updating previews were not available anywhere except one LaTeX formula-editing website and, to a lesser degree, LyX . We often wondered why, since preview.sty did most of the work for you and the editor side was pretty simple to implement. If org-latex-preview were a thrown-together external Emacs package providing many of the same features (sans polish), it could have been written over a couple of weekends. I know this because I wrote it . Twice .
Over the years, however, this feature has grown in ubiquity and there are plugins for most note-taking (Obsidian) and editing software (Neovim, VS Code) that provide this. Emacs itself has at least four active implementations of live LaTeX previews now, and a frontier LLM can probably implement a basic version for your preferred platform with one prompt.
Even so, Emacs remains the oldest platform to implement this feature, and does so in the most complete and mature form As of 2026. . Considering I spent a lot of this write-up complaining about the limitations of the Elisp runtime, this is remarkable.
But creating temporary files after every buffer change and spawning separate LaTeX processes remains a terrible way to do real-time updates. Precompilation is another hack, unsupported by LaTeX engines besides pdflatex. While org-latex-preview is a massive improvement over the previous LaTeX preview implementation for Org mode, it’s still the Elisp equivalent of a Bash script that got out of hand. Quite simply, this is the wrong level at which to address the problem. A better way to implement continuous previews would be to talk to a managed process over a pipe or socket. The right approach here is to work at the level of the TeX engine, as TeXPresso does.
But it would be even better to avoid inter-process communication entirely and use an Emacs dynamic module , linking with a modern LaTeX library that does incremental (instead of batch) compilation. “Lightweight” alternatives like KaTeX or MathJaX don’t cut it, since we need a full-fat LaTeX compiler, macros and all. One possible candidate for this is realtime-tex , the rtex library, which embeds LuaLaTeX (the most modern of the LaTeX engines) and compiles incrementally and effectively instantaneously Although I would be inclined to wait for the project to mature. . This would be a quality improvement almost as drastic as the one org-latex-preview makes over its predecessor.
Of course, a dynamic module linking an incremental compiler is a completely different architecture from what we have now, and would share at most the image display and UI layer. So projects like this and the inevitable official Typst preview package for Org are tabled for another day. Maybe you’ll be the one to implement them?

title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
body:
Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else?
Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too .
The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election.
So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”
Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.”
“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

title: Judge tosses lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska Senate race
body: A federal judge in Alaska has thrown out the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the state's Senate election results in this week's midterm elections if the Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason wrote in a 20-page order Sunday that the Justice Department did not have proper legal standing to bring the suit last week. The suit asked Gleason to block the state's election results from being certified because a teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan is also on the state's ballot, alleging that his candidacy deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name and party affiliation as the state's incumbent senator.The Justice Department argued that Daniel J. Sullivan's name on the ballot potentially diverted voters, and the Democrat running in the race, Mary Peltola, would benefit as a result.The Justice Department "provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote, adding that the it "failed to satisfy its burden to show that its alleged injury is redressable by a court order."The Justice Department filed a notice of appeal on Sunday.Earlier, a DOJ spokesperson told CBS News that the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds "but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," the spokesperson said.The suit, which argues Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include recent reporting by The New York Times on alleged efforts by people associated with Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from the Republican senator. It included a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a "conspiracy."Peltola's campaign responded to the Times story by saying the campaign "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.""I am not interested in tricking voters," Peltola said during a recent campaign event.Sen. Sullivan on Sunday told CNN's "State of the Union" that he thought the presence of a second Sullivan on the ballot would impact the election, saying: "I'm sure I'm going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery."He also said he doubted Peltola's claims that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters."There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," Sullivan said. "She got caught lying, and she's still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us."In addition to the civil lawsuit, the Justice Department is also criminally investigating an alleged plot to add Daniel J. Sullivan to the state's ballot and has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit him to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody in the race has been charged with a crime.

title: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else?
body:
Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI.
In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter . For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI .
This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending .
On the latest episode of the Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem.
Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.
Anthony Ha: There’s a lot of societal skepticism about AI, this feeling that the people running these companies don’t have our best interests at heart, that they’re out of touch. And so, you would just think, “Maybe don’t make statements like that,” because of course, people are going to see them very skeptically.
I think [CEOs] are trying to walk this delicate balance. On the one hand, there’s a tremendous financial incentive for them to make the case that you should use this technology in every aspect of your lives. But when you make that case, it actually [doesn’t paint] a very appealing picture. In some cases, it’s downright dystopian.
Kirsten Korosec: Anthony, if they took your advice, we would have nothing to talk about on this show.
But I will say this: There’s this whole idea of ChatGPT and other AI tools making your life easier when it comes to personal relationships. And in many of these cases, it just seems to overcomplicate what would be, like, observing your child. That might be hard for some people, the people who are building these products, and it doesn’t necessarily relate to everyone else out there in the world. It can just seem so incredibly disconnected when you see these quotes.
To me, it always comes back to — who are they speaking to? Are there people out there who can relate? Maybe there are.
Amanda Silberling: Other use cases we’ve seen people mention are, like, the Bumble CEO Whitney Wolf Heard has made comments about, “Well, what if we had AI concierges, your AI dates the other person’s AI. And then if the AIs have a good date together, then they introduce the people.”
Or in the New York Times article, Marissa Mayer mentioned, “Well, what if my AI could coordinate with my husband’s AI” and stuff like that. And I think that it feels like people are trying to over-optimize out of just having conversations with people.
I’ve already seen that happen in my generation, where I do notice in myself that if I’m ordering takeout, it feels weird to call a place. I’m just so used to, “Well, obviously you can do it online and you don’t have to talk to anyone. And I feel like there’s just going to be more of these things, where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring. And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.
Sean O’Kane: Yeah, but what’s the ROI, Amanda? How much revenue can you generate off of a conversation that somebody’s having in meatspace?
Amanda: That is the thing, though. Dating is really inefficient. It sucks that you have to go on a bunch of dates with different people. You might waste an evening and be like, “Well, that was a bust.” And so you can see why people are [wondering,] “What if you didn’t have to go on dates? What if your AI could go on dates for you?” But there’s just something not human there.
And then also, you are outsourcing the decision of who you are going to date to a computer that you are trusting knows you better than yourself, which I don’t think is true.
Kirsten: One thing that I think is worth going back to, and I sort of hinted about this earlier: Who are they talking to? Who is their audience for all these optimizations, in your view? Is it a product problem, or is it a messaging problem? Are they just talking about it in the wrong way, and actually, there’s this really great value in here and it just seems out of touch with reality and humanity, but if they just talked about it differently, it would be better? Or is it actually a product problem, and to your point, that we’re focusing on optimizing sort of the wrong things with AI tools?
Amanda: I think it’s a little bit of both, but I think that the marketing problem comes from when you have these high-up people at these massively valuable companies in a room together, talking about the pain points in their lives, and [they focus on] making dinner reservations, booking flights. Everybody does those things, but I’m not booking flights once a week. I’m not making dinner reservations all the time. And when I do, those aren’t really things that I find to be a particular challenge in my life.
I mean, obviously people find value from things like ChatGPT and Claude, but I think the value that the average person is finding isn’t necessarily like booking a flight for me.
Anthony: One of the things I’ve also been thinking about is, there are companies like Uber that, when it first launched, it was targeting this tech early adopter set in San Francisco, and I remember being very confident [that] this will never catch on more broadly. This is just for a very narrow audience of young urban millennials who have money to spare on cars, and it works [uniquely] well in San Francisco.
For a lot of things, the tech industry has succeeded by betting that, “People have not caught up with us, but we are the leading edge, and we reflect what the consumer of the future looks like, the family of the future looks like.”
And in this case, it just seems like that bet is not borne out yet — for a variety of reasons, partly because the society that this technology is being promoted into is very different. People are starting to say, “I don’t love the influence that this technology is having in my life. I don’t love that you’re pitching this as something where every experience in my life should be optimized out of. But actually, I want to live my own life . I actually want to parent my own children.”
Amanda: I think that it’s not a coincidence that at the same time we see this over-optimization happening among people in tech, that there’s also a movement of people that are reverting back to wanting to use flip phones, which I’ve talked about on Equity before , or people who are buying CDs because they’re tired of an algorithm telling them what they want to listen to.
And it is just an interesting cultural tension that’s happening, where we haven’t found the balance of what optimization actually helps us and what optimization just makes us feel like we aren’t as human as we want to be.

title: Learjet 60 crashes into urban area in Florida after rapid dive
body:
A Learjet 60 crashed in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday afternoon, November 1, after entering a steep descent shortly before impact. The nine people on board did not survive.
Videos shared on social media show the aircraft in a steep downward trajectory before striking the ground and exploding. The impact opened a large crater at the crash site.
According to the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , nine people, including passengers and crew, were aboard the aircraft. Emergency crews secured the area as authorities began investigating the circumstances of the accident.
The aircraft has been identified as Learjet 60 N722BD. The business jet had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was flying to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.
Flightradar24 data show an abrupt change in the aircraft's flight path during its final moments. At 17:48 UTC, the Learjet was at 35,250 feet (10,744 meters), traveling at a groundspeed of 437 knots (809 km/h) and climbing at 1,472 feet per minute.
Moments later, tracking data showed N722BD at 28,950 feet (8,824 meters), with its groundspeed increased to 505 knots (935 km/h) and a descent rate of nearly 20,000 feet per minute.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
By 17:49 UTC, the aircraft's recorded altitude had fallen to 8,750 feet (2,667 meters). The sequence indicates that the Learjet entered an extremely rapid descent before the crash, consistent with videos recorded from the ground.
It is not yet known what caused the abrupt change in the aircraft's flight path.
The Learjet 60 was developed after Bombardier acquired Learjet in 1990. Derived from the Learjet 55, the type made its first flight in 1991 and entered service in 1993, powered by two Pratt & Whitney Canada PW305A engines.
Production of the original Learjet 60 continued until 2007, when it was succeeded by the Learjet 60XR, which introduced an updated cockpit and cabin. Production of the 60XR ended in 2013.
Other models kept the Learjet production line active for almost another decade. Bombardier ended Learjet production in 2022 , nearly 60 years after the original Learjet first flew. The final aircraft, a Learjet 75, was delivered in March of that year.
Bombardier has since concentrated its business jet portfolio on the Challenger and Global families, while continuing to support the Learjet fleet in service.
