title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
body:
[This is a guest post by Frank Calegari . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy?
Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent.
Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament :
Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved. I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance.
Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved.
I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance.
The classification of finite simple groups.
I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith).
The classification of finite simple groups was in many ways a huge success, but it was also a failure in that it — apologies to my group theorist friends and collaborators — cooled a lot of the interest around the subject. The “famous problem” had gone, and mathematicians on the whole turned their attention elsewhere. And yet, there remain very rich questions in finite group theory and even about the classification itself (to name just one: John Conway’s favorite question is why does the Monster group exist? ). Perhaps for some fields, the OpenAI dump feels like how a group theorist may have felt in 1970 if the classification was dumped in their office, not in the form of the actual papers, but printed out on a spirit duplicator, smudged a little, then spread randomly like confetti all over the floor.
Right now, we need efforts like that of Gorenstein, Lyons, and Solomon and their work on the revised classification. If this was all we had to do, then it would be a fairly thankless task. But we also have the responsibility not to pronounce the subject “done” but rather — with these new tools available — ripe for further investigation. When mathematicians lament the winding paths missed by the construction of a galactic bypass, they need to realize that those old paths still exist and seek them out. And we need to reward that behavior when it comes to offering people jobs.
The promise of AI, and the (dis)-unity of mathematics:
Since I was 15, I’ve wanted to know what was. First, there was the childhood fantasy of finding a formula that Euler missed. But soon one learns more: how Grothendieck’s period conjecture, together with a sufficiently fine understanding of the geometry of mixed Tate motives (following work of Don Zagier, Sasha Goncharov, Francis Brown, and others) gives a completely satisfying structural, conjectural explanation of what’s going on. The irrationality of , or even its transcendence, is a mere shadow of the actual interesting underlying problem. Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of has inspired me for over years not because of its conclusion, but for how it reveals the tiniest hints of some still secret story relating algebraic -functions to arithmetic.
I hope AI can help mathematicians break out of the straitjacket of being constrained by the first natural conjecture they cannot prove, and work on unraveling the deeper mysteries woven throughout our subject. In the last thirty years, progress in mathematics by humans has been remarkable. But at the same time, I have felt a growing unease; the number of times I have seen mathematicians of all levels being unable to explain to someone even slightly outside their field why what they are doing is interesting has been distressing. The natural grooves of our profession have very much been bent toward more narrow technical expertise than a bigger vision. AI allows us an amazing opportunity to broaden ourselves as mathematicians.
I have tried (not always successfully) to be broad as a mathematician. I had some help by the fact that, while I knew since I was 17 that I wanted to work in algebraic number theory and the Langlands program, I grew up in the crucible of Melbourne University, which was a home to many Thurston students and low-dimensional topologists. This meant I was bathed in the sweet liqueur of hyperbolic 3-manifolds. That exposure has helped my career immeasurably. As with any two deep areas of mathematics, hyperbolic three-manifolds and arithmetic are much more closely connected than would first appear. But it’s still hard to be an expert on both, let alone pursue a crazy idea combining them. Let me get technical for a moment. For every imaginary quadratic field , there are many commensurability classes of compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds indexed by non-split quaternion algebras . Manifolds in each of these commensurability classes give rise to elements in via the decomposition of into hyperbolic tetrahedra, and their volumes are always rational multiples of . I have always had this idea that one could conceive of elements in these different commensurability classes as forming some type of geometric Kolyvagin system (“Heegner points”) associated to , which one could yoke together by some unknown integral arithmetic version of the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence. This is not a question I have pursued, for two reasons. First, there were so many underlying conjectures involved that any result I could prove was going to be conditional on many of them, something that’s not always appreciated by the mathematical community. Second, assembling all the technical background to formulate such an idea precisely would have taken a huge amount of background work. Now, with AI, the barriers to trying such a problem are much lower. It’s not trying to prove a theorem. It’s trying to explore some completely new direction that may or may not be nonsense. There are so many problems in mathematics that are still so fresh and vital but were previously untouchable that the opportunity to approach them is massively exciting. We need to be more ambitious, to create bold research plans that weren’t even conceivable a year ago.
This is not to say that everyone must (or must not) use AI. But we have to rethink and readjust what’s important. Proofs of major conjectures, using AI or otherwise, are going to remain part of the new mathematics. But working toward broader programs (new and old) and structural understanding is going to play a more fundamental role. Christian Szegedy raised the following point:
Mathematics prided itself on being meritocratic, with deep reverence for the explorers: the people who could climb what nobody else could. That specific kind of heroism will matter less, and other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world.
Mathematics prided itself on being meritocratic, with deep reverence for the explorers: the people who could climb what nobody else could. That specific kind of heroism will matter less, and other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world.
I’m ready to board the plane, because I want to see what’s there. At the same time, I would add that people who previously have been walking around on earth with their eyes closed are not going to recognize anything however high they fly; I still believe that many of the skills that mathematicians have now will not only be transferable but vital to the new world order.
The difference in reaction between the optimists and the pessimists is that, for the pessimists, the game is over. For the optimists, the game has just changed. I acknowledge that there are aspects of our mathematical culture that we treasure that won’t survive, and it is only human to grieve that loss. But there now exists an amazing new tool to study mathematics. To turn away and say that the community of mathematics as it currently exists is more important than mathematics itself would be a terrible mistake.
For all that everyone has been saying on this blog and elsewhere about how mathematics is about understanding, it takes one look at the arXiv to see many people in our profession rushing out AI-assisted papers in a somewhat unsightly rush to be the “first” to prove things. As many others have noted, there is quickly becoming a gulf between the ability to produce novel proofs and the ability to either demonstrate understanding or push the subject in new and interesting directions. As people crank out more and more results, the Leiden declaration is being honored more in name than in spirit, and it seems like “business as usual” except with a much more compressed time scale and the constant threat of being scooped hanging over people’s heads.
To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof. Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs.
Our obsession with conjectures tends to greatly undervalue the exploratory work that makes answering (or even asking) these problems possible. We are in danger of making that mistake a hundredfold now by encouraging or rewarding the rush for everyone to press the button to get these new results out as soon as possible. I would encourage all senior mathematicians (with the privilege of tenure) to take up the work of creating future problems and exploring new ideas rather than simply using AI to answer existing questions. If you, as a senior mathematician, are stressed about being scooped by AI, then you are not being ambitious enough.
Think pieces are ultimately pointless unless they propose some mechanism for actually affecting how people act. The tools that are going to be the most effective are going to be economic rather than rhetorical. Mathematicians want recognition, mathematicians want jobs, mathematicians want grants. The tools that we currently have to affect this are hiring and accepting papers at journals.
Let me offer some very basic concrete suggestions, followed by a few details.
Evaluate all work as if it is AI-assisted. Make hiring much more about personal interactions rather than a paper file. Interview postdocs and graduate students in person. Demand more from journals, and abandon those that do not adapt. Put a greater emphasis on breadth in graduate education, but do not abandon technical skills. Give better seminars. Take more ownership of the results of AI.
Nelson Cole famously spent three years of Sundays discovering the prime factorization
In , this was a contribution to mathematics. Factoring the same number in by hand would be an equally impressive feat of arithmetic, but its contribution to mathematics (even if it had not previously been known) would be far less, since this can be done on a computer algebra system in far less than a second. It’s obvious that AI is changing the economics of what is “easy” or “hard” — much has already been said about the coming collapse of the theorem economy. In time (perhaps quickly) there will emerge a new sense of what remains a substantial contribution to mathematics, whether it be asking interesting questions, developing new programs, or something completely different. In the future, I see no reason to reward a paper based purely on a result that could be produced by machine, whether it was or not. A new proof can still deserve substantial credit for the ideas it introduces, even when its conclusion is already obtainable by machine. So why not start now? Importantly, I do not think this in any way means that access to AI will be required to make progress in mathematics — as long as we continue to value human understanding. While I feel that this is the most controversial recommendation, I also feel it is the most inevitable. It requires relinquishing an aspect of our reward structure that has been around for a long time, but at the same time a structure that will make no sense in the future. Right now, the use of AI carries a stigma, and the phrasing of many AI disclosures reads more like an attempt to minimize the contribution of the machine. If we evaluate every paper as potentially AI-assisted, then we must insist that its authors explain why the mathematics is interesting, what questions it raises, and how it connects to the broader subject. Don’t we want people to be doing this anyway?
It’s not going to be possible to get people to change unless we change how we evaluate people at the level of hiring. Lazy committees in the past have sometimes pointed toward a JAMS paper, an Annals paper, or some other collection of publications to justify how a candidate is impressive. I am looking for a narrative of where you want mathematics to go, the technical ability to explain why this may be possible, being able to converse about many areas of mathematics, and a demonstrable record of having done all of this in the past. This is not in any way a radical new idea. The hiring process is going to have to be much more about personal interactions than a paper file.
It should become standard practice to interview not only for tenure-track jobs, but also for postdocs and graduate student positions. I’m sure we have all had the experience of admitting a graduate student who was “working on higher homotopy theory” to only find out after they are admitted they can’t compute the homology of the circle. At the same time, I have interviewed candidates at the tenure level whom I was initially ambivalent about, but after a 30 minute conversation in my office I was totally convinced that here was someone who not only had a deep vision of mathematics but who was also able to communicate this to their colleagues. Once we take this approach, we then have the responsibility to train our own graduate students to be better able to communicate mathematics, something that we should take much more seriously. Note there is also a difference between knowing mathematics deeply and explaining it fluently; they are related but different skills. Ideally I want both, but it is the first that I ultimately value more highly.
The journal system was in dire need of reform even before AI. Our current incentives already are to produce more and more incremental mathematics which is only flooding the system. The radical overhaul required is not going to happen through consensus agreements with editorial boards. (Do you know how hard it is to get academics to agree on anything?) Being accepted by a journal has long since ceased to be a guarantee of correctness (if it ever was) and has simply acted as an imprimatur of quality. I explained above the philosophy of how I think we should evaluate manuscripts going forward. On that basis, I would say that a significant proportion of papers posted to the arXiv should not be published anywhere. If journals demand much more from a paper in terms of writing, ideas, and exposition, I think that would make life better for everyone — editors, reviewers, and even ultimately authors.
If editorial boards are unable to adjust, then a more radical idea is to (at least temporarily) abandon journals altogether. (I still see a place for journals which emphasize exceptional utility and clarity (consider Essential Number Theory )). I am not advocating that people stop writing papers, but removing the fig leaf of journal publication forces the paper to stand on its own merits. Is the paper telling a compelling story? Is it Lean-verified? We should be producing fewer (and better) papers, not more. Autonomously AI-produced proofs, hopefully Lean-checked, also have their place, and should be recorded as part of our collective body of knowledge. (see hexagonmath .)
Graduate students, first-year courses, and seminars.
One of the thorniest issues we face is how to train graduate students. The typical thesis has always been to assign a problem in the overhang, an exercise that will teach the student the technical skills to solve a variation on some old problem, with the expectation that, as they continue, they can expand the techniques they’ve learned to new cases and then hopefully branch out to wider problems. In an age where such a thesis can be produced by the press of a button, we need to re-evaluate based on what we hope a good student will be doing in the future. Even with AI resources, no one is going to be able to explore the links between compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds and Kolyvagin systems if they don’t know what either of these terms means. (And even if somehow they could, why would they care?) It has become much more important to give students a broader overview of mathematics as a discipline. What I want a graduate student to achieve at the end of their PhD is a view of mathematics that extends well beyond their discipline, and yet with demonstrable technical skills on at least some class of problems. Often, students graduate with technical skills in a subarea, but their experience with other aspects of their area, let alone other areas of mathematics, consists of technical instruction which they have since forgotten, without any real vision. I advocated above that we need to evaluate work as if AI was involved. But this does not imply that we don’t need to teach students to do deep mathematics without AI just as the existence of computers doesn’t mean we should no longer teach children arithmetic.
This has consequences for what we teach, as well as how students learn to talk about it. A graduate course should leave students with some understanding of what the topic makes possible elsewhere in mathematics. We should expect them to retain a sense of the questions and connections, even when they have forgotten some of the technical details.
If we are to evaluate people more on how they can demonstrate understanding in person, we clearly need to be far more conscious of training our students to explain mathematics to other people, either in person, or in seminars, and to their peers. We need to work on giving our students opportunities to learn this skill. Remember that the most successful cohorts of students are the ones who learn together and who talk mathematics with each other.
We should also not forget that not everyone who completes a PhD in mathematics goes on to academia. We should also ask whether the length and structure of doctoral training serve students who will pursue careers outside academia.
Seminars are traditionally where someone presents the details of their latest result. Because math is difficult, this almost always consists of explaining some minor tweak to a previous method, often without anywhere near enough broader context to make it interesting. Instead, seminars should rarely be focused entirely on new work. They should be framed around the broader interesting questions, explaining the avenues on which we are stuck, on which we can make progress, on which we are hopeful, and then perhaps at the very end explaining some novelty, if there is any. This is how I have always encouraged my students to give talks! As senior faculty we all need to be vocal in our seminars demanding more from our speakers.
Mathematicians as a profession would do well to take more ownership of these results. What has come out of the machine has been built on the intellectual foundations of several millennia of human mathematical endeavor. Once you start to take credit on behalf of humanity (rather than attributing these results to either a Silicon Valley tycoon or a mathematical Twitter buffoon), you’ll immediately start to feel much better.
My dean recently visited New York to meet with donors and other friends of the University of Chicago, and everyone she spoke to, regardless of whether they were a math major or not, wanted to talk to her about mathematics. The world is looking at us. There are many many people who care about mathematics without necessarily having a deep technical background ( 3Blue1Brown has over six million subscribers!). All of my friends in the humanities truly believe that having mathematicians in society both as custodians of one of humanity’s oldest intellectual activities and explorers of the frontiers of knowledge is important. I understand that some part of the culture we so deeply care about will disappear, and as humans, an emotional response to that is very natural. But this is a time to explain to everyone that there are so many great new opportunities, possibilities, and reasons to be optimistic. We are on the verge of a new era of mathematics, and I am excited to see what happens.
For more context on Duminil-Copin’s remarks, see also this numberphile video . His full quote also says “We are a resilient community, and I have no doubt that we will adapt”.
Many of the themes mentioned here have been brought up in other posts. To give three examples:
The idea that mathematicians should take more ownership of the results produced by AI was also explored in Nestor Guillen’s post . The idea that AI gives us the opportunity to be far more ambitious is raised in Ben Antieau’s post . The idea that we need to revisit our reward structure to create the right incentives was explored in Bryna Kra’s post.

title: Spooky C++
body:
You want to see something… spooky? Do you want to hear a story, so haunting, so bone-chilling, it keeps you up at night? Well, let’s look at this program that grants permissions:
When I compile and run this code ( clang++-19 -std=c++17 -O0 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic cursed.cpp -o cursed_clang && ./cursed_clang ), everything works fine and my user foobarbazboo does not get root permissions:
However, if I compile this code in a forest, at midnight on halloween, on top of a Ouija board, after saying “Candyman” in front of a mirror 5 times, and changing the optimization flag to -O2 , this program will mysteriously grant foobarbazboo root permissions…
Is this the work of g-g-ghosts? Is my computer h-h-haunted?
As you can guess, this is an example of undefined behavior causing unintuitive results.
Even though this is a funny example, I doubt a bug like this will surface in the wild (nor be easily exploited) as this behavior is incredibly hard to reproduce.
For example, this only works because the string foobarbazboo is the same length as admin_id , and is passed as an inline parameter. If you change the input length or refactor the program to store foobarbazboo in a temporary variable, the behavior goes away.
Even if you didn’t know anything about UB, I think most people would think this code is ill-formed and weird. A handful of readability/refactoring principles will eliminate this particular behavior. For instance, refactoring admin_id to be a singleton/global variable will make the program behave correctly.

title: Poland sends two more MiG-29s to Ukraine as F-35 fleet grows
body:
Poland has agreed to transfer two more MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine as the country continues to phase out its Soviet-designed combat aircraft, just days after the tenth F-35A based on Polish territory arrived at Łask Air Base.
Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski confirmed on October 29 that an agreement had been reached with Ukraine for the two aircraft. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz later said both MiG-29s were being withdrawn after reaching the end of their operational service lives.
The condition of the two aircraft is different. One has already exhausted its flight-hour limit and is expected to serve primarily as a source of spare parts, while the other remains capable of flying.
The transfer is considerably smaller than a deal discussed between Warsaw and Kyiv in late 2025. Poland had considered sending its remaining MiG-29s to Ukraine in exchange for access to Ukrainian drone and missile technologies, but negotiations subsequently encountered disagreements over the aircraft and the proposed technological cooperation.
Ukraine's requirements have also changed. According to Zalewski, Kyiv's interest in additional MiG-29s has declined as it increasingly focuses on Western combat aircraft such as the F-16 and Mirage 2000.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The fate of Poland's other MiG-29s has not yet been decided. Discussions with Ukraine continue, while Bulgaria has also expressed interest in acquiring some of the aircraft, according to Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Poland has already transferred MiG-29s to Ukraine since 2023. The remaining aircraft are among the last Soviet-designed fighters in Polish service, whose missions are progressively passing to newer types including the F-16, FA-50 and F-35A.
While the MiG-29 fleet approaches the end of its Polish career, deliveries of the country's most advanced fighter are accelerating.
The tenth Polish F-35A Husarz to be based in the country arrived at the 32nd Tactical Air Base at Łask on October 27. The aircraft, numbered 3518, is the second Polish F-35 assembled at the Final Assembly and Check Out facility in Cameri, Italy.
Its arrival came five months after the first three F-35As reached Poland in May. Another five arrived in August and the ninth followed in October.
The ten aircraft at Łask do not represent the entire Polish F-35 fleet. Eight earlier jets remain in the United States, where they support the training of Polish pilots and maintenance personnel.
Meanwhile, aircraft 3520, identified as Poland's 20th F-35A, completed its first flight at Cameri on October 15. Poland is expected to have 14 F-35As on its territory by the end of 2026, followed by another 12 arrivals in 2027.
Poland ordered 32 F-35As in January 2020 under a US$4.6 billion contract. The aircraft will equip two squadrons at Łask and Świdwin as the Polish Air Force completes one of the largest fighter fleet transitions in its recent history.

title: Pratt parsing is a black box
body:
It caught my attention that most of Pratt parsing tutorials that I've stumbled on spend almost all of their time explaining Pratt's algorithm and none explaining the properties behind Pratt that actually matter. Pratt fits into just 9 lines of code if you're programming in a high-level language such as Rhombus:
And here's a secret: that's the least important thing you need to understand about Pratt's. In fact, you don't need to understand this piece at all! Imagine if you were only able to use quicksort if you understood its implementation. Imagine if you were only able to use files if you knew how to implement a filesystem from scratch. It's the same logic here. If you lack the power to abstract, you'll arrive nowhere in computer science because that's how the whole field works. In fact, I wrote the backbone of a heavily Pratt-based parsing machinery for a compiler that I've been writing since last year w/o even bothering to understand the above snippet in any detail.
Not convinced? Think for a second on how they do in traditional parsing techniques: compiler compilers! They use code generators to spit the parsing algorithm because just a minuscule crowd bothers to learn what the parsing engine is actually doing. It's no different with Pratt. However Pratt is so small that you can just copy'n'paste these 9 lines of code in your project and call it a day instead of adding a new complex dependency to your project. The algorithm hasn't changed since 1973 and it's not gonna change now.
In this article I'll go over what you actually need to keep in mind for Pratt parsing. The point won't be about memorizing any of it though. The point is about acquiring a mindset. As long as you acquire the mindset you don't need to even bother to remember even a single word of what I say here.
The only tutorial on Pratt parsing that I can firmly recommend to someone who has never been exposed to the topic is actually a talk that Douglas Crockford gave in the conference GOTO 2013 ¹ . Douglas Crockford nailed it when he stated:
Pratt takes parsing which is a really complicated thing and reduces it to one simple question: What do we expect to see to the left of a token ?
At first glance it may look like a mystical statement devoid of meaning, but that's the question that becomes the framework on how you face parsing problems and it'll rewire your brain to internalize the Pratt parsing mindset. That's the most important thing you need to understand. You register semantic actions for two categories: nuds and leds. A nud is a token that expects nothing to its left (nud stands for null denotation) while a led expects something (led stands for left denotation).
Traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules. Here's an example I took straight from GNU Bison's manual:
The text between the braces is code that executes when the BNF-like grammar on the left matches. I'm gonna repeat myself because that's really important: traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules (which by definition are non-terminal symbols). In contrast Pratt parsing registers semantic actions to the terminals themselves instead. That's a fundamental shift on how you face parsing problems.
Here's a stripped down version of the code for the tables that I have in my compiler right now:
All values on the left of each table are the lexer codes for terminal symbols. The values on the right depend on the table kind:
Functions matching the signature ExprPtr(Context&,reader,reader&) ExprPtr(Context&,reader,reader&) .
Functions matching the signature ExprPtr(Context&,reader,reader&,ExprPtr) ExprPtr(Context&,reader,reader&,ExprPtr) .
Most of the semantic actions in these tables have code whose implementation amount to one semicolon in their body at most. Here's the code for parse_unary_plus() parse_unary_plus() :
On the surface it may seem just like a different but still very similar way to organize your code, but the impact is in fact huge. Here are a few differences from traditional parsing techniques that stem from this single departure alone:
You don't need to worry about left-recursion problems that occur in traditional parsing techniques such as LL(k). Given the dispatch to a semantic action is done with its associated token already consumed from the stream, left-recursion just doesn't happen. It's a non-issue.
The parsing engine doesn't need to test alternatives or backtrack. The usual dichotomy between speed versus memory that is found in some parsers (e.g. PEG vs packrat) is gone. Pratt is fast, and it's not gonna starve for insane amounts of memoization. Pratt is just going to compare numbers, and iterate or recurse.
Related to the previous point, but worth to consider on its own: semantic actions run exactly once! That means there's no need to rollback to a previous state if a match fails. In other words your actions may contain side-effects. In my parser I use this property to do name reservation/release on lexical scope through a shared context object juggled through each layer. Just be careful to not abuse side-effects and end up with spaghetti.
Also related: your semantic action always knows it's the correct match. Therefore it may look arbitrarily far ahead if it wants to. In other words: you can further use PEG parsers (or layered Pratt parsers) in the semantic actions. While Pratt itself only eats 1 token at a time, the nuds & leds themselves may eat more tokens per round. You just unlocked the power of parser combinators.
Most of the grammar ambiguities become table collisions so you waste less time on the simpler ambiguity cases. If you combine multiple parsers then it's still possible to have grammar ambiguities. So you still have work as a grammar designer, but in my experience it's much less work. When you combine parsers you're really combining grammars. Pratt as the parsing algorithm won't act as the all-seeing oracle and detect every possible ambiguity in the full grammar amalgamation. Pratt (just like PEG) will just return the first possible match in this case.
Unfilled gaps in your tables become trivial extension points in your grammar. You may fill these gaps in response to the text parsed so far. In other words you can implement macros and even parse a language that extends its own operators. In contrast extending a pre-existing grammar based on production rules (the orthodox parsing school) is a job worth the complexity of PhD researches.
You may even find a few of these properties in the traditional school as well, but only to certain extents, or with a huge complexity toll.
Nonetheless I mentioned earlier that this organization is a mindset shift , but so far I've only mentioned properties that you can use from adopting Pratt, so where's the shift really? Consider the usual EBNF rule for parsing function calls:
How do you approach this problem when instead of production rules your toolbox contains only nuds & leds? The key observation is that the opening parentheses always expect something to its left, so it's a led. There you go: register a led for lparen and parse the function call from there. It's not immediately obvious, specially when you've only been exposed to the traditional parsing school. Hence why Douglas Crockford nailed it when he stated:
Pratt takes parsing which is a really complicated thing and reduces it to one simple question: What do we expect to see to the left of a token ?
The led for array indexing is very similar to the led for function call. Here's the variation that I use in my own parser:
Pratt is not just precedence climbing. Pratt is a way to organize your code. First learning Pratt as a black box actually helps to understand this difference. If you don't have access to the black box, you won't be tempted to reduce Pratt to precedence climbing. Hopefully by the time you want to take away the abstraction and see what's inside you won't make the mistake of treating Pratt just like a mere variation of precedence climbing because by then you'll have already been exposed to all the power unlocked by Pratt parsing. Andy Chu's blog post on Pratt parsing without prototypal inheritance is worth reading as it contrasts two opposing styles of writing Pratt parsers ² . Here's a minimal calculator written in Rhombus that is (stylistically) closer to a version that'd use prototypal inheritance than the style that Andy Chu shows:
The previous section might have been the densest in this whole blog post so I want to tune it down while you incubate the Pratt mindset and go on trivial things for now:
Pratt requires a separate lexer. Some modern parsing engines can work in a scannerless manner (e.g. PEG) or even embed the lexer definition directly in the parser itself, but Pratt requires a separate lexer. That shouldn't be a big concern, but it's something to keep in mind.
Pratt is fast. The algorithm only compares numbers and iterate or recurse. It's only looking 1 token ahead, and not doing anything else really. It doesn't go back to test alternatives or to backtrack on failed production rules. It just doesn't go back at all. It's a full-speed locomotive only looking ahead eating 1 token at a time.
Given Pratt itself is already fast, if you want to optimize anything, the only thing left is the dispatch code for nuds & leds. In my case I use global read-only dispatch tables, but most of the tutorials I've seen in the wild use dynamic objects in highly dynamic scripting languages.
Pratt can't parse statements. You have to combine it with other techniques to parse languages with statements. I've already gone through this constraint in my last blog post where you can find solutions.
Pratt is a form of recursive descent parsing meaning it's running custom user code (i.e. code in a Turing-complete language) for the semantic actions, but that's not the whole picture. The semantic actions further drive the parsing choices/direction which means that your code might look at the context (e.g. previous declarations) to decide how to parse the next piece of the input text. In summary you can have some forms of context-sensitive parsing which opens the door for more classes of languages.
You'll have to resort to modal lexing to parse some complex languages found in the wild, but I'll reserve a later section of this blog post to touch on this topic.
Pratt can't be used for incremental parsing as done in GLR parsing. However that's not a power found in most parsing algorithms anyway (I'm running out of algorithmic properties to talk about). Incremental parsing is used in tools such as tree-sitter.
My whole argument today is that Pratt is a black box abstraction, so let's go with this argument and lay down what contracts you need to respect to use Pratt:
Only tokens with associated leds need a value in the binding power table. Tutorials in the wild are usually written in a way where this property isn't obvious. It becomes more obvious when you write your parser using static tables rather than highly dynamic objects in scripting languages.
Related to the previous point: You still need a value for the binding power of prefix operators, but this value isn't used in the Pratt loop at all. Therefore it's not a requirement to inflate the binding power table with a value for the prefix operators, but that's what most of the code I've seen in the wild do anyway. If you think it's easier to just stuff the binding power for prefix operators in the same table be my guest and go ahead. Just bear in mind that this popular arrangement isn't a hard requirement. Only the nud implementing the prefix operator itself needs to know the binding power for prefix operators.
Never assign a binding power of zero to a led.
Separators such as comma and unknown/error/EOF tokens where the parser must stop should have a binding power of zero. They don't need to exist in the binding power table.
If you're writing in decimal like every human being, adopt increments of 10 in the binding power table. When reading these values, you may just ignore the final zero, but the extra room between operators enables some tricks.
So how do we implement right-to-left associative operators with Pratt? First let's look at a common left-to-right associative infix operator. Here's my code for the led + + :
If we wanted to make the operator right-to-left associative, we'd just need to use bp - 1 bp - 1 instead of bp bp :
That's a standard trick in the field of Pratt parsing. A trick of the trade so to speak. A trick you ought to know. Why does it work? It doesn't matter. It's a black box for today. Tomorrow it might matter, but today you should only be focusing on how to use Pratt, not why it works.
Why even write a section for macros when most language designers won't add them? Pratt macros are just nuds/leds implemented in the language that your code is parsing and interpreting. Therefore anything that your own nuds/leds can do is something that ought to be possible in a macro and vice-versa. Lessons learned from Pratt macros are lessons learned on Pratt parsing itself.
That's just a principle, and not a hard-truth. It's definitely not a truth in the Pratt macros of my own language, for instance, but the principle remains my guide (and hopefully yours as well).
The implementation of macros outside Lisp are traditionally very limited in many fronts. In languages such as C you have macros that are just textual substitution templates that work in the environment of a preprocessor doing textual expansion (therefore working on the lexing layer). It's also possible to design macros that work in the AST/parsing layer such as done in Lisp. However Pratt macros unify these two previously severed worlds. If you're implementing procedural Pratt macros then it's possible for the macro to use APIs that alternately invoke either the lexer or the parser. My own macro system doesn't yet have enough APIs so I can't showcase a real example, but here's how envision that it's gonna work:
These APIs are pretty much what's already used in the core nuds of many parsers using Pratt. A macro system only needs to expose them to the macros as well to get this far. This part is actually easy. Tasks actually challenging in macro systems reside elsewhere, not here. The hardest part of a macro system is hygiene ³ ⁴ , not parsing (well… parsing is gonna be easy if you use Pratt parsing at least). However this blog post is about (Pratt) parsing, not macro systems, so I'm not gonna delve on hygiene or other macro system challenges (problems which I've already battled with and ultimately won).
The takeaway here is that Pratt parsing enables languages with powerful macros that can implement beautiful unconstrained eDSLs. Pratt macros are just an interpreter for your language that has access to the lexer and the parser at the point where the macro is being expanded. Patterns that you use in your nuds & leds are patterns that you'd likely see in Pratt macros. The code being parsed is teaching the very parser that is parsing it on how to do so (tell me about meta!).
Usually the lexer is the most neglected part of a compiler. It's a solved problem. There's no reason to waste time on its design. You use a lexer generator to implement an efficient lexer, and move on to never look back again. However Pratt – the algorithm – is just 9 lines of Rhombus code. Your lexer is most likely bigger than the parser already. Just on the face of this your lexer is already playing a bigger part on your project by at least some metric (even if an unimportant one).
However it goes further than this. Every nud and led in your code is a subparser of sorts. Combining (sub)parsers is key to unlocking the power to parse even more classes of languages. The lexer becomes the single point in common that trespass the walls between all subparsers. A good lexer design improves parser composability.
As a practitioner of the Pratt school, the single most important lexing technique you should learn is modal lexing. The technique is already useful on its own even if you're not using Pratt, but it's even more so for us. As Andy Chu succinctly explains ⁵ , modal lexing is enabled by adding an extra parameter to your lexer:
There are other ways to express the same pattern. For my own project, I prefer to use separate functions instead of an enum. As a C++ programmer I've been trained well to discern between cases of static versus dynamic polymorphism, and here's a case where clearly the dispatching information is fully known statically at compile time. Hence it doesn't make sense to even use an enum. The story could be different in highly dynamic macro-enabled languages though.
Simple as it is, this single defining trait of modal lexing unlocks the ability to parse many more complex classes of languages by providing a way for the lexer to receive feedback from the parser. Lexers never know grammatical structure, but the parser always does. By feeding this information from the parser back to the lexer you enable forms of language composition where each sublanguage might have conflicting token definitions (e.g. C++11's right-shift operator spawns different tokens in template contexts) or just tokens with different meanings altogether. Andy Chu already gave comprehensive examples on where this might be useful ⁶ so here I'll only bother to contribute a single example to the corpus.
In Rust you have a different sublanguage just to express types. This type annotation happens in neatly delimited places inside the "main" language. It usually happens after the colon and ends on the equals-sign or delimiters such as commas or the closing parentheses:
My language syntax is heavily inspired by Rust's. Naturally I rely on modal lexing to parse these structures. The function reader::next_on_type_scope() reader::next_on_type_scope() shown earlier is used for the type annotation sublanguage. Then I have a Pratt parser for each – parse_expr() parse_expr() and parse_type() parse_type() . It's a simple trick that doesn't demand much explanation really, but gets you very far. The code almost writes itself after you get the idea.
The only caveat is that your lexer must adhere to a pull design instead of lexing all tokens upfront. For some reason people like to only design push APIs that fully steal execution flow, and these people are addicted to implement lexers that do all the work upfront. It's a popular arrangement, but not one that will work for modal lexing. Pratt itself is a push design so in the end you'd have a mix of designs.
Moving on to the next topic, there are more lexer tricks that I have to share, but for today I just have one suggestion: don't design your lexers to do any IO (syscalls) nor to buffer anything. Working on a copy of your lexer shouldn't have observable side-effects on the original object. Copies should be cheap and encouraged. Working on a copy of the lexer enables arbitrary lookahead which might be required by some subparser. Even if you only requires a fixed amount of lookahead (e.g. 3 tokens) this design fits the hole all the same.
Fulfilling this design is easy: just read the whole file at once (or use mmap) and make the lexer point to this shared region to do its job. Your AST alone is likely gonna use more memory than the whole input file anyway so memory shouldn't be a concern here.
Most of the code that I see on the wild has a custom type for tokens, and that's get used as argument for the nuds & leds, but I just store/pass the lexer itself instead. My lexer is cheap to copy so there's no need to create a class to pass tokens around. The layer expecting a token can decode from the matched lexeme directly anyway so the lexer only needs to store a few pointers to the original input text. Here's the code parsing decimal literals in my project to showcase the decode-from-lexeme-directly trick:
Furthermore this design allows me to rollback 1 token which is something that I use in the nud for < < :
This trick also requires a lexer that represents error as a dedicated token code instead of raising exceptions when they happen. You may still use exceptions if you want when an error is fatal for all sublanguages (e.g. non-ASCII character found on the stream).
Now what's this nud even parsing might be a valid question, so let's go over exactly what it's doing. Rust (which inspired my language's syntax heavily) allows one to access fields from a type. Field access here is done using the operator :: :: . For instance:
However what happens when referring to your type requires access to the type annotation language such as in the case for generics? Then you need an "escape hatch" in the main language to access the type annotation language explicitly, and that's done through the nud for < < :
So now you know how to parse this type of grammars with Pratt. Simon Ochsenreither once argued that using <> <> for generics is bad design ⁷ , so maybe it's no coincidence that that's the only time that I actually had to use the rollback trick (which I consider a hack) in my project. Nevertheless it was the best compromise I could find so I went with it anyway. Language design is hard.
I have a lot more of lexer tricks to share, but I'm feeling that I should postpone them to later articles. Some of them are already used in my project. Ironically perhaps, but I acquired the mindset that enabled me to come up with these lexer tricks from past experience parsing HTTP and JSON which has nothing to do with the techniques that one uses to parse programming languages.
Pratt is a shift in parsing mindset. You must get comfortable on breaking grammatical structures into nuds & leds. It's totally okay to write shortcuts that remove the boilerplate by factoring the common parts of the implementation of prefix, infix and postfix operators as done by Douglas Crockford ⁸ , but if you're changing Pratt's algorithm itself as done by Alex Kladov in 2020 ⁹ (I've done the same mistake myself once) to make accommodations because you refuse to reason in terms of nuds & leds (or any other reason), you're missing out and should start over. Using Pratt parsing as a black box abstraction will remove your ability to change Pratt's algorithm, and it may help in adapting your mindset. That's my advice to get you started.
I have a lot more of parsing tricks to share (e.g. Pratt-walk interpreters, REPLs with perfect auto-completion), but they're more advanced, and I'll postpone them to later articles.

title: Damascus seeks a security umbrella. Syria negotiates entry into the Mecca Defence Alliance
body:
Syria’s transitional authorities have entered talks to join the trilateral military pact formed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. The move represents an attempt by the new administration in Damascus to rebuild its deterrence capabilities following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s regime.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani disclosed the ongoing negotiations on Saturday during the IISS Manama Dialogue security summit in Bahrain. According to reports, Damascus is currently evaluating the terms of accession, although a formal application has yet to be submitted. The pursuit of external security guarantees stems from the urgent need to reconstitute the Syrian armed forces (a process in which Türkiye already plays a leading training role) as well as mounting military pressure in the country’s south. Al-Shaibani noted that Israeli forces have conducted over a thousand strikes in Syria since late 2024, and he called for the reactivation of the 1974 disengagement agreement. Potential membership in the bloc was previously explored during the chief diplomat’s August visit to Islamabad and President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s October talks in Riyadh.
Established on August 7, 2026, by the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, the alliance is anchored in a mutual defense clause (under Article 51 of the UN Charter) that treats an attack against one member as an act of aggression against the entire bloc. Operating with a permanent secretariat in Riyadh headed by retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood, the pact encompasses intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, counterterrorism operations, and defense technology transfers.
This October, the agreement underwent its first operational test when, in response to attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, the member states decided to urgently deploy designated military contingents to Saudi Arabia. Riyadh and Islamabad have already ratified the treaty (while the ratification process remains underway in Ankara), and admitting new states requires the unanimous consent of the three founding members.
The Manama declaration confirms a profound geostrategic reorientation in the Levant: the new administration in Damascus seeks to anchor itself within a Sunni security architecture, which for Tehran means the definitive closure of its overland logistics corridor to Lebanon.
However, Syria’s rapid and full accession faces a barrier in the risk calculus of Riyadh and Islamabad. Extending collective defense guarantees to Damascus amid regular strikes by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) would risk automatically entangling the pact in a direct confrontation with the Jewish state. Publicly signaling these talks should therefore be read primarily as an instrument of diplomatic deterrence designed to raise the cost of Israeli operations, while Syria’s actual military integration will proceed in stages—first and foremost through bilateral training and equipment agreements with Türkiye.

title: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury
body:
More broadly, the use of LLMs erodes trust in documentation, in software, and in the organizations which produce them. Perhaps engineers will begin to treat any new software project with suspicion—the signals we used to rely on as markers of a mature system are now easier to counterfeit. [...]
In the age of LLMs, what can maintainers do to ensure correct software and accurate documentation? Having done that work, how can they demonstrate its quality to users?
— Kyle Kingsbury , Jepsen results for ParticleDB 1.1.4
This is a quotation collected by Simon Willison, posted on 1st November 2026 .

title: A Specialised Haskell Processor on FPGA
body:
I follow Lennart Augustsson’s approach when he was presenting MicroHs — give the demo first.
This is a Haskell program running on a specialised processor, which is hosted on an FPGA and talks through a UART port:
There is no software runtime or “kernel trap” underneath, everything is handled by the hardware processor.
There is a more detailed demo video . If you want to reproduce this demo, either by running it on your FPGA or using our simulator, see the guidance .
My PhD study topic is about specialised hardware design for non-strict functional languages. This post talks about my recent work on adding IO capability into our Haskell processor and putting it on an FPGA, with a goal of convincing people that a Haskell processor is a cute idea.
Specialised hardware for functional languages actually has a lot of interesting history , especially in the 80s. This idea was largely abandoned during the 90s, because of better software implementation and the evolving speed of standard CPUs at the time.
For reasons well known, domain-specific architectures are becoming interesting again. We try to investigate the possibility of this old idea in today’s context. I will present the hardware architecture, IO handling, FPGA implementation results, and some limitations of this work.
Our processor is called Ouros , a combinator-based graph reduction machine. Many design details, including representation of combinators, thread management (Ouros can do automatic multi-threading!) and garbage collection, can be found in our paper 1 . The figure below is an overview of the processor architecture.
Unlike a conventional processor, Ouros does not execute a sequence of instructions. Instead, a Haskell program is compiled into combinator graphs , and execution is a process of repeatedly reducing function applications. Each application (we call it an App ) is represented by a fixed-size word containing a function and its arguments. Larger expressions are stored in the heap as multiple Apps connected by pointers.
The main components are the Dereference Heap , which follows pointers and manages threads; the Reducer , which performs combinator reduction; and the ALU , which handles arithmetic. Apps move between these components as data tokens, and each component processes them whenever its input is ready. This is why we call Ouros dataflow-driven , rather than instruction-driven. Ouros also supports relatively large combinators, which can save quite a few reduction steps. Readers interested in the combinators and how we compile Haskell into them can refer to our earlier paper 2 on structured combinators and our MicroHs fork .
Another interesting feature is automatic fine-grained multi-threading. For example, when an arithmetic operation needs two independent values, Ouros can evaluate them in separate threads without any explicit threading code in the Haskell program. These threads share the same hardware pipeline. There is also a concurrent hardware garbage collector, which reclaims unused heap cells alongside normal execution.
Adding IO allows the Ouros processor to become a standalone computer, rather than just a machine for evaluating pure expressions. The question is how to introduce side effects without hurting the graph reduction model.
We use the familiar state-passing representation of the IO monad 3 :
Here World is just a dummy Int , not a representation of the actual world. The important part is the dependency: each IO operation consumes a World token and produces one for the next operation. This gives the operations an order, even though the processor evaluates Haskell lazily.
The low-level primitive IO interface is intentionally kept simple:
They allow a Haskell program to read and write a set of registers. The compiler turns these primitives into special IO operations understood by the hardware. When an IO operation is ready, a dedicated IO unit performs the corresponding AXI4-Lite transaction, and the result goes back into the normal graph reduction pipeline. The operation only finishes after the bus transaction completes.
The AXI4-Lite details are hidden from the Haskell program. From the programmer’s point of view, it is simply reading and writing registers, some of which are connected to the outside world. This is how we get actual side effects without a software runtime.
Currently the FPGA demo only uses a UART, with the Haskell program polling its registers. The same interface could also be connected to GPIOs, timers, a hardware random number generator, etc.
The FPGA board I am using is AUP-ZU3 , which was kindly donated by people from AMD.
The current design runs at 100 MHz on this board. Its resource usage is approximately 27% of LUTs, 7% of registers and 40% of BRAM . The BRAM usage is mainly determined by the heap and code memories, so it can be adjusted by changing their sizes.
What I find quite encouraging is that the logic footprint is roughly in the range of a small pipelined RISC-V core. Of course, this is not a like-for-like comparison, and Ouros has many limitations (see below). Still, it is nice to see that we can have direct hardware support for graph reduction, automatic threading and garbage collection within a fairly small circuit budget.
An immediate question someone might ask is: how does this machine compare to a PC running GHC-compiled code? This is not easy to answer. If we only care about wall-clock speed, the FPGA demo is likely to be several times slower than a modern laptop. However, the implementation technology, circuit size, and power consumption model are all very different, making a fair comparison difficult. Also, since Ouros has a rather unusual memory organisation, we cannot simply assume that its performance would improve by several times if implemented as an ASIC using a 7nm process.
Apart from being a cute toy, does this FPGA demo show any practical value? One possibility I can imagine is something like a Raspberry Pi, but with Haskell as its bare-metal programming language. Being able to run Haskell directly on a small embedded processor might be useful in certain scenarios. More interestingly, I think a native Haskell processor could open up some research possibilities that have been difficult to explore in practice. For example, what would a small operating system written entirely in Haskell look like?
There are four related repositories for Ouros:
To compile Haskell programs, first build our MicroHs fork from the repository root:
The UART demo program lives in ouros-uart-demo in that repository; follow the README there to compile it. You can also try your own Haskell programs in the same way. Copy the compiled program image into ouros-chisel/src/main/scala/benchmarks or ouros-simulator/src/hardware/ouros/benchmarks , depending on whether you want to use the hardware implementation or the simulator.
For the Chisel implementation , run this from the ouros-chisel root:
This generates the SystemVerilog output under fpga-gen/ .
For the simulator , the UART demo can be run directly from the ouros-simulator root:
To reproduce the demo on the AUP-ZU3 FPGA board , follow the README in the Vivado repository . It covers the FPGA build and boot image generation.

IEEE, 2026. doi: 10.1109/ASAP71856.2026.00023 . ↩︎
